He worshipped Thiru-anaikka, Thiru-erumbiyur, Thiru-chirappalli, Thiru-karkudi, Thiru-parayathurai, and other sthalams. As he journeyed to reach Thiru-paingili, he suffered from weariness, hunger, and thirst on the way. Nevertheless, with an unwavering mind, Nayanar continued towards the sthalam of Thiru-paingili.

“At that time, the Lord, intending to relieve Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar’s suffering, created a grove and a pond on that path and appeared in the guise of a Brahmin traveler with a bundle of food. When Nayanar arrived at that place, the Brahmin, addressing Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar, said, “Eat this bundle of food, relieve your weariness, and proceed further.” Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar, as if knowing it was the Lord’s grace, listened to the Brahmin’s words, took the bundle of food, ate it, and refreshed himself.

“Afterwards, as he set out for Thiru-paingili, the Brahmin said he would also go there. As he also came along, when they approached the town of Thiru-paingili, the Brahmin disappeared. Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar sang, “What a mercy it is that the Lord considered even me worthy of His grace!” and with tears flowing, he fell and rose, overcome with ecstasy, and praised.

“Similarly, he worshipped and praised the Lord residing in the Thiru-koyil in Paingili.

“Next, we will contemplate the brief history of Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Two Hundred and Sixty-Seven, Thiru-nindra Charukkam, Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We are contemplating the brief history of Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar. After praising the Lord in Thiru-paingili, Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar then journeys to Thondai Nadu. He visits and worships many mountains, countries, and towns where the Lord resides, reaches Thiru-annamalai, worships, and by the path of divine grace, reaches the good land of Thondai.

First, he joins and worships in Thiru-vothur, and then proceeds further to reach Kanchipuram.

The devotees, having adorned the city of Kanchipuram, came to welcome him. He entered, reached the Thiru-ekambarar temple, worshipped, and seeing the great life of the Lord whose body was softened by the embrace of the Mother, he bowed, and with tears flowing, he was immersed and delighted in the flood of great love. He sang the Thiru-pathikam “Karavadum Vannenjarkku Ariyanai” in praise. He also worshipped Kachi Thiru-mayanam. He served there for many days. From there, he visited and worshipped sthalams such as Thiru-malperu, and thinking, “Ekamban Kan Avan En Ennathane,” he returned and worshipped in Kachi.

Afterwards, he worshipped Thiru-kazhukkundram, Thiru-vanmiyur, Thiru-mayilappur, and other sthalams, and then reached Thiru-ottriyur. There, he worshipped the Lord, who is the one who knows writing, with tears flowing, his body trembling with goosebumps, and with a melting heart, he sang the Thiru-thandakam “Vandongu Sengamalam” in praise. He stayed in that sthalam for some days, singing Thiru-kurunthogai, Thiru-ne Thiru-virutham and other pathikams, performing service, and worshipping nearby temples. From there, he worshipped Thiru-pasur, sang the pathikam “Munthi Muveyil,” reached Pazhayanur Thiru-valangadu, bowed, and proceeded north. He visited many towns, great mountains, and dense forests, worshipped Thiru-karikkarai, and reached Thiru-kalathi. He bathed in the Ponmugali Theertham, worshipped the sacred mountain, and ascended.

He fell prostrate before the Lord, who is the blazing flame on Kalathi mountain, and with a mind and eyes filled with delight, he was ecstatic. He worshipped with the Thiru-thandakam “Kalathiyan Avan En Kannullane,” and with difficulty, came out. He performed sacred services on that sacred mountain and resided there. From the indication of his worship there, he desired to directly behold the magnificent form of the Lord residing in Thiru-kailai. He worshipped Kalathi Nathar and proceeded north with great desire. After crossing great mountains, forest rivers, and the countries that followed them, he reached the Lord’s Thiru-paruppatham.

He worshipped that mountain, where Deva-jathis such as Vinjayar, Iyakkar, Kinnarar, Nagar, and Kamasarigal come daily to worship, and sang pathikams in praise.

After that, he crossed the Telugu country and the Kannada country.

Then, he crossed dense forests, mountain paths, and countries, reached and crossed the Malava country, and after crossing difficult deserts, he crossed the Ladabhoomi, where righteousness abounds everywhere.

Then, after crossing great mountains, rivers, forests, and other obstacles, he reached Madhyama Paithiram. He crossed the Ganga river and worshipped the sthalam of Kasi with devotion. Leaving those who had accompanied him there, he alone, desiring to go to Kailai mountain, crossed the Ganga. Even though the paths of Katrangal and Vanamalavu were impassable for humans, he walked and crossed them due to his intense desire. He abandoned eating roots, leaves, and fruits, and walked day and night. His feet wore down to the ankles.

With his desire fixed on Kailai, Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman crawled forward with his hands. His hands wore down to the wrists. Even though they wore down, he did not stop, but pushed himself forward with his chest through the harsh, smoky, gravelly terrain of the dense forest. His chest and flesh were bruised, and his bones were broken.

After that, he rolled forward, wearing down his entire body. When his entire body was worn down, and there was no external means to proceed further, the Tamilian remained there. Lord Shiva, who desired that he should be praised by this world with his steadfast, sweet Tamil, then, instead of granting him grace to reach Kailai, created a pond there. He himself appeared in the guise of a sage and stood directly before Nayanar, looking at him with concern. Nayanar also looked at him, and the sage asked, “Why have you come to this cruel forest, to the point of your body being destroyed?” To this, Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar replied, “O Sage, I came to behold the magnificent form of Lord Shiva with Umaiyammaiyar in the northern Kailai. This is my intention.” The sage then said, “Is Kailai mountain an easy mountain for humans to see?

“Even the Devas find it difficult to see. What have you accomplished by coming here?

“Now, it is your duty to return from this point.” To this, Thiru-navukkarasu The Nayanar refused, stating that he would not return with this perishable body unless he beheld the vision of the Lord in Kailash. Seeing his resolve, the sage vanished into the sky and, through an ethereal voice, commanded, “Arise, O King of Eloquence!” The Nayanar then rose with a body free from all ailments. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar humbly prayed, “O Lord, grant me the grace to behold Your sacred form in Kailash with my own eyes.” In response, the Lord, through an ethereal voice, commanded, “Plunge into this pond, and you shall behold that sacred form in Thiru-Aiyaru.” The Nayanar praised Him with Thiru-Thandagams such as “Vettragi Vinnagi” and, obeying the divine command, plunged into the pond. Who can comprehend the greatness of the grace of the Primal Lord?

“There, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, who had plunged into the pond, emerged from a tank in Thiru-Aiyaru. In Aiyaru, he beheld all animate and inanimate beings shining forth as Shiva and Shakti. He bowed in reverence and approached the Thiru-Koyil. That Thiru-Koyil of Thiru-Aiyaru became Mount Kailash itself. Devas such as Mal, Ayan, and Indra praised Him. The Vedas resounded.

“Siddhas, Vidyadharas, and others thronged. Apsaras sang and played musical instruments. Sacred waters like the Ganga worshipped Him. Gana-Nathas and Bhootha-Vetalas praised Him. And like another silver mountain, Rishabha-Devar stood before Him. They served before Nandi Peruman.

“Shiva-Peruman shone like a coral mountain adorned with an emerald creeper upon a silver mountain. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, the King of Eloquence, beheld this magnificent form. He drank the nectar of that vision with his eyes. He clasped his hands, prostrated, rose, and, with his body trembling, stood before Him, dancing and singing. He wept, he worshipped, he praised with Thiru-Thandagams. After he had beheld this for some time, the Lord graciously concealed that form.

“The Nayanar grieved. He praised the vision he had seen with the Thiru-Pathigam “Madhar Pirai Kanniyanai.” Afterwards, he stayed in that sacred place, praising with Thiru-Thandagams, Thiru-Kurunthogais, Thiru-Nerisais, Thiru-Viruthams, and other Pathigams, and performing sacred service.

“Then, departing from Thiru-Aiyaru, he worshipped Thiru-Neithanam and Thiru-Mazhapadi and reached Thiru-Poonthuruthi. He sang the Thiru-Thandagam “Poyyiliyai Kanden” and the Thiru-Kurunthogai “Thiruvadi Keezh Naam Iruppathu,” and a Thiru-Virutham with the sentiment “Naam Adi Potruvathae” (that we praise His feet), and performed service there.

“There, having received the Lord’s grace, he established a lofty sacred monastery and resided there. During those days, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sang various Pathigams such as Thandagam, Thani-Thandagam, Adaivu-Thandagam, and Thiru-Angamalai.

“Now, the third meeting between Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman and Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar is about to occur. While Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar was residing in Thiru-Poonthuruthi, Aludaiya Pillaiyar, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, who had parted from the Nayanar in Thiru-Maraikkadu, having defeated the Jains in debate, made the light of the sacred ash shine forth, straightened the hunchback of the Pandyan king, and proceeded to the Chola country. Hearing that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar was in Thiru-Poonthuruthi, he came to meet him. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, the Vageesar, hearing that Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman was coming to Thiru-Poonthuruthi, went forth to meet him. Outside the town, amidst the throng of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s retinue, unseen by anyone, he prostrated himself on the ground and concealed himself. He entered in that form and, along with those bearing the pearl palanquin on which Pillaiyar was riding, he too bore it, thus attaining great merit.

“The Nayanar became one of those bearing the palanquin on which Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman was riding. No one knew of this. Immediately, a thought arose in Pillaiyar’s sacred mind, and he asked, “Where is Appar?” The Nayanar replied, “Because I performed unparalleled penance before, I have now attained the blessing of bearing Your palanquin and am here.” Hearing this, Pillaiyar was greatly startled and, rising in fear, asked, “What is this that you have done?” and worshipped Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. The Nayanar, in turn, worshipped him, asking, “How else should I serve Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman?” Thus, both of them met, worshipped Poyyiliyar, conversed in the Nayanar’s sacred monastery, and inquired about each other’s journeys and well-being. They rejoiced and departed. Pillaiyar recounted the depth of Queen Mangaiyarkkarasiyar’s devotion and the greatness of Kulachiraiyar, and Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar resolved to proceed to the Pandya country.

“Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman requested him to visit the good shrines of Thondai Nadu, and accordingly, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman worshipped Poonthuruthi and departed. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman also took leave of the Lord and departed south, worshipped Thiru-Pukalur, and reached Madurai Thiru-Alavai. He joined the Lord who had researched Tamil in the assembly of refined scholars, rejoiced, immersed himself in supreme bliss, and sang the Thiru-Thandagam “Mulaithanai,” praising and exulting. Mangaiyarkkarasiyar, the Pandyan king who had received blessings through her, and Kulachiraiyar came and worshipped the Nayanar’s feet. He resided there, singing Tamil compositions such as Nerisai Thandagam. He resided there.

“From there, he departed, worshipped Thiru-Poovanam, praised it with the Thiru-Thandagam “Vadivaeru Thirusoolam,” and proceeded to Thiru-Rameswaram. He worshipped there and resided, singing Pathigams such as Thiru-Nerisai.

“Afterwards, from there, he worshipped shrines such as Thiru-Nelveli and Thiru-Kaanapper. His mind was always softened, tears flowed, and he lived in a state of constant contemplation of Shiva’s feet.

“Thus, he traveled throughout the Pandya country, then reached the Chola country, worshipping the shrines he had visited before, and came to Poonpukalur, the remover of false bonds. In Thiru-Pukalur, he worshipped the Lord’s sacred feet and resided in the sacred courtyard with great devotion. During those days, he sang countless Thiru-Pathigams such as Nindra Thiru-Thandagam, Thani-Thiru-Thandagam, Kshetra-Kovai, Kuraintha Thiru-Nerisai, Thani-Nerisai, Aaruyir Thiru-Virutham, Dasa-Puranam, Pavanaasa-Pathigam, Sara- He sang countless Thiru-Pathigams, including Parakkarai Thiru-Virutham. While Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman was performing this service, to reveal his virtuous state to the world, by the grace of the Lord, wherever his Ulavaram (hoe) touched, gold and precious gems shone forth. He considered them mere pebbles, placed them with pebbles, and cast them into a tank with his Ulavaram. Before the Nayanar, who had attained a state of non-differentiation between gold, gems, grass, and stones, celestial Apsaras descended from the heavens.

“Like lightning streaks, they came, spreading nectar in the appropriate decorative manner of full-throated melodies, their eyes wide open, singing. Their feet, like tender Kalpaka leaves, moved in circles, their fingers moved gracefully, and their hands moved in sync with their eyes, swaying and dancing like vines. As they sang and danced, showering flowers, embracing as if to unite, their hair falling loose, running and returning, performing various acts of love, the Nayanar, a great ascetic whose mind was unceasingly fixed on the Lord’s sacred feet, remained steadfast in his service, his mental state unwavering. He looked at them and sang the Thiru-Thandagam “Poymaya Perunkadalil,” saying, “I am not lacking because of you. I am a servant of Thiruvarur Ammaan. I will not fall into your ways.

“Do not wander.” The Apsaras, unable to accomplish anything, bowed and departed. All the worlds praised this state. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, the Vageesar, who was the embodiment of loving devotion, was about to attain the true grace of the Lord. He resided there for some days, as the time for attaining the true grace of the Lord was near. With his inner faculties fixed on the Lord, he sang many Thiru-Viruthams, with the premonition that “Pukalur Peruman will now place me at His sacred feet,” which became his fame. He sang the Thiru-Thandagam “Punniya Un Adikkae Pothukindren” and, becoming the very form of Shiva-Ananda Gnana, the Nayanar resided at the Lord’s sacred feet, worshipped by all the worlds.

“The celestials showered flowers. Five celestial drums resounded. On that sacred day of Sathayam in the month of Chithirai, when the Nayanar attained the sacred feet, all living beings in all wombs were filled with immense joy. This is a brief summary of the history of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Peruman.

“Now, we will extensively contemplate the Thiru-Puranam of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar through the Periya Puranam.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Two Hundred and Sixty-Eight. Thiru-Nindra Charukkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. “Unceasing great devotion, eyes that shed tears, a sacred hand holding the Ulavaram, a heart fixed on Shiva-Peruman’s sacred feet, a great ascetic’s walk, the eloquent tongue of Vageesar singing songs of wisdom, and the beautiful radiance of Shiva’s attire — let us praise and live.” This is the praise of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman composed by Srimath Sivagnana Swamigal. O wealthy devotees of Shiva!

We have contemplated the brief history of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar.

Now, according to our tradition, we will extensively contemplate the Nayanar’s Puranam as a summary, a classification, and an elaborate work. Aludaiya Adigal Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. How much merit, how much Shiva-merit, must we have accumulated to contemplate the Puranam of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, who is known by sacred names such as Appar Swamigal and Vageesa Thava Munivar? How can we praise and describe the great compassion of Shiva-Peruman, who granted us the grace to contemplate the Puranam of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar? We praise, worship, and extol the grace of Shiva-Peruman, the benefactor who has enslaved us all, and the grace of the Guru, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, and extensively contemplate the Nayanar’s Puranam. The twelve Shaivite Thiru-Murais; of these, Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal composed the fourth, fifth, and sixth Thiru-Murais.

Indeed, the fourth, fifth, and sixth Thiru-Murais of Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal are called Thevaram. The Thiru-Murais composed by Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, who composed the first, second, and third Thiru-Murais, are named Thiru-Kadaikkappu. The Thiru-Murai composed by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, which is the seventh Thiru-Murai, is named Thiru-Paattu. The Thiru-Murais composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, who composed the fourth, fifth, and sixth Thiru-Murais, are named Thevaram. Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal is one of the four great Samayacharyas of the Saiva Siddhanta, the pure Advaita Vaidika Saivism. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, holding an Ulavaram (hoe) in his sacred hand, traveled to various sacred places and performed sacred service.

The total number of Thiru-Pathigams composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman is forty-nine thousand, according to the information we have. In the Thiru-Murai Kanda Puranam, Umapathi Sivachariyar states that the total number of Thiru-Pathigams sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman is forty-nine thousand. Nambiandar Nambi also refers to this, stating, “Pathigam Ezhunooru Pagarum Ma Kavi Yogi” (The great poet-yogi who sang seven hundred Pathigams).

Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, in the second verse of his Thiru-Nindriyur Thiru-Pathigam, sings that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, the king of the sacred tongue, who gave birth to seven times seven hundred great compositions, sang a total of forty-nine thousand Thiru-Pathigams. During the time when Nambiandar Nambi compiled the Thiru-Murais at the request of King Abhaya Kulasekara, the total number of Thiru-Pathigams sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, revealed to us by Shiva-Peruman, was three hundred and twelve. Out of the forty-nine thousand Thiru-Pathigams composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, three hundred and thirteen Pathigams are available. Among these, approximately three thousand sixty-eight sacred verses have been revealed to us by Shiva-Peruman. The total number of Pathigams compiled by Nambiandar Nambi is three hundred and twenty-one. Of these, nine Pathigams are not available to us.

A total of three hundred and twelve Pathigams have currently been graciously bestowed upon us by the Lord. If we consider the general calculation of ten sacred verses per Pathigam, then for these three hundred and thirteen Pathigams, approximately three thousand sixty-eight verses are available to us. We have already seen, have we not, that the Pathigams included in the fourth, fifth, and sixth Thiru-Murais of the twelve Thiru-Murais The Pathigams included in this fourth Thiru-Murai are also referred to as Thiru-Nerisai. This fourth Thiru-Murai contains a total of one hundred and thirteen Pathigams, with a total of one thousand seventy verses. Within the fourth Thiru-Murai, Pathigams pertaining to fifty Shiva-Sthalams are included. It contains a total of ten Panns: Kolli, Thiru-Nerisai, Thiru-Virutham, Kantharam, Piyanthai Kantharam, Sathari, Kanthara Panchamam, Pazhanthakkaragam, Pazhampanjuram, Seekamaram, and Kurinji.

This Thiru-Murai contains nine miraculous Thiru-Pathigams.

Furthermore, the fourth Thiru-Murai includes many general Pathigams sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, in addition to the Pathigams sung in various Sthalams.

Furthermore, the Thiru-Pathigams found in the fifth Thiru-Murai composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman are noted as Thiru-Kurunthogai. This fifth Thiru-Murai contains a total of one hundred Pathigams, with a total of one thousand fifteen verses. Seventy-six Shiva Thiru-Sthalams are sung in this Thiru-Murai. Although these Thiru-Murai songs should be considered as natural Tamil songs, they are currently sung in the Indala Pann. These Thiru-Murai songs are composed of simple and sweet words. The sixth Thiru-Murai composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman is customarily called Thiru-Thandagam.

That is why we praise Peruman as Thandaga Vendhar and Thandaga Chathurar. It contains ninety-nine Thiru- Pathigams and nine hundred and eighty-one Thiru-Paadals, i.e., Thiru-Thandagams. These are Pathigams sung in sixty-five Shiva Thiru-Sthalams.

Additionally, many general Pathigams are included.

Now, in the Thiru-Thondar Puranam, also known as Periya Puranam, composed by Sekkizhar Peruman, the Thiru-Nindra Charukkam contains the Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. In this, Sekkizhar Peruman has structured the Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam with twenty-nine sacred verses. Sivakavimani Ayya has written extensively on this.

Furthermore, out of the three hundred and twelve Thiru-Pathigams composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, he has published this commentary with appropriate notes for two hundred and forty-four Pathigams. The publishers have noted that the remaining sixty-nine Pathigams, along with notes, should also be published as part of the Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Sivakavimani Ayya’s commentary on the Periya Puranam comprises a total of seven volumes. The third volume is divided into two parts. The first part of the third volume contains Sivakavimani Ayya’s commentary on the Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam.

Now, we will systematically delve into the Puranam. The Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam is the twenty-first Puranam in the Periya Puranam.

First, the verses about Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman in the summary work are as follows: “Thiru-Nindra Semmaiyai Semmaiyaga Ko-” “Thiru-Navukkaraiyan than adiyaarkkum adiyen.” These are the lines about Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman found in the Thiru-Thondar Thogai composed by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal.

Now, in the classification work, Thiru-Thondar Thiru-Anthathi, Nambiandar Nambi has sung about Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman in two sacred verses, numbers twenty-four and twenty-five. Those two sacred verses are as follows: “Natravan Nallur Sivan Thiruppatham than senni vaikka petravan matra ippirappara veerattar peykalal thazhvutravan utra vidam adaiyaaridavallamuthatrutravan aamoril navukku arasannum thoo maniyae. Maniyinai ma marai kaattu marunthinai vanmozhiaatchiniyena neezh kathavan thirappithana then kadalil.” “Piniyena kanmithappithana saiva perunerikkae maniyena navukkaraiyar piran than arunthamizhae.” These are the two sacred verses sung by Nambiandar Nambi about Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman in the Thiru-Thondar Thiru-Anthathi.

First, after examining the explanations for these sections of the summary and classification works, we will then continue to contemplate the Nayanar’s Puranam, along with Sivakavimani Ayya’s commentary on the four hundred and twenty-nine sacred verses found in the Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam, which is part of the elaborate work, the Periya Puranam. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Two Hundred and Sixty-Nine. Thiru-Nindra Charukkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. In the method of contemplating the Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam, we must first contemplate the lines about Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman found in the Thiru-Thondar Thogai composed by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. Those lines are as follows: “Thiru-Nindra Semmaiyae Semmaiyaga Konda Thiru-Navukkaraiyanthan Adiyaarkkum Adiyen.” These are the lines composed by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal about Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar in the Thiru-Thondar Thogai.

The meaning of this is: “I am a servant to the devotees of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, who held the enduring and sacred ultimate reality as his perfect support.” This is the meaning of those lines composed by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. The phrase begins with “Thirunindra Semmaiye,” but it should be rephrased as “Nindra Thiru.” “Thiru” signifies the wealth of liberation. “Thiru” here means the Lord’s Thiru, that is, the wealth of liberation. “Thirunindra Semmaiye” appears, where “Semmai” means the ultimate reality, the state of Shiva, or liberation.

Therefore, “Semborul” means that which bestows “Semmai,” i.e., the liberation that is the state of Shiva.

Furthermore, “Semmai” also implies the eternal, pure, unchanging nature of the Lord.

Here, it is a metonymy, referring to Lord Shiva, who possesses all these qualities.

Thus, “Thirunindra Semmai” is It refers to Lord Shiva, who bestows the wealth of liberation, which is the state of Shiva.

Now, the song continues with “Thirunindra Semmaiye Semmaiya Konda.” “Semmaiya Konda” means having firmly grasped as a supreme refuge. “Semmai” here denotes the strength and steadfastness of conviction.

Therefore, “Thirunindra Semmaiye Semmaiya Konda” means having firmly grasped the supreme reality of Shiva, which bestows the wealth of liberation, as the ultimate refuge. Following “Thirunindra Semmaiye Semmaiya Konda,” the song continues with “Thirunavukkaraiyan than adiyarkkum adiyen.” Thirunavukkarasu is the name bestowed upon Appar Swamigal by Lord Shiva. Appar Peruman’s birth Lord Shiva, appreciating the richness of the Tamil language, bestowed the name Thirunavukkarasu upon Appar Swamigal.

Thus, Thirunavukkarasu is a significant name. Thirunavukkarasu is rendered here as Thirunavukkaraiyan. We will extensively discuss the history of how the Lord bestowed the name Thirunavukkarasu upon Appar Swamigal in the hagiography of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar. Both Thirunavukkarasu and Thirunavukkaraiyar convey the same meaning. Such a Thirunavukkaraiyan, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sings, “I am a servant to his devotees.” Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sings, “I am a servant even to the devotees of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman.” Therefore, “Thirunindra Semmaiye Semmaiya Konda” The meaning of “Thirunavukkaraiyan than adiyarkkum adiyen” is, “I am a servant to the devotees of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, who has taken the supreme reality of Shiva, which bestows the eternal wealth of liberation, as his ultimate refuge.” This is the meaning of these lines from the Thiru-Thondar Thogai.

Furthermore, “Thirunindra Semmai” also refers to the steadfastness of the sacred service performed by Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. We will elaborate on this in the history of the steadfast Peruman.

Moreover, many of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s Thevarams illustrate his unwavering devotion to Lord Shiva, the ultimate reality. Such a Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal praises and sings, “I am a servant to his devotees.” This is because I am unworthy of serving Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, who, with such distinguished and steadfast sacred service, took Lord Shiva, the ultimate reality, as his supreme refuge.

Therefore, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sings, “I will serve the devotees who served Thirunavukkarasu Peruman.” Thus, the inner meaning here is that the quality of servitude, serving the devotees of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, will bestow upon us the wealth of liberation. “Adiyar adiyar adiyarkku adimaikku adiyanai nalgiradimaiyum poonden adiyar arulaal avanadigooda adiyan ivan endru adimai kondaane” is from Thirumandiram. To be a servant to servants, The nature of such service itself is a great Shiva-punya (merit).

Here, we can see Appoodhi Nayanar, who attained liberation through his devotion to Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, as an example for Sundaramoorthy Swamigal’s lines. When praising Appoodhi Nayanar, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal later emphasizes the same idea by saying, “Nambi Appoodhi adiyarkkum adiyen.” This is the meaning of the lines “Thirunindra Semmaiye Semmaiya Konda Thirunavukkaraiyanthan adiyarkkum adiyen” sung by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal about Thirunavukkarasu Peruman in the Thiru-Thondar Thogai, a collection of hymns.

Now, in the Thiru-Thondar Thiruvandhadhi, Nambi Andar Nambigal sings about Thirunavukkarasu Peruman through two sacred verses. This is a genre of literature. In the first verse, he sings: “Nattravan nalloor Sivan Thiruppadham than sennivaikkap petravan mattum ippirapparaveerattar peykalal thazhvuttravan uttraiyidam adaiyaarida ol amudhathutravan aamooril Naavukku Arasu enum Thoo Maniye.” Now, Nambi Andar Nambigal composes the second verse about Thirunavukkarasu Peruman in this genre, the Thiru-Thondar Thiruvandhadhi, as follows: “Maniyinaimamarai kaattu marundhinai vanmoliyal thiniyana neelgathavan thirappiththana thenkadalil piniyana kalmithappiththana Saiva perunerikke aniya”

Thus, “ena Naavukkaraiyar Piran than arunthamizhe” is the second verse composed by Nambi Andar Nambigal about Thirunavukkarasu Peruman.

In this way, we have contemplated the parts and verses about Thirunavukkarasu Peruman in both the collected works and the genre-specific works.

Now, we formally enter the Thiru-Thondar Puranam, also known as Periya Puranam, a comprehensive work, specifically the Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. The Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam is the twenty-first sacred puranam in the Periya Puranam. This puranam is the section that narrates the life history and character of the Nayanar with the sacred name Thirunavukkaraiyar, or Thirunavukkarasar. This puranam is the first in the Thirunindra Sarukkam.

Thus, the history of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar begins here. As we have already discussed, Sekkizhar Peruman has sung the puranam of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman in a total of four hundred and twenty-nine sacred verses. The first verse is as follows: “Thirunavukkarasu valar Thiruthondin neri vazha varugnanath thavamunivar Vaageesar vaaimai thigal perunama seer paravalurugindren perulagil oru naavukku urai seiya onnamai unaraden.” Sekkizhar Peruman begins the first sacred verse thus. He starts the puranam of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman by saying, “Thirunavukkarasu valar Thiruthondin neri vazha.” Unlike any other puranam we have seen so far, he begins this puranam by placing the Nayanar’s sacred name first. If so, we can understand the glory of the sacred name Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, Thirunavukkarasu, here. The wise ascetic, Vaageesar, who came to ensure the world lives in the path conducive to the growth of Lord Shiva’s sacred service, is Thirunavukkarasu Peruman.

Sekkizhar Peruman sings that he praises the glories of this esteemed sacred name, Thirunavukkarasar and Vaageesar. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar is the Nayanar who bears the esteemed sacred names Thirunavukkarasar, Vaageesar, and Appar Swamigal. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that he praises the glories of his sacred name through his history. In this Sekkizhar Peruman sings that he realizes his inability to describe the glories of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s sacred name in this vast world, for one tongue cannot do justice. This is the explicit meaning of the first verse.

Now, its detailed explanation: Thirunavukkarasar and Vaageesar are great names, sacred names. In the collected work Thiru-Thondar Thogai and the genre work Thiru-Thondar Thiruvandhadhi, the great teachers have proudly sung about the glories of this sacred name, Thirunavukkarasu.

Therefore, following that tradition, Sekkizhar Peruman, who began to narrate the history of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, placed the name Thirunavukkarasu first. And placed the name Vaageesar in the middle, thus beginning the first sacred verse in the Thirunavukkarasu Peruman Puranam. Sekkizhar Peruman begins by saying, “I embark upon praising the glories of that name.” All that is sung in the Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam are the glories of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s sacred name. That is why Sekkizhar Peruman refers to it as “Perunama Seer” in this verse. Thirunavukkarasu is the sacred name bestowed upon Appar Swamigal by the Lord. Vaageesar was Appar Swamigal’s sacred name in his previous birth.

It is a historical fact that Thirunavukkarasu Peruman had a previous birth and that in that previous birth, he was an ascetic engaged in penance. It is also a historical fact that the penance he performed in his previous birth was a Shiva-gnana penance, striving to attain Shiva. Gnana-thavam means penance suitable for attaining Shiva through wisdom.

Thus, it is a historical fact that Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, in his previous birth, was endowed with gnana-thavam and strove to attain Shiva, and that his name then was Vaageesar. In the Periya Puranam, in the Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam, the 1313th sacred verse states that Lord Shiva tells Thilagavathi Ammaiyar, “Your brother, having become a sage before, strove through penance to attain Me.” This is the basis for the information about Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s previous birth.

Furthermore, in the 1314th sacred verse, the passage “Pandu puri naravaththu pazhudhin alaviraivazhuvum thondar” (devotees who, in their past penance, erred slightly) undoubtedly indicates that the Nayanar was a sage who performed good penance to attain Shiva in his previous birth, and that he erred slightly in that penance.

Moreover, there are many internal evidences for this in the Thevarams composed by Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. “Nillaadha nin kurambai pinakka neenga adiyerkku niraiviththu endrum sellaadha sen nerukke selvipaanai” is from Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s Thiruchengattangudi Thevaram, Thiruththandaagam. This internal evidence is found here.

Therefore, following these ideas, Vaageesar was the name Thirunavukkarasu Peruman bore in his previous birth. Thirunavukkarasu is the sacred name bestowed upon the Nayanar by the Lord in this birth. It is also remarkable that Vaageesar and Thirunavukkarasu are two names with a common meaning. It is certain that in his previous birth, the Nayanar was a sage who followed the path of Shiva-gnana.

However, even though the author does not explicitly state his former name, Sivakavimani explains that there is no impediment to accepting the name Vaageesar found in history as fitting.

Thus, when referring to the previous births of Nayanmars, it is Sekkizhar Peruman’s tradition to interpret them in this manner, as we have already discussed. We have now contemplated the meaning of the two sacred names, Thirunavukkarasu and Vaageesar, which appear in the very first verse.

Now, the verse begins, “Thirunavukkarasu valar Thiruthondin neri vazha varum.” This should be understood to mean that this world should live by growing in the path. The world, immersed in the mire of ego, is entitled to be uplifted and live. Sekkizhar Peruman here refers to the path that enables the world, immersed in the mire of ego, to be uplifted and grow, as the “path of growth.” What does “growth” mean? It means attaining the state of non-birth, where these souls do not repeatedly take birth. This is the meaning of growth. “Valarneri” (path of growth) means the path or way that leads to such growth.

He refers to it as the “path of growth of sacred service.” Its meaning is that the path of Shiva, comprising Chariya, Kriya, Yoga, and Gnana, is the path of growth of sacred service. Its main meaning is to attain Shiva through service. The Sivagnana Siddhiyar states that the four paths to attain Shankara are Sanmargam, Sagamargam, Sathpuththira Margam, and Dasa Margam, which are Gnana, Yoga, Kriya, and Chariya, respectively. In such a path of Shiva, that is, the path of sacred service, Our Thirunavukkarasu Peruman came to enable this world to live by following that path. What does it mean for the world to live by following this sacred service? It means guiding this world by demonstrating those Shiva paths.

Our Paramacharyar, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, came to guide this world by demonstrating and walking in the path of sacred service. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, among the four paths of Chariya, Kriya, Yoga, and Gnana, stood first as the foundation for all four, demonstrating the Chariya path, also known as Dasa Margam, and guiding us in that Dasa Margam, was our guide, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar. We can understand this by observing that the Nayanar undertook and demonstrated the sacred Uzhavara service as his certainty. It is our Saivite tradition that among the four Saivite Paramacharyars, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar incarnated to explain Chariya.

Furthermore, by mentioning “Gnana-thavam,” it implies that he explained not only Chariya but also the four paths, starting from Chariya, then Kriya, Yoga, and finally Gnana.

Therefore, this Puranam elaborates on the special quality of Vaageesar, the Gnana-thava Muni, who incarnated as Thirunavukkarasar to enable the growing path of sacred service to flourish. The sacred name Thirunavukkarasu and the sacred name Vaageesar are names that cause truth to shine forth. They are sacred names of shining glory. We can also recall here the history of Appoodhi Nayanar attaining Lord Shiva by merely praising this great name, Thirunavukkarasu. “Vaimai” (truth) here signifies the state of Shiva-bhoga, which is Shiva-ananda. Such a great name is instrumental in attaining and shining in that state of Shiva-bhoga, which is Shiva-ananda.

I praise the greatness of such a glorious Thirunavukkarasar by narrating the Nayanar’s history, but praising the greatness of his sacred name or narrating the Nayanar’s sacred history, Sekkizhar Peruman says that it cannot be done by a single tongue, nor by any tongue. We shall continue our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 270. Thirunindra Sarukkam. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. When Sekkizhar Peruman sings the sacred histories of the Nayanmars, it is his tradition to sing about the country and village where the Nayanmars incarnated, their prosperity, and the greatness of the lineage and clan in which they were born.

Accordingly, Sekkizhar Peruman begins to sing about the country, lineage, and prosperity of the land where Thirunavukkarasu Peruman incarnated. The country where Thirunavukkarasu Peruman incarnated is the prosperous land called Thirumunaippadi. This Thirumunaippadi country is the region surrounding the present-day Cuddalore area. Sekkizhar Swamigal sings about the prosperity of that country. A country can have many forms of prosperity, but among all the forms of prosperity a country possesses, the greatest prosperity is to have citizens of good character living there. That is considered the most excellent prosperity, the special prosperity for a country, praised by the wise.

Thiruvalluva Devanayanar, in his Thirukkural, in the chapter on “Country,” in Kural number 731, has sung, “Thakkarum thaazhvilaa selvarum servadhu naadu” (A country is where the worthy and the wealthy without fault reside). In that, he places the worthy, those of good character, first. That is, “Thakkar” means righteous people, those who follow dharma, those of good character. This is the meaning. He places this first, and then secondly, “thaazhvu ilaa selvarum,” meaning the wealthy, he places the wealthy second.

Thus, Valluvar says that a country is where those who follow dharma and those who are wealthy live together. In that, Valluvar Peruman places those of good character and those who follow dharma, called “Thakkar,” first.

Therefore, the prosperity of a country means that it must have citizens of good character who follow dharma. Accordingly, Sekkizhar Swamigal mentions that Thirumunaippadi Nadu, where our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar incarnated, is also a prosperous country. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that Thirumunaippadi Nadu is a country where citizens of good character, excelling in Shiva devotion, live in abundance. The Thiru-munaippadi country is so rich that it can be said to be without any fault. If there is any fault, it is only the dust on the soil of Thiru-munaippadi, and there is no other fault in the soil or the country itself. Thiru-munaippadi is a prosperous land where great sages, rich in virtue and Shiva-dharma, live.

This Thiru-munaippadi country is a land where citizens of excellent and steadfast virtue reside. Such citizens, excellent in steadfast virtue, refer here to the agricultural community. This refers to the agricultural community, because the Nayanar of this history, Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman, was born into the Vellala community.

Therefore, it is the tradition of our Sekkizhar Peruman to describe the excellence of that community as the excellence of the country and the city. In Thiru-munaippadi country, there are mansions. The moon shines at the top of these mansions, as if they are adorned by it.

Thus sings Sekkizhar Peruman. What does this signify? It indicates that the great people of this land are those who stand on the path of Shiva-sadhana to attain the state of Shiva.

Therefore, the mansions there also stand and grow in the same path. That is, the moon shines at the top of the mansions, and the mansions grow as if to adorn themselves with the moon on their heads. The mansions grow there as if to adorn themselves with the moon on their heads. Adorning the head with the moon is the appearance of Lord Shiva, and those who have attained Shiva-sarupyam also wear the moon on their heads, having attained Shiva-sarupyam. All the citizens living in this Thiru-munaippadi country have attained Shiva-sarupyam by standing on the path of Shiva-sadhana to attain the state of Shiva.

Therefore, just like them, the mansions in that country also rise high as if adorning themselves with the moon on their heads.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman, while singing the glory of the mansions, has sung the glories of the Shiva devotees there. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that this country is a prosperous land. The Pennai River, which flows through this country, is the reason for this country being a prosperous land. The Pennai River originates in the Kurinji region, which is mountainous and its surrounding areas. It carries with it the pearls found in the bamboo groves of that Kurinji region. The Pennai River flows through the Mullai region, which is known as forests and their surrounding areas.

As it flows from the mountains through these forest lands, it carries with it fragrant flowers and also many precious gems.

Thus, it scatters the pearls, gems, and flowers it carries on both banks. Just as generous philanthropists, without self-interest, distribute all their valuable possessions for the benefit of others, Similarly, the Pennai River beautifully flows, scattering the pearls, gems, and flowers it brought on both sides of the Marutham lands. On both sides of the Pennai River, in the vast agricultural fields, farmers yoke buffaloes and plough the land. They carry out agricultural work. The Pennai River brings the necessary water for this. Water is the primary necessity for agriculture.

Here, the farmers do not have to make great efforts to find water. The water needed for agriculture comes naturally through the Pennai River.

Therefore, the prosperity of this Thiru-munaippadi country, due to the flow of the Pennai River, is not a newly created prosperity, but an inherent prosperity that exists there, which we can perceive here. In this Thiru-munaippadi country, just like the Thenpennai River, other great rivers including Kedilam also flow here, enriching the country. In all the water bodies of Thiru-munaippadi country, there are Varal fish in the shape of plates. Varal fish have a plate-like shape; they are wide and long and wriggle. When they wriggle, both sides glitter, so the Varal fish leap like plates. The canals through which water flows in Thiru-munaippadi country are rich in sugarcane.

Therefore, sugarcane has grown very well and flourished. Due to such abundant growth, the sugarcane juice automatically bursts and flows through the nodes of the sugarcane. In all the fields, paddy crops with ears of grain have grown luxuriantly. In the vast lands, areca nut trees with clusters of nuts are abundant. In the places ploughed with ploughshares, there are heaps of pearls. In the ponds, red water lilies have blossomed.

In every house of Thiru-munaippadi country, things are happening splendidly.

Here, in Thiru-munaippadi country, wrestlers have built canals to regulate the floodwaters and to direct them into the fields.

Here, sugarcane has grown very luxuriantly. Among these sugarcane plants, there are beehives. Due to the abundant growth of sugarcane, the nodes of the sugarcane burst, and sugarcane juice flows profusely.

Moreover, there are beehives among the sugarcane. When these beehives break, honey flows out and spreads.

Thus, sugarcane juice and honey mix and flow widely. Bees swarm there and make sounds.

In this way, sugarcane juice and honey flow like floodwaters, breaking the sluices. To block these broken sluices, jaggery blocks made from boiled sugarcane juice are used. When sugarcane juice and honey, mixed like floodwater, break the sluices in the canals, jaggery made from sugarcane is used to block them. They use jaggery blocks, made from boiled sugarcane juice, to block the flood caused by sugarcane juice. There is a type of medicine where the very source of a disease is used as its cure.

Similarly, here, the great people use jaggery blocks, made from boiled sugarcane juice, to block the flood caused by sugarcane juice. Sekkizhar Peruman sings about the prosperity of the country in this way. Some might think this is poetic imagination, but it is true. Because, even now, in Cuddalore, in many towns like Nellikuppam, sugarcane is growing very luxuriantly, and the sugar mill industry is abundant here even now.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman sings thus. Some might think this is poetic imagination, but it is not. It is the inherent prosperity and true nature of this country, explains Sivakavimani Aiya.

Let us continue our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Two Hundred and Seventy-One, Thiru-nindrachcharukkam. The Puranam of Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing about the prosperity of Thiru-munaippadi country. Sekkizhar Peruman sings about the prosperity of the Marutham land in Thiru-munaippadi country, comparing it to the four divisions of a king’s army. There are many banana trees in Thiru-munaippadi country.

The clusters of these banana trees resemble the long, trunk-like faces of elephants. The banana clusters on the banana trees there, especially a variety called ‘Aayiram Eeni’ (thousand-yielding), have clusters that resemble the face and trunk of an elephant. That is, the base of the banana clusters is thick, and the tip is thin, and the clusters are very long.

Thus, the clusters on the banana trees resemble the faces of elephants.

Therefore, the countless banana trees there, resembling countless elephant faces, are like an elephant army, sings Sekkizhar Peruman. Beside the banana trees are paddy crops. Those paddy ears are tall and well-grown. Due to their tall growth, the ripened paddy ears are bent in clusters. These are red paddy crops, so they are red in color.

Thus, the paddy crop with its mature, long, and drooping ears resembles the face of a horse with a mane.

Therefore, it is like a cavalry. There are many carts to carry these ripened ears. All these carts are like a chariot army. The servants who carry the ripened paddy and load it onto the carts are like an infantry.

Therefore, a king’s Chaturanga Balam, that is, the four types of armies, consists of elephant army, cavalry, chariot army, and infantry.

Similarly, here in the Marutham land, the clusters of banana trees are like elephant armies, the paddy ears are like cavalry, and the carts carrying the paddy ears, are like chariot armies, and the servants who pick up the paddy ears and load them onto the carts are like infantry, sings Sekkizhar Peruman. There is another point in this. Among the professions of the people called Vellalars, agriculture and warfare are important professions. Vellalars would both farm and, under the king’s command, go to war against enemies, excelling in military service. Even in this history, the news that Kalippakaiyar, who was betrothed to Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman’s elder sister Thilagavathi Ammaiyar, went to war as the king’s army chief, is also found in Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman’s Puranam.

Therefore, agriculture and warfare are the appropriate professions for Vellalars. In this verse, Sekkizhar Peruman has beautifully sung about these two types of professions. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing. The Pennai River flows in Thiru-munaippadi country. On both banks of the river, areca nut trees have grown very tall. Sekkizhar Peruman compares these areca nut trees to women.

In the section, they have clusters of flowers, unripe fruits, and ripe fruits. This appears as if women are wearing necklaces inlaid with nine gems around their necks. The leaves of those areca nut trees resemble women’s hair. It appears like women’s hair. Just as women’s necks sway under the weight of their hair, unable to bear its burden, so too, due to the dense leaves of the areca nut trees, when they sway in the wind, the neck-like part of the areca nut trees also bends and sways, unable to bear the weight of those areca nut leaves.

Thus, the areca nut trees on both banks of the Pennai River appear to form a fence for the river. Water flows full in the Pennai River. Waves appear in that river. These waves are like the tender shoots of plants, sings Sekkizhar Peruman. A plant’s tender shoot A tender shoot is soft, cool, reddish, and tasty.

Similarly, waves appear in the Pennai River. Since they are compared to the tender shoots of plants, the water in the waves of the Pennai River is also very soft, cool, and tasty, like the tender shoots of plants. Generally, the nature of water is to flow from top to bottom and to stand level.

But here, due to the wind striking the surface of the Pennai River, waves are formed. These waves appear in this manner. All these waves gently reach the groves on its banks. The song states that those waves spread and reach.

Therefore, it is understood here that they have the characteristic of spreading slowly. We can recall here the sight of waves spreading slowly upwards on the seashore, pond banks, and riverbanks.

Thus, the land prosperity and water prosperity of Thiru-munaippadi country are beautifully sung by Sekkizhar Peruman.

Now, in this Thiru-munaippadi country, there are ponds (vaavi). Flowers have bloomed there. Black buffaloes enter to graze. This is how it appears, sings the author: as if black clouds enter the upper part of the already black sea. He sings that it is like black clouds entering the upper part of the already black sea.

Thus, black buffaloes enter the pond to graze on the flowers in the pond. In that pond, there are already very plump Varal fish. These Varal fish have a leaping nature.

Now, buffaloes enter the pond and graze on the flowers in the pond.

At that time, the very plump Varal fish leap up and butt the udders of the buffaloes.

Thus, when the Varal fish butt the udders of the buffaloes, the buffaloes think that their calves are butting their udders. The buffaloes then squirt milk. That milk mixes with the water in the pond and overflows its banks. Through this scene, it is understood that the Varal fish in the pond are as plump and well-grown as buffalo calves, and that these Varal fish have the nature of leaping up and striking, and that they have the nature of calves that butt the udder of a buffalo to drink milk. The affection and love of the mother buffalo, who secretes milk when the calf butts her udder, are also conveyed to us here. In reality, it is not buffalo calves butting and causing the buffaloes to secrete milk.

It is the Varal fish themselves that go and butt the udders of the buffaloes. But due to the general dull-witted nature of buffaloes, they do not recognize the truth that it is Varal fish butting their udders, and thinking that their calves have come to butt, they squirt milk. The milk thus squirted mixes with the water in the pond, and the milk-mixed water overflows the banks.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman sings this very beautiful scene. In that place where he sings about the prosperity of Thiru-munaippadi country, now, the next song with beautiful descriptions is also arranged. Sekkizhar Peruman takes this earth as a maiden. In Thiru-munaippadi country, there are very long rows of trees, long trees, like the arms of this maiden, the earth. On these trees, which are the arms of the earth-maiden, there are flowers, and black bees surround them. This is how it appears: as if blue bangles surround the trees, which are the arms of the earth-maiden.

On these trees, there are red tender leaves. For the earth-maiden, these trees are her arms.

Therefore, the tender leaves of the trees are like her fingers, and these trees have grown tall, reaching up to the sky.

Therefore, this earth-maiden, with her arms as trees, lifts high She holds the moon in the sky like a mirror and looks at her reflection. Thus Sekkizhar Peruman describes. In the cities of Thiru-munaippadi country, there are very high places for storing paddy, that is, very high paddy granaries.

Similarly, there are very high mansions. These paddy granaries and mansions are so high that they touch the clouds. Flocks of peacocks are dancing in those mansions and beside them. Generally, peacocks have the nature of dancing as soon as they see clouds.

Therefore, in the paddy granaries and beside the mansions that stand high enough to touch the clouds, peacocks are dancing, looking at the clouds. Thus sings Sekkizhar Peruman.

Therefore, until now, Sekkizhar Peruman has described the prosperity of Thiru-munaippadi country, the prosperity of the Pennai River, how Thiru-munaippadi country is prosperous due to the Pennai River, the excellence of its land, fields, groves, etc., followed by the excellence of the ponds and flower gardens on the sides of the city, and the excellence of the mansions and high paddy granaries within this country, all in the context of singing about the country’s prosperity. We shall continue with our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 272, Thirunindracharakkam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Sekkizhar Peruman sings of the prosperity of Thiru-Munaippadi Nadu. It is in this sacred land of Thiru-Munaippadi Nadu that Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar and Sundaramurthi Swamigal, also known as Alala Sundarar, are destined to be born. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar takes birth in Thiru-Amur, within this Thiru-Munaippadi Nadu.

Sundaramurthi Swamigal is born in Thiru-Navalur, another sacred place in the same Thiru-Munaippadi Nadu.

Thus, Thiru-Munaippadi Nadu is a most excellent land, blessed with the births of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar and Sundaramurthi Swamigal, and possesses such greatness. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that the glory of Thiru-Munaippadi Nadu cannot be fully encompassed by our understanding. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman and Sundaramurthi Swamigal were born in Thiru-Munaippadi Nadu. They incarnated to transform evil paths and to bestow upon the world the true path of Shiva, the Shiva Dharma. These two great spiritual preceptors incarnated here. Evil paths lead to sin; these evil paths were to be changed so that the world might abide in the path of Shiva.

For this purpose, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar and Sundaramurthi Swamigal incarnated in this Thiru-Munaippadi Nadu. Generally, A country may possess many excellences. Among all these excellences, what is paramount? While a country’s prosperity may nourish the bodies of its people, providing benefits to the physical form, if a country exists to nourish the soul and bestow well-being upon life, then such prosperity is its greatest distinction. Thiru-Munaippadi Nadu possesses such a unique and great distinction, guiding souls and bestowing well-being upon them, because Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar and Sundaramurthi Swamigal incarnated there and caused the path of Shiva to flourish. They blessed all beings to live according to the path of Shiva.

Therefore, Thiru-Munaippadi Nadu possesses such prosperity that benefits the soul. It is by this prosperity that this land shines with glory. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman and Sundaramurthi Swamigal are those who guided souls from evil paths to the path of Shiva. What is an evil path? It is the sum total of all paths that are bound by the individual soul (pasu) and its attachments (pasam). In contrast, the path that truly benefits souls abiding in Shiva Dharma is the path of Shiva.

Therefore, all paths other than Shiva Dharma, the righteous path of Shiva, yield only the fruit of a tree (i.e., temporary, material benefits). The path of Shiva alone is the path that benefits souls. Souls It is the path that redeems. “Those who do not approach Thiru-Velimilaiyan are entering evil paths,” is the sacred utterance of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. There is an alchemy that turns copper into gold; there is an elixir for it. When that elixir touches copper, the copper becomes gold.

Similarly, when a soul enters the path of Shiva, the evil path that soul had followed until then changes on its own. When the soul abides in such a path of Shiva, its individual consciousness (pasu-bodham) transforms into Shiva-consciousness (Shiva-bodham). All the soul’s individual instruments (pasu-karanangal) become Shiva-instruments (Shiva-karanangal).

Consequently, the bonds (pasam) that tied the soul also transform to aid in the experience of Shiva. All these are Shaiva These are the truths revealed by the Siddhanta scriptures. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman and Sundaramurthi Swamigal are those who established souls in this true path of Shiva, the path of Shiva Peruman, who is Thiru-Neelakantar.

Here, Sekkizhar Peruman states, “evil paths change.” This phrase, “evil paths change,” signifies the removal of bonds (pasam). He states that souls abide in the path of Shiva, which implies the attainment of Shiva. To bestow this upon souls, two of our four supreme preceptors, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman and Sundaramurthi Swamigal, incarnated. The purpose of their sacred incarnation The benefit is the removal of the bonds of souls and the bestowal of Shiva’s grace upon them. In this particular verse, when speaking of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman and Sundaramurthi Swamigal, Sekkizhar Peruman places Thirunavukkarasu Peruman first, followed by Sundaramurthi Swamigal, also known as Alala Sundarar. Why did Sekkizhar Peruman place Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar first?

Because this Puranam is the Puranam of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar.

Therefore, due to the nature of the Puranam, he sang of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman first.

Furthermore, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman predates Sundaramurthi Swamigal. For this reason too, he sang of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman first.

Moreover, Sundaramurthi Swamigal sang In the Thiruthonda Thogai, Sundaramurthi Swamigal praised Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. For this reason, Sekkizhar Peruman sang of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman first and Sundaramurthi Swamigal second.

Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman and Sundaramurthi Swamigal were born in this Thiru-Munaippadi Nadu and blessed the world. Sekkizhar Peruman sings of such greatness and glory. By giving Thirunavukkarasu Peruman to this world, the greatest benefit of Thiru-Munaippadi Nadu is the wisdom it bestows upon this world.

Sundaramurthi Swamigal’s sacred incarnation He blessed the world by singing the Thiruthonda Thogai. Our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar has shown us the paths of Shiva Dharma, namely Chariyai, Kiriyai, Yogam, and Gnanam. Specifically, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, by his own example, demonstrated the path of Chariyai, especially Chariyai in Gnanam, in a special way. Not only that, but Thirunavukkarasu Peruman also blessed us by teaching these paths through his authoritative utterances, the Thevarams. In this glorious Thiru-Munaippadi Nadu, there are many villages. The path that always bestows truth There are many villages that possess increasing excellence.

Among them, there is one excellent village that bestows the path of Shiva upon all seven worlds. Its name is Thiru-Amur. Thiru-Amur is the village that fosters the Shiva that arises from the divine path, a village of grace. Indeed, in Thiru-Munaippadi Nadu, there are many villages that possess true wealth and bestow true wealth. When speaking of a country’s wealth, there can be water resources and land resources. Such water and land resources exist in many villages of this Thiru-Munaippadi Nadu.

But here, these water and land resources are praised by Sekkizhar Peruman as true wealth. “Wealth that bestows truth” is its Meaning. Indeed, the water and land resources in the villages of Thiru-Munaippadi Nadu serve as instruments for the path of Shiva. That is why Sekkizhar Peruman sings of them as true wealth, genuine wealth, wealth that bestows truth.

Thus, any wealth that is not an instrument for Shiva is false wealth, regardless of its nature. This is the true meaning. In Thiru-Munaippadi Nadu, there are many villages where such wealth, including the path of Shiva, land resources, and other forms of wealth, abounds. Thiru-Kovalur, Thiru-Vennainallur, Thiru-Navalur, Thiru-Thuraiyur, and many other sacred places of Shiva, with their spiritual wealth, flourish in Thiru-Munaippadi Nadu.

Moreover, the histories of supreme preceptors such as Sundaramurthi Swamigal of Thiru-Navalur, Meykandar Devar of Thiru-Vennainallur, and Arunanandi Sivachariyar of Thiru-Thuraiyur, who incarnated in these sacred Shiva sthalams and spread grace, also contribute to this Shiva wealth and true wealth. We must remember this here. As mentioned above, there are many sacred Shiva sthalams in Thiru-Munaippadi Nadu. Among them, there is a village that bestows grace upon all seven worlds. Its name is Thiru-Amur. This Thiru-Amur is a village that stood in the Shaiva path and showed the Shaiva path to the world.

Here, Thiru-Amur is the village where Thilagavathi Ammaiyar and Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, who incarnated there, guided all beings to the Shaiva path.

Thus, this village possesses the quality of bestowing the Shaiva path upon all seven worlds. This Thiru-Amur is the village of Thilagavathi Ammaiyar, the elder sister of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar is one of the four Shaiva Samayacharyas. They incarnated in this Thiru-Amur and showed the Shaiva path to all beings. How did Thilagavathi Ammaiyar show the Shaiva path to the beings of this world? Thilagavathi Ammaiyar prayed to Shiva Peruman.

She prayed to Shiva Peruman that her younger brother, who was in the alien religion of Jainism, should return to the Shaiva religion and abide in the good path of Shaivism. When Thilagavathi Ammaiyar thus prayed to Shiva Peruman, Shiva Peruman, moved by her plea, afflicted Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, who was then in the Jain religion, with a severe illness (Chulai Noi) and took him into His grace, calling him back to the Shaiva path. Our Thirunavukkarasu Peruman shines as one of the four supreme preceptors. Our Thilagavathi Ammaiyar was instrumental in this. This is how she showed the Shaiva path to all Shaiva people and all beings. Not only That, but Thilagavathi Ammaiyar also performed severe penance and undertook many sacred services.

In Thiru-Adigai, she performed the path of Chariyai, such as sweeping and cleaning the temple, and thereby showed that Shaiva path to the world. This is how Thilagavathi Ammaiyar showed the Shaiva path to all beings.

Now, how did Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar show the Shaiva path to the world? In his previous birth, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar was the sage Vakeesa Muni and performed penance. Our Vakeesa Muni guided Ravana to Shiva Peruman on Mount Kailash. He himself, in this incarnation, in this land, in this Thiru-Munaippadi Nadu, in Thiru-Amur, incarnated and was taken into Shiva Peruman’s grace. He showed the Shaiva path to all beings in this world. Not only that, but he also made the inhabitants of the celestial world abide in the Shaiva path.

Thus, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman are those who bestowed upon all beings the grace that fosters the Shiva attained through the divine path, causing it to grow more and more. The village where these two great individuals incarnated is Thiru-Amur. If we separate Thiru-Amur as Thiru-Aam-Ur, we call it Thiru-Amur. Thiru means the path of Shiva, and Aam means to increase.

Therefore, Thiru-Aam-Ur means the village that increases the path of Shiva. The path of Shiva Thiru-Amur is the village that increased it before. Thiru-Amur is the village that increases the path of Shiva now. Thiru-Amur is the village that will increase the path of Shiva in the future. The sacred name of this village is thus structured to apply to all three tenses. This Thiru-Amur is currently located in Cuddalore District, Tamil Nadu, near the towns of Panruti and Thiru-Koyilur.

The Pasupatheeswarar Temple is located here in Thiru-Amur. The name of the Goddess here is Thiripura Sundari. The Kondrai tree is the sacred tree of the sthalam. The Kedilam River serves as the sacred water body.

Here, in the Pasupatheeswarar Temple, the Moolavar (presiding deity) blesses as a Swayambhu Lingam. Opposite the Swami Sannidhi, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman is seen in a standing posture, bestowing grace. A separate Thevaram Thiru-Pathigam for this sthalam is not available to us. Nevertheless, it is our custom and tradition that the Pasupathi Thiru-Arutham sung by Appar Swamigal was composed specifically for the deity of this sthalam.

Furthermore, this sthalam is also a Thevaram Vaippu Sthalam (a place mentioned in Thevaram hymns). The place where Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal incarnated is located to the southwest of this temple. The house where he was born now stands as a sacred temple. There are also Thiruppugazh hymns by Arunagirinathar for this sacred sthalam. Such are the glories of Thiru-Amur. This is a brief note about the village of Thiru-Amur.

Let us persist in our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 273, Thirunindracharakkam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Sekkizhar Peruman sang of the glories of the sacred place called Thiru-Amur in Thiru-Munaippadi Nadu. In such a sacred place as Thiru-Amur, people of excellent character, possessing all kinds of virtues, reside. What are all kinds of virtues? One aspect is the righteous practices mentioned in the Dharma Shastras.

Not only that, but another aspect is the good practices that are traditionally followed and observed in worldly custom.

Thus, the quality of following and adhering to all kinds of ethical conduct, as described in worldly custom and Dharma Shastras, That quality is called virtue. All such virtuous people reside in that sacred place of Thiru-Amur.

Thus, in that country, Thiru-Munaippadi Nadu, in the sacred place of Thiru-Amur, all clans and all people live without deviation from good conduct. Among them, there is a distinguished clan called the Vellalar clan. That Vellalar clan is a clan that excels in domestic virtue. What does it mean for the Vellalar clan to be a clan that excels in domestic virtue? It means that they follow all the dharmas prescribed for household life, And among these, they excel in the higher Shiva Dharmas. While people of other castes also live in household life, the household life observed by the Vellalar clan is particularly special.

This is because the profession of the Vellalar clan is agriculture. By engaging in such farming, the Vellalar clan, without conscious effort, performs the service of providing sustenance for many beings to live. This is the profession of the farming Vellalar clan.

Therefore, the household life followed by this Vellalar clan is more special than the household life followed by other clans. It is most special. In this glorious Vellalar clan, there is a sub-clan called the Kurukkaiyar clan. A clan is a large division, and within that clan, there will be many sub-clans.

Thus, the Vellalar clan is a very large division. Among the many sub-clans within the Vellalar clan, one is known as the Kurukkaiyar clan. Within this sub-clan, there may also be many smaller divisions. It is customary in our country to refer to a sub-clan as a Gotra and the smaller divisions within it as Pravaram. We have previously learned in the Puranam of Chandeswara Nayanar that Chandeswara Nayanar, also known as Visarasarumanar, was born into the Brahmin clan, and his Gotra was Kashyapa Gotra. We can recall that here as well.

We can recall that here as well.

Thus, in the glorious Vellalar clan, in the Kurukkaiyar sub-clan, which is a division of that Vellalar clan, lived a great man named Pugazhanar. In that sacred place of Thiru-Amur, Pugazhanar was a great man whose glory extended in all directions. He was superior to all those who were distinguished. That great man Pugazhanar was the great leader of the Kurukkaiyar sub-clan. That great man Pugazhanar lived in and understood the exalted household dharma. He was one who possessed the greatness of providing hospitality.

There are many restraints and duties incumbent upon householders. The Thirukkural expounds extensively on the many virtues prescribed for householders. In the chapter on domestic life (Ilvaazhkai) in the Thirukkural, Thiruvalluvar has graciously bestowed upon us eleven duties for householders in the first three couplets. The first couplet is: “Enbaan iyalpudaiya moovarkkum nallaatrin nindra thunai.” Its meaning is that those who live a domestic life, that is, those who live in the Grihastha ashrama, should be a support to those in the other three ashramas. This first couplet states that they should be a support to those who live. That is, those who live in the Grihastha ashrama should support the three types of people in the other three ashramas: those living in Brahmacharya, those living in Vanaprastha, and those living in Sannyasa.

This first couplet thus states three duties. In the second couplet, Valluvar lists three more people whose duties are to be protected: “Thurandhaarkkum thuvathavarkkum irandhaarkkum enbaan thunai.” Who are these three people? Firstly, the renunciants, meaning those who have been abandoned by those who should protect them. For example, when children are young, it is the duty of parents to protect them. When parents are old, it is the duty of their children to protect them.

Thus, those who have been abandoned by those who should protect them, it is the duty of those engaged in the Grihastha ashrama to protect them, says Valluvar. This is stated as the first duty in this second couplet, and generally as the fourth duty in this chapter.

Next, the fifth duty, or the second duty mentioned in this second couplet, which Valluvar states for householders, is to protect those who suffer from poverty.

Thirdly, for those who come to them without any support and pass away, performing the water rites and other ancestral rituals after their demise is the sixth duty, the sixth duty of householders, says Valluvar. These three duties are stated in the second couplet through the verse, “Thurandhaarkkum thuvathavarkkum irandhaarkkum ilvaazhvaan enbaan thunai.” Now, in the third couplet, Thiruvalluvar states five duties. So far, Valluvar, who stated three duties in the first couplet and three duties in the second couplet, states five duties in the third couplet. They are: “Thenpulaathaar deivam virundhu okkal thaan endraangu aimpulaathaaru oombal thalai.” That is, “Thenpulaathaar” refers to ancestors, and “deivam” refers to deities. Vrundhu refers to guests, Okkal refers to relatives, and Thaan refers to oneself and one’s family members.

Thus, the third couplet states that it is the duty of householders to protect these five types of people.

Therefore, in this chapter on domestic life, Thiruvalluvar prescribes eleven duties for those engaged in domestic life in the first three couplets.

Here, Sekkizhar Peruman sings that Pugazhanar lived in Thiru-Aamoor, practicing domestic virtues and possessing the greatness of providing hospitality. The phrase “Aram porindhu” implies that Pugazhanar practiced the virtues appropriate for domestic life. These virtues are what we have seen as the eleven points mentioned by Thiruvalluvar in the chapter on domestic life in the Thirukkural. These are the eleven matters we saw that Thiruvalluvar mentioned in the chapter on domestic life in the Thirukkural. Sekkizhar Peruman specifically sings that the great elder Pugazhanar lived by continuously following these matters, that is, the virtues prescribed for householders in dharma texts like the Thirukkural, without any deviation. He also states that Pugazhanar possessed the greatness of providing hospitality and the distinction of protecting his relatives (okkal).

Welcoming and providing hospitality to guests is one of the most important duties of householders. Okkal means relatives.

Therefore, it means that a householder should protect relatives who share the same lineage, tradition, and character as themselves. What does ‘relatives’ mean? It refers to those kinsfolk who naturally gather around us. The Thirukkural states, ‘Sutraththaal sutrappada ozhugal’ (Live so as to be surrounded by relatives). Avvaiyar’s sacred saying is, ‘Sutraththirku azhagu soozha viruththal’ (The beauty of kinship is to be surrounded).

Therefore, the elders prescribe that relatives should surround us. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that Pugazhanar performed these two important duties: providing hospitality and nurturing relatives. In describing these two virtues, hospitality and nurturing relatives, Sekkizhar Peruman first mentions hospitality and then the quality of nurturing relatives. This is because hospitality is defined as giving to newcomers who have no prior connection. Relatives, on the other hand, are those with whom we have a connection.

Therefore, the duties owed to connected relatives are very significant. Nevertheless, providing hospitality to guests who arrive suddenly without any prior connection, without saying “I will come now” or “I will come at this time,” and who are completely unknown to us, is considered a most important duty. For this reason, Sekkizhar Peruman places hospitality, which is a dharma performed without prior connection, first, and nurturing relatives, which is a duty performed for those with whom we have a connection, second. In Sanskrit too, the word ‘athithi’ is used for guests. ‘Athithi’ means those who come without a ‘thithi’ (date), that is, those who arrive suddenly without prior announcement of their arrival date or time. Providing hospitality to such sudden, unknown guests, who have no prior connection to us, has been considered one of the highest duties for householders in our country and has been practiced. This is a matter of great pride for us.

The great elder Pugazhanar lived without failing in honoring such guests, nurturing relatives, and performing all the duties prescribed for householders. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, our Lord, was born as the sacred son to such a Pugazhanar.

We shall continue our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 274. Thirunindra Sarukkam. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Sekkizhar Swamigal sang about the Saivite elder named Pugazhanar, who lived in Thiru-Aamoor. The venerable lady Madhiniyar was blessed to be the wife of that greatly esteemed Pugazhanar.

Madhiniyar, the lady, came from a lineage and family of unparalleled excellence, befitting Pugazhanar and his noble heritage. Pugazhanar married such a lady, Madhiniyar, and lived with her. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that their marriage brought joy to everyone else. Can it be said that all marriages bring joy to others? Not necessarily. There are also marriages that bring other, less joyful outcomes.

However, the marriage of Pugazhanar and Madhiniyar was a marriage that brought joy to all living beings. Although Madhiniyar was the lady’s given name, her name also held a symbolic meaning: Madhiniyar, when separated as “Maadhu Iniyaar,” means “the sweetest among all women,” or “the most pleasant among all women.” Even if it is separated as “Maadhu ini yaavar,” it also carries the meaning, “who else is there like her, such an incomparable woman?”

Thus, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar was born to Pugazhanar and Madhiniyar Ammaiyar, like the Goddess of Wealth. Thilagavathiyar was born from the sacred womb of Madhiniyar. At the time of her birth, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar appeared like the Goddess of Wealth seated on a red lotus. Pugazhanar and Madhiniyar had their first female child. They named her Thilagavathiyar. Thilagam means a forehead mark, which enhances the beauty of the forehead.

Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar, however, is like a thilagam to her lineage and to the Saivite religion.

Therefore, her name Thilagavathiyar is a meaningful name. After Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar was born, some years later, a male child was born to Pugazhanar and Madhiniyar Ammaiyar. That male child is our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar. His birth name is Marulneekiyar.

Thus, after Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar was born, some years later, our Marulneekiyar was born. Sekkizhar Peruman sings about the place of his birth as follows: “Thilagavathiyar pirandhu.” “Sila murai aandu agandradhan pin alagil kalaithurai thazhaippa varunthavaththor neri vaazha ulagil varum irul neekki oli vilangu kadhirpol pin malarum maru marul neekkiyaar vandhu avathaaram seidhaar” – thus Sekkizhar Peruman sings in this verse about the birth of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar. This is the eighteenth sacred verse in the Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam, and the one thousand two hundred and eighty-third sacred verse in the Periya Puranam. When singing about the birth of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, Sekkizhar Peruman sings, “alagil kalaithurai thazhaippa” (the boundless arts flourished), “varum thavaththor neri vaazha” (the path of ascetics prospered), and “ulagil varum irul neekki oli vilangu kadhirpol” (like a radiant sun dispelling the darkness of the world). Sekkizhar Peruman sings that because Thirunavukkarasu Peruman was born and graced the world, “alagil kalai thurai thazhaippa,” meaning the field of arts flourished.

What does “kalai thazhaiththal” mean? It means that the world received the Thevarams, which are the sacred utterances of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, because of his birth.

Therefore, the field of arts flourished.

Furthermore, “kalai” refers to education and wisdom.

Thus, because Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar was born, education and wisdom flourished. This education and wisdom are referred to as “Apara Gnanam” and “Para Gnanam” in the Gnana Sastras.

Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar was born to make both Apara Gnanam and Para Gnanam flourish in this world. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, with the name Marulneekiyar, was born to make the world flourish.

Next, Sekkizhar Peruman sings, “Thavaththor neri vaazhthal” (the path of ascetics prospered). Because Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar was born and graced us, the world received the path of Gnana Chariyai and the state of renunciation that he exemplified. An Acharya should not only teach but also demonstrate. It is the nature of an Acharya to come and save the world by both teaching and demonstrating. Our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar is one of the four Saivite Acharyas.

Therefore, through his Thevarams, he taught the world the Shiva tapas. By standing in the state of Gnana Chariyai and the state of renunciation, he demonstrated to the world and established it in the Saivite path, thus saving it. Such a great Acharya, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, one of our Saivite Paramacharyas, came to save the world by both teaching and demonstrating.
