That is why Sekkizhar Peruman refers to him as “varum thavaththor neri vaazha.” Now, he says, “ulagil varum irul neekki oli vilangu kadhirpol pin malarum marul neekkiyaar vandhu avathaaram seidhaar.” Just as light dispels darkness in this world, Marulneekiyar, also known as Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, was born to dispel the delusion (marul) of living beings. The darkness in this world is removed by the sun, which is the sun. The sun removes the external darkness.

Generally, the sun does not rise to remove darkness, but when the sun rises, darkness is removed by its arrival.

Similarly, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, with the name Marulneekiyar, was born to remove the inner darkness, that is, the darkness within living beings. Just as the external sun makes lotuses bloom with its rays, Manikkavasagar Peruman was born as the sun of wisdom to make the lotus hearts of devotees bloom beautifully, as stated in the Thiruvathavoorar Puranam. We can compare that message here as well. When Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar was born, his sacred name was Marulneekiyar. This name means “one who removes delusion.” Marul means delusion. It refers to the erroneous knowledge that causes us to perceive what is not real as real.

It is the delusion that makes us mistake what is not the true meaning for the true meaning. This delusion is our seed, and it brings us more and more births. The word Marulneekiyar means “one who removes such delusion.” To remove this delusion, one must attain the sacred feet of the Lord. This act of removing delusion is what leads to attaining divine knowledge and salvation.

Thus, Marulneekiyar, also known as Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, was born to remove the delusion of living beings. He was born here. “Avathariththal” is a traditional idiom meaning “to descend.” What does “avathariththal” mean? It means that great beings take birth not for themselves, but for the sake of others, for the salvation of the living beings of this world. When such great beings take birth not for their own sake, but for the sake of others, with the intention that the living beings of this world should be saved, that is called “avathariththal” or “avatharam.” Therefore, out of great compassion for living beings, Our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, who was Vaakeesa Munivar in his previous birth, has now taken birth with the name Marulneekiyar in the sacred place of Thiru-Aamoor.

Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, as Vaakeesa Munivar, took the name Marulneekiyar and was born to guide living beings in the state of Gnana Chariyai, and so that his sacred words, the Thevaram Thirumurais, might be available to all of us, enabling these beings to find rest and remain in the path of Shiva. Our reflection now resumes. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 275. Thirunindrasarukkam. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, with the name Marulneekiyar, was born as the second child to Pugazhanar and Madhiniyar Ammaiyar, after Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar. Sekkizhar Peruman sings of him as “Pugazhanar Kaathalan.” This means Marulneekiyar, the beloved son of Pugazhanar.

Generally, a father is very fond of his male child, and similarly, a mother is very fond of her female child. Sekkizhar Peruman mentions him here as “Pugazhanar Kaathalanar aagiya Marulneekiyar,” implying this sentiment. Is not a father’s affection for his son very great? When Thadathagai Pirattiyar incarnated in Madurai, Malayathvaja Pandiyan was slightly worried that he had a daughter, as recounted in the Thiruvilaiyadal Puranam.

Thus, Marulneekiyar, who was greatly beloved by Pugazhanar, was born. After Marulneekiyar’s birth, Pugazhanar performed all the auspicious rites, or samskaras, due to him. Generally, in our tradition, samskaras begin even when a child is conceived. During the ten months of pregnancy, there are also samskaras in our tradition.

But here, Sekkizhar Peruman states that Marulneeki Pugazhanar performs the samskaras and auspicious rites for Marulneekiyar with great enthusiasm after his birth. This is because the samskaras performed during the ten months, that is, while the child is in the mother’s womb, are the first samskaras performed for a child.

Therefore, these samskaras were performed for Thilagavathi Ammaiyar. Our Marulneekiyar is the second child of Pugazhanar and Madhiniyar.

So, after his birth, Pugazhanar and Madhiniyar perform the samskaras due to a newborn child for Marulneekiyar. These are all duties and samskaras to be performed according to their family customs.

Therefore, here Pugazhanar, according to his family custom, performed the samskaras due for the first child, that is, the samskaras to be performed when Thilagavathi Ammaiyar was in Madhiniyar’s womb, for Thilagavathiyar.

Then, after the birth of the second child, Thirunavukkarasar Peruman, Pugazhanar and Madhiniyar performed the samskaras due to him, in accordance with his Vellalar lineage and family. The auspicious ceremonies performed after Marulneekiyar’s birth include the ceremonies performed for ten days after the child’s birth, the auspicious event of writing down the date, the naming ceremony called Namakaranam, and the rice-feeding ceremony called Annaprasanam. All these are prescribed for male children.

Thus, Pugazhanar and Madhiniyar performed all these auspicious ceremonies prescribed for male children for Marulneekiyar. Earlier, Sekkizhar Peruman sang about the sacred incarnation of Thilagavathi Ammaiyar, but he did not mention these samskaras after Thilagavathi Ammaiyar’s birth, nor did he state that her parents performed these samskaras. This is because, for female children, such samskaras were customarily performed as a courtesy, and only marriage is prescribed for women; other samskaras are not. For this reason, Sekkizhar Peruman has structured it this way.

Therefore, here Pugazhanar and Madhiniyar perform all these auspicious ceremonies for Marulneekiyar. While performing all these rituals, they perform the rituals with great excellence, according to the prescribed rules. They perform all these rituals with great enthusiasm and joy. As they conducted all these auspicious events, their relatives gathered, rejoiced, and were delighted.

Afterwards, they perform a samskara called Chaulam, which is the removal of hair, for him who was named Marulneekiyar. Many wise people rejoice at this. Even though Thirunavukkarasu Peruman only needed the Gnana samskara, and did not need such rituals like other worldly people, his parents, according to the custom of the Thaptham clan, perform these rituals without fail. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to this as ‘mayir neekkum mana vinai’ (the mental act of removing hair), which is known as Chaula Kalyanam. The removal of the hair present at birth at a specific age and the tying of the kudimi (tuft) according to family tradition is one of the important prescribed samskaras and rituals. Among the sixteen Shaiva samskaras, this ritual called Chaula Kalyanam is an important one.

We saw that there are sixteen Shaiva rituals; these sixteen rituals each represent a spiritual meaning. Among them, this Chaula Kalyanam is one ritual. The spiritual meaning of this Chaula Kalyanam is the Shiva It signifies the eminence of Shiva’s grace. The Agamas refer to this as Achinthiya Visvasathakkiyam. The Agamic saying is ‘Shivaprasadothkarshanthu yeththa choodakaram bhaveth’. This Chaula Kalyanam aids in the child’s good physical development.

Its spiritual meaning signifies the eminence of Shiva’s grace. Even today, this Chaula Kalyanam is performed at divine shrines, especially at the shrine of the family deity, under names such as ‘mudiyirakkuthal’ (hair-cutting) and ‘mudi vaanguthal’ (hair-receiving), as a fulfillment of vows. It continues to be a custom even today. The phrase ‘sirandha sigai varuvi thar’ also appears in the Thiruvathavoorar Puranam.

Therefore, this is not merely a meaningless ritual; it is a ritual that embodies spiritual meaning, to the delight of the wise.

Now, Marulneekiyar’s mind, which was like a bud with curled and closed petals, expanded and blossomed like the unfolding petals of a flower.

Therefore, deeming this the appropriate time and age to learn arts, his father, Pugazhanar, also had the Aksharābhyāsam, the ritual for beginning the arts, performed for Marulneekiyar.

Similarly, we have previously In the Puranam of Chandeswara Nayanar, which we saw earlier, it is stated, ‘Like the fragrance of a blossoming flower, the mind blossomed with the blossoming of the intellect.’ There, we explained in detail how Visarasarumanar’s mind blossomed due to the continuation of his previous birth, and how the Shiva-mind blossomed there. All these can be recalled and applied here. In the Kannappa Nayanar Puranam, according to their tribal custom, his parents initiated Kannappa Nayanar into the art of archery.

Similarly, in the Chandeswara Nayanar Puranam, we saw in detail how the Aksharābhyāsam ritual was performed for Visarasarumanar at the appropriate age, and how he was initiated into the sacred thread ceremony and the Brahmopadesam.

Similarly, here, Pugazhanar initiated Marulneekiyar into the learning of arts. Pugazhanar initiated Marulneekiyar into the learning of arts. The Thirukkural states, ‘The best good a father can do for his son is to make him excel in the assembly of the learned.’ What is the good a father does for his son? The greatest good a father does for his son is to make him possess knowledge that surpasses all the learned in an assembly of scholars. This is the paramount duty of a father. The greatest good a father does for his child is the greatest good.

This is the meaning of this Kural. Accordingly, Pugazhanar performs Aksharābhyāsam for Marulneekiyar. Our Thirunavukkarasar’s consciousness, which arose from the continuation of his previous birth’s knowledge, had been within his mind until now. It now began to blossom for Marulneekiyar. Sekkizhar Peruman describes this: ‘The mind blossomed, and in the rising consciousness, the skills of the rich arts were learned in the former manner.’ Sekkizhar Peruman mentions two of the sixteen Shaiva rituals here. One is the Chaula Kalyanam, the mental act of removing hair, which brings well-being to the body.

The second is the ritual of teaching the arts, called Aksharābhyāsam. This ritual, which imparts knowledge, brings well-being to the soul.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman implicitly indicates here one ritual for the well-being of the body and another for the well-being of the soul.

Therefore, all other rituals are implicitly included here. Marulneekiyar, having undergone Aksharābhyāsam, excels greatly in the arts. Generally, a father rejoices greatly and delights when his son excels greatly in art and knowledge. This is the nature of the world.

Here, our Marulneekiyar’s arts, which had resided in his mind due to his previous training, are now maturing.

Now, this The art and knowledge that were subtly within him until now are now outwardly manifested in a concrete form for Marulneekiyar. The knowledge that was within him until now becomes known to others. The age at which this occurs is approximately five years, according to the information we have here. Around the age of five, Marulneekiyar’s father performs the Aksharābhyāsam for him. From then until the age of ten, our Marulneekiyar has been learning and growing in the arts, starting with the Aksharābhyāsam. This is the indication.

Thus, Marulneekiyar, who began to learn the arts, grows and develops in them like the flawless crescent moon. Sekkizhar Peruman sings here that he grows like the flawless crescent moon. By ‘maru ozhitha ilampirai’ (flawless crescent moon), an unblemished moon is implied, and a growing moon is also implied.

Similarly, in the Thirugnanasambandha Peruman Puranam, Sekkizhar Peruman sings, ‘Vaanathin misaiyandri mannil valar madhikkozhunthai’ (a growing moon-bud not in the sky but on earth).

Thus, seeing Marulneekiyar’s growth, his proficiency in the arts, and his intellectual brilliance, his father Pugazhanar rejoices, and his mother Madhiniyar’s heart is gladdened.

At this time, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar reaches the age of twelve.

Therefore, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar’s parents wish to arrange her marriage. Her parents wish to arrange her marriage. Generally, according to our Indian tradition, the age of marriage for a girl is twelve, and for a boy, it is sixteen. This is the custom we have followed for a long time.

Therefore, as Thilagavathi Ammaiyar reached the age of twelve, her parents, Pugazhanar and Madhiniyar, decided to arrange her marriage. Let us go on reflecting. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 276, Thirunindracharukkam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thilagavathi Ammaiyar reaches the age of twelve. According to our traditional custom, the marriageable age for a man is sixteen, and for a woman, it is twelve. In the commentary on the first sutra of Iraiyanar Agapporul, it states, ‘He, being sixteen years of age, and she, being twelve years of age, possessing equal qualities, equal beauty, equal love, equal wealth, and equal education.’ This serves as proof.

Therefore, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar’s parents, Pugazhanar and Madhini Ammaiyar, decide to arrange her marriage. At this same time, Kalippa There is a devotee of Shiva named Kalippagaiyar. The meaning of the name Kalippagaiyar is ‘enemy of Kali,’ in the sense of being an enemy to Kali’s faults. Kalippagaiyar is an enemy to all the faults of Kali. The name Kalippagaiyar conveys the meaning of one who protects from the approach of any of Kali’s faults. This name is both a conventional and a descriptive appellation for him.

He belongs to the Vellalar lineage and excels greatly in his clan. He is a foremost Vellalar, meaning he belongs to the primary division among the many classifications of Vellalars, and thus shines as a foremost Vellalar. He is of a suitable clan, matching Pugazhanar, and particularly born into a matching family, excelling in matching qualities. He desires to be a true servant of Lord Shiva, the Lord with the red matted locks. Although he possesses many other good qualities, his desire for servitude to Lord Shiva is the foremost quality that stands above all others. Kalippagaiyar is desirous of servitude to Lord Shiva.

Although the age of maturity for a man is sixteen, at that age, to know Lord Shiva and the nature of servitude to Lord Shiva, and to desire to serve Lord Shiva, is generally a very rare quality to find at this age. This is because, If a person, at the age of sixteen, develops a desire for servitude to Lord Shiva, without getting entangled in the various situations and mental distractions characteristic of that age, it will gradually lead him into the path of becoming a devotee of Lord Shiva.

Therefore, our Kalippagaiyar, even at the age of sixteen, was desirous of embracing servitude to Lord Shiva. Sekkizhar Peruman mentions this as the foremost of his qualities. Not only that, but he also excels in worldly affairs. Generally, serving a king is considered a high position in the world. In that regard, he holds the profession of lovingly undertaking the tasks assigned by the king. Kalippagaiyar.

The king’s primary duty is to protect the world from harm. By protecting the world from harm, he earns the name ‘Kavalan’ (protector).

Thus, Kalippagaiyar, having received the command of the king who protects the world, and out of compassion for the living beings of this world, assists the king and carries out the king’s duty of protection. He serves as the king’s helper. Kalippagaiyar performs this military service, which is a royal duty, not for personal gain, but out of compassion for living beings. Serving in the military for the king is one of the traditional occupations of the Vellalars. For the king, Serving in the military and carrying out the king’s commands is a traditional occupation of the Vellalars. Kalippagaiyar is very brave and like a mighty male lion in warfare.

Here, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to warfare as ‘aan thagaimai thozhil’ (manly profession). This generally refers to bravery. ‘Aan thagaimai thozhil’ is a phrase Sekkizhar Peruman uses to signify bravery and as a symbol of valor. Names like ‘Muthalana’ indicate that women also engaged in warfare.

Therefore, warfare is a profession suitable for both genders. Nevertheless, warfare Sekkizhar Peruman here refers to warfare and valor as ‘aan thagaimai’ (manliness). Indeed, the qualities that symbolize womanhood are gentleness, compassion, and mercy. These are naturally associated with womanhood.

However, despite this inherent nature, there has also been a tradition of women engaging in warfare. But for men, valor is inherent.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman here refers to warfare as ‘aan thagaimai’. In such warfare, Kalippagaiyar shines like a mighty lion. This conveys his strength and valor to us.

Furthermore, he is now sixteen years old, at the age suitable for marriage. In ancient times, among the qualities considered most desirable for a bridegroom were strength and valor. It was customary in those days to test a prospective groom’s strength and valor by having him defeat an elephant or subdue a bull (eru thazhuvuthal), and then give one’s daughter in marriage to him. Kalippagaiyar possessed such valor and strength.

Moreover, what other qualifications or qualities are desired in a bridegroom? Physical radiance and an attractive appearance that pleases onlookers—these too were abundant in Kalippagaiyar. Choosing such a bridegroom was customary among the Vellalar It has been customary in the Vellalar clan. These are all examples of the qualifications and qualities that Vellalars of that era sought in a groom before giving their daughter in marriage. Sekkizhar Peruman describes these matters to us by portraying the qualities of Kalippagaiyar. It is stated here that the first and foremost desire of a father with a daughter is the groom’s character and lineage.

Thus, to arrange the marriage of Thilagavathiyar to Kalippagaiyar, they send elders from the Vellalar clan, who are distinguished by their age, wisdom, worldly knowledge, experience, and profound understanding.

Thus, it was our tradition to send elders, mature in age, wisdom, experience, and grace, to negotiate marriages.

In this manner, elders on behalf of Kalippakaiyar approached Pugazhanar to request the hand of his daughter, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar, in marriage to Kalippakaiyar. Having learned of Kalippakaiyar’s lineage and character, and moreover, his fervent devotion to Lord Shiva, which was the foremost qualification among all others, and also knowing that Kalippakaiyar served as the commander-in-chief to the king, and being apprised of his valor, beauty, and other virtues, they recognized Kalippakaiyar as a suitable groom for Thilagavathiyar.

Therefore, Pugazhanar expressed his consent to give his daughter, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar, in marriage to Kalippakaiyar. He gives his consent.

We shall proceed with our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 277. Thirunindra-ch-charukkam. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Pugazhanar and Maathiniyar give their consent to marry Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar, the elder sister of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, to a man named Kalippakaiyar.

The elders convey this news of their consent to Kalippakaiyar.

Thus, the marriage is decided by both parties. Before the wedding ceremonies could be completed, Kalippakaiyar received another assignment. We have already noted that Kalippakaiyar was the commander of the king’s army.

At this time, northern kings ...came to attack.

Therefore, the king decided to send Kalippakaiyar to that war, summoned him, and dispatched him to battle. All this happened when the marriage between Kalippakaiyar and Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar had been fixed, consent given by both sides, and the wedding arranged. In this situation, the war took place.

Thus, the marriage was completed by consent; it had happened. Only the ritual of marriage remained, as Sekkizhar composes his verses here, indicating this point. The implication is that as soon as a man and a woman agree and consent that she is his wife ...and express their approval, the act is completed then and there. At that very moment, they become husband and wife. The subsequent ceremony, the wedding ritual, is merely performed as a formality. This is its meaning.

Therefore, when a woman, thus destined for marriage, gives her consent and mentally accepts a man, he becomes her husband at that very moment, and she becomes his wife to that man. This is a virtue of the highest order in conduct. It is at this time that kings from the northern regions launch an attack towards this central region (Nadu Nadu). This Nadu Nadu, or central region, is a part of Tamil Nadu that includes many territories, including Thirumunaippadi Nadu. The Pallava kings ruled this part of Tamil Nadu at that time. In history, we can see that there were always wars between the Pallava kings and the kings of the northern lands.

In the Siruthondar Puranam, the history of Paranjothi, known as Siruthondar, going to Vadapi in the northern country and waging war is mentioned. In the Moorthi Nayanar Puranam, the news of the Vadugu Karnataka king waging war on the Pandya country is also mentioned. We can recall all of that here. The period in which the history of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, which we are observing, took place, was when Mahendravarman, also known as Gunabaran, ruled there. Kalippakaiyar was the commander of Mahendravarman’s army.

At that time, northern invaders launched an attack. The Pallava king commanded Kalippakaiyar to fight them. Kalippakaiyar marched with his army and engaged in battle. Kalippakaiyar, taking his fighting forces with him, spent some days there, confronting the enraged enemies and engaging in a fierce battle with them. In Akapporul (Tamil love poetry), a section within Karpiyal (chaste love) is the act of separation (pirivu). This is generally of two types: separation for wealth (porul vazhi pirivu) and separation for war (por vazhi pirivu).

That is, a hero separates from his heroine, either to earn wealth or to wage war.

In this context, within the Akapporul tradition of Tamil literature, the separation for the sake of war, which occurs in Karpiyal, is happening here. Kalippakaiyar departs, separating from Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar, to wage a fierce war there. A fierce battle takes place there. Sekkizhar metaphorically describes the war as an ocean. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that Kalippakaiyar swims across that ocean of war, which is difficult to cross, with his own hands. He attempts to cross the war, but Sekkizhar Peruman composes this metaphor in such a way as to convey the meaning that he will not return.

Kalippakaiyar goes and wages that war with great courage and strength. He wages the war, thinking it would conclude in a few days.

However, contrary to his expectation, the war prolonged for many days. While Kalippakaiyar was engaged in that protracted war, here, Pugazhanar, the father of Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, departed from this world and attained the celestial realm. It is the consequence of a soul’s karma that brings about the impermanent cycle of death and birth. This is a great tradition that has been happening since ancient times. Due to that karma, Pugazhanar was afflicted with illness and suffered. Even before this, according to the state of his body, Pugazhanar might have suffered from many ailments.

However, the illness that came upon him now was a terrible, incurable disease that caused him to depart from this world. Such was the persistence of that disease. Karmic actions must be experienced to be exhausted. If they are not experienced and exhausted, liberation will be hindered. That is, if we do not experience and exhaust our karmic actions, it will be an obstacle to our moksha, our liberation.

Therefore, when we experience suffering such as illness, and each time we experience illness and suffering, we should think that our karmic experience is being exhausted.

Moreover, karma ...our karmic experience is thus being exhausted, and as it is being exhausted, we are gradually progressing towards liberation. We must realize this.

Thus, Pugazhanar, who suffered from a terrible, incurable disease, endured his evil karmic actions, exhausted them through experience, and then approached Shivagati (the path to Shiva). This is the great news we receive here.

Therefore, Pugazhanar, the father of Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, departs from this earthly world and goes to the celestial world. “He who lives a virtuous life in this world will be placed among the gods in heaven” is a saying from the Thirukkural. “He who cherishes guests and awaits their arrival is a good guest to the heavenly beings” is also from the Thirukkural.

Here, in this world, Pugazhanar lived a life of excellent domestic virtue. He lived by hosting guests. He cared for all his relatives and lived a life of great distinction, giving many charities and living a good life.

Therefore, he lived a virtuous life in this world, and thus he attained the celestial world. He was placed among the gods in heaven, according to the Thirukkural.

Thus, when Pugazhanar departed his life, his holy wife, Maathiniyar, who was always inseparable from Pugazhanar, did not deviate from her path of chastity and immediately followed her husband, Pugazhanar, to the other world. His holy wife, Maathiniyar, who was always inseparable from Pugazhanar, did not deviate from her path of chastity and immediately followed her husband, Pugazhanar, to the other world. She considered her relatives and children as mere dust, leaving them all behind, and accompanied her holy husband to the celestial world. Maathiniyar Ammaiyar considered her relatives and her own children as dust, and considering her husband, whom she had married, as her sole support, she lived a life of supreme chastity. Upon her husband’s departure to the celestial world, she too went to the celestial world. It is customary to refer to relatives as a stage for a play or a gathering.

Moreover, relatives are those who cause us to form attachments.

Therefore, she renounced her relatives. Not only that, but the greatest duty of a married life, a householder’s life She considered her relatives and her own children as dust, and considering her husband, whom she had married, as her sole support, she lived a life of supreme chastity. Upon her husband’s departure to the celestial world, she too went to the celestial world. It is customary to refer to relatives as a stage for a play or a gathering.

Moreover, relatives are those who cause us to form attachments.

Therefore, she renounced her relatives. Not only that, but the greatest duty of a married life, a householder’s life ...the greatest duty is to nurture one’s children.

But she, considering even her own children as mere dust, went to the celestial world with her husband. Generally, there are some who consider their children as their very life and even sacrifice their lives for them. There are mothers who live by holding onto their lives for the sake of their children.

But here, the chastity that Maathiniyar possessed was the supreme virtue of not living separated from her husband.

Therefore, Maathiniyar believed that the virtue of not living separated from her husband was superior to her love for her children and her relatives. For such a path of chastity, for the path of chastity of not living separated from her husband, She considered it appropriate to renounce her attachment to her children and her attachment to her relatives, and thus, she renounced her attachment to her own children and her attachment to her relatives and went to the celestial world with her husband. Before such a high path of chastity, all other attachments seemed like mere dust to her.

Therefore, according to her path of chastity, she went to the celestial world with her husband. “We saw one soul in two bodies” and “one soul taking two forms” are the sacred words of Thirukkovaiyar. According to those words, a husband and wife may be two physically, but in terms of soul, they are one.

Furthermore, a hero says to a heroine, A hero says to a heroine, “I will not leave you in this birth.” To which the heroine asks, “Then will you leave me in future births?” This is how the ideal nature of a husband and wife should be. When a husband goes to the celestial world, it is our Tamil tradition to celebrate and worship those women who, unable to bear separation, give up their lives and also go to the celestial world, calling them Maasathi (chaste woman) and divine women. There is a tradition in our Tamil Nadu of erecting stones and worshipping such women who have given up their lives. Such stones are also called Maasathi stones. We can see this in various educational institutions. We can even see it in various educational institutions.

Such love that leads to the giving up of life is praised as supreme love. Generally, there are three types of chastity: supreme chastity (thalai-k-karpu), middle chastity (idai-k-karpu), and lower chastity (kadai-k-karpu). What is supreme chastity? It is when, upon hearing the news that her husband has gone to the celestial world, she too goes to the celestial world. Our Maathiniyar Ammaiyar possessed such supreme chastity. Women with such supreme chastity live eternally in the celestial world, in heaven.

This act of going to the celestial world with one’s husband was formerly known as ‘udankatta yeruthal’ (sati) and was considered a supreme path of chastity. In the northern regions, this is called ‘sahagamanam’. This is the noble quality and character of a woman who, unable to bear the sorrow of separation from her husband, gives up her life and accompanies him. It is based on this that Valluvar Peruman, in the Thirukkural, describes the love and conduct between a hero and heroine in Tamil Nadu as “like body and soul.” The Kandapuranam tells the story of Padmakoamalai, the wife of Surapadman, giving up her life upon hearing of his death. This is how the husband-wife relationship has been practiced in our country.

However, if we compare the various chaotic situations found in the marital relationships of this era with those of our ancestors, If we compare the various chaotic situations found in the marital relationships of this era with those of our ancestors, the high qualities, culture, character, chastity, and discipline of our predecessors become very clear to us. We shall continue our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 278. Thirunindra-ch-charukkam. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s parents, Pugazhanar and Maathiniyar Ammaiyar, depart to the celestial world.

After the death of their father and mother, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar and Thirunavukkarasar are greatly saddened by grief. In this verse, when referring to parents as ‘father and mother,’ Sekkizhar Peruman has placed the father first and the mother second. Generally, it is customary to place the mother first, saying ‘annaiyum pithavum’ (mother and father).

However, Here, Sekkizhar Peruman places the father first and then the mother, saying ‘thandai thaai’ (father mother). The reason for this is that he has arranged them according to the chronological order of their passing. The father, Pugazhanar, goes to the celestial world first, and then the mother also goes to the celestial world.

Therefore, he has arranged and stated it in that sequential order. There is another inner meaning to this. Generally, a child resides in the father’s womb for two months and then joins the mother’s womb. This is a tradition and science prevalent in our Bharat Desam. Regarding this method, Sivakavimani Aiya explains that Sekkizhar Peruman arranges it as father first, then mother. Even in the phrase ‘thandai thaai pen’ (father, mother, woman), we see the same order.

Thus, having lost their father and mother at a young age, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar and Marulneekiyar, who is Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, are greatly distressed. Grief overwhelms their minds. They are deeply saddened because they lost both their father and mother, who were their foremost deities, simultaneously.

Similarly, their relatives are also greatly distressed. Pugazhanar had well protected and cared for all these relatives.

But those relatives, not considering themselves, They grieved greatly out of gratitude, remembering all the favors that Pugazhanar and Maathiniyar Ammaiyar had done for them. These relatives tried to console Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. The sorrow that befell them was unbearable, yet it gradually lessened.

So, they somehow consoled themselves and performed the funeral rites, water offerings, and other rituals for their father and mother who had gone to the celestial world. These duties are to be performed on the day of death and for a prescribed number of days thereafter. All these are duties that must be performed, hence they are called ‘kadan’ (debt/duty). Hiranyan, son of Surapadman, took the form of a fish and hid in the ocean, solely to perform the funeral rites for his father. The Kanda Puranam states that after Surapadman was killed, his son Hiranyan, fearing that if all of Surapadman’s children were killed there would be no one to perform the final rites for his father, took the form of a fish and hid in the ocean for the sole purpose of performing this ‘kadan’ for his father. Generally, those who hold other philosophies, such as the Lokayata, etc.

They would say that after death, there is no other birth or death for the soul. In that vein, even today, some people, holding onto that philosophy, live without performing these ancestral rites and without belief in them.

However, in our tradition, in our Sanatana Dharma, ancestral rites are a very important prescribed duty.

Therefore, when studying and listening to such scriptural texts, one should understand and perform these duties according to their respective family customs.

Thus, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar and Marulneekiyar, who is Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, perform the funeral rites, water offerings, and other rituals for their parents. They are gradually comforting their minds.

At the same time, we read that Kalippakaiyar, to whom Thilagavathi Ammaiyar’s hand was promised, went to war. Kalippakaiyar went to war against the enemies of his king. He sacrificed his life on the battlefield and attained a body of fame. Out of compassion for the lives protected by his king, he gave his own life on the battlefield to protect them. Through this, he gained fame. To gain fame, one must give life, limbs, or wealth, or one of these, or many of these.

It is customary to attain fame. By giving life-giving organs and precious things, he would rise in fame.

But here, Kalippakaiyar gave his very life. He attained fame by giving his life out of compassion to protect the people protected by his king. In a barter system, the item one receives is more valuable than the item one gives. This is the definition of trade.

Here, Kalippakaiyar gave his life and bought fame. The idea here is that he considered fame greater than life. Leaving behind the physical body, he attained a body of fame. Kalippakaiyar attained it.

Now, for Thilagavathi Ammaiyar and Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, after the unbearable sorrow of losing both their parents simultaneously, this other great sorrow occurred even before the first sorrow had faded. They experienced immense grief when they lost their father and mother. Before they could recover even slightly from that, they were caught in this utterly inconsolable sorrow. “It falls on the trodden foot” is a proverb. The message we receive from this proverb is that sorrows naturally come one after another to a person.

Thus, the news of Kalippakaiyar attaining Veerasvargam is conveyed to Thilagavathi Ammaiyar. There is a heaven called Veerasvargam for those who attain it, and they will reach that heroic heaven. They inform Thilagavathi Ammaiyar that Kalippakaiyar has gone to such a Veerasvargam. Upon hearing this, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar, who is like Thiru-Magal seated on a lotus, what did she say? “My father and my mother, I have become theirs.

“Therefore, I will join his life.” Thilagavathi Ammaiyar says this with great determination and courage. Generally, before marriage, women follow the words of their parents, and after marriage, they follow the words of their husband. If they have to live after their husband, they follow the words of their son. This has been the practice followed by our ancestors in our Bharat Desam. After marriage, if one has to live, they would live according to the words of their son. This was the custom followed and upheld by our ancestors in our Bharat Desam.

“What Thilagavathi Ammaiyar embraced here is also the custom established by our ancestors. Accordingly, she knew her duty to stand by her parents’ consent. She stood firm in that duty. They had not yet performed the marriage, but they had expressed their consent and decided to arrange the marriage. Even at that stage, she considered this to be her parents’ consent, her parents’ decision.

“Therefore, the firmness, the mental discipline, the mental order to stand firmly by their decision, was abundant in Thilagavathi Ammaiyar.

“Therefore, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar did not arrange her own intellect, desires, and actions apart from the path set by her parents and apart from their decision. She arranged her intellect, desires, and actions according to the path set by her parents. The parents had expressed their consent to marry Thilagavathi Ammaiyar to Kalippakaiyar.

“Accordingly, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar strongly held the belief that she belonged to Kalippakaiyar. The parents Thilagavathi Ammaiyar firmly decided that the marriage had taken place and was concluded by the mere consent of her parents to arrange her marriage to Kalippakaiyar. The marriage that was to take place thereafter would only be the external ceremonies of the already decided and consented-to marriage, which had already concluded. This was Thilagavathi Ammaiyar’s principle. In reality, the mental consent of the parents was the marriage; the marriage was concluded on that very day. Marriage rituals, according to the changing times, have varied over time as told by our sages in Smriti texts, which is our tradition.

“This is the tradition. The importance of the rituals mentioned in these Smritis is limited to this extent.

“However, there are marriage rituals and customs prescribed in the Sivagamas, and these cannot be altered by anyone, which we must understand here.

“Therefore, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar’s principle was that the marriage took place on the very day the parents gave their consent.

“Furthermore, previously, when Pugazhanar passed away, Mathiniyar also accompanied him. Thilagavathi Ammaiyar took this as an example for herself. The determination to follow the path shown by her mother also took hold in Thilagavathi Ammaiyar.

“Thus, when she resolved to go with Kalippakaiyar herself, Marulneekiyar, also known as Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, fell at the feet of Thilagavathi Ammaiyar. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, who thus fell, lamented greatly, saying, “After my mother and father left, I have been seeing and worshipping you. I lived by worshipping you. If you now abandon me and leave, I too will give up my life.” Thus, Marulneekiyar, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, weeps, falling at the feet of Thilagavathi Ammaiyar. We find here the reference that Marulneekiyar, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, considered his elder sister, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar, as a mother.

“Therefore, after the mother left, he continued to worship his elder sister in that position. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, when his elder sister resolved to give up her life, lamented that he too would give up his life. The young Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, Marulneekiyar, thus laments, falling at the feet of Thilagavathi Ammaiyar.

“After their father and mother passed away, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar, like a mother, protected Marulneekiyar so that he would not feel that sorrow. This is the implication.

“Therefore, Marulneekiyar, as a younger brother, tells his elder sister, “If you give up your life, I will give up mine.” For this reason, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar explains the situation where she resolved to give up her life. Thilagavathi Ammaiyar abandons her decision to give up her life and decides that she must live for her younger brother. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, when his elder sister resolved to give up her life, lamented that he too would give up his life. The young Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, Marulneekiyar, thus laments, falling at the feet of Thilagavathi Ammaiyar.

“After their father and mother passed away, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar, like a mother, protected Marulneekiyar so that he would not feel that sorrow. This is the implication.

“Therefore, Marulneekiyar, as a younger brother, tells his elder sister, “If you give up your life, I will give up mine.” For this reason, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar explains the situation where she resolved to give up her life. Thilagavathi Ammaiyar abandons her decision to give up her life and decides that she must live for her younger brother. She decides to live here, not going to the celestial world, out of great compassion for her younger brother.

“Therefore, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar abandons her decision to give up her life. But in what state does Thilagavathi Ammaiyar live after this?

“Our reflection now resumes.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Two Hundred Seventy-Nine. Thiru-Nindra-Charukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. The affection of Marulneekiyar prevented Thilagavathi Ammaiyar, who had intended to go to the celestial world with Kalippakaiyar, to whom she was betrothed. Out of compassion for her younger brother, Marulneekiyar, who is Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, and for him to live and exist, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar set aside the state of going to the world of the gods and decided to sustain her life and live here. It was solely out of compassion for her younger brother that she decided to continue living.

She did not think of sustaining her life for herself, but she resolved to sustain her life for her younger brother. She did not think of living for herself, but she resolved to live for her younger brother. Out of a compassionate heart that her younger brother, Marulneekiyar, should live on, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar made this decision. Just as her father, Pugazhanar, lived a very distinguished life, so too should his son and her younger brother, Marulneekiyar, live a distinguished life—this was the compassion held by Thilagavathi Ammaiyar. It was Thilagavathi Ammaiyar’s wish that Pugazhanar’s family should not cease or be cut off, but should continue for a very long time in the Saivite tradition. This wish, this compassion held by Thilagavathi Ammaiyar, yielded many times greater benefit to the world and to the Saiva religion than she had imagined.

It gave to the Saiva tradition. The Saiva tradition continues even today, and that too is a result of the compassion held by Thilagavathi Ammaiyar.

Thus, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar, having made this decision, lived a life of austerity, adopting the ascetic state, without wearing ornaments of gold and gems. In the worldly state, this condition is referred to as ‘vaithaviyam’ and ‘amangalithuvam’ (widowhood), and such a custom exists. It is the way of life in our country for a wife who has lost her beloved to undertake an ascetic life. Generally, when a husband went to the celestial world, it was the custom for women to immediately follow him. We learned this even from the actions of Mathini Ammaiyar.

Therefore, it was the predominant custom in those days for chaste women to accompany their husbands. If, however, a wife had to live in this world after her husband went to the celestial world, then it also happened that she would live an ascetic life. This occurred as a minority practice in those days. Accompanying the husband was the predominant custom.

Thus, both these types of situations have existed in our tradition. We can find this even in Tholkappiyam and ancient Tamil literature like Purappattu. When classified as a ‘thinai’ (literary genre), this would be included and sung under the ‘Kanchi Thinai’.

Therefore, going to the celestial world with one’s husband Going to the celestial world with one’s husband was the predominant custom, and if, by chance, one had to remain in this world, then undertaking an ascetic life was the minority custom in those days.

Now, the act of going with one’s husband has been classified as suicide, and the government has prevented these actions through laws.

Therefore, in these days, they have ceased to exist. That is, the customs of going to the celestial world with one’s husband have all ceased. Not only that, but the customs where women who had to live here after their husbands went to the celestial world lived an ascetic life have also been abolished now in the name of women’s rights reform.

Therefore, going to the celestial world with one’s husband immediately, or if one had to remain here, undertaking an ascetic life—these customs have now become ancient tales, mere stories for us. These customs have now become ancient tales, mere stories for us.

Now, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar, out of compassion for her younger brother, decided to sustain her life and undertake an ascetic life, and she continues to do so. She lived an ascetic life not only out of compassion for her younger brother but also out of Thilagavathi Ammaiyar’s compassionate and firm conviction that all beings should be happy. That very act, in a way that brought happiness to all beings, transformed Thilagavathi Ammaiyar’s younger brother, Marulneekiyar, into a great compassionate Paramacharya and bestowed him upon this world.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman was given to this world. It was the great compassion held by Thilagavathi Ammaiyar that bestowed Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman upon this world as a Saiva Paramacharya. It was the great grace held by Thilagavathi Ammaiyar. Grace (Arul) comes in the sense of compassion that flows towards beings without attachment.

Therefore, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar undertook an ascetic life not only out of compassion for her related younger brother but also out of compassion for the beings of this world, without attachment. As a result, we received Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman.

Here, the austerity undertaken by Thilagavathi Ammaiyar is called ‘Manaithavam’ (household austerity). What is Manaithavam? ‘Manai’ means home.

Therefore, performing vows, virtues, and pujas without leaving the home is Manaithavam. All forms of austerity. Puja and meditation fall into this category. As Thilagavathi Ammaiyar lived this ascetic life out of compassion for her younger brother, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman understood the impermanence of this world.

Thus, understanding the impermanence of this world, he performed many acts of dharma. Let us go on reflecting. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Two Hundred Eighty. Thiru-Nindra-Charukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thilagavathi Ammaiyar and Marulneekiyar, who is Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, having lost both their father and mother simultaneously, are growing up. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman is gradually overcoming the sorrow in his mind. His age is steadily advancing.

At the same time, he understands the truth that worldly life is impermanent. Marulneekiyar, who is Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, as we saw earlier, when Thilagavathi Ammaiyar was twelve years old, her marriage was arranged.

At that time, Marulneekiyar was ten years old.

At that time, sorrows occurred one after another.

Therefore, at that time, ten-year-old Marulneekiyar who was ten years old, is now growing up. Many years pass. The age suitable for performing acts of dharma and for helping scholars and others by understanding their welfare arrives for our Marulneekiyar. Marulneekiyar is filled with education, wisdom, and discipline, and his age is also appropriate. In this state, he lives a life of renunciation without marrying. Moorthiyar Appar’s renunciation is a part of the Puranic history.

Accordingly, among our sixty-three Nayanmars, Moorthi Nayanar and Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman lived a life of renunciation. Marulneekkiyar, who lived in a state of renunciation, despised the worldly life of home, wealth, and family. He understood its impermanence and embraced an ascetic life. Our ancestors taught that impermanence applies to the body, youth, and wealth. While these worldly possessions may appear permanent, they are fleeting. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, formerly Marulneekkiyar, grasped this truth not through books or teachings.

He did not learn it from reading books. He understood this impermanence through the deeply ingrained feeling of experience, for his father and mother left him at a young age. The man to whom his elder sister, Thilagavathiyar, was betrothed, passed away before their marriage.

Consequently, Thilagavathiyar resolved to end her life. However, at the request of Marulneekkiyar, his sister Thilagavathiyar endured her life, embracing an ascetic state and living a life of penance. These events occurred during Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s early youth. Through these experiences, the truth of impermanence became deeply rooted in the Nayanar’s mind. These incidents served to impress upon his mind the impermanence of this world. The events that befell him were sufficient to make him realize the impermanence of the world.

Indeed, a wise person can learn many profound truths from such worldly experiences. This is true for others in the world as well. Such events can and do happen to others.

However, for most, this wisdom and understanding of impermanence are not realized. These kinds of sufferings also befall other worldly people, but they do not gain wisdom from observing them. They struggle without attaining wisdom.

But for our Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, when such continuous sorrows occurred, observing all these made the concept of impermanence deeply rooted in his mind. This is because our Arulneekkiyar, in a previous state, in a previous birth, was a sage who performed penance to attain God. That unfinished task continued with the Nayanar here, aiding him in attaining this wisdom.

Thus, Marulneekkiyar, who realized impermanence, now Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, performed many acts of charity. He used all his wealth to perform numerous charitable deeds. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman believed that giving is righteousness, as the ancient saying goes.

Accordingly, he spent all his possessions on charitable causes. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman established many charitable institutions. Although generally referred to as charitable institutions, these included अन्नசாலை (Annasaalai), places that provide food; மருத்துவசாலை (Maruthuvasaalai), hospitals; கல்வி சாலை (Kalvi Saalai), schools; and so on. Such Annasaalai, Maruthuvasaalai, Kalvi Saalai, and other charitable institutions were established by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. He spent all his wealth on these. He provided the initial capital and funding for establishing these charitable institutions.

He did this not just to help those he knew, but so that anyone who came to these charitable institutions could benefit. He is thus described as giving charity. Grace or compassion is defined as the kindness shown to those with whom one has no connection, and the love extended to them. It is said that he established Annasaalai, Maruthuvasaalai, Kalvi Saalai, and so on. He also established water pandals (shelters providing water). While other institutions are generally referred to as charitable institutions, Sekkizhar Peruman specifically mentions the water pandal.

Even though a water pandal is also a charitable institution, it is particularly effective in immediately alleviating suffering from heat, thirst, and fatigue.

Therefore, a water pandal is considered more special than other charitable institutions. Appoothi Adigal also established water pandals in the name of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman and performed acts of charity. Through this, he attained the grace of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, whom he revered as his Guru. Water, The Thiruvasagam states, “By establishing water pandals for victory, the goodness of a good water server.” According to this, Lord Shiva himself, as the divine play, established a water pandal and demonstrated this act of charity, which we can see in the Thiruvilaiyadal Puranam.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman established many charitable institutions. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to all these as “Aasil Arasaalai,” meaning faultless charitable institutions. “Aasu” means fault. Sekkizhar Peruman states that all the charitable institutions established by Peruman were faultless. The Thirukkural states, “To be free from blemish in mind is all righteousness.” Accordingly, these charitable institutions were created with a blameless mind. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman established these charitable institutions with his blameless mind.

He performs acts of righteousness. The charity performed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman now falls under the category of “Pasu Dharmam” (charity for living beings). Making one’s possessions and wealth beneficial to other living beings is called Pasu Dharmam. These Pasu Dharmams, or Pasu Punniyams (meritorious deeds for living beings), will bring fame to those who perform them in this life. In future births, they will bestow excellent merit, providing a very good life to those who performed Pasu Dharmam, and granting them a good rebirth.

However, there is a charity that transcends this Pasu Dharmam, and that is called “Pathi Dharmam.” Pathi Dharmam refers to acts of charity performed towards Lord Shiva and His devotees. The Pasu Dharmams mentioned earlier will exhaust their respective merits and benefits.

However, unlike Pasu Dharmams, Pathi Dharmam, which is Shiva Dharmam, leads us to the path of liberation. Pathi Dharmam, or Shiva Dharmam, never diminishes; it continues to grow. Nevertheless, Pasu Dharmam can serve as a cause for Pathi Dharmam.

Therefore, we must remember that the acts of charity performed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman at this stage were Pasu Dharmams.

Furthermore, Sekkizhar Peruman states that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman cultivated groves. He dug ponds. Cultivating groves and digging ponds are acts of charity that benefit not only humans but also all other living beings, such as birds and animals. These actions demonstrate Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s compassion not only towards other humans but also towards other forms of life.

Furthermore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman established these charitable institutions, and there are those who come there to receive the help they need. However, there are also people who do not come to these institutions for help, yet they still require assistance. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman identifies such individuals and goes to them to offer help. Groves and ponds also belong to this type of charity. Again, we must remember that these are all Pasu Dharmam. We previously saw that Nandanaar dug a pond in Thiru-Pungoor; that was different, that was Pathi Dharmam.

This is because Nandanaar dug the pond there with the intention of helping the devotees of Shiva who came to Thiru-Pungoor temple.

Therefore, that was Pathi Dharmam, Shiva Dharmam. The pond established by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman here belongs to the category of Pasu Dharmam.

Therefore, generally, all acts of Chariyai (service), etc., performed after being graced by divine grace, are called Pathi Dharmams. We should remember them here.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman bestows many gifts upon guests. He protects guests. He bestows wealth and other riches upon poets to enhance their prosperity. Even in giving, he acts with unwavering integrity. What does it mean to give with unwavering integrity? It means performing a gift or donation exactly as prescribed in the books of justice, without deviation.

That is called integrity in giving. The books of dharma describe the giver, the receiver, the object of the gift, and the benefit of the gift. He performs acts of charity in accordance with these principles. He does this not only with integrity but also with heartfelt joy and compassion. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman offers hospitality. Providing food and shelter to new arrivals who have no prior connection is called offering hospitality.

Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman also performs this act of hospitality. As we mentioned earlier, he bestows gifts upon poets and others. When giving these gifts, he does not consider lineage, character, goals, or principles, but performs this act of charity appropriately for everyone, wherever he finds merit. The acts of charity mentioned thus far are only some of the many performed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. He continues to perform many more acts of charity.

Let us resume our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Two Hundred Eighty-One, Thiru-Nindrachcharukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We reflected on how Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, realizing the impermanence of the world, performed various acts of charity. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing in the one thousand three hundred and second verse of the Periya Puranam, the thirty-seventh verse in the Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam: “Nillaatha ulagiyalbu kandu nilaiyaa vaazhkai allean endru araththurandhu samayangal aanavatrin nal aaru therindhu unara nambar arulaamaiyinaal kollaamai maraindhu uraiyum aman samayam kuruguvaar endru.” Sekkizhar Peruman composed this verse. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman realizes the impermanence of this world.

Therefore, he becomes a complete renunciate, declaring, “I will not struggle in this impermanent worldly life.” At this point, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman joins the Samana (Jain) religion. The Samana religion outwardly presents non-violence as a cloak, while inwardly performing many inappropriate actions.

However, the apparent principle of non-violence captivated Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, leading him to join the Samana religion. This happened because the all-powerful Lord Shiva did not bestow His grace upon Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman to discern the good path among religions. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman therefore joined the Samana religion. This is an important point in the history of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, particularly in the history of Marulneekkiyar. Sekkizhar Peruman divides the history of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman into several parts.

First, he sings about Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, stating that he was born like the sun, dispelling darkness and shining light.

Then, he mentions that he passed his childhood, stating that he “passed the stage of a young child.” Later, he states that he grew like a flawless young crescent moon.

Then, after losing his parents, he sang that he grieved and accumulated those debts. Afterwards, he sang that he fell at the feet of Thilagavathiyar, spoke, and wept, and his mental sorrow was dispelled. Sekkizhar Peruman thus far sings about his early youth. This is the first part.

Then, in the second part, Sekkizhar Peruman announces that he reached maturity and passed the stage of worldly life. He declares that he saw the impermanence of this world and performed many acts of charity. This is the third part of his life. In this part, in the second section, his mind progresses one step further from the life he lived like other worldly people. Sekkizhar Peruman describes the detail of his mind’s progression. He speaks of the compassion he held for other living beings, and how, due to that compassion, he lived performing acts of charity in this world.

Sekkizhar Peruman then states that after this, his mental maturity increased slightly, and seeing the impermanent nature of this world, he renounced it, declaring that he would not live an impermanent life, and joined the Samana religion.

Then he joined the city called Paadaliputhiram. He went there, joined the Samana religion, and rose to the position of leader of the Samana religion. Sekkizhar Peruman explains Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s entry into religious inquiry, his joining the Samana religion, his adoption of the name Dharumasenar, and his subsequent arrival in Thiru-Adigai, up to this point. Sekkizhar Peruman explains the fourth section, which is categorized as religious inquiry and spiritual inquiry. Beyond this, due to the painful disease bestowed by the Lord, he secretly left the Samana religion and reached Thiru-Adigai. Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar gave him sacred ash and the five-letter mantra, guiding Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman towards the Lord.

Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, by the grace of Thiru-Veerattar, gained the inspiration to compose Tamil garlands, the Thevarams, and lived excelling in the path of Shiva. Finally, in Thiru-Pukalur, he declared, “O Punniya, I come to Your feet,” and becoming the very form of Shiva-Ananda Gnana, he reached the feet of the Lord. This fifth part of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s history is considered the most supreme of all.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s life was We can see how he gradually ascended, reaching higher states in thought, word, and deed, and how he remained in that elevated state. Accordingly, Sekkizhar Peruman now explains to us the event of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman joining the Samana religion. We saw that Marulneekkiyar, who became Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, realized the impermanence of this world and performed acts of charity.

Now, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman realizes that even these acts of charity are impermanent and fleeting.

Therefore, he renounced his home, engaged in spiritual inquiry, and embraced complete asceticism. He firmly resolved that there was no benefit in this impermanent worldly life and that he would not live in it, thus entering into renunciation. It is understood here that he renounced his home, wealth, worldly life, and even his relatives, including his sister Thilagavathiyar, who were associated with this worldly body.

However, later, when he suffered from the colic disease, we can see in detail why he came to Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar.

Thus, the Samana religion greatly attracted Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, who had embraced renunciation. This Samana religion, while using the virtue of non-violence as a cloak, concealed its other flaws and acts of violence beneath that cloak, thus being a religion that practiced such base conduct. Generally, during the time Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman lived, the Samana religion was in such a degraded state. Researchers would say that the Samana religion was in a very high state during its initial period, the period of the first Jains.

However, that is not the case. Whether it was the medieval Samana, later Samana, or early Samana, this Samana religion would declare non-violence as the sole virtue and outwardly display it.

But the same Samana religion that proclaimed non-violence as the greatest virtue would also preach that practices like lying on a bed of stones, plucking out hair, and other body-torturing vows and severe penances should be observed as important principles. This is a policy completely contrary to its principle of non-violence.

Moreover, when Marulneekkiyar, who is Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, joined their religion, the Samana religion, he was then Dharumasenar.

Later, when Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman returned to the Saivite religion, we learn how much the Jains tormented our Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, how much they deceived him and inflicted cruelties upon him.

Therefore, the Samana religion held such a stance. Not only that, but when Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, the child-saint, was staying in Madurai, it was the Jains who set fire to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s monastery. These actions clearly demonstrate to us that they are principles contrary to the virtue of non-violence preached by the Samana religion. We can understand how cruel Jainism was from the Puranas of Naminandhi Adigal and Dhandi Adigal, from the sacred utterances of Thevaram, from earlier texts, and from our nation’s historical records. Not only that, but we can also see in history how Jainism, without patience, tolerance, or forbearance, tried to harass and destroy other religions, such as Shaivism. All the actions they performed were completely contrary to their preached principles of ahimsa and non-violence, which is an undeniable truth.

Jainism generally states that non-violence is the most important virtue, but in our tradition, there are places where even killing is said to be a virtue. There are also instances where such principles are expounded in legal texts, worldly texts, and Shaivite texts. Many such histories are found within these Puranic narratives. Jainism, ignorant of these truths, dared to commit many heinous acts of killing, and it is a religion that cunningly concealed these acts of killing under the guise of non-violence.

However, when our Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, observing the impermanence of the world, renounced worldly life and engaged in spiritual inquiry, the principle of non-violence, which appeared to be an external aspect of Jainism, greatly attracted him. It captivated his mind and drew him towards Jainism.

Therefore, he joined Jainism. Joining a spiritual inquiry is generally the beginning of a religious life.

Here, we saw why Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, also known as Marul Neekkiyar, joined Jainism. We saw that non-violence was a principle that greatly attracted him, and thus he joined Jainism. Sekkizhar Peruman gives a reason for this: Lord Shiva did not reveal to him, that is, to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, which was the true religion. Our Lord Shiva did not bestow grace upon Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman in this manner.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman sings that he joined Jainism. We already saw that sacred verse, did we not? It sings, “Because our Lord did not grant him the grace to discern and understand the good path among the religions.” This is its meaning: Lord Shiva Sekkizhar Peruman sings that Lord Shiva did not grant Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman the grace to discern which was the true religion, and therefore Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman joined Jainism. Generally, the beginning of religious life is to engage in spiritual inquiry. Religions branch out into many divisions and exist as many different faiths. The existence of so many religions is all the will of God.

According to God’s will, there are countless religions here. “To continuously argue against divinity everywhere” is the sacred utterance of Thayumanavar Swamigal. What is the good path among these religions? What is the good way? When examining each religion, this religion Sekkizhar Peruman here refers to the ‘good path of religions’ as the gradual realization of truth: that one religion holds a degree of truth, another a higher degree, and yet another an even more profound truth, until we finally understand that a particular religion embodies the complete truth. This process involves comparing and examining all religions, and then, as a result of that research, discerning the true state and embracing whichever religion is complete.

All these are referred to as knowledge and experience, or wisdom and understanding.

Here, Lord Shiva grants intellectual enlightenment to beings according to their varying levels of maturity.

Therefore, according to the varying levels of maturity of those beings, they attain intellectual enlightenment and live within the religions appropriate to their respective levels of maturity. However, the act of placing these religions in a hierarchy, comparing them, understanding which is the true religion, which is the superior religion, and then arriving at a conclusion—that mature state—is not likely to happen in an instant or within a specific period; it will not happen. This state of maturity will not come to all souls at the same time. According to the maturity of each soul, intellectual enlightenment is granted, and God reveals those souls by placing them in the religions appropriate to them. We can compare this to a mother feeding many children or a teacher instructing many students. A single teacher teaches many students, but not all those students, that is, all students studying under the same teacher, excel greatly.

Their education flourishes according to the intellectual capacity of each student, and they excel in it.

Similarly, considering the state of maturity of all beings, God Himself bestows upon them the religions appropriate to each. However, when the time comes for that maturity to realize which is the true religion, the religion that transcends all religions, God reveals it to that soul.

Here, the good path of Shaivism, that is, Shaivism, Lord Shiva, in this situation, did not appropriately bestow or explain to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman the truth that Shaivism transcends all religions. Why did Lord Shiva not bestow grace in this manner? Was it due to a deficiency in Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s penance in a previous birth, a lack of maturity, the fruit of karma, or the necessity of this for him to descend to a lower state and then refute other doctrines? All these are unknown to us, unknowable matters known only to God.

Therefore, taking it that Lord Shiva did not bestow the greatness and truth of Shaivism upon Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman at this point, we understand that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman joined Jainism. We will continue to read the Nayanar’s Purana.

Later, Lord Shiva inflicts a severe stomach ailment and, through Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar, calls him back to Shaivism. We will also examine that truth in detail at that point.

Therefore, in the history of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, at this juncture, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman joins Jainism and begins to live by its tenets. We shall proceed with our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Two Hundred Eighty-Two, Thiru-Nindrachcharukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We saw the news that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman joined Jainism.

Thus, Marul Neekkiyar, also known as Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, who was attracted to Jainism, reaches a city called Pataliputra. There, Jain schools and monasteries abound. In ancient times, in the northern country, there was a city named Pataliputra. The city of Patna, which is currently the capital of Bihar state, was formerly known as Pataliputra. The Ashoka king, who lived after the time of Adi Buddha and followed Buddhism, ruled from the capital city named Pataliputra. In the same name, here in the south, in Tamil Nadu, Jains established a city called Pataliputra, where they built their Jain schools and monasteries, making the city prominent in Jainism.

However, the Pataliputra that was once in Tamil Nadu is no longer found; it has been destroyed.

Now, there is a Shiva sthalam called Thiru-Padiripuliyur. This city of Pataliputra must have been located near this Shiva sthalam. Padalam refers to the Padiri tree. The Padiri tree is called Padalam. Thiru-Padiripuliyur is a Shiva sthalam.

Here, the Padiri tree is the sthala-viruksham (sacred tree of the place).

Therefore, this place received the name Thiru-Padiripuliyur after the name of that sthala-viruksham. Near it must have been Pataliputra, that is, the city of Pataliputra that was in Tamil Nadu. In earlier days, it must have been the capital and a major city of a Jain king. The history that is to come later states that Gunaparan, a Pallava king who converted from Jainism to Shaivism through Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, demolished the Jain schools and monasteries that were in Pataliputra and built a temple called Gunaparaveecharam.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, who was then Marul Neekkiyar, goes to that city of Pataliputra. He joins the Jain temple. He joins those Jains who have the power to preach by making falsehood appear as truth. The Jains there teach Marul Neekkiyar that Jainism alone is the path to liberation. As we have already seen, Jainism in those days was a religion that performed many cruel acts while superficially presenting the principle of non-violence, or ahimsa. Asti Nasti is the mantra of the Jains.

Similarly, their doctrine may appear to be true, but it is not true, as our Shaivite Acharyas have told us. In the Purana of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, it is stated that he considered the Jains, who are of a corrupt path, saying that an unclear thing is both false and true, to be false.

Thus, the Jains preach and teach their false path as if it were true. They taught Marul Neekkiyar in such a way that he felt the urge to abandon his former state and join the Jains.

Therefore, as far as Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman was concerned, he converted; he entered Jainism because he, on his own, investigated and considered Jainism to be the true religion, and because the principle of ahimsa in Jainism attracted him. He thus went to Jainism.

However, in modern times, those who join foreign religions like Christianity convert due to temptations such as food, wealth, and women. Marul Neekkiyar, also known as Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, was not such a convert. He was attracted to the principle of non-violence in Jainism.

Therefore, he went there, believing Jainism to be the true religion. The Thevarams of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman serve as internal evidence for this, stating, “Believing the falsehoods of the wicked to be true, I entered,” and “I spent many, many ages speaking words among the Jains,” and “Listening to the words of the Jains, I became one with them.”

Thus, Marul Neekkiyar, believing the semblance of truth to be truth, enters Jainism. The reason for this is the lack of grace from our Lord Shiva. He did not bestow grace. This is what we saw before. After going to Jainism, Marul Neekkiyar also diligently studies all the profound artistic texts of Jainism with surging emotion. Jains were skilled in many artistic texts in those days.

They composed their religious texts and many other artistic and knowledge-based texts, including mantras, and with their help, they brought this world under their control. All these are known from the history of Aludaiya Pillaiyar and other historical records. Just as Christians do now, the Jains in those days spread their religion using various tactics, employing their artistic and intellectual skills. Through this, they even brought many kings under their sway. Thiru-Sundaramoorthy Swamigal informs us of the Jains’ practices with his sacred utterances, “Gnama Gnana Gnana Gnonamenrothi.” Thiru-Sundaramoorthy Swamigal incarnated many centuries after Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. If Jainism was still prevalent enough for Thiru-Sundaramoorthy Swamigal to sing about it in those days, then what need is there to speak of the time of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman?

How strongly and widely Jainism had spread in his time! Why, even after thousands of years, Jain texts continue to have various impacts on many people. Even today, we see how those who are not Jains but belong to the Hindu religion still hold great affection for Jain principles and continue to study those principles and Jain texts. This reveals to us the strength of Jain propaganda. They are highly skilled in composing various artistic and philosophical texts and in practicing them. They used this to spread and strengthen their religion.

Even today, history bears witness to all this. It is an additional fact that they were skilled in mantras and tantras.

Here, our Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, having entered Jainism, thoroughly learns all their texts and becomes highly proficient.

Therefore, the Jains bestow upon our Marul Neekkiyar, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, the name Dharmasenar. They have also composed his history as a Jain text called Dharmasena Puranam. Generally, it has been a tradition in Jainism to have names ending with ‘sena’. “Chandrasenan, Sindhusenan, Dharmasenan, Karmasenan, Kanakasenan, and others with names like these” is from Thiru-Alavai Thevaram, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s Thevaram. He compiles all these names used by the Jains and sings about Jains with such names.

Therefore, they bestow the traditional name Dharmasenar upon Marul Neekkiyar, who entered Jainism. They give him the name Dharmasenar because the newly arrived Marul Neekkiyar is superior to them in Jainism. Marul Neekkiyar is the name given to our Nayanar by his parents. Dharmasenar is the name given by the Jains. Thiru-Navukkarasu is the name bestowed by Lord Shiva himself. Appar is the name by which Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, the child-saint, addressed him.

Vakkeesar is the name of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman in his previous birth.

Thus, our Nayanar has many names. Generally, when one formally enters a religion, it is a religious custom to change the previous name and give a new one. In Shaivism, this tradition has been known as Diksha Nama from ancient times.

Similarly, followers of other religions also held this practice, and even today, we can see that those who join Christianity, which is involved in conversion, are given different names.

Similarly, in those days, Marul Neekkiyar, who entered Jainism, studied its principles, and excelled in it, was given the name Dharmasenar by the Jains.

Thus, Marul Neekkiyar, who excelled in Jainism, defeated the Buddhists in debate. The fundamental principle of the Buddhists, based on Jainism, is that the inner instruments, such as the mind and its faculties, are the soul.

Therefore, they are ignorant of the true nature of the soul. Not only that, but they have no concept of God whatsoever. Buddhists are those who have no concept of God. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, who was highly proficient in Jainism and its principles, kept the superiority of Jainism and the inferiority of Buddhism in his heart. With that awakened mental fervor, he stood in support of the Jains and even defeated the Buddhists in debate.

Thus, at this time, when Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, under the name Dharmasenar, was excelling in a high leadership position within Jainism, his elder sister, Thilagavathiyar, was performing service (chariyai) to Lord Shiva at Thiru-Adhigai Thiru-Sthalam, continuously praying to Lord Shiva that her younger brother, Thiru-Navukkarasar, should somehow return to Shaivism. We are going to reflect on this in detail.

We shall continue our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Two Hundred and Eighty-Three, Thirunindrachcharukkam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman entered the Jain faith, where he lived a distinguished life under the name Dharumasenar.

At the same time, here in Thiruvarur, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar, who was engaged in domestic asceticism, conceived the desire to worship the holy feet of Lord Shiva. Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar lived in Thiruvarur, practicing domestic asceticism, that is, living an ascetic life from home. According to the customs of the wise, the ancient traditions, and the rules prescribed in the scriptures, she lived at home. She lived an ascetic life in Thiruvarur. Such Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar now wishes to worship the holy feet of Lord Shiva and engage in the path of Shiva. Thinking thus, she comes to the city of Thiruvathikai, to the holy sthalam.

Just as Marulneekiyar renounced his home, village, and relatives, so too Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar leaves Thiruvarur, where she was born and lived, and comes to the holy sthalam of Thiruvathikai. Sekkizhar Peruman states that familial ties are attachments that cause rebirth, and these are strong bonds of attachment.
