Thus, she casts aside all such binding relatives and comes to the holy sthalam of Thiruvathikai. She comes to the holy sthalam of Thiruvathikai to join the pure and good path of Shiva. Until now, the domestic asceticism that Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar practiced in Thiruvarur consisted of ordinary ‘pasu dharmas’ and ‘pasu punniyams’ (virtuous deeds for the soul). These ‘pasu dharmas’ and ‘pasu punniyams’ lead to rebirth.

But now, what Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar wishes to attain and join is the pure and good path of Shiva, which severs all other attachments and is capable of uniting one with the holy feet of Lord Shiva. To stand in such a path of Shiva, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar now decides and comes to Thiruvathikai. This path, which Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar wishes to stand upon, The path she wished to stand upon is the pure and good path of Shiva, the path of wisdom to attain Shiva.

Thus, to stand in the path of Shiva and worship the holy feet of Lord Shiva, she comes to Thiruvathikai. For even to stand in such a good path of Shiva, the grace of Lord Shiva is required. That is why she came to Thiruvathikai to live in that good path of Shiva and worship the holy feet of Lord Shiva. “By His grace, one worships Him” is a saying from Thiruvachagam. The Lord’s grace is completeness. The path that leads us to those holy feet is the good path, the Sanmargam.

Of all good things, the greatest is liberation, or Mukti.

Therefore, the path to attain it is a good path, a good one.

Thus, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar, who desired to be freed from the bonds of attachment, and who longed for this from Lord Shiva, arrives at the greatly glorious Thiruvathikai Veerattanam, located on the northern bank of the river called Thirukedila. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that she arrives here so that the bonds of attachment may be severed. Bonds of attachment are called inherent bonds, bonds that are not easily severed. If one loves Shiva, all these bonds will be severed. Without love for Shiva, by no other means can this bond, this bond of attachment, be broken. It is impossible to remove or displace.

Thus, to attain boundless love for Lord Shiva, the embodiment of purity, she comes to Thiruvathikai. That Thiruvathikai is located on the northern bank of the Kedila River. The Kedila River is a river with purifying waters. We have already seen the glories of the Kedila River, referred to as the Ganges of the South, in the Puranam of Thaduthatkonda. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman has sung of the excellence of its waters with phrases like “leaping Kedilam,” “wide Kedilam,” “good Kedilam,” “full Kedilam,” “flowing Kedilam,” “running Kedilam,” “deep Kedilam,” “abundant Kedilam,” and “Kedila waters.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has sung of this Kedila River as “fish-filled, clear water.”

Sundaramoorthy Swamigal has sung about this Kedila River in the Thiruvathikai Thevaram, referring to it as “iron-watered, strong-flowing Kedila.” Such Thiruvathikai, located on the northern bank of the Kedila River, is a very great Shiva sthalam. It holds the tradition and sthala history that it is the place where the event of burning the three cities (Thirupurams) occurred. The burning of the three cities is a symbol of Lord Shiva removing the three impurities.

Therefore, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar, who wished to be freed from the bonds of attachment, comes to this Thiruvathikai, which is the site of the historical event where the three cities, symbolizing the three impurities, were burned. In this Thiruvathikai, Lord Shiva burned the three cities.

Similarly, there are eight sthalams where the heroic deeds of Lord Shiva were manifested. There are eight sthalams where the heroic deeds of Lord Shiva were manifested: Thirukkandiyur, where Brahma’s head was severed; Thirukkovalur, where the slaying of Andhakasura occurred; Thiruvathikai, where the destruction of the three cities took place; Thirupariyaloor, where Daksha was punished; Thiruvirkudi, where the slaying of Jalandharasura occurred; Thiruvaluvur, where the slaying of Gajamukhasura occurred; Thirukkurukkai, where Manmatha was burned; and Thirukkadavur, where Yama was kicked to save Markandeya. These are celebrated as the Ashtaveerasthana sthalams. We can see this fact categorized in the hymn “Bhooman Siram Kandi.” Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar has come from Thiruvarur to Thiruvathikai to be freed from the bonds of attachment and to stand in the good path of Shiva. This is in Thiruvarur. If one were to ask why she couldn’t attain that means of love and be freed from attachment while remaining in Thiruvarur, or why she couldn’t stand in the good path of Shiva while remaining in Thiruvarur, it is because her home and relatives were there.

Therefore, due to that, all her past memories would repeatedly return to Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar, and the bonds of those memories would continue. These could not be eliminated.

Thus, to meditate on Lord Shiva with single-minded devotion and perform service to Shiva, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar reaches the holy sthalam of Thiruvathikai. Sekkizhar Peruman sings, “To be freed from the unceasing bonds of attachment, to attain boundless love for the Pure One, that lady, who was supported, reached the glorious Thiruvathikai Veerattanam on the long northern bank of the water-filled Kedila.” In this verse, Sekkizhar Peruman mentions this fact. In this song, by “Neerar Kedilam” (water-filled Kedilam), the glory of Thiruvathikai’s sacred water (theertham) is highlighted; by “Athikai,” the glory of the sthalam; and by “Veerattanam,” the glory of the deity (murthi).

Thus, in a single song, Sekkizhar Peruman has sung the greatness of the Murthi, Sthalam, and Theertham. He has sung these three glories pertaining to the Thiruvathikai sthalam. “Murthi, Sthalam, Theertham, if one properly begins with these, a good guru will also be found to speak the word, O Paraparame,” is the saying of Thayumanavar Swamigal. In the Puranam of Amarneethi Nayanar, Amarneethi Nayanar also left his village, Pazhaiyarai, came to Thirunallur, established a matham, worshipped, and attained Shiva-hood. We have seen that account as well.

Similarly, here, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar leaves Thiruvarur, where she lived, She arrives at Thiruvathikai Veerattanam. She prostrates and worships Veerattaneswarar, Lord Shiva, who is enshrined in Thiruvathikai Veerattanam.

From that day onwards, she bore all the symbols of Shiva and began to perform sacred services with her own hands, filled with love. Sekkizhar Peruman sings this, saying, “She went and prostrated before the coral mountain that resided in Thiruveerattanam, bore the flawless symbols of Shiva from that day onwards, and with ardent love, began to perform abundant sacred services with her own hands.” Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar wears the symbols of Shiva. Sekkizhar Peruman sings of them as “flawless symbols of Shiva.” “Kothu” means fault. “Kothil” means without fault.

So, it means flawless symbols of Shiva. The symbols of Shiva are sacred ash (Thiruneeru) and Rudraksha. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to these Shiva symbols as “Kothil Shiva Chinnams,” meaning flawless Shiva symbols. He states that they are Shiva symbols without faults. Indeed, Thiruneeru and Rudraksha are Shiva symbols that remove faults.

Now, Sekkizhar Peruman sings that Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar bore the Shiva symbols of Thiruneeru and Rudraksha. Even before this, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar had borne Shiva symbols in Thiruvarur.

However, those were generally borne for engaging in domestic asceticism.

At that time, the domestic asceticism performed by Ammaiyar consisted of ‘pasu dharmas’ performed for the benefit of other beings, acts of compassion for other beings. But here, after coming to Thiruvathikai, Ammaiyar, Sekkizhar Peruman sings that she has adorned herself with the Shiva symbols of Rudraksha and Thiruneeru.

Here, these are Shiva symbols she bore specifically to stand and abide in the good path of Shiva. There in Thiruvarur, the ‘pasu dharmas’ she performed for other beings, all those are now set aside, and she performs Shiva dharmas, embracing only love for Shiva.

Therefore, to specifically highlight these, Sekkizhar Peruman emphasizes that she bore all these Shiva symbols specially, saying “from that day onwards.” She prioritizes these Shiva symbols. She begins to stand in that good path of Shiva, where she abandons servitude to her husband, who is the lord of her body, and to other beings related to her body, and takes Lord Shiva alone as her master. Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar begins to walk in that good path of Shiva, taking Lord Shiva alone as her master, abandoning servitude to her husband, who is the lord of her body, and to other beings related to her body. “Having You as our Lord, Your glorious devotees, we will perform no service to anyone but You.” In accordance with this, Ammaiyar bears these Shiva symbols as signs of such a life. She bears them with emotion. Even though Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar had devotion to Shiva before, she also had other attachments.

But now, all other attachments have been severed, and only devotion to Shiva remains in Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to this love as boundless love.

Therefore, Standing in such love, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar begins to perform sacred services for Lord Shiva with her own hands. We will continue to contemplate what those sacred services to Shiva were that Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar performed. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Two Hundred and Eighty-Four, Thirunindrachcharukkam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar reached Thiruvathikai Veerattanam and performs sacred services to Lord Shiva there. The service performed by Ammaiyar here is a form of worship belonging to the ‘Chariyai’ path, one of the four paths known as ‘Saiva Narpadhangal’ in Saivism. Sekkizhar sings how she performs this sacred service of ‘Chariyai’: “Before dawn, she swept the holy place, purified it well with fresh, auspicious cow dung, plucked flowers, strung garlands, and performed many sacred services with a character praised by many.” Sekkizhar Peruman, in the one thousand three hundred and ninth verse, explains the sacred service performed by Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar.

Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar performs the sacred service of sweeping the holy temple before dawn, in front of the Lord. She also cleanses the temple well with the dung of a cow that has recently calved, which is full of auspiciousness, plucks flowers, strings garlands, and offers them. Sekkizhar Peruman states in this song that she performed many such sacred services with a character praised by many devotees. All the actions and sacred services mentioned here are placed within the ‘Chariyai’ path, one of the four good paths of Saivism. Sekkizhar Peruman has structured and sung this verse as an exposition of the characteristics of ‘Chariyai’. ‘Chariyai’, ‘Kiriyai’, ‘Yogam’, ‘Gnanam’ are the four paths of Saivism, the four good paths of Saivism. Among them, the first is the sacred service called ‘Chariyai’.

In this path, the most important aspect is the services rendered to Lord Shiva, to Shiva’s devotees, and to the Guru with our physical body. This is referred to as ‘Dasa Margam’ by Sivagnana Siddhiyar. In Sivagnana Siddhiyar, Sutra 8, the 19th verse, the 271st Thiruviruttam of Sivagnana Siddhiyar, the author, Arulnandi Sivachariyar Peruman, describes the characteristics of ‘Chariyai’. The verse is as follows: “Dasa Margam, if spoken, is to sweep and cleanse the temple of Shankara, to adorn it with sacred cow dung, to pluck flowers and make beautiful garlands for the Holy One, to praise and sing, to light flawless lamps, to create sacred gardens, and upon seeing the sacred form of a devotee, to ask, ‘What service shall I perform for you?’ and to perform their service. Those who perform this Chariyai will reside in the world of the Lord.” The meaning of this is as follows: Devotees who come to attain the holy feet of Lord Shiva will achieve it by standing in four paths. The first path is the Chariyai path, which is called Dasa Margam.

What are the sacred services performed by Shiva devotees who follow the Dasa Margam? They sweep and clean the temple of Lord Shiva, then cleanse it with cow dung, light lamps, maintain gardens, and gather flowers. With these flowers, they make garlands, wreaths, and other adornments for the Lord. Upon seeing the sacred form of the Lord’s devotees, they bow and serve them. These are the actions of those who follow the Chariyai path. This is the sacred service performed in the Chariyai path.

Sivagnana Siddhiyar states that it is worship directed towards the manifest form (Uruva Thirumeni). That is, Chariyai is external worship performed outwardly. Among the three forms of the Lord—namely, formless (Aruvam), form-formless (Aru-Uruvam), and manifest form (Uruvam)—those who follow the Chariyai path worship the manifest form. This Chariyai worship is an external form of worship. Those who practice this Chariyai path will attain the state of liberation, which is the world of Lord Shiva.

Thus, this verse of Sivagnana Siddhiyar describes the characteristics of the Chariyai path. Sekkizhar Peruman has composed and sung this song, incorporating those same characteristics. Sekkizhar Peruman has composed this song, depicting Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar performing all those services. What does Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar do? She rises before dawn and sweeps and purifies the Lord’s temple. According to Agamic rules, the first period of worship, known as Thiruppalli Ezhuchi, must be performed three and three-quarter naligais before sunrise.

Accordingly, what needs to be done before that worship in the Thiruppalli Ezhuchi period is to sweep and clean the Lord’s temple. For that purpose, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar rises before dawn and sweeps and purifies the Lord’s temple and its courtyard. She cleanses the Lord’s temple with fresh cow dung, sweeping and purifying it. What kind of cow dung is it? Sekkizhar Peruman mentions here that it is dung from which impurities have been removed. It is customary that for ten days after a cow has calved, its milk, dung, etc., should not be used for the Lord’s worship.

Furthermore, the dung of sick cows, barren cows, pregnant cows, or cows that eat excrement should not be used for cleansing the Lord’s temple.

Therefore, following these rules, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar brings good cow dung and cleanses the Lord’s temple. Sekkizhar Peruman also states that she cleanses it thoroughly. What does “cleanses thoroughly” mean? It means cleansing without gaps, She performs that exalted sacred service of cleansing evenly with cow dung, without spots or other imperfections, and without harming ants or other living creatures.

Then, she plucks flowers and arranges them into garlands and other floral offerings, preparing them to be adorned upon the Lord. We have extensively discussed how to pluck flowers, how to bring them, and how to string garlands in the Puranams of Eripattar Nayanar, Muruga Nayanar, and others.

Therefore, following those rules, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar here also brings floral offerings and prepares them to be adorned upon the Lord.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman has composed and sung this song, incorporating the characteristics of the Chariyai path.

Similarly, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman has sung: “O mind, if you wish to attain permanence, come! Daily enter the temple of our Peruman, before dawn, sweep and clean, adorn with garlands of flowers, praise and sing, prostrate with your head, dance, and chant ‘Shankara, hail, hail!’ and ‘Our Primal Lord with the red matted hair adorned with flowing waters!’ and ‘Thiru-Arur!’” Thus, in the Thiru-Thandakam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman has extensively described this path of Chariyai. Even in the Thiru-Vathavurar Puranam, the Lord has instructed Thiru-Manikkavasagar Peruman, also known as Vathavur Adigal, on how to perform this path of Chariyai. We can find this in the Thiru-Perunthurai Sarga of the Thiru-Vathavurar Puranam.

Thus, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar performs all these sacred services according to the tenets of Chariyai, one of the four paths of Saivism prescribed in many Saivite texts. How does she perform them? Many devotees of Shiva, who are calm and composed, praise her for these sacred services. The praise or blame of others means nothing to her. The joy and greatness that arise in the hearts of those who are not concerned with such things are shown to us. Thilagavathi Ammaiyar performs these sacred services in such a way that many true devotees of Shiva praise her.

This is how it is in the Thiru-Veerattanam temple in Thiru-Athigai. She continues to do this for many days, for a long time. At such a time, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar makes a plea at the feet of the Lord, asking that Marulneekkiyar, who had fallen into the pit of other religions and become Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, be brought back to the Saivite faith.

Our reflection now resumes. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Two Hundred and Eighty-Five. Thiru-Nindra Charukkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. In Thiru-Athigai, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar, following the path of Chariyai, performs true service to the temple of Lord Shiva. In this state, while Thilagavathiyar is performing such excellent sacred services, she is deeply distressed and saddened by her younger brother Marulneekkiyar joining another religion, Jainism.

Thilagavathi Ammaiyar, who was engaged in Shiva’s sacred service every day, performs these services with great humility and reverence. The Peruman here mentions “bowing with humility.” He mentions: “The destiny to join the Saivite religion with the quality of humility.” This is from Sivagnana Siddhiyar. The meaning of this is that when we worship the Lord, we must bow with great humility. We must remember our smallness.

At the same time, we must constantly think of the great compassion of the Lord and, therefore, serve the Lord with great humility. On such a day, while performing this sacred service, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar remembers her brother who joined another religion. The Peruman here mentions, “On the good days spent with the Lord.” The days spent with the Lord, serving the Lord, are good days. All other days are wasted.

The elders’ conclusion is that days not spoken of are days not born. The good words that say, “I have wasted days without praising,” tell us that the days we attain the Lord are good days.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman sings that Thilagavathi Ammaiyar is one whose love for her relatives overflows.

Here, relatives do not refer to those related by body, but to Lord Shiva, who is the companion of the soul, and the servitude of Shiva’s devotees, who are the relatives of the soul. “You are my father, you are my mother, you are my lord, you are my loving uncle and aunt,” says Thiru-Thandakam. “Relatives are the hosts of Rudra,” is the word of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. All these indicate that the relatives related to this body are only at the physical level, but Lord Shiva, who is the companion of the soul, and the devotees of Shiva are always the relatives of this soul.

Thus, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar lives in the discipline of Shiva, with love for Lord Shiva and the devotees of Shiva, who are the relatives who accompany the soul. Sekkizhar Peruman thus sings this as an adjective for the love that Thilagavathi Ammaiyar had. It is during these days that Thilagavathi Ammaiyar grieves, remembering her younger brother Marulneekkiyar.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman here sings this as an adjective for the love that Thilagavathi Ammaiyar had. It is during these days that Thilagavathi Ammaiyar grieves, remembering her younger brother Marulneekkiyar. She is distressed. As we said earlier, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar renounced all bodily relatives and developed love for Shiva’s devotees and Shiva, who are soul-related relatives.

At the same time, the story here states that Thilagavathi Ammaiyar grieves, remembering her brother Marulneekkiyar.

Therefore, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar’s grief for her brother Marulneekkiyar, who became Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, is not due to worldly attachment to bodily relations. It is not because he is her brother. This sorrow and distress came from Thilagavathi Ammaiyar’s firm conviction in the higher Shiva-related servitude. This is because she knew the exalted state of her brother’s soul. She knew the exalted state of her brother’s soul.

Therefore, she grieves that her brother has joined another religion that does not benefit his soul, and has not joined the Saivite religion which truly benefits his soul.

Thus, Thilagavathiyar is immersed in sorrow, thinking this. Thilagavathi Ammaiyar is like a kindled lamp of penance. Such an Ammaiyar worships Thiru-Veerattaneswarar, who is like a radiant light, and repeatedly pleads, “If you would graciously accept me as your servant, then you must rescue my younger brother from the deep pit of other religions, which is a sinful act.” Thilagavathiyar is Sekkizhar Peruman refers to her as a kindled lamp of penance. Kindled penance means the penance that inspires one to abandon worldly attachments and attain Shiva-related good deeds, which are Shiva-related attachments. Ammaiyar’s penance was that she inspired herself in Shiva’s penance. Not only that, but she also inspired her brother in Shiva’s penance.

Through that, she also inspired the people of this world in Shiva’s penance. Thilagavathi Ammaiyar was like a lamp and inspired herself.

Then, she inspired her brother, who was in another religion, to stand in the path of Shiva’s penance. Because her brother stood in this path of Shiva’s penance, he bestowed the Thevarams. Through those Thevarams, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar inspired all the living beings of this world to stand in the path of Shiva, in the path of Shiva’s penance. Thilagavathi Ammaiyar inspired all the living beings of this world to stand in the path of Shiva, in the path of Shiva’s penance.

Furthermore, the reference here is that Thilagavathi Ammaiyar is a great ascetic, like a kindled lamp that shines brightly. Sekkizhar Peruman called Thilagavathi Ammaiyar a kindled lamp of penance. Now he says that Lord Shiva, Thiru-Veerattaneswarar, who is in Thiru-Athigai, is like the light of that flame. “O Light, O Flame, O Lamp of encompassing light,” says Thiru-Vasagam.

Thus, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar, who is like a lamp of penance, worships Thiru-Veerattaneswarar, who is a radiant light, and makes a plea. Thilagavathi Ammaiyar says to Lord Shiva, “You have graciously accepted me as your servant. If your grace to me is true,” She pleads that He should also bestow His grace upon her brother. She repeatedly pleads that He should rescue her brother, who has fallen into the pit of other religions. Why?

Because it is very rare for a soul to take human birth in this world. And it is even rarer to join the imperishable Saivite faith. Marulneekkiyar was one who had attained the very rare great fortune of standing in the Saivite faith. Yet, he deviated from this Saivite faith and fell into Jainism.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to this as a sinful act and a pit of other religions. A soul takes various bodies and finally takes human birth, and that too, very rarely, is born in the land of Bharata, and that too, very rarely, stands in the Vedic path, and that too, very rarely, attains the Saivite faith. “It is very rare to attain the destiny of joining the Saivite religion with humility, escaping the delusion of life and the misery of poverty, through the high Shiva-knowledge. Those who praise the moon-crested Lord attain His grace.” This is from Sivagnana Siddhiyar.

Furthermore, Manikkavasagar Peruman has also sung in Thiru-Vasagam, Thiru-Agaval, about how a soul escapes from various sufferings and finally attains the Saivite faith. Manikkavasagar Peruman sings about how a soul takes many births, many bodies, and then Manikkavasagar Peruman has sung in Thiru-Vasagam, Thiru-Agaval, about how a soul takes many births, many bodies, and then wanders through various religions, and finally attains the feet of the Lord. In Thiru-Vasagam, Thiru-Agaval, he sings: “From elephant to ant, in faultless wombs, surviving the inner karma; in human birth, in the mother’s womb, surviving the faultless germ’s struggle; surviving the one-month’s growth, surviving the two-month’s development, surviving the three-month’s growth, surviving the great darkness of four months, surviving the five-month’s cessation, surviving the six-month’s spreading, surviving the seven-month’s falling to earth, surviving the eight-month’s confinement, surviving the nine-month’s coming sorrow; surviving the ocean of sorrow of the ten months with the mother; and in those years, having attained, having gathered and having remained, surviving many such things; morning’s filth and severe Day’s hunger, night’s sleep, surviving the journey; surviving the dark-haired, red-lipped, white-toothed, peacock-like women, whose swaying gait, close-set, swelling, firm, and budding breasts cause the waist to ache, rising and spreading wide, through whose narrow space no hair can pass, surviving the sharp-eyed women’s plunder; surviving the mad world’s vast expanse, surviving the desire for the rutting elephant; surviving the many seas of knowledge; surviving the distress of wealth; surviving the ancient poison of poverty; surviving the many paths of limited understanding; when the thought of a deity arose, and when one considered that imperishable entity, six crores of illusory powers began their various illusions. “The Vedic scholars, whose vows were supreme, showed the scriptures as truth. The proponents of various religions argued and fought, asserting their own religions as supreme. Manikkavasagar Peruman thus describes the stages by which this soul, born in various species, attains human birth, and then, after wandering through various paths, finally comes to join the good path of Saivism to attain the liberation of the Lord’s feet.

“Therefore, on that day when a soul, after much struggle, experience, and maturity, is born into the Saivite religion, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar, feeling compassion for Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, who had again fallen into the Jain religion, which is another religion, and was suffering, makes a plea to the Lord.

“Therefore, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar, deeply distressed and saddened that he had fallen into Jainism despite being born into the Saivite religion, which is very difficult to attain, makes a plea to the Lord. She pleads, “O Lord, just as you have accepted me, so too must you accept my brother.” Let us go on reflecting.”” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Two Hundred and Eighty-Six. Thiru-Nindra Charukkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing as follows: “May he not fall into the path of futility, which is to wear a mat as penance, pluck out one’s hair, and eat while standing,” thus Thilagavathiyar, who stood in the path of Shiva, prayed, and the Lord, who removes the karmas that cause birth, accepted her prayer.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman composes the forty-seventh verse. Thilagavathi Ammaiyar prays to Lord Shiva: “May he not fall into the futile path of Jainism, which involves wearing a mat as penance, plucking out one’s hair, and eating while standing.”

Thus, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar prayed to the Lord, and the Lord, who removes the karmas that cause birth, accepted her prayer. This is the meaning of this verse. In this sacred verse, the first line describes the state of the Jains, that is, the state of the followers of Jainism. The second line describes the state of Marulneekkiyar, who entered it. The third line describes the state of Thilagavathi Ammaiyar, who tried to rescue Marulneekkiyar. And the fourth line describes the state of the Lord who granted grace for that.

Sekkizhar Peruman first describes the Jains in the first line. He sings about the Jains, saying, “They wear a mat as penance, pluck out their hair, and eat while standing.” They considered these as penance. They considered these as their ascetic discipline. “Idukkuthal” means to wear tightly around the waist. Jains followed this practice of wearing tightly around the waist.

Next, plucking out hair. When someone becomes a guru in Jainism, many Jain gurus surround him and pluck out his hair one by one with their hands.

At that time, they utter some words as mantras. They utter some mantras like “Ip thuk pir suk.” They utter those words as mantras, saying “Now sorrow, then happiness,” and pluck out the hair one by one.

Thus, plucking it out is initially sorrowful and then joyful. They would utter those mantras to mean that it would be sorrowful at first and then joyful. This is one of the ascetic practices of the Jains. Our Thiru-Murai teachers have pointed this out and condemned it in many places in the Thiru-Murais, saying, “Plucking hair is pleasure.” Next, their ascetic practice was to eat while standing. They would eat while standing, holding food in their hands. This is a custom of Jain gurus.

“We have forgotten all the words that told us to remember those who eat standing,” is from Marumattru Thandakam, composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. This is an example that Jains have the custom of eating while standing. These actions are practices forbidden in our Dharma Shastras as things that should not be done. They would utter those mantras to mean that it would be sorrowful at first and then joyful. This is one of the ascetic practices of the Jains. Our Thiru-Murai teachers have pointed this out and condemned it in many places in the Thiru-Murais, saying, “Plucking hair is pleasure.” Next, their ascetic practice was to eat while standing.

They would eat while standing, holding food in their hands. This is a custom of Jain gurus. “We have forgotten all the words that told us to remember those who eat standing,” is from Marumattru Thandakam, composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. This is an example that Jains have the custom of eating while standing. These actions are practices forbidden in our Dharma Shastras as things that should not be done.

Therefore, the Jains considered and practiced these customs as penance. In reality, our Dharma Shastras condemn them as futile.

Thus, our Gnana Shastras, in the section on opposing other religions, have extensively condemned how these practices are futile. Our Acharyas have extensively condemned the principles of Jainism in their refutations of other religions.

But the question may arise in us, “Is doing all this defamation of other religions? It is defamation of other religions, isn’t it?” All these followers of external religions are deluded, believing falsehoods to be truth. Our Acharyas, observing the suffering of those who mistakenly believe falsehood to be truth, felt compassion for them and therefore condemned their external religions, such as Jainism.

Furthermore, the harms inflicted upon Shaivism by adherents of these external religions are considered offenses against Shiva. Committing offenses against Shiva incurs severe punishment.

Therefore, out of compassion for them, and to prevent them from incurring such severe punishments by committing offenses against Shiva, our Shaiva Acharyas condemned these external religions. All these actions were taken to prevent the adherents of external religions from being deceived and suffering due to their misguided state. It is also a warning that no new person should join that external religion and suffer harm.

Thus, our Acharyas have composed commentaries and texts condemning other religions. In the first line, Sekkizhar Peruman speaks of Jainism, and in the next line, he sings of the state attained by Marulneekiyar, saying, “May he not fall into the path of delusion, but be graced.” Marulneekiyar, having joined Jainism, found that his actions did not lead him to unite with Shiva; they did not allow him to perform acts for Shiva, but rather brought him futility. Such futility would gradually lead to the soul’s downfall.

Therefore, Marulneekiyar, having joined Jainism, did not unite with the path of Shiva. Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar prays that Marulneekiyar, who is united with a futile path and performing futile actions, should not fall further into such actions, and that grace should be bestowed upon him. In the third line, Sekkizhar Peruman sings, “Thilagavathiyar, who stood firm in the path of Shiva, praised.” Thus, Thilagavathiyar, who is devoted to Shiva, prays to the Lord that Marulneekiyar, who is on the futile path, should not fall further and should return to Shaivism. In the following lines, Sekkizhar Peruman sings of the divine will of Lord Shiva, saying, “He who dispels the karma that brings forth birth.” How does he sing of Lord Shiva? “He who dispels the karma that brings forth birth.”

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman sings about Lord Shiva in this fourth line. ‘Bhavam’ means birth. The past karma that causes one to be born in this life.

Here, the reason Marulneekiyar received this birth was a deficiency in his previous penance.

Lord Shiva is the one who removes such faults and deficiencies in penance. He now wills it. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that Lord Shiva, the dispeller, has now willed it.

Thus, Lord Shiva, having willed it, that is, having acceded to the request of Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar, appears as a great ascetic. He appears in the dream of Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar. Lord Shiva, who always has the bull as His vehicle, appeared in Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar’s dream and spoke as follows: “Cast away your mental sorrow. “Now, I will take him by afflicting him with the disease of colic.” Thus, Lord Shiva graciously appeared in Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar’s dream. The verse is as follows, the forty-eighth verse in the Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam, which has one thousand three hundred verses. The sacred verse where the Lord appears in a dream and speaks is as follows: “To the steadfast ascetic, in a dream,”

“The Lord of the young bull said, “Cast away your mental sorrow. Your brother, born with you, formerly became a sage and strove to attain Me through penance.

“Now, I will afflict him with colic and take him.” Thus, this verse is structured.

“Lord Shiva appears in Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar’s dream and declares, “Cast away your mental sorrow.” Furthermore, Lord Shiva Himself states that Marulneekiyar, that is, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, was a sage in a previous birth who performed penance to attain Lord Shiva, thereby implicitly referring to his past life. This history is recounted differently in the Sanskrit texts Upamanyu Bhaktavilasa and Agastya Bhaktavilasa, meaning the previous birth of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. His previous birth, where he was a sage who performed penance to attain Lord Shiva, is mentioned in these two texts. Regardless, it is confirmed by the gracious words of Sekkizhar Peruman in this historical section that our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, in a previous birth, was a sage who strove to attain the Lord, and that a slight error occurred in that endeavor, which is why he was born in this life with the name Marulneekiyar, and that he suffered in Jainism to experience and exhaust that error, and that thereafter, the Lord gave him a solution and afflicted him, and then, through divine grace, he reached his elder sister, understood the truth, and attained the Lord, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. The karma of a person is It is true that karma is exhausted only by experiencing it; if not experienced, it will not be exhausted. It is also true that people will experience only the fruit of the karma they have performed.

“These are the conclusive findings of our scriptures. Our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar was a sage who performed penance in a previous birth. That is why, in this birth, he attained the state of renunciation in his youth. Not everyone attains the state of renunciation in their youth so easily. It was a continuation of the Nayanar’s penance as a sage in his previous birth. He continued his actions in Jainism.

“Even there, he undertook penance.

“Later, even after joining and following Shaivism, he maintained the same state of renunciation in Shaivism. All these are about Thirunavukkarasu. These are references to the previous birth of Arasu Nayanar.

“Lord Shiva Himself, through His divine word, tells Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar in a dream that Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, in his previous birth, strove to attain Him, that is, Lord Shiva, through penance. “Lord Shiva says that Thirunavukkarasu Peruman performed penance in his previous birth.

“At that time, his penance remained at the level of effort. That effort would not bear fruit until the time came. Only when the time came would that effort bear fruit.

“Now, the time has come, and Lord Shiva conveys this to Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar in a dream through His divine word.

“Thus, the reference to Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s previous birth is found in the Periya Puranam through the divine word of Lord Shiva Himself.

“Similarly, we have seen here all the details about Sundaramurthi Swamigal’s previous birth. Sekkizhar Peruman has included in the Periya Puranam the accounts of his being Aalala Sundarar in Thiru Kailash, then incarnating as Sundaramurthi Swamigal in Thirunavalur, and then returning to Mount Kailash. We have also contemplated these.

“Similarly, in the Kannappa Nayanar Puranam, he was Arjuna in a previous birth and performed penance seeking the Pasupatha Astra. To this, Lord Shiva said, Since you performed penance seeking the Pasupatha Astra, I grant it to you in this birth. You will attain the liberation you requested secondarily in a future birth. We saw this in detail in the sacred verse ‘Munbusai Thavathin Eettam’ in the Kannappa Nayanar Puranam, which states that the Lord thus graced him, and as a result, he incarnated as Kannappa Nayanar.

“Similarly, in the history of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, we will see ‘Pandu Thiruvadi Marava Panmaiyor’ (those who never forgot the sacred feet).

“Thus, wherever it is necessary in the Periya Puranam, Sekkizhar Peruman has provided us with references to the previous births of the Nayanmars.

“Now, just as Lord Shiva graced Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar in a dream, how did He Let us continue to contemplate the news of how He took Naakkarasu Peruman into His fold.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Two Hundred and Eighty-Seven. Thirunindrachcharukkam. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam.

Lord Shiva appears in the dream of Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar and graciously declares that He will take Marulneekiyar, who is Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, by afflicting him with the disease of colic. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, in a previous birth, performed penance to attain the Lord. He found a slight error in that penance. When performing penance, one must strive with mind, speech, and body. These efforts should not be directed elsewhere but towards the Lord. When directing them towards the Lord, a slight lack of attention or the mind, speech, or body going elsewhere signifies a deviation from penance.

Not only that, Deficiencies in mantras, puja materials, and the rituals of performing puja also fall under the category of decline in penance.

Therefore, generally, committing faults with mind, speech, and body in the Shiva Puja, which is penance, signifies a deviation from penance. In this, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, who performed penance in his previous birth, deviated slightly. He erred slightly.

Therefore, the Lord bestows upon him the disease of colic, a stomach ailment, in this birth. He deviated only slightly, so this experience was limited to this extent. Not only that, but it also served as an aid in finding a solution for this colic disease.

At the same time, If very grave offenses had been committed, they would have become offenses against Shiva, leading to severe punishment.

Thus, because Thirunavukkarasu Peruman had slightly deviated in his Shiva penance in his previous birth, he is now joining Jainism and is about to receive the disease of colic. This is the point here. Sekkizhar Peruman sings about it in the following verse: “The Lord of the fiery forehead, in His grace, caused the severe, burning colic, like a fierce fire, to enter the belly of the devotee, Marulneekiyar, who had committed a slight error in his former good penance, to take him into His fold.” He sings that the severe, burning colic entered his belly. Marulneekiyar, the devotee who had committed a slight error in his former good penance, Lord Shiva willed to take him into His fold. As He began to take him, He bestowed the disease of colic upon Marulneekiyar. It afflicted Marulneekiyar like a fierce fire.

That very severe colic entered his belly.

Here, the terms ‘irai vazhuvum’ (slight error) appear, which we interpreted as a slight fault that occurred in Shiva Puja.

Now, Sivakavimani Aiya further writes that in previous births, when Thirunavukkarasu Peruman was the sage Sudhapa, he also had the fault of providing firewood to Ravana, who tried to uproot Kailash.

Furthermore, there is also a story that he argued that Jainism was superior to the sage Santhar, who came seeking the truth. Sivakavimani Aiya notes this history.

Thus, the disease of colic now afflicts Marulneekiyar, who is currently in Jainism under the name Dharumasenar, serving as a Jain guru. By the grace of Lord Shiva, it is generally wise to interpret the onset of poverty, disease, and other afflictions as the Lord having taken compassion on us, causing us to experience and exhaust our past evil deeds, and beginning to take us into His fold. The Devaram says, “He will surely bestow grace in distress.” Similarly, Lord Shiva also afflicted Eyarkon Kalikkamar with colic and took him into His fold.

Lord Shiva has a third eye on His forehead. He is endowed with a gracious gaze.

Here, the disease of colic is Because it afflicted Thirunavukkarasu Peruman like fire, Sekkizhar Peruman here describes Lord Shiva as having a third eye on His forehead, referring to that third eye. Even though it is a third eye from which fire emanates, it is also an expression of the Lord’s grace.

Therefore, he said ‘grace.’ Once upon a time, when the Mother Goddess Parashakti closed the Lord’s two eyes, out of compassion and grace for living beings, He opened His third eye and caused light to appear from it, thereby gracing living beings and protecting them from darkness.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman here sings that He has such a gracious third eye. That disease of colic entered the belly of Dharumasenar, who loved Jainism and followed its path. It was like the Vadavamukagni, a fire. It causes him immense suffering and torment, like a deadly poison and a diamond, and even more so if all these were combined. That disease gnaws at Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s intestines. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman suffers greatly.

Sekkizhar Peruman here uses three similes for the disease of colic. One is the Vadavamukhi, which is called Vadavamukhi in Tamil and Vadava Mukagi in Sanskrit. There is a fire with the face of a horse named Vadava. It lies dormant and submerged at the bottom of the ocean. It is customary to say that this Vadavamukhi, which is at the bottom of the ocean, grows immensely during the dissolution of the universe, drying up the ocean and destroying the world. Just as it grows from the bottom of the ocean, so too does the disease of colic gnaw from within Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s stomach.

Next, he says it causes suffering like a diamond. A diamond is a gem. There is a custom that those who decide to take their own lives will crush diamonds into powder and consume them. Such a diamond, entering the stomach, would cut through the stomach muscles and kill them.

Similarly, this disease of colic causes suffering to Thirunavukkarasu Peruman.

Furthermore, he suffers as those who have consumed deadly poison would suffer. Not only that, but the disease of colic is like the suffering caused by these three individually. And even more, the combined suffering of these three and other evil torments. Even if all these were combined, the suffering would be immense, and such suffering is caused to Thirunavukkarasu Peruman by the disease of colic. Each of the above, even individually, is capable of causing suffering to the point of death.

But when he sings that all these, and many more, combined to cause such suffering, we must consider how great that suffering must have been for him. It gnaws at his stomach, causing him extreme distress. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman himself has sung about how this disease of colic tormented him in his first Thiruppathikam, ‘Kootraayina Vaaru.’ He sang, “I cannot bear it, as it has seized and crippled my intestines within my stomach, without appearing.” He also sang, “It has seized and crippled my stomach.” He sang, “The colic burns,” and “The colic within the body,” and “It has plucked, churned, cut, and dragged within my stomach, and I am weary,” and “I am exhausted, it has stirred, churned, and devoured within my stomach, and I am pressed,” and “Sweating, tossing, falling, and rising, what is my agony?” Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman himself, in his divine words, described the terrible nature of that colic disease in his first Thiruppathikam. If he sang in such a way, we must imagine how great the suffering it caused him was. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, who was then in Jainism under the name Thiru Dharumasenar, fell into the Jain monastery. ‘Aman Pazhi’ means a place where Jain gurus reside.

There is a separate place for Jain gurus to stay. He went there and, unable to bear his body, lost control and fell down.

Our contemplation continues. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Two Hundred and Eighty-Eight, Thirunindrachcharukkam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We saw that the colic affliction reached Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, causing him great suffering. We also noted that Thirunavukkarasu Peruman was currently a Jain guru known as Dharmasenar.

Therefore, he attempted to use all the arts, including mantras, that he had learned, practiced, and mastered within the Jain religion. That is, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman tried all the arts he had learned in the Jain religion, but they were all ineffective. The colic did not diminish with the mantras he had learned in the Jain religion; instead, the suffering increased further. Generally, Jains were skilled in many arts and adept in mantras and tantras. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman had also practiced and used these mantras and tantras. He tried all these arts, using gems, mantras, and medicines, based on Jain principles.

Usually, these methods prevent diseases from worsening and eradicate them. However, in this instance, they did not reduce or eliminate Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s colic; instead, they intensified it. The Thirukkural states, “Diagnose the disease, then its cause.” Therefore, other medical efforts made without discerning the root cause of the disease, will only exacerbate the illness. This is the fundamental principle.

Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s attempts here were to employ Jain mantras without investigating the root cause of his colic. He practiced and used them, but they only increased the disease instead of reducing it. These were all self-administered remedies by Dharmasenar. As he attempted to resolve it himself, his efforts failed, and the disease reached its peak. The colic reached such an intensity that it could not progress further.

Therefore, Dharmasenar, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, then known as Dharmasenar, suffered an intensifying colic. He was affected as if by the swift venom of a poisonous snake, and consequently, he fainted and lost consciousness. The Jains witnessed his condition. The Jains are those who, under the guise of penance, speak of penance but accumulate evil deeds and follow a path devoid of good association. Such Jains observed the state of Marulneekkiyar, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. They conversed among themselves, saying, “We have never seen or heard of such a disease before.” Now, other gurus from the Jain religion arrive.

It is mentioned here that these gurus had heads with sores, because Jains have the custom of plucking the hair from their heads with their hands, hence the reference to sores on their heads. Such gurus came and observed Dharmasenar’s condition. They consecrated the water in their kundika (water pot) and made him drink it. Even then, the disease did not subside. Jains always carry peacock feathers and kundikas.

So, they consecrated the water in the kundika and made Dharmasenar drink it, but it did not cure the disease. They then tried consecrating him with the peacock feathers they always held in their hands. Even then, the disease did not subside. Jains always carry peacock feathers in their hands. When they travel, they sweep the path with the peacock feathers to clear it, so that small creatures like ants are not trapped and harmed. They always carry a bunch of peacock feathers for this purpose.

Not only that, but when diseases or other afflictions strike, they use these peacock feathers to stroke and consecrate, and they keep the bunch of peacock feathers for this purpose.

Thus, they tried making him drink consecrated water and consecrating him with peacock feathers, but even then, the disease did not subside; it only continued to increase.

Thus, Despite trying many methods, the disease that afflicted Dharmasenar did not abate; it remained and continued to grow. Seeing this situation, all the Jains were bewildered and became disheartened, wondering what they should do next. They concluded that curing this disease was extremely difficult and withdrew from the scene. Generally, doctors or others do not speak such negative words in front of a patient.

So, they left Dharmasenar’s presence and spoke among themselves, saying that this disease was very severe and difficult to cure.

Thus, even the Jain ascetics have now abandoned Dharmasenar, and the terrible colic, grips him and torments him increasingly.

Therefore, Dharmasenar, bewildered and not knowing what to do, now remembers his elder sister, Thilagavathiyar. Although the colic torments him greatly, this colic was bestowed by Lord Shiva.

Therefore, the disease is the divine power of the Lord.

Thus, as soon as that colic, as the Lord’s divine power, entered Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s stomach, the Jain delusion left him.

Now, the memory of Thilagavathiyar, the Shaivite devotee, comes to Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, due to the suffering caused by this colic.

Therefore, the Lord’s divine power, begins to operate here, is the meaning. Generally, what is the nature of the soul? It takes on the color of that to which it is attached. The soul generally attaches itself to the world and assumes its characteristics.

But if it abandons these worldly characteristics and embraces the grace of God, it will stand in non-duality with God. This is the implication.

Therefore, until now, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s soul was inclined towards Jainism. As soon as the colic, which is the divine power of God, afflicted Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, it began to align itself with God and His divine power.

Therefore, the memory of Thilagavathiyar, the Shaivite devotee, now comes to Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. In that state of bewilderment and intense suffering, it is the common nature of a soul to be distressed, not knowing who will be its support. Thirunavukkarasar, as Dharmasenar, had newly formed a relationship with the Jain religion.

Now, the followers of that Jain religion have abandoned Dharmasenar.

Therefore, the memory of his old relationship, his elder sister Thilagavathiyar, whom he had forgotten until now, comes to Dharmasenar, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Generally, when an incurable disease or great sorrow afflicts one, it is the nature of the world for memories of old relatives to arise. In the middle of a forest, for those suffering in the dead of night, a flash of lightning appears, and that flash of lightning appears and helps them. Just as a flash of lightning helps those who are lost and suffering, a good feeling arises by the grace of God in those who are bewildered and struggling, even amidst their suffering. They grasp onto it and subsequently turn to God; they come towards God.

Therefore, now, the memory of his elder sister Thilagavathiyar comes to Dharmasenar, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Dharmasenar was a guru, so he had a servant to prepare and serve him food. That servant, understanding Dharmasenar’s intention, goes to Thilagavathiyar. Sekkizhar Peruman sings this as follows: “The Jains abandoned him, and the colic took hold and intensified greatly, bewildering him. He remembered his ancient kin, Thilagavathiyar, and sent his feeder to convey his intention.”

Here, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to the cook as ‘oottuvan’ (one who feeds). Sekkizhar Peruman refers to him as ‘oottuvan’ because he prepares food and places it in Dharmasenar’s hand, feeding him. If we interpret the word ‘oottuvan’ in this context, it also carries another meaning: the one who brings about the good fortune of uniting Dharmasenar, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, with Thilagavathiyar. This other meaning is also present here. Dharmasenar, in his current state, was unable to articulate this himself.

However, the servant, understanding Dharmasenar’s inner intention, goes to Thilagavathiyar. The next verse is as follows: “Thereupon, he went to Thiruvathikai and saw the venerable Thilagavathiyar outside the fragrant flower garden, and bowed to her. He said, ‘I have come at the bidding of your younger brother.’ She asked, ‘Are there any troubles?’ And he replied.” This is the next sacred verse. What was Dharmasenar’s intention here? Dharmasenar wished to inform his elder sister, Thilagavathiyar, of his suffering from this disease and ask for her help. This was Dharmasenar’s intention.

The servant, understanding this, reaches Thiruvathikai. The Thirukkural extols the subtlety of ‘kurippu unarthal’ (understanding intentions), stating, “Those who understand intentions by observing unspoken signs, understand the intention within the intention.” Therefore, this servant was skilled in understanding and acting upon such intentions.

Thus, he reaches Thiruvathikai, the sacred place where Thilagavathiyar resides and performs sacred service, to inform her of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s condition. We shall continue our reflection.

The Thirukkural extols the subtlety of ‘kurippu unarthal’ (understanding intentions), stating, “Those who understand intentions by observing unspoken signs, understand the intention within the intention.” Therefore, this servant was skilled in understanding and acting upon such intentions.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Two Hundred and Eighty-Nine, Thirunindrachcharukkam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. There was a servant who cooked for Thirunavukkarasar in Padaliputhiram. He, understanding Thirunavukkarasar’s condition after being afflicted by colic, his suffering, and his intention to inform his elder sister Thilagavathiyar of this suffering, comes to the sacred sthalam of Thiru Adhigai to convey this to Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s elder sister, Thilagavathiyar. The time when that servant departed from Padaliputhiram, where Thirunavukkarasu Peruman resided, was night.

Therefore, When he reached the city of Thiruvathikai, it was early morning. In that early morning, the servant stood outside the Nandavanam (flower garden) of Thiruvathikai. In that fragrant Nandavanam, in the early morning, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar came out after plucking flowers for the Lord. She came out of the Nandavanam. The rule is that one should wake up in the early morning, bathe, and pluck flowers before dawn.

Therefore, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar, who performs the sacred service of ‘sariyai’ for the Lord, also went to the Nandavanam before dawn, plucked all the flowers, and came out.

At that time, the servant reached the area outside the Nandavanam. If Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar had been going to pluck flowers, she would have been meditating on the Lord and chanting the sacred five-letter mantra as she went.

Therefore, it is customary for her not to speak to anyone else at that time.

Now, the servant is standing outside the Nandavanam. Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar comes out of the Nandavanam with the plucked flowers.

Now, a conversation takes place between the two. What does the servant, who has seen Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar, say to her? He tells Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar, “I have come here at the bidding of your younger brother.” This is mentioned in the sacred verse composed by Sekkizhar Peruman: “Here I have come at the bidding of your younger brother.” It is stated in the sacred verse by Sekkizhar Peruman, “I have come at the bidding of your younger brother.” He says, “your younger brother,” addressing Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar. ‘Ilaiyar’ (younger brother) has a direct meaning of ‘your younger brother.’ However, in Tamil, ‘izhaithal’ also means to diminish or to be weary.

Therefore, if we consider that meaning, the servant says, “your younger brother.” If we look at the other side of the word, the servant is saying that even though Marulneekkiyar, Dharmasenar, has fallen into another religion, if you bless him to recover, he will no longer diminish before you in his devotion to Shiva. He will not cause you any reduction. There is also an inner meaning here: if you bless him to recover, he will not cause you any reduction. This subtlety is found in the word ‘ilaiyar’.

So, the servant says, “I have come at the bidding of your younger brother; I have come because he told me to.” To this, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar replies. Sekkizhar Peruman mentions Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar’s reply here as, “She asked, ‘Are there any troubles?’” She asks if any harm has befallen him, that is, her younger brother Dharmasenar. Generally, it is customary to ask, “How are you?” or “Are you well?” But here, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar asks if there is any harm concerning her brother. Why? Because Lord Shiva had already appeared in Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar’s dream and blessed her, saying, “We will afflict your brother with colic and take him into our fold.” Therefore, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar asks, “Are there any troubles?” with the implication that the colic, that suffering, has come upon him. Not only that, but the suffering of colic itself is a blessing from God that brings good to Thirunavukkarasu Peruman.

Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar also did not consider the colic that came upon him, that is, her younger brother, suffering. She considered it a blessing that would bring divine grace to her brother.

Therefore, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar asking, “Are there any troubles?” is appropriate in both ways. That is, the trouble that came here is a blessing, so asking “Are you well?” and asking “Are there any troubles?” become equivalent.

Moreover, the Lord had already appeared in her dream and blessed her, told her.

Therefore, Ammaiyar already knew that colic was going to come upon her brother. So, in both these ways, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar’s question, “Are there any troubles?” is appropriate.

Thus, when Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar asks if there is any harm or suffering to her brother, the servant who had come replies. suffering. She considered it a blessing that would bring divine grace to her brother.

Therefore, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar asking, “Are there any troubles?” is appropriate in both ways. That is, the trouble that came here is a blessing, so asking “Are you well?” and asking “Are there any troubles?” become equivalent.

Moreover, the Lord had already appeared in her dream and blessed her, told her.

Therefore, Ammaiyar already knew that colic was going to come upon her brother. So, in both these ways, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar’s question, “Are there any troubles?” is appropriate.

Thus, when Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar asks if there is any harm or suffering to her brother, the servant who had come replies. That verse is the one thousand three hundred and forty-second verse, the fifty-seventh verse in the Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam: “Kollaathu soolai noy kudar mudakki theeraamai ellaarum kaivittar idhu seyal en mun pirandha nallaazhpaal sendru iyambi naan oyyumbadi kettuingu al aagum pozhudhu anaivaay endru arivithaan.” This is that verse, that is, the verse that forms the servant’s reply. How does this verse begin? “Kollaathu soolai noy kudar mudakki theeraamai ellaarum kaivittar.” The first two lines of this verse describe Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s condition. The servant says, “Your brother has been afflicted with colic. It has twisted his intestines and is an incurable disease within him.

“It has spared your brother’s life, that is, it has not killed him. It is only at that level. Otherwise, all sufferings, however intensely they can cause suffering, are being caused intensely. It is only not killing him,” he says.

“Therefore, it begins with “Kollaathu” (it does not kill). She asked if any harm had befallen him. In reply, he says, “Yes, there is harm; it is a terrible colic, but its harm has not reached the extent of taking his life,” he announces first. That is, Your brother has been afflicted with colic. It has twisted his intestines and is an incurable disease within him. It has spared your brother’s life, that is, it has not killed him.

“It is only at that level. Otherwise, all sufferings, however intensely they can cause suffering, are being caused intensely. It is only not killing him,” he says.

“Therefore, it begins with “Kollaathu” (it does not kill). She asked if any harm had befallen him. In reply, he says, “Yes, there is harm; it is a terrible colic, but its harm has not reached the extent of taking his life,” he announces first. That is, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar asks about her younger brother with great sorrow and concern, asking if any harm has befallen him.

“Therefore, to alleviate her mental distress, he first announces, “Kollaathu soolai noy” (the colic does not kill). That is, he announces the news that he has colic but it has not reached the extent of taking his life, thereby alleviating Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar’s mental distress. The servant who had come, the one who had the great fortune of performing the sacred service of preparing food for Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, his servant, the servant who had come.

“So, need we speak of his eloquence?

“Furthermore, the servant says, “Ellarum kaivittanar” (everyone has abandoned him), referring to the followers of the religion to which Thirunavukkarasu Peruman belonged. All the gurus tried and gave up; all medicines, mantras, and those skilled in them also gave up, he says.

“Therefore, the messenger says, ‘Your younger brother told me this: that he has been afflicted with colic and is suffering greatly, and everyone has given up. Go to my elder sister, that good lady, tell her this, ask for a way for me to be saved, and return here before nightfall.’ This is what Marulneekiyar, Dharmasenar, told the messenger, and the messenger is now relaying this message to Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman says, ‘I am suffering in this way, so go to my elder sister, that good lady, and tell her.’ He says, ‘Go and tell her.’ He says, ‘My elder sister, that good lady.’ Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar was born before Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman.

“Similarly, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar’s devotion to Shiva is worthy of precedence. The implication here is that Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar, unlike me, did not wander in the Jain religion but remains a good person. Thiru-Navukkarasar Peruman says, ‘I was born later and wandered into a foreign religion.

“Therefore, I am an evil person worthy of standing behind. But my elder sister, that good lady Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar, did not join a foreign religion like me but remained steadfast in the Shaiva religion and is a good lady worthy of standing before me.’ To such a good lady, I Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman told the messenger, ‘Ask for a way to be saved and come here tonight.’ And the messenger relayed it exactly as it was said. We must remember one thing: the time the messenger departed from Paadali-puthiram was also night. Thiru-Navukkarasar told the messenger to return at night after meeting Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar again. This is because Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman thought that the cruel Jains there should not know about these events. If they were to find out, that is, if the Jains knew that this servant had gone as a messenger to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s sister on his behalf, then the servant’s life would be in danger.

“It would be lost. The Jains, who superficially preach non-killing, are also capable of murder.

“Therefore, fearing this, Thiru-Navukkarasar instructed the servant to leave Paadali-puthiram at night and return the following night.

“Similarly, later, when Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman departed from Paadali-puthiram and reached Thiru-Adhigai, it was also at night. We should remember this here.

“Later, after joining the Shaiva religion, when Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman was in Thiru-Adhigai, and the king of that country summoned Thiru-Navukkarasar at the instigation of the Jains, he stood before him without fear. This is because at that time, after attaining Shiva, it was the nature of his steadfastness.

“Now, however, he is in the Jain religion. He said.

“Therefore, he is afraid in this manner. After rejoining the Shaiva religion, loving Shiva, and attaining Shiva, due to the steadfastness of that love for Him, Thiru-Navukkarasar Peruman then stood without fear of the king’s command. We must remember that here.

“In this way, the messenger came as an envoy and told Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar. What was Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar’s reply to that?

“Let us go on pondering.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Two Hundred and Ninety. Thiru-Nindra-Charukkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. The messenger who came from Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman tells Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar about Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s suffering and his request for a way to be saved, for grace to be bestowed. Hearing this, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar replies to the messenger.

Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar says to the messenger, ‘Those Jains who do not know what is good, those Jains who do not stand in the right path, I will not come to the abode of such Jains, to the place of the Jains. I will not come with you to the place of the Jains. You go and tell this to my brother.’ Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar says, ‘Go and tell him.’ When Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar says, ‘I will not come there,’ the implication is, ‘Tell him to come here.’ This is the unspoken message.

Therefore, the messenger returns to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman and says, ‘Your sister says she will not come here.’ Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman understands this hidden meaning. That is, if his sister says she will not come here, it means he must go there. Understanding this, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman journeys from Paadali-puthiram towards Thiru-Adhigai.

Therefore, the ability and grace to understand the true meaning of his sister’s reply were present in him. The point we see here is that it was present in him. Even though his younger brother was afflicted with a terrible disease, Thilagavathiyar’s courage in not going to the place where evil Jains live, even to see her suffering brother, and considering it improper to do so, is a discipline that all of us should observe and follow. What did the messenger truly think when he came here? What did Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman tell him to do? Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman had told the messenger to tell the sister the news and bring her here.

Therefore, the messenger also came here, delivered the message, and intended to take Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar with him and unite her with Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. The messenger had come to Thiru-Adhigai.

But Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar, contrary to their expectations, firmly says, ‘I will not come there.’ The messenger, having received this reply, goes to Paadali-puthiram that night, as instructed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, meets Thiru-Navukkarasar, and conveys this message: ‘Your sister said she would not come here.’ Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman understands the true meaning of his sister’s reply and decides that he must now go to where Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar is. Initially, upon hearing those words, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman became disheartened and wondered what he would do now.

At that moment, the divine grace of Shiva manifested.

Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s heart He feels an emotion. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman thinks that he will go and reach the sacred feet of Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar, who stands in the righteous path of Shaivism, so that this suffering, which came from joining this unsuitable Jain religion, may cease. Initially, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman was disheartened by the news that his sister refused to come.

Therefore, he became weary. He despaired, ‘What will I do now to alleviate my suffering?’ At that moment, the divine grace of Shiva manifests there. The divine grace of Shiva unites with Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. Due to this union of Shiva’s divine grace, the thought arises in Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s mind that he will leave this Jain religion and reach the sacred feet of Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar, who is in the Shaiva path. This thought arises in Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s mind due to the union of Shiva’s divine grace.

Now, a common question will arise: if Shiva’s divine grace is uniting now, and this thought came to his mind, is there ever a time when Shiva’s divine grace is not with living beings? Is there a time when Shiva’s divine grace is not with living beings? It is not so. The Lord’s divine grace is always united with all living beings.

But it exists as the Thirodhana Shakti, the veiling power. Sekkizhar Peruman states here that it is the transformation into the Arul Shakti, the grace power, that has united. That is, as far as Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman is concerned, he joined the Jain religion. He engaged in Jain asceticism there, and he became a Jain guru there. To return from that Jain religion to the Shaiva religion, he experienced the colic disease that afflicted him as ‘the fire of fate’ and suffered. Until now, the Lord’s veiling power (Thirodhana Shakti) was with him.

That too is the Lord’s power. This Thirodhana Shakti, which was present until now, has now transformed into the Arul Shakti (grace power). It has transformed into the Arul Shakti and united with Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. The religion that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman truly found agreeable, that is, acceptable, was the Jain religion before.

Now, it is considered a foreign religion and an unacceptable religion. That truth is now revealed to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman by the divine grace of the Lord. As it is revealed, he gains the courage to leave the inferior Jain religion and join the sacred feet of Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar. The colic disease seems to be the reason for this. The suffering caused by the colic disease and the colic disease itself appear to be a reason on the surface.

But in reality, the colic disease is not the reason for the thought of returning from the Jain religion to the Shaiva religion that arose in Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. The divine grace of the Lord, who sent that colic disease, is the reason. It was due to the divine grace of the Lord that the colic disease afflicted Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, and he suffered.

Therefore, because of that, he now returns to the Shaiva religion.

Therefore, the colic disease is merely an external appearance. In reality, it is due to the divine grace that sent that colic disease that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman now has the thought of joining the sacred feet of Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar. This courage and this thought are the truth he perceived as revealed by divine grace. The colic disease merely served as an instrument for the event of divine grace.

Therefore, we must clearly understand here that the change that came to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman is not like the changes people make now, moving from one religion to another with the intention of curing their diseases. Because generally, ordinary people now Diseases come. These are diseases that come due to past karma. People now move from one religion to another, change, to get rid of diseases that come due to their accumulated karma (Prarabdha karma).

But we must clearly understand here that the religious change undertaken by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman was not such a change. Because the colic disease that afflicted Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman did not come due to his karma. It did not come due to his Prarabdha karma. It came due to the divine grace of Shiva. This is the very big difference between other living beings and Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman.

Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman suffered from colic, stomach pain. So, to relieve it Sivakavimani Ayyavargal emphasizes that it should not be simply understood that he came from Jainism to Shaivism.

Therefore, the colic pain that afflicted Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, his suffering due to it, and his coming from Jainism to Shaivism were all events that occurred due to the divine grace of the Lord.

Furthermore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman reflects that all the Jain gurus tried mantras, tantras, and so on, but they were all ineffective and failed.

Therefore, the philosophical truth that this world is operated by a power superior to them also becomes clear to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman.

Therefore, not remaining in such an inferior, false religion as Jainism, but in the righteous path of Shaivism Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman realizes the life of Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar, who lives in the Shaiva path, her steadfastness, and her adherence to the Shaiva path, due to the union of the Lord’s divine grace.

Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman thinks that he too should stand in the righteous path of Shaivism, which Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar stood in, attain that Shaiva path, and receive great blessings.

Therefore, he considered that he should join a guru to remove his mistakes and make him attain Shiva.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman decides not to think of joining Shiva’s feet, but to take Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar as his guru and join her sacred feet. Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar also stands in such a guru’s position, guides Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, and brings him into the Shaiva path. This is the history we are about to see.

We shall continue pondering. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Two Hundred and Ninety-One. Thiru-Nindra-Charukkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. When his elder sister, Thilagavathiyar, stated that she could not come to his dwelling, that she could not come to the place of the Jains, Thiru-Navukkarasar, also known as Dharmasenar and Marulneekiyar, decided that he must go to the sacred feet of Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar. The moment he thought of going to Thiru-Adhigai, of joining Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar, of attaining her sacred feet, a little of his weariness left him.

Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman made an effort to reach Thiru-Adhigai.

At that time, his exhaustion diminished slightly, not completely. The colic disease was not completely cured or removed, but it receded slightly, not causing Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman extreme suffering.

Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman attempts to go to Thiru-Adhigai even with the colic disease. His current state is that he is a guru in the Jain religion.

Therefore, he possesses the water pot, peacock feather, and other items that Jain gurus always carry.

Now, as soon as he thought of going to the Thiru-Adhigai Thiru-Sthalam, the Jain symbols such as the mat, water pot, and peacock feather, which are the hallmarks of Jains, disappeared, and Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sets out to go to Thiru-Adhigai. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sets out. This is because these Jain garbs would be obstacles to reaching the Thiru-Adhigai Thiru-Sthalam. One should not go to the Thiru-Adhigai Thiru-Sthalam wearing such Jain garbs.

Therefore, he set out for the Thiru-Adhigai Thiru-Sthalam, shedding these Jain symbols.

Here, Sekkizhar Peruman did not sing that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman ‘shed’ the Jain symbols, but that they ‘disappeared.’ Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman did not make great efforts to shed these symbols. Sekkizhar Peruman uses the word ‘disappeared’ to indicate that as soon as he thought of reaching Thiru-Adhigai, the Jain symbols vanished on their own, falling away by themselves. Nayanar, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, by reaching Thiru-Adhigai, those false Jain garbs disappeared from him. Not only that, but the Jain garbs worn by other people in the world also disappeared. This is another point here.

Therefore, to make himself worthy of reaching the Thiru-Adhigai Thiru-Sthalam, he abandoned the garbs he had previously worn. Leaving all those, he now approaches, allowing a white cloth to envelop his body. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, having abandoned the Jain garbs, wore a pure white garment. This white color is a color associated with purity and fame.

Therefore, with a white garment on his sacred body, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sets out. This is because he is going to the Thiru-Adhigai Thiru-Sthalam. The rule is that one must go to Thiru-Sthalams wearing the attire of an ascetic, suitable for performing penance.

Therefore, it is also known to us here that one should not go to Thiru-Sthalams with other garbs, without such ascetic attire. Generally, in the Shaiva religion, ascetics wear red garments. For Shaivites other than ascetics, the appropriate and suitable attire and color is white. Specifically, it is known to us through this that those who go to Thiru-Sthalams should wear such white garments. The rule is that one should not wear garments of other colors. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sets out, wrapping this white cloth around his body.

He is suffering from the severity of the ailment, and therefore cannot properly wear the garment. So, he somehow wraps it around his body and departs.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman sings that he goes, wrapped in a white cloth. Generally, the word ‘pudavai’ (cloth) was once a general term for clothing.

However, nowadays, it mostly refers to the attire worn by women. But in earlier times, ‘pudavai’ was used in the general sense of a garment to be worn.

Thus, he resolved to go to Thiru-Adigai Thiru-Sthalam and set forth. His weariness slightly abated, and he gained more resolve. Leaving the place of the false religion, Jainism, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman journeys, becoming one who attains the good path of Shiva Peruman, who bestows truth, and accordingly, wrapping a white cloth around his body. Due to the severe colic, he cannot walk alone.

Therefore, with helpers accompanying him, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sets out. Leaning on those who support him, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman departs. He leaves at night so that no Jains can see him. In that state of weakness, unable to walk on his own due to the colic. With the help of those who support him, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman proceeds, leaning on their strength.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman walks with the help of others. Having set out in this manner, he reaches Thiru-Adigai, where great ascetics who perform penance reside. In Thiru-Adigai, great ascetics live. The penance they perform is a worthy penance.

Therefore, ‘Maathavar’ here means those who possess penance.

Thus, Thiru-Adigai Veera-Ttaanam is a Thiru-Sthalam where great ascetics live. The Kural states that penance is for those who have performed penance.

Accordingly, even to perform penance, one must have performed penance before. Such great souls. Thiru-Adigai Veera-Ttaanam is the Thiru-Sthalam where they reside.
