In this, the “Kootraayina Vaaru” Thiru-Pathikam possesses the qualities of being a poetic Thiru-Pathikam, a blossoming Thiru-Pathikam, a pure Tamil Thiru-Pathikam, a sweet-worded Thiru-Pathikam, a powerful Thiru-Pathikam, and a garland-like Thiru-Pathikam. The first attribute is “paavuru Thiru-Pathikam” (poetic Thiru-Pathikam), because this Thiru-Pathikam is a Thiru-Pathikam that fully adheres to the poetic rules of Tamil grammar. All the Thiru-Pathikams composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman are Thiru-Pathikams that are entirely structured according to the rules of Tamil grammar, following the grammatical conventions of Tamil. “Paavutru”

As it comes, “alarnda,” we have seen the explanation for “paa uruthal.” Now, the ethereal voice states that this is a “alarnda Thiru-Pathikam,” a Thiru-Pathikam with the quality of blossoming. “Alarthal” means that the meaning is not confined within the words but expands further and further. The words and their meanings continue to expand.

Next, the attribute “Senthamizh” (pure Tamil) appears in the Thiru-Pathikams composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. “Senthamizh” refers to a Thiru-Pathikam that adheres to Tamil literary grammar and is composed without the use of colloquialisms or other dialects.

Next, “Insol” (sweet words) is mentioned as another quality of this Thiru-Pathikam. “Insol” means a Thiru-Pathikam with sweet words. Not only is the word sweet, but the sweetness of meaning is also abundantly present in this Thiru-Pathikam.

Next, this Thiru-Pathikam is said to be a powerful Thiru-Pathikam. “Vanmai” means richness or abundance. Richness means a Thiru-Pathikam that is full of inexhaustible words and meanings. It is rich in both word and meaning, never diminishing no matter how much it is drawn upon.

Furthermore, just as it was then, so it is now and forever, this pathikam fulfills the requests of those who sing, recite, and supplicate it, granting them benefits without fail. Next comes “Thodai.” This is a garlanded pathikam, hence “Thodai.” It is garlanded as ten verses, hence it is called “Thodai.” Thus, Sivakavimani Aiyya explains the phrase “paavutru alar senthamizhin sol vala pathika thodai” as an attribute to the Thiru-Pathikam beginning with “Kootraayina Vaaru,” sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. Because our Nayanar sang such a glorious, flawless, and enduring Thiru-Pathikam, the Lord bestowed upon him the name Navukkarasu. Navukkarasu is the name given to the Nayanar by the Lord. The Thiru-Pathikam “Kootraayina Vaaru,” bestowed by the Lord, earned him this name. That is why our Sekkizhar Peruman thus expounds the greatness of that Thiru-Pathikam.

Therefore, the Lord bestows the name Navukkarasu upon our Marul Neekkiyar, our Nayanar.

Furthermore, the Lord blesses that this name, Navukkarasu, shall endure and be glorious throughout the seven worlds. “Nannuga” in the seven worlds means that whoever in any world praises this name, Navukkarasu, shall be saved. We are also going to see the history of Appoothi Nayanar, who was saved by praising this sacred name, Navukkarasu.

Therefore, the truth obtained from the Thiru-Thondar Thogai is that the sacred names of the Nayanmars themselves are capable of protecting and saving those who praise them.

Similarly, we have contemplated the history of how the Lord bestowed the sacred name “Van Thondan” upon Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, and by that divine grace, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sang the first Thiru-Pathikam, “Piththa Pirai Soodi.” We can recall that here as well.

Therefore, just as the Lord bestowed the name Van Thondan upon Sundaramoorthy Swamigal and graced him to sing the first Thiru-Pathikam, “Piththa Pirai Soodi,” so now, by virtue of the first Thiru-Pathikam sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, the Lord bestows upon him the name Navukkarasu.

Therefore, it is our Saivite tradition that the names of our religious preceptors themselves are capable of protecting and saving those who praise them. Just as the Lord has the Five Letters, so too do the names of our religious preceptors, Thiru-Navukkarasu, Gnanasambandar, and Nambi Aaroorar, possess five letters. Thiru-Navukkarasu, Gnanasambandar, Nambi, If we count the letters in the sacred names “Yaroorar” after removing the single letters, there will be five letters.

Therefore, we should remember that just like the sacred Five Letters of the Lord, the sacred names of our religious preceptors also consist of five letters, and we should praise the names of our preceptors.

Thus, the ethereal voice arose in the sky, to the astonishment of all, saying, “May the auspicious name Thiru-Navukkarasu be bestowed upon you, and may that name be fitting and endure throughout the seven worlds.” Therefore, this name, Thiru-Navukkarasu, is a name bestowed upon our Nayanar by the Lord Himself. That is why Sekkizhar Peruman, even when beginning the Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam, places that name, bestowed by the Lord upon the Nayanar, first, saying, “Thiru-Navukkarasu valar Thiru-Thondin neri vaazha.” The name Vaakeesar was our Nayanar’s name in a previous birth. Marul Neekkiyar was the name given by his parents. Dharma Senar was the name given to Marul Neekkiyar by the Jains when he joined the Jain faith. Thirunavukkarasar is a descriptive name given by the Lord due to the richness of his sweet Tamil words.

Appar is the name given by Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman.

Thus, the Lord Himself bestowed the name Thirunavukkarasu upon our Nayanar.

Therefore, our Nayanar, the king of the tongue’s language and a devotee, contemplating the great compassion of the Lord, thought, “For so long, I harbored evil deeds in my mind. How could I, such a wicked person, attain such a great blessing? Is this great blessing truly worthy of me?” and worshipped the Lord.

We shall proceed with our reflection.

I had only evil deeds in my mind for so long. How could I, such a wicked person, attain such a great blessing? Is this great blessing truly worthy of me?“ and worshipped the Lord.

We shall continue our reflection.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Three Hundred, Thirunindracharukkam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We reflected on how the Lord bestowed the name Thiru-Navukkarasu upon our Nayanar, and thereafter, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, contemplating the Lord’s compassion, prostrated himself in worship. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, melting with emotion, worshipped the Lord, thinking, “Am I worthy of attaining such a blessing?” Knowing the true nature of the Lord’s great grace, which extends even to Ravana, he prostrated himself before the Lord, taking it as his duty to praise the Lord’s power. He melted with emotion, thinking, “How am I worthy of receiving such great compassion, I who for so long harbored only evil in my mind?” He contemplated the boundless greatness of Lord Shiva’s grace and his own boundless insignificance.

As he contemplated thus, he realized that such grace is indeed the greatness of the Lord’s divine grace, and that the greatness of the Lord’s divine grace is such that it embraced even Ravana, who had committed an offense against Shiva. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, having been in the Jain faith without knowing the greatness of Lord Shiva and having committed a mistake, now found that the Lord had also graced him.

Similarly, he remembered and worshipped the Lord’s greatness and the nature of His divine grace, knowing that Lord Shiva had also graced Ravana, who, like himself, had committed the offense of not knowing Lord Shiva’s greatness. What was that compassionate act of grace shown to Ravana? What was that compassionate power of the Lord? Ravana was one who had insulted the Lord Himself and committed a great offense. Nevertheless, when he approached and praised Lord Shiva, our Lord Shiva forgave his offense against Shiva. Not only that, but Lord Shiva, the greatly compassionate one, also bestowed upon Ravana the Chandrahasam sword and a lifespan of three and a half crores of years.

Ravana had performed severe penance and received many boons.

Therefore, he was arrogant about his strength. He traveled in his chariot to many directions.

Similarly, he went towards Mount Kailash in his chariot. Mount Kailash was in his way.

Therefore, upon Mount Kailash, He attempted to drive his chariot through the aerial path of Mount Kailash. He tried to pass over Mount Kailash from his chariot.

At that time, Ravana’s charioteer warned and stopped him. But without listening, he drove his chariot swiftly. He attempted to fly through the sky over Mount Kailash.

At that time, the chariot was stopped by the command of Thiru-Nandi Devar.

Therefore, Ravana, in anger, tried to uproot Mount Kailash, saying, “I will uproot this Mount Kailash, which obstructs my chariot.” He tried to uproot Mount Kailash with his ten mighty arms.

At that time, Lord Shiva, with just a slight pressure of His toe on His sacred feet, As soon as he pressed it, Ravana was trapped and crushed beneath Mount Kailash, losing his strength, and wept for a long time. That is why he was named Ravana, the one who weeps.

Thus, Ravana was trapped beneath Mount Kailash for a long time, suffering and weeping.

At that time, the sage Vaakeesar was performing penance there. It is said that this sage Vaakeesar is now incarnated as Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. Such a sage Vaakeesar was circumambulating Mount Kailash. Seeing Ravana suffering in distress, he took pity on Ravana.

At that time, with compassion that Ravana should escape from that suffering, he told Ravana, “Shankaran is fond of Sama Gana, so you can please the Lord with music.” The sage Vaakeesar revealed the means to escape the offense against Shiva that Ravana had committed. Ravana, too, accordingly, took out his nerves, made them into a veena, and sang the Sama Veda. Lord Shiva, the Lord, out of compassion, appeared and blessed Ravana, granting him a lifespan of three and a half crores of years. That very sage Vaakeesar, who advised Ravana, is now incarnated as Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman.

Therefore, because of his connection to his previous birth’s history, and contemplating the compassion the Lord showed to Ravana, he melts with emotion and praises the Lord, realizing that the Lord has shown him similar compassion. Just as He graced Ravana, who committed the offense against Shiva, Lord Shiva has also graced him, who joined the Jain faith and committed the offense of insulting. This is His nature. And just as He graced Ravana, who committed an offense, and showed him the way to escape that offense, so too does He grace him who committed an offense. This is the true nature of Lord Shiva’s divine grace. Knowing this, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman here praises the Lord.

Appar Swamigal, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, has sung this history of Ravana in the tenth verse of most of his Thiru-Pathikams.

Therefore, in most of the tenth verses of our Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s Thiru-Pathikams, we can see him singing about Ravana.

Similarly, in the Thiru-Pathikams of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, a similar arrangement can be found. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman has sung about Ravana in the eighth verse of his Thiru-Pathikams. In the first Thiru-Pathikam, “Kootraayina Vaaru,” composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, which we saw, we can also recall that in the tenth verse, he sang, “Aarthaan arakkan thannai maal varai keezh adarthittu arul seytha athu karuthaay.” Similarly, in the general Thiru-Pathikam, Dasapuranam, the tenth verse; in the Payattur Thiru-Pathikam, the tenth verse; in the Thiru-Pukalur Thiru-Pathikam, the tenth verse; and in many other Thiru-Pathikams, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman has sung about this history of Ravana and the Lord’s grace upon him in the tenth verse.

Therefore, among the Thiru-Pathikams of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, Except for a few Thiru-Pathikams, in all other Thiru-Pathikams, in the Thiru-Kadaikaappu (that is, the tenth verse), we can find the history that speaks of Ravana lifting Mount Kailash, suffering, and then receiving grace by singing to the Lord.

Thus, when Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman suffered from colic disease and came to Thiru-Athikai Thiru-Veerattanam, Thilakavathi Ammaiyar, reciting the sacred ash and the sacred Five Letters, gave them to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. When he entered the temple and sang the Thiru-Pathikam “Kootraayina Vaaru,” his colic disease was cured.

Then, his heart melted with emotion, contemplating the Lord’s divine compassion, and he praised the Lord.

At that time, Lord Shiva Himself, as an ethereal voice, bestowed the name Thiru-Navukkarasu upon our Nayanar. Recalling that compassion, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman offered praise.

Thus, as the path of the Jains was ruined and destroyed, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman came here and received grace, and thereby this world was saved. So, the devotees of Shiva gathered from all sides in the great city of Thiru-Adigai. Drums, tambourines, udukkai, mridangam, yazh, mulavam, kilai, thundhubhi, and bells resounded everywhere. Conches blared everywhere. Shiva Peruman, the great one praised by the Three, the Devas, and all others, is praised even by the secular text Silappathikaram as ‘the great one of unborn form.’ Thus, by the grace of Shiva Peruman, who is praised even by secular religions, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman came here and received grace, and thereby the world was saved.

Thus, the devotees of Shiva celebrated. The grace received by a good person means that all who see him as a guide will receive that grace. And with the belief that the Saiva religion, by attaining a Paramacharya, saved this world, the devotees of Shiva praised there and continue to praise even now.

Therefore, as a symbol of this, the sound of various instruments arose here, as Sekkizhar Peruman mentions. The instruments mentioned above resounded individually. Many conches gathered and were blown in sequence. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, who emerged from the confusing secular path of Jainism, and whose greatness grew with joy, performed Shiva Thiru-Thondhu with his mind, speech, and body. He began to perform Shiva Thiru-Thondhu.

Therefore, he adorned himself with the appropriate Shiva symbols: Thiru-Neeru and Rudraksha. The Thiru-Thondhu that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman performed was a true service, performed with mind and truth. Thiru-Thondhus must be performed with the mind, speech, and body united.

Furthermore, Shiva Thiru-Thondhus should not be performed without wearing the Shiva symbols of Thiru-Neeru and Rudraksha.

Therefore, with Thiru-Neeru and Kandigai (Rudraksha) shining on his sacred body, and with his mind, speech, and body united, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman performs that Thiru-Thondhu. We see that he performed Thiru-Thondhu with these three instruments—mind, speech, and body—united. What he did in his mind signifies his constant meditative awareness of Shiva Peruman. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman is one whose mind is fixed and united with Shiva Peruman, the Lord.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, whose mind is fixed and united with Shiva Peruman, attains a state of unwavering devotion to Shiva Peruman. He remains in that state of awareness. This is what he did with his mind.

Now, with his sacred speech, he bestows many Thiru-Pathigams that arise continuously and ascend higher. This is the service Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman rendered with his speech. What occurs in speech is the word, that which is Sekkizhar Peruman here refers to as ‘Thiru-Vasagam that arises without end.’ This refers to the Thevara Thiru-Pathigams bestowed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. It is mentioned here as ‘Thiru-Pathigam that arises without end.’ ‘Thiru-Pathigam that arises without end’ means that as soon as one verse in a Thiru-Pathigam ends, the next song follows. As soon as one Thiru-Pathigam ends, another Thiru-Pathigam begins.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman continuously sings these Thiru-Pathigams with his sacred speech, as if speaking from his prior memory. Our Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar continuously sang and bestowed Thiru-Pathigams like this, always. That is why it is recorded in history that he sang a total of forty-nine thousand Thiru-Pathigams. “Ezh-ezhu-nooru irum panuval eenravan Thiru-Navinukku Arasan” (He who begot seven times seven hundred great compositions, the King of Sacred Tongue) is from Sundaramoorthy Swamigal’s Thiru-Nindriyur Thiru-Pathigam. “Pathigam ezh-ezhu-nooru pagaruma kavi yogi” (The Yogi who speaks seven times seven hundred Pathigams) is from Nambiandar Nambigal’s Thiru-Ekadasa Malai.

Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman continuously bestowed Thiru-Pathigams through his sacred tongue. This is why he was able to bestow a total of forty-nine thousand Thiru-Pathigams.

Thus, we have seen the Thiru-Thondhus Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman performed with his mind and speech.

Now, our Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman also performs Thiru-Thondhu with his body, with his physical self. He always sat with an Uzhavarappadai in his sacred hands. This Uzhavarappadai served as the sacred symbol of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. This Uzhavarappadai served as his emblem. With the help of this Uzhavarappadai, he performed Uzhavara service in the Thiru-Koyils where Shiva Peruman resides. He removed unnecessary items, such as straw and stones, from the streets inside the Thiru-Koyil, the Thiru-Sutrus, and the streets outside the Thiru-Koyil, and always carried this Uzhavarappadai, the tool for cleaning the sacred streets, in his hands.

He traveled to various sacred places and performed this Uzhavara Thiru-Thondhu as his physical service.

Thus, our Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, with his mind always continuously fixed on Shiva Peruman, with the Thiru-Pathigams arising ceaselessly from his speech, through the Thevara Thiru-Pathigams, and by performing Uzhavara service with his body, performed Shiva Thiru-Thondhu with all three instruments: mind, speech, and body. Adorning his entire sacred body with Thiru-Neeru and Rudraksha, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar thus served with his hands, melting and overflowing with devotion.

Thus, Thilagavathiyar sees Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar performing Thiru-Thondhu with his mind, speech, and body in Thiru-Adigai. We must also remember here that Thilagavathiyar herself, in a similar manner, stood in the path of Chariyai and performed Thiru-Thondhu with her mind, speech, and body.

Thus, she sees her prayer, that her younger brother Marulneekiyar should return to the Saiva religion, fulfilled. She sees her desire fulfilled. She sees that Shiva Peruman has bestowed a boon. Thilagavathiyar, the female ascetic, had prayed to Shiva Peruman, saying, ‘You must take charge of my younger brother who came after me.’ She had asked for a boon that her younger brother Marulneekiyar should find peace. Thinking of the immense compassion with which the Lord had granted a boon beyond what she had asked, beyond the measure she had requested, Thilagavathiyar prayed to the Lord, saying, ‘Who else here has received such grace, as if He has taken even us, who are so small, as worthy objects and taken us into His service?’ Great people who have received the Lord’s grace, reflecting on the immense greatness of the grace they have received, praise it and revel in that grace. Manikkavasagar Peruman sings, “Arabu ammayanakku aruliyavaaru aatr peruvaar achchove” (How can others receive the grace that was bestowed upon me, a woman, alas!).

Thilagavathiyar had prayed to the Lord, saying, “Just as you have taken me into your service, you must also take my younger brother into your service.” Accepting her prayer, the Lord reveals in a dream that He will bestow the disease of colic upon her brother and take him into His service. Accordingly, when the disease of colic was given, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, leaving the Jain religion, came here and received Thiru-Neeru, chanted with the five letters, from the sacred hands of Thilagavathiyar, the female ascetic. As Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sang the Thiru-Pathigam “Kootraayina Vaaru,” the disease of colic disappeared by the grace of the Lord.

The Lord Himself bestowed the name Thiru-Navukkarasu upon our Nayanar.

Thus, melting with emotion, contemplating the compassion with which the Lord took him into His service, Thilagavathiyar, the female ascetic, asked, “Who else here has received this grace that I have received?” Melting with devotion, she praised and worshipped the Lord.

Thus, Thilagavathiyar, who had been living in this manner, shed her bonds of attachment, worshipped the Lord alone, stood firm in the path of Shiva, performed penance, and attained Shiva, as Sekkizhar Peruman concludes and sings the sacred history of Thilagavathiyar here: “Meimai pani seytha veruppu athanaal vinnor thani nayakanaar kadalil tham ichchai niramba varamperum aththanmai pathimeviya thaapathiyaar poimai samaya pini vittu avar munpothum pini vittu aruli porula emmai pani kol karunai thiram ingu yaar petranar enna irainjinare” (Because of the true service she performed, the unique Lord of the heavens, in the ocean of His grace, granted her desire fully. The ascetic, having attained that state, abandoned the false bonds of religion and, having been freed from the former bonds, prayed, ‘Who here has received the power of grace that takes us into service as a worthy object?’).

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman sings.

Therefore, Thilagavathiyar, the female ascetic, thus shed her bonds of attachment. Sekkizhar Peruman concludes the history of Thilagavathiyar in this song, showing that she worshipped at Thiru-Adigai Veerattanam, stood firm in the path of Shiva, performed penance, and attained Shiva.

Thus, at this point, the section on the history of Thilagavathiyar in the Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam concludes. We will continue to contemplate the Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Three Hundred and One, Thiru-Nindrachcharukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman thus attained the path of Shiva and, having received the immense grace of Shiva Peruman, was freed from suffering, was he not? The Jains in the city called Pataliputra heard all these tidings. The city of Pataliputra mentioned here is a city that was in Tamil Nadu. The city of Pataliputra in the north, which was established in North India during the time of Gautama Buddha and served as the capital for Buddhist kings like Ashoka, was a very large city for Buddhists.

According to that memory, the Jains here in the south established a Pataliputra near Thiru-Padiripuliyur in Cuddalore district, which is currently Thiru- Thiru-Padiripuliyur. We have already contemplated that the Jains here established a Pataliputra near Thiru-Padiripuliyur in Cuddalore district, and there they established Jain schools and monasteries and reigned.

Therefore, the city where Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman joined the Saiva path and engaged in religious service was Thiru-Adigai. The Jains in Pataliputra hear and learn about all these events that took place in this city. We must also remember here that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, as Dharmasenar, was formerly in Pataliputra before coming to Thiru-Adigai. The Jain gurus in such a Pataliputra hear that Thiru-Navukkarasu has joined the Saiva religion, been cured of colic, and is performing sacred service. They could not tolerate it. Jains are those who preach non-violence, patience, and other virtues, yet they are people who do not possess this patience themselves, lacking even a little bit of the quality of patience.

The incurable colic that afflicted Dharmasenar while he was in their Jain religion was cured after he joined the Saiva religion. If Dharmasenar had remained, what should he have done? They should have truly rejoiced at the well-being of other beings and at the removal of their suffering and their happiness. If they were truly acting according to their religious principles, they should have rejoiced.

But instead, the Jains became envious when they learned that the colic that afflicted Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman had been cured. Just as it is said, ‘A change in character indicates impending ruin,’ the time had come for these Jains to be destroyed.

Therefore, they were overcome by evil qualities such as envy. The severe colic that afflicted Dharmasenar remained incurable despite all the efforts of the Jains here.

Therefore, in order to be cured of that disease, Dharmasenar went there, became a Saivite, and was relieved of his affliction. Because of this, the Jains became disheartened, thinking that their great religion, Jainism, had fallen. On this very day, their Jain religion is about to fall. As if giving a prelude to this, they themselves declare with their own words, ‘Our Jain religion has fallen.’ Now the Jains think that the Jain religion was sustained by Thiru-Navukkarasar, who was named Dharmasenar, having conquered many religions that differed from Jainism. That Jain path, which was so, is now going to be destroyed. This is because Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman left the Jain religion and joined the Saiva religion, and so the Jain path is now going to be destroyed here.

Saying all this, all the Jain gurus gathered together.

Thus, the Jains, who were distressed by shame, gathered among themselves and discussed.

Here, Dharmasenar, having become Thiru-Navukkarasu by joining the Saiva religion and being cured of his affliction, If the king of our country hears about these events, he too will become a Saivite. He will become angry with us and destroy our profession and our religion.

So, what should we do now? the Jains fretted. This is because the king is currently a follower of the Jain religion. The Jains feared that even he would become a Saivite, hearing about the greatness of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. This is because they had been deceiving and deluding the king until now by falsely claiming that their Jain religion possessed unique glories that it did not. If the king were to learn this truth, he would become angry.

Furthermore, the Jains had similarly deluded and deceived the people by telling lies.

Therefore, the Jains feared that the king would also become angry about the royal justice, which states that deceiving people by telling lies is a crime. If the king were to learn that the true religion is the Saiva religion, then leaving the false religion of Jainism, which he had believed to be the true religion until now, and joining the Saiva religion, which he found to be true, would be the first action the king would take. If he were to hear about all these events.

Therefore, before that, the Jains conspired and deceived, deciding that they should go to the king and tell him more lies, deluding him, and continue to live as they are living now. Their means of livelihood. The Jains conspire to prolong the situation, just as the king had supported their means of livelihood until now. Jains are skilled at making the non-existent appear existent and the existent appear non-existent. They are capable of fabricating and presenting anything with falsehoods.

Thus, these Jains decide that they must go and tell the king this news. How should they tell it? They should say that Thiru-Navukkarasar, who was Dharmasenar here, a Jain guru, decided to join his elder sister, Thilagavathiyar. Thilagavathiyar is a Saivite.

Therefore, Dharmasenar himself pretended to have colic, acting out a drama. He pretended that the colic could not be cured by the methods available in the Jain religion. He then dramatically abandoned the tenets of our Jain religion, blasphemed our deities, and went to join his elder sister. They decided to tell the king that he fabricated this colic as a pretense for this. This is because the king was a follower of the Jain religion.

Therefore, if they told the king that Thiru-Navukkarasar had falsely acted, abandoned the Jain religion, left the Jain religion, and blasphemed the deities of the Jain religion, the king would punish him for these two crimes. These two crimes, namely abandoning the Jain religion and blaspheming the deities of the Jain religion, would incur royal punishment. Murder and other acts are also part of the royal and Jain religious tradition.

Therefore, based on this, the Jains conspired to go to the king, tell him such lies, protect their Jain religion, and also ensure that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman received punishment. Having conspired thus, all the Jains decided to go to the king’s palace, saying, ‘We will tell the king exactly this.’ Indeed, before the king could learn about the miracles performed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, they rushed to tell him this false information with the evil intention of protecting the Jain religion and ensuring that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman received punishment.

Therefore, all the Jains, like a dark multitude, went and reached the Pallava city where the king resided, inside the city of Pataliputra.

Here, the Peruman metaphorically refers to the Jains as a ‘dark multitude.’ Darkness has the characteristic of obscuring the true nature of things.

Therefore, he sings that they went like a dark multitude. The place where the king stayed in that city of Pataliputra was called Pallavanagar. There were palaces and other structures there. The place where the Jains’ monasteries and schools were located was different.

Furthermore, the place where citizens and others resided was also different.

Thus, because the city of Pataliputra was structured in this way, the Jain schools in the outskirts, and the Jain gurus, who eat while standing, reached the gate of the king’s palace and told the gatekeepers there, ‘Inform the king that all of us have gathered and come.’ The gatekeepers were also followers of the Jain religion.

Therefore, they were close associates. So, knowing that the Jain gurus had gathered and come, they waited for the opportune moment, went inside, and informed the king. The gatekeepers went to the king and informed him that all the Jain gurus. The guards inform the king that the suffering people have come together and are waiting at the palace gate. The king, who was a follower of the Jain religion, asks his gatekeepers with concern what trouble has befallen them that they have gathered so quickly. He orders the gatekeepers to let them in.

The gatekeepers allow the Jains to enter, and they approach the king. Our reflection now resumes. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 302. The assembled Jains approach the king and complain about Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman. They tell the king that Dharma-sena, their leader, feigned a stomach ailment, acted out a drama, went there, became a devotee of Shiva, and abandoned their religion. Sekkizhar Peruman condemns these Jains as “wandering Jains,” meaning Jains whose only profession is to walk around alive. They have life, they walk; that is the only thing they truly do.

Otherwise, they do not perform righteous deeds that benefit life, nor do they gain any advantage from them. Performing such deeds is the proper creative work for people. The Jains are those who do not engage in any such work. They present all their actions as if they were dharma, speaking as if they were righteous, but in reality, these Jains are those who commit unrighteousness. What do they tell the king? They say that Dharma-sena has abandoned your religion, your Jain religion, and has joined Shaivism.

This is because they are truly the Jain religious leaders, yet they tell the king, “This is your religion.” Therefore, they thought that the king had more right to this religion than they did, and they intended to use the king’s support to carry out all their schemes.

Thus, they speak. The king was swayed by the Jains’ statement. He believed what the Jains said.

So, he addresses the Jains who spoke thus: “Dharma-sena, with a wicked mind, feigned illness to join the Shaiva religion, abandoning our glorious Jain religion. Is this proper? Is this right?

“Therefore, O ascetics of immeasurable penance, what should we do about this?” The king, greatly angered, asks the Jains what should be done regarding Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman. The Jains immediately reply, “Our Jain religion is a most exalted religion. That Dharma-sena, who destroyed such a Jain religion and offended you, O King—” —“You must torment that ignorant man,” they declared without the slightest fear, those cruel Jain ascetics. Truly, they are supposed to live by the principle of non-violence, yet these wicked people, these Amanas, speak in such a way, deviating from it.

“Here, they accuse Dharma-sena, Thiru-navukkarasar, of two crimes: destroying the religious path of Jainism and offending the king. They tell the king that he must torment the one who did this.

“Here, they only said “torment,” but in reality, their intention was to kill, because Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman— —the Jains inflict these four punishments upon him. We are about to see that all four of these punishments are aimed at murder. The Jains, who are truly supposed to adhere to the path of non-violence, give the king wrong advice, suggesting that he should inflict upon Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman a cruel act that is not even fit to be spoken by their mouths. A king should be compassionate and merciful. Without such compassion, he deviates from the good path, mistakes delusion for wisdom, and becomes confused. Justice is established on the basis of compassion, and accordingly, the fundamental quality required of a king— —this emotion is compassion.

“Without the slightest trace of this compassionate feeling, he deviates from the good path. He mistakes something devoid of wisdom for wisdom and becomes deluded. It is common for people to mistake delusion for wisdom. This delusion is the action of the anava mala (ego impurity). This is referred to as marul mayakkam (delusion) or piral unarthal (misperception). Sekkizhar Peruman here refers to that king as a deluded king, a king possessed by marul, because he considers the Jains, who are devoid of wisdom and virtue, to be wise and virtuous, and acts according to their words.

“As prescribed in the Dharma Shastras, a king— —a king should elevate his good wisdom and adhere to its path. But here, that king was swayed by the Jains who deluded him.

“Therefore, without even a trace of wisdom or compassion, the king, in his delusion, acts according to the Jains’ words. This king, who was caught in delusion, then addresses his ministers as follows: “Ministers, you must punish that wicked man according to what these wise Jains have said.

“Therefore, seize that wicked man and bring him here. Do not take money from that wicked man and let him escape. Seize him and bring him here.” He tells the ministers, “I must punish him.” We still see today that kings entrust great and responsible ministers with the task of imprisoning important people. The same custom existed then.

“Therefore, the king orders his ministers to imprison Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman, who was formerly a great guru, a Jain guru, under the name Dharma-sena, when he was in the Jain religion, and bring him back. He also adds, “Do not take money, that is, cash or other valuable items, and let him escape.” This further advises them. It is known that even in those days, those who performed royal duties would accept bribes and neglect their duties, or deviate from their duties. It is known to us that even in those days, as they now call it ‘bribe,’ there was a custom among those who performed royal duties to accept bribes and deviate from their duties.

“Furthermore, there is another meaning here: “Do not consider Thiru-navukkarasu, the great one, to be righteous, to be one who adheres to dharma, to be a good person, and let him go.” There is also room for this interpretation.

“Moreover, the king says, “Do not let him go with minor punishments like fines; imprison him and bring him here. I will punish him myself.” The populace must obey the king’s command and adhere to the rule of justice. One must act in fear of the king’s command and the rule of justice. Not only that, but one must also act in accordance with God’s rule. This was the principle held and the life lived by our ancestors. Without that, letting guilty people escape by taking money from them, or guilty people trying to escape the king’s command by giving money or goods, or trying to escape by blaming others for their own crimes, saying they did not commit them but someone else did, are all wrong actions in the eyes of God’s justice.

“It is very regrettable that these things are developing today. The king’s— —Having received this command, the ministers, along with their armies, with drums beating, reach the city of Thiru-vathikai. It is natural and necessary to go with an army and announce by beating drums when going to imprison great people.

“Thus, the ministers, with their armies, reach the city of Thiru-vathikai, where Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman resides. These ministers go to Thiru-navukkarasar, who is characterized by having severed his attachments to external religions.

“Here, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman as one who has severed his attachments to external religions. “Para-samayam” here refers to the Jain religion. By stating “para-samaya pattu arutha” (severed attachment to external religions), Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman severed his attachment to the Jain religion, which is an external religion. Not only that, but the meaning here also implies that he severed the attachments of other people as well, so that they would not be deluded and suffer in the Jain religion.

“Furthermore, in Tamil, the word “panmai” also carries the meaning of “destiny” or “fate.” Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman was already a sage who had severed all attachments.

“Therefore, the meaning also arises that this act of severing attachments was accomplished with the help of destiny.

“Thus, the king’s ministers and soldiers, who had reached the city of Thiru-vathikai, stand before Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar. They surround Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar, the devotee of Lord Shiva, who is a Brahmin with shining matted locks, and say— —“The king has commanded you to come to him and has sent us here.

“Therefore, come,” they say. “You must come with us immediately. This is an urgent royal command,” they state. “The king has sent us to bring you,” they tell the Nayanar. What does Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar, who possesses perfect penance, say in response?

“Let us go on reflecting.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 303. Thiru-nindra-charukkam. Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. The ministers sent by the king, accompanied by soldiers, surround Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman and tell him that he must come with them immediately to be presented to the king, as it is a royal command. What does Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar say in response?

The 1358th verse, the 93rd verse in Sekkizhar’s composition of Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam, is this: “Naam aarkkum kudi allom” (We are not subjects to anyone), he began, and sang the rich Thiru-thandakam, a garland of sweet Tamil, praising the Lord of the four Vedas, the one with matted locks where the cool moon and river reside, and declared, “We are not of the kind that you can summon.” This is that— —verse.

Thus, the ministers tell him that he must come with them.

Then Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar begins with “Naam aarkkum kudi allom” (We are not subjects to anyone) and graciously declares that he is not of the kind that they can summon, having sung the rich Thiru-thandakam, a garland of sweet Tamil, praising Lord Shiva, the chief of the four Vedas, whose matted locks bear the cool moon and the river Ganga. In response to the ministers’ summons, he recites the Thiru-thandakam hymn, “Naam aarkkum kudi allom.” Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar responds to the king’s summons by saying, “Naam yaarkkum kudi allom” (We are not subjects to anyone). Through the Nayanar’s hymn, “Naam” is plural. Generally, it is customary to say “I” (நான்), but here Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar refers to himself as “we” (நாம்). It is the nature of Shiva’s devotees to bow their heads in servitude only to Shiva and His devotees. Without that, in all other places, except for Shiva’s devotees and Lord Shiva, to stand tall as a servant of Shiva and not bow to anyone else, to signify that pride and valor, our devotees traditionally use the plural “we.” Therefore, Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar says, “Naam aarkkum kudi allom” (We are not subjects to anyone).

When he says “to anyone,” the meaning here is “to anyone except Lord Shiva, the chief, and His devotees.” The meaning of this is “to anyone else.” He says, “kudi allom” (we are not subjects). He says, “Naam yaarkkum kudi allom” (We are not subjects to anyone). “Kudi allom” means “I am not a subject of your king; I am not a citizen of your king’s country.” They say, “The king has summoned you.” Therefore, a king has the right to summon only his subjects. His scepter and rule do not extend to anyone other than the subjects under him. The king’s command is valid only for the subjects within his country’s borders.

But here, Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman says, “I am not a citizen of this country, subject to your king’s command.”

Therefore, implying that your king has no right to summon me, he says, “Naam yaarkkum kudi allom.” Thus, beginning with “Naam aarkkum kudi allom,” he bestows the Thiru-thandakam. This is called “Marumaatru Thiru-thandakam” (The Responding Thiru-thandakam).

In this way, as a reply to them, beginning with “Naam aarkkum kudi allom,” Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar praises and glorifies Lord Shiva and bestows this Thiru-thandakam hymn. He refers to Lord Shiva here as “Naanmaraikku Komanai, Nadiyudan Kulirmathi Vaal Sadaiyanai” (The Lord of the four Vedas, the one with matted locks where the cool moon and river reside). “Naanmaraikku Koman” implies that Lord Shiva is the primal being revealed by the four Vedas and all other scriptures.

Therefore, he is the king of all kings. This implies that he is the king of all kings.

Furthermore, he refers to Lord Shiva as “Nadiyudan Kulirmathi Vaal Sadaiyanai” (the one with matted locks where the cool moon and river reside). The river Ganga and the moon are on Lord Shiva’s matted locks. By sustaining the river Ganga and the moon, Lord Shiva reveals His immense grace.

Similarly, Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar, who came to Lord Shiva, was also blessed with imperishable life by His grace. Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman sings this to indicate that.

Thus, praising Lord Shiva, Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman sings the “Themaalai Senthamizhin Sezhunthiru-thandakam.” The Thiru-thandakam is a type of hymn composed by Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman. This is the first place where the Thiru-thandakam hymn needs to be mentioned.

Therefore, regarding that Thiru-thandakam, he says, “Themaalai Senthamizhin Sezhunthiru-thandakam.” It says “Themaalai.” “Theam” means a word that possesses sweetness and melody. “Maalai” (garland) refers to the characteristic of a poem where many names follow continuously and conclude at one point.

Therefore, this is a “Themaalai.” Not only that, but it is a “Senthamizh Themaalai,” meaning it possesses abundant Tamil sweetness and pleasant meaning, and richness. This is a Thiru-thandakam.

Therefore, this type of poetic meter, which describes the nature of God, is called “Thandakam.” This “Thandakam” refers to the poetic structure and melodic type in which songs are composed.

Therefore, the epithets “Themaalai Senthamizhin Sezhunthiru-thandakam” are generally applicable to all Thandakams and specifically to this— —this Marumaatru Thiru-pathikam Thiru-thandakam. Only Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman has composed Thevaram in the Thandakam poetic form. That is why Peruman is known by the names Thandaka Venthar (King of Thandakam) and Thandaka Chathurar (Master of Thandakam). Thandakam is one of the poetic forms in Tamil. That is, prosody (yaappu) describes the grammar of how a poem should be. Thandakam is one such poetic form.

The grammar of this Thandakam poetic form can be found in the grammatical texts Panniru Paattiyal and Yaapparungala Viruthi. According to this, in this Thandakam form, each line has six or eight feet (seer), and it is the characteristic of Thandakam to praise men or gods in four lines. Among them, Panniru Paattiyal states that those composed with six feet are called Kurunthandakam (short Thandakam), and those with eight feet are called Nedunthandakam (long Thandakam). “Moovirandenum iru naankenam seer vagai naatti seyyulin aadavar kadavular pugazhvana thandakam avatruL arruseer kuriyathu nediyathu en seeram” is the verse from Panniru Paattiyal. In the history of Tamil literature, Appar Swamigal was the first to compose songs in the Thandakam poetic form. That is why Sekkizhar Swamigal praises Appar Swamigal, Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar, as Thandaka Chathurar.

Earlier, in the Puranam of Kungiliyakalaiya Nayanar, at Thiru-kadavur, when Thiru-gnanasambandha Peruman and Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman arrived at the holy monastery of Kungiliyakalaiya Nayanar, Sekkizhar Peruman referred to Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman as Thandaka Chathurar. We may recall what he mentioned here. Sivaprakasar, the treasury of imagination, states that Appar Adigal is the father of such Thandaka meter.

Therefore, this Thiruthandaka Thirupathigam, beginning with ‘Naam Aarkkum Kudiyellom,’ sung by Appar Swamigal, is found in the Sixth Thirumurai among the twelve Thirumurais. Among the twelve Thirumurais, the Fourth, Fifth, and Sixth Thirumurais, beginning with ‘Kudiyallom,’ this is the ninety-eighth Thirupathigam, a general Thirupathigam.

The elders also refer to this as Marumaatra Thiruthandakam.

Now, Marumaa The other Thiruthandaka Thirupathigam.

We are not subjects to anyone, nor do we fear Yama. We shall not suffer in hell, nor are we troubled. We know no fear nor disease, nor are we subservient. We know only joy, never sorrow. We have attained the sacred feet of the Lord, who is not subject to anyone, Shankara, who wears a white conch shell earring in one ear, and to whom we are eternal servants.

The wide world is our abode; those who cook and eat in every town, those who offer food, those who light lamps, their alms are our refuge. The temples are our refuge. Mother Earth will not turn away if we lie with her; this is not false, but true. He who has the bull as his mount He has accepted us. Now we lack nothing; our troubles are over. We are not bound to heed the words of those who wear fine clothes and gold ornaments; we are free from blemish.

We do not enter the homes of women with adorned breasts. By praising ‘Mahadeva, Mahadeva,’ we have bathed in the sacred waters of dawn. We have attained the sacred form adorned with water. As tears flow like rain from dark clouds, our stony hearts have melted into good hearts. We are not bound to heed the commands of those who rule the land and come riding on elephants; we are free from attachments. Our kin are the hosts of Rudras; their attire is but a loincloth and a tattered garment.

Those who are hostile will not approach; even evil Even evil itself becomes good. We shall not be reborn. We are capable of uttering the glorious ‘Namashivaya’ of the Lord who wears the fragrant garland of golden cassia flowers. With our tongues, we have attained the luminous light of the Lord with fiery eyes, who reduced the fierce, poisonous one to ashes. We shall never yield to anyone, nor is there anyone equal to us on this vast earth. We shall not seek minor deities; we have attained the sacred feet of Lord Shiva.

We are not those who possess but one garment. Those afflicted by disease have fled, leaving us. We are among the blessed who have attained the Holy One, whose head is adorned with a garland of skulls of the deceased, the primordial form of the three, the eight-formed Lord. The three times ten (thirty) Devas and the Devas of this world praise and worship Him. He is Shiva, whose sacred form is like red coral, and He is our Lord who rules us, whose tongue utters His name. Even if the protectors, who are the lords of the island of Navalam, were to send us away, we have shed the severe impurities of karma.

He who is the standing and moving, the earth and water, fire and air, and the vast sky; He who is both minute and vast, and rare; He whose intimacy with His devotees cannot be measured; He who is the Supreme, the Sadasiva, and who is both Himself and I; Him we shall speak of with goodness and splendor. We are free from error, speaking what the Pēyar (demons) speak. We have been blessed to constantly meditate on the Lord, who is the Lord of all worlds, the Peruman of the Himalayas, the effulgent one like fire, whose sacred body is red and adorned with white ash, the beloved of the golden daughter of the mountain king. We have forgotten all the words spoken by those who stand and eat, telling us to remember them. Who is that king who came? He is the Lord with matted locks, wearing a conch shell earring in one ear, whose body is adorned with ash and snakes.

He is the Lord with the bull mount, whose upper garment is tiger skin, and whose attire includes the skin of a spotted deer. He is our Lord; behold, He is the Lord who commands the hosts of those who are with you and others. We are not those who cast away the bonds of illusion. We have been blessed to sing of our Lord with our tongues. We have attained good fortune, having shed our ego. He is the Lord of the Devas, the one who rules us, the one who is an immeasurable fire, unknowable to Brahma and Vishnu.

Even if the King of the Southern Direction himself were to come and serve Him with devotion, we would not consider it a virtue, for we are in His virtues. Even if the King of the Southern Direction himself were to come and serve Him with devotion, we would not consider it a virtue, for we are in His virtues. We would not consider it a virtue, for we are in His virtues.

This is Thirunavukkarasu Peruman himself. This is the Marumaatra Thiruthandakam, which begins with ‘Naam Aarkkum Kudiyallom,’ spoken as a reply to the king’s ministers and soldiers who came to take him, and also praising Lord Shiva. This Thiruthandaka Thirupathigam also contains ten sacred verses.

Let us continue to contemplate the meanings of those ten sacred verses. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Three Hundred Four. Thirunindrachcharukkam. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We saw that Thirunavukkarasu Peruman bestowed the Marumaatra Thiruthandakam, beginning with ‘Naam Aarkkum Kudiyallom,’ as a reply to the king’s ministers and soldiers who came to take him, and also praising Lord Shiva. This Marumaatra Thiruthandakam contains ten sacred verses.

Let us briefly contemplate their meanings. The first verse of this Thirupathigam is as follows: ‘Naam Aarkkum Kudiyallom, Namanaianjom, Naragaththil Idar Padom, Nadalai Illom, Emaappom Pini Ariyom, Panivom Allom, Inbame Ennalum Thunbamillai, Thaamaarkkum Kudiyal.’ The nature of Shankara, who wears a good conch shell and a white earring in one ear, to Him alone we are eternal servants, and we have sought refuge at His sacred feet adorned with freshly plucked flowers. This is the first sacred verse. Its meaning is as follows: First, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman begins by singing ‘Naam Aarkkum Kudiyallom.’ We have already contemplated its meaning. ‘Naam Aarkkum Kudiyallom’ means he tells the king, ‘I am not your subject. I am not a citizen living in your country.

Therefore, your command is not valid for me.’ We saw that he says this. He then gives the reason by saying, ‘Namanaianjom.’ ‘Naam Aarkkum Kudiyallom,’ I am not your subject, because Yama We do not fear Yama. That is, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman says, ‘We do not even fear Yama.’ This is because Thirunavukkarasar is one who attained the Lord who kicked Yama.

Therefore, ‘We do not even fear Yama. Yama’s command cannot control me. How can your command control me?’ says Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Generally, a king’s command is only valid for the subjects living under him in that country. His command is not even valid for a citizen in a neighboring country.

Therefore, his command is valid only within the territory under his rule. But Thirunavukkarasu Peruman sought refuge in the Lord who kicked Yama himself. He became a servant of Lord Shiva. He became a servant.

Therefore, to me, who has sought refuge in Lord Shiva, the King of all kings, your royal decree, which rules a small part of this earthly world, is not valid. Generally, in Saiva Siddhanta, in the Saiva religion, it is said that at the time of death, Shiva’s messengers will come to take the souls that have received Samaya Diksha (initiation). Yama’s messengers will come to take ordinary souls at the time of death.

But Yama does not even have the authority to take souls that have received Samaya Diksha. Shiva’s messengers will come and take those souls. Srikantarudra is the lord of these souls, according to Saiva Siddhanta.

Here, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman is in the position of an Acharya of the Saiva religion. He has sought refuge in Lord Shiva.

Therefore, according to that principle, even Yama’s messengers cannot approach him, and he is not subject to Yama’s jurisdiction. A common king’s command cannot bind me. I have sought refuge in Lord Shiva. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman says, ‘Naam Aarkkum Kudiyellom, Namanaianjom.’ Generally, in Dharma Shastra, there is a rule that those who escape the king’s punishment will go to hell. That is, if someone commits a crime here, the king punishes that crime.

But that punishment received Now, when he says ‘Nadalai Illom,’ it means falsehood. When he says ‘Nadalai Illom,’ Thirunavukkarasu Peruman states that there is no falsehood in him. He says ‘Emaappom,’ which means ‘we have received Shiva’s great protection.’ Therefore, your command is not valid for me, who has received Lord Shiva’s great protection. There is no falsehood in me, so there is no need to fear Yama. I do not even have the state of suffering in hell. After saying all this, he says ‘Aduththom.’ ‘Pini’ should be taken as disease, and ‘Pinippu’ should be taken as bondage.

I, who have sought refuge in Lord Shiva and served Him, having become His servant, now have no bondage in this world. Nothing else can bind me, he says.

Now, after singing ‘Emaappom Pini Ariyom,’ he sings ‘Panivom Allom.’ Therefore, for these reasons, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman states that he has no need to bow to anyone other than Lord Shiva and Shiva’s devotees, and he will not bow. Because he has served Lord Shiva and Shiva’s devotees, he now sings, ‘Inbame Ennalum Thunbamillai’ (Only joy always, no sorrow). This refers to future times.

Therefore, he sings that there will be no sorrow for him, neither in the present nor in the future. Why no sorrow always? Because ‘Thaamaarkkum Kodiyallaa Thanmaiyaana Sangaranar Sanga Ven Kuzhai Or Kaathil.’ The answer to ‘Komarkke Naam Endru Meelaa Vaazhaai Koymalar Sevadiyinaiye Kuruginome’ is that we will henceforth always experience joy and never sorrow. This is because we have joined the sacred feet of Lord Shankara, Lord Shiva. Such a Shankara wears an earring in one ear. Who is such a Lord Shiva?

He is one whose nature is not to be subject to anyone. That is, He has no master; He is the master of all.

Therefore, I have joined the sacred feet of Lord Shiva, who has no master. My master is Lord Shiva, and He has no master. There is no one. He is the King of all kings. Such a Shankara grants only joy to those who attain Him. He does only good.

Therefore, for us who have attained Him, there will be no sorrow from now on; there will only be joy, says Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. This is the meaning of the first sacred verse.

Now, the second sacred verse: ‘Agalidame Idamaga Oorgal Thorum Attunbar Ittunbar Vilakkaar Aiyam Pugaliidam Ambalangal Bhoomi Devi Udan Kidanthal Purattaal Poyandru Meyye Igaludaiya Vidaiyudaiyaan Enru Kondaan Ini Ethum Kuraivilom Idargal Theerndhom Thugil Uduththu Pon Poondru Thrivaar Sollum Sorketka Kada.’ We are not bound to heed the words of those who wear fine clothes and gold ornaments; we are free from blemish. This is the second sacred verse. Its meaning is as follows: This vast earth is my abode; it belongs to me. I am a complete renunciate.

Therefore, in all towns, those who lead household lives, those who live in the Grihastha ashrama, they offer food to those who come begging, without saying no. So, as long as they exist, I have no worry about food. Not only that, but in this world, there are public forums and public places in all towns; all of them are my places. Not only that, but I will lie down and sleep on this earth. If I need a place to sleep, this earth I will lie down and sleep. Even Mother Earth will not reject me if I lie down and sleep.

Therefore, this entire world is my place. Those who live in the household dharma will not deny me food. Mother Earth will not reject me.

Furthermore, Lord Shiva, who has the bull as His vehicle, has accepted me as His servant.

Therefore, I have no shortcomings now. So, I am not bound by any obligation or duty to accept the words of your king, says Thirunavukkarasu Peruman in this second verse.

Let us continue to contemplate the meanings of the Marumaatra Thiruthandaka Thirupathigam. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Three Hundred Five. Thirunindrachcharukkam. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We are contemplating the meanings of the Marumaatra Thiruthandaka Thirupathigam.

Now, the third verse: ‘Vaaraanda Kongaiyar Ser Manaiyil Serom Mahadeva Mahadeva Endru Vaazhththi Neeraanda Purothayam Aada Pettrom Neeraniyum Kolame Nigazha Pettrom Kaaraanda Mazhai Pola Kanneer Sora Kalmaname Nal Manamaai Karaiya Pettrom Paaraandu Pagaderi Varuvaar Sollum Pani Ketka Kadavomo Patratrrome.’ This is the third sacred verse. Its meaning is as follows: In this, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman first sings about his state of renunciation. I will not join and live in a household, that is, household life I do not live. By repeatedly uttering the names of Lord Shiva, ‘Mahadeva, Mahadeva,’ I have bathed in the early morning and adopted the Saivite sacred form of adorning myself with sacred ash. Previously, having been in the Jain religion, my heart, which was like a stone for many years, has now melted into a good heart by joining Lord Shiva, and tears flow like rain from a cloud. My heart has melted to such an extent that tears come.

Therefore, I am detached from worldly things.

Thus, the commands issued by kings who rule the entire earth and come riding on elephants do not bind me, who is detached from worldly affairs. He states that he is not obligated to accept royal commands.

Now, the fourth verse: ‘Uravaavaar Rudra Palganathinorgal Uduppana Kovanamodu Keezhuzhavaam Andre Seruvaarum Serumaattaar Theemai Thaanum Nanmaiyaai Sirappathe Pirappir Sellom Naravaar Pon Idazhi Narunthaaron Seeraar Namashivaya Sollavallom Naavaal Suravaarum Kodiyanai Podiya Kanda Sudar Nayana Jothiyaiye Thodarvutrome.’ This is that verse. Its meaning is as follows: ‘Uravaavaar Rudra Palganathinorgal,’ that is, Shiva’s devotees in Shiva’s guise are my kin. A loincloth and rags are the clothes I wear.

Therefore, even enemies will not approach me. I utter with my tongue the sacred Namasivaya mantra of the glorious Siva-peruman, who wears a garland of good Konrai flowers, full of honey and golden. Siva-peruman is the one with the fiery eye that reduced Manmatha, the god of love with the sugarcane bow, to ashes. He is of the form of light. Having reached such a Siva-peruman, I have no more births. Others who have not attained Siva-peruman will also die and wander.

Manmatha, who dared to shoot an arrow at Siva-peruman, was burned by Siva-peruman’s third eye.

Similarly, Siva-peruman is capable of burning anything that comes to destroy us. Thus sings Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman in this fourth hymn. Now for the fifth hymn, “We are not to anyone...” We are not subject to anyone, nor do we have adversaries in this vast world. We will not seek out minor deities. We have attained the sacred feet of Siva-peruman.

We are not lacking in anything. Indeed, the diseases fled and ran away. We are in the blessed state of having attained the holy one who wears a garland of skulls of those who perished. This is the fifth Thiru-paadal. Its meaning is as follows: We are those who have attained the sacred feet of Siva-peruman. Siva-peruman is the one who wears the skulls of Brahma and Vishnu as a garland.

We have attained such a state.

Therefore, we will not retreat before anyone. In this vast world, we have no enemies. We will not search and seek out minor deities to worship.

Here, by minor deities, Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman refers to those souls that are born, exist, and die, which some religions celebrate and worship as gods. He states that we will not worship such minor deities. We have joined with Siva-peruman, the one supreme being, the God who has neither birth nor death.

Therefore, we have no deficiencies. Even diseases will flee without troubling us, sings Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman in this fifth hymn. Now for the sixth Thiru-paadal: “The first form of the three, the eight-formed one, the red coral-bodied Siva, whom the thirty-three devas and the great ones praise with excellence.” We are those whose tongues praise thus. He is our master. Even if the king, the lord of Nava-lan-theevu, sends an order, we are not bound by it, nor are we harsh or deceitful.

This is the sixth Thiru-paadal. Its meaning is as follows: Siva-peruman is above Brahma, Vishnu, and Rudra, being the first among them all. He pervades through his eight forms. We are those whose tongues praise Siva-peruman, the red coral-bodied one, whom the thirty-three devas and the great rishis always joyfully praise.

Thus, we are enslaved to Siva-peruman. He is our ruler.

Therefore, we, who know not even a speck of deceit, are not bound to obey the command of the king, the ruler of this entire Nava-lan-theevu, even if he sends for us. The implication here is that the Pallava king, who ruled a small part of Bharat, called Nava-lan-theevu, sent for Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman.

Therefore, Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman states that even if the king of the entire Bharatadesam, called Nava-lan-theevu, calls, we are not obliged to obey him. Hence, we are not obliged to obey your king, who rules a small part of this great Nava-lan-theevu. This is the implication. Now for the seventh hymn: “The standing and the moving...” The standing and the moving, the earth and water, fire and wind, and the vast sky; the small and the great, the rare and the easy for the loving; the immeasurable, the supreme, the Sadasiva, the one who is both Himself and I. We are bound to speak of the goodness and splendor of such a one.

We speak not the words of demons, and we are blameless. This is the seventh Thiru-paadal. Its meaning is: We are bound to praise Siva-peruman, who is the standing and the moving, the earth and water, fire and wind, the vast sky, the small and the great, the rare and the easy for the loving, the immeasurable, the supreme, and Sadasiva, and who is both Himself and I, speaking of His goodness and splendid qualities.

Therefore, we are blameless. So, will we speak like demons, bowing before the king and pleasing him? Will we praise as they do? No, we will not, is the meaning of this seventh Thiru-paadal. Now for the eighth Thiru-paadal: “We have been blessed to always remember Isan, the Lord of all worlds, the great one of the Himalayas, the fiery and radiant one, the red-bodied one with white ash, the beloved of the golden goddess, the daughter of the mountain king. We have forgotten all the words that those who stand and eat told us to remember.

“Who are you who have come now, and who is the king?” This is the eighth Thiru-paadal. Its meaning is as follows: We daily remember Siva-peruman, who is the Lord and master of all worlds, the chief of the devas, the one with a fiery, radiant light, the one who wears white ash on his red body, and the beloved of the golden goddess, the daughter of the mountain king, whom he loves and who loves him.

“Therefore, we have forgotten all those words of assurance that the Jains, who eat standing, told us to never forget. In this state, Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman asks, “Who are you who have come to me, and who is the king?” Siva-peruman is the lord of all worlds. Not only that, he creates, protects, and destroys all worlds as a sport. We, who are servants of such a Siva-peruman, do not need to fear or be subservient to a king who rules a small part of one world, in one universe, in one cosmos, in one earth, within the totality. This is the meaning. Kanippu aakum iththakaiya mannan vanthiruntha Thiru-navukkarasu Perumanai paarththu ivanai enna seyvathu enru Samanarkalidam ketkiran Thiru-navukkarasu Perumanai orumaiyil ivan enru alaikkiran enenral avanin Samana gurumaarkal erkanave avanathu moolaiyai salavai seythu vaiththiruntharkal enave athile aatpatta antha mannan ivvaru orumaiyile nam Nayanarai alaikkiran ivvaru antha mannan kettathum dharmam enpathu sirithum illatha ketta mathiyinai udaya Samanarkal sirithum achchamo koochamo illamal Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanarai kothikkum neetraraiyil idungal enru sonnarkal ivvaru kodum paathaka seyalai seyyumaaru arasanidam sonnarkal Samana samayaththile ahimsa enpathe muthanmaiyana dharmam Now for the ninth hymn: “He with matted locks, with a conch earring in one ear, with a body adorned with ash and snakes, with a bull as his mount, wearing a tiger skin as an upper garment, and a deer skin as his lower garment.

“He is our master, you see. We are not servants who obey the commands of you and your army. We are those who cast off all bonds.” This is the ninth Thiru-paadal. Its meaning is as follows: Siva-peruman, who has matted locks, wears a conch earring in one ear, has a body adorned with ash and snakes, has a bull as his mount, wears a tiger skin as an upper garment, and a deer skin as his lower garment, is our master.

“Therefore, we have attained the state of completely casting off all bonds. So, Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman sings, “We are not those whose duty it is to obey the commands of the king who has you and your soldiers.” and other soldiers. Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman sings that we are not those whose profession is to listen to the commands of the king. Now for the tenth Thiru-paadal: “We were blessed to sing of our Lord with our tongues. We were blessed to be rejected by the Jains who wear no clothes.

“The Lord of the celestials, who took us into his grace, Siva, the God of gods, who stood as an unknowable pillar of fire to Brahma and Vishnu, has entered my heart. Even if the Lord of the South comes and commands us to serve him, we will not consider it good, for we are of the eight virtues.” This is the tenth Thiru-paadal. Its meaning is as follows: Our tongues are filled with joy as we sing of Siva-peruman.

“Therefore, the Jains, who wear no clothes, rejected us without desiring us.

“The Lord of the celestials, Siva-peruman, in his compassion, took us into his grace. He is the one who stood as an unknowable pillar of fire to Brahma and Vishnu. Siva-peruman, the God of gods, resides in our thoughts. Such a Siva-peruman possesses eight virtues. We are servants of Siva-peruman, who possesses these eight virtues.

“Therefore, not only the messengers of Yama, but even Yama himself, if he comes and commands us, we are not obliged to do so. We are servants of Siva-peruman.

“Therefore, Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman sings in this tenth Thiru-paadal that we will not submit even if we are kicked by the sacred feet of Siva-peruman. Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman composed this Maru-maatra Thiru-thhandakam as a reply to the ministers and armies sent by the king with the command to capture and bring him. This Thiru-pathikam, which begins with “Namaarkkum kudiyallom,” is compiled as the ninety-eighth Thiru-pathikam in the sixth Thiru-murai of Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman’s Thevaram, within the twelve Thiru-murais. This Thiru-pathikam was composed by Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman with a fearless heart, stating that he would not fear anyone.

“Therefore, the benefit of this Thiru-pathikam is that those who recite it need not fear anyone. Fear will not approach those who recite this pathikam. The state of being subservient to Siva-peruman will be attained, and the fearless nature of not fearing anyone in this world, will come to those who recite this pathikam by the grace of God. The state of being proud like Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman will come. This is the benefit of reciting this Thiru-pathikam.

“Let us continue to contemplate the sacred life of Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 306, Thiru-nindra-ch-charukkam, Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We saw that Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman composed the Maru-maatra Thiru-thhandakam, beginning with “Naam aarkkum kudiyallom,” in the presence of the king’s envoys, the ministers, and the armies who had come to take him. We also contemplated the meanings of that Thiru-pathikam.

Thus, Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar sings the Maru-maatra Thiru-thhandaka Thiru-pathikam.

After that, the ministers and other armies who had come to imprison Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar fall at the sacred feet of Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman and worship him. Now they humbly request Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman, saying, “Peruman, Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar, you must come with us.” They make a request to Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar. Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman refuses to come. The ministers who had come to take him by force were afraid.

Therefore, they humbly request him, saying, “You must come with us.” Not only that, they also say that if they do not bring Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman, the king will punish them.

Therefore, to escape the king’s punishment, to protect themselves, they humbly bow to Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman and the armies. Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman, the sacred devotee of Siva-peruman, who has the bull banner, showed compassion to the ministers and armies who had come. Out of compassion for them, he did not want them to be punished by the king. He agrees to go with them, with the conviction that our Siva-peruman will be a helper in the difficulties that come. Sekkizhar Peruman mentions the conviction that Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman held: “Our Lord is with us for the difficulties that come.” He goes with the conviction that Siva-peruman will be a helper for the actions that will come now that he is going to the king. The actions that will come now are the evils that the Jains and the king inflicted upon Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman: putting him in the lime kiln, giving him poisoned rice to eat, setting an elephant on him, and tying him to a stone and throwing him into the sea.

These are the future events that are to occur. Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman goes with the conviction that Siva-peruman will be a helper in these future events. If Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman had not agreed, it would have been impossible for the ministers and others who had come to bring Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman to the king.

Therefore, out of compassion to protect them from the king’s punishment, Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman agrees to go to the king. This is the first reason. The second reason is the principle of upholding the worldly justice that stands by the king. This is the second reason. For this too, he agrees to go to the king. The third reason is to establish the glory of Saivism, to show the glory of Saivism. to the king and to the people of the world.

This is the third reason.

Therefore, for these three reasons, Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman agrees to go to the Pallava king. So, the ministers and armies take Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman and present Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar to the king. In this hymn, Sekkizhar Peruman states that Thiru-navukkarasu is the sacred devotee of Siva-peruman, who has the bull banner. He mentions Siva-peruman’s banner as the bull banner here, because raising a banner, displaying a banner, is a sign of starting a war. Not only that, it is also a sign of victory.

Now, Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman is going to the Jain king. This is a sign of bringing the good path of Saivism to the people of the world. and a sign of the beginning of the war to remove the suffering caused to the Vedic path and the Saivite path by the inferior religion, Jainism, which is contrary to the Vedas. And in this, Sivakavimani Ayya writes that Sekkizhar Peruman mentions Siva-peruman, who has the bull banner, as a sign that the Vedic path, which is the Saivite path, will win.

Thus, Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar goes to the Pallava Jain king. Seeing him, the Pallava king becomes angry. He turns to the cruel Jains beside him and asks, “Tell me what to do with him now.” This king, the Pallava king, belongs to the Pallava lineage, which was one of the Chola dynasties. The Pallava king who ruled during this period was Mahendravarman. He was also known by the name Gunabharan.

His inscriptions are found in Thiru-ch-chirappalli. Based on his inscriptions, we can determine the period of Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar.

Similarly, these inscriptions of Mahendravarman Pallavan help to confirm the period of Thiru-gnanasambandha Peruman and the period of the Vathapi war undertaken by Siru-thondar.

Therefore, his reign is estimated by historians to be around 640 CE. This king, seeing Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman who had arrived, asks the Jains what to do with him. He refers to Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman in the singular, as “him,” because his Jain gurus had already brainwashed him.

Therefore, the king, influenced by them, addresses our Nayanar in the singular. When the king asked this, the Jains, who had no dharma and possessed evil minds, without any fear or hesitation, said, “Put Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar in the boiling lime kiln.” Thus, the Jains told the king to commit this heinous act. In Jainism, non-violence is the foremost dharma. Thirukkural states that the greatest virtue is non-killing. Yet, the Jain gurus, whose primary dharma is such non-violence, without a shred of mercy, tell the king to put Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar in the boiling lime kiln and seal him in. They tell the king to kill Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar by putting him in the boiling lime kiln.

Such Jains are those with evil minds who do not know the two benefits that are certain for a soul: the benefit in this world and the benefit in the next world. Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman had already suffered from colic, which could not be cured by Jainism, and by the grace of Siva-peruman, the Lord, Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman had overcome that colic. Such a Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman would also escape the punishments imposed by the king. If he escaped, the king would abandon Jainism and convert to Saivism, and thus their Jain religion would be destroyed. Without considering any of this, they tell the king to inflict this cruel punishment on Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar. Hearing this, the king also ordered Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar to be placed in the boiling heat of the lime kiln.

As soon as the tyrannical king spoke, his servants prepared the lime kiln, which had the great heat of fire that could melt even stone. The servants of that tyrannical king prepare the lime kiln, which always has immense heat, heat that can melt even stone, and fire. In such a lime kiln, where fire was boiling, they placed Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar inside and guarded the room so that he could not come out, and then locked it.

At that time, Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar, from inside the lime kiln, without doing any harm or thinking any harm to the king or his servants who had done this to him, sought only the grace of Isan. Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar, the king of the states, Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar, that Upon entering the lime kiln, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, with a resolute heart, meditated on the sacred feet of Lord Shiva, who performs the dance of grace in Thiru-Ambalam. He sang a Thiru-Pathikam, questioning whether sorrow could afflict or approach the devotees of the Lord. With such courage, he worshipped Lord Shiva, the Primal Being, and sat within the kiln.

At that moment, remembering the shade of Lord Shiva’s sacred feet, he began to sing the Thiru-Pathikam starting with “Maasil Veenaiyum.” In it, he refers to the shade of the Lord’s sacred feet. The Lord’s feet provide shade to all beings; that is the pervasiveness of divine grace. Those sacred feet perform the dance of Thiru-Thandavam. The Thiru-Thandavam is a dance of grace. It is the Lord’s sacred feet that take possession of souls out of compassion, even before the souls realize themselves. Among these, the raised foot in the Lord’s sacred dance posture is the foot capable of bestowing grace.

Therefore, those sacred feet provide shade to all beings.

Lord Shiva alone is capable of rescuing souls from the heat of birth.

Thus, taking refuge in the sacred feet of the Lord, and remaining sheltered in the shade of those feet, is the state that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar now experienced within that scorching lime kiln, that fiery chamber. Within that fiery chamber, under the shade of Lord Shiva’s sacred feet. He was absorbed within. The shade of Lord Shiva’s sacred feet served as a fortress for Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar at that time. His mind became one with the Lord’s sacred feet, contemplating whether any sorrow could truly exist for devotees who had taken refuge in the Lord. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar stood, his entire being focused on the Lord’s sacred feet.

In accordance with the Nayanar’s sacred words, “Unite and meditate,” Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar’s entire intellect worshipped the Primal Being. As stated in Siva Gnana Siddhiyar, “Those who perceive the Supreme through supreme knowledge will only see the Supreme; Jivanmuktas will only see Shiva.” In such a state of Jivanmukti, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, within that fiery chamber, was absorbed in Lord Shiva. He meditated on the sacred feet and took refuge in the shade of those sacred feet. Even amidst the intense heat of the fire, our Nayanar clung to the sacred feet of Lord Shiva as his shade.

Therefore, that lime kiln, that fiery chamber, became for Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, because he was in the shade of the Lord’s sacred feet, like a gentle breeze in the spring season, like a cool pond with refreshing water, like the cool rays of the moon, and like the sweet sound of a melodious veena. This was because he was cool and absorbed in the grace of Lord Shiva’s sacred feet. He is cool, absorbed in the very essence of grace. That is why he now remembers the sacred feet of Lord Shiva and sings the Thiru-Pathikam beginning with “Maasil Veenaiyum.” Now, that Thiru-Pathikam: Thiruchitrambalam. Maasil veenaiyum maalai madhiyamum, Maasil veenaiyum maalai madhiyamum, Veesu thendralum veengizhavenilum, Maasil veenaiyum maalai madhiyamum, Veesu thendralum veengizhavenilum, Moosu vanda poygaiyum pondrathe. Isan endaiyadi neezhale namachchivaayave.

Gnanamum kalviyum namachchivaayave. Naan arivichchaiyum namachchivaayave. Naan avindredhume namachchivaayave. Nanneri kaattume. Aalahaara laanaarai adaindhuyaar meelaachcheydhu meymmaiyul nirkilaar. Tholaadha sooraiyo thozhumbevi vaazha maayndhu mannaagi kazhivare.

Re nada vaazhvu kondu en seydheer naaneer sudalai servadhu sorpiramaaname. Kadalin nanjamudhundaavar kaivittaal udalinaarkidoormuni pandame. Pookkai kondaran ponnadi potrilaar naakkai kondaran naamam navilkeelaar. Aakkaikke irai thedi alamandhu kaakkaikke irai aagi kazhivare. Kurigalum adaiyalamum koyil. The paths and their unique nature, even if a thousand Vedas were to speak of them, why does your mind, devoid of understanding, not enter them?
