My Lord, who gave me a mouth to praise, a humble heart to contemplate, and a bowed head to prostrate, alas, I, a sinner, have wasted a long time without offering flowers and praising Him. The good woman, like a painted doll, left me, and I, who worshipped and stood, was surrounded by the world. The heart that cried out, like a farmer plowing, is now being plowed. In the hearts of those who constantly remember Him, the Lord with golden matted locks, the virtuous one, stands without deceit. Those who are deceitful, seeing His flowers and water, will laugh at themselves in shame. Like fire in wood, like ghee in milk, the Lord, a great gem of light, stands hidden.

If one churns with the churning stick of relationship and the rope of awareness, He will appear before you.

This is the Thiru-Pathikam that begins with “Maasil Veenaiyum.” It is the Thiru-Pathikam composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman when he was in the lime kiln, sheltered by the shade of Lord Shiva’s sacred feet.

We will continue to contemplate its meaning. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 307, Thiru-Nindrachcharukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We saw that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sat in the fiery, boiling lime kiln, absorbed in the shade of Lord Shiva’s sacred feet, and then sang the Pathikam “Maasil Veenaiyum.” We also examined that Pathikam.

Now, let us contemplate the meaning of that Pathikam. This Pathikam, which begins with “Maasil Veenaiyum,” is found in the fourth, fifth, and sixth Thiru-Murais composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman among the twelve Thiru-Murais. This Pathikam is located in the fifth Thiru-Murai, compiled as the ninetieth Thiru-Pathikam in the fifth Thiru-Murai. This Pathikam belongs to the category of general Thiru-Pathikams. This Pathikam was composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman from within the lime kiln in Pataliputra. It is a cool Thiru-Pathikam of the lime kiln, but it is not composed in the name of a specific sthalam.

That is, generally, Devarams are sung in praise of the deity of a particular Shiva Thiru-Sthalam.

Therefore, those Pathikams are revered as the Pathikams of that sthalam, belonging to that sthalam. However, this Thiru-Pathikam was composed generally, not in the name of any specific Thiru-Sthalam.

Therefore, it is called a general Pathikam.

Similarly, later, when the Pallava king, instigated by the Jains, sent an elephant to attack him, The Thiru-Pathikam “Sunnaven Chandanachchaandhu” that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sang there also falls under the category of general Thiru-Pathikams.

Furthermore, when Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman was tied to a stone and cast into the sea, the Thiru-Pathikam “Sotrunaithiyan” that he sang in the middle of the ocean was also a general Thiru-Pathikam, not about a specific sthalam. It was directed towards the Lord who is omnipresent. This is structured as a unique Kurunthogai.

Now, we must contemplate the meanings of the ten sacred verses of this Pathikam. The first sacred verse is: Maasil veenaiyum maalai madhiyamum veesu thendralum veengizhavenilum moosu vandarai poygaiyum pondrathe Isan endaiyinaiyadi neezhale. This is the first sacred verse. The meaning of this verse is as follows: We saw that Appar Peruman sang this from within the fiery chamber, meditating on the shade of the Lord’s sacred feet, didn’t we?

Therefore, he sings about how the shade of the Lord’s sacred feet is. He sings that the shade of Lord Shiva’s sacred feet is like the sound of a pure veena, like the coolness of the moon appearing in the evening, like the gentle breeze and the grandeur and coolness of the abundant spring, and like the coolness of a pond where bees swarm, thus bringing joy. In this first sacred verse, he enumerates how the shade of the Lord’s sacred feet is.

First, he sings “Maasil Veenaiyum.” Maasu means blemish or fault. Maasu il means faultless. He sings that the shade of the Lord’s sacred feet is like the faultless sound emanating from a veena. Faultless sound refers to the rules of musical notes (swara lakshanas). He sings that the shade of the Lord’s sacred feet is like that faultless sound, completely full and played without any deviation from the swara lakshanas.

Next, he sings “Maalai Madhiyamum.” He sings that it is like the moon that appears precisely in the evening. Unlike the moon before or after evening, the moon that appears at dusk is like a full moon, cool to the eyes. He sings that the shade of the Lord’s sacred feet is like this.

Next, he sings “Veesu.” He sings of the “Veesu Thendral,” a gentle breeze that carries a pleasant fragrance. He sings that the shade of the Lord’s sacred feet is like that fragrant breeze.

Next, he sings of the “Moosu Vandu Arai Poygai,” meaning a pond where bees swarm. He sings that it is as cool as such a pond. There is a pond, and its water is cool and abundant. There are water lilies in it, and bees swarm around these lilies.

Thus, he sings that the shade of the Lord’s sacred feet is like the water in that cool pond where bees swarm. He sings that the shade of the Lord’s sacred feet is as cool as the spring season. This is the meaning of this first sacred verse. As if commenting on this sacred verse, Peruman has composed a sacred verse. When Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman was placed in the lime kiln, Sekkizhar Peruman, who sang, “Are there any sorrows for the devotees of the Lord?” and “With a resolute mind, he worshipped the Primal Being,” then sings: “The scorching lime kiln itself became like the abundant spring season, like the gentle southern breeze, like a cool lotus pond, and like the bright, cool moonlight, as the grace of the Lord’s sacred feet cooled it.” In this verse, Sekkizhar Peruman has provided an explanatory commentary, an elaborate explanation, for the first sacred verse, “Maasil Veenaiyum.” In this verse, Sekkizhar Peruman describes how that lime kiln. What was that kiln like?

It was a chamber where fire constantly burned. The heat in that lime kiln became cool for Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman because he was cooled by the grace of Lord Shiva’s sacred feet, and he was absorbed in that grace. That is why even the lime kiln became cool for him. How would that fiery chamber be? It would be hot and harmful to the five senses and their perceptions. The sound of the fire burning in that fiery chamber, where Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar was placed, would torment the ears.

The light of that fire would torment the eyes. The poisonous air produced in that fiery chamber would be harmful to the nose. The taste of the lime would burn the tongue. The heat in that lime chamber would harm the body and cause damage. The light of that fire would torment the eyes. The poisonous air produced in that fiery chamber would be harmful to the nose.

The taste of the lime would burn the tongue. The heat in that lime chamber would harm the body and cause damage.

Thus, that lime kiln, that fiery chamber, was a cruel chamber capable of harming the five senses—eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body—causing damage to the body and taking life. But Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, who was there, was mentally absorbed in the shade of the Lord’s sacred feet.

Therefore, All these, through the Lord’s cool grace, became five cool things, like a feast for the five senses of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. Even while in the fiery chamber, due to the Lord’s cool grace, that fiery chamber became for Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman as sweet as the sound of a yazh for his ears, as cool as the fully bloomed moonlight for his eyes. Just as a gentle breeze carries fragrance, he received a pleasant scent. It was as delicious as the cool water of a pond. That fiery chamber provided a cool sensation like the spring’s source.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, in this first verse, has placed things that bring joy to the five senses.

Therefore, even though he was in the fiery chamber, the natural pleasures that provided a feast for the five senses of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar were like the natural beauty of the world. The sound of the yazh, like the sound of a veena, was a very gentle and sweet sound, cool to his ears. The full moon that appears in the evening brings coolness to the eyes; through its nectar-like rays, it benefits the eyes.

Similarly, that fiery chamber brought coolness to Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar’s eyes, like the cool moon.

Next, just as a gentle breeze carries fragrance, a pleasant scent appeared to Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. The gentle breeze, born in the Pothigai hills and flowing northwards to the Thondai country, carries the fragrance of sandalwood trees and other aromatic trees, as well as fragrant flowers from the groves it passes through.

Thus, it brings a pleasant fragrance. Peruman praises this breeze as “Pongu Tamil Pothiyamalai pirandhu poonjanathin konganaaindhu kulirchaaral idai valarndha kozhuthendral” (The rich Tamil breeze born in the Pothigai hills, embracing the breasts of the earth, growing amidst cool slopes). Although wind is generally associated with the sense of touch, here it is described in relation to the sense of smell because it carries fragrance.

Furthermore, just as the cool water in a pond is delicious, so too for Thiru-Navukkarasu. Indeed, that fiery chamber, which was supposed to destroy and annihilate the five senses, became for our Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar a time that offered cool natural pleasures. How so? Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings that these natural pleasures are like the coolness provided by the shade of the Lord’s sacred feet. These joys and sorrows, experienced by the physical body—whether the suffering in the fiery chamber or the joy provided by nature—are all experienced by the body.

But can these worldly experiences, which truly bring suffering to the body, transform into joy if one worships Lord Shiva? Can they truly transform into joy? Sivakavimani Aiyya writes a research commentary on how things that truly cause suffering transform into joy when they are sheltered in the shade of the Lord’s sacred feet. Generally, for someone in a very ordinary state, if they suffer from physical or mental illness, the nature of the things they perceive changes. If someone has a bilious illness, all the foods they eat will taste bitter to them. Even if they eat something sweet, it will taste bitter to them.

This is not a fault of the food; the nature of the food is indeed sweet. But for them, if they have a bilious illness, There is a bilious disease, and because of this bilious disease, even the sweets he eats taste bitter to him. We see that those who, unable to bear the suffering of the disease, wished to die and consumed poison, did not die, but the disease left them. We also see in the world instances where those who consumed ambrosia to live, lost their lives because of that very ambrosia.

Therefore, the knowledge that resides in the intellect, this knowledge of the five senses, even if it remains in its original nature without changing the nature of the substance consumed or experienced, its nature will change because the nature of those who consume it has changed. This is evident from this. For those who have mastered the art of Agnistambhana, fire does not burn them; we see this. If there is an expert in hypnotism, we see that for a person hypnotized by him, the fire does not burn them according to the path laid out by the hypnotist. Thayuumanavar Swamigal speaks of these achievements, such as being able to walk on fire and attain unparalleled Siddhi, in the section on Siddha Ganam.

Therefore, to prevent fire from harming someone, or to prevent the suffering of water from affecting someone, these can all be included under the category of Siddhis. There are eight great Siddhis, are there not? These can all be included in those eight great Siddhis.

Therefore, for those who have attained Siddhis, if they wish, fire will burn; if they do not wish, fire will not burn.

Thus, Siddhas control the nature of things through the Siddhis they have attained. All these fall under the category of the eight great Siddhis.

However, even these are Siddhis that stand at a certain level. But here, we see that even when Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar was in the fire chamber, the fire did not burn him; instead, he felt coolness. This means that what Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar experienced here does not fall into this type of Siddhi. All these Siddhis are at a very basic level. It is an experience.

Therefore, what our Nayanar experienced or undertook here does not fall into the category of Siddhi.

Similarly, when Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, during the fire debate in Madurai, wrote the Thiru-Nallatru Thiru-Padigam, ‘Bhogamartha Poonmulaiyal,’ on a palm leaf and placed it in the fire, we see that the leaf did not burn, but remained green. This is because the fire that was placed there, being one of the eight forms of the Lord, protected the palm leaf on which the Thevaram Padigam was written.

Therefore, here, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar is truly united with Shiva-Peruman and is in a very high state of Jivanmukta. He is in the divine grace of Shiva-Peruman’s Thiru-Adi Nezhil (sacred feet’s shade).

Therefore, for one in such a high state, the ordinary illusions and the objects of this world, which are made of illusion, have no effect. This is its meaning.

Therefore, the fire chamber, which is suffering experienced by the gross body, became a cool experience for Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar because he was in an advaitic union with Shiva-Peruman in the state of Jivanmukta. How is this so? There are the gross body and the subtle body. Of these, the subtle body is the primary cause of the gross body. The primary cause of this world is Maya. When the soul stands with the Anava mala (impurity), for the good and bad deeds of that soul, the Lord creates and bestows upon souls the body, instruments, and experiences from Maya.

Therefore, the body, external instruments, internal instruments, and experiences that souls possess are all created and given by the Lord from Maya. Maya is one of the three malas.

Therefore, when the soul, freed from this mala called Maya, unites with Shiva-Peruman and with Shiva-Peruman’s Thiru-Arul (divine grace), this Maya becomes inactive. The worldly matters, bodily matters, and matters of external and internal instruments created from this Maya will not affect the soul. How? When the soul is united with Shiva-Peruman’s Thiru-Arul in an advaitic manner, if we need light in the dark, we light a lamp.

But when the sun rises, the light of this lamp becomes unnecessary.

Moreover, the light of the lamp merges and subsides in the light of the sun. The light of the lamp is like Maya and its effects (Mayeyam). That is, when Maya and the effects of Maya are under the power of Thirodhana Shakti without the connection of the Lord’s Thiru-Arul Shakti, souls remain in darkness.

Therefore, just as a lamp’s light is needed for eyes in the dark, so too is the lamp of Maya needed for the soul, that is, for souls afflicted by mala. From Maya, the world, body, and instruments, which are like a lamp, are created and needed. When the same soul becomes one with Shiva-Peruman’s Thiru-Arul, just as the need for a lamp disappears when the sun comes, so too, when united in an advaitic manner in the shade of the Lord’s sacred feet, the need for Maya and its effects, namely worlds, bodies, and instruments, disappears for this same soul. Or, these are not even perceived as things by souls. These Mayas and their effects, the Mayeyams, will subside in Shiva-Peruman’s grace and stand as grace itself for these souls. After souls stand as grace itself, the body (Thanu) and instruments (Karanas), both internal and external, which are the abode of that soul, all become Shiva-Peruman’s grace itself.

When the soul is united with Shiva-Peruman’s Thiru-Arul, the Thanu, Karana, Bhuvana, and Bhoga created from Maya all become grace itself.

Therefore, the soul’s instruments become Shiva’s instruments. The individual instruments become the Lord’s instruments.

At that time, the soul loses the name ‘Pasu’ and gains the name ‘Jivanmukta.’ Therefore, when the bonds (Pasam) are removed, and the name ‘Pasu’ is also removed, and the soul stands as a Jivanmukta, united with Thiru-Arul, at that time, the pervasive Mayas and the effects of Maya, like Thirodhana Shakti, lose the name ‘Pasam’ (i.e., the name ‘Malam’), and even that Maya stands as the very form of grace. Madhavashivagnana Munivar elaborates in the Sivagnana Ma-Padiyam that it stands as darkness itself. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman was one who stood in such a high state. That is why, even when he was placed in the fire chamber, he had such an experience, because he was united and stood in the shade of the Lord’s sacred feet.

We shall proceed with our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 308, Thiru-Nindrachcharukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We have been reflecting on how Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, who was united in the pervasive grace of the Lord’s sacred feet, experienced the heat of the fire chamber, which is an effect of ordinary Maya, as coolness. According to Saiva Siddhanta, Sivakavimani Ayya explains how this happens. ‘The consciousness, which is the sacred form of the First One, adheres to the First One, and being of the same color as the First One, in that body, it is thus full of grace.’ This is from Sivagnana Ma-Padiyam. The consciousness, which is the sacred form of the First One, Shiva-Peruman, is contained within the pervasive grace of the First One, and in the bodies of souls, it is full of grace. ‘Making Thuriya (the fourth state) manifest in Jagrat (the waking state), and performing deeds for the devotees, He is their own.’ This is the 69th Thiru-Padal of Thiru-Kazhitruppadiyar. ‘Are there any sorrows for the devotees of the Lord?’ Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar is in the fire chamber. With mental fortitude, holding onto the shade of the Lord’s sacred feet in his mind, united in that advaitic state, in the Jivanmukta state, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar is in the fire chamber, wondering if sorrow would come to those who have taken refuge in the Lord.

Thus, for the Nayanar who had worshipped Shiva-Peruman, all his past karmas had ended, He had already been made pure.

Therefore, the lime chamber, the fire chamber, is a product of Maya. For Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, that fire chamber stood as the Lord’s Thiru-Arul.

Therefore, its effects, the five elemental experiences perceivable by the five senses, did not appear to him as feelings of pleasure or pain. That fire chamber stood as the very grace of the Lord for Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar.

Therefore, all of them showed only the coolness of grace to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. That is why Sekkizhar Peruman writes in his commentary, ‘It became cool as grace.’ We can understand Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar’s state here from the commentary on the second verse of the eleventh Sutra, as expounded by Arunanthisivachariyar in Sivagnana Siddhiyar. Arunanthisivachariyar has expounded here in Sivagnana Siddhiyar the methods by which a soul, freed from mala, attains the liberation of Shiva-Pethu. How does a soul live as a Jivanmukta? Since it is stated that all malas perish with the body, a mature soul, after the body is shed and the three malas are removed, becomes a pure soul. That soul must adhere to and understand the right to be thus served by the Lord in an advaitic manner.

Therefore, that soul, having become advaitically united with the Lord through that connection, must worship the Lord’s sacred feet and remain in the pervasive presence of those sacred feet. The desire for this will occur without interruption.

Thus, the knowledge and desire of that soul will not attach to any other object, but will solely cling to the advaitic state and occur entirely within the pervasive presence of the Lord’s sacred feet, unitedly.

Thus, being united, after this body perishes, the mala will be removed, and the soul will stand pure. However, this state of standing pure can be attained even while the body exists.

Therefore, having removed and destroyed all malas in this birth, Kriya, Gnana, and Iccha (action, knowledge, and desire) will all be united and remain in the shade of the Lord’s sacred feet.

Therefore, that soul will attain the sacred feet of Shiva-Peruman, the Lord, and live in an unchanging Shiva-Anubhuti, considering that Shiva-Anubhuti as its own Anubhuti.

Therefore, it is understood that that soul lives as a Jivanmukta.

Thus, the Lord will be with that soul, united, one, and inseparable.

In this way, for the Jivanmukta, the removal of mala (i.e., the removal of Pasam) and the attainment of Shiva-Pethu occur. This is the state of having attained Para-Gnana. Through such Para-Gnana, Jivanmuktas will clearly perceive Shiva-Peruman Himself and love Him.

Therefore, they will not be affected by Prarabdha Karma. They will not see even the slightest of those objects that are capable of causing Prarabdha Karma to strike. This Para-Gnana is called Nishthai, which is Shiva-Gnana. This Shiva-Gnana alone is the special knowledge that does not perceive objects.

Therefore, one who has attained this Shiva-Gnana, which is Para-Gnana, is a Jivanmukta. He will constantly perceive Shiva-Peruman alone.

Therefore, he will not come into the experience of Prarabdha by perceiving other objects. He will not be affected by that experience.

Therefore, it is understood that since a Jivanmukta does not perceive anything else, there is no Maya-Mayeya association at all.

Therefore, it is understood that there is no Prarabdha Karma or its effects arising from Maya-Mayeya association. All these are beyond Chariya, Kriya, Yoga, and Gnana, Having transcended the stages of hearing, clarifying, contemplating, and Nishthai, and having attained Shiva-Gnana, those Jivanmuktas who have attained Para-Gnana, which is Shiva-Gnana, will thus constantly gaze upon the shade of Shiva-Peruman’s sacred feet.

Therefore, they will not be affected by Prarabdha Karma or by the objects arising from the association of Maya and its effects, which are called Pasas. They will not experience any of these. This is what Arunanthisivachariyar Peruman states in the second verse of the eleventh Sutra of Sivagnana Siddhiyar: ‘Those who have perceived the Supreme through Para-Gnana will perceive only the Supreme; they will not perceive objects. The knowledge that comes to perceive is manifold knowledge, the delusion of ignorance, the knowledge of the expressed and the expressor, the knowledge that causes confusion of the five states, the knowledge of the experiencer and the experienced, the knowledge of the conceived, is all mental knowledge.’ Thiru-Gnanam is the knowledge that transcends all these.

Therefore, the verse states that Shiva-Muktas will perceive only Shiva. This is the state in which our Thiru-Navukkarasar stood. It is said that he perceived only Shiva-Peruman.

Here, the Nayanar worshipped only Shiva-Peruman, was united in an advaitic manner, and was in the Jivanmukta state.

Therefore, the fire chamber did not affect him. The chamber did not act as an effect of Maya, but stood as the very grace of the Lord.

Therefore, the Nayanar experienced the coolness of divine grace.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasar’s state is explained in terms of Saiva Siddhanta scriptural principles by Sivakavimani Ayya.

Similarly, just as the fire chamber did not affect Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, so too, subsequently, poison was given to Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, elephants were set upon him, and he was tied to a stone and thrown into the sea. Yet, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar was not harmed by any of these.

Therefore, we can apply this scriptural explanation we have just seen to these actions and narratives, and thus understand the true meaning of these miracles.

Thus, when Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sang the Thiru-Padigam ‘Maasil Veenaiyum’ in the fire chamber, Sekkizhar Peruman wrote a poetic commentary on the first verse, which begins with ‘Maasil Veenaiyum,’ Sivakavimani Ayya elaborates on it, explaining various subtle points of Saiva Siddhanta scriptures.

Thus, we will continue to reflect on the meanings of the remaining sacred verses. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 309, Thiru-Nindrachcharukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We have been reflecting on the meaning of the Thiru-Padigam ‘Maasil Veenaiyum’ sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman in the lime chamber. We reflected on the meanings of the first sacred verse and how it aligns with Saiva Siddhanta scriptural concepts.

Now, the second sacred verse: ‘Namachivayave gnanavum kalviyum / Namachivayave naan arivichaiyum / Namachivayave naa navindru ethume / Namachivayave nanneri kattume.’ This is the second sacred verse.

Here, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman refers to ‘Namachivaya’ as the sacred name of Shiva-Peruman. When Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman arrived at Thiru-Adhigai and came to Thilagavathi Ammaiyar’s sacred monastery, when he arrived, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar gave him the sacred ash along with the Panchakshara.

Thus, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar guided Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman by chanting the Panchakshara. From that moment, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman was immersed in the sacred five letters, the Sri Panchakshara, ‘Namachivaya.’ Therefore, he sings about this Sri Panchakshara, ‘Namachivaya,’ in the second sacred verse. He sings that this ‘Namachivaya’ itself becomes education and knowledge.

Here, he has mentioned ‘education’ and ‘knowledge’ separately.

Therefore, education is distinct from knowledge. Education serves as the cause for knowledge. What is knowledge? To know and attain Shiva-Peruman, gnana (divine wisdom) is the means. Gnana can be understood as para-gnana (supreme knowledge), and education as apara-gnana (worldly knowledge).

Therefore, Namasivaya itself is gnana. Namasivaya itself is the education that leads to gnana.

Next, he sings, “Namasivaya is the knowledge I have been taught.” Vitchai means vijnai, vidhai, or porul vitchai, meaning the mantra revealed to me.

Therefore, he sings, “Namasivaya is the mantra revealed to me.” Now, next, he sings, “Namasivaya is what I recite and praise.” Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman states that the sacred five-letter mantra, Namasivaya, was revealed to him.

Therefore, his tongue constantly recites that mantra. This is the meaning of the third line, “Namasivaya is what I recite and praise.” Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sings, “I hold the five letters of Your name as my weapon on my tongue.” Is it not so? He sings that his tongue always praises such a sacred five-letter Namasivaya. “Praises” here means incessantly. “Even if I forget You, O good one, my tongue will utter Namasivaya” is from Sundaramoorthy Swamigal’s Thevaram.

Now, next, he sings, “Namasivaya will show the good path.” “Good path” means gnana. This means the path that serves as the foundation for attaining Shiva-Peruman is the good path. It signifies the way to achieve the liberation of mukti. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sings that this too is Namasivaya. We reflected on the meaning of the first hymn, did we not? In it, we saw that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman found the intense fiery chamber to be very sweet and cool because he was sheltered in the shade of Shiva-Peruman’s holy feet.

This signifies the outcome.

Now, in this second hymn, starting with Namasivaya, he sings the glories of the sacred mantra Namasivaya. In the first hymn, Peruman Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman showed the outcome of Shiva-ananda Shiva-bhoga. In the second hymn, he glorifies Namasivaya, the mantra that serves as the means to attain that Shiva-ananda Shiva-bhoga.

Thus, the first two Thiru-hymns are structured.

Now, the third Thiru-hymn, and the five Thiru-hymns from three, four, five, six, and seven, are gracious instructions given by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman out of compassion for the souls of this world.

Therefore, the next five Thiru-hymns are Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s gracious instructions to the souls of this world, that is, to us. He asks, “Why do you needlessly wander in this worldly life? Serve Shiva-Peruman!” and thus, he tells us the way to serve Shiva-Peruman. He describes the path to servitude.

Therefore, the third hymn is: “Aalaakaar aalaanaarai adainthu uyyaar meelaa aatseythu meymmaiyul nirkilaar tholaatha suraiyo thozhumbar sevi vaazhaa maaynthu mannaakik kazhivare.” This is the third Thiru-hymn. It describes how those who do not serve Shiva-Peruman, the Lord, waste their time. “Aalaathal” means to be in servitude. He sings, “Aalaakaar,” addressing the souls of this world, saying, “You will not serve Shiva-Peruman, you will not surrender to Shiva-Peruman. And you will also fail to worship those who have surrendered to Shiva-Peruman and serve Him. You will not attain salvation by reaching Shiva’s

“You will not attain salvation by reaching the devotees. He sings, addressing the worldly people who waste their time without serving Shiva-Peruman or Shiva-Peruman’s devotees. If one serves Shiva-Peruman or Shiva-Peruman’s devotees, those worldly souls will find the path to salvation. To be liberated from this cycle of birth and death and attain the bliss of mukti, one must serve Shiva-Peruman or Shiva-Peruman’s devotees.

“Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman states that both of these are ways to find rest. We have contemplated the sacred stories of those who attained mukti by serving Shiva-Peruman. We have also greatly contemplated the sacred stories of those who reached Shiva-Peruman’s devotees and served them. We have contemplated in the great ancient puranas.

“Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman states that by contemplating all these histories, one should serve Shiva-Peruman and Shiva-Peruman’s devotees. He says one should serve Shiva-Peruman with unwavering devotion and abide in that truth. Truth is the nature of God, Sat. He addresses the people of the world, saying, “O people of the world, you do not attain that God, you do not serve God, and you do not abide in that path of truth!” Next, he sings, “Tholaatha suraiyo thozhumbar sevi.” He says that the ears that serve Shiva-Peruman and listen to the glories of Shiva-Peruman, the sacred names of Shiva-Peruman, the sacred puranas of Shiva-Peruman, and the Shiva-shastras are truly Ears. Without these, ears that do not do all these things are merely holes, he says, addressing the people of this world.

“Therefore, an ear that is not pierced by thoughts about Shiva-Peruman is merely an ear with a hole.

“Similarly, taking other senses, those worldly people who do not experience Shiva-related matters through all their other senses waste the body they have received.

“Thus, they waste their lives, die in vain, and turn into dust, he sings in this third Thiru-hymn.

“Now, the fourth Thiru-hymn: “Nadalaivaazhvu kondu en seithir naan” The fourth Thiru-hymn is structured as: “Sudalai seruvathu sorpiramaname kadalin nanju amuthu undavar kaivittal udalinaar kidanthu oor muni pandame.” Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar addresses the people of this world, calling them shameless. For what will you do with this life full of suffering, which you lead in vain? It is certain that you will eventually reach the cremation ground. The words of the wise are proof of this.

“Therefore, if Shiva-Peruman, the Lord who consumed the halahala poison that arose from the milky ocean as nectar, abandons you, your body will become an object despised by the villagers.

“Therefore, instead of shamelessly wasting your time, serve Shiva-Peruman and He advises them to serve Shiva-Peruman’s devotees. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar calls this life a life full of suffering. He sings that it is certain that everyone who lives such a life full of suffering will eventually reach the cremation ground. This is “sorpiramanam,” meaning “shabda pramanam” in Sanskrit, which he renders as “sorpiramanam” in Tamil. It is the saying of the wise that wasting days and eventually reaching the cremation ground is certain.

“Moreover, it is also a truth we directly observe as “pratyaksha pramanam.” Therefore, you waste your days in vain. Shiva-Peruman is the one who consumed even the halahala poison as nectar. If He abandons you, if He who has protected you until now If he abandons you without protecting you, your body will become an impure object. Until now, you have cherished your body with great affection, enthusiasm, and desire. If Shiva-Peruman does not protect it, this body that you have cherished until now will become an impure object despised by these villagers, warns Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, and advises them to follow the path of Shiva.

“Now, the fifth hymn: “Poo kai kondu aran ponnadi potrilaar naakkai kondu aran naamam navilkaar aakkaikke irai thedi alamandu kaakkaikke iraiyaakik kazhivare.” Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman addresses the people of the world. He first sings, “You will not show love to Shiva-Peruman’s holy feet by holding flowers in your hand. You will not worship Shiva-Peruman’s golden feet by offering flowers.” Here, when he sings, “holding flowers in your hand,” it can be understood to encompass all the actions according to the flower ritual we have already seen: selecting, searching, arranging, stringing, and offering appropriate flowers.

“Thus, you will not worship Shiva-Peruman’s holy feet with flowers. You will not utter Shiva-Peruman’s holy name with your tongue. You are always searching, searching, searching for food to nourish this body.

“Thus, after running around all your life to nourish this body, these corpses, which are eventually taken to the cremation ground, Will be torn apart and eaten by crows. Is it to become food for crows that you run around all your life nourishing your body?

“Therefore, instead of nourishing this body that will become food for crows, hold flowers in your hand and worship Shiva-Peruman’s golden feet. Utter Shiva-Peruman’s holy name with your tongue. This is the meaning of the fifth Thiru-hymn.

“Thus, he speaks of the impermanence of this world and the impermanence of this body, and also provides the means of what we should do. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman.

“We will continue to contemplate the meanings of the remaining five Thiru-hymns of this Thiru-pathikam.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 310, Thiru-Nindrachcharukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We are contemplating the meanings of the hymns of the pathikam that begins with “Maasil Veenaiyum.” We have contemplated the meanings of five Thiru-hymns.

Now, the sixth Thiru-hymn: “Kurigalum adaiyalamum koyilum nerigalum avar nindrathor nermaiyum ariya aayiram aaranam othilum poriyileer manam enkol pugathathe” he sings. This is the sixth Thiru-hymn. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sings, addressing the souls of this world. He asks, “Thousands of Vedas and Agamas speak of Shiva-Peruman, His symbols, the temples where He resides, the paths to attain Him, and the righteousness in which He stands. Why do these not enter your minds, O ignorant ones?” Vedas, Agamas, all these speak.

Here, what is called “Aaranam” is the sacred word of Shiva-Peruman. These are the Vedas and Shiva Agamas. What do all these say? They speak of the signs, that is, the places where Shiva-Peruman manifests and bestows grace. The places where Shiva-Peruman manifests and resides are the sacred form of the Guru, the sacred attire of the devotees, and the Shiva-lingam. The Vedic Agamas state that Shiva-Peruman manifests and bestows grace upon beings in these three places: Guru, Linga, and Sangama.

Furthermore, the sacred words of Shiva-Peruman, the Vedas, Agamas, and Puranas, describe all the symbols of Shiva-Peruman. The Vedas, Agamas, and Puranas, which are the sacred words of Shiva-Peruman, describe the symbols of Shiva-Peruman. The matted crown, the crescent moon, the Ganga, the Konrai flower, the serpent, all these are on His matted hair. His three sacred eyes, His sacred ears adorned with earrings and ear-studs, His coral-red lips, His sacred chest adorned with serpent ornaments, His sacred body smeared with sacred ash, His sacred body adorned with tiger skin, deer skin, elephant skin, and lion skin, His sacred hands holding the battle-axe, His sacred feet adorned with heroic anklets and silambu – all these sacred symbols of Shiva-Peruman are described by the Vedas, Agamas, and Puranas. The Puranas speak of the temples where Shiva-Peruman resides and bestows grace. Shiva-Peruman’s clear The Shiva temples and the hearts of devotees are said to be the places where Shiva-Peruman resides clearly.

The Thiru-mantram states, “The heart is the great temple, the body is the shrine.” The Sivagnana Bodham states, “The form of those filled with love and the temple itself, worship them as Aran.” Thus, the Vedas and Agamas speak of Shiva-temples and the sacred hearts of great devotees as the places where Shiva-Peruman lovingly and clearly resides.

Furthermore, the Agamas clearly describe the four paths of Shiva-dharma—Chariya, Kriya, Yoga, and Gnana—as the ways to attain Shiva-Peruman.

Moreover, the Vedas and Shiva-Agamas speak of the nature of Shiva-Peruman, who is clearly present for those who love Him and obscure for those who do not. The Vedas and Shiva Agamas speak of how Shiva-Peruman is present everywhere and in everything, and how He stands prominently in specific places with a unique quality. In the Nindra Thiru-thandakam, Sri Rudram, and other texts, it is described how He is pervasive. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman asks in this sixth Thiru-hymn, “Do all these, the sacred words of Shiva-Peruman, the Vedas and Shiva Agamas, not reach your minds?” Until now, in the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth Thiru-hymns, he spoke of the way to serve Shiva-Peruman and the places to worship Shiva-Peruman.

Now, he is going to speak of the manner of worshipping Shiva-Peruman in the seventh Thiru-hymn.

Now, he sings: “Vaazhtha vaayum ninaikka mada nenjum thaazhtha chenniyum thantha thalaivanai soozhtha maa malar thoovi thuthiyaathe veezhtha va vinaiye nedungalame.” Shiva-Peruman gave humans the organ of the mouth to praise Shiva-Peruman. He gave humans the heart, the mind, to remember Shiva-Peruman. He gave humans the head to bow to Shiva-Peruman.

Thus, Shiva-Peruman, the Lord who gave the mouth to praise, the heart to remember Him, and the head to bow to Him, has given these out of compassion for living beings.

Therefore, he sings, “Alas, I have wasted a long time without praising Him by scattering great flowers.” Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sings, “He has given the mouth to praise.” Therefore, the meaning here is that we should use our mouth only to praise Shiva-Peruman, the Lord, and for nothing else.

Similarly, the head should be used only to bow to Shiva-Peruman, and only to Shiva-Peruman. The mind should only think of Shiva-Peruman and nothing else.

Now, next, the eighth Thiru-hymn. He sings that when we worship Shiva-Peruman, the Lord, in this way, sins will depart from us. In this eighth Thiru-hymn, he sings: “Ezhuthu paavai nallaar thiram vittu naan thozhuthu potri Even as I stood worshipping and praising, the mind, like a ploughman who ploughs again along the furrow already ploughed, was surrounded and drawn to the charms of beautiful women. This is the eighth Thiru-hymn. In this world, we experience various pleasures.

“Thus, we repeatedly experience without aversion the very things we have already experienced. We have melted like ghee in worldly enjoyments.

“But if we join Shiva-Peruman, all these will leave us.

“Therefore, he sings, “Praise Shiva-Peruman and Shiva-Peruman’s devotees; serve them.” Next, the ninth Thiru-hymn: “Nekku nekku ninaibavar nenjule pukku nirkum ponnaar sadai punniyan pokkamikkavar poovu neerum kandu nakku nirpar avar thammai naaniye.” This is the ninth Thiru-hymn. He sings in this ninth Thiru-hymn about how the intensity of our love for God will be if we worship Him in this manner. “Nekku nekku ninaibavar” means those who remember Shiva-Peruman with melting hearts. The meaning is those who remember Shiva-Peruman with a melting, softening heart. Shiva-Peruman lovingly and clearly resides brightly within the hearts of such devotees.

“But without this, that is, without love that melts the heart, God stands smiling with shame at those who merely worship Him with flowers and water, he sings. “Naani” means It means without clarity, not openly.

“Thus, he sings in this ninth hymn that God exists in two ways in two different places.

“Now, in the tenth Thiru-hymn, he explains the state in which God stands, as mentioned above. The tenth Thiru-hymn is as follows: “Virakil theeyinan paalil padu neybol maraiya nindrulla maamani sothiyan uravu kolnattu unarvu kayitrinaal muruga vaangak kadaiya munnirkume.” This is the tenth Thiru-hymn. In this, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sings about how Shiva-Peruman manifests and bestows grace when Shiva’s devotees worship Him with love. Just as fire is in wood, just as ghee is in milk, Just as light is in a gem, so too is the Lord, he sings. The fire within the wood is hidden; it is not manifest.

“But when it comes into contact with fire, the wood, through the fire that was within it and the fire that approached it, connects and the fire becomes visibly apparent in the wood.

“Similarly, ghee is in milk, but it is not visibly apparent to us; it is hidden within the milk.

“Likewise, light is in gems, but that light is not naturally manifest; it is hidden. As the gems are polished, the light within them increases and appears clearly. Until polished, that light remains hidden.

“Thus, fire is hidden in wood, ghee is hidden in milk, and light is hidden in a gem. But when two arani sticks are rubbed together, the fire within them appears. When milk is churned and processed, the ghee within it becomes apparent. When gems are polished, the light that was hidden until then becomes visible.

“Similarly, God is hidden within our minds. Just as fire is hidden in arani sticks, just as ghee is hidden in milk, just as light is hidden in a gem, so too is God hidden within our minds, not overtly manifest. So when will He appear? Just as fire appears when arani sticks are rubbed, just as ghee appears when milk is churned, just as light appears when gems are polished, so too can we overtly see the God within our minds. When? If we plant the staff of ‘relationship’ and churn vigorously with the rope of ‘awareness,’ the God who is unmanifest within our minds will manifest brightly.

“This is what Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman sings: “Planting the staff of relationship, and drawing with the rope of awareness, He will stand before you.” We must plant the staff of relationship, and tie the rope of awareness to that staff. When we churn with this rope of awareness tied to the staff of relationship, God will appear. It is said, “planting the staff of relationship,” so what does that mean? It means that God and souls have a relationship. What is the relationship between God and souls? God is a sentient being, and souls are sentient beings.

“Therefore, the relationship between God and souls is that both belong to the same category, called ‘chit’ (consciousness). The right and love that arise from this single category of ‘chit’ constitute the connection and relationship between God and souls. This relationship itself should be the staff. To this, the rope of ‘awareness’ must be tied. What is meant by ‘awareness’ here? As taught by the Shiva-acharyas to souls, it is the ‘sadhana gnanam’ (knowledge gained through practice) of knowing with Shiva-gnanam (divine knowledge) as the eye.

“Such When we churn, taking the ‘sadhana gnanam’ (knowledge gained through practice) that knows with Shiva-gnanam (divine knowledge) as the eye, bestowed by the Shiva-acharyas, as the rope, and the love of possession for Shiva Peruman as the staff, then God will manifest and bestow His grace. The God who is unmanifest within our minds will manifest brightly and bestow His grace. This manifestation, this standing, is explained as His ‘standing righteousness.’ This is the meaning of this tenth Thiru-padal (sacred verse).

“Thus, we have contemplated the meanings of the ten Thiru-padals of this Thiru-padigam (sacred hymn) that begins with “Masu il veenaiyum malai madhiyamum” (Spotless lute and evening moon). In this Thiru-padigam, many truths of Saiva Siddhanta are conveyed: the fruit of Shiva-ananda (divine bliss) and Shiva-bhoga (divine experience) which is the shade of Shiva Peruman’s sacred feet, the mantra which is the means to attain it, and His dominion and the path to submission, the places where Shiva Peruman is seen and worshipped, the ways of worshipping Him, what is to be abandoned when worshipping Shiva Peruman, the power of love placed upon Shiva Peruman, and the state in which Shiva Peruman manifests and bestows His grace.

“Let us go on contemplating.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 311. Thiru-nindrachcharakkam. Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We saw that Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman composed the Thiru-padigam “Masu il veenaiyum” while in the fire chamber. That fire chamber was pleasant and cool for Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman, who was united in the shade of Shiva Peruman’s sacred feet.

It was pleasant and cool, just like the shade of Shiva Peruman’s sacred feet. We saw all those details. Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman remained in this fire chamber for seven days. After seven days, that is, seven days after Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman was placed inside the lime kiln, by the king’s command, his guards came and opened the lime kiln. They opened the fire chamber.

Thus, Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman remained in that fire chamber for seven days. Sekkizhar Peruman also sings extensively about these events. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing that Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman remained in that fire chamber, meditating solely on Shiva Peruman, and was in advaitic union with Shiva Peruman. In this verse, Sekkizhar Peruman describes how Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman remained pleasantly, contemplating and worshipping the sacred feet of God: “Masin madhi needu punal manni valar chenniyanai pesa iniyanai ulagalaudaiya pinjaganai isanai emperumanai evvuyirum tharuvanai adi vanangi inidhu irundhar.” He describes how Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman remained pleasantly there, worshipping the sacred feet of Shiva Peruman, who has a head where the flawless moon and the ever-flowing Ganga reside and grow, who is sweet to speak of, who is the Pinjagan (one with matted locks) who rules all worlds, who is the Lord, our Peruman, who creates all beings, and who is the inexhaustible nectar born of love. In this Thiru-padal, Sekkizhar Peruman describes Shiva Peruman in seven ways: as Chenniyan, Iniyan, Pinjagan, Isan, Emperuman, Tharuvan, and Amudhu.

He states seven attributes because Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar remained in the lime kiln for seven days, worshipping and praising Shiva Peruman.

Therefore, to subtly convey this, he describes Shiva Peruman in seven ways in this Thiru-padal.

First, he sings about Shiva Peruman as “Masin madhi needu punal manni valar chenniyanai” (One whose head is adorned with the flawless moon and the ever-flowing Ganga). He first sings about Shiva Peruman as having matted locks where the moon (pirai chandran) and the Ganga (punal) reside and grow. The moon, which was waning daily, became a waxing moon upon reaching the Lord’s sacred head. The Ganga, which flowed with a thousand great faces, when held by Shiva Peruman in His matted locks, became small like dew, remaining steadfast on Shiva Peruman’s sacred head.

Furthermore, the moon on Shiva Peruman’s matted locks possesses the nectarine kala (digit). We have contemplated in the history of Kachi, in the Kanchi Puranam, when we looked at the history of Nila Thingal Thundapperumal inside the Ekambaranathar Temple, that when poison arose from the Milk Ocean, Vishnu was saved because the moon’s digit on Shiva Peruman’s sacred head spread its influence.

Similarly, the Ganga is also cool nectar.

Thus, we see that the Ganga and the moon on the Lord’s sacred head are both nectarine kalas and nectar.

Here, when our Thiru-navukkarasu Peruman was seated in the fire chamber, that fire chamber became cool through Shiva Peruman’s grace.

Therefore, for Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar, who was inside, the cooling elements that grew and filled the Lord’s sacred head, namely the moon and the Ganga, became apparent. He praised Shiva Peruman as Chenniyan, who possesses that Ganga and moon. This is the first way he praised Shiva Peruman, calling Him Chenniyan.

Now, secondly, in this song, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to Shiva Peruman as “Pesa Iniyan” (sweet to speak of). He sings that Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar was seated in the fire chamber, contemplating the one who is sweet to speak of. Every time one thinks, every time one speaks, always and in everything, He is the one who showers the honey of joyful smiles. This is the implication. Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar has praised the Lord in this Thiru-padigam, which begins with “Masu il veenaiyum,” saying, “Namashivaya, I utter and praise,” and “Those who do not utter the Lord’s name with their tongue,” and “The Lord who gave me a mouth to praise, a mind to think, and a head to bow,” and “I stood worshipping.” Thus, he has spoken about Shiva Peruman within this Thiru-padigam.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman sings that Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar remained pleasantly in the fire chamber, worshipping such a sweet one, the one who is sweet to speak of, Shiva Peruman.

Now, thirdly, he sings that he remained contemplating “Ulagu aludaiya Pinjagan” (the Pinjagan who rules the world).

Here, Shiva Peruman is referred to as the Lord who has all beings as His servants.

Therefore, the implication here is that the Lord has the duty and compassion to protect those who are His servants.

Now, fourthly, he sings “Isan” (the Lord). Sekkizhar Peruman sings that Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar remained in the fire chamber, contemplating Shiva Peruman, who is Isan. Isan means one who possesses sovereignty. The term ‘Ishvara’ (Isan) by yogic convention and etymological derivation refers exclusively to Shiva Peruman. This is a truth we observe. That the term ‘Ishvara’ refers only to Shiva Peruman is a truth discovered and proven by the elders of the Saiva faith.

This universe is sustained by Ishvara; it cannot exist without Ishvara. Such an Ishvara must be one, a singular being. It is inappropriate for Him to be many. The term ‘Ishvara’ and its meaning do not apply to other deities besides Shiva Peruman. The Vedas proclaim such an Ishvara. Although the term ‘Ishvara’ may, through yoga, refer to other gods, by yogic convention, it refers only to Shiva Peruman.

Therefore, the term ‘Ishvara’ is a name exclusive to Shiva Peruman. It is a Mimamsa tradition that yogic convention is stronger than yoga.

Therefore, the lexicon called Amaracosam, like the names of Shiva and other names of Shiva Peruman, recites the term ‘Ishvara’ as a name of Shiva.

Therefore, the term ‘Ishvara’ and ‘Isan’ refer only to Shiva Peruman. This has been explained by Sabha-pathi Navalar, a scholar of the Thiru-kailaya Paramparai Thiru-avaduthurai Adheenam, in his work ‘Chaturveda Tatparya Sangraham,’ which is a garland of Vedic hymns.

Now, fifthly, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to Shiva Peruman as ‘Emperuman’ (Our Lord) in this song. He sings that Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar remained in that fire chamber, contemplating Emperuman. Emperuman means that although Shiva Peruman is the Lord of all beings and the Isan for everyone, He is especially our own Lord, our leader. This is the meaning of the word ‘Emperuman.’ Next, sixthly, he refers to Shiva Peruman as ‘Evvuyirum Tharuvan’ (One who gives all life). ‘Tharuthal’ means to create. It also means to protect. No matter what nature a being possesses, no matter where it is, Shiva Peruman, the Lord, stands within that being as its life, protecting those beings and showing compassion.

Thiru-gnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred words state, “He created various wombs and stood within them as the life of those beings.” Just as it is said, “He is the true one who lovingly provides nectar to the embryo, the egg, and the frog within the stone,” here it is implied that He is the protector of the life within the lime kiln.

Now, seventhly, Sekkizhar Peruman sings here about Shiva Peruman as ‘Asaiyil Ara Amudhu’ (the inexhaustible nectar of desire). Asaiyil Ara Amudhu means that Shiva Peruman is like an inexhaustible nectar that never cloys, no matter how much one desires and consumes.

Here, ‘asai’ (desire) comes in the sense of ‘anbu’ (love).

Therefore, its meaning is ‘the inexhaustible nectar born of love.’ ‘Anbinil vilaindha ar amudhe’ (the rare nectar born of love) is from Thiru-vasagam. Sekkizhar Peruman here sings of one who is like nectar as nectar. Nectar is something that prevents death; this is the implication here.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman sings in this song that Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar sat pleasantly in that fire chamber, worshipping the sacred feet of Shiva Peruman, who is the Chenniyan adorned with the flawless moon and the ever-flowing Ganga, who is sweet to speak of, who is the Pinjagan who rules the world, who is Ishvara, who is Emperuman, who gives all life, and who is the inexhaustible nectar of love. Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar, who was inside the fire chamber, felt no heat; moreover, he experienced great joy. He was in great bliss. It is said that those who attain the sacred feet of Shiva Peruman experience the removal of bonds and the attainment of Shiva-peru (divine grace).

Accordingly, Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar was seated in the shade of the Lord’s sacred feet, and thus this experience came to him. This means that Sekkizhar Peruman sings that he remained pleasantly in the fire chamber, having attained the shade of Shiva Peruman’s sacred feet and always worshipping that shade. Before this, it was sung that he worshipped only the First One; that refers to the ‘sariya’ (charya) and ‘kiriya’ (kriya) that occur in gnanam (knowledge). The Saiva Siddhanta scriptures, known as the Dasakaryas (ten stages), state that Tattva Suddhi (purification of principles) brings about Atma Darshanam (vision of the soul).

Thereafter, it performs the eight stages up to Shiva Darshanam (vision of Shiva). What is mentioned here refers to the paths of Yoga and Gnanam. This performs the actions of Shiva Yoga and Shiva Bhoga. Shiva Yoga grants only a pleasant light, while Shiva Bhoga is an ocean of supreme bliss. Shiva Yoga is called Turiyam, and Shiva Bhoga is called Turiyatitam.

Therefore, the idea of ‘inidhu irundhar’ (remained pleasantly) refers to this. “Are there any sorrows for the devotees of Isan?” he said. Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar first said this before entering the lime kiln.

At that time, he had the three types of awareness: sorrow, devotee, and Isan, and he knew and worshipped Shiva Peruman. That was that state.

But now, Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar is in the state of ‘inidhu irundha nilay’ (pleasant abiding). Without any of the aforementioned feelings, forgetting the world and himself, he became one with Him. That path is the Shiva Yogic state of being one and serving the Lord. This is called ‘Jākirathaiyil Turiyam Purithal’ (experiencing Turiyam in the waking state) in the scriptures. Siddhanta states this as ‘Turiyathai Jākirathaiyil Seytharuli’ (having performed Turiyam in the waking state). These are the means and the fruits.

Thus, praising Shiva Peruman in seven ways, for seven days, Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar remained in that fire chamber, the lime kiln, did he not? The seven things mentioned here are like seven crore great mantras, capable of redeeming souls in all seven types of births. This is its subtlety.

But did Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar realize that seven days had passed? Did he realize that seven days had passed? His awareness did not go to the knowledge of whether these seven days had passed. He was absorbed in the grace and pervasiveness of the Lord’s sacred feet.

Therefore, it can be said that he had no opportunity to perceive the time calculations of days, which arise from the earth revolving around the sun and rotating on its own axis.

Similarly, even the gnanis (sages) who wander outside would not contemplate these time calculations. We can recall the Thiru-vasagam, “Engu ezilan gnayiru emakku elorembavai” (Where is the beautiful sun for us, O maidens?).

Furthermore, Sivakavimani Ayyavargal quotes a verse from the Thiru-vilaiyadal Puranam as an example of Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar’s state. That is, he explains that the verse illustrates that for a soul united with the shade of Shiva Peruman’s sacred feet, the time calculations of this world, such as day and night, are of no consequence. The thirty-ninth verse in the chapter titled ‘Vadavoor Adigalukku Upadesitha Padalam’ (Chapter on the Instruction to Vadavoor Adigal) in the Thiru-alavai Kandam of the Thiru-vilaiyadal Puranam is: “Karavu il ullamam visumbu idai kasara vilangum parasuyila sudarkku udayam eeru inmaiyal paga The verse states: “Pagalum iravu nerpada kandilar” (They saw neither day nor night). Its meaning is that for a soul without the veil of mala (impurity), the Nishkala Shiva (formless Shiva) continuously appears without interruption. That state is a state of permanent existence, without beginning or end. For that soul, day and night, which are referred to here as Sakala Kevalam (the state of being with attributes and being alone), are not perceived.

“That state is referred to here as the pure state of Jagirathatitam (beyond the waking state). Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar was seated in the lime kiln in such a state.

“Therefore, the idea conveyed here is that small time calculations like whether seven days had passed were of no consequence to him. This is the state of being immersed in Shiva-ananda (divine bliss). Sivakavimani Ayyavargal writes that the shloka “Chidadityo hrudakase pratibhati nirantaram nastameti nacchodeti katham sandhyamupasmake” (The sun of consciousness shines continuously in the sky of the heart; it neither sets nor rises, so how can we perform evening worship?) also conveys the same idea. In such a state of immersion in Shiva-ananda, Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar remained pleasantly for seven days in the fire chamber of the lime kiln.

“We shall proceed with our contemplation.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 312. Thiru-Nindra-Charukkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar remained blissfully in that lime kiln for seven days.

After these seven days, the Pallava king summoned the Jains and instructed them to inspect the fiery chamber. It was a clear conclusion that if someone remained inside that intensely hot chamber for seven days, they could not possibly be alive. Nevertheless, these Jains, filled with suspicion, opened the fiery chamber. As these Jains, like a dark multitude, opened that dreadful fiery chamber, they beheld Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar seated there, immersed in the abundance of Shiva-ananda, having partaken of the ambrosia from the honey-dripping, lotus-like feet of Ambalavanar, thereby attaining clarity and being devoid of any deficiency, filled with joy. The cruel Jains were astonished, wondering if he had not suffered even a slight affliction, what a marvel! Inside the fiery chamber, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar was submerged in the state of Shiva-ananda param-bhoga, oblivious to all else, standing in that flood of bliss.

This state is the Shiva-bhoga state; it is ananda that does not diminish like other joys, ananda that is without lack, unlike other joys, ananda that does not cause sorrow, unlike other joys, and ananda that does not wane but rather increases evermore.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar remained in that flood of bliss. There, he continuously meditated upon the sacred feet of Shiva-peruman, abiding in that fullness of grace. The sacred feet of Shiva-peruman are supreme bliss, the ambrosia that bestows joy by removing birth and death.

There, within the lime chamber, Thiru-Navukkarasu peruman was immersed in this fullness of grace. The Jains who witnessed this observed a difference between the state in which Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar entered the lime chamber and the state in which they found him after seven days. That difference was that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar appeared clearer than before. That clarity arose from having partaken of the ambrosia of the Lord’s sacred feet.

Therefore, it is understood that those who have attained the sacred feet of Shiva-peruman are the ones who have achieved clarity; others remain unclear. Seeing Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar in that state, without any deficiency, the Jains were greatly astonished and amazed.

However, the Jains, fearing that the king, upon hearing this, might realize the greatness of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, now conspired to deceive the king.

Therefore, they approached the king and stated that it was no miracle that he remained alive in the lime chamber, because Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, when he was previously in their Jain religion, had performed many spiritual practices.

Therefore, using the mantras he learned from their Jain religion, he survived without dying inside the fiery chamber of the lime kiln by employing those mantras now, thus misleading the king. The Jains did this because they did not want the king to consider it a miracle.

Therefore, to prove that it was not a miracle, the Jains spoke this falsehood.

Furthermore, the Jains told the king, “O King, administer a deadly poison to him.” These Jains dared to commit the great sin of further blaspheming Shiva. They spoke unspeakable things with their mouths.

Therefore, Sekkizhar peruman, in this verse, refers to them as “foul-mouthed Jains.” He further mentions that the Jains, believing that brushing their teeth would kill worms, would not brush their teeth and thus had foul-smelling mouths.

Therefore, he refers to them as “foul-mouthed Jains” here. These Jains, who would not brush their teeth to avoid killing even a worm, cast aside that principle and, with their very words, advocated for the great sin of murder.

Here, they instruct, “Administer poison to Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar.” The king, who was corrupted by the influence of these Jains, also, being swayed by their delusion, commanded, “Administer the poison.” This king was not inherently evil-minded; he was corrupted by associating with the Jains, by associating with evil people, he became corrupted through that connection. This is because, in a few days, very soon, he would realize that the words of the Jains were false, understand the truth, embrace Shaivism, and undertake Shaivite service.

Therefore, this king was inherently of good intellect, but by associating with the Jains, he became subject to their delusion and issued such cruel commands. The deceit of the Jains, their falsehoods, their contradictory principles, their injustice, and all the conspiracies they orchestrated made it impossible for the king to perceive these things. Just as severe mental illness, potent poison, and the like, when they ascend to the head, obscure the intellect, so too, the king’s excessive trust in the Jains here seized his ability to discern truth and deluded him.

Therefore, the Jains here brought the king under their control, deluded him, and through his words, obtained commands due to that delusion. All these were the desires of the Jains, the decisions of the Jains. That is, these sinful acts—placing Thiru-Navukkarasu peruman in the fiery chamber, giving him poison, unleashing an elephant, tying him to a stone and casting him into the sea—all these were the desires of the Jains. They obtained them from the king’s words, deluding the king, and carried them out as royal decrees. It is the duty of a king to punish murderers, but here, if they are making someone administer poison and kill someone through his own words, then we can see how much the king’s intellect was deluded by the Jains and how skilled the Jains were in this trickery.

Similarly, in Madurai, the Jains set fire to the sacred monastery where Thiru-Gnanasambandha peruman was staying. They even obtained the royal decree for this by bringing the Madurai king, Koon Pandiyan, under their control.

In the same way, here, next, they say that poison should be administered to Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. The king also issues such an order. They obtained an order to administer poison into the sacred mouth of Thiru-Navukkarasar, who possessed ambrosial speech. The sacred mouth of Thiru-Navukkarasu peruman, who possessed ambrosial speech, though it was fitting to offer ambrosia, they, contrary to that, made the king agree to administer poison. The king also issued such an order.

Therefore, they mixed poison in milk and rice, which they prepared, and offered it to Thiru-Navukkarasu peruman. The term “pal adisil” appears in the verse here. “Pal adisil” means rice cooked with milk. This is known as payasam. “Parchoru” is the Tamil term.

So, they poured poison into that payasam, mixed poison into that milk rice, and offered it to Thiru-Navukkarasu peruman to eat. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar was capable of making the glories of Shiva-peruman manifest in this world. The Jains, with their deceitful minds, even knowing that the milk-rice, prepared by their deceitful act, was mixed with poison, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar partook of it. How did he partake of it? With the conviction that for the devotees of Shiva-peruman, our Lord, poison is also ambrosia, he ate the milk-rice given by those cruel Jains and remained unharmed. “Nanjum amudham engal nadhar adiyaarkku endru vanjamigu nenjudaiyaar vanjanaiyaam padiyarindhe senjadaiyaar seer vilakkum thiral udaiyaar thee vidaththaal venjamanar iduviththa paal adisin misainthirundhaar” is the sacred verse placed here by Sekkizhar peruman.

It states that Thiru-Navukkarasu peruman, convinced that “poison is ambrosia for the devotees of our Lord,” partook of it.

Therefore, it is revealed to us that “poison is ambrosia for the devotees of our Lord” is the inner meaning of the Thevaram pathigam sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar at this time. The Thiru-pathigam sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar is not available to us now; it has been lost. This is a deficiency in the spiritual merit of both the Shaivite world and the Tamil world. Even after partaking of the poison-mixed milk-rice given by the Jains, Thiru-Navukkarasu peruman remained well, without any suffering. Even knowing, he desired and lived, remaining splendidly. In Greece, there was a great philosopher named Socrates.

His enemies also administered poison to him. He also calmly and steadfastly partook of it.

Similarly, some people here equate these two incidents and say that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar also partook of it with peace of mind, and they conduct research. “Peyakandu nanjundu amaivar nayaththakka naagarigam vendupavar” is a Kural.

Here, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar partaking of poison is not like that. The conviction that for the devotees of the Lord, that is, the devotees of Shiva-peruman, poison is ambrosia, and the steadfastness in his devotion to Shiva-peruman’s sacred service, stand foremost here. We must understand that this is not the case for others, such as Socrates of Greece, who is cited as an example here. We must also note that the Greek philosopher, having partaken of the poison, died there. Even if he had not died then and there, he would not have been worthy of comparison with our Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar here. This is because Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar here embraced the servitude of Shiva-peruman, the love he held for Shiva-peruman’s sacred feet, and the manner in which he received divine grace.

Therefore, Sivakavimani Ayya writes in his commentary that it is an unnecessary act to compare the actions of other people who died without receiving divine grace with the actions of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, who was a Jeevanmukta, possessing the great life of Shiva-ananda. As we have already seen, the Thiru-pathigam sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar at this time is not available to us; it is lost. Nevertheless, from Sekkizhar peruman’s sacred verse, we understand a little that the pathigam must have been structured around the meaning that “for the devotees of the Lord, even poison is ambrosia.” This Thiru-pathigam is lost, but we find internal evidence for this incident in the fifth Thiru-pathigam of Thiru-Nerisai, sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu peruman: “Thunjirul kaalai maalai thodarchiyai marandhiraadhe Anjezhuththu Odhi naalum Aran adikkku anbaagum Vanjanai paarchoraakki vazhakkilaa amanar thandha Nanju amudhaakku viththaar Nanippalli adigalaare” This is from Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar’s Thevaram. In this Thevaram, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar himself, through his sacred words, presents this incident as internal evidence to all of us. If the dreadful Halahala poison, which has the power to destroy all worlds, became ambrosia for Shiva-peruman, the sacred Lord with the sacred ash-adorned body, then for the devotees of that Pasupathi, poison becoming ambrosia is not a miracle; it is a very ordinary matter.

Previously, when the Devas and Asuras churned the milky ocean, the Halahala poison arose. It had the power to destroy all worlds. Such poison became ambrosia for Shiva-peruman. For those who are in servitude under the protection of such Shiva-peruman, the primordial Shiva-peruman, poison becoming ambrosia is an ordinary matter. This implies that those who are in servitude to Shiva-peruman’s sacred feet will be protected by Shiva-peruman, their Lord.

Therefore, for such devotees of Shiva, poison becoming ambrosia is a natural occurrence. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar thus transformed the poison into ambrosia. The Jains were terrified that even deadly poison had become ambrosia. The Jains panicked, thinking that if Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar remained unharmed even after consuming the poison, then their end was near.

So, they immediately rushed to the king. They told the king, “He is still alive even after we administered the milk-rice mixed with poison, because when he was formerly in our Jain religion as Dharmasena, he learned mantras that cure poison.

“Therefore, with the help of those mantras, he prevented the poison from affecting him. If we leave him like this, it is certain that our lives and your kingdom will be destroyed,” said those deceitful Jains to the king. The Jains, with their deceitful ways, spoke to the king. The foolish king, upon hearing their words, asked how he should punish him now. To this, the Jains suggested that an elephant should be unleashed upon Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar.

“Let us continue to contemplate the Puranam of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar.

“The Jains, with their deceitful ways, spoke to the king. The foolish king, upon hearing their words, asked how he should punish him now. To this, the Jains suggested that an elephant should be unleashed upon Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar.

“Let us continue to contemplate the Puranam of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 313. Thiru-Nindra-Charukkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. The Jains demand that an elephant be unleashed to trample Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. Until now, they had placed him in a fiery chamber and made him eat poison-mixed rice.

What did they say then? Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar was truly well and happy by the grace of Shiva-peruman.

But what did these Jains say? They claimed he had escaped by using the mantras he had learned when he was previously in the Jain religion.

Therefore, as a third measure, they ask the king to unleash an elephant. So, the king might now ask them, what if he escapes again by using the mantras he learned in the Jain religion?

Therefore, before he could ask, the Jains declared, “You unleash the elephant upon him; we will perform mantra-sadhana so that all the mantra-sadhana uttered by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar will not be effective.” Even after witnessing the ineffectiveness of the Jains’ words twice, the foolish king, succumbing to their conspiracy, agreed to this. It is a method proven by the elders in our country that a greater mantra can nullify the power of a lesser mantra. This is what the Jains tell the king here. Unleashing a rutting elephant against Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar and having it trample him with its feet, because a rutting elephant cannot be controlled by mantras, is the Jains’ belief. That was the thought of those Jains.

Therefore, those Jains, who were the greatest of sinners, unleashed a rutting elephant upon Thiru-Navukkarasu peruman, the sacred Vaageesa Adigal, upon Thiru-Navukkarasu peruman, the devotee of Kapali. Shiva-peruman is Kapali. Kapali means Shiva-peruman, who holds the skull of Brahma in his hand. He is the devotee of Shiva-peruman, the Lord who holds the head of Brahma, the creator of worlds, and who is imperishable.

Therefore, he will remain imperishable even by an elephant. Sekkizhar peruman reiterates the same idea here, as he said before, “Is it a wonder that poison becomes ambrosia for the devotee of the Lord who consumed poison?” Indeed, a king is called Bhoopalan, meaning one who protects all living beings on this earth. It is the duty of a king to protect. Such a king here performs a cruel act, an act of murder. “Pulaitozhil” means unjust killing.

A king is obligated to stand impartially, without leaning to one side, and protect this world without deviating from justice. Such a king, here, in anger, commanded that an elephant be unleashed upon Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. That elephant is referred to here as a “killer elephant.” That elephant was trained to kill others, because killing humans is not the nature or characteristic of an elephant.

Therefore, to make an elephant act contrary to its nature, it must be thoroughly trained. So, the king commanded that a trained killer elephant be unleashed. The guards also unleashed the killer elephant. That elephant moves like a great dark mountain, a huge hill, moving. On its way, it demolishes mansions and destroys halls. It is as if Yama has come in the form of this rutting elephant.

Sekkizhar peruman here refers to it as “coming in the guise of an elephant.” It is as if Yama, among the many forms he assumes in this world, came here in the guise of an elephant. Killing humans is not the nature or characteristic of an elephant.

Therefore, to make an elephant act contrary to its nature, it must be thoroughly trained. So, the king commanded that a trained killer elephant be unleashed. The guards also unleashed the killer elephant. That elephant moves like a great dark mountain, a huge hill, moving. On its way, it demolishes mansions and destroys halls. It is as if Yama has come in the form of this rutting elephant.

Sekkizhar peruman here refers to it as “coming in the guise of an elephant.” It is as if Yama, among the many forms he assumes in this world, came here in the guise of an elephant. The common understanding is that Yama, the god of death, takes lives in the form of diseases, enemies, or wild animals like tigers.

However, these are merely the apparent causes for the departure of life. In truth, it is Yama himself who, hidden within these forms, takes lives. Such a Yama now appears in the form of an elephant, approaching with great speed and ferocity. It breaks the chain that bound it, snapping the tether to which it was tied, and advances, causing flocks of circling birds to flee in terror. It disregards all obstacles, breaking through them as it moves forward, swaying. With its trunk swaying like a pendulum, the elephant approaches with immense fury and anger.

Its rut, fragrant like a downpour, flows abundantly, as this mountain-like elephant, in rut, comes forward. It trumpets like thunder as it charges. Even the Dik Gajams, the elephants of the directions, are terrified by its charge. Dik Gajams refers to the directional elephants. Our tradition holds that to protect this world, eight elephants are stationed in the eight directions. Even these Dik Gajams are terrified as this elephant charges.

These eight elephants in the eight directions are Airavatam in the east, Pundarikam in the southeast, Vamanam in the south, Kumudam in the southwest, Anjanam in the west, and in the northwest, Pushpadantam, in the north Sarvabhoamam, and in the northeast Supradeepam—these are the names of the eight elephants guarding the eight directions, according to our tradition.

Now, that murderous elephant charges rapidly. Its footprints sink into the earth, causing the ground to tremble. It rushes like a storm. Just as the Vadavamukha Agni, the submarine fire within the ocean, erupts during the dissolution of the universe, so too does this elephant charge like that Vadavamukha Agni. This mountain-like elephant, with its destructive trunk, charges forward. The surrounding herds of horses scatter and flee.

Those horses that did not flee, or could not flee, were caught by the elephant and perished. The elephant destroys the walls and platforms as it approaches. The Jain ascetics, who commit sinful and cruel acts, harbored deep-seated malice and treachery in their hearts, intending to kill Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar. These cruel Jain ascetics bring this murderous elephant before Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. They unleash the elephant, which possesses a trunk capable of fighting enemies, as if launching a dark mountain against him. All the treachery, lies, murder, and betrayals that the Jain ascetics had committed against Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, all those terrible evil deeds, accumulate and mature, as they perform this act with great malice, intending to kill Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar.

They command the elephant to kill him. This is because elephants trained in this manner would be unleashed with the command to kill.

Therefore, trained elephants are capable of understanding and executing such commands.

Thus, these cruel Jain ascetics unleash the murderous elephant upon Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar. At that moment, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, without the slightest fear, was clearly contemplating and meditating upon the golden holy feet of Lord Shiva, who shines upon the bull.

Let us resume our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 314, Thirunindrachcharukkam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. The Jain ascetics unleash the murderous elephant upon Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar.

At that moment, the great Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal, without the slightest fear, was clearly contemplating the golden holy feet of Lord Shiva, who shines upon the bull. Sekkizhar Swamigal sings: “Seeing the command of the great king of arduous penance approaching him, he joyfully sings the Thiru-pathikam, beginning with ‘Sunnaven Sandanachchaandu,’ in praise of the Lord of the celestials, the Peruman who delights in riding the bull, so that the world may be saved.” Thus sings Sekkizhar Swamigal. The next verse describes the great and rare ascetic king, Thiru- Seeing the elephant approaching him, he praises Lord Shiva. He praises Lord Shiva, the leader of the celestials, who delights in riding the bull vehicle, and sings the Thiru-pathikam, beginning with “Sunnaven Sandanachchaandu,” with great joy, so that all the inhabitants of this earthly world may be saved.

Here, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal as “Annal,” meaning a person of greatness. He also refers to him as “Thava Vendar,” meaning the king of ascetics, as Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal is the leader of all those who perform penance.

Therefore, he is referred to as Thava Vendar here. Such a Thirunavukkarasu Peruman praises Lord Shiva and sings the Thiru-pathikam.

Here, “Vinnvar Tham” (Lord of the celestials). Peruman.
