Here, Sekkizhar Swamigal has structured it as “praising Lord Shiva, who is the Peruman of the celestials.” The epithet “Peruman of the celestials” for Lord Shiva is very apt in this context. This is because the elephant is charging towards Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal.

At that moment, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar praises Lord Shiva. If he sings here, using the epithet “Peruman of the celestials” for Lord Shiva, what does it mean? It means that for every tree, plant, animal, and so on in this world, there is a presiding deity. These are referred to as mantra leaders.

Thus, for every object and every For every destructive force and every animal, there is a presiding deity. However, it is Shiva-Shakti who, standing within the mantras of those respective presiding deities, bestows benefits. In the ninth sutra of Sivagnana Bodham, in the section on Garuda-sanam, “Thirvidam Potran,” Madhava Sivagnana Munivar has commented in the Padhyam. We can consider it here in this context. That is, we see here an object, its presiding deity, and its corresponding mantra. As an example, we can reflect on what Madhava Sivagnana Munivar said.

Here, he takes Garuda. In ancient times, if someone was bitten by a snake and poisoned, a sorcerer would come and remove the poison. He would remove it by means of his Garuda-yoga Bhavana.

At that time, the sorcerer would identify himself with Garuda, chant the Garuda mantra, and look at the poisoned person with his Garuda gaze. Through that Garuda gaze, the poison would be removed, and the person bitten by the snake would recover. How does this happen? In reality, Garuda exists in three forms: Adhi Bhautika Garuda, Adhi Daivika Garuda, and Adhi Atmika Garuda. Garuda is of three types. The Garuda we ordinarily see in the world is called Adhi Bhautika Garuda.

That is, the Garuda we ordinarily see openly in the sky is called Adhi Bhautika Garuda. This Garuda has a presiding deity. The mantra that is the presiding deity of this Garuda is Adhi Daivika Garuda. The sorcerer would constantly chant and practice this Adhi Daivika Garuda, that is, the mantra-form Garuda.

Therefore, whenever someone was bitten by a snake, the sorcerer would use and apply the mantra-Garuda, called Adhi Daivika Garuda, which he had been chanting and practicing, and identify himself with Garuda.

Thus, from the state of Garuda-yoga Bhavana, the Adhi Daivika, mantra-form, When he looks with the Garuda gaze, using the Garuda mantra he has practiced, the poison leaves the body of the affected person. But beyond this, there is a third, Adhi Atmika Garuda. What is this? We saw earlier that the mantra-form Garuda, which is the presiding deity, is called Adhi Daivika Garuda. The Shiva-Shakti that bestows benefits to the sorcerer from that mantra is called Adhi Atmika Garuda. That is, when the sorcerer chants the Garuda mantra, it must yield results, must it not?

The chanted mantra itself will not remove the poison. Within that mantra, Shiva-Shakti must exist as Adhi Atmika and give the benefit of that mantra. That Shiva-Shakti is called Adhi Atmika Garuda.

Thus, Madhava Sivagnana Munivar explains Adhi Bhautika Garuda, Adhi Daivika Garuda, and Adhi Atmika Garuda.

Similarly, for every living being, plant, animal, bird, etc., in this world, there is a presiding deity. But it is Shiva-Shakti, our Lord Shiva, who stands within all those presiding deities and bestows benefits.

Therefore, when he sings, addressing Lord Shiva as “Peruman of the celestials,” what does it mean? It means that for every bird and so on found in this world, the mantra leaders, the celestials, are the presiding deities who bring about their actions.

Lord Shiva is their leader, meaning that Lord Shiva is the one who, standing within them as Adhi Atmika, directs even them. Including this, he has sung here, referring to Lord Shiva as “Peruman of the celestials.” Here, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sees the rutting elephant approaching him with anger, intending to kill him.

Therefore, to appease, calm, and control that rutting elephant, the great seers, who have attained clarity regarding the mantra-form of the elephant’s presiding deity, contemplate Lord Shiva, the Peruman of those celestial deities.

Here, he next sings that the Peruman of the celestials desires to come.

Therefore, singing of Lord Shiva as the Peruman of the celestials, the Peruman who delights in riding the bull, brings joy. These are also referred to as Nigraha Anugraha and Kopa Prasadam.

Therefore, for this reason, to appease the elephant approaching him in anger, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar praises and sings of Lord Shiva, our Peruman of the celestials, who delights in riding the bull, who bestows grace as the presiding deity of the elephant and as the Adhi Atmika of that presiding deity. How does he sing? Sekkizhar Peruman states that he sings the Thiru-pathikam beginning with “Sunnaven Sandanachchaandu,” and sings it with joy so that this earthly world may be saved. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that by Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar singing this Thiru-pathikam, “Sunnaven Sandanachchaandu,” this earthly world will be saved and find rest. The Thiruvachakam states, “This earth is for Shiva to save.” According to that, If those living in the celestial worlds above and the netherworlds below wish to attain salvation by performing Shiva’s meritorious deeds, they must come to this earthly world.

Therefore, when it is mentioned here that “this earthly world may be saved,” we must understand it to mean that this earthly world, as well as all the upper and lower worlds, may be saved. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar is constantly meditating on the holy feet of Lord Shiva. That alone would save him from the elephant. Does he need to sing a separate pathikam to appease the elephant? No, that is not necessary. The mere thought of Lord Shiva’s holy feet would save him.

However, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sings the Thiru-pathikam here.

Therefore, this is for the benefit of the people of this earthly world. It is with the intention that they should benefit, out of compassion for us, that he sings this pathikam. If the living beings on this earth offer this Thiru-pathikam to the ears of the Lord, they will receive Lord Shiva’s divine grace. That is why, out of compassion for us, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sings this Thiru-pathikam beginning with “Sunnaven Sandanachchaandu.” Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman here explains why Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sings this pathikam. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing: “Looking at the fierce, rutting elephant of war, unleashed by the deceitful ones, he sang the beautiful Tamil song, declaring, ‘We are the devotees of the Lord of the red matted locks, the long-haired dancer, the Lord of Lords, the one with the fiery trident, the Veerattar. We fear nothing.’”

He continues the next verse, stating, “We are not afraid,” and sings the beautiful Tamil song. Sekkizhar Peruman structures it continuously. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, looking at the elephant, which was full of rut and anger, unleashed by the deceitful Jain ascetics, sang this Tamil pathikam, declaring, “We are the devotees of the Lord of the red matted locks, the long-haired dancer, the great Lord of all celestials, the one who holds the fiery, three-pronged trident, Thiru-Veerattaneswarar. We have nothing to fear.” He sings this Thiru-pathikam towards the rutting elephant. This is because the power of his unwavering contemplation on Lord Shiva’s holy feet must reach the elephant and change its anger and ferocity.

Therefore, he sings this Thiru-pathikam towards the elephant.

Furthermore, it is a truth established by Gnana Sastras and worldly texts that looking with such an intention will be effective. That is the inner meaning of Nayana Deeksha (initiation through the gaze). If the compassionate gaze of a Guru, which is Nayana Deeksha, can subdue the ego, the Anava Malam, that has bound the soul from eternity, then is it a great thing for the rut of this ordinary elephant to subside? No, it is not.

Here, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sings, addressing Lord Shiva as “Senjadai Neen Mudi Koothar” (the dancer with long, red matted locks). The nature of the Lord, who wears the crescent moon and the Ganga, openly reveals to everyone His nature of protecting those who seek refuge in Him.

Next, there is a reference to Lord Shiva as “Devar Peranar” (Lord of the Devas). “Devar Peranar” means the great leader or Mahadeva. We can also apply the meanings we saw earlier for “Vinnvar Tham Peruman” here.

Furthermore, there is a reference here to Lord Shiva as the one who holds the fiery, three-pronged trident. The trident here, while generally referring to a weapon, specifically indicates the ankus (elephant goad) that controls the elephant. We can also reflect here on Lord Shiva’s gracious forms holding the noose and the ankus. The term “Venjudar” (fiery glow) here indicates that the mere glow of the trident, without even being used, is capable of producing the desired effect. This indicates that such a Lord Shiva resides in Veerattam.

Here, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sings about Thiru-Adhigai Veerattaneswarar. While the pathikams sung during the other three torments inflicted by the Jain ascetics were general pathikams, this Thiru-pathikam, beginning with “Sunnaven Sandanachchaandu,” was sung by Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, contemplating Thiru-Adhigai Veerattaneswarar.

Therefore, this pathikam is celebrated as the pathikam belonging to the holy place of Thiru-Adhigai. In that pathikam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sings, “I am a devotee of the Lord who lovingly resides in such Thiru-Adhigai Veerattaneswaram.” The phrase “Thamar Nam” appears in that pathikam, which Sekkizhar Peruman specifically highlights here. “Anjuvathu” (to fear). Sekkizhar Peruman states here, “There is nothing to fear.” Therefore, this Thiru-pathikam is structured to mean that there is no fear in the present, and there will be nothing to fear in the future. The phrase “Anja Varuvathum Illai” (nothing to fear in the future) refers to the cruel act that the Jain ascetics are yet to commit, where they tie him to a stone and cast him into the sea. Not only that, but this phrase also arose for the sake of others, implying that Shiva’s devotees in this world need not fear any future suffering.

Such is the nature of this rare Tamil pathikam.

Therefore, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar expresses his conviction through this beautiful Tamil song, this Thiru-pathikam.

Thus, Sekkizhar Swamigal explains the incident where Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sang the Thiru-pathikam beginning with “Sunnaven San- Sandanachchaandu” towards the elephant that came against him. This Thiru-pathikam is compiled as the second Thiru-pathikam in the Fourth Thirumurai among the twelve Thirumurais.

Now, that Thiru-pathikam: Sthalam: Thiru-Adhigai Veerattanam. Pan: Gandharam.

Nothing will ever come to cause fear. For His devotees, there is nothing to fear; nothing will ever come to cause fear. Anjuvathu yaathonrum illai anja varuvathum illai. Pala pala kaamaththaraaki pathaiththezhuvaar manaththulle kalamala kittu thiriyum ganapathi ennum kalirum valamenthirandu sudarum vaan kayilaaya malaiyum nalamaar kedila poonalum udaiyaar oruvarthamar naam anjuvathu yaathonrum illai anja varuvathum illai anjuvathu yaathonrum illai anja varu. There is nothing to fear; nothing will ever come to cause fear. He who has Ganesha, the elephant-faced one, who stirs the minds of those with many desires and makes them tremble, who has the two shining lights (sun and moon) on His right, the celestial Thiru-Kailash mountain, and the auspicious Thiru-Kedila river, for His devotees, there is nothing to fear; nothing will ever come to cause fear. There is nothing to fear; nothing will ever come to cause fear. Illai karanthana kolli vilakkum karangkooththudiyin mulakkum parantha pathinenkanamum payintthariyathana paattum arangidai noolarivaalar ariyappadaathathorkooththum nirantha kedila punalum udaiyaar oruvar thamar naam anjuvathu yaathonrum illai anja varuvathum illai anjuvathu yaathonrum illai anja varuvathum illai kolai vari vengai.

Nothing. He who has the hidden lamps of the cremation ground, the resounding drumbeats, the songs unknown even to the eighteen hosts of celestials, the dance unknown to scholars of the arts, and the full Thiru-Kedila river, for His devotees, there is nothing to fear; nothing will ever come to cause fear. There is nothing to fear; nothing will ever come to cause fear. The fierce striped tiger. Athazhum kulavodilangu potthodum vilai peru sanga kuzhaiyum vilaiyil kapaala kalanum malaimagal kai konda maaniyaar thilangumidarum ulavu kedila punalum udaiyaar oruvar thamar naam anjuvathu yaathonrum illai anja varuvathum illai anjuvathu yaathonrum illai anja varuvathum illai aadal purintha nilaiyum araiyil asaiththa aravum. And the shining golden earring, the precious conch ear-ornament, the priceless skull-bowl, the radiant throat held by the Daughter of the Mountain, and the flowing Thiru-Kedila river, for His devotees, there is nothing to fear; nothing will ever come to cause fear.

There is nothing to fear; nothing will ever come to cause fear. The state of performing the dance and the snake tied around His waist. Paadal payinra palbootham pallaayiram kolkaruvi naadarkkariyatho kooththum nankuyar veerattam soozhnthu odum kedila punalum udaiyaar oruvar thamar naam anjuvathu yaathonrum illai anja varuvathum illai anjuvathu yaathonrum illai anja varuvathum illai soozhum arava thukilum thukil kilikopan keezhum yaazhin mozhiyaval anja anja. The many Bhootas who learned to sing, the dance with thousands of instruments, difficult to find, and the Thiru-Kedila river flowing around the lofty Thiru-Veerattam, for His devotees, there is nothing to fear; nothing will ever come to cause fear. There is nothing to fear; nothing will ever come to cause fear. The encircling serpent garment, the parrot-like lower garment, and the one with the voice of a lyre, fearing, fearing.

The state of flaying the elephant like a mountain, and the Thiru-Kedila river flowing around the expansive groves of Thiru-Veerattam, for His devotees, there is nothing to fear; nothing will ever come to cause fear. There is nothing to fear; nothing will ever come to cause fear. He who, holding the veins, made the Goddess tremble, and lifted the mountain with all his strength, causing the nine and one (heads) to cry out, and then bestowed boons. Seyvaan valar pozhil veerattam soozhnthu nirampu kedila punalum udaiyaar oruvar thamar naam anjuvathu yaathonrum illai anja varuvathum illai anjuvathu yaathonrum illai anja varuvathum illai Thiruchitrambalam ithuve sunnavan santhana saanthum enru thodangum antha thiruppathikam ithil irukkinra paththu thiruppaadalkalin arththangalai thodarnthu sinthippom Thiruchitrambalam. He who bestows boons, who possesses the Thiru-Kedila river flowing around the flourishing groves of Thiru-Veerattam, for His devotees, there is nothing to fear; nothing will ever come to cause fear.

There is nothing to fear; nothing will ever come to cause fear.

This is the Thiru-Pathikam beginning with “Sunnavan Santhana Saanthum.” We shall continue to contemplate the meanings of the ten sacred verses contained within it. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 315, Thiru-Nindrachcharukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We have seen the Thiru-Pathikam beginning with “Sunnaven Santhana Saanthum.” We are now to contemplate its meanings. The first sacred verse of this Thiru-Pathikam is as follows: Sunnavan Santhana Saanthum sudar thingal soozhaamaniyum vanna urivai udaiyum valarum pavala niramum annal aran muran erum akalampalaay aravum thinnan kedilappunalum udaiyaar oruvar thamarnam anjuvathiyaathonrumillai anjavaruvathum illai. Its explanation is as follows: It begins with “Sunnaven Santhana Saanthum.” This should be understood by combining “Saanthu” with “Sunna Ven” and “Santhanam,” meaning “Sunnaven Saanthu” and “Santhana Saanthu.” The first “Sunna.” The white paste, being white paste, refers to sacred ash, because other sandalwood is red in color.

Therefore, white paste refers to sacred ash. This is the sacred ash on the Lord’s divine form. When the Nayanar remembers the divine form of Shiva in his mind, the first thing that appears to him is the sacred ash worn by Shiva on His divine form. That sacred ash greatly captivated Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. He therefore sings first of the white sacred ash showered on the Lord’s divine form.

Next, what captivated his heart was the red sandalwood paste on the Goddess’s half. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, in his heart, meditated on the Lord’s form as a mantra, conceived to remove the elephant’s anger, as its presiding deity.

Thus, the sacred white ash and the red sandalwood paste worn by the Goddess, which captivated the Nayanar in the divine form of Shiva, appear before him first.

Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar begins by singing “Sunnaven Santhana Saanthu.” “Ilam kongaiyil sengungumam polum odiyani maarbu ilangumenru punniyar pottrisaipa” is a Thiru-Isaippa. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, who begins singing thus, throughout this Thiru-Pathikam, describes the ways in which he clearly established the Lord’s sacred feet in his mind.

Therefore, beginning with “Sunnaven Santhana Saanthu,” he sings of the growing coral hue, the shoulders like mountains, the mark of the two worlds, and the two shining lights on the right. The chest held by the Daughter of the Mountain, the radiant throat adorned with gems, and other parts of His divine body; the crescent moon as a crown, the snake encircling His chest, the boar’s tusk, the tortoise shell, the sacred white thread, and the two sacred waistbands; the pearl necklace, the Rudraksha, the tiger skin, the golden earring, the ear-ornament, the skull-bowl, the serpent garment, the parrot-like lower garment, and other adornments He wears; the banner with the bull, the trident, the fawn, the golden deer, the axe, the snake, the veena in one hand, the celestial Thiru-Kailash mountain, the hidden lamps of the cremation ground, the drumbeats, and other divine possessions; the practice of the dance with the bent bow, the dance unknown to scholars of the arts, and thousands of instruments. The dance difficult to find, the state of flaying the elephant, and other divine acts; the Lord’s fierce bull, Ganesha the elephant-faced, the eighteen hosts of celestials, the songs unknown even to them, and the many Bhootas who learned to sing—thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sings throughout this Thiru-Pathikam of the ways in which he clearly established the Lord’s sacred feet in his mind.

Now, let us continue to contemplate the meanings of the first sacred verse. We contemplated the meaning of “Sunnavan Santhana Saanthu,” which he sang.

Next, he sings “Sudar Thingal Soozhaamaniyum.” On the Lord’s sacred head, on the Lord’s half, is the radiant crescent moon. On the Goddess’s half is the crest jewel.

Therefore, he sings of these two as “Sudar Thingal Soozhaamaniyum.” Next, He sings “Vanna Urivai Udaiyum.” The Lord wears a beautiful tiger skin garment. This is sung here as “Vanna Urivai Udai.” The coral hue, which is the color of the Lord’s divine body, is mentioned here as “Valarum Pavala Niramum.” Such a Lord comes riding on a bull. This bull vehicle protects those who have attained the Lord, like a fortress, and bestows grace upon those who have not attained Him, standing as an obstacle. Such a Lord, riding on a bull vehicle, comes adorned with snakes on His sacred chest. Such a Lord resides in Thiru-Athikai, a Thiru-Veerattam, on the banks of the Thiru-Kedila river.

Therefore, I am a devotee of such Shiva.

Therefore, there is nothing for me to fear. Nothing will ever come to cause me fear. This is the meaning of the first sacred verse.

Now, the second sacred verse: Poondathor Kezhal Eyirum Pon Thigal Aamai Porul Neenda Thin Thol Valam Soozhnthu Nilaakkathir Pola Venn Noolum Kaandagu Pullin Siragum Kalantha Kattanga Kodiyum Eendu Kedila Punalum Udaiyaar Oruvar Thamar Naam Anjuvathu Yaathonrum Illai Anja Varuvathum Illai. Its meaning is as follows: Shiva wears the boar’s tusk on His chest. That is the tusk of Vishnu who came as the Varaha avatar.

Next, He wears the tortoise shell on His sacred chest. That is the back shell of Vishnu in the Kurma avatar.

Thus, Shiva adorned Himself and bestowed grace. He wears a crane feather on His sacred matted hair. On His sacred chest, He wears a white sacred thread that shines like the moon. Such Shiva bestows grace in Thiru-Athikai Thiru-Veerattam, on the banks of the Thiru-Kedila river. We are the devotees of Thiru-Athikai Thiru-Veeratteshwarar.

Therefore, we have nothing to fear; nothing will ever come to cause fear.

Now, the third sacred verse: Ottha Vadaththila Naagam Oruththira Pattamirandum Muththu Vadakkandikaiyum Mulaiththazhu Moovilaim Velum Chiththavadamum Athikai Senuyar Veerattam Soozhnthu Thaththum Kedila Punalum Udaiyaar Oruvar Thavar Naam Anjuvathu Yaathonrumillai Anja Varuvathum Illai. Shiva wears a young serpent like a garland on His shoulder. He also wears the Rudra-Pattam. The Rudra-Pattam is a yogic waistband.

Furthermore, He wears a pearl necklace and Rudraksha beads. The pearl necklace is on the Goddess’s half of the Lord’s divine body, and the Rudraksha is on the Lord’s half. Along with these, He holds the trident, known as the three-pronged spear, in His sacred hand. It is customary to refer to this as the three-pronged spear or three-pronged trident. Such Shiva is enshrined in a sacred monastery called Chiththavadam, located outside Thiru-Athikai. We have contemplated the history of how the Lord bestowed foot-initiation upon Sundaramoorthy Swamigal in this Chiththavadam monastery in the Puranam of Thaduthaatkonda.

Such a Chiththavadam monastery. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings of it here. We are the devotees of Shiva who resides in such a Chiththavadam monastery and in the Thiru-Veerattam temple on the banks of the Thiru-Kedila river.

Therefore, we have nothing to fear; nothing will ever come to cause fear.

Now, the fourth sacred verse: Madamaan Mari Porkalaiyum Mazhuppaambu Oru Kaiyil Veenai Kudamaal Varaiyathin Tholum Kuni Silai Kooththin Payilvum Idamaal Thazhuviya Paakam Irunila Netra Suvadum Thadamaar Kedila Punalum Udaiyaar Oruvar Thamar Naam Anjuvathu Yaathonrumillai Anja Varuvathum Illai. Its meaning is as follows: The Lord holds a fawn in one sacred hand. In another hand, He holds the axe weapon. He wears deer skin as a garment. In another hand, He holds a snake. In another hand, He holds a veena.

The sacred shoulders of Shiva shine like the western mountains. Such Shiva performs the dance. In one half of Him, Thiru-Mal (Vishnu) is seated. Such Shiva is seated in Thiru-Athikai Thiru-Veerattam on the banks of the Thiru-Kedila river. We are His devotees.

Therefore, we have nothing to fear; nothing will ever come to cause fear. This is the meaning of the fourth sacred verse.

We shall continue our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 316, Thiru-Nindrachcharukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We are contemplating the meanings of the verses of the Thiru-Pathikam beginning with “Sunnaven Santhana Saanthum.” The fifth verse: Palapala Kaamaththaraaki Pathaiththezhuvaar Manaththulle Kalamalakittu Thiriyum Ganapathi Ennum Kalirum Valamenthu Irandu Sudarum Vaan Kayilaaya Malaiyum Nalamaar Kedilap Punalum Udaiyaar Oruvar Thamar Naam Anjuvathu Yaathonrumillai Anja Varuvathum Illai. “Palapala Kaamaththaraaki Pathaiththezhuvaar” refers to the Asuras with evil intentions. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sings here of Ganesha, the elephant-faced one, who created confusion in the minds of such Asuras and destroyed them.

Therefore, he sings here of Ganapathi, Lord Ganesha, who destroyed Gajamukhasura. It is said in the Puranas that Ganapathi Murthy came to destroy Gajamukhasura, who tormented the Devas. He sings here that Shiva is the father of such Ganapathi.

Therefore, just as Ganapathi destroyed Gajamukhasura, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman implicitly sings that Shiva, the father of such Ganapathi, is the one who removes the suffering caused by the elephant unleashed upon him. “Pidiyathan uruvumai kola migu kadiyathu vadikodu thanathadi vazhipadum avaridar kadikkan pathivara arulinan” is from Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s Thiru-Valivalam Thevaram. Such Shiva has the sun. And the moon as His two eyes. He who resides on Thiru-Kailash mountain bestows grace in Thiru-Athikai Thiru-Veerattam on the banks of the Thiru-Kedila river. We are the devotees of such Shiva.

Therefore, we have nothing to fear; nothing will ever come to cause fear.

Now, the sixth sacred verse: Karanthana Kolli Vilakkum Karangu Thudiyin Muzhakkum Parantha Pathinen Kanamum Payintthariyathana Paattu Arangidai Nool Arivaalar Ariyappadaathathor Kooththum Nirantha Kedila Punalum Udaiyaar Oruvar Thamar Naam Anjuvathu Yaathonrumillai Anja Varuvathum Illai. Its meaning is as follows: It begins with “Karanthana Kolli Vilakkum.” The place where Shiva dances is the cremation ground.

There, the half-burnt logs from the cremation. Those logs serve as lamps. In such a cremation ground, the Lord dances as the sound of the Thudi musical instrument spreads everywhere. That dance and song are such that the eighteen hosts of celestials cannot hear or see them anywhere else; it is a unique dance and sound. The next line is “Arangidai Nool Arivaalar Ariyappadaathathor Kooththum.” The meaning of this is that the Lord is unknowable through worldly knowledge (Pasu Gnanam) and individual soul knowledge (Pasa Gnanam). We can apply what we contemplated in the first verse of the Periya Puranam, “Ulagellam Unarnthu Odarkkariyavan,” here to understand the meaning.

Such Shiva, who dances, is seated in Thiru-Athikai on the banks of the Thiru-Kedila river. We are His devotees.

Therefore, we fear. There is nothing to fear, nor will anything fearful come.

Now, the seventh Thiru-paadal: “He who wears the skin of a fierce tiger, who has a radiant golden earring and a conch-shell earring of great value, who holds a skull-bowl of no price, whose chest is embraced by the Daughter of the Mountain, whose throat shines like a sapphire, and who possesses the waters of the Thiru-Kedila river—we are His devotees. There is nothing to fear, nor will anything fearful come.” The meaning of this verse is: Lord Shiva wears the skin of a striped tiger. This tiger was slain by Him, a tiger sent by the Rishis of Thaarukaavanam against the Lord. He killed it and wears its skin. He wears a radiant, substantial golden earring in His sacred ears, and an earring made of conch-shell of immense value. He holds that skull-bowl, which is priceless.

He has a sacred chest, one part of which is adorned by Devi Parvati. He possesses a sacred neck that shines like a blue gem. Such a Lord Shiva is enshrined at Thiru-Adigai Veerattaanam on the banks of the Kedila river. We are His devotees, therefore there is nothing to fear, nor will anything fearful come.

Now, the eighth Thiru-paadal: “He who delights in dance, who has a serpent tied around His waist, who is surrounded by thousands of Bhoothas singing praises, whose dance is unknown to the gods, and who possesses the waters of the Thiru-Kedila river that flow around the well-elevated Veerattam—we are His devotees. There is nothing to fear, nor will anything fearful come.” Its meaning is as follows: The Lord delights in dancing. He has a serpent tightly bound around His waist. Thousands of Bhoothas surround Lord Shiva. The dance performed by such a Lord Shiva is unknown to the scriptures and beyond the scope of artistic knowledge; He cannot be understood through scriptural knowledge, nor can His dance be comprehended. Such a Lord Shiva resides as Veerattaaneswarar in Thiru-Adigai on the banks of the Kedila river.

We are His devotees, therefore there is nothing to fear, nor will anything fearful come.

Now, the ninth Thiru-paadal: “He who wears a serpent as a garment, and a loincloth torn from another cloth, whose form, like a mountain, terrified the sweet-voiced lady (Parvati) when He slew the elephant, and who possesses the waters of the Thiru-Kedila river that flow around the fragrant groves of Veerattam—we are His devotees. There is nothing to fear, nor will anything fearful come.” Its meaning is: As follows: Lord Shiva wears a garment encircled by a serpent. He wears a loincloth, a kowanam, torn from another cloth, adorned with a waist-cord. He is the one who, when a mighty, mountain-like elephant in rut came, tore off its skin and wore it, terrifying Devi Parvati, whose voice is sweet like the sound of a Yaazh.

Lord Shiva manifested as Gajasamhaara Moorthy. Such a Lord Shiva is enshrined at Thiru-Adigai Veerattaanam, which has the sacred waters of the Kedila river flowing in a depression, surrounding the groves of Veerattam on one side. We are the devotees of such a Lord Shiva, therefore we have nothing to fear, nor will anything fearful come.

Now, the tenth Thiru-paadal: “With sinewy hands, he (Ravana) tried to lift the mountain, causing the Lady (Parvati) to tremble. He who granted boons when the ten (heads of Ravana) cried out, and who possesses the waters of the Thiru-Kedila river that flow around the flourishing groves of Veerattam—we are His devotees. There is nothing to fear, nor will anything fearful come.” Its meaning is as follows: Once, Ravana attempted to uproot Mount Kailash.

At that time, Devi Parvati trembled and embraced Lord Shiva.

The Lord then pressed lightly with the tip of His sacred big toe, causing Mount Kailash to crush Ravana, who suffered greatly as his ten heads cried out. Afterwards, he sang the Saama-gaanam. Hearing that Saama-gaanam, Lord Shiva granted him boons and bestowed His grace. The sacred temple where such a Lord resides is Veerattam. It is located On the banks of the Kedila river in Thiru-Adigai. We are the devotees of Veerattaaneswarar, who is enshrined in such a Veerattam.

Therefore, we have nothing to fear, nor will anything fearful come. This is the concise meaning of the ten Thiru-paadal-s in this Thiru-pathigam.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, having sung these cool Tamil garlands, shines with the conviction of having taken his Peruman as his sole refuge. These Thevaram-s sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal are Tamil garlands, his own Tamil garlands, which are always cool. The meaning of ‘cool’ here is that they are pleasing to the ear when heard, and they also impart wisdom.

Furthermore, this cool Thevaram, this Tamil garland, therefore, removes heat. It alleviates the heat of birth, the heat of existence, and serves as a means to impart wisdom that transforms it, thus providing coolness. While this generally applies to Tamil, this epithet particularly suits the Tamil of the Nayanmars. He refers to them as his own Tamil garlands. Each Thiru-paadal within this Thiru-pathigam is a distinct garland.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, in a state of Shivoham-bhavana, composed this Thiru-pathigam. He is the very embodiment of love for the Lord. Despite all the evils and cruelties committed by the Jains, the king of that country, and the elephant sent to torment him, he harbored not the slightest anger towards them, but meditated solely on the sacred feet of Lord Shiva. He was completely consumed by love. As Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal remained thus, the elephant that had been sent against him, that sacred devotee Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, circumambulated him, bowed low before him, and prostrated itself at his feet. It prostrated itself before Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, falling to the ground in reverence.

The elephant, for all to see, bowed to Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, rose, and then departed. The elephant, its anger quelled by the Thiru-pathigam of Tamil Thevaram sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, understood the greatness of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar.

Thus, it worshipped Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. Indeed, this elephant was a greatly meritorious elephant, because Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, having been blessed with his gracious gaze, understood the truth, abandoned its former association with Jainism, and worshipped and bowed to its Guru, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, who had bestowed upon it a gracious gaze and Nayana-deeksha. These are all the ways in which wise people worship.

In the same manner, that elephant also worshipped Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, the Acharya. Circumambulating, bowing low, prostrating on the ground, and rising—these are the methods of worshipping the sacred form and the temple of the devotees of Lord Shiva. The elephant performed these actions exactly.

Thus, the elephant worshipped Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar and departed.

Therefore, the cruel mahouts who had sent this elephant against Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, tried to torment the elephant. They tried to force and manipulate it, again attempting to send it against Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, inflicting cruelty upon it.

But at that moment, the elephant did not act as they wished; instead of going towards Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, it threw and killed the very mahouts who had sent it, and also killed the Jains, then ran away in opposition. The elephant trampled, gored, and pursued many Jains, killing them and causing great commotion in the city. Like the Mandara mountain churning the great ocean of milk, the elephant caused the city to be agitated and distressed. Some Jains, who were evil-doers and managed to escape from this rampaging elephant, the remaining Jains, all lost their honor, became confused, and distressed, fell individually at the feet of the king of that city, And lamented. Generally, the Jain gurus held a position of spiritual authority; they were gurus to the king himself. In such a situation, they were gurus who would have the king fall at their feet and worship them.

But now, they were forced to fall at the king’s feet and lament, because their nature was not asceticism but deceit and cruelty. Seeing these Jains who had come and fallen, the angry king asks what should be done next. To this, the Jains say, “O King, if this humiliation that has befallen you is to be removed, then that Dharumasenan must die.” When the Jains said this, the king, who was about to commit a great and terrible sin, asked the Jains, “What should be done with Dharumasenan, who has destroyed our religion And caused us suffering? Tell me,” he asked. Those Jains, who were the embodiment of deceit, said that Dharumasenar, that is, our sacred Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, should be tied to a stone with a rope and thrown into the sea. Those cruel Jains said this.

We shall continue our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 317, Thiru-Nindrachcharukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. The king, having heard the evil counsel of the Jains, commanded his guards, who served under him, saying, “Do not let the wicked Dharumasenan escape. Take him, tie him with a rope to a stone, put him in a boat, and cast him into the sea.

“Then return.” Sekkizhar Peruman here refers to the boatmen and those who perform the cruel act of tying our Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar to a stone and throwing him into the sea as ‘maakkal’. ‘Maakkal’ means those who are like unintelligent animals, because even though they possess the ability to discern for themselves, they carry out evil deeds even when commanded to do so by others. Thus they act.

“Therefore, they are like unintelligent animals.

“Here, a doubt may arise in us: those who perform the commanded task act according to the king’s order.

“Therefore, they do whatever the king tells them to do. How can this be wrong? Since they are simply doing what the king told them to do, isn’t that correct? How can it be wrong?

“Here, it is said that this is wrong and that those who do so are like unintelligent animals. Why? Because it is not so. Have we not seen before, at the beginning of the Periya Puranam, the history of Manu Needhi Chozhan? In that story, Manu Needhi Chozhan’s son, the prince, accidentally runs over a calf with his chariot, taking its life.

“Therefore, as punishment, he commands his minister to tie his son, The prince, to a chariot in the same manner and take his life. But what does that minister do? He explains to the king that the king’s command is not right according to his conscience and the principles of Dharma. He says, “I cannot do this,” and gives up his own life.

“Therefore, it is not mandatory to simply do whatever the king says. One can use one’s experiential knowledge, wisdom, Dharma Shastras, and other forms of intellect to analyze and offer advice. It is not necessary to simply carry out the king’s command.

“Similarly, our Sekkizhar Peruman was also the chief minister in the court of Anabaya Chozhan. When Anabaya Chozhan Was idly passing his time reading the sensual story of Seevaka Chinthamani, our Periya Puranam author, Sekkizhar Peruman, guided that king. He explained that the Seevaka Chinthamani he was reading would not benefit him in this life, nor in the next, nor would it lead to liberation. He then narrated the stories of our Nayanmars to the king, guiding him towards the right path. This should be the duty of a minister, or of someone serving under a king.

“But here, these Pallava kings, influenced by the Jains, simply carry out the tasks they are told to do. They inflict harm upon our Thiru-Navukkarasar. That is why Sekkizhar Peruman refers to them as ‘maakkal’, unintelligent, animal-like people.

“Similarly, in Kamba Ramayanam, The day for Sri Rama to go to the forest was decided by the astrologers as the day for his coronation. Kamban refers to them as ‘Kanitha Maakkal’ (unintelligent astrologers) in Kamba Ramayanam. So far, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman has remained unharmed by the three torments inflicted by the Jains through the king, and is peacefully seated. This is the fourth punishment.

“Therefore, the king is very careful in this matter. The king very cautiously orders that our Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar be securely tied to a stone with a rope, placed in a boat, taken to the middle of the sea, and then thrown into the sea along with the stone. This is because the Jains had thoroughly indoctrinated him, confusing his mind, telling him that if Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman escaped this time, then Jainism would be destroyed, And their kingdom would also be destroyed.

“However, we are going to see in detail how, after this punishment, the king reforms, embraces the path of Shiva, and becomes a Shaivite. So, for now, the king’s guards are carrying out his orders. Our Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar also went with those guards. The guards, who were the king’s servants, went deep into the sea as the king had commanded and completed their task.

“Here, it is said in history that the Jains also went along in that boat. It was not necessary for those Jains to go in the boat with the guards to witness that cruel act. Nevertheless, Those cruel Jains, like wild animals, boarded the boat and went along. This reveals the malice and cruelty in their hearts. Those Jains, with their cruel, animal-like minds, boarded the boat and went along, wanting to witness the events firsthand and rejoice. They also went with the intention and concern that if the king’s servants made any mistake, they themselves would directly carry out the act.

“This allows us to understand their cruel minds.

“Meanwhile, our Thiru-Navukkarasar, in his sacred heart, was filled with great joy and steadfastness, without any sorrow or worry. The guards also carried out the king’s orders. Wherever we look in Sekkizhar Peruman’s Periya Puranam, Wherever devotees face suffering, he avoids describing those incidents with his own words. He has made it a tradition not to speak of them with his own words. That is why he briefly sings, “They carried out the king’s orders.” Even in the story of Meypporul Nayanar, when Mutthanathan met Meypporul Nayanar, Sekkizhar Peruman, while singing about the cruel act committed by Mutthanathan, concludes by singing, “Mutthanathan did as he had intended.” Similarly, here too, he sings that the guards carried out the king’s orders. If so, then there are places in the Periya Puranam that describe how Thiru-Navukkarasar was given poison, how an elephant was sent against him, and how he was placed in a heated chamber.

“All those descriptions were not presented as the author’s (Sekkizhar Peruman’s) own narrative. They were presented as the statements of the Jains and the king.

“Thus, the guards and the Jains, having completed the task they came to do, returned to the shore.

“At that time, in the incomparably deep sea, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, who was steadfast in his true devotion, with the courage that no matter what situation arose, he would praise and worship Shiva, his father and Peruman, invoked the sacred five-letter mantra of Shiva through Tamil verses. Our Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar was steadfast in his true devotion to the sacred feet of Lord Shiva. ‘Uraippu’ means to remain unwavering in that state, no matter what happens. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar remained fearless in these four evil acts committed by the Jains. This was the state of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, because of the mental fortitude he held as a devotee of Lord Shiva. Sekkizhar sings what Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar thinks while in the sea: “No matter what situation arises, I will worship Lord Shiva.” It is mentioned here that he praises Lord Shiva. The phrase “No matter what situation arises” is a reference to the fact that he was previously thrown into fire and now into water.

“Therefore, the inner meaning is that no matter what situation arises, he will continue to remember and worship Lord Shiva, his father. Some interpret “No matter what situation arises” here to mean whether the stone thrown into the sea floats or sinks. This interpretation is not appropriate here, because if he thought whether the stone thrown into the sea floated or sank, then Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar is one who remains steadfast with the conviction that divine grace will surely protect him.

“Therefore, it is unlikely that he would think in such a way. So, that interpretation should not be taken.

“Therefore, how should it be interpreted here? It should be understood that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, the steadfast true devotee, thought that whether he was thrown into fire or into the water of the sea, no matter what situation he was in, he would not forget the Lord’s sacred feet and would worship Him. This is the most accurate interpretation.

“Thus, in that state, bound to a stone in the sea, our Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar invokes the five-letter mantra of Lord Shiva. “No matter what situation arises, no matter what happens, I will praise my Father,” he resolves. “No matter what situation arises, I will worship Lord Shiva,” he resolves. He completes this by invoking the five-letter mantra. He invokes the five-letter mantra. The sacred five-letter mantra of Lord Shiva is the great mantra that encompasses Shiva, the primordial mantra.

“The five letters are mentioned in the Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman Puranam. This great mantra has the power to lead one to Shiva and to bestow Shiva’s grace. That is the sacred five-letter mantra.

“Thus, at that moment when our Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar was bound to a stone with a rope and was in the sea, he began the Namasivaya Thiru-pathigam, starting with “Sotrunai thiyan.” It is a beautiful Tamil garland that begins with the pure sacred words “Sotrunai thiyan.” This Thiru-Pathikam of Namasivaya was composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. Namasivaya is the Holy Five Letters that protect us in times of distress. With abundant love and unceasing devotion to these Holy Five Letters, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sang this Thiru-Pathikam, which begins with “Sotrunaivedhiyan.” The Tamil of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar is good Tamil, composed of words that bring purity and goodness. This Tamil brings goodness; it is purifying Tamil.

“Therefore, by purifying, it completely removes all previous evils and obstacles. This is a wondrous Thiru-Pathikam that brings goodness.

“Therefore, it is a Thiru-Pathikam that will now bring the perfection of Shivathuvam. Previously, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar reached Thiru-Adhigai. Having reached the Thiru-Sthalam and attained spiritual realization by the grace of the Lord, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sang the Thiru-Pathikam “Kootraayina Vaaru.” At that very moment, his sufferings ceased, and he attained the blissful state of Shiva. If so, why is it said that he sang this Pathikam, “Sotrunaivedhiyan,” now to remove suffering and attain good fortune? Because when he sang “Kootraayina Vaaru,” his suffering was removed, and he attained the blissful state of Shiva.

“Now, he is fully engaged in the righteous path of Shiva, so that the sufferings caused by the illusory forces that tried to destroy that blissful state are completely overcome.

“Therefore, the same meaning is attributed to this Thiru-Pathikam here. Sotrunai Vedhiyan enum thoo mozhi Narsamil maalaiyaha Namasivaya endru Atram mun kaakkum anjezhuththai anbodhu Patriya unarvinaal pathikam paadinaar endru Sekkizhar Peruman inge Thiruppaadalai amaikkindraar. Sekkizhar Peruman states that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar composed this Thiru-Pathikam, beginning with “Sotrunaivedhiyan,” as a garland of pure and good Tamil words, with Namasivaya. This Thiru-Pathikam is structured so that “Namasivaya” concludes each verse, appearing at the end of all the songs. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar composed this Thiru-Pathikam with a feeling of loving devotion to the Five Letters, Namasivaya, as stated by Sekkizhar Peruman. In this Thiru-Pathikam, the best support is Namasivaya itself.

“That which cuts off sin is Namasivaya itself. That which bestows great good is Namasivaya itself. That which illuminates the good heart is Namasivaya itself. That which is the good path is Namasivaya itself.

“Thus, in each instance, the Five Letters, Namasivaya, appear as the conclusion.

“Therefore, Saivism celebrates this Thiru-Pathikam as the Namasivaya Thiru-Pathikam. The Peruman sings of those Holy Five Letters here as the Holy Five Letters that protect us from harm. “Achcham” means suffering or harm. Whatever suffering may come, the Holy Five Letters, the sacred mantra of Shiva’s holy name, stand guard to protect those who remember them. When one contemplates those Holy Five Letters, they sever our sins and destroy the trembling we experience, as stated in The Thevarams declare. Not only that, it is said that “Namasivaya bestows great good,” not just removing suffering.

“Therefore, these Holy Five Letters also bestow goodness. This is called the Namasivaya Pathikam.

“Similarly, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman sang the Panchakshara Pathikam. Sundaramurthy Swamigal sang, “Even if I forget You, O good ascetic, the word I utter is Namasivaya.” Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar composed this Thiru-Pathikam with a feeling of devotion to these Holy Five Letters, Namasivaya. There are many methods for chanting and abiding in the Holy Five Letters. The benefits also vary according to these methods. The teachings regarding these Holy Five Letters should be understood from the gracious lineage of Gurus. They should be understood in that manner, through the Guru, through the Acharya.

“What is stated in this Thiru-Pathikam is the Holy Five Letters, Namasivaya, beginning with the letter “Na.” Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings this Thiru-Pathikam with a feeling of loving devotion to these Holy Five Letters. He sings with love for these Holy Five Letters, with firmness, contemplating them in his consciousness, becoming one with them. He sings with a feeling of devotion to the Holy Five Letters. It is said that he sings with a feeling of loving devotion. The feeling of devotion to the Holy Five Letters is the feeling of contemplating and grasping their inner meaning. The greatness of these Holy Five Letters and their truths can be found in the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophical texts such as Thiruvarutpayan, Unmai Vilakkam, Sivagnana Bodham, Sivagnana Siddhiyar, and others.

“Furthermore, in Thiru-Moolar’s Thiru-Mandiram, in the ninth Tantra, in sections such as Sthoola Panchaksharam, Sookshma Panchaksharam, Adisookshma Panchaksharam, Thiru-Koothu Dharisanam, Sivananda Koothu, and in other Shaiva Siddhanta gnana texts, they can be found. These should be properly learned and understood from enlightened teachers, from Gnana Desikars, who possess grace and experience. This Namasivaya Thiru-Pathikam, which begins with “Sotrunaivedhiyan,” is compiled as the eleventh general Thiru-Pathikam in the Fourth Thiru-Murai. The tune is Gandhara Panchamam.

“Now, the Namasivaya Thiru-Pathikam.

“Sotrunaivedhiyan. Potrunai theerndadi porundha kai thozha Katrunai poottiyor kadalil paichchinum Natrunaiyavadhu Namasivayaave Poovinu karungalam pongu thaamarai Aavinu karungalam aran anjaadudhal Kovinu karungalam koottamilladhu Naavinu karungalam Namasivayaave Vinnura adukkiya viragin vevvazhal Unniya pogil avai ondrum illaiyaa Panniya ulaginil payindra paavaththai Nanni nindraruppadhu Namasivayaave Idhu kan pattirukkinum irandhiyaaraiyum Vidukkil piraan vinavuvom allom Adukkil keezhkeeda keenum arulin naam Utra nadukkaththai keduppadhu Namasivayaave Vendha neerum kalam viradhigarkkellaam Andha narkarungalam arumarai aarangam Thingal karungalam thigazhu neenmudi Nammalukkarunga Namasivayaave Salamilan Sankaran saarndhavar kallaal Nalamila naador nalkuvaan nalan Kulamila raagilum kulaththirkketpadhor Nalam miga koduppadhu Namasivayaave Veedinaar ulaginil vizhumia thondargal Koodinaaran neri koodi sendralum Odinen odi sendru uruvam kaandalum Naadinen naaditru Namasivayaave Illaga veezhakkadhu irul Keduppadhu Sollaga veezhakkadhu jothi ulladhu Pallaga veezhakkadhu palarum kaanbadhu Nallaga veezhakkadhu Namasivayaave Munnariyaagiya mudhalvan mukkaNNan Thanneriye saraN aadal thiNName Anneriye sendranggu adaindhavar kellaam Nanneriyavadhu Namasivayaave MaappiNai thazhuviya maadhor paagaththan PooppiNai theerndadi porundha kai thozha NaappiNai thazhuviya Namasivaya paththu Eththavallaar thamakku idukkal illaiye NaappiNai thazhuviya Namasivaya paththu Eththavallaar thamakku idukkal illaiye Thiruchitrambalam.

“Let us continue to contemplate the meanings of the Namasivaya Thiru-Pathikam.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 318, Thiru-Nindrachcharukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We saw that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman composed the Namasivaya Thiru-Pathikam while bound to a stone in the ocean.

Now, let us contemplate the meanings of that Thiru-Pathikam. This Thiru-Pathikam begins with “Sotrunaivedhiyan.” Its first verse is: “Sotrunaivedhiyan sothivaanavan Potrunai thirundhadi porundha kaithozha Katrunai poottiyor kadalil paichchinum Natrunaiyavadhu Namasivayaave.” We saw that this is the Namasivaya Thiru-Pathikam because “Namasivayaave” appears at the end of each verse. He begins by placing that first, singing “Sotrunaivedhiyan.” Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. “Sotrunaivedhiyan” should be separated as “Sol Thunai Vedhiyan.” Sivakavimani explains the meaning of these words, “Sotrunaivedhiyan,” as the one who expounded the Veda, who is the meaning of the Veda, and who is a helper in every way. “Sotrunai” or “Sol Thunai” means “Sabdapramanam” or “word measure.” Thus, the Veda, which is Sabdapramanam, exists in the form of words.

The Lord exists as the object of those words. He is the Vedhiyan, as stated here. Why does he begin by calling Him the Vedhiyan, who is the object of the Vedas? Because this is the Namasivaya Thiru-Pathikam, and the word “Siva” shines in the midst of the Vedas. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, taking the word “Siva” as his sole support, proceeds to sing the Five Letters, the Holy Five Letters.

Therefore, he sings, taking Him as the one who shines as the meaning of the Veda. Primarily, this Namasivaya is called Sri Panchaksharam. When Manikkavasaga Peruman began the Sivapuranam, the first part of Thiruvasagam, he also began with “Namasivaya Vazhga.” This Panchaksharam is in the middle of the Vedas. The Vedas are called “Trayi,” and they are divided into three forms: Rig, Yajur, and Sama. The Yajur Veda is in the middle of these three. This Yajur Veda is arranged in seven sections.

The middle section is the fourth section, the Satarudriyam. In its Middle is the fifth Prashna. In the middle of the Anuvaka “Nama Somayacha,” the Panchakshara Mantra “Nama Sivaya” shines. For this reason, this Siva Mantra shines as the jewel of all Vedas, as supremely purifying, as highly secret, and as the essence of all Vedanta. This is the true meaning of the four Vedas and is the mantra chanted during Sandhya times. Sri Gnanasambandha Peruman, who drank the milk of Sivagnana, the essence of the Vedas, sang in his Thevara Thiru-Pathikam, “The true meaning in all four Vedas is the Lord’s name, Namasivaya.” He also explained and sang, “For the righteous Brahmins who maintain the sacred fire, the mantra in the evening is the Five Letters.”

The object of this Sri Panchaksharam, Namasivaya, is Sambhu, Parameswaran. This Parameswaran, bearing the Siva Bija “Sim” in the middle of the Sri Panchaksharam on His face, and placing the Amrita Varuna Bija, “Vam,” next to it, shines by the name “Sivaga” as the secret of all Vedas and their life-gem. This word “Siva” stands as a great ornament in the Rig, Yajur, Sama, and Atharva Vedas, illuminating the Turiya state. It stands as a conventional name for the Para-Brahman. The Mandukya Upanishad, Narasimha Tapaniya Upanishad, Atharvasiras Upanishad, and all other Upanishads praise it immeasurably. Among all texts, the Veda is supreme.

Within it, the great mantra The collection known as Satarudriyam is most excellent. Within that, the Sri Panchakshari “Namasivaya” is most excellent, and within that, the two letters “Siva” are most excellent.

Therefore, for the Veda Purusha, the Panchaksharam is like the pupil of the eye, and the word “Siva” is like the eyesight. Just as the soul, in its subtle form, resides in the heart in the middle of the body and animates the entire body, so too the word “Siva” resides in the middle of the Veda and makes the entire Veda contemplate Shiva. For this reason, all Vedic scholars, with discerning minds, have declared that the essence of the fourteen Vidyas, that which destroys all sins, and that which is the signifier of the Para-Brahman, is the name of Shiva. Thayumanavar Swamigal also said, “The hundred and eight Vedas, when expounded, are like A grammar that is sufficient, yet even that is not enough; it is beyond that, becoming the eye of grace.” It is said in a verse in the Mundaka Upanishad that even if one is a Chandala, if he utters the word “Siva,” one should converse with him, reside with him, and eat with him. This very meaning of the Shruti was expounded by Madhava Sivagnana Swamigal, the great scholar of Dravidian Mahabhashyam, who said, “If even a vile Chandala utters the word ‘Siva,’ converse with him, speak with him, and eat with him,” thus explaining the meaning of the Shruti through this simile.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, who composed this Namasivaya Thiru-Pathikam by placing the Holy Five Letters, Namasivaya, at the end of each verse, for this reason He begins this Pathikam with “Sotrunaivedhiyan.” Namasivaya is the Lord’s Five-Letter Mahamantra. This is called Sthoola Panchaksharam. “Namaha Sivaya” comes in Tamil as “Namasivaya” according to Sanskrit grammar. Its meaning is “Salutations to Shiva.” The Shaiva Siddhanta spiritual scholars explain that each letter of this Five-Letter Mahamantra signifies a different meaning. Appar Swamigal referred to this as “Padham Anjum” (Five Letters), and Sundaramurthy Swamigal sang, “Andhiyum Nanbagalum Anju Padham Solli” (uttering the Five Letters morning and noon). In Namasivaya, the letter “Na” signifies Tirodhana Shakti, “Ma” signifies Malama, “Si” signifies the Lord, “Va” signifies the power of divine grace, and “Ya” signifies the soul.

This It signifies that the soul, in its bound state, is led through birth, subjected to karma, purified of its impurities, and then attains liberation through the grace of the Lord. This also signifies the Lord’s selfless great grace. That is why Manikkavasaga Peruman begins the Sivapuranam and the Thiruvasagam with “Namasivaya Vazhga.” Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman begins with “Sotrunaivedhiyan.” He refers to Shiva as “Sothivaanavan.” The “Sothi” mentioned here refers to Shiva, who is the Supreme Light.

The Lord guides us when darkness comes.

Therefore, he says “Sothivaanavan.” “Irulidathu Unnai Sikkana Pidithen” (I held You firmly in the darkness) is from Thiruvasagam.

Next, he sings, “Potrunai thirundhadi porul.” He sings, “Porundha kaithozha.” “Potrunai thirundhadi” should be separated as “Pon thunai thirundhu adi,” meaning “golden feet, supporting feet, perfect feet.” It should be understood as the Lord’s golden holy feet, the Lord’s supporting feet, the Lord’s perfect feet. He sings, “Porundha kaithozha,” meaning to worship with hands joined in a fitting manner. He sings, “Porundha kaithozha.” This means that our heart should cling to the Lord’s holy feet with great devotion, and our hands should be joined in worship.

Therefore, he sings, “Sotrunaivedhiyan sothivaanavan Potrunai thirundhadi porundha kaithozha,” and then, “Katrunai poottiyor kadalil paichchinum Natrunaiyavadhu Namasivayaave.” “Katrunai poottiyor kadalil paichchinum” refers to the event that occurred in the history of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. “Katrunai pootti” should be understood as “Kal thunai pootti,” meaning “bound firmly with a stone.” Even if one is bound firmly with a stone and thrown into the ocean, “Natrunaiyavadhu Namasivayaave” he sings, meaning Namasivaya is the good support. Namasivaya is a good support. Even if one is bound to a stone and thrown into the ocean, the Holy Five Letters, Namasivaya, are the support. When?

When we worship the Lord’s golden, perfect feet with devotion, Namasivaya is the good support, the excellent support. If the Holy Five Letters, Namasivaya, can rescue souls from the great ocean of birth and bestow the bliss of liberation, then is it necessary to say that it will rescue one from this ordinary ocean with a stone?

Now, the next verse, the second verse, is structured as: “Poovinukku arungalam pongu thaamarai Aavinukku arungalam aran anjaadudhal Kovinukku arungalam koottamilladhu Naavinukku arungalam Namasivayaave.” In this, the word “arungalam” appears. “Arungalam” means “most excellent.” It means “most excellent among many benefits.” So, the first line is “Poovinukku arungalam pongu thaamarai,” meaning among all flowers, the lotus is the most special. “Poovenappaduvadhu porivaazh poove” is a saying.

Therefore, among all flowers, the lotus is the most special and good. The lotus flower is like an ornament to all flowers, yielding benefit. The three goddesses, Saraswati, Lakshmi, and Parvati, are seated upon it.

Therefore, the lotus is the ornament to flowers.

Next, it is said that the ornament to cows is the fivefold ablution of Aran. Aran refers to Lord Shiva, and the fivefold ablution means He who performs ablution with the Panchagavya. ‘Aa’ means cow.

Thus, the good benefit derived from cows is the Panchagavya offered as ablution to Lord Shiva. That is the best benefit among all benefits derived from cows.

Therefore, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sings, ‘The ornament to cows is the fivefold ablution of Aran.’ We have already learned about the glories of Panchagavya. We have seen it in great detail in the Nayanar Puranam and the Chandesvara Nayanar Puranam.

Now, next, he sings, ‘The ornament to a king is impartiality.’ ‘Ko’ means king. A king should be without partiality. ‘Kottam’ means leaning to one side. A king should be neutral and not lean to one side.

Therefore, ‘The ornament to a king is impartiality.’ Next, he sings, ‘The ornament to the tongue is Namasivaya.’ This means that the benefit of the tongue is the Namasivaya mantra. Uttering the Namasivaya mantra is the ornament to the tongue. It is the best benefit among all benefits derived from the tongue. The Namasivaya Thirumandiram is like a good ornament to the tongue.

Now, the third sacred verse: “If the fierce fire of wood piled high to the sky were to consume, there would be nothing left. The sins accumulated in the created world, if approached, Namasivaya will destroy them.” They have piled wood up to the sky. If a small fire is placed at its base, that fire will consume all the wood piled up to the sky, reducing it to nothing, to ashes. Just as such a large pile of wood, similarly, even if the sins committed by people who have lived for a long time in this world created by God are piled up as high as the sky like huge logs, if one practices the small fire of the sacred five letters, Namasivaya, and utters it, That sacred five-letter Namasivaya will reduce even such a huge pile of sins to nothing.

Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar describes the greatness of the Namasivaya Thirumandiram through this analogy. Even if a huge amount of wood is piled up, a small fire is enough to burn it all to ashes and make it disappear.

Similarly, even if people have accumulated immense sins, the single Thirumandiram of Namasivaya is enough to make all those sins disappear.

Here, the sins accumulated by people refer to the sins committed by people before coming into this world, which caused their birth here, and then the accumulation of sins multiplied by their actions after being born in this world.

Thus, however great the accumulation of sins may be, However great the piles of sins may be, the sacred five-letter Namasivaya will stand by and destroy them all. We will continue to contemplate the meanings of the sacred verses of the Namasivaya Thiruppathikam. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 319, Thirunindrachcharukkam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We are contemplating the meaning of the sacred verses of the Namasivaya Thiruppathikam, which begins with ‘Sotrunaivedhiyan’. We have contemplated the meaning of three sacred verses.

Now, the fourth sacred verse: “Though afflicted by distress, we will not abandon Him and inquire of anyone else, saying, ‘O Lord, release us.’ Even if a mountain falls upon us, Namasivaya will remove the trembling with His grace.” This is the fourth sacred verse. Its meaning is as follows: However much we may be afflicted by poverty and suffering, we will not abandon our Lord and worship anyone else. We will not ask anyone else to remove our suffering. We will only make our supplication to Lord Shiva, our Lord. Whatever suffering comes to us, of whatever kind, Whatever suffering comes, we will not ask anyone other than Lord Shiva, ‘O Lord, remove this suffering.’ Even if a mountain falls on our head and buries us, we will believe that the sacred five letters, Namasivaya, will remove our suffering. We will believe that our Lord, Lord Shiva, is the Lord who removes our sufferings.

Now, the fifth sacred verse: “Sacred ash is the ornament for all ascetics; the sacred Vedas and their six ancillaries are the ornament for Brahmins; the crescent moon is the ornament for the glorious long crown; for us, the ornament is Namasivaya.” This is the verse. Its meaning is as follows: Here, ‘arungalam’ (ornament) is used in the sense of ‘that which is desired.’ Therefore, in the first line, ‘Sacred ash is the ornament for ascetics,’ Its meaning is that for all ascetics who have undertaken vows, sacred ash is what is desired. Sacred ash is the best ornament.

Next, it says, ‘The sacred Vedas and their six ancillaries are the ornament for Brahmins.’ For all Brahmins, what is desired and essential is the recitation of the four Vedas and their six ancillaries.

Thirdly, it says, ‘The crescent moon is the ornament for the glorious long crown.’ For the crescent moon, what is desired is Lord Shiva’s beautiful matted hair. Being on that matted hair is the glory and ornament for that moon. In the fourth line, it says, ‘For us, the ornament is Namasivaya.’ For devotees like us, the best ornament and what is desired is the sacred five letters, Namasivaya. In the first line, ‘Sacred ash is the ornament for all ascetics,’ there is the following commentary in the book ‘Dharmapuram Adheenam Thirumurai Vilakkam’: ‘Ascetics’ refers to those who have undertaken vows. What are vows? Vows are the acceptance of doing certain good deeds and eradicating certain sins.

Therefore, these vows are undertaken to remove our karmic impurities and purify our inner instruments. That is why Thiruvalluvar, in the section on asceticism in Thirukkural, divides asceticism into two parts: ‘vow’ and ‘knowledge,’ and Parimelazhagar explains it. In the section on vows, Valluvar has graciously placed virtues like compassion, abstaining from meat, penance, Not engaging in improper conduct, not learning (what is evil), truthfulness, freedom from anger, not harming, and non-killing as separate chapters. Parimelazhagar has commented on this as follows: Through such vows, the inner instruments of the mind and others become pure. When these inner instruments are purified, awareness arises, which is true awareness. That which is realized by this true awareness, that is, by true knowledge, is the ultimate reality.

The sacred ash constantly reminds us of that ultimate reality, Lord Shiva.

Therefore, in this first line, it is said that for ascetics, that is, for those who have undertaken vows, the sacred ash is what is desired and is an ornament.

Similarly, such It is a good deed to behold the devotees of Shiva who wear the sacred ash. When one sees Shiva’s devotees wearing the sacred ash, it reminds the beholders of the Supreme Being, Shiva.

Therefore, for Shiva’s devotees and ascetics, there is no other ornament better than the sacred ash. This is its meaning.

Now, the next verse, the sixth verse: “Shankara is without deceit; He is not benevolent to those who do not cling to Him. He bestows good daily. Even if they are without lineage, Namasivaya bestows abundant good appropriate to their lineage.” This sacred verse begins with ‘Shankara is without deceit.’ The Lord is Shankara. Shankara means one who brings happiness, one who brings joy. ‘Sam’ means happiness, joy. ‘Kara’ means one who does. Such a Shankara, Thirunavukkarasar Peruman sings, ‘He is without deceit.’ ‘Sallam’ means partiality. ‘Sallam ilan’ here means ‘He is without desire or aversion.’ Therefore, ‘Shankara is without deceit’ means Shankara is without desire or aversion.

Next, he sings, ‘He is not benevolent to those who do not cling to Him.’ This means that even though Shiva is without deceit, without desire or aversion, only those who cling to Lord Shiva will prosper. In the Sivagnana Padiyam, in the commentary on the Thiruvellipava verse, ‘It is the duty of leaders to protect those who seek refuge in them,’ it is said that it is the duty of noble people to protect those who seek refuge in them.

Therefore, Lord Shiva, as the Primeval Being, protects only those who cling to Him. He protects those who cling to Him. If so, how is He without deceit? That is, how can it be said that God is without partiality, without desire or aversion, as sung in the beginning? This is because protecting those who cling to Him does not in any way diminish Lord Shiva’s impartiality and His state of being without desire or aversion. This is because Lord Shiva establishes those Shiva devotees who cling to Him, who have made themselves His servants, and who are capable of remaining in His service, as Himself.

Therefore, He destroys the future karma that comes to such Shiva devotees and protects those Shiva devotees who cling to Him.

Thus, This means that Lord Shiva bestows the fruit of karma upon those who do not cling to Him. He causes those who do not cling to Lord Shiva to experience the fruits of their respective karmas. For those who cling to Lord Shiva’s feet and are Shiva devotees, He stands as those Shiva devotees themselves, destroys their future karma, and does good for them.

Therefore, He does good for those who cling to Him. For those who do not cling to Him, that is, for those who do not cling to Him, He bestows grace to the extent of giving them the fruits of their karma. Some say that protecting only those who cling to Him and abandoning those who do not is not impartiality. Even if that were the case, it is still a quality of leadership.

Therefore, this is an example of God’s leadership quality. It is a quality of leadership and does not diminish Him, according to Saivite scholars.

Therefore, Lord Shiva, through His knowledge, removes the two karmas of those who attain Him and bestows upon them the bliss of liberation. To those who do not cling to Him, He bestows only the fruits of their two karmas.

Next, it says, ‘Even if they are without lineage, Namasivaya bestows abundant good appropriate to their lineage.’ This means that for devotees who cling to Lord Shiva, no matter what lineage, caste, or ashrama they belong to, God disregards all of that and considers only their penance, bestowing His grace upon them.

Now, the seventh sacred verse, The eminent devotees in the world who have renounced attachments, having joined that path, I ran, ran, and upon seeing their form, I sought, and Namasivaya sought me. The pure devotees, Shiva’s devotees, have renounced worldly attachments. They stand in the path of Shiva, having attained Shiva Yoga, and are in that exalted state. Seeing their state, I desired to quickly join them and attain that very path, that good path. Upon seeing the form of those Shiva devotees standing in the light of Shiva, and seeking divine grace through that path, the five letters sought me. This is the essence of the twelfth sutra of Sivagnana Bodham: ‘To be with the loving ones after the impurity is removed.’ Now, the next sacred verse, the eighth verse, The lamp within the house dispels darkness.

The lamp of the word is luminous. The lamp of many is seen by many. The lamp of the good heart is Namasivaya. Its meaning is that the lamp in the house dispels the darkness within the house. Just as that lamp dispels the outer darkness, the sacred five letters dispel the inner darkness. That light of the sacred five letters exists in all three times.

This sacred five-letter Namasivaya is the inner light of all souls. No matter what state or religion all souls are in, this sacred five letters stands within them, unseen by them, yet visible to them. Among the ‘Ya’, ‘Na’, and ‘Ma’ in the sacred five letters, all other religions are contained, while ‘Va’ and ‘Si’ are unique to Saivism. Such a sacred five-letter mantra is a good inner lamp. It is a lamp that shines within the form of knowledge. A heart filled with knowledge is a good heart.

Sivagnana Sastram states that if the sacred five-letter mantra is chanted according to the prescribed method, one can behold God. Why does Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar refer to it as a lamp here? This can be seen in the extensive commentary on Sivagnana Bodham Sutra Nine, Adhikaranam Three. When the knowledge of the self ceases and one beholds the knowable through knowledge, and when one attains the state of being one with everything, the mind’s tendency to grasp external objects due to long-standing habit, which is a partial knowledge, is restrained from going outwards and is focused on an inner point. When one attains the state of absorption, the method of chanting the five letters is seen and contemplated, and because it illuminates the vision of Shiva, it is called a lamp. Because it completely removes the partial knowledge that grasps external objects due to habit and leads to a state of fullness, it is an excellent means to remove habits.

If one can behold the Lord, who is the ultimate reality, unlike the soul and bonds that are perceived as objects of consciousness, within one’s own heart through the method of chanting the five letters, then just as fire appears from wood when a stick is rubbed with a rope, so too will the Lord appear there and shine as the knowledge of knowledge.

Therefore, it is called the lamp of the good heart, Namasivaya. This is the explanation given in the Dharmapuram Adheenam commentary on this sacred verse. This explanation is to be understood by directly studying the Saiva Siddhanta Sastras under a guru.

Now, verse number nine: “The path of the First One, the Three-Eyed Lord, is indeed the refuge. For all who have gone and attained that path, the good path is Namasivaya.” The path of Lord Shiva, who is the foremost path, is the refuge for all. The Three-Eyed Lord is the guide to liberation, which is salvation. One must firmly cling to that path which He has revealed. For all who stand on that path and attain His sacred feet, the Namasivaya mantra, the sacred five letters, serves as the best path. If living beings desire liberation, The path of the First One, Shiva, must be the refuge.

That is certain. For all who stand on that path and attain Him, Namasivaya is the good path. The greatest good that living beings can attain is liberation, known as moksha. Namasivaya is the excellent path that leads to it. That knowledge is called the good path, according to the Mahapadiyam. Although knowledge and Namasivaya are different, when knowledge shines and the knowable is perceived, the sacred five letters, which are the means to remove the habit of focusing on the bonds that were previously observed due to habit, are considered equal to knowledge, and therefore it is the good path.

This is the extensive commentary on Sivagnana Mahapadiyam Sutra Nine. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman also sings, “It leads to the good path those who, with love, melt and shed tears as they chant.”

Now, the tenth verse: “For those who can praise the Namasivaya Pathu, which embraces the tongue, by placing the sacred feet of the Lord, who holds the deer and has Uma as one half, in their hearts, there will be no distress.” The Lord holds the deer in His hand and has Goddess Parvati as one half of His body. He has sacred feet adorned with flower garlands. The sacred five letters will be the support for me to place those sacred feet in my heart and worship them with my hands.

Therefore, we must utter the sacred five letters until our tongue is calloused.

Thus, for the devotees who can worship these ten verses about the sacred five letters, that is, this Namasivaya Thiruppathikam, for the devotees who chant this, no suffering No suffering will befall them, no distress will come, as Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar graciously states in the tenth sacred verse as a phalashruti (statement of benefits). This is the only Thiruppathikam among the Thevara Thiruppathikams of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman that mentions the benefit within it. He states this to convey that worshipping Lord Shiva and attaining benefit is the sure benefit for people.

Thus, we have contemplated the meanings of the ten sacred verses of this Namasivaya Thiruppathikam, which begins with ‘Sotrunaivedhiyan,’ for the devotees who chant this sacred verse daily. We saw that this is the Thiruppathikam graciously composed by our Thirunavukkarasu Peruman when he was tied to a stone and thrown into the sea. We saw that this is the Thiruppathikam graciously composed by our Thirunavukkarasu Peruman.

We will continue to contemplate the life story of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 320, Thirunindrachcharukkam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, while in the ocean, recited and praised the sacred Namasivaya mantra, and bestowed the sacred hymn of Namasivaya. With overflowing devotion, holding fast to that mantra, Thirunavukkarasar thus praised. The sacred five-lettered mantra, which is difficult even for Brahma and other primordial celestials to praise, was thus praised by Thirunavukkarasar, and the stone floated within the ocean. He always praised the sacred Namasivaya mantra with great love and without weariness.

This sacred five-lettered mantra is the sacred five-lettered mantra, which is very difficult even for celestials to praise. This is because celestials possess abundant ‘pasu punyam’ (meritorious deeds) performed with the intention of enjoying heavenly pleasures. Due to these ‘pasu punyams’, they attain the status of gods and experience heavenly pleasures.

Therefore, for those who are in such a state due to an abundance of merit, it is very rare to completely forget themselves in love and meditate solely on Lord Shiva.

Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman praises the five-lettered mantra, which is difficult even for the celestials to praise.

At that time, the stone floated in the ocean. The Jain ascetics had tied Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar tightly to a stone with a rope and cast him into the ocean, had they not? That stone floated in the ocean. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar was seated upon that stone, being carried along. A stone is naturally prone to sinking in water. Would such a stone float?

Here, the stone floats. If we consider the order of creation, the inherent taste of water is contained within the earth.

Therefore, in the order of creation, water appears first, and only then does the earth, which is ‘prithvi’, appear. The hardness of that earth is stone.

Thus, it is understood here that if there is the divine grace of Lord Shiva, the Creator, a stone will float in water. The Jains tied Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar to a stone and cast him into the ocean, intending for him to drown.

But that very stone became a raft for him. and floated. This is the divine ordinance of the Lord, who is the chief of the five cosmic functions, including creation. What is an ordinance? It is the decree that appoints and establishes individuals to experience the fruits of the actions they perform.

Therefore, here, it is the divine ordinance that no harm should befall Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar. According to that ordinance, the stone, which would naturally sink in the ocean, floats. When one person, with the intention of killing another, gives a poisonous substance, the person who consumes that poison, contrary to dying, finds that a severe illness previously afflicting their body is cured. That very poison becomes the medicine for the severe illness, protecting the one who consumed the poison from death and curing the disease. We commonly observe this in the world.

Similarly, here, the stone, which should have sunk and remained submerged in the ocean, floated. This is because the fruit of the sin of attempting to kill Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar must accrue to the Jains. The benefit of salvation, which removes suffering, must accrue to Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar.

Therefore, for these two ordinances to occur and be preserved, the stone floated. Accomplished Siddhas who have attained the eight great Siddhis through the grace of Lord Shiva are capable of performing such deeds through Siddhis like Laghima, Mahima, and Garima. Even Siddhas who have attained such Siddhis perform such actions.

At this time, our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar is in the state of a Jivanmukta.

Therefore, all these actions are very ordinary. Our Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, Sundaramurthy Swamigal, and other Saiva Samaya Paramacharyas have demonstrated such wonders. This does not mean they performed these wonders through Siddhis. Our Paramacharyas’ vital organs were transformed into divine organs, enabling them to perform such great deeds that no one else could.
