Therefore, we should not compare our Paramacharyas with those who are merely Siddhas who have attained Siddhis at an initial stage. Our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar was placed in a fiery chamber, and the fire cooled.

Now, he has been tied to a stone and cast into the ocean. In this ocean, the stone floats. That large stone floated as a raft for our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar to be seated upon.

At that time, the rope that bound the sacred body of our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar also broke. It is said that the great stone floated as a raft. Such a large, broad, tall, and strong stone floats here as a raft. If we separate ‘perum kal’ (great stone) as ‘perumai kal’ (stone of greatness), it also implies that the stone attained the greatness of bearing our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar. The sacred body of our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, like a palanquin, is being carried; we must consider how fortunate that stone must have been. Just as the stone that should have sunk floated, so too did the rope tied to the sacred body of our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar break.

Thus, upon that stone, floating in the ocean, our Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal appeared as a great and glorious true devotee. “Perugiya anbinar piditha petriyāl arumalarōn muthal amarar vāzhththatharku ariya añjaluththaiyum arasu pōttrida karunidum kadalin ul kal mithanthathē apperum kallum angu arasu mēl kola theppamāy mithaththathil serintha pāsamum thappiyathu athanmisaiyiruntha thāvil sīr meypp- perum thondanār vilangi thōntrinār” are two sacred verses composed by Sekkizhar Swamigal at this point. Sekkizhar Peruman here praises Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar as “thāvil sīr meypp-perum thondanār” (the faultless, glorious, true, great devotee). Our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar is one whom the Jains, with great envy, tried to destroy in many ways but could not.

Therefore, Sekkizhar uses the word “thāvil” here, meaning that which is always indestructible and enduring. This is a divine greatness, so he uses the word “sīr” (glory). He calls him “meypp-perum thondanār” (true great devotee). He uses the phrase “thāvil sīr meypp-perum thondanār” here, meaning “mey” (true) because he stands firm without deviation from truth, and “perum” (great) because the greatness of our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar is immeasurable. Sekkizhar Swamigal has used it. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing: “Iruvinai pāsa mummala-k-kal ārththalin varu pavakkadalil vīzh mākkal ēridda arulum mey añjeluththu arasai ikkadal oru kal mēl ēttridal uraikka vēndumō?” (When souls, bound by the stone of the three impurities of karma and anava, fall into the ocean of birth, should it be said that the true five-lettered mantra, which grants grace, lifted the king onto a stone in this ocean?) We saw that Thirunavukkarasu Peruman praised the sacred five-lettered mantra.

We saw that the stone floated as a raft. The sacred five-lettered mantra, Namasivaya, is capable of lifting souls out of the ocean of birth. Those souls are fallen into the ocean of birth, bound by the stone of anava (ego) and the ropes of good and bad karma. They are bound by the ropes of good and bad karma to the stone of anava.

Thus, souls bound by the ropes of good and bad karma to the stone of anava are fallen into the ocean of birth. The sacred five-lettered mantra has the power to rescue such souls from the ocean of birth. If it can make that stone float as a raft, preventing our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar from drowning in this ordinary small ocean, then there is no wonder, no surprise, sings Sekkizhar Peruman.

Here, Sekkizhar Peruman uses three metaphors. He metaphorically refers to the births taken by souls as the ocean. He metaphorically refers to the impurity of anava (ego) that accompanies souls as a stone. This impurity of anava is like a stone, and the two karmas are metaphorically represented as the rope that binds souls to this stone. He metaphorically refers to good and bad karma as a rope. He metaphorically refers to the impurity of anava as a stone because the impurity of anava is very strong, firm, and like darkness, it covers the intellect of living beings, preventing it from shining even a little.

Therefore, he metaphorically refers to the impurity of anava as a stone. He metaphorically refers to the two karmas, good and bad, as a rope because this rope, these good and bad karmas, binds these souls to the stone of anava, making them subservient and inactive. He metaphorically refers to the impurity of karma, which consists of two karmas, as a rope here.

Thus, the soul, bound by the ropes of good and bad karma to the stone of anava, is floundering and sinking in the ocean of birth.

Therefore, he metaphorically refers to birth as the ocean. Generally, it is customary to refer to the ocean as the seven seas. The births that living beings experience are also of seven types.

Thus, birth, in this manner, tosses and turns souls, causing them suffering.

Therefore, he metaphorically referred to birth as the ocean. Generally, it is our spiritual tradition to refer to birth as the ocean, ‘bhavasagaram’, and ‘bhava kadal’. Generally, although karma and maya are also impurities for living beings, if ‘mala’ (impurity) is mentioned without any qualifier, it refers only to ‘anava mala’ (ego impurity). This is because the two impurities of maya and karma come and attach themselves to living beings.

But ‘anava mala’ is inherent, like the verdigris on copper.

Thus, the scriptures of wisdom speak of ‘anava’ itself as ‘mala’ (impurity) because it obscures the pervasive intellect of the soul and reduces the soul to an atomic state.

Thus, birth is given to souls by the two impurities of ‘anava’ and ‘karma’.

Therefore, birth does not come to souls on its own; someone must bring it about. That one is God. “Valvinaiyēn thannai marainthida mūdiya māya irulai aram pāvam ennum arum kaiyitrrāl katti” (The dark illusion that covered me, the one with strong karma, bound by the rare rope of dharma and sin) is from Thiruvachagam, Sivapuranam.

Therefore, what is the way for souls sinking in the ocean of birth to reach the shore? It is by worshipping the sacred feet, which are the grace of God. If one worships thus, then rising above this ocean of birth and coming ashore will occur. For this, the sacred five-lettered mantra will serve as a means. One must recite it according to the rules and benefit from it.

Therefore, reciting the sacred five-lettered mantra according to its rules and benefiting from it is the action of souls.

Thus, with this as a means, souls cross this ocean of birth. The sacred five-lettered mantra, Sri Panchaksharam, serves as the means for this. “Than kadan adiyenaiyum thānguthal en kadan pani seythu kidappathē” (It is His duty to bear me, His servant; it is my duty to serve and remain) — thus, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, at this point, meditated upon Lord Shiva, our Father, and praised the sacred five-lettered mantra.

Therefore, that sacred mantra, which is the unchanging Sat, the sacred five-lettered mantra, rescued him.

Thus, the sacred five-lettered mantra is capable of saving souls from the ocean of birth when they are bound by the rope of two karmas to the stone of anava mala and fallen into the ocean.

Therefore, the floating of this ordinary stone is not a surprising matter at all. The ocean into which souls fall is the great ocean of birth, but here, Navukkarasu Peruman was cast into a small ocean. Souls are bound by the stone of anava mala, but here, the Jains bound Navukkarasar with an ordinary black stone. Souls are bound by the ropes of good and bad karma, but here, Navukkarasar was bound by an ordinary rope.

Therefore, the sacred five-lettered mantra is capable of rescuing and making float souls who are floundering in the ocean of birth, bound by the ropes of two karmas to such a great stone of anava. This ordinary stone, rope, and ocean are nothing to the sacred five-lettered mantra of Namasivaya. This is its meaning.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman sings here that Thirunavukkarasar, who recited and praised such a sacred five-lettered mantra, made the stone itself his palanquin and floated, and that is not a surprising matter at all. Our contemplation continues.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman sings here that Thirunavukkarasar, who recited and praised such a sacred five-lettered mantra, made the stone itself his palanquin and floated, and that is not a surprising matter at all. Let us go on contemplating. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 321, Thirunindrachcharukkam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. By the grace of God, Varuna Deva himself performed great penance to embrace with his wave-like hands Thirunavukkarasar, who was the embodiment of compassion, sustained by the sacred five-lettered mantra. Our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar is the embodiment of compassion. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar is skilled in speech. Whatever Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, who is skilled in speech, says, happens exactly as spoken.

Such a possessor of perfect speech is our Navukkarasu Nayanar. Parimelazhagar stated that a word of perfect speech, whether spoken with grace or with anger, will yield those very results.

Thus speaks Parimelazhagar. Such a gracious speaker of perfect words is our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, and he is the embodiment of compassion. The Jains cast our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar into a fiery chamber, fed him poison, set an elephant upon him, and tied him to a stone and cast him into the ocean. Despite all these injustices and great sufferings inflicted upon him, our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar did not show the slightest anger towards the Jains, nor towards the cruel king who, having lost his mind to the Jains’ words, issued such commands. Whatever the situation, he only recited the sacred five-lettered mantra, believing that Lord Shiva, his Father, would protect him. He did not utter even a single word of anger towards the Jains or that cruel king, nor did he even think of it.

If our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar had uttered even a single such word, the Jains would have been destroyed by the power and might of that word. But our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar did not utter any such word towards them, nor did he even think of it in his mind.

Similarly, in a future incident in the life of our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, at the sthalam of Pazhaiyarai, even when he witnessed the cruel act of the Jains concealing and defiling the Pazhaiyarai Vadathali temple, he did not show the slightest anger towards the Jains. but observed a fast. This also demonstrates the compassion of our Navukkarasar. Varuna Deva attained great merit by bearing such a Navukkarasu Peruman on his head with his wave-like hands, because Varuna Deva knew the greatness of our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar.

Therefore, knowing that one must worship the devotees of Shiva by bearing them on one’s head, and knowing that one must perform great penance to attain that meritorious blessing, Varuna Deva thus bears our Navukkarasu Nayanar on his head with his wave-like hands. He must have performed great penance in the past to attain such great fortune. The celestials are indeed part of the flock of souls who must worship the devotees of Shiva, receive their grace, and attain liberation. Such celestials attaining the fortune of bearing devotees and serving them is only possible as a result of great penance performed in the past, and it is very rare for them to attain such great fortune easily. We are about to see the history where Indra, Vishnu, Brahma, and other celestials came to meet and escort our Sundaramurthy Swamigal from Thiru Anjaikkalam to Mount Kailash.

Similarly, now Varuna Deva worships our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar and bears him on his head. In the history of Manikkavasagar Swamigal, at the time of the debate with the Buddhists, as per the grace and command of our Vadavooradigal to Saraswati, the goddess of learning, Saraswati left the tongues of the Buddhists, and consequently, those Buddhists became mute. This is also found in the history of Manikkavasagar Swamigal. We have also read in the Periya Puranam that in Thiruvarur, outside the Devasiraya Mandapam, all the celestials stand outside, awaiting the moment to receive the grace of Shiva’s devotees.

Therefore, it is clear from these histories that the celestials worship Shiva’s devotees and await or have received their grace.

Thus, Varuna, who possessed such greatness, bore our Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar upon his head. He transformed the black stone upon which Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar was seated into a palanquin, carried it, and brought him ashore near the Thiru-Sthalam of Thiru-Padirippuliyur. He caused our Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar to alight on the shore near Thiru-Padirippuliyur. Thiru-Padirippuliyur takes its Sthala-Vriksham (sacred tree) from the Padiri tree. Due to the worship of Vyagrapada Muni, it gained the name Puliyur. As the Padiri tree was the Sthala-Vriksham, it was named Padirippuliyur.

With the addition of Thiru-, this Sthalam is known as Thiru-Padirippuliyur. The place where our Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar came ashore is currently known as Kuraiyeravitta Kuppam. It is located south of Thiru-Padirippuliyur.

Now, the sea has receded far eastward from that village.

Thus, when Thiru-Navukkarasar, the devotee who arrived at this Thiru-Sthalam of Thiru-Padirippuliyur, came ashore, all the assemblies of devotees, the Meythavakkuttam, gathered to welcome him. They rejoiced with great shouts. From all directions arose the cry of “Hara Hara.” Even the great ocean made a sound.

The devotees, knowing that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar had come to them, rejoiced.

Thus, the ocean, realizing that its task of bringing Thiru-Navukkarasar had been completed, rejoiced. The sacred names of Shiva resonated in all directions, in accordance with the words of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, “Let all be surrounded by the name of Hara.” Sekkizhar Peruman states that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, worthy of worship by all, went with the Thondars to Thiru-Padirippuliyur, worshipped the Lord who wears the crescent moon on His matted locks, fell prostrate with love, rose, and sang to make the path of divine grace manifest. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar is worthy of worship by all, including the Devas and all others. He went with the Thondars and worshipped Shiva, who is enshrined in Thiru-Padirippuliyur, wearing the white crescent moon on His matted locks. He worshipped Shiva in Thiru-Padirippuliyur, fell prostrate with love, rose, and sang in his mellifluous Tamil, so that the path of divine grace might manifest in this world. The ways in which the Lord bestows grace upon His devotees are immeasurable, but they become clear to us only when illuminated by Acharyas like Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar.

To make such a path of grace manifest here, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar praises and extols Shiva in Thiru-Padirippuliyur, beginning with “Eentraalumai enakku enthaiyum aagi” and singing a Thevaram Thiru-Padigam. We shall continue to contemplate the sacred history of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar.

Thiruchitrambalam (Sacred Hall) Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 322, Thiru-Nindra Charukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We saw that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar reached the shore at a place called Karaiyeravitta Kuppam near Thiru-Padirippuliyur, and that he entered the Thiru-Sthalam of Thiru-Padirippuliyur and had Darshan of the Lord Padaleeswarar there. We also saw that he then sang the Thiru-Padigam beginning with “Eentraalumai.” Therefore, before we examine this Thiru-Padigam of “Eentraalumai,” let us briefly consider the special features of this Thiru-Sthalam of Thiru-Padirippuliyur. This is because it is our custom and tradition that when a Sthalam is mentioned for the first time in the Periya Puranam, we contemplate its Sthala-Visheshas and Sthala-Puranas as extensively as possible, and then continue with the Puranam.

Accordingly, this Thiru-Sthalam of Thiru-Padirippuliyur is mentioned for the first time in the Periya Puranam.

Therefore, let us briefly contemplate the Sthala-Purana and Sthala-Visheshas of Thiru-Padirippuliyur, and then consider the Padigam belonging to this Sthalam, which begins with “Eentraalumai.” Thiru-Padirippuliyur is currently located very close to Cuddalore town in Cuddalore district, Tamil Nadu. The sacred name of the Lord here is Padaleeswarar, Thondra Thunainathar, Kannivanathathar, Sivakkuzhandeesar, Uttharanathar, Karaiyetrum Piran. The sacred name of the Goddess is Pragyanayaki, Periyanayaki, Thogaiyambikai, Arunthava Nayaki. The Sthala-Vriksham here is Pattalam, that is, the Padiri tree.

Therefore, this Sthalam is called Padirippuliyur after the name of this Sthala-Vriksham. The Theerthams are Brahma Theertham, Sivakara Theertham, and the Kedila River. In this Thiru-Sthalam, Agastiyar, Upamanyu Muni, Vyagrapadar, Ganga, Agni, and others have worshipped. The Shiva Lingams worshipped by them are inside this Thiru-Koyil. This Thiru-Sthalam has many sacred names such as Kadai Gnazhal, Kannivanam, Pattalapuram, Adimanagar, Uttharapuram, Padirippathi, Pulisai. Literary scholars say that Kadai Gnazhalur became Cuddalore.

Did not Varuna bear Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar in his hands and bring him ashore near Thiru-Padirippuliyur? That place is called Karaiyeravitta Kuppam. It is currently known as Vandipalayam. If you ask for Apparsami Kulam in Vandipalayam, everyone will know it. There is a tank and a small four-pillared mandapam on its bank. The stream next to this tank must have been a continuation of the Kedila River in the past.

In this Thiru-Padigam beginning with “Eentraalumai,” Appar Swamigal has sung about the Shiva of Thiru-Padirippuliyur as “Thondra Thunaiyaa irunthaargalukke” (He who was an unseen help to them). Hence, the sacred name Thondra Thunai Nathar is prevalent for the Shiva here. This Sthalam has been sung by Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman and Appar Swamigal. One of Arunagirinathar’s Thiru-Pugal also belongs to this Sthalam. The street inside the Thiru-Koyil is called Padaleeswarar Sannidhi Veethi. The east-facing temple has a front mandapam.

The adjacent Sivakara Theertham is in good condition with well-built steps. The Raja-Gopuram appears with five tiers. There are numerous stucco sculptures on the Gopuram. Passing through the entrance, one can behold the Balipeetam, Kodimaram (flagstaff), and Nandi at a height. This Sthalam has two Padiri trees as Sthala-Vrikshams. The Padiri flower on these trees blooms but does not bear fruit.

It is said that the Padiri flower blooms throughout the month of Chithirai. After circumambulating the temple, one can worship Duvara Vinayagar and Duvara Subramaniyar. Turning left after passing the entrance, in the inner circumambulatory path, after Chandra, there are separate shrines for Thiru-Navukkarasar Utsavamurtham and then the Moolamurtham. Appar, in a seated posture, with folded hands and an Uzhavara-Padai, is seen. Next to it is the Palliyarai (bedchamber). Uniquely in this Thiru-Koyil, the Palliyarai is within the Lord’s temple.

Every day, the Ambikai (Goddess) proceeds to the Palliyarai within the Lord’s temple. This is a unique feature not found in any other Sthalam. After passing the Moolamurthams of the Sixty-Three Nayanars, one can have Darshan of the Sthala Vinayagar, Sonnavaru Ari Vinayagar. He is a Valampuri Murthi, and he is also known as Kanni Vinayagar. When Ambikai worshipped the Lord in this Sthalam, this Vinayagar assisted Ambikai, and thus he is seen holding a Padiri flower in his hand. Next are the shrines of the Utsava Thiru-Menis.

The Lingams worshipped by Vyagrapadar, Agastiyar, and others, as well as the shrines of Meenakshi Sundareswarar and Arumugar with Valli and Deivanai, are located here. Opposite this, on the right side, the ancient Padiri tree, the Sthala-Vriksham, is protected by a covering. Next to the Gajalakshmi Sannidhi, at the spot where Durga is a Goshtamurthi, is the place where Ambikai performed penance in an formless state. This is revered as the Arunthava Nayaki Sannidhi.

Here, Ambikai has no form; only a Peetam (pedestal) exists.

Next, one can worship the Natarajar Sabai, Navagraha Sannidhi, Bhairavar Sannidhi, and Surya, thus circumambulating and then ascending the steps to reach the Moolavar Sannidhi. The stucco sculptures in the front mandapam are beautiful. After worshipping the Dvarapalakas, one can enter and have Darshan of Padaleeswarar. He is adorned with a Kavacham and appears charming to the eye. The Ambikai temple is separately located next to it. In the front mandapam of the east-facing Ambikai temple, sculptures of Rishabaroodar, Kalinganarthanar, Mohini Dance, Kamadhenu worship, Veenavani, Avirchadai Peruman, Anjaneyar, and others are carved on stone pillars.

In the inner circumambulatory path, there are shrines for Vinayagar, Arumugar, and Utsava Ambikai. The standing posture of Ambikai is very beautiful. Adjacent to the Ambikai Sannidhi, on the roadside, is the Pidari temple, which was consecrated later. All monthly festivals, Navaratri, Sashti, Karthigai, Somavarams, Masi Magam, Kadalattu, and all others are celebrated. The grand festival called Brahmotsavam is celebrated in Vaikasi, and Vasanthotsavam is celebrated in Chithirai. The Pidari Utsavam is also celebrated for a week in Vaikasi.

The Appar Sathaya Vizha is celebrated with great pomp in Chithirai Sathayam. The street procession on the silver Rishabam, the Kailasa Darshan at Thiru-Vaiyaaru, and the Appar Aikyam tradition at Thiru-Pugazhur, etc., take place during this Utsavam. On one day, Arulmigu Padaleeswarar proceeds to Vandipalayam, that is, to the Appar Swamy Kulam at Karaiyeravitta Kuppam, where a Theppa Vizha (float festival) is held. Thiru-Avaduthurai Adheenam Ilakkanam Chidambara Munivar has composed the “Sri Padaleeswarar Sthala Puranam” for this Sthalam. There is also a Kalambagam work for this Sthalam. A compilation of songs sung by many devotees, titled “Thiru-Padirippuliyur Thothira Koththu,” has also been published.

This temple is estimated to be about 1300 years old. Parantaka Cholan, Rajaraja I, Rajendra I, Rajendra II, Veerarajendra, Kulothunga I, Vikrama Cholan, and subsequently the Pallavas and Pandiyas, have maintained this temple by performing renovations and offering donations.

Here, Shiva bestows grace as a Swayambhu Murthi. Every Karthigai Monday, Angabhishekam and Kalasabhishekam are performed for the Lord.

Here, Shiva resides with a thousand arts.

Therefore, the Mother, who performed penance and worshipped Shiva and understood His mind, comes to the Palliyarai here. We saw that there is a Theertham called Sivakara Theertham here. This Sivakara is the place where Shiva, as a Siddhar, played and placed His hand, and it became the Sivakara Theertham. A part of the Ganga is mixed in it. It is special that this Theertham is in the Easana corner according to Vastu. This is the Sthalam worshipped by Vyagrapadar, the sage with tiger’s feet.

Therefore, this Sthalam is called Puliyur. The Padiri tree is the Sthala-Vriksham, hence it is called Padirippuliyur. Its Sthala-History is as follows: Once, the Lord, intending to perform a divine play for the salvation of the world, played a game of dice with the Goddess. Even after playing many times, Shiva was defeated, but He claimed that He had won. When He said this, the Goddess covered Shiva’s sacred eyes with her sacred hands. This caused the world to be plunged into darkness, and all activities ceased.

Seeing this, the Goddess, regretting the troubles caused by her action, sought forgiveness.

The Lord then told the Goddess to go to Bhuloka and worship the Shiva Sthalams there. He said that while she was worshipping, at whichever Sthalam her left eye and left shoulder twitched, He would take her as His own at that Sthalam.

Accordingly, the Goddess came here, visited many Sthalams, and when she arrived at Thiru-Padirippuliyur, her left eye and left shoulder twitched.

Therefore, this Thiru-Sthalam of Thiru-Padirippuliyur is the Sthalam where she stayed and worshipped the Lord in an formless state and received blessings. This is the Sthalam where the Lord, in the form of a Siddhar, removed the sufferings of the people. These are the Sthala-Visheshas of this Thiru-Sthalam of Thiru-Padirippuliyur.

Let us continue to contemplate the meaning of the Thiru-Padigam beginning with “Eentraalumai.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 323, Thiru-Nindra Charukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We briefly contemplated the Sthala-Visheshas of the Thiru-Sthalam called Thiru-Padirippuliyur.

Now, our Appar Peruman reached Thiru-Padirippuliyur and sang the Thevaram Thiru-Padigam beginning with “Eentraalumai” on the Lord enshrined there. We must contemplate the meaning of that Thiru-Padigam. This Thiru-Padigam sung by Appar Peruman is compiled as the ninety-fourth Thiru-Padigam of the Fourth Thiru-Murai, the Thiru-Padirippuliyur Thiru-Padigam.

Now, let us contemplate the meaning of this Thiru-Padigam.

The first verse: Eentraalumai enakku enthaiyumai udan thondrinarai moondraai ulagam padaithu ugandhaan. Manathul irukka entraan imaiyavarkku anban Thiru-Padirippuliyur thondraa thunaiyaai irunthanan than adiyongalukke. Its meaning is as follows: Shiva is enshrined in Thiru-Padirippuliyur. He is an unseen support to His devotees. Such a Lord is a support to me, being my mother, my father, and my sibling.

He created this world in three parts and rejoices. The Shiva, who is dear to the Devas, agreed to reside in my mind. This is the meaning of this song. He begins by singing, “Eentraalumai enakku enthaiyumai udan thondrinarai,” and by “Eentraalumai,” he begins this song by placing the mother first. As in “Annaiyum Pithaavum,” he places the mother first and then refers to the father as “Enthai.” “Eentraal” here refers to Sakthi, and “Enthai” (my father) refers to Shiva. By singing “Eentraalumai Enthaiyumai,” he means that Shiva is with His graceful power, with His grace.

Next, he sings “Udan thondrinarai” (my sibling). If “Udan thondrinar” here refers to Thilagavathi Ammaiyar, then if “Eentraalumai Enthaiyumai” (my mother and my father) refers to Pukazhanar, the father of our Navukkarasu Peruman, and Mathiniyar, his mother, according to worldly custom, they are considered a support.

But in truth, the only support is Shiva Himself.

Therefore, he sings that Shiva Himself is his mother, father, and sibling, and is his unseen support. According to worldly custom, there is a tendency to consider them as support.

But truly, the one who is a support is Shiva Himself.

Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sings that He is his mother, father, and sibling, and is his unseen support. Such a Shiva has created this world in three parts and rejoices. This world is referred to as “He, She, It” in the Siddhanta scriptures. Such a Shiva has consented and accepted to reside within my mind. It is a great act of compassion by Shiva that He has graciously allowed Himself to reside in my heart without concealment. Such a Lord, the Lord enshrined in Thiru-Padirippuliyur, is an unseen support to all beings.

He manifests to us, His devotees, and remains hidden in other places, supporting all beings.

Now, the second verse: Patraai ninainthida podhu nenje intha paarai matrum sutraai alai kadal moodinum kanden pugan namakku utraan umaiyavarkku anban Thiru-Padirippuliyur mutraamozhi mathi kanniyinaan than moygaley. Its meaning: In this song, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar addresses his heart, saying, “O heart, even if the ocean, which surrounds this entire world, comes and covers this world, the one who is our steadfast support is Shiva, who is in Thiru-Padirippuliyur. He is dear to Uma Devi and wears the crescent moon. I have realized that the dense sacred feet of such a Shiva are our refuge.

“Therefore, O good heart, always contemplate the sacred feet of such a Shiva as our support.” Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar advises his heart.

“Now, song number three: Vidaiyaan virumbi en ullaththu irunthaan ini namakku ingu adaiya avalam aruvinai saara namanaai anjom pudaiyaaar kamalaththayan polbavar Padirippuliyur udaiyaan adiyaar adi adiyongarkku ariyathundey. Its meaning is as follows: Thiru-Peruman, Lord Shiva, whose vehicle is the bull, lovingly resides within the heart of His devotees. Henceforth, no sorrows shall approach us, no evil deeds shall draw near, and we shall not fear the Lord of Death. In Thiru-Padiri-Puliyur, where Brahmins like Brahma reside and lotuses bloom on all four sides, Lord Shiva is enshrined. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar asks, “Is there any rare deed that is impossible for us, the humble servants of the devotees of that Lord Shiva?” Now, hymn number four: “Mayamellam utra vittiru neenga malaimake neyanilavirundaan avan than thiruvadikke theyamellam nindru irainjum Thiru-Padiri-Puliyur meya nallaan malarppatham en sindaiyul nindranave.” (All illusions have departed; the Lord, who is ever united with the Daughter of the Mountain, resides in Thiru-Padiri-Puliyur, where all lands bow before His sacred feet. The lotus feet of that good Lord, who abides there, remain within my thoughts.)

“The meaning of this is as follows: Lord Shiva is the one whose love is firmly established with Parvati, the Daughter of the Mountain. All the worlds come to worship at His sacred feet, and He lovingly resides in Thiru-Padiri-Puliyur. The lotus-like sacred feet of such a great being are permanently enshrined in my thoughts. Because of this, all illusion has completely vanished. He sings that the sacred feet of the Lord are firmly established within his thoughts, so that ego may depart. Hymn number five: “Vaitha porul namakkam endru solli manathadaithu sittam orukki Sivaya Nama endrirukkinallal moiththa kathirmathi polvar avar Padiri-Puliyur aththan arul peralamo arivila pedai nenje.” The meaning of this is as follows: His Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar addresses his mind, saying, “O ignorant mind, devoid of true understanding!

“The treasure that is our eternal reserve, our stored wealth, is Lord Shiva Himself. Meditate upon Him in your mind, focus your thoughts, and always chant the sacred five-letter mantra, ‘Sivaya Nama.’ If you do not thus focus your mind and chant ‘Sivaya Nama,’ how can you attain the grace of Lord Shiva, who resides in Thiru-Padiri-Puliyur?

“Therefore, O mind, always chant the sacred five-letter mantra, ‘Sivaya Nama.’” Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar advises his mind to remain in ‘Sivaya Nama.’ In common worldly parlance, elders would say, “Remain in Shiva.” Here, he says, “Remain in ‘Sivaya Nama.’” Elders would say, “Remain in Shiva.” Here, he says, “Remain in ‘Sivaya Nama.’” Indeed, in the Thiru-Pathigam known as “Sotrunaithunaiyan,” he structured the hymn to conclude with “Namashivaya” and sang that Thiru-Pathigam of Namashivaya. The “Namashivaya” mentioned there is the Sthula Panchaksharam.

“Here, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar addresses his mind, saying, “Remain in ‘Sivaya Nama.’” This is the Sukshma Panchaksharam. In the Thiru-Pathigam “Sotrunaithunaiyan,” he sang “Namashivaya,” and throughout the hymn, he sang “Nattrunaiyavathu Namashivaya.” But now, when speaking to the mind, when chanting in the mind, he considered “Sivaya Nama” as beginning with the letter ‘Si.’ This is the point here.

“Therefore, controlling the mind and unifying the consciousness, he says, “Remain in ‘Sivaya Nama.’” O mind,” thus he advises the mind in this fifth sacred hymn.

“We shall proceed with our contemplation.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 324, Thiru-Nindracharkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We contemplated the meaning of the fifth sacred hymn. In it, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar advised the mind to focus its thoughts, unify its consciousness, and remain in “Sivaya Nama.” Now, this is the sixth sacred hymn. In this too, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has sung, incorporating the sacred five-letter mantra “Sivaya Nama.” The sixth hymn is as follows: “Karuvayk kidanthun kazhale ninaiyum karuthu udaiyen uruvay thirindrunran namam payindren unatharulaal thiruvaypoliya Sivaya Nama endru neeru anindhen tharuvay Sivagathi nee Padiri-Puliyur arane.” He sings, “O Lord of Thiru-Padiri-Puliyur, O Lord of Thiru-Padiri-Puliyur! Even when I was in my mother’s womb, I was blessed to meditate upon Your sacred feet.

“Even after emerging from the womb and receiving a form, by Your grace, I have now learned to repeatedly utter Your sacred names after careful consideration. To make this mouth shine as a treasure, I chanted the sacred five-letter mantra and now wear the sacred ash.

“Therefore, grant me, Your servant, the auspicious path.” This is its meaning. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, who sang the sacred five-letter mantra “Sivaya Nama” in the fifth sacred hymn, has also sung the sacred five-letter mantra “Sivaya Nama” in this sixth sacred hymn. He sings, “Thiruvaypoliya Sivaya Nama endru neeru anindhen” (I wore the sacred ash, chanting “Sivaya Nama” to make my sacred mouth shine). He sings that the sacred ash itself is wealth, and as he applied that sacred ash, he uttered the sacred five-letter mantra “Sivaya Nama” to make his tongue shine. In the Thiru-Pathigam known as “Sotrunaithunaiyan,” he sang, “Navinukku arungalam Namashivayave” (The precious ornament for the tongue is Namashivaya).

“Similarly, here he sings, “Sivaya Nama endru neeru anindhen” (I wore the sacred ash, chanting “Sivaya Nama”). As we have already seen, in the Thiru-Pathigam “Sotrunaithunaiyan,” he bestowed upon us the Sthula Panchaksharam, which begins with the letter ‘Na’ as in “Namashivaya.” In this sacred hymn, he bestows upon us the Sukshma Panchaksharam, which begins with the letter ‘Si’ as in “Sivaya Nama.” The Maha Mantra known as Sri Panchaksharam, comprising the five sacred letters, is described in the Shiva Agamas as having five types, depending on the method of chanting, suitable for the maturity of the sadhakas (practitioners). According to the maturity of the sadhakas (practitioners), this Sri Panchaksharam is described in five ways in the Shiva Agamas. They are Sthula Panchaksharam, Sukshma Panchaksharam, Karana Panchaksharam, Maha Karana Panchaksharam, and Maha Manu. Among these, Sthula Panchaksharam is the sacred five-letter mantra “Namashivaya,” which begins with the letter ‘Na.’ Sukshma Panchaksharam is “Sivaya Nama,” which begins with the letter ‘Si,’ with ‘Nama’ coming after ‘Sivaya.’ Similarly, Karana Panchaksharam is “Sivaya Shiva,” Maha Karana Panchaksharam is “Shiva,” and Maha Manu is “Si.” These are the five types of Panchaksharam mentioned in the Shiva Agamas. In our Thiru-Murais, the Sthula Panchaksharam is mostly Predominantly featured.

“As we have already seen, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has bestowed the Namashivaya Thiru-Pathigam, which begins with “Sotrunaithunaiyan.” Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, in the Thiru-Pathigam that begins with “Kadhalagi Kasindhu,” sings, “Kadhalagi kasindhu kannir malki othuvardammai nannerikka uyppathuve Vedam nankilum meipporulavathu Nathan namam Namashivayave” (Those who chant with love, melting and shedding tears, are led to the good path; the true essence in all four Vedas is the Lord’s name, Namashivaya). Throughout that Thiru-Pathigam, he has sung, incorporating the Sthula Panchaksharam “Namashivaya.” Our Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, in the Thevara Thiru-Pathigam for the sacred sthalam of Thiru-Pandik-Kodumudi, has sung, incorporating “Indiya Namashivaya.” “Matra patru enakkinri nin thiruppathame manam pavithen petralum piranthen ini piravatha thanmai vandhu eithinen katravar thozhuthethum” In Seerkaraiyur, Thiru-Pandik-Kodumudi, “Nattrava unai naan marakkinum sollum naan Namashivayave” (O righteous one, even if I forget You, my tongue will utter Namashivaya).

“Thus begins this Namashivaya Thiru-Pathigam, bestowed by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal for the sacred sthalam of Thiru-Pandik-Kodumudi.

“Therefore, this is the Namashivaya Thiru-Pathigam, which includes the sacred mantra of Sthula Panchaksharam, “Namashivaya,” bestowed by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal.

“Now, in Thiru-Vasagam, Manickavasaga Peruman sings, “Potri om Namashivaya Puyangane mayangukindren Potri om Namashivaya pukalidam pirithu ondrillai Potri om Namashivaya puram ena pokkal kanday Potri om Namashivaya sayasaya potri potri” (Praise be to Namashivaya, O Lord with the serpent, I am bewildered. Praise be to Namashivaya, there is no other refuge. Praise be to Namashivaya, You have seen me as an outsider. Praise be to Namashivaya, victory, victory, praise, praise).

“Thus, he has sung, incorporating the Sthula Panchaksharam “Namashivaya.” In this way, in the Thiru-Murais, the Sthula Panchaksharam, “Namashivaya,” is predominantly found. Nevertheless, The Sukshma Panchaksharam, “Sivaya Nama,” is rarely bestowed by our great Acharyas in a very few places in the Pathigams. Why is it that the Sthula Panchaksharam, “Namashivaya,” is abundant, and the Sukshma Panchaksharam, “Sivaya Nama,” is found in very few places, bestowed by our great Acharyas? It is because the Sthula Panchaksharam, “Namashivaya,” is chanted with ‘Na’ at the beginning and ‘Ya’ at the end. It is taught by both the Bodhaka Acharya and the Sadhaka Acharya. It bestows benefits in this life and the next.

“It is suitable for all castes to chant.

“Therefore, our Samayacharyas have sung many Thiru-Pathigams incorporating “Namashivaya.” In “Namashivaya,” the letters ‘Na’ and ‘Ma’ at the beginning represent the bonds (pasam), and the letters ‘Si’ and ‘Va’ in the middle Represent the Lord (Pathi), and the final letter ‘Ya’ represents the soul (Pasu). This reveals the truth that the Lord is the one who activates both the unconscious (achith) in the form of bonds and the conscious (chith) in the form of the soul. This is the specialty of the Sthula Panchaksharam, “Namashivaya.” Here, when Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar was placed in the fiery chamber by the Jains, he sang the Pathigam “Masila Veenaiyum,” and in the second verse of that Pathigam, he sang, “Namashivayave Gnanamum Kalviyum” (Namashivaya is knowledge and education), incorporating “Namashivaya.” When our Nayanar was tied to a stone and cast into the sea, he sang the Namashivaya Thiru-Pathigam beginning with “Sotrunaithunaiyan.” Now, in Thiru-Padiri-Puliyur, in this Pathigam beginning with “Eendraalumai,” in the fifth and sixth sacred hymns, he has sung, incorporating “Sivaya Nama.” Our Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has sung the Panchaksharam. This Sukshma Panchaksharam, “Sivaya Nama,” is chanted with the letters ‘Si’ and ‘Va’ at the beginning, ‘Ya’ in the middle, and ‘Na’ and ‘Ma’ at the end. This is taught for the sake of liberation to those who have attained maturity through initiation, having regularly practiced the Sthula Panchaksharam.

“This Sukshma Panchaksharam, “Sivaya Nama,” if we carefully examine this sacred five-letter mantra, “Sivaya Nama,” we will understand that it stands in three parts. “Siva” is the first part, “Ya” is the second part, and “Nama” is the third part. In this, “Siva” represents the Lord (Pathi), “Ya” represents the soul (Pasu), and “Nama” represents the bonds (Pasam). The letter ‘Si’ in the first part represents Shiva, and the letter ‘Va’ represents His power of grace. The third The letter ‘Ma’ in the section represents the anava mala (ego), and the letter ‘Na’ represents the Tirodhana Shakti (concealing power). Maya and Karma act as instruments for the Tirodhana Shakti and are subservient to it.

“Therefore, Maya and Karma are contained within this Tirodhana Shakti, that is, they are contained within the letter ‘Na.’ Between the first part, “Siva,” and the third part, “Nama,” lies the letter ‘Ya.’ The letter ‘Ya’ represents the soul.

“Therefore, the soul, represented by ‘Ya,’ has the nature of standing with the bonds (pasam) that follow it and with the Lord (Pathi) in “Siva.” The “Siva” in the first part is Sat (Being), the “Nama” in the third part is Asat (Non-being). The soul, represented by ‘Ya,’ in the middle, is Sat-Asat (Being-Non-being).

“Therefore, this soul is on both sides, on the side of the bonds and It has the nature of being able to lean towards the side of the Lord. It takes on the color of whichever side it leans towards, thus acquiring the name Sat-Asat. This soul, represented by ‘Ya,’ is of such a nature. The soul, represented by ‘Ya,’ in the middle, is subject to the anava mala (ego) represented by ‘Ma’ behind it, immersed in ignorance, and driven by the Lord’s Tirodhana Shakti (concealing power) represented by ‘Na,’ associating with maya and karma, and immersed in worldly experience.

“Therefore, the two letters ‘Na’ and ‘Ma’ respectively represent the Sakala state and the Kevala state. The state where the soul is immersed in ‘Nama’ is the state of bondage. It is the bound state. The ‘Si’ and ‘Va’ that precede the soul ‘Ya’ are Shiva and His Shakti, who are like father and mother. That is, Lord Shiva and His inseparable sacred power of grace. This ‘Si’ (Shiva) and ‘Va’ (sacred power of grace) signify their inherent presence within the consciousness of the soul.

“Therefore, this ‘Si’ and ‘Va’ signify their presence as the Divine Mother and Father, mingled with the soul.

“Thus, the soul, instead of striving to perceive the Divine Mother and Father before it in its consciousness, only perceives and experiences the world that lies behind it, that is, it perceives and experiences ‘Nama.’ Thus, the pure state is when the soul abandons ‘Nama’ and takes refuge in ‘Va,’ the sacred grace. The sacred grace unites the soul with Shiva. The state of the soul being immersed in Shiva is the state of bliss.

“Thus, this Sukshma Panchaksharam, ‘Sivaya Nama,’ is the letter ‘Si.’ When spoken first, each letter signifies a subtle meaning, indicating that the soul must be freed from bonds and attain Shiva through grace.

“Therefore, it is called Sukshma Panchaksharam. In the Saiva Siddhanta tradition, the Sthula Panchaksharam, ‘Namashivaya,’ is taught in Samaya Diksha (initiation into the religion), and the Sukshma Panchaksharam, ‘Sivaya Nama,’ is taught in Vishesha Diksha (special initiation). Those who receive Vishesha Diksha, those who receive the teaching of ‘Sivaya Nama,’ must have, to some extent, renounced worldly attachments.

“Therefore, it is the tradition of the Shiva Agamas that those who are in the path of Charya (ritualistic worship) should utter the sacred five-letter mantra beginning with ‘Na,’ and those who are in the path of Kriya (devotional service) and Yoga should utter it beginning with ‘Si.’ Thus, this Sukshma Panchaksharam, ‘Sivaya Nama,’ is also known as ‘Oruthalai Manickam’ (the unique gem) and ‘Mukti Panchaksharam’ (the liberation Panchaksharam).

“Therefore, those who desire liberation should not utter ‘Namashivaya,’ Instead of chanting the Sthula Panchaksharam ‘Namashivaya,’ one should chant the Sukshma Panchaksharam ‘Sivaya Nama.’ When chanted thus, the letter ‘Va,’ which is grace, unites the soul with the letter ‘Si,’ which is the refuge of the soul, and immerses it in the ocean of bliss.

“Here, it is said that ‘Sivaya Nama’ should be chanted for liberation. Chanting here refers to meditating in the heart. The method of chanting mantras is of three types: Manasa, Manda, and Urai. Among these, Manasa is meditation by the mind, that is, thinking in the heart. Manda is chanting in a subtle, inaudible voice, audible only to oneself. The third, Urai, is chanting in a gross, audible voice, audible to oneself and others.

“Among these three, pure Manasa, which is thinking and contemplating with knowledge, is the most excellent.

“Therefore, when it comes to ‘Urai,’ chanting audibly to oneself and others, the ‘Manda’ method, chanting only to oneself, yields a thousand times more benefits. And the first method, chanting in the mind, yields millions of times more benefits than that. Such is the special, sound-producing Sukshma Panchaksharam, ‘Sivaya Nama.’ This Panchaksharam, as instructed by the Acharya, should be firmly impressed upon the heart and chanted, completely abandoning the gross dance of ‘Na’ and ‘Ma’ which leads to birth and death. Instead, one should embrace the dance of knowledge, ‘Si’ and ‘Va,’ and as the vast expanse of grace, ‘Va,’ increasingly manifests, one should even abandon the chanting as an internal thought and become immersed in it, losing the sense of individual self, becoming one with it. That grace, as ‘Si,’ It will immerse one in knowledge and make one stand in the form of pure consciousness. That alone is Parama Mukti, the Suddha Advaita Ananda Mukti.

“This is what Manickavasaga Peruman sings in Thiru-Vasagam: “Naneyo thavam seidhen Sivaya Nama ena petren” (Did I perform austerities? I received ‘Sivaya Nama’).

“Furthermore, in the Koyil Mootha Thiru-Pathigam, Manickavasaga Peruman sings: “Udaiyal undhan naduvirkum udaiyal naduvul neeyiruthi adiyen naduvul iruverum iruppathanal” (Because You are in the midst of Your devotees, and You are in the midst of Your devotees, and both of You are in my midst). However, all these experiential secrets must be learned by joining the sacred feet of Shiva Acharyas, surrendering to them, worshipping the Shiva Acharya, the Desika, in the proper manner, and understanding them through his teachings and the method of chanting. All these secrets must be taught by a qualified The Desika himself must teach; he alone is qualified to teach, and he alone has the right to teach according to the Shiva Agamas.

“Thus, the meanings of the Sthula Panchaksharam and Sukshma Panchaksharam, ‘Namashivaya’ and ‘Sivaya Nama,’ which we have seen, can be found in Saiva Siddhanta philosophical texts such as ‘Unmai Vilakkam’ and ‘Thiruvarutpayan.’ The Taittiriya Narayaniya also sings this: ‘Sivaya Namaha Sivalingaya Namaha.’ Thiru-Vasagam says, ‘Naneyo thavam seidhen Sivaya Nama enappatren’ (Did I perform austerities? I received ‘Sivaya Nama’). Thiru-Mandiram sings, ‘Thellamuthuvurach Sivaya Nama endru ullamuthuvura orusal uraithidum’ (Let the inner nectar flow, chanting ‘Sivaya Nama’ once). Avvai Pirattiyar sings, ‘Sivaya Nama endru sindhithu irupporku abayam orunalum illai’ (For those who meditate on ‘Sivaya Nama,’ there is no danger ever).

“Thus sings Avvai Pirattiyar. Such is the glory of the Sri Panchaksharam, the Sukshma Panchaksharam, ‘Sivaya Nama.’ If we expand further, the meanings will multiply.

“Therefore, we have briefly contemplated its meanings thus far. In this sacred sthalam of Thiru-Padiri-Puliyur, in the Pathigam beginning with ‘Eendraalumai,’ our Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has sung this Sukshma Panchaksharam, ‘Sivaya Nama,’ in the fifth sacred hymn as ‘Sittam orukki Sivaya Nama endru irukkin allal’ (Unless one focuses the mind and remains in ‘Sivaya Nama’), and in the sixth sacred hymn as ‘Thiruvaypoliya Sivaya Nama endru neeru anindhen’ (I wore the sacred ash, chanting ‘Sivaya Nama’ to make my sacred mouth shine).

“We will continue to contemplate the seventh sacred hymn.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 325, Thirunindrachcharukkam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We are contemplating the meaning of the hymns of the Thiruppathiripuliyur Thirthalam, beginning with “Eendraalumai.” So far, we have contemplated the meaning of six hymns.

Now, the seventh hymn: “Ennaathu amarar irakka paravaiyul nanjai undaay thirunnaar asurar thiripuram theeyazhach chettravane pannaarnthu amaintha porulgal payil paathiripuliyur kannaar nuthalaay kalanam karuththil udaiyanave.” Its meaning is as follows: The Devas churned the ocean of milk for nectar, but they did so without first meditating on You. As a result, poison emerged from the ocean.

Then, the immortals, upon entreating You, consumed the poison and protected the immortals, O Lord Shiva! You are the one who destroyed the three fortresses of the mighty Asuras, the Tripuras. O Lord with the eye on Your forehead, who resides in Pathiripuliyur, where beautiful musical hymns resonate, Your sacred feet are in our hearts, he sings.

Now, the next hymn, the eighth hymn: “Puzhuvaay pirakkinum punniyaa unnadi en manaththai vazhuvaathu irukka varam thara vendum ivvaiyakaththae thozhuvaarkku irangi irunthu arul sey paathiripuliyur sezhuneer punal gangai senjadai mel vaiththa theevannane.” This is the eighth sacred hymn, well-known to most devotees. This is an imperishable sacred hymn. Thirunavukkarasar Peruman sings to the Lord of Thiruppathiripuliyur. O Lord Shiva, who resides in Thiruppathiripuliyur, showing compassion and bestowing grace upon devotees in this world! O Lord Shiva, who holds the Ganges water in Your red matted hair! O Lord with a fiery red hue!

Even if I am born as a worm in my next birth, I pray that Your sacred feet, which are the embodiment of virtue, will never leave my mind. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sings in this hymn, “Even if I am born as a worm, Your sacred feet should always be in my mind. I should always be meditating on Your sacred feet. You should grant me such a boon.” So sings Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar.

Therefore, no matter what birth one takes, one should not forget the Lord; one should serve the Lord. This is Thirunavukkarasar Nayanar’s plea here. He asks the Lord for a boon: even if he is born as a worm, he should not forget His sacred feet. For those born as humans, what their next birth will be is unknowable. Now we have obtained human birth; we do not know what birth will come next.

Therefore, he asks for such a boon. “Even if I am born as a worm” means “even if I take any birth.” So, whether I am born as a worm or in any other birth, in any body, I should always be meditating on Your sacred feet. You should grant me such a boon, he prays to the Lord of Thiruppathiripuliyur. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar makes this plea to the Lord of Thiruppathiripuliyur. If one asks whether it is permissible to make such requests to the Lord, Manikkavasagar Peruman sings in Thiruvachakam, in Kuzhaiththapattu: “You know what creatures need; You grant all that they ask for. You are unknown to Brahma and Vishnu, yet You willingly enslaved me.

“Whatever You graciously bestow, that alone I desire. If there is anything else I desire, that too is Your will.” The Lord knows what creatures need.

“Therefore, You know what creatures need, and You will grant whatever they ask for.

“Thus, You willingly made me Your slave. Henceforth, whatever You graciously bestow upon me, that alone I shall desire.

“Therefore, if there is anything I desire from now on, that too is only the love I have for You. So, Manikkavasagar Peruman sings here, “I now desire only the love I have for You.” It is a rule not to ask for boons from the Lord. Although Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar was a complete renunciate, he would ask for some boons. This is one of the very few boons Thirunavukkarasar asked of the Lord: that in whatever birth he takes, His sacred feet should remain in his mind. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar asks the Lord for only a few such boons. Nevertheless, the goal of all those boons is one and the same, namely, It is certain that death will come to people.

“When dying, one needs the boon to remember and utter Shiva’s name.

“Then, in whatever birth comes, one must not forget Shiva.

“After that, in subsequent births, Lord Shiva must bestow His grace. This is the one goal that underlies all the boons Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar asked for. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar has sung, “Thunjum pothu nin naamam thiru ezhuthu anjum thondra arulum aiyaraare.” Furthermore, “Thunjum pothaaga vanthu thunai enakku aagi nindru anjal endru arula vendum aavadu thuraiyulaane,” and “Saathal naal naayen unnai engutraay endra pothaa ingutraen en kandaaye,” and “Saam andru urai Karuthi kandaa engal sangarane” and “Unnai ninainthe kazhiyum en aavi kazhinthathan pin ennai marakkap peraa em piraan unnai venduvathe” and “Irappan iranthaal iru visumbu eruvan erivanthu pirappan piranthal pira ani vaar sadai pingyakan per marappan kolo endru en ullam kidanthu marugidume” - all these Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar has sung in his Thevarams. All these illustrate the heartfelt thoughts of our Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar. The Nayanar asks this boon for himself. In the hymn beginning “Ponnaar thiruvadikku ondru undu vinnappam,” in that song, he asks the Lord, “Engrave the three-pronged trident upon me.”

“He asks the Lord, “Engrave the bull upon me and accept me.” He asks, “Anoint me with sacred ash.” He asks the Lord for the boon, “Engrave Your flower-like footprints upon me.” All these were asked of the Lord for himself by Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar. “Nin thal saran endrem palippaarkkarku irangukandaay” he sang in Pasupathi Thiruviruttam; those lines and similar ones were asked for the devotees. We too should strive and practice to ask for boons in this manner. This song, beginning “Puzhuvaay pirakkinum,” is familiar to all devotees and is recited by many devotees daily as a prayer to the Lord. Among the hymns recited and chanted, this is one. If one asks whether even a worm can possess the quality of not forgetting the sacred feet, it is one of the tenets of Saiva Siddhanta that all types of creatures are capable of worshipping the Lord and attaining blessings.

“Furthermore, in this hymn, the Lord of Thiruppathiripuliyur is a Lord who shows compassion and bestows grace upon those who come and worship Him.

“Therefore, this hymn is structured as a plea.

“Now, the next hymn, hymn number nine: “Man paathalam pukku maal kadal moodi matreazhulagum vinpaal thisai kettiru sudar veezhinum anjal nenje thinpaan namakku ondru kandhom thiruppathiripuliyur kanpaavu netrik kadavul sudaraan kadal inaiye.” Its meaning is as follows: Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sings to his heart, O heart, even if this world plunges into the netherworld due to an earthquake, the ocean floods the earth, the other seven worlds scatter from their celestial positions, and the sun and moon fall from their fixed abodes, do not fear, O heart! We know that the firm support of the sacred feet of the Lord with the eye on His forehead, who resides in Thiruppathiripuliyur, and who is the radiant light, is our protection.

“Therefore, do not fear anything, O heart, sings Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar.

“Now, the tenth sacred hymn: “Thirunthaa amarar than thee neri pattu thigaiththu muththi tharum thal inaikke saranam pugunthen varaiyeduththa porunthaa varakkanudan eriththaay paathu Irunthaay adiyen ini piravaamal vanthu endru kolle.” This is the tenth hymn, and its meaning is as follows: O You who crushed the body of Ravana, who tried to uproot Mount Kailash! O You who reside in Thiruppathiripuliyur! Having been bewildered and entangled in the evil path of the unrepentant Jains, I have now sought refuge in You. I have taken refuge at Your sacred feet, which grant liberation. Henceforth, accept me so that I may not be born again. In this tenth sacred hymn, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar makes this plea to the Lord.

“Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar makes a plea to the Lord in this tenth concluding hymn, asking for the boon of not being born again.

“Now, even if I am to be born again due to the remaining karma, Even if I am to be born as a worm in that birth, I pray for the ability to not forget You in that birth, he asked earlier.

“Now, in this tenth hymn, he asks for freedom from rebirth.

“Similarly, in the Puranam of Karaikkal Ammaiyar, the boon Karaikkal Ammaiyar asked for is also structured thus: “I desire freedom from rebirth; if there is rebirth again, I desire never to forget You.” When Karaikkal Ammaiyar asks this, it comes to our mind here. When listening to this tenth sacred hymn of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, it comes to our mind. This is the first sacred hymn sung by Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar after he completely triumphed over the bonds of other religions and embraced Shiva’s feet.

“Therefore, this sacred hymn shines with the unique glory of teaching many truths of Saiva Siddhanta This sacred hymn possesses the greatness of being structured to ferry souls across the ocean of birth. Sivakavimani mentions how the truths of Saiva Siddhanta are explained in this sacred hymn. In the first sacred hymn, it says, “Moondraay ulagam padaiththu ugandaan.” This explains the concept found in the first sutra of Sivagnana Bodham: “Avan aval athu enum avai muvinaiyamil thotriyathithiye odungiya malarthu ulatham antham aathi ennaar pulavar.” The second sacred hymn, structured as a plea, “Moigale patraay ninainthida pothu nenje,” explains the truth of the eighth sutra of Sivagnana Bodham: “Tham muthal guruvaay thavaththinil unarththivittu anniya inmaiyin arankazhal selume.” The fifth sacred hymn, “Vaiththa porul namakkaam endru solli manaththadaiththu siththam orukki sivaaya nama endru irukkinallaal aththan arul peralaamo,” and the ideas of the sixth hymn, “Kazhale ninaiyum karuththudaiyen un naamam payindren sivaaya nama endru thiruneeru aninthen,” also convey the meaning of the ninth sutra of Sivagnana Bodham, “Vithi ennum anjaluthe.” It is also conveyed here that there is no other support for souls besides the five letters, as understood through the grace of the Guru, and that one then practiced accordingly. We should also consider that these hymns are located in the middle of this sacred hymn. The fourth sacred hymn, “Maayamellam utra vittu irul neenga thiruvadikke theya nilaava malarpaatham en sinthaiyul nindranave,” explains The fourth sacred hymn, “Ekanagi irai pani nirka mala maayai thannodu valvinai indre” from the tenth sutra of Sivagnana Bodham, explains the state of anubhuti.

“The seventh sacred hymn, “Kalanam karuththil udaiyanave,” and the eighth sacred hymn, “Puzhuvaay pirakkinum punniyaa unnadi en manaththai valuvaathu irukka varam thara vendum,” and the tenth sacred hymn, “Adiyen ini piravaamai vanthu endru kolle,” all describe the nature of the experiential state found in the eleventh sutra of Sivagnana Bodham, “Kaana ullaththai kandu kaattalin ayara anbin aran kazhal selume.” The third sacred hymn, “Udaiyaan adiyaar adi adiyongatkku ariyathu unde,” explains the state of Jivanmukti and teaches the truth of the twelfth sutra of Sivagnana Bodham, the twelfth One must understand that it teaches the truth of the second sutra. It is for us to see and attain salvation through these truths that the author of Periya Puranam, Sekkizhar Peruman, sang here, clarifying the path of grace, saying, “He adorned with his Tamil garlands.” The path of grace is the path of the Sivagamas bestowed by Lord Shiva. It is the path that unites one with Shiva’s grace, the divine grace.

“Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sang the sacred hymn beginning “Eendraalumai” on the Lord of Thiruppathiripuliyur. We shall continue our contemplation.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 326, Thirunindrachcharukkam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We saw that Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal, having been saved in Thiruppathiripuliyur, sang the sacred hymn beginning “Eendraalumai enakku enthaiyumai” to the Lord of Thiruppathiripuliyur. We also saw the explanations of the meanings of the hymns in that sacred hymn.

In this manner, Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal stayed in that holy place and sang many such rich Tamil garlands. The other sacred hymns sung in this manner are not available to us now; they are lost. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, who was staying in Thiruppathiripuliyur, then desired to worship the sacred feet of Thiruvathigai Veerattaneeswarar. As this desire arose in him, he decided to go to Thiruvathigai, the holy place where the Veerattaneeswarar temple is located.

The Lord enshrined in Thiruvathigai Veerattaneeswaram is the victorious one who destroyed the three cities (Tripura). He is the Lord who protects those who seek refuge in Him.

Here, He is the victorious Lord who saved and accepted Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, who sought refuge in Him, from the Jains. As Thirunavukkarasar contemplated the benevolence of Thiruvathigai Veerattaneeswarar, who protected him from the Jains and took him as His own, his desire to see Thiruvathigai Veerattaneeswarar grew. Having accepted Thilakavathiyar as his Guru to guide him to the Lord, and responding to her plea, Thiruvathigai Veerattaneeswarar, the primordial Guru, bestowed His grace, imprinted the divine power of the trident, drew him to Himself, and made him His own, inspiring him to sing the Tamil garlands known as Thevaram.

Therefore, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar’s desire to see Him grew. Such a Lord Shiva, that Veerattaneeswarar, resides eternally and with pleasure in the holy place called Thiruvathigai. It is a place where He has resided from a certain time and never left, always choosing to remain. That holy place, Thiruvathigai, is a place that grants life to those who reach it. As the desire to worship Thiruvathigai Veerattaneeswarar grew, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman Thirunavukkarasu Peruman began his pilgrimage from Thiruppathiripuliyur to Thiruvathigai Veerattanam. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, who started from Thiruppathiripuliyur, visited and worshipped the holy places of Thirumanikkuzhi and Thiruthinaingar.

On the way from Thiruppathiripuliyur to Thiruvathigai, there are the holy places of Thirumanikkuzhi and Thiruthinaingar.

Therefore, although Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar went with a great desire to reach Thiruvathigai, he followed the custom of visiting and worshipping these holy places found along the way. It is a rule that a person undertaking a pilgrimage to a specific temple should visit other holy places along the way.

Therefore, following that rule of pilgrimage, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, on his way to Thiruvathigai, visited and worshipped the Lord with garlands of words (Thevarams) at the holy places of Thirumanikkuzhi and Thiruthinaingar. We have already seen the greatness of these holy places, Thirumanikkuzhi and Thiruthinaingar, in the Puranam of Thaduththaatkonda. We have contemplated the special features and greatness of these places in the section where Sundaramurthy Swamigal, on his pilgrimage to Thiruchitrambalam, visited these two holy places along the way. The Thevarams sung by Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar for these holy places, Thirumanikkuzhi and Thiruthinaingar, are not currently available to us.

Thus, after visiting these two holy places, he proceeds to the holy place of Thiruvathigai. Along the way, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar crosses many flower gardens. He crosses many gardens filled with blooming flowers and reaches the rich Thirukedila River. The Thirukedila River is a river flowing in Thiruvathigai. It is the rich Thirukedila, meaning it possesses the wealth that creates true Saivite prosperity. Like the Ganges, it is the Thirukedila that has the nature of creating true Saivite prosperity.

Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar crosses the holy Kedila River and reaches the holy place of Thiruvathigai. So that all the evil and cruel deeds committed by the Jains would cease, Having triumphed over the Jains and arrived at Thiruvathigai Veerattanam, this sweet Tamil king’s arrival in Thiruvathigai is met with great joy, enthusiasm, and acclamation by all the residents of Thiruvathigai. They welcome and honor Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar. The news of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar’s arrival at Thiruvathigai Veerattanam is announced through drums, making this auspicious news known throughout the town. They rejoice that Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, who sang sweet Tamil, has arrived. “Sweet Tamil” means Tamil that brings sweetness to life.

The Thevarams sung by Thirunavukkarasu Peruman always bring joy to lives and endure.

Moreover, without harming enemies, but protecting us from them, it acts as a fortress and brings joy. All the people living in Thiru-Athigai welcome Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, who sang such Thevaram Tamil. On that great day when Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal arrived, those who were blessed there were truly fortunate. Those who lived in Thiru-Athigai city at that time were blessed with the great fortune of welcoming Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, our Samayachariyar. To welcome Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, they erected long festoons. They tied banana trees with areca nut clusters as festoons.

They adorned all the gopurams with beautiful garlands. They decorate the gopuram of Thiru-Veerattanam. Not only that, but all along the path where Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar is to come, they set up decorative gopurams and adorn them with highly luminous gems. They smear red paste on the ground and on platforms. The city, which is naturally beautiful, now appears even more beautiful.

Now, with auspicious sounds, many people gather throughout the city and decorate it in this manner. As Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar thus arrives in Thiru-Athigai city, the men and women there welcome him with great joy. They make sweet sounds of various kinds. They produce auspicious sounds from various instruments such as flutes and drums. Women make sounds of the seven notes. They scatter turmeric-mixed fragrant powder, paddy, puffed rice, and flowers all along the path where Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar is coming.

Scattering turmeric-mixed fragrant powder, paddy, puffed rice, and flowers is one of the auspicious traditions. It is our tradition to welcome great people who come to our town from the very entrance of the town, from the beginning of the city. In the previous Puranam of Thaduthatkonda, we saw that the residents of Thiruvarur city welcomed Sundaramoorthy Swamigal from the very boundary of Thiruvarur city. Just as we saw that they escorted him, here too, they welcome Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar from the boundary of Thiru-Athigai city and lead him into Thiru-Athigai city.

We shall go on reflecting. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Three Hundred and Twenty-Seven, Thiru-Nindra Charukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman arrives at Thiru-Athigai city, at the sacred site of Thiru-Athigai.

At that time, Sekkizhar Peruman describes the sacred appearance of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman in his song. The one thousand four hundred and fifth song, the one hundred and fortieth song in Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar’s Puranam, is composed as follows: “Thooya venniru thuthaintha pon meniyum thazh vadamum Nayagan sevadi thaivaru sinthaiyum nainthorugi Paivadhu pol anbu neer pozhi kannum padhiga senchol Meya sevvaiyum udaiyar pugundhanar veedhiyulle.” How is the sacred appearance of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman? He has a pure, white sacred ash abundantly applied to his golden body, adorned with Rudraksha garlands. He possesses a mind that caresses the sacred feet of Lord Shiva, his soul’s master. His eyes, melting with devotion, continuously shed tears of love as if overflowing. He has a sacred mouth that utters the perfect words of the Thevaram hymns.

Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar thus enters the sacred street of Thiru-Veerattanam in Thiru-Athigai. This sacred verse, when Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar entered the sacred street of Thiru-Athigai, depicts the sacred form of the Nayanar and his inner and outer states as if a painter were to paint them. Sekkizhar Swamigal brings it before our eyes, as if to say that no one could paint it so wonderfully. He sings, “Thooya venniru thuthaintha pon meniyum,” meaning pure white sacred ash. “Venniru” means pure white ash, sacred ash. Only pure white sacred ash is fit to be worn.

It should be understood as “Thooya venniru,” that is, sacred ash that purifies. It also implies that the sacred ash is not placed in places where it should not be, and that it is free from impure substances. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has adorned his sacred body with such pure sacred ash. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar possesses a golden body adorned with such pure sacred ash. “Thuthaiyal” means to be abundant and overflowing. The sacred utterance is, “He smeared much sacred ash.” As pure sacred ash and tears of love flow abundantly on Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar’s sacred body, the Nayanar’s body is adorned with the sediment of tears and sacred ash.

The Nayanar’s sacred body is referred to here as a golden body, which signifies its color, beauty, and preciousness. He wears a Rudraksha garland, a “Thazhvadham,” on his sacred body. The author, who described his golden body, eyes, and sacred mouth, only mentions in this verse that he wears a Rudraksha garland, a “Thazhvadham.” Therefore, the rule is to wear Rudraksha garlands on the head, neck, shoulders, chest, hands, and other places.

Thus, we see here that our Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar presents a sacred vision, adorned with Rudraksha garlands on his head, sacred neck, sacred shoulders, sacred chest, and hands. The word “Thazhvadham” appears, and “Thazhthal” also has the meaning of desiring.

Thus, the first line, “Thooya venniru thuthaintha pon meniyum thazh vadamum,” paints a picture of the Nayanar’s sacred body for us.

Now, Sekkizhar Swamigal sings about how his mind is: “Nayagan sevadi thaivaru sinthaiyum,” he sings. “Thaivarudhal” means to gently caress, to gently stroke. It is stated here that he possesses a mind that gently caresses the sacred feet of Lord Shiva, his master. By referring to Lord Shiva as “Nayagan,” it implies that a devotee should contemplate the sacred feet of Lord Shiva with a state of mind similar to a beloved gently caressing the feet of her master.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar possesses a mind that gently caresses the sacred feet of Lord Shiva. The Nayanar’s sacred heart is always contemplating the sacred feet of Lord Shiva, that is the meaning here. Great souls who have transcended the tattvas and tattvikas of this world and attained Shivattva, Lord Shiva will manifest in their intellect. All their senses, like grass thrown into a salt pan, lose their individual consciousness and become illuminated by Shiva’s consciousness. As stated in the twelfth sutra of Sivagnanabodham, “By making their intellect, thus transformed, know itself through the contemplation of ‘Shivoham,’ and by giving its own form to know itself, and by dwelling within itself to know itself,” and as interpreted in the commentary on the twelfth sutra of Sivagnanabodham, “By making that devotee know himself through the contemplation of ‘Shivoham,‘” the mind that stands in service to the Lord as one with Him, focused solely on the Lord’s grace, is the mind of great souls who have attained Shivattva. “The senses that perceive all become supreme bliss, and the devotees who cherish it,” says Thiruvasagam.

Accordingly, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar possesses a mind that always gently caresses the sacred feet of Lord Shiva in his contemplation. Swamigal sings, “Nayagan sevadi thaivaru sinthaiyum.” Now he sings, “Nainthu urugi paivadhu pol anbu neer pozhi kannum.” Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar’s mind is melted and dissolved, and therefore, tears of love continuously flow from his sacred eyes. Due to the abundance of the Nayanar’s love, that love melts and seems to flow out through his eyes.

Therefore, he is with eyes that shed tears as if the water of love springs from within and continuously flows out through his eyes. “Marpare pozhi kannir mazhai varum thiruvadivum” is a sacred utterance. Tears flow from the eyes due to various reasons such as sorrow and worry, but Sekkizhar Swamigal sings here, “Anbu neer pozhi,” to make us understand that this is not such tears, separating it from those. “Is there a latch to contain love?” asks the Thiru-Kural. Sekkizhar Swamigal continues to sing, “Padhiga senchol meya sevvai.” From the speech of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, garlands of Thevaram hymns continuously emanate. All that comes from his sacred mouth are “senchol,” words that bestow upon us the perfect Shiva.

Therefore, that mouth, the source of such “senchol,” is referred to here as “sevvai,” the sacred mouth. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has sung in Thiru-Anga Malai, “May my mouth praise.” In his Thiru-Padhigam, “Maasil Veenaiyum,” he has sung, “The Lord who gave me a mouth to praise, a mind to contemplate, and a head to bow.” As he sang thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar possessed that sacred mouth which always uttered praises. A mouth that does not always praise Lord Shiva would not be called a sacred mouth.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, possessing a golden body adorned with pure sacred ash, a Rudraksha garland, a mind that caresses the sacred feet of the Lord, eyes that shed tears of love as if overflowing from a melted heart, and a sacred mouth that utters perfect hymns, entered the sacred streets of Thiru-Athigai. Sekkizhar Peruman sings of such Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar as “Em Udaiyar.” “Udaiyar” means our Lord, our master. “Neyam malindhavar vedamum” is from the third adhikaranam of the twelfth sutra of Sivagnanabodham, where it is taught what those who have associated with Shivagnanis should do thereafter. In this twelfth sutra, Madhava Sivagnana Yogigal, who wrote the commentary, states in his Maha Bhashyam, “Now, worship the sacred form of the devotee and the Shiva temple as Parameshwaran.” He said that the sacred form of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar shines as the best example for the term “sacred form.” Sekkizhar Peruman describes the nature of such a sacred form in this sacred verse. The same sacred form is described in the two hundred and seventieth sacred verse of Thiru-Gnanasambandhar Puranam: “Unceasing love in the mind, movement in the sacred body, the thought that a loincloth is sufficient, a hoe in hand, tears flowing like rain, and the sacred ash adorning the form, the boundless sacred form of the king.” Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman sings of the sacred appearance of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. The twelfth sutra of Sivagnanabodham states that such a sacred form and a Shiva temple should be worshipped as Shiva.

Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, possessing such a sacred appearance, walks through the streets of Thiru-Athigai. All the common people who see him fold their hands and worship him. Seeing him, who appears as if compassion itself has taken form, how could those Jains have inflicted such harm upon him? Seeing this compassionate appearance of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, how did anger arise in those Jains? How did anger come to them, they wonder. Those who saw Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar there, those who saw the Nayanar’s sacred form when he entered the sacred street, spoke among themselves.

Even after seeing this compassionate form of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, the Jains became angry and even inflicted harm upon him. They wonder how those Jain ascetics could have had such a mind; it is truly astonishing. They saw Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar as the very embodiment of compassion. They say that he was not just an embodiment of compassion, but compassion itself, the quality of compassion walking. When people see such a compassionate form, anger does not arise; only love blossoms. This is a natural characteristic even for evil people and fierce animals.

Yet, even after seeing this compassionate form, the Jains committed cruel acts. Even though the Jains inflicted harm in this manner, our Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar was protected and given to us by Lord Shiva.

Thus, the people there continuously praise Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar and Lord Shiva.

In this way, countless people speak and praise. All the groups of devotees shining in the radiant form of sacred ash accompany Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. It is customary to distinguish between the general public and the devotees of Shiva in this way. The help rendered to the general public is categorized as “pasu punyam” (merit for the soul), and as a result of this “pasu punyam,” benefits such as heaven are obtained, which again leads to rebirth.

However, the services rendered to the devotees of Shiva are categorized as “pathi punyam” (merit for the Lord), and the gnana shastras state that these services lead to the cessation of rebirth.

Thus, both the general public and the devotees adorned with sacred ash accompany Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar.

In this way, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, who has attained the state of Jivanmukta filled with Shivattva and become Shiva, enters the temple of Veerattaneswarar at Thiru-Athigai. There, he enters the temple and worships his Lord, the Lord of all gods. Lord Shiva, enshrined in the Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam temple, protected the devas by destroying the three cities. As the Lord of the devas, Lord Shiva merely smiled a little without them doing anything, and burned the three cities.

Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar worships Lord Shiva, the Lord of the devas, who is the master of such devas. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar worships Lord Shiva, who is his master.

The Lord who bestowed the colic disease and enslaved him, the Lord who resides in Thiru-Athigai, for such a Lord, he is immersed in the love that is born of trust and melts there. The love placed on Lord Shiva is a trusting love, that is, love done with the belief that Lord Shiva is the master and will protect us. That is why the Lord is called “Nambar” (one who is trusted). That love is an unending blissful love. As that love overflows and intensifies, it becomes a desire, and as it matures, it grows into a profound love. As that love matures, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar is immersed in Shivanantham.

Thus, he comes and worships Lord Shiva of Thiru-Athigai. Having worshipped Lord Shiva in this manner, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar bestows the Thiru-Thandagam hymn called “Ezhai Thiru-Thandagam” here.

We shall continue our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Three Hundred and Twenty-Eight, Thiru-Nindra Charukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar comes to the sacred site of Thiru-Athigai and, seeing Veerattaneswarar, sings the Thiru-Padhigam called “Ezhai Thiru-Thandagam.” Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar is currently visiting the sacred site of Thiru-Athigai for the second time. The first time, he came with colic disease, received sacred ash from Thilagavathi Ammaiyar, abandoned Jainism, embraced Shaivism, and was blessed with the removal of his colic disease by singing a Thiru-Padhigam on Thiru-Athigai Veerattaneswarar. That was the first time.

Now, he has come to Thiru-Athigai for the second time. On this second visit, he sings the Thiru-Padhigam called “Ezhai Thiru-Thandagam.” This “Ezhai Thiru-Thandagam” consists of eleven sacred verses. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has bestowed this Thiru-Thandagam hymn, with each sacred verse ending with “Ezhaiyen naan pandu igazhndhavare.” “Ezhai” here means foolishness in knowledge. Each verse ends with “Ezhaiyen naan pandu igazhndhavare,” does it not? “Ezhai” here refers to foolishness in knowledge.

“Pandu” refers to the long period before he was afflicted with colic disease and taken into service.

Thus, he was in the Jain religion for a long time before the colic disease, and during that time, he listened to the words of the Jains and reviled the Lord. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar now laments having previously reviled the Lord and therefore sings this Thiru-Pathikam.

Thus, at the end of each Thiru-Pathikam, he sings, “Why did I, a wretch, revile Him before?” He grieves that even though he reviled the Lord for a long time, the Lord bestowed upon him the sacred grace of the colic disease and enslaved him, and this Thiru-Pathikam is structured to recall that divine compassion. The first time he came before the Lord, he arrived with colic.

At that time, to sever the delusion and the disease, he sang the Thiru-Pathikam “Kootraayina Vaaru Vilakkagaleer” and was cured of the colic.

Now, for the second time, again, when Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar stood before Thiru-Vathikai Veerattaaneswarar, such thoughts arose in his sacred heart: even though he had forgotten the Lord, remained in the Samana faith, and reviled the Lord, Shiva-Peruman bestowed upon him the grace-filled colic disease, removed him from Samanam, drew him to His sacred presence, and enslaved him.
