After this, even when the Samanas placed Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar in a fiery chamber, fed him poisoned milk-rice, unleashed a killer elephant upon him, and cast him into the sea bound to a stone, in all those times of suffering, the Lord stood by him, protected him, saved him from those perils, and drew him back to His sacred presence. Thiru-Vathikai Shiva-Peruman, who thus bestowed grace, is Shiva-Peruman. The thought, “I, listening to the words of the Samanas when I was in the Samana faith, reviled His great compassion and such great dignity of Shiva-Peruman,” deeply impressed Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar’s sacred heart and caused him great remorse.

Therefore, with such remorse, he sang and praised this Thiru-Pathikam, the Ezhai Thiru-Thandakam. As Sekkizhar Peruman sings here, “He lived, proclaiming the pure Tamil of Thiru-Thandakam with his remorse, saying, ‘I, a wretch, reviled my Peruman before, the Lord who is the King of the celestials and the Master of all.’” means they attained salvation. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, realizing his past error, grieved and praised the Lord with devotion.

Therefore, all his degradation was removed, and the suffering from the Samanas would no longer occur in any way, and he lived. This is the meaning. Due to ignorance, having listened to the words of the Samanas before, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, with deep remorse, composed this Ezhai Thiru-Thandakam, saying, “What a sin it was that I, a wretch, reviled our Peruman!” This is the second Thiru-Pathikam among the Thiru-Thandakam Thiru-Pathikams composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. Since each verse concludes with “Ezhaiye naan pandu igazhndhavaare” (I, a wretch, reviled Him before), it is known as Ezhai Thiru-Thandakam. His previous reviling of the Lord, having listened to the words of the Samanas, and how, even though he reviled Him, the Lord did not abandon him but swiftly came, removed his suffering, and bestowed grace, and the degradation of the Samanas’ ways, are described in the fifth, seventh, eighth, tenth, and eleventh Thiru-Paadals. In the other Thiru-Paadals, he speaks of the Lord’s greatness and laments, “Alas, I, unknowingly, reviled such a great and dignified being!” Now, this Ezhai Thiru-Thandakam Thiru-Pathikam is compiled as the third Thiru-Pathikam in the Sixth Thiru-Murai among the twelve Thiru-Muraigal.

Veriviravu koovizhanal thongalaanai veerattaththaanai vellerrinaanaip poriyaravinaanaip pullurthiyaanaip ponniraththinaanaip pugazhthakkaanaai Aritharkariya seer ammaanthannai athiyaraiyamangai amarnthaanthannai erikedila thaanai iraivan thannai ezhaiye naan pandu igazhndhavaare. (I, a wretch, reviled Him before, the Lord of rare glory, who resides in Thiru-Athigai Mangai, the Lord of the fiery Kedilam, the Lord who rides a white bull, who wears a spotted serpent, who rides a bird, who is golden-hued, and worthy of praise.) Velli kundranna vidaiyaan thannai vilvalaan vilvattangaayndhaan thannai pulli vari naagam poondaandannai pon pithirntha sadaiyaan thannai valli valai thol muthalvan thannai vaaraa ulagarula vallaan thannai ezhuga vidu pichai yerpaan thannai ezhaiye naan pandu igazhndhavaare. (I, a wretch, reviled Him before, who rides a bull like a silver mountain, who destroyed the bow of Manmatha, who wears a spotted serpent, who has golden matted locks, who is the primal one with a crescent moon and a deer, who can bestow the world of no return, who accepts alms.) Munthiyulagam padaiththaan thannai moovaa muthal thannai santha ven thingal aninthaan thannai thavanerigal saathikka vallaan thannai sinthaiyil theervinaiyai thenai paalai sezhungedila veerattam mevinaane enthai perumaanai eesan thannai ezhaiye naan pandu igazhndhavaare. (I, a wretch, reviled Him before, who created the world first, who is the ageless primal being, who wears the cool white moon, who can accomplish paths of penance, who is honey and milk to the mind’s karma, who resides in the fertile Kedilam Veerattam, my Father, the Lord, the Ruler.) Manthiramum maraipporulum aanaan thannai mathiyamum nyaayirum kaatrum theeyum malai kadalum aanaan thannai athiyaraiyamangai amarnthaan thannai kantharuvam seythiruvar kadal kai kooppi kadimalargal pala thoovi kaalai maalai inthiranum vaanavarum thozhachchelvaanai ezhaiye naan pandu igazhndhavaare. (I, a wretch, reviled Him before, who became the mantra and the secret meaning, who became the moon, the sun, the wind, the fire, the sky, the mountains, and the seas, who resides in Thiru-Athigai Mangai, whom the two Gandharvas, with folded hands, offering many fragrant flowers, morning and evening, Indra and the celestials worship.) Oru pirappilaan adiyai unarnthum kaanaar uyar kathikku vazhi thedi poga maattaar varu pirappondrunaraathu maasu poosi vazhi kaanaathavar polvar manaththanaagi aru pirappai arruppikkum athikai ooran ammaanthann adiyai anainthu vaazhaathu iru pirappum veruviyaraay irunthaar solkettu ezhaiye naan pandu igazhndhavaare. (I, a wretch, reviled Him before, having listened to the words of those who, though they do not perceive the feet of the unborn, do not seek the path to higher liberation, who, not realizing the futility of rebirth, smear themselves with dirt and are like those who cannot find the way, and whose minds are like theirs, and who, not embracing the feet of the Lord of Thiru-Athigai, who cuts off the cycle of birth, lived in vain for both births.) Aaretrka valla sadaiyaan thannai anjanam polum midatrraan thannai kooretrka kooramara vallaan thannai kolvalaikaai maatharaal paagan thannai neeretrka poosum agalaththaanai ninma thannai nimalan thannai eeretrka eerumaavallaan thannai ezhaiye naan pandu igazhndhavaare. (I, a wretch, reviled Him before, who has matted locks that can hold the Ganga, whose throat is like collyrium, who can stand as the sharpest, who is the half of the woman with bangled hands, who smears sacred ash on His broad chest, who is pure, who is blemishless, who can ride a bull.) Kundakka naay ulanru kaiyil undu kuvimulaiyaar thammunne naanam indri undiyuganthamane nindraar solkettu udanaagiyoli thanthaen unarvondru indri vandulavu kondrayang kanniyaanai thisaikkum moorthiyaay nindraan thannai ezhaiye naan pandu igazhndhavaare. (I, a wretch, reviled Him before, having listened to the words of those who, like dogs, wander and eat with their hands, shamelessly standing before women with full breasts, and having been with them and given them light without understanding, the Lord who wears the garland of konrai flowers where bees hum, who stands as the deity for all directions.) Uri mudiththa kundigai than kaiyil thookki ooththai vaay samanaarkor kundakka naay kariviravu neychchoru kaiyil kandaarkku pollaatha kaatchiyaanen marithirai nirppavva nanjundaandannai marithorukkaal valvinaiyai ninaikka maatten erikedila naadar perumaan thannai ezhaiye naan pandu igazhndhavaare. (I, a wretch, reviled Him before, who, carrying a water pot with a sling, was like a dog to the foul-mouthed Samanas, and who, eating ghee-mixed rice with his hand, became an unpleasant sight to behold, the Lord who drank the ocean’s poison with its surging waves; I will not think of evil deeds again, the Lord of the land of fiery Kedilam.) Niraivaarntha neermaiyaay nindraan thannai netri mel kannondru udaiyaan thannai maraiyaanai maasondru ilathaan thannai vaanavar mel malaradiyai vaiththaan thannai karaiyaanai kaathaar kuzhaiyaan thannai kattangam enthia kaiyeenaanai iraiyaanai enthai perumaan thannai ezhaiye naan pandu igazhndhavaare. (I, a wretch, reviled Him before, who stands with perfect nature, who has an eye on His forehead, who is the Vedas, who is blemishless, who placed His flower-like feet on the celestials, who is the shore, who wears earrings, who holds a skull-staff, who is the Lord, my Father, the Master.) Thollai vaan soozhvinai soozha poonthu thoottriyen aatriyen sudaraay nindru vallaiye idaththeerththungku adimai konda vaanavarkkum thaanavarkkum perumaan thannai kollai vaay kurunthosiththuk kozhalum oothum kovalanum naan muganum koodi engum ellai kaanpariyaanai emmaan thannai ezhaiye naan pandu igazhndhavaare. (I, a wretch, reviled Him before, who, having been surrounded by ancient karmic bonds, I endured and became a light, the Lord who enslaved the celestials and the demons, who broke the kuruntha tree in the pasture and played the flute, whom Kovalan and Naanmugan together could not find the limits of anywhere, our Lord.) Mulai maraikkappattu neeraada pengal murai muraiyaal nam theyvamendru theendi thalai parikkum thanmaiyargalaagi nindru thavameyanravam seythu thakkathoraar malai marikkach chendra ilangai konai mathanazhiya setra sevadiyinaanaai ilai mariththa kondrayan thaaraan thannai ezhaiye naan pandu igazhndhavaare. (I, a wretch, reviled Him before, who, when women bathed with breasts covered, touched Him in turn as ‘our deity,’ and who, standing as those who pluck their hair, performed penance that was not penance and did not achieve what was proper, whose sacred feet crushed the pride of the King of Lanka who went to lift the mountain, who wears the garland of konrai leaves.) This is the Ezhai Thiru-Thandakam sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal.

We will continue to contemplate the meaning of its eleven sacred verses. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 329. Thiru-Nindra Charukkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We have seen the Ezhai Thiru-Thandakam sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar in Thiru-Vathikai. Let us contemplate its meaning.

The first sacred verse of this Thiru-Pathikam is: Veriviravu koovizhanal thongalaanai veerattaththaanai vellerrinaanaip poriyaravinaanaip pullurthiyaanaip ponniraththinaanaip pugazhthakkaanaai aritharkariya seer ammaanthannai athiyaraiyamangai amarnthaanthannai erikedila thaanai iraivan thannai ezhaiye naan pandu igazhndhavaare. Its explanation is as follows: The Kedilam river is a river with surging waves. On the banks of the Kedilam river, Shiva-Peruman, our Lord, appears adorned with a fragrant Vilva garland inside Thiru-Vathikai Veerattaaneswaram. He is Rishabhaakan, the one who rides the bull. He is Vishnu, and He is Brahma. He is the one who is within Vishnu and Brahma and makes them function.

He is worthy of praise that brings merit. He is the Lord whose greatness is difficult for even the enlightened to comprehend. He is the one who graciously resides in the sacred place called Thiru-Athigai Mangai. In this first verse, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings, expressing regret for his past actions: “It is regrettable that I, an ignorant person, in the early part of my life, did not worship such a great Lord but instead reviled Him. I repent for that.” In this sacred verse, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has sung that Shiva-Peruman Himself is Vishnu and Brahma. He has sung that Shiva-Peruman is Vishnu, who rides the Garuda, and Brahma, who is golden-hued.

Shiva-Peruman, it is stated in Sivagnana Siddhiyar, graciously assumes the nine forms known as Navam Tharu Bhedam. These nine forms—Sivam, Sakthi, Naatham, Bindu, Sadashivam, Maheswaran, Rudran, Thiru-Maal, Ayan—appear sequentially, one from another. All these are called Navam Tharu Bhedam. Among these, Sivam, Sakthi, Naatham, and Bindu, the first four, are formless divine bodies. Sadashivam, in the middle, is a form-and-formless divine body. Maheswaran, Rudran, Vishnu, and Brahma, the four, are embodied divine forms.

Thus, Sivagnana Siddhiyar states that the Lord alone graciously assumes these nine forms.

Therefore, here, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings that Shiva-Peruman Himself is Brahma and Vishnu.

Now, the second verse: Velli kundrenna vidaiyaan thannai vilvalaan vilvattam kaayndhaan thannai pulli vari naagam poondaandannai pon pithirntha sadaiyaan thannai valli valaiththol muthalvan thannai vaaraa ulagu arul arulavallaan thannai elkavidu pichai yerpaan thannai ezhaiye naan pandu igazhndhavaare. Its meaning is as follows: Shiva-Peruman alone can bestow liberation, the supreme liberation where there is no need for rebirth. He has a bull as His vehicle, like a silver mountain. Shiva-Peruman is the one who angered Manmatha, who held a bow. He is the one who wears a spotted and striped serpent as an ornament. He has reddish matted locks.

He is the primal one who wears a crescent moon and a deer. He is the Lord who accepts alms. I, a wretch, reviled such a Lord before. I regret that, he sings.

Now, the third verse: Munthi ulagam padaiththaan thannai moovaa muthalaaya moorthi thannai santha ven thingal aninthaan thannai thava nerigal saathikka vallaan thannai sinthaiyil theer vinaiyai thenai paalai sezhungedila veerattam mevinaane enthai perumaanai eesan thannai ezhaiye naan pandu igazhndhavaare. Its meaning is as follows: Shiva-Peruman is my Father, the Lord, who graciously resides in the fertile Kedilam river-flowing Thiru-Vathikai Veerattam. He is the ruler of all. He is the primal being that is never destroyed. He is the one who created the worlds first. He is the one who wears the beautiful white crescent moon and enables devotees to accomplish the path of penance.

He is sweet like honey and milk to the karma of actions performed by the mind and other instruments. I, when I was in the Samana faith before, reviled such a Lord. I regret that, he sings.

Now, the fourth sacred verse: Manthiramum maraipporulum aanaan thannai mathiyamum nyaayirum kaatrum theeyum antharamum malai kadalum aanaan thannai athiyaraiyamangai amarnthaan thannai kantharuvam seythiruvar kazhal kai kooppi kadimalargal pala thoovi kaalai maalai inthiranum vaanavarum thozha chelvaanai ezhaiye naan pandu igazhndhavar. The two Gandharvas, with folded hands, singing Samagana, praise Shiva-Peruman. They offer fragrant flowers at Shiva-Peruman’s sacred feet. These two Gandharvas, Ashvatharan and Kambalan, performed penance, praying to Shiva-Peruman, and asked for the boon to reside as earrings in Shiva-Peruman’s sacred ears, singing so that their music would reach His sacred ears.

The Lord graciously granted it. They continue to delight Shiva-Peruman by singing in His sacred ears. I worship such a Shiva-Peruman, who appears simply for Indra and other celestials to worship. Shiva-Peruman is the Vedic mantra and its meaning. He is the moon, the sun, the wind, the fire, the sky, and the ocean with its waves, standing within them and making them function. He graciously resides in the sacred place called Thiru-Athigai Mangai.

I, a wretch, spoke ill of such a Lord in the past. I regret that. Verse number five: Oru pirappilaan adiyai unarnthum kaanaar uyar kathikku vazhi thedi poga maattaar varu pirappondru unaraathu maasu poosi vazhi kaanaathavar polvar manaththanaagi aru pirappai arruppikkum athikai ooran ammaanthann adiyinaiye anainthu vaazhaathu iru pirappum veruviyaraay irunthaar solkettu ezhaiye naan pandu igazhndhavaare.

Here, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar recalls his past state when he joined the Samana faith and acted according to the words of the Samanas. He also sings about the nature of the Samanas here. The Samanas are those who do not even think of the sacred feet of Shiva-Peruman, the great one who is unborn.

Therefore, they do not seek the path to attain higher liberation and do not lead their lives on that path. The Samanas are those who do not understand the cause of the continuous cycle of birth. The Samanas are like those who smear dirt on their bodies and are blind in their inner eye. I acted with a mind like that of such Samanas. In the past, I performed actions that were useless for both this world and the next. Having listened to the words of those Samanas as instruction, I, a wretch, did not take refuge in the sacred feet of the Lord of Thiru-Vathikai Veerattam, who completely removes the terrible cycle of birth, and instead reviled that Lord.

I regret that, he sings. Verse number six: Aaretrka valla sadaiyaan thannai anjanam polum midatrraan thannai kooretrka kooramara vallaan thannai kol valai kai maatharaal paagan thannai neeretrka poosum agalaththaanai nirmalan thannai nimalan thannai eeretrka eerumaavallaan thannai ezhaiye naan pandu igazhndhavaare. Shiva-Peruman has matted locks that can contain the Ganga. He has a throat as black as collyrium. He is capable of being the support for all things. He is capable of pervading as knowledge, both subtly and grossly, within and without.

He is the one who has a part of Parvati Devi, who wears bangles on her hands. He has a broad chest smeared with sacred ash. He is pure and removes the impurities of others. That is, he explains the meanings of the words Nimalan and Nirmalan here. Nimalan means Shiva-Peruman is naturally free from all bonds. Nirmalan means He removes the impurities of living beings.

Such a Shiva-Peruman comes on a bull as His vehicle. I, a wretch, reviled such a Lord before. That is regrettable, he sings.

Now, verse number seven: Kundakka naay ulanru kaiyil undu kuvi mulaiyaar thammunne naanam indri undi yuganthamane nindraar solkettu udanaagi uli thanthaen unarvondru indri vandulavu kondrayang kanniyaanai vaanavargal yetrappaduvaan thannai en thisaikkum moorthiyaay nindraan thannai ezhaiye naan pandu igazhndhavaare.

Here, after speaking about the Samanas, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman speaks of the Lord’s glory. The Samanas are ignorant. They stand shamelessly naked even in front of women. Samana ascetics have the habit of eating food received in their hands while standing. I, without any understanding, associated with them and gave them light, having listened to the words of such people. I, a wretch, reviled Shiva-Peruman, our Lord, who wears a garland of konrai flowers where bees hum, who is praised by the celestials, and who stands as the Lord for all eight directions, having listened to the words of the Samanas.

He sings with regret.

Now, verse number eight: Uri mudiththa kundigai tham kaiyil thookki ooththai vaay samanaarkor kundakka naay kariviravu neychchoru kaiyil undu kandaarkku pollaatha kaatchiyaanen marithirai neer pavv Thirunavukkarasu Peruman recounts the glory of the Lord, lamenting that he had previously scorned Lord Shiva, the master of all directions, adorned with a garland of Konrai flowers frequented by bees, and praised by the Devas. He regrets having been misled by the words of the Jain ascetics, who are described as shameless, even in the presence of women, and who consume food from their hands while standing. He then sings, in verse number eight: “Urimuḍitta kuṇṭikai tam kaiyil tūkki ūttai vāy samaṇarkōr kuṇṭākkanāy kariviravu neyccōṟu kaiyil uṇṭu kaṇṭārkku pollāta kāṭciyāṉēṉ maritirai nīr pav” (Carrying the water-pot with a sling in their hands, I became a rogue among the foul-mouthed Jains, eating ghee-mixed rice from my hand, a sight unpleasant to behold, amidst the surging waves of the sea). I, a humble one, once scorned the Lord of Thirukedila, who swallowed the poison from the ocean. I will not think of the Lord who consumed poison and destroyed the mighty karma.

Here, he sings about the Jains, disparaging them. The Jains have foul mouths, carry a pot of gruel tied in a sling, and are brutish. They eat rice mixed with ghee and charcoal, holding it in their hands, a sight repulsive to onlookers. I, who associated with such Jains, once scorned Lord Shiva. I, a sinner, listened to the words of the Jains and scorned my Lord, the Lord of the land through which the surging Kedila River flows, who consumed the poison that arose from the ocean. My family has worshipped Lord Shiva for generations.

Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar laments, “How could I have scorned Lord Shiva, forgetting my family’s tradition and failing to follow it, by listening to the Jains?” This is the ninth verse. “Niraivaarndha neermaiyaay nindran thannai netrimel kan ondru udaiyaan thannai maraiyaanai maasu ondru ilaadaan thannai vaanavar mel malaradiyai vaithaan thannai karaiyaanai kaadhaar kuzhaiyaan thannai kattangam endhiya kaiyinaanai iraiyaanai endhai perumaan thannai ezhaiye naan pandu igazhndhavaare.” Its meaning is as follows: My father, Lord Shiva, resides in everyone’s heart. He is perfect and complete, without blemish. He has an eye on his forehead. He is the embodiment of the Vedas, without any impurity. He placed his sacred feet upon the heads of the celestials.

He has poison in his throat. He has sacred ears adorned with ear-rings. He holds a weapon called Kattangam in his hand. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar laments, “How could I, a humble one, have scorned such a Lord in the past?” Now, the tenth sacred verse: “Thollai vaan soozhvinaigal soozhapposthu thootriyen aatriyen sudaraay nindru vallaiye idar theerthu ingu adimai konda vaanuvarkkum thaanavarkkum perumaan thannai kollai vaay kurunthosithu kuzhalum oothum kovalanum naanmuganum koodiyum ellaikkaan pariyaanai emmaan thannai ezhaiye naan pandu igazhndhavaare.” In this verse, he sings about how Lord Shiva stood as a pillar of fire, making it impossible for Thirumal and Brahma to find his head and feet, even after searching.

Here, when describing Thirumal, he sings about how Thirumal was born into a cowherd family, played the flute, and captivated the cowherd girls by returning their clothes after they had bathed. He sings about Thirumal, who incarnated as such a cowherd. Our Lord Shiva stood as a pillar of fire, making it impossible for both Thirumal and Brahma, despite their utmost efforts, to find the limits of his head and feet. He is the Lord of the Devas and Asuras, and my Lord forever. Because ancient evil karmas surrounded me, I went astray and spoke many disparaging words about Lord Shiva. Yet, He stood as the knowledge within my intellect, swiftly cured my colic disease, and took me as His own.

Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar laments, “How could I have scorned such a Lord in the past?” Verse eleven: “Mulaimaraikkappattu neer.” The Jain ascetics, who bathe without covering themselves, consider it their duty to pluck their hair by hand, believing it to be penance. They perform unrighteous acts, adhering to their own doctrines, unable to discern what is right. There are also female ascetics in the Jain religion who do not bathe to remove dirt, but only wear clothes to cover their nakedness. These Jain female ascetics perform inappropriate acts in the name of penance, and I, associating with such Jain ascetics, once scorned Lord Shiva. Lord Shiva, whose red feet tormented Ravana, who tried to uproot Mount Kailash when it obstructed the path of his Pushpaka Vimana, and who wears a garland of Konrai flowers, showed me grace and compassion even though I scorned Him.

Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar laments in this eleventh verse, “How could I have scorned such a Lord in the past?” Thus, we have contemplated the meaning of the eleven sacred verses of this ‘Ezhai Thiruththandakam’. Our contemplation continues. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 330, Thirunindrachcharukkam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We contemplated the meaning of the ‘Ezhai Thiruththandakam’ sung by Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar in Thiruvathikai. Sekkizhar Swamigal continues to sing that the great Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sang many beautiful Tamil songs and performed sacred service in Thiruvathikai. Lord Shiva, enshrined in Thiruvathikai, is unknowable to Thirumal and Brahma, but easily accessible to His devotees. He is unknowable to the great Devas, yet easily accessible to His devotees.

He is difficult for those who approach with arrogance to perceive, but easily reveals Himself to those who surrender to Him. Such a Lord Shiva, the effulgent one, is enshrined in Thiruvathikai Veerattanam, surrounded by flowing waters. ‘Viripunnal’ here refers to the Kedila River. In this sacred place of Thiruvathikai, the Kedila River flows widely and merges with the nearby ocean, hence it is called ‘Viripunnal’.

Thus, Lord Shiva, who is enshrined in Thiruvathikai Veerattanam, is praised by Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar with many beautiful Tamil songs. Who is Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar? He is a great and unknowable personality. The greatness of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar is discernible only to true jnanis. The Jains, through their falsehoods, inflicted immense harm upon Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar. Yet, he did not become angry with them.

We can also understand the greatness of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar from the history of Appoothi Adigal.

Thus, through the history of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, we come to know a certain extent of his greatness. However, the true greatness of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar is indeed something that can only be perceived by jnanis. Such a Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, with a heart full of compassion, sang many beautiful Tamil songs and praised Thiruvathikai Veerattaneswarar. As love overflowed in the heart of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, those many songs arose.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Swamigal here refers to them as ‘Parivuru Senthamizh Paattu’ (songs of compassionate beautiful Tamil). Even today, the Thevara Thiruppathigams of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar cause love to well up in the hearts of those who learn them, the love for Lord Shiva. He bestows such sacred Tamil hymns, the Thevara Thiruppathigams, which cause love to well up.

Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar bestows the Thevara Thiruppathigams, singing of the Lord who is unknowable, yet simple, and the nectar.

At this time, the hymns sung by Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar on Thiruvathikai Veerattaneswarar are thirteen in number. These are the total hymns bestowed by Thirunavukkarasu Peruman on the sacred place of Thiruvathikai. Among them, the first hymn, ‘Kootraayina Vaaru’, was sung when Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar suffered from colic. Next is the hymn ‘Sunnavan Santhana Saanthum’, and then the hymn ‘Ezhai Thiruththandakam’. We have seen these three hymns so far.

At this time, Sekkizhar Peruman mentions that he sang many Thevara Thiruppathigams, and we should understand that to be thirteen Thiruppathigams.

Thus, a total of sixteen Thiruppathigams for this sacred place of Thiruvathikai Veerattanam.

Now, among the thirteen hymns sung by Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, ‘Kedila Vaanar’ is one Thiruppathigam. ‘Koonan Mathi Ettu Naan Malar’ are two Thirukkurunthogai hymns. ‘Irumbu Koppulitha Vennila Mathiyam’, ‘Nambane Engal Kove’, ‘Madakkinar Puliyin Tholai’, ‘Munbelam Ilaiya Kaalam’ are five Thirunerisai hymns. ‘Maasil Olvaal Pol’ is one Thiruviruttham. And ‘Adaiyaala Thiruththandakam’, ‘Potri Thiruththandakam’, ‘Thiruvadi Thiruththandakam’, ‘Kaappu Thiruththandakam’ are four Thiruththandagams.

Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar now bestows a total of thirteen Thiruppathigams. As I mentioned earlier, including the three hymns we previously discussed, Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal bestowed a total of sixteen hymns on Thiruvathikai Veerattanam. Although the Thiruththandakam ‘Naamaarkkum Kudiyallom’ was sung in Thiruvathikai, it is revered as a general Thiruppathigam.

Therefore, when Sekkizhar Swamigal states in this verse, ‘Parivuru Senthamizh Paattu Pala Paadi’ (singing many compassionate Tamil songs), it refers to the thirteen hymns we have already seen. While bestowing these Thiruppathigams, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar also performed the ‘Ulavara Thiruppani’ (physical service) in the sacred place of Thiruvathikai. That Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sang and performed service is known from his own words, ‘En Kadan Pani Seithu Kidappathe’ (My duty is to serve and remain).

Thus, the Nayanar, who sang these thirteen Thiruppathigams at this time, later embarked on a pilgrimage and visited many sacred places from here. Before we delve into that continuous history, let us look at the thirteen Thiruppathigams the Nayanar sang at this time. The first of these Thiruppathigams is dedicated to Thiruvathikai Veerattanam and is called ‘Thirukedila Vana Thiruppathigam’. Its ‘Pan’ (melody) is Kantharam. This Thiruppathigam begins with ‘Mulaikkathir Ilampirai’. It is compiled as the tenth Thiruppathigam in the fourth Thirumurai.

Now, that Thiruppathigam: Seyya pon kilai tholi thondridum Kedilavaanare. Erinar erinai ezhai thannoru koorinar koorinar vedam angamum aarinaraaridai sadaiyar pakkamum keerina udaiyinar Kedilavaanare. Vidanthigal kezhutharu midatra vellai neer udambala kezhuthuvar muzhuvathum vennila padanthala kezhutharu sadaiyil paayppunal kidanthala ezhuthiya Kedilavaanare. Velumaniyalaiyar ambu vaiyathor kozhumani nedumalai kozhuvi kottinar sezhumanimeedattrinar seyyar vaiyathor kezhumaniaaravinar Kedilavaanare. Kuzhuvinar thozhuthezhum adiyar melvinai thazhuvina kazhuvar pavalameyniyar mazhuvinar maanmari kaiyar mangaiyai kezhuvinayokinar Kedilavaanare. Angaiyil eri endhiyarum mangaiyai sadaiyadai mana.

Parumaalvarai nangaiyai paagamoo nayapparthen thisai gangaiyai thenappadum Kedilavaanare. Kazhindhavar thalai kalan endhi kaadurai thizhindhavar oruvar ezhuga vaazhbavar vizhindhili maathu karam milatra mandhigal kizhithathai nookar tharum kidandha paambarugu kandarivai pedhoora kidandha paambavalaiyor mayilandraiyura kidandha neer sadai meesai piraiyum engave. Idandhuthaan aguthalai Kedilavaanare. Veriyuru veeri sadai purala veesiyor poriyuru puliyuri araiyathagavum neriyuru kuzhalumai paagamagavum giri pada uli tharvar Kedilavaanare. Poonda therakkanai poruvil maalvarai thoondutholavai pada adartha thaalinar eendu neer kamalavaay medhi paay thara keenduthen soori tharum Kedilavaanare.

This is the first of the thirteen Thiruppathigams currently sung by Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, known as ‘Thirukedila Vaanar Thiruppathigam’. Because the name ‘Kedila Vaanar’ appears in every verse of this Thiruppathigam, it is called ‘Thirukedila Vaanar Thiruppathigam’. Let us contemplate its meaning briefly. The first verse: “Mulaikkathir ilampirai moozhga vella neer valaithazhu sadaiyinar mazhalai veenaiyar thilaithathor maan mari kaiyar seyya pon kilaith thuli thondridum Kedilavaanare.” The Lord, who is pleased to reside on the banks of the Kedila River, where red gold appears just by digging the earth, has matted locks that hold the Ganga floodwaters, causing the crescent moon with its rays to be submerged. He plays the sweet Veena.

He holds a joyful deer in his hand. He appears to the eyes of his devotees.

Now, the second verse: “Eriner erinai ezhai thannoru koorinar koorinar vedam angamum aarinaraaridai sadaiyar pakkamum keerina udaiyinar Kedilavaanare.” Lord Shiva, the Kedilavaanar, has a bull as his vehicle. He is the consort of Parvati. He taught the four Vedas and their six angas to his devotees. He has matted locks where the Ganga resides. He wears torn clothes.

Here, ‘torn clothes’ refers to the deer, tiger, and elephant skins he wears. The third sacred verse: “Vadam thigazh kezhutharumidatra vellai neer udambazhagezhuthuvar muzhuthum vennila padarnthazhagezhutharu sadaiyil paayppunal kidanthazhagezhuthiya Kedilavaanare.” Its meaning: Lord Shiva, the Kedilavaanar, whose matted locks are adorned by the flowing Ganga, where the white light of the crescent moon spreads beautifully, is the blue-throated one, adorned with the mark of poison. He beautifully smears sacred ash all over his body. The fourth verse: “Vizhumani iyal eyir ambu veyyathor kozhumani nedumalai kozhuvi kottinar sezhumanimidattrinar seyya veyyathor kezhumaniaaravinar Kedilavaanare.” Lord Shiva, the Kedilavaanar, bent the desirable great gem-studded Meru mountain as his bow, and the gem-studded serpent as its string, to shoot arrows with sharp teeth. He is the blue-throated one, adorned with fierce, red, gem-studded serpents as ornaments.

Now, verse five: “Kuzhuvinar thozhuthalum adiyaar mel vinai thazhuvina kazhuvavar pavalame.” He removes all future karmas from his devotees. He has a coral-like red body. He holds an axe and a deer in his hands. He is the consort of Parvati, yet remains in yoga. Although he has Parvati as one half of his body, the verse states he is a yogi.

This means that Lord Shiva, as a yogi, helps beings attain yogic liberation, and as a bhogi (enjoyer), he nourishes them. Verse six: “Angaiyil analari endhi aaru enum mangaiyai sadaiyidai manappar maalvarai nangaiyai paagamum nayappar thenthisai gangai athu enappadum Kedilavaane.” The Ganga of the South, the Lord who resides in Veerattanam on the banks of the Kedila River, which is revered as such, holds fire in his palm and has embraced the maiden Ganga in his matted locks. He lovingly accepts Parvati as one part of his sacred body.

Now, verse seven: “Kazhindhavar thalai kalan endhi kaadu urainthu ezhindhavar oruvar endru ezhuga vaazhbavar tharum Thiruvathigalil keezhe irangugindrana. Avvaaru vandugal olikka ivvaaru ozhugum thenai pen kurangugal arungugindrana. Iththagaiya valamikka Thiruvathigaiyil kizhi.” Lord Shiva, the Kedilavaanar, lives in such a way that the ignorant mock him, saying he holds the skull of the dead as a begging bowl and resides in the cremation ground, being of a low state.

Now, verse eight: “Kidandha paambarugu kandar ivai pedhoora kidandha paambavalaiyor mayil endru aiyura kidandha neer sadai misai piraiyum iyangave kidandhuthaan aguthalai Kedilavaanare.” A snake lies on Lord Shiva’s chest. Seeing this snake near her, Goddess Parvati faints. The snake doubts if the Goddess is a peacock. Even the crescent moon on the Lord’s matted locks is distressed upon seeing the snake. The Kedilavaanar, who holds a laughing skull in his hand, witnesses all this. This verse is a very beautiful and delightful one, a dramatic one.

The scene depicted here is that Lord Shiva wears a snake on his sacred body. Seeing this snake, Goddess Parvati, who occupies half of Lord Shiva’s sacred body, faints and is afraid upon seeing the snake on Lord Shiva’s chest.

But the snake is afraid of Goddess Parvati, who resembles a peacock, because a peacock is an enemy of a snake, isn’t it? A snake is afraid of a peacock.

Therefore, the snake on Lord Shiva’s sacred body is afraid of Umayammaiyar, who is green like a peacock, with a dark blue body. But seeing this same snake, the moon on Lord Shiva’s matted locks is afraid, because the moon has Rahu and Ketu as its enemies. The moon, fearing snakes, is terrified upon seeing the snake adorning Lord Shiva’s sacred chest. Witnessing all these scenes, which resemble a dramatic play, the skull in Lord Shiva’s hand laughs. Is not Lord Shiva the one who holds the skull of Brahma? That skull, the kapala, laughs at this sight.

Such is Lord Shiva, the Lord of Thiru-Kedila, who holds that skull in His hand.

Now, hymn number nine: “Veriyoruvirichadai puralaveesiyor poriyaru puliyuri arayathagavum neriyuru kuzhal umai bhagamagavum giripada ulithar avar Kedilavanare.” Its meaning: The Lord of Thiru-Kedila, with fragrant, flowing matted locks, shakes His head, wearing a spotted tiger skin around His waist, with Uma Devi, whose hair is curly, as a part of His sacred body, performs a very subtle dance of illusion.

Now, the tenth hymn: “Poonda ther arakkanai poruvin mal varai thoonduthol avai pada adartha thalinar eendu neer kamalavai methi pai thara keendu then soritharum Kedilavanare.” Its meaning: The Lord of Thiru-Kedila, who resides in Thiru-Athigai, where buffaloes leap into lotus-filled waters, tearing the petals and causing honey to flow, is praised as the one whose sacred feet crushed the shoulders of Ravana, who once drove the Pushpaka Vimana and attempted to uproot Mount Kailash.

Thus, we have contemplated the ten sacred hymns of this Thiru-Pathigam. We shall continue our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 331. Thiru-Nindra-Charukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Sekkizhar Swamigal sings that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has presently composed thirteen Thiru-Pathigams at the sacred Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam. When viewed alongside the history of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, he had already composed three Thiru-Pathigams.

Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar composed a total of sixteen Thiru-Pathigams for the sacred Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam. Among these, we have already examined three Thiru-Pathigams in the context of the Nayanar’s history. Of the remaining thirteen Thiru-Pathigams, we have contemplated the Thiru-Pathigam beginning with “Mulaikkathir Ilampirai” and its meaning.

Therefore, we must contemplate the remaining twelve Thiru-Pathigams. The second Thiru-Pathigam, a Thiru-Kurunthogai, begins with “Konan Ma Mathi Soodiyor.” This Thiru-Pathigam is compiled as the fifty-third Thiru-Pathigam in the fifth Thiru-Murai. This Thiru-Pathigam is structured as an Akathurai song, a devotional poem in the Akathurai genre. In Tamil literature, there is a genre called Akathurai, which describes the hero and heroine. This Thiru-Pathigam was composed when the heroine, separated from her hero, was unable to bear the separation and suffered from sleeplessness.

This Thiru-Pathigam states that her eyes will only find sleep if she sees the Lord, who resides in Thiru-Veerattanam. Will her eyes find sleep without seeing Him? They will only find sleep after seeing Him, meaning, the heroine will find solace. The verses of this Thiru-Pathigam are structured as the heroine lamenting, thinking of Thiru-Veerattaneswarar, her hero.

Now, this Thiru-Pathigam.

The first verse: “Konan mamathi soodiyor kovanam nanil vazhkai nayanthum payanilai panil veenai payindravan veerattam kanin allathu en kan thuyil kollume.” In this verse, the heroine sings, thinking of Thiru-Veerattaneswarar, her hero. Lord Shiva, who resides in Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam, wears the crescent moon. He prefers to wear a loincloth.

Lord Shiva is skilled in playing the Veena. The heroine sings that her eyes will only find sleep after seeing and worshipping Thiru-Athigai Veerattam, where such a Lord Shiva resides. The heroine sings that her eyes will find sleep.

Here, the heroine sings that Lord Shiva is skilled in playing the Veena. “Kangalaraai varum kadan meela nindru emmirai nal veenai vasikkume” is the sacred utterance of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar in another Thiru-Pathigam. “Veyuru thozhippangan vidamunda kandan miga nalla veenai thadavi” is the sacred utterance of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman.

Therefore, the image of Lord Shiva playing the Veena is mentioned in many places in the Thevarams. In the creation of the world, during the time of creation, the Nada Tattva that emanates from the Lord is metaphorically referred to as the Veena.

Therefore, in this first verse, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, in the mood of a nayaki (heroine), sings, thinking of Thiru-Veerattaneswarar Peruman.

Now, the second sacred verse: “Panninai pavala thiral mamani annalai amarar thozhum aathiyai sunna ven podi on thiru veerattam nannil allathu en kan thuyil kollume.” The heroine sings that her eyes will find sleep only if she reaches Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam, where Lord Shiva, who is the form of melody, the great jewel-like Lord with a coral-like body, the primal Lord worshipped by the celestials, and adorned with sacred white ash, resides. Otherwise, she will not find sleep. Hymn number three: “Uttravar tham oru noi kalaipavar petram eru.” pirangu sadaiyinar sutrum pai punal soozh thiru veerattam karkil allathu en kan thuyil kollume.“ Lord Shiva is the one who removes the great sorrows of those who seek refuge in Him. He rides on a bull and has matted locks. The place where He resides is Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam, which is surrounded by the pure waters of the Kedila river. The heroine sings that her eyes will find sleep only after learning about Lord Shiva, who resides in such a Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam.

If she does not praise such a Lord Shiva, will her eyes find sleep? No, they will not.

Now, hymn number four: “Muttra venmathi soodum muthalvanar settraar vazhum thiripuram theeyazha.” ittran kondu eyil eythavar veerattam katral allathu en kan thuyil kollume.” The heroine sings that her eyes will find sleep only if she praises Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam, where Lord Shiva, the primal Lord who wears the unblemished white crescent moon and who bent the Meru mountain as a bow to burn the three cities of His enemies, resides.

Now, hymn number five: “Pallaarum pala thevar panipavar nallaarum nayan thethappadupavan villal mo veyil eythavan veerattam kallen aagil en kan thuyil kollume.” Lord Shiva is worshipped by various celestials. He is praised by good people. He is the one who shot the three cities with His bow. The heroine sings that her eyes will find sleep only if she praises Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam, where such a Lord Shiva resides. The heroine sings, “Will I find sleep otherwise?” Now, hymn number six: “Vandarkondraiyum matham valarsadai kondan kola mathiyodu aravamum vindar mummathil eythavan veerattam kandal allathu en kan thuyil kollume.” Lord Shiva, who holds the bee-filled Konrai flower, the Datura flower, the crescent moon, and a snake in His growing matted locks, is the one who shot the three cities of His enemies. The heroine sings that her eyes will find sleep only after seeing Thiru-Athigai Veerattam, where He resides.

Now, hymn number seven: “Arayar kovan aadiyan ar ellam thiraiyar on punal pai kedila karai viraiyar neetran vilangu veerattan pal karaiyen aagil en kan.” thuyil kollume.“ The heroine sings that her eyes will find sleep only if she sings about Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam, where the Lord, who wears a loincloth around His waist and is adorned with fragrant sacred ash, resides on the banks of the Kedila river, where waves of water flow.

Now, hymn number eight: “Neerudai thadantholu ninmalan arudai punal pai kedilakkarai erudai kodiyan thiru veerattam kooril allathu en kan thuyil kollume.” The heroine sings that her eyes will find sleep only if she speaks of Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam, located on the banks of the Kedila river, where Lord Shiva, the pure one with broad shoulders adorned with sacred ash, who bears the bull banner, resides.

Now, hymn number nine: “Senganmal vidaiyeria selvanar paingan aanaiyin eer.” uri porththavar angann gnalamathagiya veerattam kangulaga venn kan thuyil kollume.” The heroine sings that her eyes will find sleep even at night only if she sees Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam, where the Lord, who is the wealthy one riding the bull, who is Vishnu with red eyes, and who wore the green skin of the elephant, and who owns this entire world, resides.

Now, hymn number ten: “Poonanaram poruntha udaiyavar empinal eythavan veerattam kanen aagil en kan kollume.” Lord Shiva, who is adorned with garlands and other ornaments, and who destroyed the three cities of His enemies with an arrow from the beautiful Meru mountain as His bow, is the one who resides in Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam. The heroine sings that her eyes will find sleep only if she sees Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam, where He resides.

Now, hymn number eleven: “Varaiyarntha vaira thiral manikkam thiraiyarntha punal pai kedilakkarai viraiyar neetran vilangiya veerattam uraiyen aagil en kan thuyil kollume.” The Kedila river, flowing with waves, carries collections of diamonds and rubies from the mountains and surrounds Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam. In such a Thiru-Veerattanam, the Lord, adorned with fragrant sacred ash, shines. The heroine sings that her eyes will find sleep only if she praises such a Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam. Otherwise, her eyes will not find sleep.

Now, hymn number twelve: “Ulanthar venthalai unkalanaagave valanthan mikka avvalarakkan thannai.” silambar sevadi oondrinan veerattam pulambe nagil en kan thuyil kollume.“ Lord Shiva is the one who uses a skull as a begging bowl. He subdued the arrogance of Ravana by pressing him with His sacred toe. The heroine sings, thinking of Thiru-Veerattaneswarar, her hero, that if she does not lament and sing about Thiru-Veerattanam, where He resides, will her eyes find sleep? No, her eyes will not find sleep.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has composed this Thiru-Pathigam as if the heroine is singing. Our contemplation shall continue.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 332. Thiru-Nindra-Charukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We are contemplating the Thiru-Pathigams composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar in Thiru-Athigai. In that context, we must now contemplate the third Thiru-Pathigam. This Thiru-Pathigam, which begins with “Ettu Nan Malar,” is included in the collection called Thiru-Kurunthogai.

It is compiled as the fifty-fourth Thiru-Pathigam in the fifth Thiru-Murai. This Thiru-Pathigam refers to worshipping the Lord by offering eight types of flowers, known as Ashtapushpam. In each verse of this Thiru-Pathigam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has sung about the method of offering Ashtapushpam to the Lord. The first verse begins with “Ettu Nan Malar,” and similarly, “Enmalar malar or iru nanku poongothu aayina moonrodu or ainthu pothugal moonrodu or ainthu ezhithu on malar on malar ettu attapu” — in each verse, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar mentions these Ashtapushpams. The types of Ashtapushpam and the requirement to offer them to the Lord at three different times are mentioned in the Agamas. These eight flowers generally refer to Alari and Senthamarai.

These Ashtapushpams are common and suitable for all times. When offering Ashtapushpam, not even one flower should be missing from the count for the Lord. If the specified flowers are not available, other available flowers should be added to maintain the count and offered.

Furthermore, the Ashtapushpams offered mentally in inner worship are non-violence, control of the five senses, patience, compassion, wisdom, truthfulness, penance, and love. The Agamas state that these Ashtapushpams should be offered with the intention that those who have attained Paramasivan, the cause of the five cosmic functions, should not again be caught in the cycle of the five cosmic functions. Although these eight flowers are generally referred to as Ashtapushpams, the book “Pushpavidhi” states that Ashtapushpams should be offered separately for each of the three times of the day. The Ashtapushpams to be offered during morning worship are Alari, Nayuruvi, Malligai, Erukku, Vilvam, Nandiyavartam, Thamarai, and any white flower. The Ashtapushpams to be offered to the Lord at noon are Pon Oomathai, Pulinakonrai, Vellaippathiri, Vanni, Kathari, Mantharai, Venkakkannam, Thumbai. The Ashtapushpams to be offered in the afternoon, evening, and midnight are Malligai, Kattumalligai, Maramalligai, Magizh, Vetiver, Sanbagam, Sirushanbagam, Marukkozunthu.

Thus, the book “Pushpavidhi” has explained what is stated in the Agamas.

Now, let us look at each of the verses of this Thiru-Pathigam.

The first verse: “Ettu nanmalar kondu avan sevadi matta alariduvār vinai māyumāl kattithen kalanthannu.” Kedilaveerattanar adiserum avarukku kannar thenum kalanthathaip ponru inikkum Kedilaveerattanar. Those who reach His sacred feet will worship Him by offering these eight types of honey-laden flowers. The karmas of those who worship in this manner will vanish. As we have already seen, the common Ashtapushpams are Punnai, Vellarukku, Sanbagam, Nandiyavartam, Pathiri, Kuvalai, Alari, Senthamarai.

The Lord possesses eight qualities, bears eight names, performed eight heroic deeds, and pervades everywhere as Ashtamurti. The scriptures state that such a Lord should be worshipped with eight flowers. Thiru-Navukkarasar himself states it here. Hymn number two: “Neelama ninainthu enn malar ittavar kolavalvinaiyum kuraivipparal vazhamalizhiyum kedilakkarai veli soozhnthu azhagaya veerattare.” The Lord residing in Thiru-Veerattam, which is beautifully surrounded by the Kedila river flowing broadly and deeply like a fence, will remove the severe karmas of those who constantly remember Him and worship Him with eight types of flowers.

Next, hymn number three: “Kalli nan malar or iru nanku kondu ulguvar avar valvinai ottuvar thellu neer vayal pai kedilakkarai vellai neerani meni veerattare.” Lord Shiva, who resides in Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam on the banks of the Kedila river, where clear water flows into the fields, and who has a body adorned with white sacred ash, will drive away the severe karmas of those who worship Him by offering eight fresh, honey-laden flowers.

Next, hymn number four: “Poongothu aayina moonrodu or ainthu ittu vangi nindravan valvinai ottuvar veengu than punal pai kedilakkarai vengai tholudai aadai veerattare.” The Lord, who resides in Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam on the banks of the Kedila river, where abundant cool water flows, and who wears a tiger skin as His garment, drives away the severe karmas of the devotees who stand and worship Him by offering eight types of flower clusters.

Now, hymn number five: “Thenappothugal.” moonrodu or ainthudan thana pothiduvār vinai theerppavar meenaththan punal pai kedilakkarai venalanai uriththa veerattare.“ The Lord, who resides in Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam on the banks of the Kedila river, where cool waters filled with fish flow, and who flayed the elephant, removes the karmas of those who worship Him by offering eight types of fragrant, honey-laden flowers. Hymn number six: “Ezhithon malar kondu paninthavar oozhitholvinai oda agattruvar pazhithan punal pai kedilakkarai velathin uri porththa veerattare.” The Lord, who resides in Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam on the banks of the Kedila river, where powerful cool waters flow, and who wore the skin of the elephant, will drive away the ancient karmas of the devotees who worshipped Him with Konrai flowers. He will remove the old karmas of the devotees who worship Him by offering eight types of flowers. Hymn number seven: “Uraisai nool vazhi on malar ettu ida thiraigal pol varu valvinai theerpparal varaigal vanthu ezhiyum kedilakkarai viraigal soozhnthu azhagaya veerattare.” Lord Shiva, who resides in Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam, which is beautiful and surrounded by fragrance on the banks of the Kedila river, which flows from the mountains, removes the severe karmas that come like waves for the devotees who worship Him by offering eight types of radiant flowers according to the Agamic scriptures. Hymn number eight: “Oli vandarai.”

The Lord of Thiru-Athigai Veerattam, surrounded by beautiful fences on the banks of the Kedilam River, where the waters flow, removes the karmic bonds of those who worship Him at the appropriate time with eight kinds of flowers, accompanied by the humming of bees. Song number nine: “Those who can praise Him with eight kinds of fragrant, large flowers will have their karmic bonds removed.

The Lord of Veerattam, on the banks of the Kedilam River with its clear, surging waves, has a fragrant, red matted lock of hair.” The Lord Shiva, who has a fragrant, red matted lock of hair, is present in Veerattam on the banks of the Kedilam River, which has powerful, clear, and flowing waves. The Lord, such a Shiva Peruman, destroys the karmic bonds of devotees who, bearing His sacred form in their hearts, contemplate Him and praise Him with eight kinds of flowers. Song number ten: “Those who reach the feet of Thiru-Athigai Veerattanar are devotees who, with the eight flowers offered according to ritual, approach the Lord, who is the eight-formed and beginningless, and worship Him in a manner that unites with Him.” This Thiru-Kurunthogai Thiru-Pathigam, beginning with “Ettu Naan Malar” (eight four flowers), which speaks specifically about the eight flowers, was composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman at Thiru-Athigai Veerattam. This is the third Thiru-Pathigam composed at this time.

Now, we must contemplate the fourth Thiru-Pathigam. Let us go on contemplating.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 333. Thiru-Nindra-Charukkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We have seen three of the thirteen Thiru-Pathigams composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar at Thiru-Athigai.

Now, the fourth Thiru-Pathigam. This is called the “Koppalitha Thiru-Nerisai Thiru-Pathigam.” Because the word “Koppalitha” (overflowing/abundant) appears throughout this entire Pathigam, it has received the sacred name “Koppalitha Thiru-Nerisai.” The meaning of the word “Koppalithal” is when a substance, or its quality, becomes exceedingly abundant and appears outwardly. For example, “Koppalitha Karumbu” (overflowing sugarcane), “Koppalitha Vambu” (overflowing fragrance), “Koppalitha Paravu” (overflowing praise). Since the word “Koppalitha” appears repeatedly throughout this Pathigam, it is named “Koppalitha Thiru-Nerisai.” This “Koppalitha Thiru-Nerisai Thiru-Pathigam” is arranged as the twenty-fourth Thiru-Pathigam in the Fourth Thiru-Murai.

Now, the Thiru-Pathigam.

“Irumpi koppaLiththa yaanai eeruRi poorththa eesan karumbu koppaLiththin sol kaarigai paagamaaga surumbu koppaLiththa gangai thuvalai neer sadaiyil etra arumbu koppaLiththa senni athigai veerattanare kombu koppaLiththa thingaL koNaL veN piRaiyum soodi vambu koppaLiththa ko ndrai vaLarsadai melum vaiththu sembu koppaLiththa moonRu madiludan surunga vaangi ambu koppaLiththa eythaar athigai veerattanare vidaivum koppaLiththa paadham viNNavar paraviyeththa sadaiyum koppaLiththa thingaL saanthavin neeru poosi udaiyum koppaLiththa naagam uLguvaar uLLaththenRum adaiyum koppaLiththaar karaiyum koppaLiththa kaNdar kaamavel uruvam manga iRaiyum koppaLiththa kaNNar eththuvaaridargaL theerppar maRaiyum koppaLiththa naavar vaNdu paadum konRai aRaiyum koppaLiththa senni athigai veerattanare neeru koppaLiththa maarpar nizhal thigal mazhuventhi kooRu koppaLiththa kodhai kolvaLai maathor paagam eRu koppaLiththa paadham imaiyavar paraviyeththa aaRu koppaLiththa senni athigai veeratta naare vaNangu koppaLiththa paadham vaanavar paraviyeththa piNangu koppaLiththa senni sadaiyudai perumai aNNal sunangu koppaLiththa kongai suriguzhal paagamaaga aNangu koppaLiththa meni athigai veerattanare soolam koppaLiththa kaiyar sudarvidu mazhuvaal veesi noolum koppaLiththa maarbin nuNpoRi aRavam serththi maalum koppaLiththa paagar vaNdu paNpaadum konRai aalam koppaLiththa kaNdaththu athigai veerattanare naagam koppaLiththa kaiyar naan paadi megam koppaLiththa thingaL virisadai melum vaiththu paagam koppaLiththa maathar paNNudan paadiyaada aagam koppaLiththa thoLaar athigai veeratta naare paravu koppaLiththa paadal paNNudan patthar eththa viravu koppaLiththa gangai virisadai mevaiththu iravu koppaLiththa kaNdar eththuvaar idargaL theerppar aravu koppaLiththa kaiyar athigai veeratta naare thoNdai koppaLiththa sevvaay thudiyadai paRavai koNdai koppaLiththa kodhai kolvaLai vaNdu koppaLiththa thenthen varigaiyil parugi maantha keNdai koppaLiththa theNneer kedila veeratta naare Thiruchitrambalam. These are the ten verses in this Pathigam. Let us contemplate the concise meaning. First verse: “Irumpi koppaLiththa yaanai eeruRi poorththa eesan karumbu koppaLiththa in sol kaarigai paagamaaga surumbu koppaLiththa gangai thuvalai neer sadaiyil etra arumbu koppaLiththa senni athigai veerattanare.” We saw that “Koppalitha” means an excessive manifestation of a quality of an object.

“Therefore, if we apply it here, it first comes as “Irumpi koppaLiththa yaanai eeruRi poorththa eesan.” “Irumpi” can be split as “iruL poo,” meaning a very dark elephant, as if darkness itself is overflowing.

“The Lord is He who flayed that elephant and wore its hide. He has Parvati, whose words are as sweet as overflowing sugarcane, as one part of His body. He has received the water of the Ganga, where bees abundantly drink and overflow with honey, into His matted locks. He is the Lord of Thiru-Athigai Veerattam, whose head is adorned with buds overflowing with honey. He is the Lord of Thiru-Athigai Veerattam, who has received that water, the Ganga, adorned with flowers where buds abundantly manifest honey, into His matted locks, and whose sacred head is adorned with buds that abundantly manifest honey.

“Now, the second verse: “Kombu koppaLiththa thingaL koNaL veNpiRaiyum soodi vambu koppaLiththa konRai vaLarsadai melum vaiththu sembu koppaLiththa moonRu madiludan surunga vaangi ambu koppaLiththa eythaar athigai veerattanare.” He is Thiru-Athigai Veerattaneswarar, who wore the crescent moon with its increasing sharpness, and above it, placed the fragrant Konrai flower on His growing matted locks. He bent His bow and shot arrows with increasing power, burning the three strong, copper-like fortresses so that they shrank and were destroyed.

“Now, the third sacred verse: “Vidaivum” koppaLiththa paadham viNNavar paraviyeththa sadaiyum koppaLiththa thingaL saantham veNNeeRu poosi udaiyum koppaLiththa naagam uLguvaar uLLaththenRum adaiyum koppaLiththa seer ar athigai veerattanare.” The Lord Shiva, whose sacred feet are adorned with the marks of mounting the bull, so that the celestials praise Him, has applied sacred white ash on His sacred body, like the light of the moon hidden within His matted locks, and has snakes adorning His sacred body. He, such a Shiva Peruman, will forever remain in the hearts of those who meditate on His sacred feet. Such a one is enshrined as Veerattaneswarar in Thiru-Athigai.

“Now, song number four: “Karaiyum koppaLiththa kaNdar kaamavel uruvam manga iRaiyum koppaLiththa kaNNar eththuvaar idargaL theerppar.” maRaiyum koppaLiththa naavar vaNdu paadum konRai aRaiyum koppaLiththa senni athigai veerattanare.” On the sacred body of Shiva Peruman, the blue stain of poison appears abundantly on His sacred throat. Shiva Peruman is He who has a forehead eye that emitted a small amount of fire to destroy the form of Manmatha. He removes the sorrows of those who praise Him. The Vedas abundantly manifest on His tongue. Thiru-Athigai Veerattanar appears with a head adorned with Konrai flowers, where bees hum. Song number five: “Neeru koppaLiththa maarpar nizhal thigal mazhu onRu enthi kooRu koppaLiththa kodhai kol vaLai maathor paagam eRu koppaLiththa paadham imaiyavar paraviyeththa aaRu koppaLiththa senni athigai veerattanare.” On the sacred body of Shiva Peruman, the sacred ash shines abundantly.

“It shines extensively. He holds a radiant battle-axe in His hand. He appears as Thiru-Athigai Veerattanar, with Parvati, who is praised by all, adorned with garlands of fame and abundant bangles, seated as one part of His body. He rides on a bull, with His sacred feet praised by the celestials, and has matted locks where the Ganga flows abundantly. Song number six: “VaNangu koppaLiththa paadham vaanavar paraviyeththa piNangu koppaLiththa sennichchadaiyudai perumai aNNal sunangu koppaLiththa kongai suriguzhal paagamaaga.” The celestials stand before and praise the sacred feet of such a Shiva Peruman, which are abundantly associated with worship through Vedic mantras. He is the great Lord with matted locks on His head, and with Parvati Devi, whose breasts are adorned with beauty marks and whose curly hair is one part of His body, manifesting divine nature.

“He appears as Thiru-Athigai Veerattanar, whose sacred body manifests divinity. Song number seven: “Soolam koppaLiththa kaiyar sudarvidu mazhuvaal veesi noolum koppaLiththa maarbin nuN poRi aRavam saaththi maalum koppaLiththa paagar vaNdu paNpaadum konRai aalam koppaLiththa kaNdaththu athigai veerattanare.” On the sacred throat of Shiva Peruman, who is enshrined as Veerattaneswarar in Thiru-Athigai, the black mark of poison appears abundantly. In His sacred hand, the sacred trident radiates light abundantly.

“Similarly, He holds a radiant battle-axe in His hand. On His chest, the sacred thread shines abundantly. He wears a snake with fine spots on His sacred chest. He wears Konrai flowers, where bees hum melodies. He, as Kesavarthamoorthy, has Vishnu as one part of His sacred body. He is enshrined in Thiru-Athigai.

“Song number eight: “Naagam koppaLiththa kaiyar naanmaRai aayapaadi megam koppaLiththa thingaL virisadai melum vaiththu paagam koppaLiththa maathar paNNudan paadiyaada aagam koppaLiththa thoLaar athigai veerattanare.” In the sacred hand of Shiva Peruman, the snake resides joyfully. Shiva Peruman sings the four Vedas, places the crescent moon, which is like an overflowing cloud, on His expansive matted locks. As Uma Devi, who is one part of His body, sings with melody, the Lord dances. As He dances, His sacred body swells and expands. Such a one with swelling shoulders is Thiru-Athigai Veerattaneswarar. Song number nine: “Paravu koppaLiththa paadal paNNudan patthar eththa viravu koppaL” aLiththa gangai virisadai mevaiththu iravu koppaLiththa kaNdar eththuvaar idargaL theerppar aravu koppaLiththa kaiyar athigai veerattanare.” Devotees sing praises and express abundant blessings.

“Devotees sing such songs with melody. Shiva Peruman is He who removes the sorrows of those who worship and praise Him in this manner. He is enshrined in Thiru-Athigai as Athigai Veerattaneswarar, with snakes joyfully dancing in His hands, the crescent moon and the Ganga in His matted locks, and as the dark-throated Neelakantha. Song number ten: “ThoNdai koppaLiththa sevvaay thudiyadai paRavai algul koNdai koppaLiththa kodhai kolvaLai paagamaga vaNdu koppaLiththa thenthen vari gayal parugi maantha keNdai koppaLiththa theNneer kedila veerattanare.” Shiva Peruman has Parvati Devi as one part of His body. Who is Parvati Devi? She has red lips that radiate the beauty of a ThoNdai fruit, a waist like a drum, a broad hip like the sea, and hair adorned with a Kondai, one of the ways of decorating hair, which shines brightly.

“Parvati Devi wears abundant bangles. Shiva Peruman has such a Parvati Devi as one part of His body. He is pleased to reside in Thiru-Athigai Veerattam, located on the banks of the Kedilam River, whose clear waters are full of leaping carp and KeNdai fish. He appears as the Lord in Thiru-Athigai Veerattam. This is the meaning of the ten sacred verses of this Thiru-Pathigam.

“We shall continue our contemplation.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 334. We must now contemplate the fifth Thiru-Pathigam among the thirteen Thiru-Pathigams sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar in Thiru-Athigai. This Thiru-Pathigam, a Thiru-Nerisai Thiru-Pathigam, begins with “VeNNilaa Mathiyam Thannai.” It is compiled as the twenty-fifth Thiru-Pathigam in the Fourth Thiru-Murai.

Now, the Thiru-Pathigam.

“VeNNilaa mathiyam thannai virisadai meva vaiththu unnilaa pugunthu ninRangu uNarvinukku uNara kooRi viNNilaar meeyachchooraar veNdovaar veNdovaarkke anniyaar perithum seyyar athigai veerattan” paadinaar maRaihal naanGum paayiruL pugunthathen uLLam koodinaar koodalaala vaayilaar nalla konRai soodinaar soodal mevi sooL soodar soodalai veNNeeRaadinaar aadal mevi athigai veerattanare oonaiye kalikka veNdill uNarmingaL uLLaththuLLe thenaiye malarhal koNdu sinthaiyuL sinthikkiNRa enaiye palavumaagavar eththa ninRu aanaiyin urivai poorththaar athigai veerattanare thuruthiyaam koorambai thannil thonnooRangu aRuvar ninRu viruththi thaan tharuganRu vethanai palavum seyya varuthiyaal vallavaRu vanthu vanthu adaiya ninRa aruthiyaarkku anbar polum athigai veerattanare paththiyaal eththi ninRu paNipavar neNjaththuLLaar thuththi ainthalaiyanaaga sooLsadaimudimel vaiththu uththara malaiyarppai umaiyavaL nadunga anRu aththiyin urivai poorththaar athigai veerattanare varimuRi paadi enRum vallavaRu adainthu neNje kariyuri moodavalla kadavuLai kaalaththaale suripuri viriguzhalaal thudiyadai paRavai algul aRivaiyor paagarpolum athigai vee rattanare neethiyaal ninaisai neNje nimalanai niththamaaga paathiyaam umai thannodum paagamay ninRa entha sothiyaay sudar vizha kaa aathiyum eerumaanaar athigai veerattanare elliyum pagalum ellaam thuNjuverku oruvar vanthu pulli manaththu koyil pukkanar kaaman ennum villi ain kaNaiyinaanaai venthuga nokkiyittar alliyam pazhanaveli athiga veerattanare onRave yuNarthiraagil om kaaraththu oruvanagum venRa aimpulangaL thammai viLakkutharkku uriya nanRavan naaraNanum naadi kaaNkuRravarkku aRiyavar polum athiga vee rattanare thadakkaiyaal eduththu vaiththu thadavarai kolugaarththu kidakkaiyaal idargaLonga kiLarmaNi mudigaL Thiruchitrambalam. This is that Thiru-Pathikam. Let us contemplate its concise meaning. The first verse: “Vennilaa madhiyam thannai virisadai meva vaiththu unnilaa pugundhu nindrangu unarvinukku unarakkoori vennilaar meeyachchoora venduvaar venduvaarke anniyaar adhigai veerattanare.” This verse states that Lord Shiva holds the cool moon on His extended matted locks. He enters within the heart, bestows consciousness, and is compassionate, granting understanding to consciousness.

He resides in the world of the Devas and also in this earthly world, primarily in Thiru-Meeyachchur. He dwells in sacred sthalams. He is near to those who desire Him, and far from those who do not. Such a Lord Shiva, entering my heart, illuminating it with the light of wisdom, imparts what needs to be understood for the mind to grasp it, and is enshrined in Thiru-Adhigai Veerattam. Verse number two: “Paadinaar maraigal naangum paayurul pugundhen ullum koodinaar koodal aalavaayilaar nalla kondrai soodinaar soodan mevi soozh sudar sudalai vennneeru aadinar aadan mevi adhigai veerattanare.” In this sacred verse, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sings that Lord Shiva is enshrined within the Aalavai temple in Madurai, the city of Koodal. Such a Lord Shiva, singing the four Vedas and lovingly adorning Himself with a Kondrai garland, is enshrined in Thiru-Adhigai Veerattam, having smeared Himself with the radiant ashes of the cremation ground and delighting in the divine play of destroying the three cities.

Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sings that Lord Shiva, who is thus, has also entered his heart. Although this Thiru-Pathikam belongs to Thiru-Adhigai Veerattanam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sings that Lord Shiva is enshrined within the Thiru-Aalavai temple in Madurai, the city of Koodal. Sivakavimani, who wrote the commentary for this passage, states that there are many pieces of evidence to suggest that Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar considered the Lord of Thiru-Aalavai in Madurai as his spiritual master and performed spiritual Shiva Puja. He points to this passage as evidence.

Furthermore, he cites many other instances where Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sang about Aalavai Appan, quoting: “Aalavaayil appane arul seyyaye” (O Lord of Aalavai, bestow Your grace!), and “Thenkoodal Thiru-Aalavaay Sivanadiye sindhikka petren naan” (I was blessed to contemplate the feet of Shiva in Southern Koodal Thiru-Aalavai), and “En mel oonamadhu ellaam ozhiththaan” (He removed all the flesh from me), and “Matroru patrillla adiyerku” (To me, a devotee without other attachments), and “Sirandhaanai” (The excellent one), and “En thalai in uchchi” (The crown of my head), and “Thaavi thirundhaanai” (The one who leaped and reformed), and starting with “Enjalil pugazhi” (Unending glory), and “Malaradi kaanum vannam anjalendru” (So that I may see Your lotus feet, saying ‘fear not’), and “Valuvillaadhu unai vaazhththi vazhipadum thondan en un sezhumalar paadham kaana” (I, a devotee who worships and praises You without faltering, to see Your glorious lotus feet), and “Narumalar neeram kondu naal thorum eththi vaazhththi serivana siththam vaiththu thiruvadi serum vannam” (With fragrant flowers and water, praising and blessing daily, setting my mind on devotion to reach Your sacred feet), and “Pundhiyondri pidiththu nin thaalgal” (Holding Your feet with a unified mind), and “Pithathri naan irukka maatten” (I cannot remain babbling). Sivakavimani quotes all these passages. Sivakavimani also quotes evidence that Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar performed spiritual Shiva Puja. “Thondan en pattadhu enne thooya kaaviriyin nannneer kondiru kothiyaatti kungumak kuzhambu saaththi indai kondu era nokki eesanai embiraanai kandane kandiraathe kaalaththai kazhiththavaare” (What did I, a devotee, suffer? Having taken the pure good water of Kaveri, bathing, anointing with saffron paste, looking up with a garland, seeing the Lord, my Master, without seeing Him, how did I spend my time?) This is a general Nerisai verse. And “Paangariya en poligal pariththu itta ilaiyum mugaiyum ellaam” (All the leaves and buds that my ignorant self plucked and offered).

Citing this Thiruviruttam, Sivakavimani writes in his commentary that Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar performed Shiva Puja according to the rules of spiritual worship. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar himself established a monastery and lived there for a long time, performing penance. That place is called Thiru-Poonthuruthi Thirumadam. The Shiva Puja site and the Shiva Puja platform where he performed worship are still visible today. Sivakavimani writes that it is one of the highest duties of Shaivite devotees to protect and cherish such historical sites, like the Thiru-Poonthuruthi Thirumadam where Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar resided and performed Shiva Puja, and other similar places associated with great acharyas.

Let us continue to contemplate the meanings of the verses. The third sacred verse: “Oonaiye kazhikka vendil unarminhal ullaththulle thenaiya malargal kondu sindhaiyul sindhikkindra enaiya palavumaagi imaiyavar eththanindru aanaiyin urivai porththaar adhigai veerattanare.” Its meaning is: Lord Shiva is enshrined in Thiru-Adhigai Veerattam. Meditate upon Him and realize Him, because if you wish to completely eradicate the suffering of this birth, which is the taking of a body, meditate upon Lord Shiva and realize Him.

Lord Shiva resides in all thoughts that arise within the heart. He is enshrined in Thiru-Adhigai, having covered Himself with the skin of an elephant, while the Devas praise Him, holding flowers that attract bees. Meditate upon Him and realize Him. Verse number four: “Thurutthiyaam kurambai thannil thonnootru angu aruvar nindru viruththithaan tharuga endru vedhanai palavum seyyavaruththiyaal vallavaaru vandhu vandhadaiya nindra aruththiyaarku anbar polum adhigai veerattanare.” This body, which torments the soul, is like a bellows. A bellows is a device that provides air to blow a forge. In iron foundries, the forge is always burning.

To keep the fire or embers from dying out, they use something like a bellows. When it is pressed and expanded, air comes out of the bellows. With the help of that air, the fire does not die out. This body is like such a bellows, because just as it contracts and expands, releasing air, so too this body breathes through the two nadis, Ida and Pingala.

Therefore, because it blows like a bellows, this body is sung as a bellows-like body. In such a bellows-like body, ninety-six entities stand and cause much suffering. These ninety-six refer to the ninety-six Tattvas. There are thirty-six Tattvas and sixty Tatvigas, which are their effects, making a total of ninety-six. We have already extensively discussed these ninety-six Tattvas in the legend of Kannappa Nayanar.

Thus, these ninety-six entities stand and torment this body, causing distress to the soul. These ninety-six Tattvas afflict living beings, demanding the objects necessary for their existence.

Therefore, living beings should seek Lord Shiva as much as possible. If they do so, Lord Shiva, who resides in Thiru-Adhigai, helps His devotees who seek refuge in Him, preventing their suffering. Verse number five: “Patthiyaal eththi nindru panibavar nenjaththullaar thuththi aindhalai naagam soozh sadai mudimel vaiththu utthara malaiyarppai umai aval nadunga anatthiyin urivaip porththaar adhigai veerattanare.” He who is steadfast in the hearts of those who worship with devotion, who wears a five-headed serpent with hoods on His expansive matted locks, who covered Himself with the skin of an elephant, making Uma Devi, the daughter of Himavan, the king of the northern Himalayas, tremble, is Veerattaneswarar of Thiru-Adhigai. Verse number six: “Varimuri paadiyendrum vallavaar adaindhum nenje kariyuri moodavalla kadavulai kaalaththaale suripuri viri kullalaal thudiyadai paravai algul arivaiyor paagar polum adhigai veerattanare.” O heart, Adhigai Veerattanaar shines as the Lord who is the partner of Parvati, who has coiled and flowing hair, a waist like a drum, and an ocean-like vulva, and who covered Himself with the elephant’s skin. Let us always sing His praises with melodic and rhythmic songs and seek refuge in Him as best we can. Verse number seven: “Neethiyaal ninai sey nenje nimalanai nitthamaaga paadhiyaam umai thannodum paagamai nindra endhai sodhiyaay sudar vilakkaay sunnavin neerathu aadi aadhiyum eerumaanaar adhigai veerattanare.” O heart, our Father, who stands as a part with Uma, who is pure, who is light, who is a radiant lamp, who smears Himself with sacred ash, and who is the beginning and end of all worlds, is Adhigai Veerattana Eswarar.

Meditate upon that pure one daily according to the prescribed method. Verse number eight: “Elliyum pagalum ellaam thunjhuverku oruvar vandhu pulliya manaththuk koyil pukanaar kaaman ennum villi aingkanaiyinaanai vendhuga nokkiyittaar alliyam pazhanaveli adhigai veerattanare.” Lord Shiva, who looked at Manmatha, the archer with five arrows, and made him burn to ashes, is the one who came to me, a devotee who spends all day and night without any activity, and entered the temple of my humble mind, making it His abode. Verse number nine: “Ondrave unardhiraagil omkaaraththu oruvanaagum vendra aimpulangal thammai vilakkudharku uriyeer ellaam nandravan naaranan naanmugan naadik kaangul andravarkku ariyarp polum adhigai veerattanare.” Adhigai Veerattanaar was the one who was difficult for the great Vishnu and Brahma to find, even when they searched for Him. If all of you, who are capable of conquering and illuminating the five senses, meditate upon Him with a united mind, He will appear to you as the true essence within Omkara. Verse number ten: “Thadakkaiyaal eduththu vaiththu thadavarai kulunga aarththu kidakkaiyaal edugaloonga kilar mani mudigal saaya mudakkinaar thiruviral thaan murugamar kodhai paagaththu adakkinaar ennai yaalum adhigai veerattanare.” Adhigai Veerattanaar, who has taken me as His slave, is the one who, when Ravana tried to lift Mount Kailash with his mighty hands, causing the great mountain to tremble and roar, simply bent His sacred toe, crushing Ravana’s ten jeweled crowns and causing him distress.

He holds Parvati Devi, adorned with fragrant garlands, on His left side.

Thus, we have contemplated the meaning of the ten sacred verses of this Thiru-Pathikam. Let us press on with our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 335. The sixth Thiru-Pathikam sung by Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar in Thiru-Adhigai, beginning with “Nambane Engal,” is compiled as the twenty-sixth Thiru-Pathikam in the Fourth Thirumurai. Thiru-Nerisai Thiru-Pathikam.

“Nambane engal kove naadhaneyaadhi moorththi pangane paramayogi endrendre paravinaalum sempone pavalakundre thigazh malar paadham kaanbaan anbane alandhu ponen adhigai veeratta neere.” “Poyyinaal midaindha porvai purai purai azhugi veezha meyya naayvaa” maatten venditronraivar vendaar seyya thaamaraigal anna sevadi irandum kaanbaan aiyanaan alandhu ponen adhigai veeratta neere.“ “Neethiyaal vaazha maatten nitthalam thooyan allen oodhiyum unara maatten unnai ul vaikka maatten sodhiye sudare unthan thoomalar paadham kaanbaan aadhiye alandhu ponen adhigai veeratta neere.” “Thiruzhumaa thirulamaatten theevinai sutram ennum porulule azhundhinaalum povadhor neriyum kaanen” irulumaa mani kandanaanin inaiyadi irandum kaanbaan arulumaara vendum adhigai veeratta neere.” “Anjinaal iyattrabatta aakkai petradhanul vaazhum anjinaal adarkappattingu ozhidharum aadhanenai anjinaal oyikkum vannam kaattinaaykseerndhen anjinaal pozhindha sennneer adhigarvoosal pola ondru vittondru pattri maru kayiroosal pola vandhu vandhulavu nenjam perugayiroosal pola pirai pulgu sadaiyaayppaa” tharugayiroosalaanen adhigai veeratta neere.“ “Kazhiththilen kaama vennnoy kaadhamai ennum paasam ozhiththilen oon kan nokki unarvenum imai thirandhu vizhiththilen veliyuru thondra vinaiyanum sarakku konden azhiththilen ayarththu ponen adhigai veeratta neere.” “Mandraththu punnai pola marambadu thuyaram eydhi ondinaal unara maatten unnai ul vaikka maatten kandriya kaalan vandhu karukkuzhi vizhuppadharke andrinaan alamandhitten adhigai” veeratta neere.” “Pinividaa aakkai petren petram ondrenruvaane panividaa idumbai ennum paasanaththazhundhuginren thunivilen thooya nallen thoomalaadham kaanbaan aniya naariyamaatten adhigai veeratta neere.” “Thiruvinaal kozhunaarum thisaimugam udaiya kovum iruvarum ezhundhum inaiyadi kaanamaatta oruvane embirane ung thiru paadham kaanbaan aruvane arula vendum adhigai veeratta neere.” The essence of this Thiru-Pathikam is: Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sings, addressing Lord Shiva in Thiru-Adhigai: “O Veeratta Neere, O Lord enshrined in Veerattanam! I have suffered greatly to behold Your sacred feet. You must bestow Your grace upon me.” The entire Pathikam is like an appeal. This is the essence of this Pathikam.

He pleads, “I have suffered immensely to behold the Lord’s sacred feet, therefore, that Lord must bestow His grace upon me.” This is the plea of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar throughout this Pathikam. The meaning of the first verse is as follows: “O Lord enshrined in Thiru-Adhigai Veerattanam, O beloved of all, O our King, O Primordial Being, O partner of Parvati, O supreme Yogi, O one like pure gold and a coral mountain, O beloved!” Thus, for a long time, I called out to You and suffered greatly to behold Your lotus-like feet. Please bestow Your grace upon me. The meaning of the second verse is as follows: This body is a covering made of perishable, false materials. Each orifice will gradually cease to function and decay. Such is its nature.

It is impossible to live a true life with this. I desire unparalleled supreme knowledge, but my five senses do not desire that supreme knowledge and cause me trouble.

Therefore, O Lord Shiva enshrined in Thiru-Adhigai, I stand in distress, unable to behold Your two sacred feet, which are like red lotuses. Please bestow Your grace upon me.

Now, the meaning of the third verse is: O Light, O Lamp of Wisdom, O Lord of Adhigai! I am not pure. I, a devotee, do not live according to the path daily. Even though I have studied all the scriptures and moral texts, I am unable to understand what I have learned and live by it. I am unable to keep You steadfastly in my heart and meditate upon You.

Therefore, O Primordial Lord, I stand in distress, unable to behold Your sacred feet, which are like pure flowers. Please bestow Your grace upon me.

Now, the meaning of the fourth verse is: O Lord of Adhigai, with a throat like a dark blue gem! My mind has not attained clarity, even after reaching the path to clarity. I am associated with material possessions, which are like relatives that aid in evil deeds.

Therefore, I am ignorant of the exalted path that should be taken.

Therefore, I, a devotee, pleads that You must bestow Your grace upon me so that I may behold Your two sacred feet.

Here, when he sings, “I have reached the path to clarity, but my mind has not attained clarity,” that ‘path’ refers to the justice prescribed in the Vedas and Shaiva Agamas, which is the niyathi (rule).

Now, the meaning of the fifth verse is: O Lord Shiva, whose sacred head is anointed with Panchagavya! I, an ignorant devotee, having obtained this body made of the five elements and living within it, am tormented by the five senses. You showed me the right path to follow through the sacred five letters, thereby freeing me from fear.

Now, verse number six, the meaning of the sixth verse is: O Lord of Adhigai, with matted locks bearing the crescent moon, my heart swings like a rope swing, moving from one place to another, grasping it, and then returning to the starting point. My heart wanders like that swing rope. Just as the ground supports a swing without a rope, just as the ground cradles a ropeless swing like a mother, so too have I attained the nature of resting in Your feet as my abode.
