Now, the meaning of the seventh verse is: O Lord of Thiru-Adhigai! I am afflicted with the terrible diseases of desire, attachment, and lust, and they have not left me. I have not abandoned the bond of desire. I have focused on bodily life.

Therefore, the veil of ego, which is the cause of all this, has not been removed, and I have not attained that state of true realization; I have accumulated much of the commodity called karma, which obstructs it.

At the same time, I have forgotten to remove the attachments that cause these to multiply. What shall I do? Please bestow Your grace upon me.

Now, the meaning of the eighth verse: In the middle of a village, there is a common tree that blossoms beautifully, bears fruit, and has many ripe fruits.

Therefore, those who see it, knowing it is a common tree for all, throw stones at it and torment it. Just as they torment the tree, I am constantly suffering, tormented by my five senses. I am suffering, yet I fail to realize the truth. I do not even cherish You, who can make me realize that truth, within my heart. In this state, the wrathful Yama approaches to cast me back into rebirth. Seeing this, I am bewildered.

O Peruman of Thiru-Athigai Veerattam, please bestow Your grace upon me, thus he sings.

Now, the meaning of the ninth verse: O You who ride the bull, O Peruman of Thiru-Athigai! Diseases always reside in this body. I am closely associated with these sufferings. I lack the purity and mental fortitude necessary to completely eradicate these good and bad karmas. Please bestow that purity and courage. I am unable to perceive You, unable to see Your pure, lotus-like sacred feet.

Therefore, O Peruman, please bestow Your grace upon me.

Now, the meaning of the tenth verse: O Peruman of Thiru-Athigai Veerattam! Both Thirumal, the consort of Thirumagal, and Brahma, who has four faces for the four directions, searched and strived, yet they could not see Your sacred feet or Your crown; they were distressed by their inability to see. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sings that You, such an incomparable Peruman, should bestow Your grace so that this humble servant may see Your sacred feet. This is the seventh Thiru-Pathigam and its meaning.

Let us continue to contemplate the eighth Thiru-Pathigam. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 336. We are now to contemplate the seventh Thiru-Pathigam among the thirteen Thiru-Pathigams sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar in Thiru-Athigai. This Thiru-Pathigam, which begins with “Madakkinar Puliyin Tholai,” is compiled as the twenty-seventh Thiru-Pathigam in the fourth Thiru-Murai. Thiru-Nerisai Thiru-Pathigam.

Madakkinar puliyin tholai mamani nagam kachchadar thondai sevvaithudiyaparavai algul adakkinar kedilaveliyathigai veerattanare soodinar. Gangaiyalai soodiya thoolani kettangoodinal nangaiyalum oodalai ozhikka vendi padinar sama vedam padiya paniyalai adinar kedilaveli athigai veerattanare kombinar kuzhaiththa vener komagan kola nirmmai nambinar kanalaga vagaiyathor nadalai seithar vembinar mathilgal moonrum villidai eriththu vizhththa ambinar kedilaveli athigai veerattanare maripada kidantha. Kaiyar valarila mangai pagam serippada kidantha sekkar sezhmathi kozhundhu soodi porippada kidantha nagam pugaiyumizhndhu azhalavikki giripada nadappar polum kedila veerattanare narivaral kavva senru nattra sey therivaral mal kol sinthai thirppathor sinthai seyvar varivaral uzhagum thennir kazhani soozh pazhana veli arivaral vayalgal soozhntha athigai veerattanare pullalai thundavottil undu poi. Palasankombin sullalai sudalai vennir aninthavar mani vellerru thullalai pagan thannai thodarthinge kidakkinrenai allalai kadappiththalum athigai veerattanare niritta nuthalar velai nilam ser kandar mathar kooritta meyyaragi koorinar arum nankum kiritta thingal soodi kilartharu sadaiyin ullal arittu mudippar polum athigai veerattanare kanilar karuththil varar thiruththalar poruththalagar enilar. Irappum illar pirappilar thoorakkalagar nanilar aivarodum ittanai viravi vaithar analar pennumallar athigai veerattanare thirthama malaiyai nokki seruvali arakkan senru perththalum pedaiyanja peruviral athanai oonri sirthama mudigal paththum viththu avanai anru arththavai alara vaithar athigai veerattanare Thiruchitrambalam.

This Thiru-Pathigam has a total of ten sacred verses, but the ninth sacred verse is damaged and unavailable to us.

Therefore, nine sacred verses. We have now seen.

Let us now contemplate the meaning of those sacred verses. The meaning of the first verse: Thiru-Athigai Veerattanar, whose boundary on one side is the Kedila River, wears a tiger skin as His garment. He has tightly bound a large serpent as a belt over that garment. He holds Goddess Parvati as one part of His body. Such is Thiru-Athigai Veerattan Peruman. The previous Thiru-Pathigam was a supplication, addressing Him as “Veeratta Neere” and asking for His grace.

This Thiru-Pathigam is structured to praise His grace with wonder. The meaning of the second verse: The Lord wears the Ganga in His matted locks. Hearing the sound of the Ganga, Goddess Parvati takes offense. To dispel that offense, Thiru-Athigai Veeratta.

The Lord Shiva sings the Sama Veda. And He dances to the rhythm of that song.

Now, the meaning of the third verse: Manmatha, the king of spring, was sent by Brahma, Indra, Thirumal, and others to shoot an arrow at Lord Shiva. Lord Shiva, in a way that those who sent Manmatha could not perceive, burned Manmatha’s body and tormented him. Such a Lord Shiva resides in Thiru-Athigai. How? He resides there holding the arrow that burned the three cities. The meaning of verse four: Lord Shiva holds a fawn in His hand.

He has Goddess Parvati on His left side. He has tightly bound a spotted serpent around His waist.

Therefore, those serpents emit smoke and. They are very angry.

Thus, Lord Shiva, who has bound the serpent around His waist, moves about so that the false consciousness in the hearts of devotees is destroyed.

Now, the meaning of the fifth verse: The fields surrounding Thiru-Athigai have clear water where Varal fish leap. Thiru-Athigai thus shines as a fertile land surrounded by fields, says Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, and tells a parable. A fox already has a piece of flesh in its mouth, its food. That fox goes to catch a Varal fish. When it goes to catch the Varal fish, it loses the food it already had in its mouth.

Similarly, human life has the nature of losing what it has by thinking of what it cannot obtain.

Lord Shiva is the one who, with a sacred heart, bestows the means to remove the delusion that arises in the hearts of wise people who examine such human life, thus he sings.

Now, the meaning of the sixth verse: Lord Shiva is one who smears ashes in the cremation ground. What kind of cremation ground is it? Vultures with the smell of flesh chase and tear apart the bodies in that cremation ground and eat them. There are skulls there. In that cremation ground, the small branches of Palasa trees wither due to its heat. In such a cremation ground, Lord Shiva is present, smeared with white ashes, leaping onto a bull and driving it.

He is the one who makes me, who has been continuously clinging to this world for a long time, cross the mire of the disease of birth and enslaves me, O Athigai Veerattan.

Now, the meaning of the seventh verse: Thiru-Athigai Veerattanar, with sacred ash on His forehead, is the Blue-Throated One, the consort of Parvati, the speaker of the four Vedas and six Shastras, wearing the crescent moon, and holding the Ganga in His matted locks, having tied His matted locks.

Now, the eighth sacred verse: Thiru-Athigai Veerattanar, who is neither male nor female, is unknowable to others’ sight, unattainable by thought, impossible to correct, and impossible to make conform to oneself. He is without any specific state, without death or birth. He is inseparable from us, yet not ours, impossible to abandon. He is unashamed of His states that are contrary to worldly ways, and He has kept me in this world, mingling with the five senses and causing me to wander. In this verse, the Lord’s nature of being inseparably with living beings, Even though He is inseparably with living beings, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings in this verse about the nature of that Lord whom we cannot see, and the benevolent nature of the Lord who gives bodies to living beings, makes them experience karmas, and removes them, and other benevolent acts and characteristics of the Lord. The ninth verse is not available to us.

Therefore, the tenth verse: Thiru-Athigai Veerattanar resides on the pure Kailasa mountain. When Ravana came to uproot the Kailasa mountain, the Lord pressed it down with His toe, making Goddess Parvati fear, scattering his ten heads, and making his mouths, which were roaring with joy, cry out in sorrow in an instant. This is the meaning of the tenth verse. So far, we have contemplated seven Thiru-Pathigams.

We will continue to contemplate the eighth Thiru-Pathigam. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 337. Thiru-Nindrachcharukkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We must now contemplate the eighth Thiru-Pathigam among the thirteen Thevaram Thiru-Pathigams sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar in Thiru-Athigai. This Thiru-Pathigam, which begins with “Munbellam Ilaiya Kalam,” is a Thiru-Nerisai Thiru-Pathigam.

It is compiled as the twenty-eighth Thiru-Pathigam in the fourth Thiru-Murai.

Now, the verses of the Thiru-Pathigam and their meanings.

First verse: Munbellam ilaiya kalam murthiyai ninaiyathu odi kan kana erumi nalum karuththu azhindhu aruththamindri pinpagal unangal attum pedaimar ponren ullam anbanai vazhamatten athigai veeratta nire munbellam ilaiya kalam murthiyai. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings, “Ninaiyathu odi kan kana erumi nalum karuththu azhindhu.” This implicitly indicates the advanced age of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar when he converted from Jainism to Shaivism. “Pinpagal unangal attum pedaimar” is a proverb. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings that he is like a foolish woman who, when hungry all day and her family is hungry, wastes time all day without cooking, spending it in idle talk, and then starts cooking in the evening. That is, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, during his youth, the early part of his life, did not meditate on the sacred feet of the Lord.

Having wandered, and now having reached old age, he sings with tears in his eyes, “O Peruman, I have come to You in this old age, coughing with a ‘kan-kan’ sound, with my mind destroyed.” For all this time, without thoughts of Shiva, without doing beneficial deeds, just as a housewife does not cook all day and starts cooking rice in the pot in the evening, similarly, after being in Jainism throughout my life, I have now come seeking You in this old age, which is the evening of my life. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings to the Peruman of Thiru-Athigai, “I am unable to live with heartfelt true devotion.” Now, the second verse: Karai perum kandaththane kaykathir nama. Anji nirai perum kadalum kanden nilvarai uchchi kanden pirai perum senniyane pinjaga ivai anaiththum aruththor upayam kanen athigai veeratta nire. This is the second sacred verse. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings, “O Peruman of Athigai, O great Blue-Throated One, O You with the crescent moon as Your head ornament! Fearing Yama, who comes with wrath upon living beings, I have bathed in the sea and reached the summit of tall mountains and performed austerities there, yet I have not found a way to remove the fear of birth and rebirth.” That is, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings to Lord Shiva, “Even if I perform austerities in mountain caves or at the bottom of the sea, fearing birth and death, fearing prosperity and decline, I do not know the way to remove the suffering of the fear of birth and death.”

Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings to Lord Shiva, “I do not know the way to remove the suffering of the fear of birth and death.” Now, verse number three: Nathanar enna nalum nadunginaragi thangal ethangal ariyamaattar inaiyadi thozhuthom enbar athana avan enru ezhugi athigai veerattanene nin pada nan paravathu pazhavinai parisilene. In this, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings about the nature of Shiva devotees. Great people, those who possess learning and listening, if someone calls them “You are our leader,” they will tremble at that very moment. They will consider it a great fault to think of themselves as leaders. Great people who possess learning and listening, Shiva. In this austerity, great people who have passed through the three stages of Chariya, Kriya, and Yoga, and possess the first two stages of Gnana, namely learning and listening, will never consider themselves leaders.

They will only consider themselves devotees. They will consider themselves devotees of the Lord, and not only that, they will tremble at the very mention of the name “leader,” apart from the name “devotee of the Lord.” They are those who have Lord Shiva alone as their leader. Such is the state of great people.

But what is my state? I have spent many ages without worshipping Your sacred feet.

Therefore, I possess that ancient evil karma.

Therefore, unlike those great people who possess learning and listening, I have not been free from the arrogance of ‘I’ and ‘mine.’ I have remained ignorant. I have thought of myself as the leader and scorned You. He sings regretfully about all this, referring to his past time in Jainism, in this third sacred verse.

Now, the fourth sacred verse: Sudalai ser sunna meyyar surumbuna virintha konrai padalai ser alangal marbar pazhanam ser kazhanai thengin madalai nir kiliya odi athanida manigal sinthum kedila veerattameyaki kilar sadai mudiyanare. In this, he praises the richness of the Kedila River. Thiru-Athigai is a fertile land full of fields belonging to the Marutham region. The Kedila River flows, hitting and splitting the coconut fronds that grow near those fields.

Thus, the waves of the Kedila River rise to the height of coconut fronds, scattering gems upon them. Our Peruman, who lovingly resides in Thiru-Athigai Veerattam on the banks of such a Kedila River, has a body smeared with cremation ground ashes and a chest adorned with a garland of Konrai flowers. Verse number five: Now, let the mantra be within, let the churning ocean be the ghee, let the color of the flame that arose from Indra’s sacrificial fire be seen wonderfully, and let them be enlightened. They come to steal, and in the groves where the Kandiram bird sings, they are seen by the Kedila. This is the fifth sacred verse. In this, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings, referring to the churning of the ocean of milk.

Indra is the lord of sacrifices. One attains the position of Indra by performing many sacrifices. Such an Indra, the son of. Bhagapathi, therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasar compares his churning of the ocean of milk to a sacrifice here. Indra performed the sacrifice of churning the ocean of milk, with the Mandara mountain as the churning rod and the ocean of milk itself as the ghee. The Kalakala poison emerged as the flame of that sacrificial fire.

The Peruman Himself consumed it and appeared as Thiru-Nilakandar. This event reveals the supremacy of Shiva to the devotees.

Thus, that sacred throat remains blue-throated even today, revealing the supremacy of Shiva to the devotees. Such a Peruman has come to this earthly world and resides in Thiru-Athigai Veerattam on the banks of the fragrant Kedila River, which has groves. This is the meaning of the fifth sacred verse. The meaning of this hymn: the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth verses are lost due to our misfortune and are not available to us.

Therefore, we will now consider the meaning of the tenth verse.

Now, the tenth sacred verse: “Maingala manaiya kannaal panganmaa malaiyai odi meignaram puthiram pilka visai thanindhu arakkan veezhndhu kaingaram pezhivi kondu kaadhalaal inidhu sonna kinnaram kettugandhaar Kedila Veerattanare.” Thiru-Adigai Veerattana Peruman, Lord Shiva, is accompanied by Parvati. Normally, women apply kohl to their eyes to make them beautiful, but Goddess Parvati has applied kohl to her sacred eyes.

Therefore, the kohl applied to Goddess Parvati’s sacred eyes has now gained beauty. He is the one who has such a Parvati on His left side. When Ravana tried to uproot Mount Kailash, he was crushed by one of Shiva’s sacred great toes, his nerves and blood gushing out. His speed diminished, and Ravana, using his own hand-nerves as the strings of a veena, played a sweet song filled with love. Lord Shiva, pleased by that song, bestowed His grace upon him. This is how the tenth sacred verse is structured.

This is the meaning of the verses from the Thiru-Padigam that begins with “Ilaiya Kaalam” (Youthful Age). Let us go on contemplating. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 338. Thiru-Nindra-Charukkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Of the thirteen Thiru-Padigams sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman in Thiru-Adigai, we have so far contemplated the verses of eight Thiru-Padigams and their meanings.

Now, the ninth Thiru-Padigam, which begins with “Maasilol Vaazhpol,” is a Thiru-Virutha Thiru-Padigam. It is compiled as the 104th Thiru-Padigam in the Fourth Thiru-Murai.

Now, the Thiru-Padigam.

The first verse: “Maasilol vaazhpol mariyum mani neer thirai thoguthi oosalai aadi angu on sirai annam urangalutraal paasarai neelam parugiya vandu pan paadal kandu veesum Kedila vadakaraitte endai Veerattame.” The first three verses in this Thiru-Padigam speak of our Father, Lord Shiva, residing in the temple called Thiru-Veerattam. In this first verse, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings that the waves of the Kedila River, like a shining sword, rise and fall, casting waves like crystal clear water. These waves of the Kedila River bring the swans to the shore. This is like the bees that drink honey from the flowers in the groves on the banks of the Kedila River and sing songs. Just as the bees sing, the Kedila River, as if offering a reward, brings gems and jewels to the shore, sings Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar.

He sings that the sthalam called Veerattam is located on the banks of such a Kedila River.

Now, the second sacred verse: “Paingal thavalai parai kotta paasilai neerpadugar angal kuvalai mel aavi uyirppa arugulavum sengal kurugu ivai serum seri Kedila karai thengal kurusilai veeran arul vaitha Veerattame.” Lord Shiva, the warrior with the golden Meru mountain as His bow, established His grace by destroying the three cities in Thiru-Adigai Veerattam.

Here, green-legged frogs make sounds like drums. As the water of the Thiru-Kedila River overflows, the water collects in the hollows. In it, water lilies spread their fragrance. Nearby, red-legged storks approach the water lilies.

Thus, Thiru-Adigai Veerattam is located on the northern bank of the water-rich Kedila River.

Now, the third sacred verse: “Ammalar kanniyar anjanam senthuvar vaayilaiyaar vemmulai saantham vilai perum maalai eduthavargal tham arungil kirangaar thadanthol kudaivaar vimmu punal Kedilakkaraitte entha azhagiya maiyezhuthiya kangalai udaiya sivandha pavalam pondra vaayinai udaiya azhagiya maalaigalai anindha pengal intha Kedila nadhiyil neeraadugindraargal iththagaiya Kedila nadhiyin.” Beautiful women with kohl-lined eyes, red coral-like lips, and wearing beautiful garlands bathe in this Kedila River. Such a Kedila River’s northern bank is where our Lord’s Thiru-Adigai Veerattam is located.

Now, the fourth sacred verse: “Meen udai than punal Veerattare nummai vendugindradhu yaanudai sil kurai ondru ulladhaal narum than nerukkin then udai kondrai sadai udai Gangai thirai thavalum koon udai thingal kuzhaviyappodhum kurikkonmine.” O Veeratteshwara, who resides in Thiru-Adigai where cool waters with fish flow, I, your servant, have a small request. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings, making a very tasteful plea to Lord Shiva, “I have a request for you.” He asks Lord Shiva to pay attention so that the crescent moon in His matted locks does not drown in the Ganga that flows through His matted locks. He sings, “With cool Erukku flowers and honey-laden Kondrai flowers, you hold the Ganga in your matted locks. The crescent moon, which floats on the waves of that Ganga, is always swimming.

“Therefore, please take good care of it. Please ensure that the crescent moon does not drown in the Ganga in your matted locks.” Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar makes this request. The meaning of this is that the moon sought refuge in the Lord to be relieved of its suffering.

“Therefore, by making the request, “O Lord Shiva, just as you protect the moon who sought refuge in you, please protect your devotees who, like the moon, have sought refuge in you,” Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar makes the plea that just as you protect the moon who sought refuge in you, we too have sought refuge in you, so please protect us. This is its implication.

“Now, the fifth sacred verse: “Aaratta thenum irandhu undu agamagavandririndhu veratta nirppiththidugindradhaal viri neer paravai sooratta velavan thaathaiyai soozh vayalaar Adigai Veerattaththaanai virumbaa varum paavavedanaiye.” In this sacred verse, it is described that Lord Shiva, the father of Lord Muruga, is seated in Thiru-Adigai. The sea is vast with water. Lord Muruga is the one who destroyed Soorapadman in that sea. Lord Muruga wields the spear that destroyed Soorapadman. The father of such a spear-wielding Lord Muruga, Lord Shiva, is seated in Thiru-Adigai Veerattam. Those who do not worship such a Supreme Being, the Lord, those who have not worshipped in previous births, accumulate terrible sins.

“As a result of those terrible sins, in this birth, they will wander, begging for food, sings Navukkarasar. The suffering that comes as a result of committing terrible sins will befall a person in this birth.

“Therefore, because of this, they will wander from house to house, sweating, and their lives will be such that they have to beg for and eat whatever food is prepared by anyone. All this happens to those who do not accept and worship the Lord.

“Thus sings Thiru-Navukkarasar.

“Now, the sixth sacred verse: “Padar porchadaiyum paguvaai aravum pani madhiyum sudalai podiyum ellaam ulave avar thooya thenneer Kedila karai Thiru-Veerattar aavar ketthenai adaindhaar nadalaikku natthunaiyaagum kandir avar naamangale.” This is the sixth sacred verse.

“Lord Shiva is seated in Thiru-Adigai, located on the northern bank of the pure, clear-watered Kedila River. He has golden-glowing matted locks, a serpent with a split tongue, a cool crescent moon, and cremation ground ashes, all of which are His symbols. The sacred names of Lord Shiva are a great support that dispels the suffering of those who seek refuge in Him, sings Thiru-Navukkarasar. Lord Shiva’s names serve as a support to alleviate the sufferings of devotees.

“Here, the term ‘naamam’ refers to the sacred five-letter mantra. Even so, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar laments, saying, “Even though I am foolish, I tried to cling to Lord Shiva but then abandoned Him and hid myself.” Now, the seventh sacred verse: “Kaalang kadandhadhor kandaththaraagi kannaar Kedila naalam kadikkor nagaramum maadhirkku nangu isaindha thaalangal kondu kuzhal kondu yaazh kondu thaam anggane vedangal kondu visumbu selvaar avar Veerattare.” This is the seventh sacred verse.

“Lord Shiva is Thiru-Neelakantha. At the request of Parvati, He held the poison of time in His sacred throat, thus becoming Thiru-Neelakantha. He is the Lord who possesses the heroic feat of burning the three cities. The place where He resides, adorned with snakes, playing well-matched rhythms, flutes, and lutes, is the city of Thiru-Adigai. That city is on the bank of the Kedila River.

“Lord Shiva is also the one who possesses such a Kedila River, sings the poet. Lord Shiva, after burning the three cities, travels through the sky to Thiru-Kailash.

“At that time, He performs a dance of victory. He performs that dance of victory in the sky. Thiru-Adigai Shiva is Thiru-Purantaka, and therefore, He has eight arms. With those arms, He holds the rhythms, flutes, and lutes and dances. It is a tradition for those who win a war to perform a victory dance.

“Therefore, Navukkarasu Peruman mentions here that the Lord of Thiru-Adigai Veerattanam, who conquered the three cities, performs such a victory dance.

“Similarly, in the invocation to God in Kalithogai, we can see the sacred dance of Lord Shiva who burned the three cities. In the invocation to God in Kalithogai, it says: “Padubarai pala empa pal oruvam peyarththu nee kodu kotti aadum kaal kodu uyar agal algul kodi purai nusuppinaal konda seer tharuvaalo” and “Mandu amar pala kadandhu madhu kaiyaal neeru anindhu pandarangam aadum kaal panai ezhil anai men thol vandu aratrum koondhalaal valar thookku tharuvaalo.” After burning the Asuras of Tripura, the dance performed by the Lord is mentioned in the invocation section of Kalithogai.

“Similarly, here, after burning the three cities, the Lord, with eight arms, holding various rhythms, lutes, flutes, and other instruments, performs a sacred dance and ascends to Thiru-Kailash in the sky. He is Lord Shiva residing in Thiru-Adigai, sings Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. In this Thiru-Padigam, the eighth, ninth, and tenth verses are lost and are not available to us.

“Therefore, we will conclude this Thiru-Padigam with this seventh sacred verse.

“We must continue to contemplate the tenth Thiru-Padigam.

“We shall proceed with our contemplation.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 339. Thiru-Nindra-Charukkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Of the thirteen hymns composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar in Thiru-Adigai, we have contemplated nine hymns.

Now, we must contemplate the tenth Thiru-Padigam. This Thiru-Padigam is called Adaiyaala Thiru-Thandagam. It is compiled as the fourth Thiru-Padigam in the Sixth Thiru-Murai. This belongs to the Thiru-Thandagam melodic structure and hymn arrangement. In this Thiru-Padigam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar describes the sacred symbols of the Lord one by one. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings that Lord Shiva possesses all these symbols and resides in Thiru-Adigai.

Therefore, this hymn is named Adaiyaala Thiru-Thandagam.

Now, the hymn.

“Chandiranai maa Gangai thiraiyaal modha sadamukuda thiruththume saamaveda Gandharuvam virumbume kapaala mendhu kaiyane meyyane kanagamenai pandhanavu melviralaal paaganaame pasu erume paramayogiyaame aindhalayamaasunam kondaraiyargumme avanaagil Adigai Veerattanaame.” “Ereru ezhu ulagum ozhi tharuvaane imaiyavargal thozhudhaiththirukkiraane paareru paduthalaiyil bali kolvaane pada aravan thada maarbil payil veeththaane neer eru sembavala.” If he is the one who, with the great Ganga’s waves striking the moon, adorns his matted crown, who delights in the Gandharva music of the Sama Veda, who holds a skull in his hand, who is the truth, who has a golden body, who has a soft finger, who rides a bull, who is the supreme yogi, who wears the five-headed serpent around his waist, then he is the Lord of Adigai Veerattam. If he is the one who rides the bull and illuminates the seven worlds, who is worshipped by the celestials, who receives offerings in the great skull, who has the serpent coiled on his broad chest, who is like a red coral mountain in the water, who placed a single eye on his forehead, who placed the crescent moon on his matted crown, then he is the Lord of Adigai Veerattam. If he is the one whose body shines in the cremation ground, who is the beginning, middle, and end, who has a white mark on his throat, who dances with a fierce serpent, who is the nature of the body, who is the great earth, water, fire, air, and ether, who is beyond the universe, then he is the Lord of Adigai Veerattam. If he is the red one, the dark one, the one with a green-eyed serpent in his throat, the one who removes sins, the one who has a cool Kondrai flower in his matted locks, the one who holds a shining axe and trident, the one who is the three times, the one who burned Kama, the one with the mighty bull, then he is the Lord of Adigai Veerattam. If he is the one whose four Vedas sing without ceasing, whose matted locks shine, who wears the moon on his head, who has a deer skin and a serpent around his waist, who has Uma with coral lips as a part of him, who dances with the sound of Kudamuzhavu, Veena, and Thalam, with small goblins making sounds, who holds fire, then he is the Lord of Adigai Veerattam.

If he is the one who hides in the hearts of those who contemplate him, who with a single eye burned Kama to ashes, who brought down the great Ganga to his red matted locks, who is the seven worlds, who destroyed the moving three cities with a single arrow, who is the primordial great ascetic, then he is the Lord of Adigai Veerattam. If he is the one who dances with the sound of the flute, Kokkarai, and Thalam, with the goblins singing in front, who performs karanam with his anklet-wearing sacred toes, who shows his sacred form in dreams, who dances waving his beautiful deer skin, who dances with fire in the cremation ground at every cremation, who is the eight forms, then he is the Lord of Adigai Veerattam. If he is the one who killed the mighty elephant, the demon, and wore its skin, appearing neither above nor below, as if the flesh and blood were mixed, who churned the ocean with the great mountain and the serpent, causing the waves to roar, who drank the deadly poison and has a dark throat, then he is the Lord of Adigai Veerattam. If he is the one whose red matted locks are like gold, the Lord, the divine one, the beloved husband of Uma, whose hair is adorned with fragrant flowers, the one who wields the axe in his right hand, the Lord, the one who stands to be worshipped by the four Vedas, the one who shot the arrow that made the three cities tremble without trembling, the one who is in the cosmic sphere, then he is the Lord of Adigai Veerattam. If he is the one whose growing matted locks are adorned with the moon, wet with the spray of the rising river, the one who, with his coral-red lips, fought with Kama and took on a beautiful form, the one whose chest bears the mark of battle, who wears the sacred thread, whose sacred form is smeared with fragrant sandalwood and sacred ashes, then he is the Lord of Adigai Veerattam. If he is the tall one whom Vishnu and Brahma could not find, the one without an equal, the one with the beautiful jewel on his banner, the one with the fierce tiger skin, the one who wears a loincloth, the one whose body is covered with ashes, the one who begs for alms and wanders the world, the one with the sacred thread, the one who makes his devotees rule the heavenly world, then he is the Lord of Adigai Veerattam.

This is the Adaiyaala Thiru-Thandagam. It contains eleven verses.

Therefore, we will contemplate the meanings of the eleven verses briefly. As we have already seen, this hymn, throughout its eleven verses, describes and illustrates the symbols of Lord Shiva. The meaning of the first verse, as we saw, is that Lord Shiva holds the Ganga in his matted locks, and the Ganga strikes his matted locks with its waves.

Furthermore, Lord Shiva holds the moon in his matted locks. He who greatly loves the music of the Sama Veda, who holds a skull in His sacred hand, whose sacred body is like gold, who has Parvati Devi as one part of Himself, that Parvati Devi holds a ball in Her fingers.

Lord Shiva has a bull as His vehicle, is a supreme yogi, and has a five-headed serpent tightly bound around His waist. The Peruman with such deeds and attributes is enshrined in Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam.

Now, the meaning of the second verse: Lord Shiva, riding on a bull, travels around the seven worlds, existing so that the Devas may worship and praise Him. He takes alms in a skull bowl where vultures come to feed. He has a hooded serpent crawling on His great chest. He who has a body like a rich coral mountain, adorned with sacred ash, who has an eye on His forehead, who wears the crescent moon on His matted locks where the Ganga resides. Such a Peruman is enshrined in Athigai Veerattanam. The meaning of the third Thiru-Padal: Lord Shiva has a sacred body that shines with the garland of skulls of deceased Brahmas.

He wears the skulls of Brahmas as a garland on His sacred body. He is responsible for creating, sustaining, and ultimately destroying this world. In His neck, Lord Shiva wears the tusk of the great boar (Maha Varaha) as an ornament on His sacred neck. He dances, holding an angry serpent in His hand, presenting a divine spectacle. He is the support for the tattvas that are the causes of this body. He is present as the five great elements, pervading both outside and inside the universes.

Such a Peruman is the Peruman of Athigai Veerattanam.

Now, the meaning of the fourth verse: Lord Shiva is red in color, His throat is dark. He wears serpents, wearing hooded serpents with hungry eyes and white teeth. He is an enemy to the karmas of His devotees, causing them to cease. He has matted locks adorned with a cool Konrai garland. He holds a trident in His sacred hand. He is present in all three times.

Lord Shiva is the Lord who angered Manmatha, who has a sugarcane bow. He comes on a bull vehicle, which is tall and stout. Such is His greatness. Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam is Lord Shiva.

Now, the meaning of the fifth Thiru-Padal: Lord Shiva continuously chants the four Vedas. He wears the crescent moon such that its light falls on His garment. He has a tiger skin and a serpent wrapped around His waist. He has Uma Devi, whose mouth is like a Kovvai fruit, as one part of His sacred body. He is surrounded by small Bhootas. These Bhootas have a small gait.

These Bhootas play instruments like the Kudamuzha, Veena, and Thalam. Lord Shiva, thus surrounded by Bhootas, performs the supreme dance of the five actions (Panchakritya dance). He holds fire in His beautiful long hand. Such a Lord Shiva is seated in Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam.

Now, the meaning of the sixth Thiru-Padal: Lord Shiva resides in the hearts of those who meditate on Him. He removes all internal enemies like lust and other ailments from the hearts of those who meditate on Him. He looked at Manmatha with His third eye, causing him to turn to ash. He made the Ganga descend and reside in His red matted locks. He Himself is the cause of the movement of the seven worlds. He destroyed the three flying cities with a single arrow.

He performs supreme penance. Why? To show the path of penance to His devotees.

Therefore, He performs penance. Such a Lord Shiva is seated in Thiru-Athigai Veerattanam.

Now, the meaning of the seventh Thiru-Padal: Around Lord Shiva are short Bhootas. These short Bhootas are always present, playing instruments like the Kuzhal, Kokkarai, and Munthai, and clapping their hands. As these small Bhootas sing, Lord Shiva dances in accordance with their song. With His sacred fingers, which move at His sacred feet, Lord Shiva activates and moves the subtle bodies of living beings.

Lord Shiva reveals His sacred form to His devotees in their dreams.

Lord Shiva dances, rapidly moving His beautiful shoulders.

Lord Shiva dances every night in the cremation ground outside the village, standing in fire. He has eight forms. Such a Lord Shiva is seated in Thiru-Athigai.

Now, the meaning of the eighth Thiru-Padal: Lord Shiva killed an elephant and flayed its skin, covering His entire sacred body with it as a garment. The Devas, making a great clamor, churned the great milky ocean, its waves roaring, by setting Mount Mandara as the churning rod and Vasuki as the churning rope. He has a blue throat from consuming the great poison that arose then. Such a Lord Shiva is seated in Thiru-Athigai.

Now, the meaning of the ninth verse: Lord Shiva has red matted locks. He is the abode of love for Uma Devi, whose hair is adorned with flowers possessing a naturally divine fragrance.

Lord Shiva is Uma Devi’s husband. He holds a battle-axe in His right hand. He is desired by us. He exists so that the four Vedas may worship Him. He destroyed the three cities of the fearless Asuras, causing them to tremble. He is omnipresent in all worlds.

He stands pervading all. Such a Lord Shiva is seated in Thiru-Athigai.

Now, the meaning of the tenth verse: He wears the Ganga on His sacred head.

Lord Shiva holds the Ganga. The crescent moon in His matted locks is thought to be from the drops of waves emerging from the Ganga.

Lord Shiva is the husband of Uma Devi. That Uma Devi has a mouth as soft as a fruit. Uma Devi has a mouth as red as coral. That Uma Devi, enshrined in Kanchi-Kamakottam in Kanchipuram, embraced Her life’s Lord, Ekambaranathar, so that Her two breasts rested on His chest.

Thus, Lord Shiva has a chest bearing the marks of breasts and bangles from Uma Devi’s embrace. He has a chest that displays these marks. On that sacred chest, Lord Shiva wears the sacred thread. He wears sacred ash on His red body, where sandalwood and fragrant pastes are smeared like mud. Such a Lord Shiva is enshrined in Thiru-Athigai.

Now, the meaning of the eleventh verse: Lord Shiva is the Lord who has no equal or superior. He is the Lord. He assumed a tall form that Vishnu and Brahma could not find, even with their efforts. He is Thiru-Neelakandan. He wears the skin of a tiger, which is a killer, as a garment over His loincloth. He has a body smeared with sacred ash.

He is the Peruman who wears the sacred thread. He wanders in the upper worlds and the seven worlds to beg for alms. He makes His devotees rule the world of the Devas. Such a Peruman, Lord Shiva, is seated in Thiru-Athigai. This is the meaning of the eleven Thiru-Padal-s (verses) in this Thiru-Pathigam, which is a Thiru-Thandagam of identification. We must continue to contemplate the eleventh Thiru-Pathigam.

We shall continue our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 340. Thiru-Nindra-Charukkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We have contemplated ten of the thirteen Thiru-Pathigams composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar in Thiru-Athigai. The eleventh Thiru-Pathigam is the Thiru-Thandagam called ‘Potri Thiru-Thandagam’.

Because this Thiru-Thandagam contains ‘Potri, Potri, Potri’ in praise of Lord Shiva, it is named ‘Potri Thiru-Thandagam’. This is the Potri Thiru-Thandagam composed in Thiru-Athigai.

Similarly, there are three Potri Thiru-Thandagam Pathigams for Thiru-Kailai. ‘Potri’ means ‘protect’. This is the meaning given by Nachinarkiniyar. ‘Potri’ also means ‘salutation’. This Pathigam received its name because it contains many praises like ‘Potri, Potri’ to Lord Shiva. This Pathigam, the Potri Thiru-Thandagam, is the fifth Thiru-Pathigam in the sixth Thiru-Murai.

Now, the Thiru-Pathigam: Thiruchitrambalam. Potri, You who stand as all things, saying ‘all is Shiva’! Potri, Lord who stands as the fiery light! Potri, You whose weapon is the deadly battle-axe! Potri, You who kicked the killer Yama! Potri, You who are unknown to the sight of the unlearned!

Potri, You who remove the suffering of the learned! Potri, You who shot the great fortress with a bow! Potri, Immaculate One, beloved of Veerattanam! Potri, Essence of song and dance! Potri, You who created many eons! Potri, You who delight in eating from a skull!

Potri, You who dwell in the hearts of those who meditate! Potri, You who delight in dancing in the cremation ground! Potri, You whose throat is like a dark cloud! Potri, You who tied the serpent that makes one dance! Potri, Lord of Thiru-Kedila Veerattanam! Potri, You whose crown is adorned with Mullai flowers!

Potri, Form smeared with sacred ash all over! Potri, You whose virtues are boundless! Potri, You who created the sound of the seven strings! Potri, You who eat from a small, hairless skull! Potri, You who remove the evil deeds of those who seek refuge! Potri, You who reside in Thillai Thiruchitrambalam!

Potri, Our Lord in Thiru-Veerattanam! Potri, You who are unique in the vast ash! Potri, You who established the paths of penance! Potri, You who speak the small services of those who worship with folded hands! Potri, O Youth! Potri, You who kept the serpent, moon, and water together, ending their enmity!

Potri, You who adorned Yourself with Ambal flowers! Potri, Lord of Thiru-Kedila Veerattanam! Potri, You whose throat is dark with water! Potri, You who hold the shining white battle-axe! Potri, You who hold Uma as one part of Your body! Potri, O Youth who makes the fierce serpent dance!

Potri, You who have the Ganga on Your head! Potri, You who became the rare nectar for devotees! Potri, You who always delight in riding the bull! Potri, Our Father in the great Thiru-Kedila Veerattanam! Potri, You who delight in the songs of those who sing! Potri, You who reside in Pattiswaram near Pazhaiyaru!

Potri, You who are capable of granting liberation to those who seek it! Potri, O Lord! Potri, You who are difficult for those who seek to find! Potri, O Lord who tied the serpent around His waist! Potri, You who delight in the five sacred offerings! Potri, Lord who rules the world from Thiru-Kedila Veerattanam!

Potri, You who delight in dancing amidst the roaring sounds! Potri, You who became the great ocean and the great sky! Potri, You who shot the three cities, causing the heavens to tremble! Potri, O Unique One who covers Himself with elephant skin! Potri, You who practiced singing with ancient melodies! Potri, O Supreme One who pervades the entire world!

Potri, You who burned Manmatha in ancient times, seen by the world! Potri, O Kapali who holds the skull, beloved of the dark Kedila! Potri, You who have a fierce white bull as Your vehicle! Potri, You who held the Ganga flood on Your matted locks! Potri, O Supreme One who begs for alms without sleep! Potri, You who remove the suffering of those who worship!

Potri, O Lord whose throat holds poison! Potri, You who are the four Vedas and the six Angas! Potri, You who have the sweet-speaking Uma as Your part! Potri, Lord of Thiru-Kedila Veerattanam! Potri, Shiva who stands in thought! Potri, You who meditated on Sri Parvatam!

Potri, You who are wisdom and the lotus heart! Potri, O Virtuous One! Potri, O Pure One! Potri, You who stand as the three junctions! Potri, O Truth! Potri, My Father!

Potri, You who stand as the ultimate refuge! Potri, Lord of Thiru-Kedila Veerattanam! Potri, O Three-Eyed One! Potri, O Primeval One! Potri, You who begot Muruga! Potri, O Dakshina!

Potri, O Dharma! Potri, O Truth! Potri, My Father! Potri, You who stood as a blazing light, unmoving, when the two, Vishnu and Brahma, folded their hands! Potri, O Father, I have no other eye! Potri, Lord of Thiru-Kedila Veerattanam!

This is the Potri Thiru-Thandagam. It contains eighty-two praises of ‘Potri’.

Now, let us contemplate its meaning. The first verse: He who is mingled in all things, as if to say that all things are connected to Shiva! He who stands as the three lights: fire, sun, and moon! He who wields the battle-axe, a weapon of destruction! He who kicked Yama, who separates souls from bodies! He who is unknown to the mental perception of those who have not learned the truth from a wise guru!

He who removes the sorrow of those who have received proper initiation from a guru! He who destroyed the great fortresses with a bow! He who is the blemishless one, enshrined in Athigai Veerattanam! I praise You, I worship You. The meaning of the second verse: He who has singing and dancing as His attributes! He who created many eons!

He who delights in accepting as food what He receives as alms in a skull! He who has the hearts of those who meditate on Him as His dwelling place! He who delights in dancing in the cremation ground! He whose throat is dark like a dark cloud! He who tightly binds the serpent, which should be made to dance by withdrawing, around His waist! He who rules living beings from Athigai Veerattanam, by the banks of the wave-lashing Kedila river!

I worship You. The meaning of the third verse: He who is crowned with a garland of Mullai flowers! He whose entire body is smeared with sacred ash! He who possesses boundless good qualities! He who created the seven types of sounds from the seven strings of the Yazh! He who receives food in a round, hairless skull!

He who removes the evil deeds of those who come to worship Him! He who is enshrined in Thillai Thiruchitrambalam! Our Lord who is enshrined in Athigai Veerattanam! I worship You. The meaning of the fourth verse: He who is smeared with sacred ash on His chest! He who ensures that the paths of penance undertaken by devotees yield their respective benefits!

He who is the Youth, ready to bestow grace upon those who control their five senses with their minds and perform small services to You, keeping them in His heart! He who, with the attribute of keeping the serpent, moon, and Ganga together in His matted locks without enmity! He who is adorned with Ambal flowers! He who rules everyone from Athigai Veerattanam, located on the banks of the wave-filled Kedila river! I worship You.

Now, the meaning of the fifth verse: O blue-throated one smeared with sacred ash! O You who hold the shining white battle-axe! O You who have Uma Devi as a part of Your body, fitting as one half! O Youth who makes fierce serpents dance! O You who have the Ganga on Your head! O You who became the rare nectar for devotees!

O You who always delight in riding the bull as Your vehicle! O Our Father, enshrined in the great Athigai Veerattanam on the banks of the Kedila river! I worship You.

Now, the meaning of the sixth verse: O You who delight in listening to the songs of devotees who sing with love for You! O You who are enshrined in Pattiswaram, belonging to Pazhaiyaru! O You who are capable of granting liberation to devotees who have renounced worldly attachments! O You who covered Yourself with an elephant skin, causing Uma Devi to fear! O You who are difficult for those who seek to attain You through their own efforts to understand! O You who have tightly bound a serpent around Your waist!

O You who delight in the Panchagavya Abhishekam! O Lord who rules the world from Thiru-Kedila Veerattanam! I worship You.

Now, the meaning of the seventh verse: O You who delighted in dancing so that the earth trembled! O You who became the great ocean and the sky! O You who destroyed the three fortresses by shooting an arrow, causing the celestial world to tremble! O You who are distinct from worldly ways, covering Your body with elephant skin! O You who are accustomed to singing with melodies! O Supreme One who pervades the entire world!

O You who, in ancient times, destroyed Manmatha with a mere glance! O Kapali who holds the skull, beloved of Thiru-Kedila Veerattanam, which is dark due to the depth of its waters! I worship You.

Now, the meaning of the eighth verse: O You who have a white bull of great anger as Your vehicle! O You who made the Ganga flood reside on Your expansive matted locks! O Supreme One who begs for alms without sleep! O You who remove the suffering of devotees who worship You with discipline! O Lord whose throat holds poison! O You who are the four Vedas and the six Angas!

O You who are the consort of Parvati Devi, who speaks sweet words! O Lord of Thiru-Kedila Veerattanam! I worship You. The meaning of the ninth verse: O Shiva, who is established in the hearts of devotees as their dwelling place! O You who reside in the lotus of the heart as the form of wisdom! O You who are the embodiment of virtue!

O Pure One! O Supreme One who exists as the three junctions: morning, noon, and evening! O Truth! O My Father! O Refuge who exists as the excellent twilight among times! O Lord who rules the world from Veerattanam!

I worship You.

Now, the meaning of the tenth verse: O Three-Eyed One! O Primeval One! O Father of Muruga! O God of the South! O Embodiment of Dharma! O Truth!

O My Father! O You who stood as an unmoving pillar of light when Vishnu and Brahma, together, called out ‘O Lord!’ and folded their hands! O Lord! This is the meaning of the ten Thiru-Padal-s of the Potri Thiru-Thandagam.

Following this, the twelfth Thiru-Thandagam, Thiru-Vadi Thiru-Thandagam, is arranged as a Thiru-Pathigam. We will contemplate it next. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 341. Thirunindra Sarukkam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We have contemplated eleven of the thirteen Thiru-Pathigams composed by Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar in Thiru-Adigai. Currently, this is the twelfth Thiru-Pathigam. It is called Thiruvadi Thandagam, or Thiruvadi Thiru-Thandagam.

This Thiru-Pathigam is named Thiruvadi Thiru-Thandagam because it praises the nature of the sacred feet of Lord Shiva. The sacred feet of the Lord signify the pervasive grace of God. It is our tradition to metaphorically refer to the pervasive grace of God as His sacred feet. In each verse of these Pathigams, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar extols the sacred feet, describing their greatness. He describes it. This is compiled as the sixth Thiru-Pathigam in the sixth Thiru-Murai.

Now, the Thiru-Pathigam.

First verse: “Aravanaiyaan sindhiththu aratrum adi arumaraiyaan sennikku aniyaam adi saravanaththaan kaithozhuthu saarum adi saarndhaarkkellaam saranaam adi paravuvaar paavam paraikkum adi pathinkanangalum paadum adi thiraiviravu thenkedila naadan adi Thiru-Veerattaanaththu em selvan adi.” Its meaning: The sacred feet of our Lord Shiva, who graciously resides in Thiru-Adigai Veerattanam, where the Kedila river flows, are meditated upon and praised by Thirumal. They adorn the heads of Brahma. The sacred feet are approached and worshipped by Murugapperuman. The history of Murugapperuman performing Shiva Puja in Thiru-Sengalur and Thiru-Sendur (also known as Thiru-Chendil) is found in the Kanda Puranam. Such are the sacred feet of Shiva, worshipped and approached by Murugapperuman.

These sacred feet offer refuge to all devotees who hold them as their support. They remove the sins of those who worship them. They are sung by the eighteen hosts of celestials.

Now, verse number two: “Koduvinaiyaar endrum kurugaa adi kuraindhadaindhaar aazhaamai kaakkum adi padu muzhavam paani payitrum adi pathaiththezhundha vem kootrai paaindha adi kadumuranaeru oordhaan kalar sevadi kadal vaiyam kaa.” The sacred feet are desired by Thirumal, who protects the world surrounded by the sea. The sacred feet are adorned by the crescent moon. The sacred feet never leave the Thiru-Veerattam of Kedila. The sacred feet of Shiva, who rides on a bull, and who is enshrined in Thiru-Adigai Veerattanam on the banks of the Kedila river, can never be approached by those with evil deeds. They protect those who seek refuge, preventing them from perishing.

They teach the beating of drums and the rhythm of music. They leaped upon Yama, the fierce god of death, who rose in fury. They are desired and praised by Thirumal, who performs the act of protecting this world surrounded by the sea.

Now, verse number three: “Vaithazhuvaar kaamam poi pogaa adi vanja valaippaadu ondru illaa adi.” The sacred feet, which we worship with our hands and see, transcend all calculations and accounts. The sacred feet, which we worship with ghee, pierce through the vast sky and stand firm. The sacred feet of the Lord of the divine river Kedila, our Lord of Thiru-Veerattanam. The sacred feet of Shiva do not fulfill the desires of those who wake up reviling the Lord.

Here, the Lord’s power of concealment is sung. The sacred feet of the Lord are not caught in the net of deceit. They offer us the opportunity to worship with our hands, praise with our tongues, and see with our inner eye. These sacred feet transcend the limits of calculation by worldly beings. As devotees, we worship with our bodies, praise with our tongues, and offer ghee with our hands. They are long, They are the sacred feet that pervade the vast heavens and are omnipresent.

Now, verse number four: “Arumbiththa sengnyaayiraikkum adi azhagazhudhalaaga arul sevadi surumbiththa vandinangal soozhndha adi somanaiyum kaalanaiyum kaaindha adi perumbiththar koodi pithatrum adi pizhaiththaar pizhaippariya valla adi thirundhu neer thenkedila naadan adi Thiru-Veerattaanaththu em selvan adi.” The sacred feet of our Lord Shiva, who is enshrined in Thiru-Veerattanam, are like the red sun that appears in the morning, causing lotuses to bloom, in terms of color and light. The beauty of those sacred feet is such that it cannot be captured in a painting. They bestow grace upon devotees. They provide an opportunity for bees and beetles to swarm around them. They are the sacred feet that raged against the god of death. They are the sacred feet praised by a multitude of greatly devoted devotees.

They are the sacred feet capable of discerning the faults of those who have erred.

Now, verse number five: “Oru kaalaththu ondraagi nindra adi oozhithoru oozhi uyarndha adi poru kazhalum pal silambum aarkkum adi pugazhvaar pugazhthagaiya valla adi irunilaththaar inbutru angu eththum adi inbutraar itta poo aerum adi Thiru-Adigai then Kedila naadan adi Thiru-Veerattaanaththu em selvan adi.” The sacred feet of our Lord Shiva, the Lord of Thiru-Adigai Veerattanam in Kedila Nadu, stand as one during creation and remain in their own state during dissolution, not engaging in Maya. The sacred feet are arranged so that one anklet sounds on one foot and another on the other. They are the sacred feet capable of preventing the praises of those who praise from reaching an end. They offer an opportunity for the inhabitants of this great earth to rejoice and praise. They are the sacred feet that bear the flowers offered by such joyful devotees. Verse number six: “Thirumagarkku senthaamaraiyaam adi sirandhavarkkuth thenaay vilaikkum adi porulavarkku pon uraiyaay nindra adi pugazhvaar pugazhthagaiya valla adi uru irandu ondrodu ondru ovvaa adi uruvendru unarappadaadha adi Thiru-Adigai then Kedila naadan adi Thiru-Veerattaanaththu em selvan adi.” The sacred feet of our Lord Shiva, the Lord of Thiru-Adigai Veerattanam in Kedila Nadu, are like a red lotus to Thirumagal.

To excellent devotees, they are sweet like honey. To the wealthy, they are a touchstone, discerning their ability to spend their wealth. They are the sacred feet capable of preventing the praises of those who praise from reaching their limit. The two feet, right and left, are arranged as male and female, not resembling each other. They are the sacred feet that transcend the states of form and formlessness, unable to be perceived as having a form as their inherent nature.

Now, verse number seven: “Urai maalai ellaam udaiya adi uraiyaal unarappadaadha adi varai maadhai vaadaamai vaikkum adi vaanvargal thaam vanangi vaazhththum adi arai maaththiraiyil adangum adi agalam alakkil paarillaa adi karaimaang kalikedila naadan adi kamal veeratta kapaaliyadi.” The sacred feet of Shiva, who graciously resides in Thiru-Veerattanam, fragrant with blossoms, in the land where the Kedila river flows with the great clamor of people on its banks, They are the sacred feet of Shiva, who holds the skull. They possess garlands of words, both songs and prose. They are the sacred feet that cannot be fully comprehended by words. They keep Uma Devi joyful and unwithered. They are worshipped and praised by the celestials. They are the sacred feet that are contained within the half-measure sound of the Pranava.

They are the sacred feet that pervade everywhere, their expanse immeasurable by anyone.

Now, verse number eight: “Narumalaraay naaru malarchchevadi naduvaay ulaga naadaayavadi seri kadhirum thingalumay nindra adi theeththiralaay ulle thigazhndha adi marumadhiyai maasu kazhuvum adi mandhiramum thandhiramumaay adi serikedila naadar perumaanadi Thiru-Veerattaanaththu em selvanadi.” The sacred feet of our Lord Shiva of Thiru-Veerattanam, The sacred feet of our Lord Shiva of Thiru-Veerattanam are adorned with fragrant flowers. They manifest righteousness and justice as their form, bringing about worldly and national affairs. In the world, they stand as the sun and moon, providing external light. They illuminate the hearts of yogis as a mass of light. They cleansed the blemish of the moon. They are mantras and the actions that implement them.

Now, verse number nine: “Aniyanavum seyyanavum allaavadi adiyaarkkarku aar amudamaay adi panibavarkku paangaaga valla adi patratraar patrum pavala adi maniyadi ponnadi maanpaam adi marundhaaypini theerkka valla adi thanipaadu than Kedila naadan adi thagaisaar veerattaththu thalaivan adi.” The sacred feet of Shiva, the Lord of Thiru-Adigai Veerattanam, The sacred feet of Shiva, the Lord of Thiru-Adigai Veerattanam, are near to devotees and far from non-devotees. They are like rare nectar to devotees. They are capable of being a support to those who worship. They are coral-colored sacred feet, clung to by sages who are free from worldly attachments. They are sacred feet of immeasurable greatness, like gems and gold. They are capable of completely curing the disease of birth, acting as medicine.

Now, the tenth verse: “An thaamarai podhu alarndha adi arakkanaiyum aatral azhiththa adi mundhaagi munne mulaiththa adi muzhangazhalaay neenda em moorththi adi pandhaadu mel viralaal paagan adi pavalaththadavaraiye polvaan adi vendhaar sudalai neeru aadum adi veerattam kaadhal vimalan adi.”

Lord Shiva is in the form of a towering blaze of fire. Our Lord Shiva, who is the consort of Parvati with soft fingers that play with a ball, who is like a great coral mountain, and who is the pure one residing in Adigai Veerattam, has sacred feet that have bloomed like lotus flowers. Those sacred feet destroyed the power of Ravana. Those sacred feet appeared before all other creations. They are the sacred feet that are smeared with the ashes of those cremated in the cremation ground.

These are the ten verses of the Thiruvadi Thiru-Thandagam and their meanings.

Our contemplation continues. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 342. We have contemplated twelve of the thirteen Thiru-Pathigams composed by Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar in Thiru-Adigai.

Now, we must contemplate the thirteenth Thiru-Pathigam. This is called Kaappu Thiru-Thandagam. Each verse in this Thiru-Pathigam concludes with the phrase ‘the Lord’s protection.’ Therefore, it is named Kaappu Thiru-Thandagam. Kaappu means protection. It means to be under the Lord’s protection. This is a metonymy, referring to the protected place.

It was composed by Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, describing how the Lord, in this southern direction of great penance, in various places, protects us. He mentions many sacred places throughout the verses of this Pathigam, where the Lord resides and protects us.

Thus, the essence of this Pathigam is that the Lord resides in many sacred places and protects us.

Therefore, it is named Kaappu Thiru-Thandagam. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar has listed many sacred places in this Thiru-Pathigam.

However, since each verse mentions ‘Kedila Veerattam’ and ‘Thiru-Adigai,’ it has been compiled among the Thevarams pertaining to the Thiru-Adigai sacred place. The phrases ‘Selvappunal,’ ‘Siraiyaarpunal,’ ‘Theerththappunal,’ and many others describe the excellence of the Kedila river’s water. Since Thiru-Veerattam is mentioned in connection with the Kedila, this Thiru-Pathigam has been compiled as a Thevaram pertaining to the Thiru-Adigai sacred place. This Thiru-Pathigam is compiled as the seventh Thiru-Pathigam in the sixth Thiru-Murai.

Now, the Thiru-Pathigam.

First verse: “Selvappunal Kedila Veerattamum Sitraemum Perunthan Kutraalamum Thillaichitrambalamum Then Koodalum Then Aanaikkaavum Siraappalliyum Nalloorum Devan Kudi Marugalum Nallavargal Thozhudheththum Naaraiyoorum Kal Alagu Nedumburuvak Kapaalam Endhik Kattangaththodu Uraivaar Kaappukkale.” In this first verse, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sings about several sacred places where Lord Shiva resides.

Lord Shiva resides in Thiru-Adigai Veerattam, which is blessed with wealth by the water-rich Kedila river.

The Lord resides in the sacred place called Sitraemam.

The Lord resides in the cool sacred place of Kutraalam. He resides in Thillaichitrambalam. He resides in Madurai in the south. He resides in the beautiful sacred place called Thiru-Aanaikka. He resides in Siraappalli, also known as Thiru-Siraappalli. Nalloor, Devan Kudi (this is the sacred place Thiru-Thirundhu Devan Kudi), Thiru-Marugal, and Thiru-Naaraiyoor, worshipped and praised by the virtuous, are places where the Lord resides.

He is Shiva, who holds a skull with long eyebrows and the weapon called Kattangam. He graciously resides in all these sacred places. Verse number two: “Theerththappunal Kedila Veerattamum Thiru-Koval Veerattam Thiru-Vennainalloor Aarththaruviveezh Sunai Neer Annaamalai Arayani Nalloorum Araneriye Eththumingal.” The Lord, who stands to be praised by you, resides in Thiru-Idaimarudhu, Thiru-Innampar, Thiru-Ekamparam, and Thiru-Kailasam, with its dense, beautiful groves, and is the protection of the one with an eye on his forehead. In this verse, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sings about the sacred places where Lord Shiva resides: Thiru-Adigai Veerattam, Thiru-Kovalur Veerattam, Thiru-Vennainalloor, Thiru-Annaamalai with its roaring waterfalls and spring water, Thiru-Arayani Nalloor, Thiru-Araneri, Thiru-Idaimarudhu, Thiru-Innampar, Thiru-Ekamparam, and Thiru-Kailasam. He sings, “Praise our Lord in these places.” The term ‘Araneri’ here not only refers to the path of Shiva but also to the sacred place Aaroor Araneri in Thiruvarur.

Now, the third verse: Siraiyaarpunal Kedila Veerattamum Thiru-Paadhirippuliyoor Thiru-Aamaaththoor Thuraiyaar Vana Munigal Aththanindra Sotrutthurai Thurutthi Neyththaanamum Arayaar Punal Ozhugu Kaaviri Soozh Ayyaatru Amudhar Pazhanam Nalla Karaiyaarpuzhil Pudaisoozh Kaanapperum Kazhukkundrum Thammudaiya Kaappukkale. In this verse, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sings about the sacred places where the Lord resides: Thiru-Adigai Thiru-Veerattam with the Kedila river, Thiru-Paadhirippuliyoor, Thiru-Aamaaththoor, Thiru-Sotrutthurai, Thiru-Thurutthi, Thiru-Neyththaanam, Thiru-Kaanaapperur (also known as Kaalaiyaar Kovil), and Thiru-Kazhukkundram. The Lord, who is like nectar, resides in Thiru-Aiyaatru, surrounded by the flowing waters of the Kaveri.

Now, the fourth verse: “Thiraiyaarpun.” The Kedila Veerattam with its wavy waters, Thiruvarur, Thevoor, Thiru-Nellikka, Thiru-Otthiyoor, where the eloquent worship, Otthoor, Maarpere, Maanthurai, Maanadhi surrounded by mountain waterfalls, Maakkaalam, Kedaaram, Maameru, and Kadambanthurai, surrounded by the flowing waters of the Kaveri, are the places where the Lord resides, and they are His protection. In this verse, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sings about the sacred places where the Lord resides: Thiru-Adigai Veerattam, where the Kedila river flows, Thiruvarur, Thiru-Thevoor, Thiru-Nellikka, Thiru-Otthiyoor, worshipped by eloquent sages, Thiru-Otthoor, Thiru-Maalperu, Thiru-Maanthurai, Maanadhi surrounded by mountain waterfalls, Maakkaalam, Kedaaram, and Maameru. The sacred places of Shiva, who is Kadambavaneswarar in Kadambanthurai, also known as Kadambar Kovil, surrounded by the Kaveri, are mentioned. He sings. Maanadhi, Maakkaalam, and Maameru in this verse are Vaippu-Thalams (places mentioned in devotional hymns but not necessarily major pilgrimage sites).

Now, verse number five: “Sezhuneer Punal Kedila Veerattamum Thripuraanthagam Thennaar Dheveechcharam Kozhuneer Pudai Suzikkum Kottukkaavum Kudamookkum Kokaranam Kolakkaavum Pazhi Neermaiyillaa Punangaattoorum Panaiyoor Payatroor Paraayththuraiyum Kazhuneer Madhuviriyum Kaalingamum Ganapatheechcharaththaar Tham Kaappukkale.” In this verse, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sings about the sacred places: Thiru-Adigai Veerattam on the Kedila bank, Thripuraanthagam, the beautiful Dheveechcharam, Kottukkaa with its swirling waters, Thiru-Kudamookku (Kumbakonam), Thiru-Kokaranam, Thiru-Kolakkaa, Thiru-Panangaattoor, which is beyond reproach, Thiru-Panaiyoor, Thiru- Payatroor, Thiru-Paraayththurai, and Kaalingam, where honey flows from water lilies. Lord Shiva, who resides in all these places, has graciously chosen Ganapatheechcharam. He sings that these are all sacred places of Lord Shiva.

Here, Thripuraanthagam, Dheveechcharam, Kottukkaa, and Kaalingam are Vaippu-Thalams. Ganapatheechcharam is Thiru-Sengattangudi, the sacred place where the history of Siruththonda Nayanar took place. Kudamookku refers to Kudanthai, also known as Kumbakonam.

Now, verse number six: “Dheivappunal Kedila Veerattamum Sezhunthan Pidavoorum Sendru Nindru Pavvan Thiriyum Paruppadhamum Pariyaloor Veerattam Paavanaasam Mavvam Thiraiyum Mani Mutthamum Maraikkaadum Vaaimoor Valanjoliyum Kavvai Varivandu Pannae Paadum Kazhippaalai Thammudaiya Kaappukkale.” In this verse, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sings about the sacred places of Shiva: Thiru-Adigai Veerattam on the Kedila bank, the prosperous and cool Pidavoor, Thiru-Paruppadham (Srisailam), which is approached by ocean floods, Thiru-Pariyaloor Veerattam, Paavanaasam, Thiru-Manimuttham, Thiru-Maraikkaadu, Thiru-Vaaimoor, Thiru-Valanjoli, and Thiru-Kazhippaalai, where noisy striped bees sing melodies. He sings that Lord Shiva resides in these places. Pidavoor and Paavanaasam here are Vaippu-Thalams. Pidavoor is in Chola Nadu. It is the place where Maasaththanar revealed the Gnana Ula, which Cheraman Perumal Nayanar heard in Kailasam, to the earthly world. Manimuttham is also a Vaippu-Thalam.

Now, verse number seven: “Thenneer Punal Kedila Veerattamum Seerkaazhi Vallam Thiru-Vettiyum.” Unneeraar Edagamum Ooral Ampar Uraiyoor Naraiyoor Arananalloor Vinnaar Vidaiyaar Vilamar Vennni Meeyachchoor Velimizhalai Mikka Kannaar Nudhalaar Karapuramum Kaappaaliyaar Avardham Kaappukkale.“ The sacred places mentioned in this verse are Thiru-Adigai Veerattam, Seerkaazhi, Thiru-Vallam, and Thiru-Vetti. This Thiru-Vetti is the sacred place Thiru-Vetteeswarampettai in Chennai. Next are Thiru-Edagam, Thiru-Ooral, Thiru-Ampar, Thiru-Uraiyoor, Thiru-Naraiyoor, Thiru-Arananalloor, Thiru-Vilamar, Vennni, Thiru-Meeyachchoor, Thiru-Velimizhalai, and Karapuram. Lord Shiva, who holds the skull, graciously resides in these sacred places. Thiru-Vetti, Arananalloor, and Karapuram here are Vaippu-Thalams.

Uraiyoor is the sacred place Thiru-Mukkeechcharam.

Next, Thus, hymn number eight: Thiru-Kedilam Veerattam, Thindeeswaram, Thiru-Pugalur, Thiru-Idaithanam, Eiyeeswaram, Nallemkoodal, Thiru-Kodikka, Kuranganil Muttram, Kurumbalaa, and Thiru-Karonaam, which are meditated upon and praised by those who have attained Sakthi Nipada for spiritual knowledge, are the sacred abodes of Lord Shiva. These are Thiru-Adigai Veerattam, Thiru-Thindeeswaram, Thiru-Pugalur, Thiru-Idaithanam, Eiyeeswaram, Emam Koodal, Thiru-Kodikka, Kuranganil Muttram, Kurumbalaa, and Nagai-Karonaam and Kudanthai-Karonaam, which are meditated upon and praised by those who have attained Sakthi Nipada for spiritual knowledge. These are the sacred abodes where Lord Shiva, who has a host of Bhootas and performs the dance, resides. The term ‘Koodal’ here refers to Madurai. Thiru-Thindeeswaram, Idaithanam, and Nallemam are all Vaippu Sthalams (places mentioned in hymns but not necessarily visited by the Nayanars). Kurumbalaa refers to Kurumbalaanathar in Thiru-Kutralam.

Now, the ninth hymn: Thiru-Kedilam Veerattam, Thiru-Kattuppalli, Thiru-Venkaadu, Pai-Ngeeli, Panthanai Nallur, Paasoor Nallam, Thiru-Nindriyur, Thiru-Nedungalam, Thiru-Nelvennai, Thiru-Nelvaayil, and Kadavur Veerattam are the sacred abodes where Lord Shiva resides, as sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar in this hymn.

Now, the tenth hymn. The hymn mentions Thiru-Kedilam Veerattam, Thiru-Vanchiyam, Thiru-Nallaru, Ayoganthi surrounded by beautiful groves, Aakkur, Aavur, Aanpatti, Idaichuram, Thalaichangadu, Karaveeram, and Kadambur Karakkoyil as the sacred abodes of our Peruman. In this tenth hymn, the sacred abodes mentioned by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, which the Lord has lovingly accepted, are Thiru-Adigai Veerattam, Thiru-Vanchiyam, Thiru-Nallaru, and the Thiru-Sthalam called Ayoganthi, which is also known as Ayavanthi. This is the name of the temple in Thiru-Sathamangai.

Also, Thiru-Aakkur, Thiru-Aavur, Thiru-Aanpatti. This Thiru-Aanpatti is the Thiru-Sthalam called Thiru-Perur, a Kongu Nadu Thiru-Sthalam near Coimbatore. Thiru-Idaichuram, Thiru-Thalaichangadu, and the fragrant Karaveeram. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings that the sacred abodes of Kadambur, which has a Chakra temple, are the places where our Lord lovingly resides.

Now, hymn number eleven: Thiru-Kedilam Veerattam, Thiru-Chemponpalli, Thiru-Poovanam, Mananjeri worshipped by celestials, Mathil Anjai Mahaalam, Varanasi, Veguleeswaram praised by others, Ilangar Paruppatham, Thodainar Solai, Kaanar Mayilar, Karumari, and Karaimidatrar are the sacred abodes of our Lord. In this eleventh hymn, the sacred abodes mentioned by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar are Thiru-Adigai Veerattam, Thiru-Chemponpalli, Thiru-Poovanam, Thiru-Manjeri, Thiru-Unjai Mahaalam, Varanasi, also known as Kashi, Veguleeswaram, Thiru-Paruppatham, also known as Srisailam, and Karumari, among others.

Now, the twelfth hymn. The twelfth hymn, sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, mentions Thiru-Kedilam Veerattam, Thiru-Alappur, Siddhavadam to the south, Ma-Niruppam, Mylappil, Brahmapuram, Suzhiyal, Pennagadam, Thiru-Kalathi, and Kailayam as the sacred abodes where the Lord lovingly resides. These are the sacred abodes that Lord Shiva has lovingly accepted, as sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar.

This is the Kaappu Thiru-Thandagam. These are the twelve hymns from the Thiru-Thandagam and the sacred abodes mentioned in those hymns where the Lord lovingly resides and protects us.

Let us go on meditating.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 343, Thiru-Nindra Sarukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We saw that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar composed thirteen Thiru-Pathigams at Thiru-Adigai at this time. We have meditated on those thirteen Thiru-Pathigams and their meanings. As we have already seen, we have examined the Thiru-Pathigams ‘Kootraayina Vaaru’, ‘Sunnavan Santhana Santham’, and ‘Ezhai Thiru-Thandagam’ in the context of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar’s history and the circumstances in which he sang them.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar composed a total of sixteen Thiru-Pathigams for Thiru-Adigai Veerattanam. In addition to this, in the history of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, we have also seen the general Thiru-Pathigams ‘Naamarkkum Kodiyallo’, ‘Maasil Veena’, and ‘Sotrunai Thiyan’. We have also seen the three general Thiru-Pathigams, along with his history.

Thus, we have meditated on the hymns pertaining to Thiru-Adigai. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing the history of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. At the time when Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar composed these hymns in Thiru-Adigai and was performing his service there, the Jain king, the ruler of that country, who belonged to the Jain religion, listened to the words of the Jains and tried to inflict suffering on Thiru-Navukkarasar. That king, now, due to the removal of his old karmic bonds, was freed from the suffering of the Jain religion and came to Thiru-Adigai. He bowed down to Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, abandoned the Jains, and joined the feet of Lord Shiva. He entered the Saiva religion.

That Pallava king, who had listened to the words of the ignorant Jains, had continuously committed evil deeds until then. His causing suffering by listening to the Jains was due to his old karmic bonds.

Now, it was time for these old karmic bonds to be removed.

Therefore, he was freed from the state of suffering caused by the Jains, and his bonds were broken and destroyed.

Thus, he now understood the truth and was freed from the suffering of Jainism. He arrived at Thiru-Adigai. Until then, he had committed offenses against Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar out of ignorance, listening to the Jains.

Therefore, to atone for that sin, he bowed down to Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar and asked for forgiveness.

Thus, after seeking forgiveness, he entered the Saiva religion and became one who serves Lord Shiva. To attain the path of Shiva, a Guru’s guidance is essential.

Therefore, that Pallava king first bowed down to Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, and as guided by him, the king embraced the Saiva path of loving devotion to Lord Shiva’s feet. He entered the Saiva religion. The Jains, who did not know the path to liberation, their words were all false. The Pallava king, also known as Kadava Arasan, now realized the truth, seeing that all that the Jains had said was false. He abandoned the Jain religion, which makes one perceive as real things that are not real, and embraced the Saiva religion, which grants liberation. He entered the Saiva religion.

That king, having entered the Saiva religion, demolished the Jain schools and monasteries in Pataliputra, which was near Thiru-Padiripuliyur at that time, and brought the materials to Thiru-Adigai to build a new temple for Lord Shiva called Gunaparaveecharam. This Gunaparaveecharam is the name of that temple. It is a tradition for a temple to be named after the king who built it. For example, the temple built by Rajaraja Chola in Thanjavur is named Rajarajeswaram.

Similarly, the temple built by Rajendra Chola, who was known as Gangai Konda Chola, is named Gangai Konda Choleeswaram. The name is prevalent.

Accordingly, this Kadava king, that is, this Pallava king, was called Gunaparan. He also had the name Mahendravarman. This name Mahendravarman is found in inscriptions. History tells us that he built many cave temples, that is, many cave temples carved out of rock. This is the history we learn from inscriptions. In the Sanskrit inscription of his time found in the Thiru-Chirappalli cave, his act of converting from Jainism to Saivism is mentioned.

Another name for this king is Gunaparan. He is also known as Gunatharan.

Therefore, the temple built by this king, Gunaparan, is named Gunaparaveecharam. How did he build this Shiva temple called Gunaparaveecharam? He demolished the Jain schools and monasteries in Pataliputra and built a temple for Lord Shiva here. Even though the king was capable of building a new temple, Sivakavimani explains why he demolished the Jain monasteries and schools and built a temple here. His intention was to destroy the means that deluded the world with falsehoods.

Therefore, he decided to destroy the Jain schools and monasteries, which were the means that spread falsehoods and caused worldly delusion.

Furthermore, he wanted to transform those very things that had been instruments of spreading falsehoods and deluding the world into sacred instruments.

Therefore, he built a temple for Lord Shiva using them.

Thus, this act illustrates his conversion from Jainism to Saivism and his subsequent steadfastness in the Saiva religion.

Similarly, in Thiru-Perur, which is currently near Coimbatore in Kongu Nadu, Maran Sadaiyan built a temple for Thirumal twelve hundred years ago. It later fell into disrepair.

Then, about five hundred years ago, a person named Thiru-Kanambi Maathaiyan took the stones from that temple and built the steps for the sacred tank in front of the current Perur Patteeswarar temple. This history is also present there.

Similarly, there are other histories as well. We can also meditate on all of them here. On this day, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, the sage Vakeesa, performs services in Thiru-Adigai for many days. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar performed services with his mind, speech, and body. In this hymn, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar as Vakeesa Thiru-Muni. The term ‘Muni’ indicates the complete ascetic state attained by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. ‘Vakeesar’ is the Sanskrit equivalent of ‘Naavukku Arasu’.

In this period, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar intends to embark on a pilgrimage from Thiru-Adigai to visit and worship many sacred places where Lord Shiva resides, and to sing hymns praising His name and perform service. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar had been in Thiru-Adigai for many days, performing the physical service of Uzhavara Pani and meditation. There were no days when he did not perform service; he served every day, every hour, every moment. He performed his sacred service so that good days followed one after another, without any evil days interrupting. As he was doing this, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar set out from Thiru-Adigai to visit many sacred places where the Lord resides. As explained in the twelfth Sutra of Siva Gnana Bodham, ‘Aalayam Thaanum Arananath Thozhume’ is that twelfth Sutra.

Accordingly, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar undertakes this pilgrimage to demonstrate it in his life. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar was a teacher who came to explain ‘Sariyai’ in ‘Gnanam’.

Therefore, to demonstrate the nature of the enlightened in his own life, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar set out to visit and worship many sacred places and sing hymns, according to the twelfth Sutra of Siva Gnana Bodham, ‘Aalayam Thaanum Aranenath Thozhume’.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, who set out from Thiru-Adigai, worshipped many sacred places near Thiru-Adigai, such as Thiru-Vennainallur, Thiru-Aamathur, Thiru-Kovalur, and others, and sang many rich Tamil hymns. ‘Thiru-Adigai Pathi Marungu Thiru-Vennainallurum Arulu Thiru-Aamathur Thiru-Kovalur Muthalam Maruvu Thiru-Pathi Piravum Vanangi Valaththamizh Paadi Perugu Viruppudan Vida’. Sekkizhar Peruman’s composition states that he arrived at Pennagadam, where the Lord rejoices.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman sings that he worshipped Thiru-Vennainallur, Thiru-Aamathur, Thiru-Kovalur, and other sacred places, and then arrived at Pennagadam.

Here, Thiru-Vennainallur is mentioned as the first sacred place Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar visited after leaving Thiru-Adigai. We have already meditated on the special features of Thiru-Vennainallur in the history of Sundaramurthy Swamigal, in the section on Thaduthatkonda Puranam. The hymn composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar for Thiru-Vennainallur is not available to us due to our lack of merit.

Here, after worshipping the Lord in Thiru-Vennainallur, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar reaches the sacred place called Thiru-Aamathur. Two hymns composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar for this sacred place are now available to us. This sacred place, Thiru-Aamathur, is the twenty-first among the Thevaram-sung Sthalams in Nadu Nadu. It is a Sthalam sung by all three, Thiru-Gnanasambandhar, Thiru-Navukkarasar, and Sundaramurthy Swamigal. Aamathur is the name of this place. By adding ‘Thiru’ before it, it is called Thiru-Aamathur.

In Sanskrit, it is called Go Mathrupuram. It is a place where the Lord blesses as the mother of cows.

Therefore, it is called Go Mathrupuram. In Tamil, it is Thiru-Aamathur. ‘Cows’ should also be understood as ‘living beings’.

Here, the name of the Lord is Azhagiyanathar, Abirameswarar. The name of the Goddess is Mukthambigai, Azhagiyanayagi. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar praises the Lord here as Azhagan in Thiru-Kurunthogai and Azhagiyare in Thiru-Thandagam. The Theertham is Pampaiyaru. The Sthala Vriksham here is the Vanni tree. This sacred place is near Villupuram in Tamil Nadu.

Those who worshipped here include Bringi Munivar, Sri Rama, Kamadhenu, Thiru-Gnanasambandhar, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, Sundaramurthy Swamigal, Kapiladeva Nayanar, and Paranadeva Nayanar. Dasaratha Rama worshipped the Lord here. In Thiru-Kurunthogai, composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, he sings, ‘Rama also worshipped the Lord’.
