This is the place where Bringi Munivar worshipped and was freed from a curse. This is the history. Bringi Munivar had a vow not to worship Shakti.

Thirumoolar’s saying is that if Shakti blesses, then Sattan’s (Shiva’s) grace will be received. Accordingly, Shakti and Shiva are not different; they are one and the same, being the quality and the qualified.

Therefore, when the Goddess received the left half of Lord Shiva, Bringi Munivar took the form of a beetle and drilled through, worshipping only Lord Shiva. Since he lost Shakti, he suffered from a lack of strength to walk.

At that time, by the grace of Lord Shiva, Bringi Munivar received a third leg. Due to Shakti’s curse, Bringi Munivar stood here as a Vanni tree. As a Vanni tree, By standing and worshipping the Lord, he was freed from the curse by the grace of Lord Shiva. As evidence of this, the Vanni tree stands as the Sthala Vriksham in the corner of the Goddess’s temple. A special feature of this place is that the Swami Sannidhi faces east, and opposite it, the Goddess’s temple faces west, being separate. The Thiru-Vattapparai Shiva Linga Murthy here is very special.

History states that Rama and Sugriva sat before it and made a friendship pact to kill Ravana, with Hanuman as a witness.

The Lord here blesses as a Swayambhu Murthy. The Ambika appears in a standing posture facing west. Inside the temple courtyard are Mal Thuyarthirtha Vinayagar, Murugan, Natarajar, Dakshinamurthy, Lingothbavar, Brahma, Durga, Bikshada. Sahasralingam, Sattanathar, Kasi Viswanathar, Arunachaleswarar, Rama, Sapthamathar, Nalvar, sixty-three Nayanmars, Chandeeswarar temple, Bhairavar, and Navagraha shrines are present. Passing through the gopuram entrance, one sees a large stucco Nandi, a Pathala Nandi, a flagstaff, and a Balipeetam. Inscriptions in the temple belong to the periods of Kopparakesarivarman, Rajaraja I, Rajendra Chola I, Veerarajendra, and Kulothunga I.

Rama, who killed Ravana, performed Abhishekam to Shiva here with Thandatheertham to remove his Brahmmahatthi Dosham. Murugan worshipped Shiva and Parvati here to destroy Surapadman. Vinayagar, Murugan, Parvati Devi, Rama, Sita, Lakshmana, Naradar, Agasthiyar, Vasishtar, Durvasar, Bringu Munivar, Parasarar, Viswa. Vyasar, Romashar, Mathanga Muni, Ashtavasukkal, and Bringi Munivar have worshipped the Lord Shiva of this place. Arunagirinathar has sung about the Murugan of this place in Thiru-Pugal. It is believed that at one time, cows did not have horns, and therefore, wild animals tormented them.

The distressed cows prayed to Shiva here for protection and worshipped Him, and through this, they received horns.

Therefore, this place is called Thiru-Aamathur.

Thus, this place is known as the town that is the mother of cows. It is believed that the Lord of this place, Abirameswarar, blesses with a cow’s hoof mark on His head. These are the special features of the Thiru-Aamathur Sthalam.

We will continue to meditate on the two Thiru-Pathigams composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar for this Sthalam. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Three Hundred Forty-Four, Thirunindrachcharukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We saw that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar departed from Thiru-Athikai, visited Thiru-Vennainallur, and then arrived at Thiru-Aamaththur. We contemplated the special features of Thiru-Aamaththur Sthalam. There are two Thiru-Pathikams composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar for this Thiru-Aamaththur Thiru-Thalam. The first Thiru-Pathikam begins with “Maamaaththaakiya.” This Thiru-Pathikam is compiled as the forty-fourth Thiru-Pathikam in the fifth Thiru-Murai.

It is a Thiru-Kurunthokai Thiru-Pathikam.

Now, the verses of the Thiru-Pathikam and their meaning.

The first verse: “Maamaaththaakiya maal ayan maalkodu thaama thediyum kaankilar thaazhmudi Aamaaththur arane arulaay” endra emaappu They attained and saw the Lord. Thirumal and Brahma, in their great quarrel and arrogant delusion, searched on their own, but Shiva-Peruman was not found by them. They could not see the sacred feet or the sacred crown of the Peruman.

But after repeatedly and lovingly calling out, “O Arane of Aamaththur, bestow your grace,” they saw the Lord.

Now, verse number two: “Sandhiyaanai samaathi seyvaar thankal pundhiyaanai puththelar thozhappadum Andhiyaanai Aamaaththur azhakanai sindhiyaathavar theevinaiyaalarē” Its meaning: Shiva-Peruman is worshipped at dawn and dusk. He resides in the intellect of those who follow the path of yoga. Shiva-Peruman is worshipped by the Devas. He has a sacred form of crimson color, like the evening sky. Such a Shiva-Peruman resides as a beautiful one in Aamaththur. Those who do not contemplate such a beautiful one of Aamaththur are indeed evil-doers, he sings.

Now, the third verse: “Kaama tham enum kaar valaippattu naan pōmaa thai ariyaathu pulampuven Aamaaththur arane endru azhaiththalum thēmaa theenkani pōla thiththikkumē” Its meaning: Caught in the dark net of desire and wealth, I, a devotee, lament, not knowing the way to escape. I call out, “O Arane of Aamaththur!” As soon as I call, the Peruman becomes sweet like a delicious mango fruit.

Now, the fourth verse: Fearing to fall into the net of the five elements, I, too, contemplated the beautiful one of Aamaththur in my heart. As soon as that thought came, the treacherous rivers dried up, behold! Its meaning: I feared falling into that net made of the five great elements. I, a devotee, contemplated the beautiful one of Aamaththur in my heart. At the moment that thought came to me, the treacherous rivers dried up. You too, behold! he sings.

Now, the fifth sacred verse: “Kuraa mannum kuzhalaal oru kooranaar araamannum sadaiyaan Thiru-Aamaaththur Iraamanum vazhipaadu seyya niraamaiyan thannai naalum ninaminē” Its meaning: Shiva-Peruman has Uma Devi, whose hair is adorned with Kuraa flowers, as one part of his body. He has a sacred matted lock where snakes reside. Such a Shiva-Peruman is the Shiva-Peruman worshipped by Rama in Thiru-Aamaththur. He is Niraimaiyan (one without blemish). Contemplate such a Peruman daily, he sings. This Thiru-Aamaththur Sthalam is a place where Rama worshipped Shiva-Peruman.

It has such a Sthala Puranam.

Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasar sings about that history in this verse.

Now, verse number six: “Piththanai perunthēvar thozhappadum aththanai ani Aamaaththur mēviya muththinai adiyēn ul muyarralum paththi vellam paranthathu kaanminai” Its meaning: I, a devotee, strive to think in my heart of that Peruman, who is mad (with love for devotees), the master worshipped by great Devas, the pearl-like Shiva-Peruman who lovingly resides in beautiful Aamaththur. A flood of devotion arose and spread from it; you shall see it.

Now, verse number seven: He whose sacred body is covered with sacred ash, who has a beautiful woman as one part, who has a river (Ganga) in his cool, beautiful matted locks, such a Shiva-Peruman lovingly resides in beautiful Aamaththur. He is mounted on a bull (Rishabha Vahanam). He is the Lord who rules over us.

Now, the eighth sacred verse: “Pannil paadalgal paththi sey viththakarkku anniththaakum amuthinai Aamaaththur sannippaanai thamarkku aniththaayathōr kannīr paavai annaan avan kaanminē” Its meaning: Shiva-Peruman is like sweet nectar to those skilled in singing songs with melody and devotion to him. He is like sweet nectar to those who skillfully sing songs with melody and devotion to him. He resides in Aamaththur. He is very close to his devotees, like the pupil of an eye. Behold him!

Now, verse number nine: “Kundar peeligal kollum gunamilaa mindarōdu ena vērupaḍuththu uyya konda naathan kulir punal veerattaththu anḍanaaridham Aamaaththur kaanpinē” Its meaning: He is the Lord who separated me from the Jains, who are Kundars (those who do not wear clothes) and arrogant ones who do not possess the quality of killing peacock feathers, and saved me. He is Shiva-Peruman, the Lord of the Devas, residing in Veeratttam, surrounded by cool waters. His abode is Aamaththur. Behold! he sings.

Now, the tenth verse: “Vaanam saadum The moon, along with the snake, was placed in his matted locks without fear. He is the Lord of Aamaththur, who accepts honey and other Panchamirtham, tender coconut water, and Panchagavyam as ablutions.

“Now, verse number eleven: “Vidalaiyaay vilangal aduththaan mudi adaraōr viral oondriya Aamaaththur idamathaakkonda eesanukku en ullam idamathaakkondu inpurriruppanē” Its meaning: When the unruly Ravana tried to lift Thiru-Kailayam, Shiva-Peruman pressed down with one finger so that his crowns were crushed. He is the Lord who has Aamaththur as his abode. I, a devotee, reside in joy, making my heart the abode for that Lord, sings Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar.

“These are the eleven verses of this Pathikam and their meanings. The note for this Pathikam is: Brahma and Thirumal, who could not find Shiva, who is unknowable through ignorance, saw him by worshipping him as “Arulāy.” Those who do not contemplate such a Shiva-Peruman are evil-doers. I contemplated Shiva-Peruman within. As soon as I did, the rivers dried up, and a flood of devotion surged. He is the Lord who rules over us, like the pupil of an eye.

“He is the one who performs the five dances. His abode is Aamaththur. I will reside in joy, making my heart his abode. As soon as I called out “Arane,” it became sweet like a mango fruit.

“Therefore, you too, contemplate that Shiva-Peruman daily, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar guides the people of the world in this Thiru-Pathikam, the Aamaththur Thiru-Pathikam. There are two Thiru-Pathikams composed for this Thiru-Aamaththur Thiru-Thalam, and we have seen one of them.

“We will continue to contemplate the second Thiru-Pathikam.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Today is Vaikasi Poosam, the auspicious day of the Guru Puja of Sekkizhar Swamigal, the author of Periya Puranam. I bow to the golden sacred feet of Sekkizhar Swamigal, who bestowed upon us the Thiru-Thondar Puranam, known as Periya Puranam, which we contemplate daily, and who has kept us all on the path of Shiva. Today marks one year since the contemplation of Periya Puranam began. Last year, on the auspicious day following Sekkizhar Swamigal’s Guru Puja, Vaikasi Poosam, we began contemplating Periya Puranam. Today marks the completion of one year.

Throughout this year, we have been listening to and contemplating Periya Puranam daily. By the grace of the Peruman and the grace of the Guru, in between, during the month of Margazhi, due to the Thiru-Vembavai festival, the Arudra Utsavam, we contemplated Thiru-Vembavai for ten days. This was in accordance with the tradition that other Thiru-Murais should be preserved.

Therefore, excluding those ten days, we have been listening to and contemplating Periya Puranam daily throughout this entire year. On this auspicious day, I praise and worship the sacred grace of Shiva-Peruman. I praise and worship the grace of the Guru. I bow to the sacred feet of Sundaramurthi Swamigal, the author of Thiru-Thonda Thokai, the collection of works that is the source of Periya Puranam. I bow to the sacred feet of Nambiandar Nambi, who compiled and presented it. I bow to the sacred feet of Sekkizhar Swamigal, who expanded upon it.

I bow to the sacred feet of Sivakavimani Ayya Arumuga Navalar Ayya and other great scholars who wrote commentaries on this Periya Puranam. I bow to the sacred feet of our Sath Sangha Guru Natha Vengiyanna, who commanded us to contemplate this in our Sath Sangha, and I offer my gratitude. I express my salutations and countless thanks to Anna, who gave this humble one such a great responsibility and opportunity at this moment. Not only that, but I also bow to the sacred feet of our Sangha, who daily listened to this, gave me many pieces of advice, clarified my doubts, and encouraged me. I also bow to the sacred feet of other revered elders and great souls who are not part of our Sath Sangha but helped me in many ways. I extend my gratitude to everyone at this moment.

Furthermore, to continue contemplating this Periya Puranam, Let us pray for the Guru’s grace and submit our petition at the sacred feet of Shiva-Peruman. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Three Hundred Forty-Six, Thirunindrachcharukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, after worshipping the Lord in Thiru-Aamaththur, performing sacred service, and composing two Thiru-Pathikams, now arrives at the sacred Sthalam called Thiru-Kovalur. This Thiru-Kovalur is one of the Veeratttana Sthalams. Thiru-Kovalur Veerattta Sthalam is the sacred place where the slaying of Anthakasura, one of the eight heroic deeds performed by the Lord, took place. In the Puranam of Meypporul Nayanar, which we have already contemplated, we discussed the special features and Sthala Puranams of Thiru-Kovalur.

Thiru-Kovalur Sthalam is the sacred place where the sacred history of Meypporul Nayanar occurred. In the Malaiyaman country, on the banks of the Pennai River, a king named Malaiyaman Thiru-Mudikari ruled, with Thiru-Kovalur as his capital. It is known from ancient historical texts like Paththuppaattu that this king was one of the Kadaiyezhu Vallalgal (seven last great patrons) praised by Kapilar.

Here, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman undertook a pilgrimage and came here. Of the rich Tamil Pathikams he sang in praise of the Lord of Thiru-Kovalur, only one Pathikam is currently available to us. This Thiru-Pathikam begins with “Setthaiyēn Sidambanaayēn.” It is compiled as the sixty-ninth Thiru-Pathikam in the fourth Thiru-Murai. The tune is Thiru-Nērisai. The general note for this Thiru-Pathikam is as follows: Humans, deluded and unaware of the evils of this birth, serving their senses, immersed in worldly pleasures, and caught in the cage of family, wife, and relatives, and suffering, should change their thoughts from these things and live a righteous life. They should give to those who ask and praise and cling to the Lord.

If they do so, they will attain goodness and joy. This note can be seen throughout this Pathikam. This Sthalam is a place that removes karma.

Therefore, the Pathikam for this Sthalam also carries a similar note.

Now, the Thiru-Pathikam.

The first verse: “Setthaiyēn Sidambanaayēn sediyanēn azhukku paayum potthaiyēn pōtri naalum pukalidam ariyamaattēn eththai naan patti nirkēn irul ara nōkkamaattaa kotthaiyēn seyvathannai O Lord of Koval Veeratttam! Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sings, addressing the Lord of Thiru-Kovalur Veeratttam: “O Peruman, I am like refuse (setthai means useless rubbish).

“Therefore, I am like useless rubbish. I am devoid of any good quality. I am like a dog. I am full of faults. I am putrid. I cherish this body, which is a decaying, dirty, leaking vessel, and protect it every day.

“Therefore, I am unable to know what is truly a place for a soul to reach. I am mentally blind, unable to perceive with my mind to dispel darkness. What should I, a wretched one, do? What should I do?” he sings.

“Now, the second verse: “Thalai sumanthu iru kai naatri tharanikkē poraiyaathaaki nilaiyilaa nenjam thannul niththallum aivar vēndum vilai koduththu arukkamaattēn vēnditrē vēndi eyththēn kulai kol maangkanigal sinthum Kōval Veerattta Neerē” In this second sacred verse, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings: “O Peruman, who resides in Thiru-Kovalur, where mangoes fall in clusters! I carry my head, letting my two hands hang, becoming a burden to the earth. In my unstable heart, my five senses daily demand things, and I live under their influence. I am unable to overcome the dominance of the five senses. I have desired and pursued only what these five senses crave, and I am ruined. Bestow your grace upon me,” pleads Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar.

“Now, the third verse: “Vazhiththalai padavum maattēn vaikalum thooymai seythu pazhiththilēn paasamattru parama naan paravamaattēn izhiththilēn piravi thannai en ninainthu irukkamaattēn kozhiththu vanthu alaikkum thenneer Kōval Veerattta Neerē” This Thiru-Kovalur is a Thiru-Kovalur with abundant good water. “O Peruman, who resides in such a Thiru-Kovalur! I am unable to walk on the good path indicated by the wise and great. I do not purify my heart daily, nor do I condemn worldly attachments and praise you, the Supreme Being. I am unable to praise you. I should despise this birth, but I am unable to do so.

“I waste time thinking many irrelevant thoughts,” he sings.

“Now, the fourth verse: “Saattruvar aivar vanthu santhiththa kudimai vēndi kaattruvar kanalap pēsi kan sevi mookku vaayul aattruvar alanthu pōnēn aathiyai arivu ondru inri kootruvar vaayil pattēn Kōval Veerattta Neerē” “O Peruman of Thiru-Kovalur! This soul lives as a tenant in the house of this body. Like the owners of the house who dominate this body, these five senses demand what they desire, I live, unable to eradicate the dominion of the five senses and their five organs. I have been ruined by desiring and indulging in these very sensory pleasures. Grant me grace, thus implores Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar.

“Now, in the third hymn, he says: “I will not follow the path, nor will I purify myself daily and revile attachments. I will not praise the Supreme Being, nor will I despise this birth, nor will I dwell on it. O Lord of Thiru-Koval Veerattam, whose waters surge and churn!” This Thiru-Kovalur is a Thiru-Kovalur rich in good water resources. O Lord enshrined in such a Thiru-Kovalur! I am unable to walk the good path indicated by the wise and the elders. Daily purifying the heart and reviling worldly attachments I shall not praise You, who are exalted beyond all, standing before You.

“I am unable to praise You. This birth ought to be considered lowly, but I am unable to consider it so. I waste my time thinking of many inappropriate things, thus he sings.

“Now, the fourth hymn: “The messengers of Yama come and seek to take away life, speaking harshly. They cause the eyes, ears, nose, and mouth to suffer. I am weary and distressed, without any knowledge of the Primal Being. I have fallen into the mouth of Yama, O Lord of Thiru-Kovalur Veerattam! O Thiru-Kovalur Peruman! This soul dwells in this body, like a solitary tenant in a house.

“The five senses, like the owners of this body-house, assert their dominance and seek what they desire.” and they harshly speak to me, ordering me to provide all these things. These five senses—eye, ear, nose, mouth, and skin—harshly speak to me, demanding that their five desired objects be provided to them.

“Therefore, I suffer greatly. Without the knowledge to know you, who are the origin of everything, I have fallen into the mouth of Yama,” sings Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar.

“Now, the fifth sacred verse: “Thaduththilēn aivar thammai thaththuvaththu uyarvu nērmai paduththilēn parappu nōkki pan malar paatham uttra aduththilēn sinthaiyaara aarvaliththu anbu thinnam koduththilēn kodiyavaa naan Kōval Veerattta Neerē” “O Peruman of Thiru-Kovalur! I have not restrained the five senses. I am unable to make my soul immerse itself in the truth of the real substance, my Peruman. I am unable to realize that You are omnipresent. I have not gathered many flowers and offered them to You at Your Thiru-feet. I have spent my time as a very cruel person, without having abundant love in my heart and directing that love towards You, Peruman, sings Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar.

“Now, song number six: “Ma seytha kurambai thannai mannnidai mayakkam eythu naasseythu naalum ainthum nallanavaaythal vaithu kaasseytha kaayam thannul nithalum aivar vanthu kosseythu kumaikkavaatren Koval Veeratta neere.” O Peruman of Thiru-Kovalur, this body, made of the five great elements, is like a hut with nine openings for the taste of the tongue. Within this body, which carries life, these five senses rule daily.

“Therefore, I am unable to bear their harms, sings Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar.

“Now, song number seven: “Padaigal pol vinaigal vanthu patri en pakkal ninrum vidagilaavathalaale vithithanai virumbi ettum idaiyilen en seyken naan irappavar thangatku enrum kodaiyilen kolvathe naan Koval Veeratta neere.” Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings: O Peruman of Thiru-Kovalur, karmic actions come like armies and cling to me, refusing to leave, tormenting me. I never give anything to those who come to me asking for something. Instead, I make it my business to receive from others. I have not had the opportunity to lovingly praise You, Peruman.

“Therefore, I am living a useless life, he sings.

“Now, song number eight: “Pichilen piravi thannai pedaiyen pinakkam ennum thuchule alunti veeltu thuyarame idumbai thannul achanaay aathimoorthikku anpanaay vaalamaatta kochaiyen seyvathenne Koval Veeratta neere.” Its meaning is: O Peruman of Thiru-Kovalur, I, a foolish person, am unable to completely shatter and remove the disease of birth. I am like a blind person, unable to live with my inner eyes, making the soul within this body, which is immersed in the attachment to this body and destined to experience suffering, devoted to You, the Primal Being, he sings with sorrow in this song.

“Now, song number nine: “Ninathidai yaakkai peni niyamam seythirukka maatten manathidai aattam pesi makkale sutram ennum kanathida aattappattu kaathalaal unnai penum kunathidai vaalamaatten Koval Veeratta neere.” Its meaning is: O Peruman of Thiru-Kovalur, I desire and cherish this body, which is formed by the union of fat, he sings.

“Here, he sings of this body, designed and joined by fat.

“Therefore, since fat is one of the seven humors, by mentioning one, we should understand that he refers to all the other humors, and that he lives cherishing this body, which is formed and joined by the seven humors.

“Thus, I protect and nurture this body, but at the same time, I am unable to perform the duties of worship that I ought to perform. I live, swayed by the crowd of people and relatives, desiring marriage. I am unable to live with the good quality of loving You with affection, he sings.

“Now, the tenth song: “Verikadal Ilangai konai viyan Kailayathin keezh irupathu tholum pathu sirangalum neriya unri paraviya paadal kettu padai koduthu aruliccheythaar kuravodu kongu soozhntha Koval Veerattanare.” Its meaning is as follows: Lord Shiva, who pressed down the twenty shoulders and ten heads of Ravana, the king of Lanka surrounded by the sea, beneath the vast Mount Kailash, and upon hearing the songs of praise he sang, bestowed upon him the sword, Chandrahasam. He resides in Thiru-Kovalur, surrounded by Kurava and Kongu trees.

“This is the Thiru-Pathikam and its ten songs, along with their meaning, that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar offered to the Peruman of Thiru-Kovalur.

“Our contemplation shall continue.”” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 347. Thiru-Nindrachcharukkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We saw that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, who set out on a pilgrimage from Thiru-Athigai, reached Thiru-Vennainallur and sang a Thiru-Pathikam there. We saw two Thiru-Pathikams sung by the Nayanar in Thiru-Aamathur.

Following that, we saw a Thiru-Pathikam sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar when he came to Thiru-Kovalur Veerattam. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, having come to Thiru-Kovalur, worshipped many other Thiru-Sthalams, sang Tamil songs, and reached Pennagadam. The song mentions “Thiru-Kovalur muthala maruvu Thirupathi piravum.” Thus, he visited many Thiru-Pathis, including Thiru-Kovalur, he sings. Such Thiru-Pathis are considered to be Thiru-Idaiyaru, Thiru-Thiru-Nelvennai, and other Thiru-Sthalams. It seems that the Pathikams sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar for these Sthalams are not available to us. We can also infer that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar worshipped Thiru-Arayani Nallur on his way from Thiru-Aamathur to Thiru-Kovalur.

The Nayanar has mentioned these Sthalams in the Thiru-Thandagam of “Annamalai Arayani Nallurum Araneriyaum” and “Nalvennai Nelvayilum.” Therefore, we can assume that he worshipped all these Sthalams and reached Pennagadam. Pennagadam is a town with mansions where clouds reside. Pennagadam is a prosperous city where Brahmins, who foster the sound of the Vedas, live. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar arrived at that Pennagadam. Within Pennagadam, where Lord Shiva is permanently enshrined, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar worships Lord Shiva in the Thiru-Thoongai Maadam Thiru-Koyil, which is inside the Thiru-Sthalam of Pennagadam. This town of Pennagadam is a town where many Brahmins live.

The Brahmins there study the Vedas according to tradition. They perform sacrifices according to Vedic injunctions.

Therefore, as a result, clouds are always above that city, making it prosperous. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar goes inside the temple called Thiru-Thoongaanai Maadam in the town of Pennagadam and worships Lord Shiva.

Now, let us briefly contemplate the special features and history of the Pennagadam Sthalam. The town of Pennagadam is located in Virudhachalam, Cuddalore district, Tamil Nadu, near Thittakudi.

Here, the name of the Lord is Sudarkozhundeesar, Prallayakaleswarar. The name of the Goddess is Aamothanaambaal, Kadainayagi, Azhagiya Kaathali. The Sthala Vriksham here is the Champaka tree. The Theerthams are Kedila Nadi, Vellaru, Kailai Theertham, Parvati Theertham or Paramaananda Theertham, Indra Theertham, and Mukkulam. This town was named Kadanthai Nagar because six thousand Kadanthaiyars, or brave people, lived here. The name of this town, Pennagadam, came from the combination of Penn, Aa, and Kadam.

Penn, meaning celestial maidens, Aa, meaning Kamadhenu, and Kadam, meaning elephant. This is the Sthalam worshipped by these three.

Therefore, it is named Pennagadam.

Once, celestial maidens came to this Sthalam to pluck flowers for Indra’s puja. They were delighted to see the Lord here, worshipped Him, and stayed here. Indra, seeing that no flowers were coming for his puja, sent Kamadhenu. It also came here, worshipped the Lord of this Sthalam, and stayed here. Indra sent his white elephant to search for Kamadhenu, and that elephant also came here, worshipped the Lord, and remained here. Indra, understanding nothing, came searching himself, learned of the situation here, and worshipped Lord Shiva, so goes the history.

Thus, this Sthalam was worshipped by the celestial maidens (Penn), Kamadhenu (Aa), and the white elephant (Kadam).

Therefore, Penn Aa Kadam became Pennagadam. It is believed that the milk that flowed when Kamadhenu performed puja filled the Kailai Theertham and became a pond. To the north of the Moolasthanam, on a built-up hill, is the Soundareeswarar shrine, which is a temple with a separate gopuram. It is said that this temple was built so that Soundaravalli, a devotee who lived in Soundara Chozhapuram near this Sthalam, could worship from the market street when she came to this Sthalam to exchange goods. There is also a legend that a Chola king, who came to worship this Sthalam on the banks of the Vellaru, performed penance on the opposite bank due to a flood in the river, and to bless him, the Lord appeared to him, rising to a height visible to him, and that is this hill temple. This Thiru-Sthalam of Pennagadam is the town where Kalikkamba Nayanar was born and lived.

There are Thiru-Devarams by Thiru-Gnanasambandar and Appar Swamigal for this Sthalam. The temple in this Sthalam is called Thoongaanai Maadam. This Thiru-Koyil is built in the shape of a reclining elephant. The front of the temple is elevated like the face of an elephant, and the back is bulky and round like the hindquarters of an elephant.

Therefore, it is called Thoongaanai Maadam. Thiru-Gnanasambandar refers to it as Kadanthai Thadam Koyil in his Thiru-Devaram. There are three windows around the Garbhagriham. This is a special architectural feature of this temple. This Thiru-Sthalam of Pennagadam is the town where Achutha Kalappalar, the father of Meykandar Deva Nayanar, a Saiva Siddhanta Santhana Paramacharyar, lived. It is also the Thiru-Sthalam where Maraijnana Sambandar, one of the Saiva Santhana Acharyars, was born.

We saw that the Moolasthanam here is shaped like an elephant; this is called Gajaprishta architecture.

Here, the shrine of Chandeswarar is located under the Sthala Vriksham. This Sthalam has names such as Dhayarajapathi because Airavatham worshipped here, Pushpavanam or Pushparanyam because it was a flower garden in ancient times, Mahendrapuri because Indra worshipped here, Parvatipuram because Parvati worshipped here, and Shokanashanam because it is the Sthalam that relieved the weariness of the Lord who consumed poison. It is also called Shiva Vasam because it is a beloved abode of Shiva. To the west of the village, there is a place called Kalappalar Medu, named after Achutha Kalappalar, the father of Meykandar Deva Nayanar. There is a small temple for Meykandar there. Many Chola-era inscriptions are found in this temple.

These inscriptions refer to the Lord of this Sthalam as Thoongaanai Maadam Udaiya Nayanar.

Here, the Lord bestows grace as a Swayambhu Murthy. The Nandi, which turned its direction to protect the earth from the flood, still faces the entrance today.

The Lord here is named Prallayakaleswarar.

Once, when this world was destroyed by Lord Shiva, all places except this Sthalam were submerged by the flood. The Devas, knowing this, came here and requested that the lives be protected in this Sthalam.

Lord Shiva commanded Nandi to stop the flood. Nandi, who was facing Shiva, then turned towards the village, and the direction of the flood changed, saving the earth.

Therefore, the Lord here is named Prallayakaleswarar. This is the 213th Thevara Sthalam among the 274 Shiva temples praised in Thevaram. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar comes to this Thiru-Sthalam of Pennagadam and has a darshan of the Lord.

We will continue to contemplate the history of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 348. Thiru-Nindrachcharukkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar worships in the Thiru-Thoongaanai Maadam Thiru-Koyil in Thiru-Pennagadam.

Here, in this Thiru-Sthalam, an important event is about to occur in the sacred history of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, having worshipped the Lord here, pleads with Lord Shiva: “I cannot bear to live with this body, which has been tainted by the evil path of the Samana religion.

“Therefore, my Lord, Lord Shiva, You must imprint Your seal upon me, that is, upon this body, for me to wear it.” Thus, he makes his appeal and sings a garland of rich Tamil Thiru-Pathikams. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar pleads with Lord Shiva to imprint His Rishabha (bull) and Shula (trident) marks on this body, which has been tainted by the Samana religion. Sekkizhar’s sacred verse states: “Pun neriyam aman samaya thodakkundu pontha udal thannudane uyir vaazhath thariyen naan tharipatharku ennutaiya nayaka nin ilacchinaiyittu arul enru pannu sezhunthamil maalai munninru paaduvaar.” Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings: “I cannot bear to live with this body, which has been tainted by the Samana religion.” He sings that this body is a defiled body, and therefore, his mind does not agree to live bearing it. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings that if there is impure action and association, even this body will become impure and defiled. Just as milk poured into an impure vessel becomes unusable, an impure body will be an obstacle to standing in the path of righteousness.

“Therefore, our scriptures strongly emphasize physical purity.

“Here, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has left the Samana religion. Even after that, even though Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar is now in the Saiva religion, if the question arises as to what the taint of having been in the Samana religion before will do, it is not so. This body, if it has once, at some point, been defiled by evil association, then the seven types of humors, including the blood in this body, will all become defiled and toxic.

“Therefore, just as medicine is given for a disease, and a vessel fallen in impure mud is purified by fire, this body also needs to be purified as prescribed. This is called Prayaschittam in Sanskrit and Kazhuvai in Tamil. For the first time, when Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar suffered from colic and came to Thiru-Athigai, Thilagavathiyar Ammaiyar recited the Anjali and gave him the sacred ash.

“From that day, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, wearing the sacred ash and becoming a complete Saivite, a Saiva Acharyar, has visited and worshipped many Thiru-Pathis so far. Even after all this, is the body that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has an impure body? Was the body not purified before by the sacred ash? It is not so. It is true that this body was purified before. When Thilagavathiyar recited the five letters and gave the sacred ash, and when Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar wore it on his sacred body, this body was purified then and there.

“However, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has until now considered that the growth of this body, having been subjected to the taint of the Samana religion, is ignoble. We can see this in the “Ezhai Thiru-Thandagam” and many other sacred utterances. The application of sacred ash is a ritual called Agneya Snanam, which purifies the body from time to time. Each time we fully apply sacred ash, it is called Agneya Snanam and purifies this body.

“Thus, the parts such as Sukshma Deha Suddhi, Sthula Deha Suddhi, Sharira Dahana, and Amrita Abhilavanam are all performed daily in the Shiva Puja Krama. These all indicate the state of burning the body and purifying the gross and subtle bodies for that day, every day. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar performed and worshipped these daily. All these are appropriate rituals for all those who worship Shiva to purify themselves.

“However, these are different.

“Here, the appeal that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has now made is different. How so? It is that the ignominy of his body having grown up in the Samana religion must be atoned for. This body must be made worthy of being worn by the soul, freed from that ignominy. This is Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar’s view. Why is this?

“Because he had previously been in the external Samana religion and had reviled Lord Shiva, and then returned to the Saiva religion, wasn’t he? What special atonement is appropriate when returning thus? It is to have the marks of the Lord, the Shula (trident) and Rishabha (bull) marks, imprinted on this body. This is what is desired, and the Sivagamas refer to it as Saiva Mudra Diksha. It is one of the types of Diksha prescribed by the Sivagamas. What does it mean to engrave the Rishabha symbol and the Trishula symbol on the body?

“It means that these symbols are to be impressed firmly upon our shoulders, leaving an indelible mark.

“Similarly, Vaishnavites also perform the Shankha Chakra Mudradharanam, which is a ritual among them. It is likely that a similar ritual existed in the Saiva tradition in the past. The doubt that arises here is that Saivites do not seem to follow it as Vaishnavites continue to do. If such a tradition did not exist, there would be no reason for the Nayanar to make such a request.

“Therefore, This tradition must have existed in the Saiva faith at one time.

“Moreover, the message we receive from this is that those who had strayed into an alien, external religion and suffered there, when they returned to their mother religion, had to perform such a penance that afflicted the body.

“Here, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar requests the Lord to engrave His insignia on his body. These are the Trishula and the Rishabha, meaning the Rishabha insignia. The idea is that by engraving these insignia, the body is purified and becomes the property of Shiva, removing the defilement it incurred when it was previously in the Samana faith. Just as impure gold becomes pure gold when refined in fire, so too, a fault- If the offering of a faulty person becomes Shiva’s property, that fault is removed; it is like that.

“Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar here, in Thiruppennagadam, at the Thiruthunganaimadam temple, sings, “My petition to the golden feet,” as Sekkizhar Peruman sings. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar offers a Thiru-pathikam here, requesting the Lord to engrave the Trishula and Rishabha symbols on his body.

“We shall continue with our reflection.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 349, Thirunindrachcharukkam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We saw that in Thiruppennagadam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar requested that the Trishula and Rishabha symbols be engraved on his body. Sekkizhar Swamigal sings about this: “My petition to the golden feet,” he begins, “He who stood before all things and as their end, He who held Uma as a part of His body, Shankara, I sing the Thiruviruttam of His good names, that its goodness may flourish.” Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar begins to sing, “My petition to the golden feet.” He sings of Him who stood before all things and as their end, and who held Uma as a part of His sacred body. Sekkizhar Peruman states in this verse that he sings the Thiruviruttam pathikam, which praises the good names of Shankara, who holds Uma Devi as a part of his sacred form, so that its goodness may flourish. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar began by singing, “My petition to the golden feet.” This is the opening reference to the Thiru-pathikam that Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar bestowed at this time.

Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar begins this Thiru-pathikam by singing, “To the golden feet, there is a petition.” Sekkizhar Peruman refers to this here. “Pon Aarntha Thiruvadi” (golden feet) appears as “Ponnar Thiruvadi” in the Thiru-pathikam. The author has expounded this as a verbal compound applicable to all three tenses. The sacred feet of the Lord are as beautiful as gold and appear as beautiful as gold.

Similarly, they possess the quality of bestowing benefit and goodness like gold. This quality did not newly appear in those sacred feet today, nor will it come in the future; it has existed from time immemorial, sings Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar. He sings, “My petition to the sacred feet,” “There is a petition to the sacred feet.” In this Thiru-pathikam, which begins with “There is a petition to the sacred feet,” only three verses have reached us.

Now, in these three verses, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar makes three petitions. However, even though he makes three different Even though he made these petitions, they all share the single purpose of requesting the insignia to purify the body, which had been defiled by contact with external religions. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sings, beginning with “To the golden feet, there is a petition,” addressing Lord Shiva. Sekkizhar Peruman mentions here that Lord Shiva stood before all things and as their end. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sings of Him who stood before all things and as their end. The meaning of this is that the Lord existed before all things and will exist after them, and He pervades all things.

By saying “before,” it refers to the leadership of creation, and by saying “stood,” it refers to the leadership of protection. By saying “stood,” it refers to the leadership of protection, and by saying “as the end,” it refers to the leadership of destruction.

Thus, the three functions are indicated in this one line. By “He who stood before all things and as their end,” the three functions of the Lord are indicated. To signify that the Lord is the head of these three functions, He holds the three-pronged Trishula in His sacred hand.

The Lord holds the Trishula, which has three prongs and a base. Why? It is to signify that “I am the first in all three functions.” Therefore, Shiva holds the Trishula in His sacred hand.

Therefore, such a Trishula should be engraved on His Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar makes his first request, asking that the Trishula be engraved as a mark on his shoulder, that this mark should always remain on his shoulder. He makes this first request. This is because the Trishula of the Lord, the Lord holding the Trishula, signifies His nature as the one who creates, protects, and destroys.

Furthermore, there are three prongs in the Trishula, which the holy ones sing of as the “kudukadai” that pierces the three malas (impurities). That is, the idea here is that the Trishula has three prongs that remove the three impurities of souls.

Here, it is understood that the Trishula represents the three prongs that remove the three impurities of souls. “He who rules without defilement and bestows grace, He who holds the ‘kudukadai’ in His hand and bestows grace” is from Thiruvachakam, Keerthithiru Agaval.

Therefore, Shiva holds the Trishula to signify that He is the primal one who performs the three functions of creation, preservation, and destruction. He holds the Trishula as a symbol of removing the three impurities of souls.

Furthermore, the Trishula also signifies Vama, Jyeshta, Raudri, and Janani, Rodhayathri, Harini, which are names that perform the cutting of bonds in initiation. Shiva, the Lord, is the one who presides over the three functional deities, and by presiding over these powers, the primal one It explains that they are known as Brahma, Vishnu, and Rudra, respectively. The worship of Brahma and others in the base, middle, and top parts of the Shivalingam is also related to this concept.

Therefore, Shiva holds the Trishula in His sacred hand to signify that He, by presiding over Brahma, Vishnu, and Rudra, is the one who performs the three functions of creation, preservation, and destruction. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar requests that such a Trishula be engraved on his body, on his shoulder, as an identifying mark, an insignia. Such a Shiva holds Uma Devi as one part of Himself. Grace is the sacred form of Shiva. Shiva is the one whose sacred form is grace, or compassion. That grace or compassion is the form of the Mother.

The sacred ash is also the form of the power called ‘Parai’. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings of this very thing: “Paravanamavathu Neeru.” Therefore, he places a petition, requesting the Lord to apply the sacred ash of His feet. This is the second petition Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar makes to the Lord here in Pennagadam. Requesting to apply the sacred ash of the feet signifies desiring to receive the power of grace. Such a Shiva is called Shankara. Shankara means “one who brings happiness.” Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar requests that the Rishabha insignia be engraved, which implies the desire to receive happiness.

It implies the desire to give happiness. Since it is mentioned in this verse, “He who stood before and as the end,” it refers to the Lord’s quality of Sat (existence). Since it is mentioned, “He who held Uma as a part of Himself,” it refers to the Lord’s quality of Chit (consciousness). He who is full of happiness is the one who gives happiness. Such a giver of happiness, Shankara, refers to the Lord’s quality of Ananda (bliss).

Therefore, this one verse is structured to refer to the Lord’s three qualities of Sat, Chit, and Ananda. The quality of Sat refers to the qualification to bestow grace, Chit refers to the possession of that grace suitable for giving, and Ananda refers to the Lord’s qualification to bestow happiness. Based on these ideas, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar makes three petitions in this sacred verse: “The Trishula insignia should be engraved on me,” “The sacred ash of the feet should be applied,” and “The Rishabha insignia should be engraved.” He makes these three petitions in the three sacred verses of this Thiru-pathikam. This Thiru-pathikam belongs to the ‘Thiruviruttam’ category of hymns. It is said that he sings this Thiruviruttam so that goodness may flourish. “Nalame Sirakka” means “may goodness abound, may goodness shine.” Previously, Thilagavathi Ammaiyar had applied the sacred ash given by chanting the sacred five letters.

Therefore, Thirunavukkarasar had already received that goodness through the grace of the Lord in Thiru-athikai, which brought about great spiritual awareness. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, who had previously received those blessings, sings this pathikam so that those blessings may further flourish here. “I cannot bear to live with this body, which has been defiled by the Samana religion.

“Therefore, engrave your insignia, the Trishula and Rishabha, on this body, and apply the sacred ash of your feet.” Thus, three petitions are made in the three verses of this pathikam that we have received. The remaining verses are not available to us due to our lack of merit.

“Now, let us reflect on the three verses of this pathikam.

“The first verse: “To the golden feet, there is a petition. If you desire to protect my soul, which praises you, then to remove the great Yama, engrave the lightning-like three-pronged Trishula on me.” O Lord, who is the blazing flame within the Thiruthunganaimadam temple, located in Pennagadam where clouds reside!

“Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar first addresses the Lord. When he sings, “O blazing flame!” he is referring to one of the sacred names of the Lord of this sthalam, “Sudarkkozhuntheesar.” He mentions it here. “O Sudarkkozhunthu Nathar, O blazing flame! I, your servant, place a petition, a request, at your golden feet. That is, if you desire to protect my soul, then to remove the ignominy of having wasted a large part of my life in the Samana faith, so that it may be evident that you have accepted me as your servant, please engrave the three-pronged Trishula insignia on my body.” He makes this request in the first verse. In this first verse, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sings, “I cannot keep this body any longer.

“I am not ready to keep this body, because it is a body that has been corrupted by the Samana faith.

“Therefore, I have no desire for my soul to live in this body. So, only if this body is purified, then” If the soul lives within it, it will be useful; otherwise, that life will be wasted, is the conclusion of the wise.

“Therefore, if my petition, this petition of mine, is agreeable to your sacred heart, then please engrave the Trishula symbol on me.

“Now, the second verse: “O Lord, if you do not protect this humble servant, thinking, ‘What did he, a small devotee, think?’ and if the great disease of suffering mixes with me, then blame will fall upon you, O Lord, who is loved by devotees. Apply the sacred ash of your feet, O our virtuous one, in Thunganaimadam of Kadanthai, where the lotus blooms.” The meaning of this is, “O our virtuous one, who resides in the Thiruthunganaimadam temple in Thiruppennagadam, I am I am a small, lowly servant among your devotees.

“Therefore, you should not think that he is asking for things beyond his worth. My body and the Samana defilement, which is mixed within it like leprosy, are present in my body. Even though I am unworthy, even though I am unworthy, I have come and reached you.

“Therefore, even if I am unworthy, it is your nature to protect and sustain a devotee who has come to you, is it not? If you do not protect and sustain a devotee who has come to you, even if he is unworthy, then that blame will fall upon you.

“Therefore, are you not the God whom lovers adore?

“Therefore, to attain the fullness of your divine grace, As a symbol, make me apply the sacred ash. This is the second petition he makes in this second sacred verse, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar.

“Now, the third sacred verse: “When the wheel of time could not pass, you placed one sacred toe on Kailash, crushing him who came. Engrave the Rishabha, like the great snowy mountain, and accept me, O my true essence, in Thunganaimadam of Kadanthai, where the moon touches the great groves.” This is the tenth sacred verse. “O my true essence, who resides in the Thiruthunganaimadam temple in Thiruppennagadam! O Lord, who crushed Ravana’s body with one of your great toes when he tried to uproot Mount Kailash! Please engrave the Rishabha symbol, which is in the form of a white bull like the great Himalayas, on my body, and accept me as your servant.” This is the third petition made by Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar in the third sacred verse, which is the request to engrave the Rishabha insignia on his body.

“Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sings this Thiru-pathikam by making these petitions.

“As soon as this Thiru-pathikam was sung, a Bhootha, one of Shiva’s ganas, appeared there. These Bhoothas, as Shiva’s ganas, are capable of carrying out any command given by Lord Shiva.

“Thus, one of these Bhoothas, without anyone else knowing, engraved the sacred insignia of the Rishabha and the Trishula on Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar’s shoulders and departed. Thirunavukkarasar’s heart rejoiced upon seeing these sacred insignia on his shoulders. Remembering the grace of his Lord, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar’s eyes began to shed tears like an unceasing waterfall. He cried out, “I have lived!” and then rose. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar saw the insignia engraved on his shoulders, but he did not see the Bhootha that engraved them, nor the act of engraving.

“Therefore, he believed that Shiva, his rightful Lord, had bestowed them upon him as soon as he made his petition, and his heart melted. Let us persist in our reflection.”” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 350, Thirunindrachcharukkam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We saw that in Thiruppennagadam, when Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar requested that the Rishabha insignia and the Trishula insignia be engraved on him, one of Shiva’s Bhootha ganas, at the command of Lord Shiva, came and engraved the Rishabha and Trishula insignia on Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar’s shoulders and departed.

After this, Thirunavukkarasar worshipped the sacred feet of Sudarkkozhunthanathar, who resides in Thiruthunganaimadam in Thiruppennagadam, for a long time. After performing many regular services in that sacred place and residing there with devotion for some days, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar departed from there and proceeded to the sacred place called Thiru-araththurai. Thiru-Aṟattuṟai, a sacred sthalam, is sung by Sekkizhar Peruman as the incomparable Thiru-Aṟattuṟai, where the fragrance of flowers wafts. Here flows the Niva River. The floods in this Niva River carry flowers from the forests, making the river fragrant. On its banks lies the sacred sthalam called Thiru-Aṟattuṟai.

In his hymn, Sekkizhar Peruman sings of Thiru-Aṟattuṟai as a place where the fragrance of flowers wafts, implying its incomparability. “Poruvil Thiru-Aṟattuṟai” means the incomparable Thiru-Aṟattuṟai, a place where the incomparable Lord Shiva resides.

Therefore, this Thiru-Aṟattuṟai is an incomparable sacred sthalam.

Here, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has composed a Thiru-Pathikam. This Thiru-Pathikam begins with “Kadavulai” and sings of “Oppar illatha em madalulanai,” meaning the Lord who has no equal.

Thus, this sthalam is where Lord Shiva, possessing such unique qualities, is spoken of.

Therefore, the special feature of this sacred Thiru-Pathikam for this sthalam is that it describes Lord Shiva as one who transcends all comparisons, having no equal, and yet is present for us to worship, with qualities that make Him comparable in certain ways throughout the entire Pathikam. This Thiru-Aṟattuṟai, also known as Thiru-Nelvayil Aṟattuṟai, is considered the foremost among the Thevaram-sung sthalams in Nadu Nadu. This sthalam, Thiru-Nelvayil Aṟattuṟai or Thiru-Aṟattuṟai, is located in Kongu Nadu. This sthalam, Thiru-Nelvayil Aṟattuṟai or Thiru-Aṟattuṟai, is the first sthalam encountered when crossing the border from the west into Nadu Nadu. It is the sthalam where Lord Shiva bestowed the pearl palanquin, pearl umbrella, and pearl insignia upon Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. This sacred sthalam has the distinction of being sung by the three great saints.

It is located on the northern bank of the Niva River, near Virudhachalam in Tamil Nadu. The name of this sacred sthalam is Thiru-Nelvayil, and the name of the temple is Aṟattuṟai.

Here, the Lord’s sacred names are Anandeeswarar, Theerthapureeswarar, and Aṟattuṟainathar. The Goddess’s sacred names are Anandhanayaki, Thiripurasundari, and Aṟattuṟai Nayaki. The Sthala Vriksham here is the Banyan tree, and the Theertham is the Niva River. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, Nambiandar Nambigal, Sekkizhar Swamigal, Valmiki Munivar, and Aravan are among those who worshipped at this sthalam. This sthalam is currently known as Thiru-Vatturai. Upon entering through the main gateway, to the right are shrines for Vinayagar, the four Samaya Kuravargal, Valmiki Munivar, the Saptha Kanniyargal, the Bhuta Bhavishya Varthamana Lingams, Maha Vishnu, and the Jyotirlingam.

Further on, one can worship the shrines of Annamalai, Adiseshan, Murugaperuman with Valli and Deivanai, Dandayuthapani, and the Linga Moorthies named after the Chera, Chola, and Pandya kings. Kasi Viswanathar also appears with Visalakshi. There are also shrines for Gajalakshmi, Santhana Kuravargal, Bhairavar, Surya, and Chandra. After worshipping in the outer circumambulatory path, upon entering, to the left is the Navagraha shrine, with a separate shrine for Sani Bhagavan. There are separate flagstaffs, balipeetams, and Nandis for the Lord and the Goddess. When the Niva River flooded, Nandi turned its head to prevent damage, and the floodwaters receded.

Therefore, Nandi’s head is slightly turned. The Koshta Moorthies include Vinayagar, Bhikshadana, Dakshinamurthy, Lingodbhavar, and Brahma. After worshipping the forms of Natarajar, Sivakami Darshanam, Durga, Ardhanareeswarar, Chandeeswarar, and Bhairavar, one can worship the Moolavar. The Moolavar is a Swayambhu Lingam, facing east. Since this sthalam also bears the name Theerthapuri, the Lord is known by the sacred name Theerthapureeswarar. This sacred sthalam is located on the banks of the Vellar River and is considered an important one among the seven “Thurai” sthalams.

That is, the seven “Thurai” sthalams on the banks of the Vellar River are Aadhi The seven “Thurai” sthalams are Thurai, Kariyanur Thiru-Alandurai, Thirumanthurai, Thiru-Aaduthurai, Thiru-Vattathurai (Thittakudi), Thiru-Nelvayil Aṟattuṟai, and Thiru-Karanthuthurai. Among these, Thiru-Nelvayil Aṟattuṟai stands as a significant sthalam. In these seven sacred “Thurais,” the Lord resides and bestows grace to remove the sins of the people. It is believed that the Saptharishis called out “Nee Vaa” (Come) to worship in these seven “Thurais,” and thus this became the Nee Vaa River, which is also said to have transformed into the Vadavellar River. These are the special features of the sthalam known as Thiru-Nelvayil Aṟattuṟai, or Thiru-Aṟattuṟai. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has composed a Thiru-Pathikam for this sthalam, which is a Thiru-Kurunthogai Thiru-Pathikam.

It is compiled as the third Thiru-Pathikam in the fifth Thiru-Murai. This is compiled as the third Thiru-Pathikam.

Now, let us contemplate the ten sacred verses of this Thiru-Pathikam and their brief meanings.

The first verse: “Kadavulai kadalul ezhunju unda udal ulanai oppar illatha em adal ulanai arathurai meviya sudar ulanai kandeer nam thozhuvathe.” Its meaning: Lord Shiva is the God we worship. He has a graceful form, having consumed and held the poison that arose from the ocean. There is no one who can be compared to Lord Shiva; He is incomparable. Such a powerful Lord has graciously and willingly resided in this sacred sthalam called Aṟattuṟai. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar begins this first verse of the Thiru-Pathikam with “Kadavulai.”

Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar begins with “Kadavulai.” “Kadavul” means one who transcends feeling and speech. It means one who transcends the six Adhvas. Sekkizhar Peruman mentions this in the first verse of Periya Puranam as “Ulagellam unarnthu odarku ariyavan.” Here, it is indicated that the Lord is incomparable, as He reveals Himself from within. “Thanaku uvamai illathan” is a quote from Thiru-Kural.

Now, the second sacred verse: “Karumoppanai karumbinil kattiyai virumbu oppanai vinnoru arugila arumbu oppanai arathurai meviya surumbu oppanai kandeer nam thozhuvathe.” I will worship Lord Shiva who resides in Thiru-Nelvayil Aṟattuṟai. He is like sugarcane and the sugar candy within sugarcane. He is like a bud unknown even to the Devas. He sings that Lord Shiva is like sugarcane.

Lord Shiva is like the juice in sugarcane for the devotees, remaining hidden in their spiritual practices and manifesting as the sweet nectar of love that arises from their achievements.

Therefore, Lord Shiva is like sugarcane. For the true devotees, the Jivanmuktas, He is the ever-present, blissful love that manifests without ceasing.

Thus, the Lord is sung as “karumbinil katti” (sugar candy). The same Lord Shiva, if their ego of “I and mine” does not subside, remains unmanifest to them.

Therefore, He is unknown even to the Devas, as sung in this verse.

Furthermore, for those who practice Shiva Dharma, Shiva Yoga, and Shiva For those who practice Shiva Gnanam, these spiritual disciplines cause Him to sprout and appear as blissful love within their hearts, expanding and blossoming.

Thus, He is sung as being like a bud. Thiru-Navukkarasar sings that after being a bud, the primal Lord Shiva, with His rays of grace, removes the coils of ignorance from their lotus-like hearts, causing them to blossom, and the Shiva-mind blossoms within the Jiva.

Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar also states that He is like a bee. Such a Lord Shiva resides willingly in this sthalam called Thiru-Aṟattuṟai, so that beings may come here, perceive Him intimately, worship Him, and attain salvation.

Now, the third verse: “Eroppanai ella uyirkkum irai veroppanai vinnoru Arugila arapanai arathurai meviya urappanai kandeer nam thozhuvathe.” Its meaning: The Lord has no other object comparable to His glory. He stands supreme as the Lord of all beings. He is like a path unknown even to the Devas. Such a Lord Shiva exists as an entity in the sthalam of Aṟattuṟai.

Now, the fourth verse: “Parappoppanai pagal irul nannila irappanai ilamathi soodiya arappappanai arathurai meviya surappanai kandeer nam thozhuvathe.” Its meaning: The Lord whom we lovingly worship resides in Thiru-Aṟattuṟai. He wears the crescent moon. He is like the expanse of daylight and the growth and playfulness of the beneficial waxing moon in darkness, and the flow of milk due to love. The primal Lord Shiva, who is like the flow of milk due to love, resides here.

The Lord is sung as being like the light of day. The great light of day is the great light of the sun.

Similarly, the Lord is sung as being the great consciousness pervading everywhere. He is sung as being like the growth of the waxing moon that brings benefit in darkness.

Here, it means that the Lord, residing within the intellect of beings, gradually removes the inner darkness and causes Shiva Gnanam to flourish.

Therefore, the Lord is like the growth of the moon that waxes in the night.

Now, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings that He is like playfulness. Playfulness means sport. This means that Lord Shiva is capable of performing His actions with ease, like a sport. This means that Lord Shiva is capable of performing His actions with ease, like a sport. “Surappu oppanai” comes next.

The Lord manifests and bestows grace like milk flowing immediately for yogis who worship Him with mantras dedicated to Shiva Lingams and other sacred forms.

Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings that He is like a gush. For Shiva Gnanis who worship with true love, just as a cow that has recently given birth to a calf secretes milk when it thinks of its calf, Lord Shiva manifests and bestows grace whenever Shiva Gnanis desire it. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings this scriptural truth here.

Now, the fifth verse: “Ney oppanai neyyil sudarpolvathor mey oppanai vinnorum arugilar aiyappanai arathurai meviya kaiyappanai kandeer nam thozhuvathe.” Its meaning: Lord Shiva, the deity we worship, is like ghee and the truth that shines like a flame in ghee, and a great wonder. He is unknown even to the Devas. He resides willingly in this sthalam called Aṟattuṟai.

Now, the sixth sacred verse: “Nedhiyappanai nedhiyil kizhavanai vidhi oppanai vinnorum arugilar adhiyappanai arathurai meviya gathiyoppanai kandeer nam thozhuvathe.” Its meaning: What we worship is Lord Shiva. He is unknown even to the Devas. He is the refuge for beings in the sthalam of Aṟattuṟai.

Now, the seventh verse: “Punal oppanai porunthalar thammaiye minal oppanai vinnorum arugilar anal oppanai ara Aṟattuṟai meviya kanal oppanai kandeer nam thozhuvathe.” Its meaning: Our Lord Shiva is like water, like lightning to those who are not in harmony, and like fire. He is unknown even to the Devas. He resides in Aṟattuṟai like a blazing fire.

Here, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings that Lord Shiva is like water. Water has the nature to nourish anything.

Similarly, the Lord resides within every being and nourishes their intellect. He is like lightning to those who are not in harmony. This means He is like thunder to enemies.

Next, He sings of the Lord as being like fire. A swirling, blazing fire is compared to the sacred form of the Lord.

Now, the eighth sacred verse: “Pon oppanai ponnil sudarpolvathor” Minoppanai vinnorum arugilar annoppanai arathurai meviya thannoppanai kandeer nam thozhuvathe.“ Its meaning: Lord Shiva, the Lord we worship, is like gold, like the lightning that shines like a flame in gold, and like a mother. He is unknown even to the Devas. He resides in Aṟattuṟai, incomparable to Himself, for us to worship. He sings of the Lord as being like gold. The sacred words “Ponnar Meniyane” (He of the golden form), “Ponvannam Evvannam Avvannam Meni” (His form is like whatever color gold is), and “Namo Hiranyabhagave Hiranyavarnaya” (Salutations to Him whose share is gold, whose color is gold) reveal to us that the Lord is like gold.

Now, verse nine: “Kaliyanaik kanvidaiyurum mey vazhiyanaik val Ellorum enru innavar azhiyan piramarkkum arathurai uzhiyanai kandeer nam thozhuvathe.” The Lord we worship is the God who resides in Sirkazhi. He is the one with an eternal sacred form, riding on a majestic bull. He is the one who is the ultimate refuge even for Vishnu and Brahma, who are called powerful by others. He is Lord Shiva who resides in Thiru-Aṟattuṟai.

Now, verse ten: “Kalai oppanai kattarkku or amudhinaimalai oppanai mani mudi unriya alai oppanai arathurai meviya nilai oppanai kandeer nam thozhuvathe.” Its meaning: The Lord we worship is like art, like nectar to the learned, like a mountain. He is the one who crushed Ravana, who tried to lift the mountain, causing his jeweled crowns to scatter and be tossed about. Such a Lord resides in Aṟattuṟai.

These are the ten verses of the Thiru-Pathikam for the sacred sthalam called Thiru-Nelvayil Aṟattuṟai and their brief meanings.

Let us proceed with our contemplation.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 351. Thiru-Nindra Charukkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We have contemplated the Thiru-Pathikam composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, worshipping the Lord at the sacred sthalam of Thiru-Nelvayil Aṟattuṟai. From here, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar proceeds to the sthalam called Thiru-Muthukunram, also known as Virudhachalam.

There, he composes a Thiru-Thandagam in praise of the Lord. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar composes a Thiru-Thandaga Thiru-Pathikam beginning with “Karumaniyai Kanagathin Kundru Oppanai.” The sthalam of Virudhachalam is located in an important place in North Tamil Nadu. Let us briefly contemplate the special features of this sthalam.

Here, the Lord’s name is Virudhagireeswarar, Pazha Malainathar. The Goddess’s sacred names are Virudhambikai and Balambikai. This sthalam, known as Thiru-Muthukunram in Tamil and Virudhachalam in Sanskrit, is an ancient sthalam. It is one of the Thevaram-sung Shiva sthalams in Nadu Nadu. This Virudhachalam has the distinction of being sung by the three Shaiva Acharyas: Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, and Sundaramoorthy Swamigal.

In addition, there are Thiru-Pugazh hymns composed by Arunagirinathar for this sthalam. Guru Namasivayar, Kumaradevar, Sivaprakasa Munivar, Sokkalinga Adigal, and others have also sung about this sacred sthalam. In Tamil Nadu, there are several sthalams with the name “Kundram” (hill), such as There are several such sthalams, including Thiru-Kazhukunram, Thiru-Parankunram, and Thiru-Kodukunram.

Similarly, this sacred sthalam is also called Thiru-Muthukunram. However, in other sthalams ending with “Kundram,” there are hills corresponding to the name.

But here in Virudhachalam, only the name Muthukunram exists, and we might wonder if there is no hill. The Sthala Varalaru (temple history) states that this hill is buried beneath the earth.

Accordingly, this area is indeed bedrock beneath the surface. Since it existed before all other mountains, it was named Pazhamalai (ancient mountain) or Muthukunram (first mountain). In Sanskrit, it is called Virudhachalam.

Here, the sacred Theertham is the Thiru-Manimutharu River. Siddhiananda Kobam, Agni Theertham, Chakra Theertham, Kubera Theertham, and other five Theerthams. The Sthala Vriksham here is the Vanni tree. It is customary to first bathe in the Thiru-Manimutharu River, which is located directly to the north of the northern gopuram entrance of this temple. This very spot is renowned as a sacred bathing place, and it is here that bones turned into stone. The Thiru-Manimutharu River flows to the north and east of the town, then turns southeast.

Wide streets for chariot processions are laid out around the temple. Including these, there are five prakarams (circumambulatory paths) in this temple. Generally, it is a tradition to say that all special features in this temple are in fives. There are five prakarams: the Chariot-running Thiru-Chutru, the Kailasa Thiru-Chutru, the Vanniyadi Thiru-Chutru, the Arupathu Moovar Thiru-Chutru, and the Panchavarna Thiru-Chutru. There are five Vinayagars: Azhathu Vinayagar, Maatruraitha Vinayagar, Muppillaiyar, Dasabhuja Ganapathi, and Vallabha Ganapathi. The five who had darshan of the Lord here are Romasa Munivar, Vibhajithu Munivar, Kumaradevar, Nadhasarma, and Anavarthini.

There are five gopurams: East, West, North, South, and Kandaraadithan Gopuram. The temple is very large. The Azhathu Pillaiyar temple is located inside the temple, facing east, at a depth of eighteen feet. In the Kailasa Prakaram of the temple, in the northwest corner, there is a temple for the twenty-eight Agamas. This temple was established because Lord Muruga worshipped the twenty-eight Siva Agamas as Shiva Lingams in this region.

Therefore, the Lingams are named after the Agamas. The Lingams are named after the Agamas: Kamikeswarar, Yogajeswarar, Chinthesvarar, Karaneswarar, Ajitheswarar, Deeptheswarar, Kusumewarar, Sahasreswarar, Amsumaneswarar, Suprabhedeswarar, Vijayeswarar, Niswaseswarar, Suvayambeswarar, Analeswarar, Veereswarar, Rauraveswarar, Magudeswarar, Vimaleswarar, Chandrajanesvarar, Mukabimbeswarar, Purodgeedeswarar, Laliteswarar, Siddhesvarar, Santhanesvarar, Sarvottameswarar, Parameswarar, Kiranesvarar, and Vathuleswarar. In the northern Kailasa Prakaram, the temple of Mother Periyanayagiyar is located facing east. It has a single, separate circumambulatory wall. In the northern mandapam of the Goddess’s temple, there is a Chandeswari temple. The Amman shrine is structured with a sanctum sanctorum, an ardha mandapam, and a maha mandapam.

In the sanctum sanctorum, Mother Virudhambikai, Periyanayaki, shines with a compassionate, tender face, like a mother feeding milk to a hungry, crying child. Outside the Periyanayaki temple, in the decorative mandapam, there is a flagstaff and Nandi. Nearby, on the north side, is Lord Muruga in a cave. In the southeast corner of that mandapam, facing east, is the Nadhasarma temple. Directly east of it, outside, facing west, is the Anavardhani temple. Nadhasarma and Anavardhani attained Sarupa status in this Thiru-sthalam, which is why temples have been established for them here.

In this Thiru-koyil, there is an utsava murthi named Periyanayakar. There is a circumambulatory path called the Sixty-Three Nayanars’ circumambulatory path. Within the temple, on the south side of the inner southern circumambulatory path, there are shrines for the four Saivite Acharyas: Thiru-gnanasambandhar, Thiru-navukkarasar, Sundarar, and Manikkavasagar, along with Pillaiyar, the sixty-three Nayanars who are Siva’s devotees, ten great devotees, Rishabaroodar, Yoga Dakshinamurthi, the Sapta Matrikas, the eleven Rudras, and Pillaiyar who changed the measure of gold, among others. On the upper side of the inner circumambulatory path, from south to north, there are shrines for Chinna Pazhamalainathar, the small utsava murthi, Lord Arumuga with Valliammai and Deivanai, Vallabhai Ganapathi, Bindu Madhava Perumal, Mayura Muruga Kadavul, and others.

Here, the Bindu Madhava Perumal shrine within this Thiru-sthalam is associated with the Kasi Kshetram. That is why, because it resembles the Kasi Kshetram, this Kshetram is known as Virudhakaasi. The Puranic history states that it possesses greater glory and significance than Kasi itself. In the northwest corner of this circumambulatory path is the Balambikai shrine.

There, Balambikai, the embodiment of compassion, the youthful goddess, shines with a blossoming face. In the northern inner circumambulatory path, on the north side, facing south, is the Chandeswarar temple. In the northeast corner is Kala Bhairavar. In front of this inner circumambulatory path is the Maha Mandapam. Next to it, inside, is the Snapan Mandapam, where Thiru-manjana items are kept and mantra japa is performed. Adjacent to the Snapan Mandapam is the Idaikkali Mandapam.

It has two entrances, one facing south and one facing north. In the middle are the inner Nandi and the Balipeedam. Next to it, inside, is a separate central temple with an ardha mandapam. In this sanctum sanctorum, our Lord Pazhamalainathar, Virudhagireeswarar, shines as one mouth, six mouths, and six forms.

Now, let us briefly look at the Puranic history of this temple. In the beginning, Brahma, intending to create the earth, first created water.

At that time, Thirumal had to cut down and defeat the evil Madhu and Kaitabha. The severed parts of their bodies fell into the water created by Brahma and floated. Brahma saw this. He prayed to Lord Shiva for the water and the body tissues to merge and for the earth to appear.

Lord Shiva appeared in the form of a mountain and stood before him. However, Brahma could not recognize it and created many other mountains. Brahma was greatly saddened and confused, thinking there was no place for the mountains he had created.

Lord Shiva then Upon being enlightened, Brahma gained wisdom and worshipped Lord Shiva, who stood before him in the form of a mountain.

Lord Shiva blessed that the tissues and water would merge, and the earth would appear.

Therefore, Brahma named this world ‘Medini’ and also provided space for the mountains he had created. Addressing Brahma, Lord Shiva said, ‘I myself appeared in the form of this mountain. I am not separate from this mountain. Only after this mountain appeared did you create many mountains.

Therefore, let our mountain be known as Pazhamalai or Virudhagiri.’ Lord Shiva then disappeared, having blessed that anyone who worships this Pazhamalai, which stands as the axis of the earth and shines as a Shiva Lingam above, will attain their desired benefits and be joyful.

Once, Thirumal and other Devas came to this Pazhamalai They stayed in this Thiru-sthalam and performed severe penance. Due to the heat of that penance, a flood of supreme bliss overflowed. Virudhagireeswarar, with His sacred hand, caressed it, causing it to flow as the Thiru-Manimuththa River here.

Thus, this Manimuththa River, which is the embodiment of divine grace and the fire that burns away sins, stands. Countless people have benefited from it. Even today, the bones of the deceased are immersed in this river. All of them turn into stone. Devas and sages attained eight types of siddhis by bathing in this sacred Thiru-Manimuththa River and worshipping Pazhamalainathar. Sukracharya bathed and worshipped, becoming the guru of the Asuras.

Yajnavalkya Muni bathed and worshipped, attaining the mantra siddhi of Mritha Sanjeevini. Chitrasikandi and Koshikan bathed and worshipped, becoming Vedic sages. Vithargana Chetti bathed and worshipped, becoming a Siva Gana. A man born blind bathed and worshipped, regaining his sight. Six people suffering from severe illnesses bathed and worshipped, recovering from their ailments and attaining well-being. Vibhajithu Muni bathed and worshipped, attaining liberation.

This Vibhajithu Muni was the one who originally renovated the temple for Pazhamalainathar. Devas bathed and worshipped, receiving the vision of the sacred dance. Guru Muni bathed and worshipped, getting rid of the karma of consuming flesh. Kalingan bathed and worshipped, getting rid of his demonic form. Sages bathed and worshipped, causing the power of Kali to diminish.

King Swetha bathed and worshipped, attaining the status of Nandi. Nadhasarma and Anavardhini bathed and worshipped, attaining Sarupa status. All these histories are extensively narrated in the Virudhachala Sthala Purana. Thiru-navukkarasu Nayanar He sang the Thiru-thandagam ‘Karumaniyai Kanagathin Kundrappanai’ on Pazhamalainathar, worshipped, and found joy. Thiru-gnanasambandha Peruman sang seven types of Thevara Pathigams, including ‘Matthavarai Niruvia,’ worshipped the Lord of this Thiru-sthalam, and found joy.

Here, in Virudhachalam, Lord Shiva bestowed twelve thousand gold coins upon Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. We will see that history in detail in the sacred history of Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. About nine hundred years ago from today, there was a Sivagnana Selvar named Gnana Koothar. He was the great person who sang the Thiru-mudukundra Sthala Purana in Tamil. About four hundred years ago from today, there was a Siva devotee named Guru Namasivayar. He was traveling from Thiru-vannamalai towards Thiruchitrambalam.

On the way, He had to stay one night in Thiru-mudukundram. After worshipping Virudhachala Nadhar and Virudhambikai, he lay down on one side inside the temple. Hunger tormented him. Whenever he was very hungry, he would sing to Ambikai and eat the food she provided; he made it a habit.

So, according to that custom, he sang a song remembering Virudhambikai, Periyanayaki, who resides in this Thiru-sthalam: ‘Nandri Punaiyum Periya Nayaki enum Kizhathi endrum Sivanar Ida Kizhathi Nindra Nilai Kizhathi Meni Muzhu Nilakkizhathi Malai Kizhathi Soru Kondu Vaa’ (O Periyanayaki, the old woman who always adorns goodness, the old woman on Shiva’s left, the old woman who stands firm, the old woman whose body is the whole earth, the mountain old woman, bring food). He sang a Venpa on Virudhambikai, the Ambikai of this Thiru-sthalam. Virudhambikai means ‘old woman,’ doesn’t it?

So, it came as ‘Kizhathi’. He sang a Venpa in such a way that it referred to her as ‘Kizhathi’ (old woman). In front of him, Periyanayaki Virudhambikai appeared like an old woman and asked, ‘Why do you sing about me as an old woman so many times? If I am an old woman, how can I bring food and water?’ Guru Namasivayar, seeing this old woman, sang another song: ‘Muttha Nathi Soozhum Mudukundru Uraivaale Patthar Paniyum Pathathaale Atthan Idathaale Mutra Ila Mulai Mel Aara Vadathaale Soru Kondu Vaa’ (O dweller of Mudukundram surrounded by the Muttha River, O one whose feet devotees worship, O one on the left of the Lord, O one with fully developed young breasts, bring food). In this, he sings about Virudhambikai as a youthful goddess, Balambikai. Immediately, the joyful Ambikai, as a youthful goddess, gave him food and water.

Guru Namasivayar ate it and appeased his hunger. Only after this did a separate shrine for Balambikai come into existence in this town.

Therefore, Here, Virudhagireeswarar has two Ambikais: Virudhambikai and Balambikai. About a hundred years ago from today, Mr. Charles Hyde, who was then the District Collector of South Arcot, laid the floor for the Kailasa Prakaram of this temple and named it ‘Hyde Thala Varisai’ (Hyde’s Floor Arrangement) after himself. He also had an iron chain made for raising the chariot and a silver pot for performing Kumbha Aarathi. That British Collector served Pazhamalainathar in many ways with sincere devotion. All these are still recorded in the South Arcot District Gazetteer, the English historical record.

Many kings have performed renovations here, and there are many inscriptions. In all those inscriptions, the names of the following The names of kings are mentioned: Parantaka Chola, Gandaraditya Chola, his wife Sembiyan Madevi, Uttama Chola, Rajaraja Chola, Rajendra Chola, Rajadhiraja Chola, Vikrama Chola, Rajaraja Chola II, Kulothunga Chola III, Kulothunga Chola Kadavaradithan who was Ezhisa Mohan, Veerasekhara Kadavarayan, Arasarayanan, Kachirayan, Kopperunjingan, Vikramapandiyan, Veerapandiyan, Sundarapandiyan, Maravarman Pandiyan, Konerinmai Kondan, Ariyanna Udaiyar, Pokkana Udaiyar, Kampana Udaiyar, Veera Vijayarayar, Muppidi Krishnapathi, and other rulers. Two major festivals are held in Thiru-mudukundram. One is the Thiru-kalyana festival held on the Poora star in the month of Aadi. The other is the Mahotsava festival held in the month of Maasi. Among these, the Thiru-kalyana festival is a celebration for people to understand the truth that Lord Shiva performs all actions while being united with His divine power.

The Maasi Mahotsava festival is a celebration to make people realize the truth that the Lord is the one who performs the five great cosmic functions. Before the Maasi Mahotsavam, first, festivals are held for Aiyanar for one day, for Kaliyamman, the village deity, for eight days, and for Pillaiyar for ten days. Only after that does the festival begin at the Pazhamalainathar temple. The first day is the flag-hoisting ceremony, which signifies the function of creation. The seven-day festivals from the second day to the eighth day signify the function of protection. Among these, the sixth Thiru-nal (sacred day) is very special.

Only on that day does Pazhamalainathar, seated directly on a silver Rishabha vahana, proceed through the streets, granting the vision of the festival and bestowing grace. On the ninth day, the chariot festival takes place, which signifies the function of destruction. The tenth day is the Theerthavari festival, which signifies the function of bestowing grace. On that night, the flag-lowering ceremony takes place, which is called Maunotsavam (festival of silence), and it signifies the function of concealment. On the eleventh night, the Theppotsavam (float festival) takes place. This temple has many sub-temples: Siddhi Vinayagar Temple, Koothadum Pillaiyar Temple, Aiyanar Temple, Kaliyamman (Selli) Temple, Perumal Temple, Thropathaiyam Temple, East Thropathaiyam Temple, Mariyamman Temple, Lord Muruga Temple known as Kolanjiappar, Venmalaiyappar Temple, Karumbayiram Kondappar Temple, and so on.

As we have already seen, Sambandhar, Appar, and Sundarar, the three, have blessed this Thiru-sthalam with Thevara Thiru-pathigams. There is also a Thiru-pugal sung by Arunagirinathar for this Thiru-sthalam. The Thiru-mudukundra Sthala Purana was composed by Gnanakoothar.
