Now, verse number ten: “Naadinaranan naanmugan endru ivar, Thediyum thirindhum kaanavallaro, Maada maaligai soozh Thillai Ambalaththu, Aadi paadham en nenjullirukkave.” The meaning of this is: Can Vishnu and Brahma, who searched and wandered, thinking they would find the Primal Lord, ever find Him? The feet of the Dancer in the Thillai Ambalam, surrounded by mansions and palaces, reside within my heart, which remembers Him with love.

Now, verse number eleven: “Madhuravaaimozhi mangaiyor panginan, Chathuran Chithrambalavan Thirumalai, Adhira aartheduththaan mudi paththira, Midhigol sevadi sendradaindhu uymin.” The meaning of this is: He who has Parvati, whose words are sweet, on His left side; He who is the skillful one, capable of creating, protecting, and destroying all worlds without effort; He who is enshrined in Thiruchitrambalam. Go and attain salvation by worshipping the sacred feet that gently pressed down the ten heads of Ravana, who roared with arrogance and lifted the sacred mountain, Thirumalai (Mount Kailash), where this Lord is enshrined, causing it to tremble.

These are the eleven verses of this sacred hymn, beginning with “Annam Palikkum Thillai Thiruchitrambalam,” and their meanings.

Our reflection now resumes. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 360. Thirunindrachcharukkam. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. While Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar was performing these sacred services in Thiruchitrambalam, he departed from Thiruchitrambalam and went to Thiru-Vetkalam. He went before the Lord Shiva, who has the bull-emblazoned flag, enshrined in Thiru-Vetkalam, and worshipped Him.

Sekkizhar Peruman sings, “Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, on the days he performed and shone in his chosen services, went and worshipped before the Lord who has the bull-emblazoned flag in Vetkalam, and sang.” Here, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to the Lord as “Sevu-uyar Kodiyar.” “Se” means bull or Rishabam. “Uyar Se Kodiyar” means “He who has raised the bull flag.” It also means “He who has the exalted Rishaba flag.” As we saw, “Se” can mean Rishabam, or it can be taken to mean “cow species,” implying the flag that elevates by removing the enmity of attachment that exists among cows. “Saalavum edhilaar thun enna mel vilangi erkaattum Kodhilaa eraam kodi” is from Thiruvachagam, Thiruththasangam, tenth Thiruppadal. When asked what the Lord’s flag is, this Thiruththasangam, in the voice of a parrot, states that the Lord’s flag is the faultless Rishabam (bull) depicted on it, which appears above, causing enemies to tremble greatly in fear.

Here, “Kodhillaa E” refers to the Lord’s faultless Rishabam, which is the embodiment of dharma.

Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar went to Thiru-Vetkalam, where Lord Shiva, who has the Rishaba flag, is enshrined. He worshipped before the Lord there and sang a sacred hymn. This sacred place, Thiru-Vetkalam, is very close to Thiruchitrambalam. It is believed to be the place where Pasupatham was bestowed upon Arjuna.

Here, the Lord’s name is Pasupatheswarar.

Furthermore, in this place, the standing form of Arjuna and the form of the Lord holding the Pasupatham are enshrined and worshipped. Through the reference in Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar’s Thirukkurunthogai, where Lord Shiva is addressed as “Vedanar” (hunter), this truth is revealed to us: that this place is where Pasupatham was granted to Arjuna. Annually, on the full moon Visaka day in the month of Vaikasi, the festival where the Lord, disguised as a hunter, fights with Arjuna and bestows the Pasupatha weapon, is celebrated here. This sacred place is also known as Thiru-Porkalam. It also bears the name “Bamboo Forest.” Here, the Goddess’s name is Nalla Nayaki, Sarkunambal. This sacred place has received hymns from Thirugnanasambandar and Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal.

Thirugnanasambandar Peruman, after worshipping the Thillai Koothan, came to this place and worshipped the Lord. Afterwards, he stayed here for several days.

Similarly, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar also worshipped Thillai, and then ...came here, worshipped this sacred temple, then worshipped Thiru-Kazhippalai, and returned to Thillai. The temple faces east. Opposite the temple are a Nagalinga tree and a tank. After worshipping the gopuram and entering through the gateway, one finds shrines for Siddhi Vinayagar and Somaskandar in the circumambulatory path. Beyond the Nalvars (four great devotees), Chokkanathar and Meenakshi are seen, followed by shrines for Subramaniar and Mahalakshmi. The Sthala Vriksham (sacred tree) here is bamboo, which is present.

After circumambulating the prakaram, upon entering the front mandapam, to the right is the Ambika shrine. The Goddess is in a standing posture here.

The Lord Shiva Linga form is Pasupatheswarar, who blessed Arjuna, a beautiful sight. In the Mahamandapam, there is the Natarajar Sabha and the darshan of Sivakami Ambal. Nataraja Peruman is seen here wearing a crown, which is ...special. Among the Utsava Murthams (processional deities), there is also the deity of Arjuna with the Pasupatha Astra. To illustrate the history associated with this sacred temple, on the pillars of the front mandapam, there are sculptures depicting the Lord and Goddess in hunter forms with dogs, and fighting with Arjuna. On another pillar, there is a sculpture of Arjuna performing penance, with Mookasuran coming below to obstruct him.

As Koshtamurthis (deities in niches), there are Uchchi Vinayagar, Narthana Ganapathi, Dakshinamurthy, Lingodbhavar, and Brahma. There is a Chandeswarar shrine. The grand temple festival takes place as a one-day Utsavam during Vaikasi Visakam. On that day, the scene of bestowing Pasupatham and the procession of the Panchamurthis (five deities) occur. All these are notes about this sacred place, Thiru-Vetkalam. These are the notes about the sacred place called Thiru-Vetkalam.

Here, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar came, worshipped the Lord, and bestowed the sacred hymn beginning with “Nandru naaldhorum nam vinai poy arum.” This sacred hymn is a Thirukkurunthogai Thiruppathigam. It is compiled as the forty-second sacred hymn in the Fifth Thirumurai. Sivakavimani writes that the note for this hymn is: “Naldhorum nam vinai poy arum” (Our karma will greatly diminish day by day). There is no trouble, no sorrow, no difficult karma, no suffering, no more misery. All karmas will cease.

Therefore, come to Thiru-Vetkalam, worship the Lord with folded hands, and let your heart be steadfast. If you praise the sacred feet of the Lord, He with the dark throat will protect us. This is the note for this sacred hymn.

Now, let us look at the ten sacred verses of this hymn and their brief meanings.

First verse: “Nandru naaldhorum nam vinai poy arum, Endrum inbam thazhaikka irukkalaam, Sendru neer Thiru-Vetkalaththu ullurai, Thundru porchadaiyaanai thozhumine.” Worship Lord Shiva, who resides in Thiru-Vetkalam, the Lord with dense, radiant matted locks. If you worship Him thus, our karma will greatly diminish day by day, and we can live flourishing in eternal bliss and attain salvation. Verse number two: “Karuppu venjilai kaamanai kaaindhavan, Poruppu venjilaiyaal puram chettrravan, Viruppan mevviya Vetkalam kaithozhudhu, Iruppanaagil enakku idar illaiyee.” Manmatha, who has a sugarcane bow, is the one. That bow of Manmatha causes desire.

Lord Shiva is the one who burned such a Manmatha. He is the one who destroyed the three cities with Mount Meru as His bow. He is fond of His devotees. If I worship Thiru-Vetkalam, where such a Lord Shiva resides, with folded hands, I will have no troubles. If I worship Thiru-Vetkalam, where such a Lord Shiva resides, with folded hands, I will have no troubles. Verse number three: “Vetkalaththu urai vedhiyan em irai, Aakkal eruvar aanainjum aaduvar, Pookkal kondu avan pon adi pottrinaal, Kaappar nammai karaimidatru annale.” Lord Shiva, who resides in Thiru-Vetkalam, is our Lord, the Vedian (one who knows the Vedas).

He is the Lord with the dark-throated neck. He delights in riding the bull. He loves to bathe in the five products of the cow (panchagavyam). If we praise His golden feet with flowers, He will protect us. Verse number four: “Allal illai aruvinai thaan illai, Malku venpirai soodum manaalanaar, Selvanaar Thiru-Vetkalam kaithozha, Vallar aagil vazhiyathu kaanmine.” If we are able to worship with our hands the gracious Lord of Thiru-Vetkalam, who is the bridegroom adorned with the abundant white crescent moon, that itself will show us the path to Shaivism. If we stand on that path, we will have no sorrows, no difficult karmas, and no troubles.

If we are able to worship with our hands the gracious Lord of Thiru-Vetkalam, who is the bridegroom adorned with the abundant white crescent moon, that itself will show us the path to Shaivism. If we stand on that path, we will have no sorrows, no difficult karmas, and no troubles.

Now, the fifth verse: “Thunbam illai thuyar illai yaam ini, Nambanaagiya nan manikandanar, Enbanaar urai Vetkala nannagar, Inban sevadi eththiyiruppadhe.” Since we remain praising the sacred feet of the Lord, who is our beloved, the good blue-throated one, the golden one, who resides in the good city of Thiru-Vetkalam, there will be no more sorrow or suffering for us.

Now, the sixth verse: “Kattappattu kavalaiyil veezhaadhe, Pottavalluyir povadhan munnam neer, Chittanaar Thiru-Vetkalam kaithozha, Patta valvinai aayina paarume.” Do not be bound by worries and fall. Before your life quickly departs, go to Thiru-Vetkalam, where the exalted Lord resides, and worship Him with folded hands. If you do so, all your powerful karmas will be destroyed.

Now, the seventh verse: “Vatta menmulaiyaal umai panganar, Ettum ondrum irandum moondru aayinaar, Chittar ser Thiru-Vetkalam kaithozhu, Ittam aagi iru mada nenjame.” O ignorant heart, worship with love Thiru-Vetkalam, which is the abode of the exalted ones and where the Lord resides, who has Uma Devi with round, soft breasts as one half, who is the eight-formed one, the one supreme being, the two (Shiva and Shakti), and the three (Trimurtis). O ignorant heart, worship with love Thiru-Vetkalam, which is the abode of the exalted ones and where the Lord resides, who has Uma Devi with round, soft breasts as one half, who is the eight-formed one, the one supreme being, the two (Shiva and Shakti), and the three (Trimurtis).

Now, the eighth verse: “Nattamaadiya nambanai naaldhorum, Ittaththaal inidhaaga ninaminno, Vattavaar mulaiyaal umaippanganar, Chittanaar Thiru-Vetkalam thannaiyee.” Remember with love and sweetness, day by day, the Lord who performed the sacred dance, and Thiru-Vetkalam itself, where the exalted Lord resides, who has Uma Devi with round, beautiful breasts as one half.

Now, the ninth verse: “Vattamaamadhil moondrudai val aran,” O ignorant heart, worship with love Thiru-Vetkalam, which is the abode of the exalted ones and where the Lord resides, who has Uma Devi with round, soft breasts as one half, who is the eight-formed one, the one supreme being, the two (Shiva and Shakti), and the three (Trimurtis).

Now, the eighth verse: “Nattamaadiya nambanai naaldhorum, Ittaththaal inidhaaga ninaminno, Vattavaar mulaiyaal umaippanganar, Chittanaar Thiru-Vetkalam thannaiyee.” Remember with love and sweetness, day by day, the Lord who performed the sacred dance, and Thiru-Vetkalam itself, where the exalted Lord resides, who has Uma Devi with round, beautiful breasts as one half.

Now, the ninth verse: “Vattamaamadhil moondrudai val aran,” “Sutta kolgaiyar aayinum soozhndhavar, Kutta valvinai theerththu kulirvikkum, Chittar pottriru-Vetkala selvare.” The gracious Lord of Thiru-Vetkalam, though He is the one who burned the three strong, circular fortresses, is also the exalted one who removes the powerful karmas of those who surround Him and cools them.

Now, the tenth verse: “Sedanaar uraiyum sezhu maamalai, Odi aangkeduththaan mudi paththira, Vaada oondri malaradi vaangiya, Vedanaar urai Vetkalam sermine.” Go and join Thiru-Vetkalam, where the hunter-Lord resides, who pressed down His sacred feet, causing the ten heads of Ravana, who ran and lifted the glorious great mountain, Thirumalai (Mount Kailash), where the great Lord resides, to wither and suffer.

This is “Nandru.” The Thiru-Kurunthogai Thiru-Pathigam, beginning with “Naalthorum nam vinai poyarum,” comprises ten verses dedicated to Thiru-Vetkalam, along with their concise meanings. After reverently worshipping at Thiru-Vetkalam and singing a pathigam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar proceeds to Thiru-Kazhippalai, where he composes another pathigam.

We shall continue to contemplate this history. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 361, Thiru-Nindra-Charukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Having worshipped at Thiru-Vetkalam and sung a pathigam there, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar reaches the sacred sthalam known as Thiru-Kazhippalai. Sekkizhar Peruman sings of this in the Periya Puranam: “Kaviyang Kandar mannum Thiru-Kazhippalai thannil Navinukku Arasar sendru nanninar mannoru vazha.” This means that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar proceeds to Thiru-Kazhippalai, where Lord Shiva, with His beautiful blue throat, is eternally enshrined. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar visits this sacred sthalam and sings a pathigam so that those living on this earthly plane may find repose. Just as Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar did, those dwelling on this earth should follow the Nayanar and this sthalam.

It is stated, “Navinukku Arasar sendru nanninar mannor vazha,” meaning the King of Tongues went and attained salvation for the welfare of kings, so that they may praise the Lord and be saved. This sthalam, Thiru-Kazhippalai, is one of the sacred sthalams on the northern bank of the Kaveri River. Previously, it was located at Karaimedu on the northern bank of the Kollidam River. The temple was damaged by the Kollidam River.

Therefore, the Thiru-Kazhippalai temple is now established as a separate temple in Shiva-Puri, known as Thiru-Nelvayil. This sthalam was worshipped by Sage Valmiki.

Here, the Lord’s name is Palvannanathar, meaning “Lord of Milk-White Hue,” with a beautiful white form. The Goddess is Vedanayaki. There are a total of eight pathigams associated with this sthalam. The sthala vriksham here is the Bilva tree, and the sacred water is the Kollidam. The temple, which was damaged on the banks of the Kollidam, The person who built the temple near Shiva-Puri, performed the sacred services for this sthalam, and permanently established the daily rituals is Thiru-Kazhippalai Palaniappa Mudaliar, a great landlord and a highly meritorious soul. The Thevara Patasalai, which he first established and continues to operate in Thiruchitrambalam, is a noble institution that serves as a guide for all other Thevara Patasalais.

This virtuous person had great affection for Sekkizhar Peruman. He himself consecrated the Lord, the Goddess, and other attendant deities at Thiru-Kazhippalai and performed sacred services.

Here, the Lord bestows grace as a Swayambhu Murthi. Behind the Shiva Lingam, Lord Shiva and Goddess Parvati are depicted in their wedding attire. This is the fourth of the two hundred and seventy-four Thevara-praised sacred sthalams. This sacred sthalam features a Bhairavar, similar to the one in Kashi, but without a dog as a vehicle. He is adorned with twenty-seven skulls, a sacred thread, a serpent as a waist-cord, matted locks, and prominent fangs, gracing a separate shrine. It is believed that worshipping the Bhairavar of this sthalam yields the same benefits as worshipping the Bhairavar of Kashi.

This is also one of the sthalams where Lord Shiva granted the wedding vision to Agastya. The Natarajar here has his matted locks tied up. The presence of Shiva-Kamy-Amman with her companions, Vijaya and Saraswati, nearby is a unique feature. When Sage Kapila was visiting various Shiva sthalams, he decided to stay in this area, which was a Bilva forest, and perform Shiva puja. Because cows in this area naturally secreted milk, the entire sand appeared white. The sage took this white sand, formed a Lingam, and worshipped it.

One day, the hoof of a king’s horse, passing by, struck the sand Lingam, causing it to crack slightly. The grieving sage intended to remove the cracked Lingam and consecrate another.

At that moment, the Lord appeared with Parvati and graciously commanded him to consecrate the cracked Lingam made of white sand mixed with cow’s milk just as it was. These are some notes about this sthalam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar comes to this Thiru-Kazhippalai sthalam and worships the Lord. Sekkizhar Peruman states that he sings the Thiru-Pathigam beginning with “Vanappavala vaaythirandhu vaanuvarkkum thaanavane.” “Sinavidai yeru ugaithu yeru ma” Manavazha Nambi kadal sendru thaazhndhu vanapavala vaaythirandhu vaanuvarkkum thaanavane enkindraal“ — thus, with such a Thiru-Pathigam, he sang Tamil verses filled with love and stayed there. “Ninaivariyaarthamai potri needu Thiru-Puliyoorai ninaindhu meezhvaar” — this is the verse from Periya Puranam.

At this point, the meaning of this verse is that he went and worshipped the feet of the Lord, who is Manavazha Nambi, riding the angry bull. He sang such a Thiru-Pathigam, saying, “Opening her coral-like mouth, she says, ‘He is the Lord even to the celestials.’” After singing Tamil garlands of powerful love and staying at that sthalam, he praised Lord Shiva, who is beyond comprehension, and then, remembering Thiru-Needu Puliyoor, he reached there. The Thiru-Pathigams said to have been sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar at this time include the Thiru-Pathigam beginning with “Vanappavala Vaay” and several other Thiru-Pathigams, as stated by Peruman. This Thiru-Pathigam, which begins with “Vanappavala Vaaythirandhu Vaanavarkkum Thaanavane,” is composed in the Akathurai style, imbued with the flavor of Akapporul (love poetry). This Thiru-Pathigam is presented as if spoken by the foster mother or mother, observing the emaciation of the heroine separated from her beloved.

Therefore, in keeping with the Akapporul style, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to Lord Shiva as “Manavazha Nambi” in this song. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar is said to have bestowed this Thiru-Pathigam, which begins with “Vanappavala Vaay,” along with several other Thiru-Pathigams. During his stay at Thiru-Kazhippalai, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar composed many such pathigams. Among them, one each from Thiru-Thandagam, Thiru-Nerisai, Thiru-Kurunthogai, and Thiru-Virutham are currently available to us. Including the Thiru-Pathigam beginning with “Vanappavala Vaay,” a total of five Thiru-Pathigams by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar are dedicated to this sthalam.

Furthermore, two Thiru-Kadaikkappu pathigams by Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman and one Thiru-Pattu pathigam by Sundaramurthi Swamigal are also dedicated to this sthalam, making a total of eight Thiru-Pathigams currently available for Thiru-Kazhippalai. Not only this, but Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman and Appar Swamigal have also mentioned and sung about this sthalam in their pathigams for other sthalams and in general pathigams. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s This sacred sthalam is mentioned in Thiru-Kshetra-Kovai Thiru-Pathigam by Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, and in Appar Swamigal’s Kaappu Thiru-Thandagam, Aroor Araneri Thiru-Thandagam, and Kshetra-Kovai Thiru-Thandagam. In the thirty-fourth verse of Shiva-Peruman Thiru-Andhadhi by Paranadeva Nayanar, which states, “Thamenna naamenna verillai thathuravil thaamenna veraaga thanithirundhu thaamen Kazhippalai serum karaimidatrar enno Kazhippalai serum kadan,” he specifically mentions and sings about Thiru-Kazhippalai.

Additionally, in the Periya Puranam, the twelfth Thiru-Murai, Sekkizhar Swamigal has sung about Thiru-Kazhippalai in the Puranams of Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, and Eyarkon Kalikkama Nayanar. Among the five Thiru-Pathigams composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, “Vanapavala” The Thiru-Pathigam beginning with “Vaaythirandhu” is the sixth Thiru-Pathigam in the Fourth Thiru-Murai. The Thiru-Pathigam called “Nangaiyai Paagam Vaithaar” is the thirtieth Thiru-Pathigam in the Fourth Thiru-Murai. The Thiru-Pathigam beginning with “Neithar Kuruguthan” is the one hundred and sixth Thiru-Pathigam in the Fourth Thiru-Murai. The Thiru-Pathigam beginning with “Vannammum Vadivum” is the fortieth Thiru-Pathigam in the Fifth Thiru-Murai.

The Thiru-Pathigam beginning with “Oonuduthi” is the twelfth Thiru-Pathigam in the Sixth Thiru-Murai.

Thus, the five Thiru-Pathigams sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar are compiled in the Fourth, Fifth, and Sixth Thiru-Murais. We shall continue to contemplate these Thiru-Pathigams and their concise meanings.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 362, Thiru-Nindra-Charukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We have seen that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman bestowed the Thiru-Pathigam beginning with “Vanapavala” at Thiru-Kazhippalai, along with several other Thiru-Pathigams. A total of five Thiru-Pathigams were bestowed upon this sthalam by Appar Swamigal. Among them, the first Thiru-Pathigam, beginning with “Vanapavala Vaaythirandhu,” is the sixth Thiru-Pathigam in the Fourth Thiru-Murai. Its melodic mode is Gandharam.

We also noted that this Thiru-Pathigam is composed in the Akathurai style, imbued with the flavor of Akapporul (love poetry). Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar bestowed this Thiru-Pathigam in the manner of a heroine’s mother or foster mother speaking, observing the emaciation of the heroine separated from her beloved. He has bestowed it here. The beloved here is Lord Shiva, Palvannanathar, enshrined in Thiru-Kazhippalai. This sthalam, Thiru-Kazhippalai, belongs to the Neythal land, with the sea nearby. In Tamil, Neythal Thinai is characterized by “Irangal Naruneythal,” meaning lamentation due to separation.

Therefore, in this Thiru-Pathigam of Thiru-Kazhippalai, located in the Neythal land, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has composed it as if the heroine, separated from her beloved Lord Shiva, is lamenting, and her mother is speaking about it. The heroine, having seen and enjoyed her beloved, now dwells solely on his memory, thinking of his separation. She describes his form, his beauty, and all his attributes. She raves and laments, becoming emaciated. Observing this—that is, hearing the words she utters, forgetting herself and raving—her mother speaks, and this Thiru-Pathigam is structured as such. This theme runs throughout the entire pathigam.

Now, the verses of this Thiru-Pathigam and their meanings.

The first verse: “Vanapavala vaaythirandhu vaanuvarkkum thaanavane enkindraalaal Sinappavala thinthol mel serthilanggu vennitran enkindraalaal Anapavala megaliyoode appalaikku appalaan enkindraalaal Kanapavalam sindhum Kazhippalai servaanai kandaal kolo.” This is the first verse. A woman, One day, a woman goes to the sthalam called Thiru-Kazhippalai.

There, she beholds Palvannanathar, Lord Shiva, who is enshrined there. She does not stop at seeing Him once; she sees Him repeatedly, absorbing the sacred form of Lord Shiva through her eyes and embedding it in her loving heart.

Now, when she closes her eyes, the beautiful form of Lord Shiva stands before her inner vision. After seeing Him many times in this manner, she returns to her village with the memory of the beautiful form of Lord Shiva, which she sees with her inner eyes. Until now, she had been speaking normally, as is natural for ordinary women.

Now, her speech has completely changed. The woman, having seen Palvannanathar of Thiru-Kazhippalai many times, Now she always speaks only of Lord Shiva. Whatever she sees, it reminds her of Lord Shiva. Her mother observes this change in the girl from her previous state. She hears her daughter always speaking of the Lord of Kazhippalai. Everyone asks the mother, “Your daughter seems different; she doesn’t speak like other girls.

“What is the reason?” To this, the mother replies, “Yes, I too have noticed. Her speech has changed completely. If she opens her beautiful coral-like mouth to speak, it’s like a parrot, and even now, that sweetness is undiminished.

“But all she talks about is Lord Shiva of Kazhippalai.” She speaks of Lord Shiva as the one who bestows good life upon all celestials. I heard her say that. How did this young woman come to know of the Lord’s glory? “Vanapavala vaaythirandhu vaanuvarkkum thaanavane enkindraalaal,” says the mother.

“Furthermore, the girl’s mother says, “My daughter has seen Lord Shiva and has captured His image in her heart, hasn’t she? She has developed a desire to embrace Lord Shiva’s shoulders.

“Therefore, she praises the firmness of Lord Shiva’s sacred shoulders. On Lord Shiva’s coral-red, firm shoulders, Lord Shiva has applied His sacred ash, His emblem. My daughter, speaking of that white ash and the shoulders adorned with it, is filled with joy,” says the mother. My daughter, says the mother, is ecstatic, speaking of the shoulders adorned with the white ash. This is the meaning of the next line.

“Therefore, the girl has keenly observed the white sacred ash on Lord Shiva’s red, firm shoulders. Amidst that application of sacred ash, she has seen and delighted in Lord Shiva’s reddish form. This girl also knows that Lord Shiva is dear to women, because the next line says, “Aana pavala megaliyoode.” In this verse, Goddess Uma is adorned with a coral girdle.

“Thus, this girl has seen Lord Shiva enshrined with Uma, who wears a coral girdle. She yearns, “Will I also attain such a state?” That is, she yearns, “Will I also attain the state of Uma?” Such a yearning arises in her heart. She yearns thus. Yet, she also knows that Lord Shiva is beyond all, and she laments this. The next line says, “Anapavala megaliyoode appalaikku appalaan enkindraalaal.” She has also realized that Lord Shiva is not easily accessible to everyone.

“Therefore, she sings of Lord Shiva as “appalaikku appalaan,” meaning “He who is beyond even that.” “Beyond even that” implies that Lord Shiva, in His true nature, is beyond the five elements, beyond the five senses, beyond the mind, beyond the thirty-six tattvas, and beyond the unreachable beyond. Realizing this, the girl sings and says that He is beyond even that. When she thinks that Lord Shiva is with Uma, who wears a coral girdle, the thought arises in her that she too might attain that state.

“But the very next moment, the thought that He is beyond everything and transcends all comes to her, and she sighs. The girl’s mother ponders, “Who is worthy of all these descriptions that this girl is uttering?” She realizes that everything the girl raves about are the symbols of Lord Shiva.

“So, she thinks, “How did she come to know all this about the Lord who manifests with these symbols?” The girl’s mother wonders why this sudden change has come about, as she never spoke like this before. She realizes the truth. What truth does she realize? This girl went to Thiru-Kazhippalai with her friends. Her mother agreed to let her go, thinking she could enjoy the sights there.

“But after returning from Thiru-Kazhippalai, she doesn’t seem to be present in this village anymore. She raves as if she is still standing before Lord Shiva in Thiru-Kazhippalai, gazing at Him without blinking. There is a sea at Thiru-Kazhippalai, where the sea brings corals to the shore. She did not see any of these. The girl did not see the sea at Thiru-Kazhippalai; she only saw Lord Shiva, the ocean of grace. This girl, instead of seeing the corals in the sea, has seen the coral-like sacred shoulders of Lord Shiva.

“That is why she speaks like this. It seems to me that she speaks thus after seeing Lord Shiva of Thiru-Kazhippalai, says the mother of the girl who is in love with Lord Shiva. The concluding line is, “Kanapavalam sindhum Kazhippalai servaanai kandaal kolo.” Thus, Appar Swamigal sings, as if a mother is speaking about her daughter: “Vanapavala vaaythirandhu vaanuvarkkum thaanavane enkindraalaal Sinapavala thinthol mel serthilanggu vennitran enkindraalaal Anapavala megaliyoode appalaikku appalaan enkindraalaal Kanapavalam sindhum Kazhippalai servaanai kandaal kolo.” The meaning of this song unfolds. The girl sings of Lord Shiva as the one who bestows upon the celestials. This means that the Lord grants positions to the Trimurtis and other deities, enabling them to perform their respective duties.

“The Lord possesses valiant shoulders, and thus, in this song, those shoulders are referred to as “thin-thols” (firm shoulders). The eight sthalams of heroic deeds, known as Ashta Veerattanams, proclaim the valor of His firm shoulders. It is natural for women to be attracted to the masculine shoulders of men.

“Here, the girl’s mind is completely absorbed in the red sacred shoulders of Lord Shiva, those valiant shoulders, and those coral-colored sacred shoulders. The sacred ash smeared on those holy shoulders remains etched in her mind, and thus she laments.

“Here, it mentions Uma Devi adorned with a coral girdle. It means Uma Devi wearing an ornament made of coral around her waist. This Thiru-Kazhippalai is on the seashore, where waves bring corals ashore.

“Thus, it became natural for Uma Devi there to wear a coral girdle. It is human nature to frequently speak what one has seen and imprinted in their mind.

“Thus, the meaning of the first verse of this Thiru-Pathikam, spoken by Appar Swamigal, unfolds. On this basis, we can briefly contemplate the meaning of the other verses as well.

“Now, the second. The verse: “She says, ‘He has a red matted lock adorned with honey-laden Konrai flowers, where bees roam.’ She says, ‘He has a fresh, fragrant white Erukku flower, fully bloomed, on his matted lock.’ She says, ‘He wears a silk upper garment that appears nearby.’ Did she see the one who resides in Thiru-Kazhippalai, which appears nearby?” The meaning: The mother of the girl, who is in love with the Peruman, says, “This girl laments about Shiva Peruman. She laments that he has red matted locks adorned with Konrai flowers where bees roam. My daughter laments that a fresh, fragrant white Erukku flower, fully bloomed, is also on his matted lock. She also laments that he wears a silk upper garment that appears nearby. Because my daughter has seen the Peruman of Thiru-Kazhippalai, who resides near the seashore.

“That is why she laments thus,” sings the mother.

“Now, the third verse: “She says, ‘The young crescent moon is on our Peruman’s head.’ She says, ‘His body’s color is that of radiant saffron.’ She says, ‘He has a jewel-like throat, like the eyes of Parvati, whose eyes are like a spear that stirs trees.’ Did she see the one who resides in Thiru-Kazhippalai, which is full of unceasing bounty?” The girl’s mother says, “My daughter laments about Shiva Peruman. She says he is the Peruman adorned with the young crescent moon, and that the color of Shiva Peruman’s sacred body is the color of radiant saffron, and that he has a blue throat, like the pupil of Parvati Devi’s eyes, which are like a spear that reveals valor. She laments that he has a blue throat, like the pupil of Parvati Devi’s eyes, which are like a spear that reveals valor. She must have seen the Peruman who graciously resides in Thiru-Kazhippalai.

“Now, the fourth verse: “She says, ‘He holds a trident made of iron and a white battle-axe.’ She says, ‘He is adorned with Konrai flowers where bees swarm, and with sacred white ash.’ She says, ‘He is the great one, with a golden-hued form.’ Did she see the one who resides in Thiru-Kazhippalai, where sugarcane flowers bloom?” The girl, who is in love with the Peruman, sings about the Peruman. “Shiva Peruman holds a trident made of iron and a battle-axe. He is adorned with Konrai flowers where bees swarm, and with sacred ash. He has a large left side as the part of Parvati, and in that part, he has a prominent coiffure,” my daughter laments. She must have seen the Peruman of Thiru-Kazhippalai, says the girl’s mother.

“Now, the fifth verse: “She says, ‘He is blameless, glorious, adorned with milk-white ash, and rides a bull.’ She says, ‘He has not two, but three large, wide eyes.’ She says, ‘He has matted locks where the swirling, dry Ganga resides.’ Did she see the one who resides in Thiru-Kazhippalai, surrounded by joy?” “Our Peruman, Shiva Peruman, is blameless, glorious, adorned with milk-white ash, and rides a bull. He has three eyes. He has matted locks where the Ganga, flowing with swirling waters, resides,” my daughter laments. She must have seen Shiva Peruman of Thiru-Kazhippalai, says the girl’s mother.

“Now, the sixth verse: “She says, ‘He has fingers skilled in playing the melodious Veena.’ She says, ‘He is our Father, who burned the three cities of the enemies.’ She says, ‘He dances and sings to the rhythm of the melodious drum.’ Did she see the one who resides in Thiru-Kazhippalai, with its beautiful, eye-catching groves?” “Our Peruman, Shiva Peruman, has fingers that play the Veena, an instrument that produces melodious sounds. He is the great one who consumed the three cities of the enemies with fire. He performs the dance, singing to the rhythm of the drum, a percussion instrument,” my daughter laments. She must have seen the Lord of Thiru-Kazhippalai.

“Now, the seventh verse: “She says, ‘A young serpent is hidden in his dense, matted locks.’ She says, ‘Seeing that, a young crescent moon appears near it.’ She says, ‘A four-sided white crystal earring shines in his ear.’ She says, ‘A four-sided white crystal earring shines in his ear.’ Did she see the one who resides in Thiru-Kazhippalai, where radiant pearls are scattered?” “The Lord, Shiva Peruman, has a young serpent hidden in his dense, matted locks. Seeing that, and with the thought that the serpent will not harm us, the crescent moon shines near it. A well-crafted white crystal earring shines in the Lord’s sacred ear,” my daughter laments. She must have seen Shiva Peruman of Thiru-Kazhippalai, says the girl’s mother.

“Now, verse eight: “She says, ‘He recites the Vedas and wanders the world for alms.’ She says, ‘He has red matted locks that rise as the Ganga’s waters rise.’ She says, ‘His body’s color is that of red coral in the ocean that surrounds the world.’ She says, ‘Did she see the one who resides in Thiru-Kazhippalai, which is full of dark waters?’ Its meaning: “Shiva Peruman is the one who recites the Vedas and wanders the world for alms. He has red matted locks that rise as the Ganga’s waters rise. The red coral in the ocean that surrounds the world is the color of our Peruman’s sacred body,” my daughter laments. She must have seen the Peruman of Thiru-Kazhippalai, says the girl’s mother.

“Now, the ninth verse: “She says, ‘He has red matted locks where the moon, which wanders in the sky, resides.’ She says, ‘He wanders from town to town for alms, holding a white skull that smells of flesh.’ She says, ‘He has a sacred chest where honey-laden Konrai flowers bloom.’ Did she see the one who resides in Thiru-Kazhippalai, surrounded by beautiful groves?” “He has red matted locks where the crescent moon, which should wander in the sky, resides. He wanders from town to town for alms, holding a white skull that smells of flesh. He has a sacred chest where Konrai flowers bloom beautifully,” my daughter laments about our Peruman. She must have seen Shiva Peruman of Thiru-Kazhippalai. She laments about our Peruman, saying he has a sacred chest where Konrai flowers bloom beautifully. She must have seen Shiva Peruman of Thiru-Kazhippalai.

“Now, the tenth verse: “She says, ‘He crushed the mighty Ravana under the mountain.’ She says, ‘He has a radiant sacred body adorned with sacred white ash.’ She says, ‘He once taught dharma to the four sages under the great Banyan tree.’ Did she see the one who resides in Thiru-Kazhippalai, surrounded by the sea?” “He tormented Ravana under Mount Kailash. He has a radiant, glorious sacred body adorned with sacred ash. He once taught dharma to the four sages, Sanaka and others, under the great Banyan tree with large leaves. My daughter laments about Shiva Peruman, saying all this. She must have seen Palvannanathar, Shiva Peruman, who graciously resides in Thiru-Kazhippalai, surrounded by backwaters,” says the girl’s mother.

“Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman composed this Thiru-Pathikam as the words of the girl’s mother, who is in love with Shiva Peruman, who graciously resides in Thiru-Kazhippalai. We will continue to contemplate the other Thiru-Pathikams.””” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Three Hundred and Sixty-Three. Thiru-Nindra-Charukkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We contemplated the first of the five Thiru-Pathikams composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar in Thiru-Kazhippalai. The second Thiru-Pathikam begins with “Nangaiyai Bhagam Vaithar.” This is compiled as the thirtieth Thiru-Pathikam in the Fourth Thiru-Murai.

It is a Thiru-Nerisai Thiru-Pathikam.

Now, the verses of this Thiru-Pathikam and their brief meanings.

The first verse: “Nangaiyai Bhagam Vaithar Gnanamathai Navizha Vaithar Angaiyil Analum Vaithar Aanaiyin Urivai Vaithar Tham Kaiyin Yazhum Vaithar Thamarai Malarum Vaithar Gangaiyai Chadaivul Vaithar Kazhippalai Cherppanare.” In this verse, the reference to Shiva Peruman as “Kazhippalai Cherppanare” appears. Cherppan means the lord of the seashore. The Peruman, who is the lord of the seashore in Thiru-Kazhippalai, is the consort of Parvati, the one who teaches to bestow Shiva-Gnana, the one who holds fire in his palm, the one who wears the elephant’s hide, the one who holds a Yazh in one hand, the one who wears a lotus flower befitting the Brahmin’s attire, and the one who holds the Ganga in his matted locks.

Now, the second verse: “Vinninai Virumba Vaithar Velviyai Vetka Vaithar Panninai Paada Vaithar Bhakthargal Payila Vaithar Manninai Thava Neenda Maalinukku Arulum Vaithar Kanninai Netri Vaithar Kazhippalai Cherppanare.” Shiva Peruman, who is the Cherppanar of Thiru-Kazhippalai, blesses devotees to desire liberation. He is the one who enables the performance of sacrifices, the singing of melodies, and the practice of worshipping his sacred feet. He is the one with an eye on his forehead, and he blessed Thirumal, who took a long form to measure the worlds. That Peruman with an eye on his forehead blessed Thirumal, who took a long form to measure the worlds.

Now, the third verse: “Vamanai Vananga Vaithar Vayyinai Vazhtha Vaithar Somanai Chadaiyil Vaithar Sodiyul Sodi Vaithar Aamanai Aada Vaithar Anbenum Pasam Vaithar Kamanai Kaintha Kannar Kazhippalai Cherppanare.” Shiva Peruman, who is the Cherppanar of Thiru-Kazhippalai, made everyone worship his consort, his Shakti. He bestowed mouths upon everyone so they could praise. He placed the crescent moon in his matted locks. He placed his light of wisdom within the light of the devotees’ spiritual essence. He granted devotees the opportunity to anoint him with pure ghee. He also created the bond of love.

Furthermore, he has the third eye on his forehead that burned Manmatha to ashes.

Now, the fourth verse: “Ariyana Angam Vedam Andanarkku Arulum Vaithar Periyana Purangal Moonrum Per Azhal Unna Vaithar Pariya Thivannaragi Pavalam Pol Nirathai Vaithar Kariyathor Kandam Vaithar Kazhippalai Cherppanare.” Shiva Peruman holds the Vedas and their auxiliary branches (Angas) for the Brahmins. Shiva Peruman, the Cherppanar of Thiru-Kazhippalai, who bestows compassion, made the three cities consumed by fire, shining with the light of wisdom like a great fire, having a red color like coral, and having a dark throat.

Now, the fifth verse: “Koor Irul Kiliya Nindra Kodumazhu Kaiyil Vaithar Per Irul Kiliya Malku Pirai Punal Chadaiyil Vaithar Aar Irul Andam Vaithar Aruvagai Samayam Vaithar. Karu Irul Kandam Vaithar Kazhippalai Cherppanare.” Shiva Peruman, who is the Cherppanar of Thiru-Kazhippalai, holds a fierce battle-axe in his hand to dispel dense darkness. He placed the crescent moon and the Ganga, which shine to dispel great darkness, in his matted locks. He placed all worlds within the darkness of his Maya. He created the six types of religions and shines with a dark throat.

Now, the sixth verse: “Uttangu Sinthai Vaithar Olguvarkku Ullam Vaithar Vittangu Velvi Vaithar Ven Thuyar Theera Vaithar Nattangu Nadamum Vaithar Gnanamum Navil Vaithar Kattangan Tholmel Vaithar Kazhippalai Cherppanare.” Shiva Peruman, who is the Cherppanar of Thiru-Kazhippalai, bestows an unwavering mind upon those who meditate on him. He holds that mind as his dwelling place within. He established sacrifices that gods desire and accept offerings from, and through those sacrifices, he ensures the removal of severe suffering in the land. The Peruman who dances at midnight has bestowed the ability to study scriptures related to wisdom upon the tongue. He holds the Kattanga weapon on his shoulder.

Now, the seventh verse: “Oonapper Ozhiya Vaithar Othiyee Unara Vaithar Gnanapper Navizha Vaithar Gnanamum Naduvum Vaithar Vanapper Aaru Vaithar Vaikundar Kaali Vaithar Kanapper Kathal Vaithar Kazhippalai Cherppanare.” Shiva Peruman, who is the Cherppanar of Thiru-Kazhippalai, removes names associated with this fleshy body and bestows the name ‘his devotee’ upon his devotees. He established the path to attain wisdom by reciting the scriptures of wisdom. He made them utter the name of God, which is suitable for a body of wisdom, and bestowed the wisdom of the sacred feet and the heart for that wisdom to reside. He placed the Ganga in his matted locks, bestowed the discus upon Thirumal, and lovingly resides in the sacred place called Thiru-Kanapper, also known as Kalaiyar Kovil.

Now, the eighth verse: “Konginum Arumbu Vaithar Kootrangal Kedukka Vaithar Sanginul Muththam Vaithar Sambarum Poosa Vaithar Angamum Vedam Vaithar Aalamum Undu Vaithar Kangulum Pagalum Vaithar Kazhippalai Cherppanare.” Shiva Peruman, who is the Cherppanar of Thiru-Kazhippalai, placed pollen in the bud. He established the good path of reciting Thiru-Murai to eliminate evil speech. He placed pearls within conches. He is the one who has sacred ash as a substance for smearing. To uplift the world, he made the four Vedas and six Angas spread. To uplift the world, he consumed poison.

He established night for all beings to sleep happily and day for them to work. Verse nine: “Chathurmukan Thaanum Maalum Thammile Igalak Kandu Ethirmugam Indri Nindra Eriyuru Adhanai Vaithar Pithirmugan Kaalan Thannai Kaaranir Pithira Vaithar Kathirmugam Chadaiyil Vaithar Kazhippalai Cherppanare.” Shiva Peruman, who is the Cherppanar of Thiru-Kazhippalai, seeing Brahma and Thirumal arguing among themselves about who was the supreme being, stood as a pillar of fire, without a beginning or end, visible to their eyes. He scattered the fierce-faced Yama with his foot. He placed the crescent moon in his matted locks.

Now, the tenth verse: “Maalinaal Nangai Anja Mathil Ilangaikku Mannan.” Velinaan Vegundu Edukka Kaandalum Vedanavan Noolinaan Nokki Narku Nodippathor Alavil Veezha Kaalinaal Oondriyittar Kazhippalai Cherppanare.“ Shiva Peruman, who is the Cherppanar of Thiru-Kazhippalai, saw Ravana, the king of Lanka with its ramparts, angrily attempting to lift Mount Kailash. Seeing this, and seeing Parvati Devi, who had great affection for him, become frightened, he, the reciter of the Vedas and wearer of the sacred thread, looked at Ravana with his mind, and in an instant, pressed him down with his toe, crushing him at the base of the mountain, causing him to lose his strength and fall. This is Shiva Peruman, the Cherppanar of Thiru-Kazhippalai.

This is the Thiru-Pathikam beginning with “Nangaiyai Bhagam Vaithar” composed by Navukkarasar in Thiru-Kazhippalai and its meaning.

Let us go on contemplating.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Three Hundred and Sixty-Four. Thiru-Nindra-Charukkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. The third Thiru-Pathikam composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar for the sacred place of Thiru-Kazhippalai begins with “Neithar Kuruguthan.” This Thiru-Pathikam is compiled as the one hundred and sixth Thiru-Pathikam in the Fourth Thiru-Murai. It is a Thiru-Viruttam Thiru-Pathikam.

In this Pathikam, only three verses are available to us.

Now, the three verses of that Thiru-Pathikam and their brief meanings.

The first verse: “Neithal Kuruguthan Pillai Endru Enni Nerungi Sendru Kaithai Madal Pulgu Then Kazhippalai Adhan Uraivai Paithar Piraiyodu Paambudan Vaitha Parisariyom Eydherin Irangathu Ka. Kandai Nam Iraiyavane.” Thiru-Kazhippalai is a sacred place in the Neithal region (coastal land). There are backwaters there. A stork residing there embraces a white screwpine leaf, thinking it is its child.

The Lord residing in such a beautiful Kazhippalai holds the moon and a serpent in his matted locks. Even though the moon is near the serpent, if the moon approaches the serpent, the serpent will mercilessly swallow the moon. “Don’t you know this, our Lord?” sings Thiru-Navukkarasar. The second verse: “Paruma Maniyum Pavalamuthum Parandhu Undhi Varai Porumaal Karai Meethirai Konarndhetra Polindhu Ilangum Karuma Midarudai Kandan. Emman Kazhippalai Endhai Peruman Avan Ennai Aaludaiyan Ipperunilathe.” On the seashore, which is as high as a mountain in this vast world, the ocean waves bring and deposit large gems, corals, and pearls. Our Lord, my Father Peruman, the blue-throated one, who resides in such a sacred place called Kazhippalai, is the one who has me as his servant in this great world.

Now, the third verse: “Naarpattu Irundhu Inbam Eythalutringu Naman Thamaral Kotpattu Ozhivadhan Mundhurave Kuliraar Thadathu Thaatpatta Thamarai Poigai En Than Kazhippalai Annalku Aatpattu Ozhindham Andre Valla Ma Iv Agalidathe.” In this vast world, living for a long time and attaining worldly pleasures, before being seized by Yama’s messengers and perishing, I became a servant to the Lord of Kazhippalai, who resides in a cool pond with blooming lotus flowers. Before being killed and destroyed by the agents of Yama, let us become servants of Thiru-Kazhippalai Shiva Peruman and be freed from the fear of Yama, he sings. That Thiru-Kazhippalai is a beautiful, cool Thiru-Kazhippalai with cool waters and ponds with long-stemmed lotuses.

This is the brief meaning of the three Thiru-Pattikams that we have now received in this Thiru-Pathikam. The next Thiru-Pathikam, the fourth Thiru-Pathikam, composed by Thiru-Navukkarasar for Thiru-Kazhippalai Thiru-Thalam, is the fortieth Thiru-Pathikam of the fifth Thiru-Murai, beginning with “Vannamam Vadivum.” This is a Thiru-Kurunthogai Thiru-Pathikam. Sivakavimani Aiya, who wrote the commentary on Periya Puranam, in his commentary, wherever our Samayachariya Perumakkal have composed Thevara Thiru-Pathikams, he explains the meaning of the Pathikam and the meaning of the first and last verses of that Pathikam, and then continues his commentary. Based on that, we too will contemplate the first and last verses of each Pathikam and then continue with the Periya Puranam commentary.

Accordingly, we will contemplate the first and last verses of this Thiru-Pathikam.

The first verse: “Vannamam Vadivum” (Color and Form). I did not see her directly in Thiru-Kazhippalai.

The Lord of Thiru-Kazhippalai knows the nature of this woman who, without seeing him, loves him and raves about him, even if she counts his sacred names. This ninth verse is corrupted. The tenth verse is as follows: “Ponsei Maamudivaal Arakkan Thalai Anju Naankum Ondrum Irutthaan Avan En Seyyaan Kazhippalaiyul Empiraan Thunjum Podhum Thunai Enal Aagume.” Shiva Peruman, who crushed the ten heads of Ravana, the great demon with a golden crown, and who resides in Thiru-Kazhippalai, our Lord, will be our help even when we sleep.

The fifth Thiru-Pathikam composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar for Thiru-Kazhippalai Thiru-Thalam. Among the total five Thiru-Pathikams, this fifth Thiru-Pathikam is compiled as the twelfth Thiru-Pathikam in the sixth Thiru-Murai. It is a Thiru-Thandaka Thiru-Pathikam. Its first and last verses are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. The first verse: “Oon Udutthi Onbadu”

Vasal Vaithu Ol Elumbu Thoonai Uromam Meinthu Thaam Eduttha Koorai Thavirappovaar Thayakkam Pala Padaithaar Thaamaraiyinaar Kaanedutthu Maa Mailkalaalum Solai Kazhippalai Meya Kapaalappanaar Vaanidathai Oodarutthu Vallai Sellum Vazhi Vaiththaarkku Avvazhiye Podhum Naame.“ Shiva Peruman, who resides in Thiru-Kazhippalai, will go and bestow grace upon those who are worthy. This body we have received is like a hut. The flesh of this body is the wall of this hut. There are nine doors in this hut-like body. The white bones are the pillars of this hut-like body. The hair is the roof spread over this hut.

Shiva Peruman, who bestows grace upon the worthy by going to them, so that this hut, this body, may depart. He is the Lord who holds the leaping deer in his hand. Such a Shiva Peruman bestows grace in many forms. He lovingly resides in Thiru-Kazhippalai, which has groves where peacocks with spread tails dance. Shiva Peruman, who holds a skull, has shown us the path to the world of liberation, the path by which we can quickly transcend all these worlds. He has also given us this body, as mentioned above.

Therefore, the purpose of receiving this body is to follow the path laid out by Shiva Peruman, the path of the Vedas and Agamas, and that is the only thing we can do. This is the only thing we can do in return for Shiva Peruman; there is nothing else, he sings. The last verse of this Pathikam, the tenth verse: “Poruthalangal Neelmudiyaan Por Arakkan Putpakandhaan Poruppin Meethu Odaathaaga Iru Nilangal Nadukkeyd Edutthu Iduthalum Ennizhaiyaal Thaan Veruva Iraivan Nokki Kara Thalangal Kathir Mudiyaar Anjinodu Kaal Viralal Oondru Kazhippalaiyaar Varuthalangam Maaya Kurambai Neenga Vazhi Vaiththaarkku Avvazhiye Podhum Naame.” Its meaning: Ravana, the demon skilled in war, had his Pushpaka Vimana on Thiru-Kailasa.

Therefore, when he tried to uproot Thiru-Kailasa, causing the earth to tremble, Uma Devi was frightened. Shiva Peruman then, with a glance, crushed his twenty arms and ten heads with his toe. That Peruman is graciously present in Thiru-Kazhippalai. He has revealed the way for the impermanent connection of this perishable body to permanently cease for the soul. Such is Shiva Peruman.

Therefore, following the path of the Vedas and Agamas revealed by Peruman, we will walk that path so that the connection of this body with the soul may permanently cease, sings Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, having departed from Thiruchitrambalam, visited the two sthalams of Thiru-Vetkalam and Thiru-Kazhippalai, and having sung Pathikams there, is now journeying back towards Thiruchitrambalam. As he journeys towards Thiruchitrambalam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar composes a Thiru-Pathikam, remembering the Koothapperuman of Thiruchitrambalam. “Manai Padappil Kadal Kozhundu Valai Soriyum Kazhippalai Marungu Neengi Nanaichinai Men Kulir Nyaazhal Pozhil Oodu Vazhikkonddu Nannum Podhil Ninaippavartham Manam Koyil Kondda Arulum Ambalaththu Niruththanaarai Thinaiththanaiyaam Pozhudhu Marandhu Uyvano” thus sings Sekkizhar Peruman, as he reached Thillai. Thiru-Kazhippalai is a sacred place rich in marine resources. The sea there, through its waves, brings all the conches from the sea and deposits them in the courtyards of the houses in Thiru-Kazhippalai. From such a Thiru-Kazhippalai, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar departs and travels through groves dense with Punnai trees towards the city of Thiruchitrambalam.

As he travels to Thiruchitrambalam, he composes a Thiru-Pathikam remembering Thillai Koothapiran. Which Thiru-Pathikam is it? It is the Thiru-Pathikam with the theme, “Ninaippavartham Manam Koyil Konddu Arulum Ambalaththu Niruththanaarai Thinai Thanaiyaam Pozhudhum Marandhu Uyvano.” It means, “If I forget the Thiru-Ambalakoothar, who graciously resides in the minds of those who remember him as a temple, even for a moment, will I be saved?” Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar goes to the city of Thillai, singing this Thiru-Pathikam with the theme, “If I forget the Thiru-Ambalakoothar, who graciously resides in the minds of those who remember him as a temple, even for a small moment, will I be saved?” The Thiru-Pathikam that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sang at this time is the Thiru-Pathikam that begins with “Panaikkai Mummatha Velam Uriththavan.” The first verse of that Pathikam is “Panaikkai Mummatha Velam Uriththavan Ninaippavar Manam Koyilaa Kondavan Anaiththum Vedamaam Ambalakooththanai Thinaiththanai Pozhudhum Marandhu Uyvano.” Sekkizhar Peruman, here, takes the theme of that Pathikam and states that he reaches Thillai, singing a Pathikam with such a theme. Sekkizhar Peruman mentions that this Pathikam was sung while going to Thillai from outside Thillai, remembering the Thillai Kootha Peruman.

Similarly, there are some other Pathikams as well. There are Pathikams like “Enthaiyaar Inaiyadi En Manaththu Ullave” and “Muthukunru Adaivome” and “Avanathu Aroor Thozhuthu” and “Arooranai Marakkalumaame.” These are Pathikams sung while going towards those respective sthalams from outside. Such historical references are contained within those Pathikams as internal evidence.

Therefore, we will now continue to contemplate this Thiru-Pathikam, composed on the way to Thillai, and the other two Thiru-Pathikams sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar at that sthalam after reaching Thillai. after reaching Thillai, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar continued to contemplate the other two Thiru-Pathikams sung at that site.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 365. Thiru-Nindrachcharakkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Departing from Thiru-Kazhippalai on the way to Thillai, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar composed the Thiru-Pathikam beginning with “Panaikkai Mummatham Vezham Uriththavan,” remembering Thillai Koothapiran.

Accordingly, in every verse of this Pathikam, he sings, “Will I be saved if I forget Shiva Peruman? Will I be saved if I forget Thiruchitrambalam Koothapperuman?” Now, let us contemplate the first and last verses of that Pathikam.

First verse: “Panaikkai Mummatha Vezham Uriththavan Ninaippavar Manam Koyilaa Kondavan Anaiththum Vedamaam Ambalakooththanai Thinaiththanaippozhudhum Marandhu Uyvano.” Its meaning: “Pana” Shiva Peruman, who makes the minds of those who remember him his temple, who assumes all forms, is the Ambalakoothan. Will I live if I forget such a Chithambala Koothan even for a moment, he sings. Shiva Peruman, who flayed the skin of an elephant and wore it, who is in the form of Gajasamhara Murthy, sings first in this verse. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings that he is the one who flayed and wore the skin of an elephant with a trunk like a palm tree and with three ichors.

“Panaikkai” means a hand like a palm tree. An elephant’s trunk is like a palm tree. A palm tree is thick at the bottom and tapers towards the top, and is black.

Similarly, the elephant’s trunk is like a palm tree, he sings. This elephant has three ichors: Kannamatham, Kapola Matham, and Beeja Matham.

Therefore, “Panaikkai Mummatha Velam” appears in this verse. Shiva Peruman is the one who flayed the skin of such an elephant. The “Velam” here refers to Gajasura. Gajasamharam is one of the eight heroic deeds of the Lord.

Thus, Shiva Peruman, who flayed the skin of the elephant with a trunk like a palm tree and with three ichors, is the one who makes the minds of those who remember him his temple. Although the Lord is omnipresent, the Lord will graciously manifest and reside in the hearts of those who remember him with love. While the Lord is unmanifest in other places, he will shine brightly in the hearts of devotees. He performs the sacred dance in the Ambalam. The implication here is that he prefers the hearts of devotees as his temple even more than the Ambalam. “Ullam Perunkoyil” is a Thiru-Manthiram composed by Thiru-Moolar.

Parimelazhagar, in his commentary on the Kural “Malarmisai Ekinan Manadi Sernthar,” explains “Malarmisai Ekinan” as “because he quickly joins the lotus-like hearts of those who remember him with love, in the form they remember.” Such a Shiva Peruman assumes all forms, meaning he takes all these worlds as his sacred body.

Moreover, Shiva Peruman assumes forms of enjoyment, yoga, and speed. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman mentions this in the Kolaru Thiru-Pathikam as “Pala Pala Vedamaam Paran.” He sings, “Thinaiththanai Pozhudhum Marandhu Uyvano,” meaning, “Will I be saved if I forget such an Ambalakoothan even for a moment?” “Thinaiththanai Pozhudhu” means a very small amount of time. “Thinai” is a measure indicating a small quantity. It means, “I will not forget even for a moment.” It is implied here that if one forgets, one will not be saved. This state of being constantly mindful of the Lord, not forgetting even for a moment, is a state experienced only by those who have truly realized and experienced the Lord. This is the meaning of the first verse.

In the second verse, it says, “Thirththanai Sivanai Sivalokanai.” Sivakavimani, in his commentary on “Thirththan,” writes that it means one who is pure and one who purifies. “One who is pure” means one who is eternally free from bonds and who purifies those who reach him by removing their bonds. “Aarttha Piravi Thuyar Keda Naam Aartthaadum Thirththan” is from Thiru-Vasagam. “Sendraadum Thirththangal Aartthaame” is from Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar’s Thiru-Pathikam, the Thiru-Alangattu Thiru-Pathikam. Continuing, the other sacred verses of this Thiru-Pathikam: “Thirththanai Sivanai Sivalokanai Murththiyai Muthalaaya Oruvanai Paartthanukku Arul Seytha Chitrambala Kooththanai Kodiyen Marandhu Uyvano.” “Kattum Paambum Kapaalam Kai Maan Mari I” Thittamaayidu Kaatteriyaaduvaan Sittar Vaazh Thillai Ambalakooththanai Ettanai Pozhudhum Marandhu Uyvano.

Maani Paal Karanthaatti Vazhipada Nee Nuzhalalaam Aazha Koduttha Ven Aaniyai Sempon Ambalaththul Nindra Thaanuvai Thamiyen Marandhu Uyvano. Pitthanai Perungadarangavudai Mutthanai Mulai Venmathi Soodiyai Chitthanai Sempon Ambalaththul Nindra Atthanai Adiyen Marandhu Uyvano. Neethiyai Niraivai Marai Naankudan Othiyai Oruvarukkum Arivunaa Sothiyai Sudar Semponnin Ambalaththu Aathiyai Adiyen Marandhu Uyvano. Maikol Kanddan Enthoelun Mukkaninan Pai Kol Paambarai Aarttha Paramanaar Seyya Maathurai Chitrambalaththu Engal Aiyanai Adiyen Marandhu Uyvano. Muzhudhum Vaanulakaththula Thevarkal Thozhudhum Potriyum Thuya Semponninaal Ezhuthi Meyntha Chitrambala Kooththanai Ezhuthaiyen Marandhu Enganam Uyvano. Kaarula Malarkondraiyaaranai Vaarula Mulai Mangai Manaalanai Therulaaviya Thillaiyul Kooththanai Aarkila Amuthai Marandhu Uyvano.

Ongumaalvarai Enthaluttran Siram Veengi Vimmura Oondriya Thaalinaan Thengu Neer Vayal Soozh Thillai Kooththanai Paangila Thondan En Marandhu Uyvano.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings this Pathikam and reaches Thillai. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing: “Ariyaanai Endru Edutthe Adiyavarukku Ezhiyaanai Avar Tham Sinthai Piriyatha Periya Thiru-Thandaka Senthamizh Paadi Pirangu Sothi Viri” Nindru Evvulakam Vilangiya Pon Ambalaththu Meviyaadal Poriyana Nindravarthammai Panindhu Thamizhaal Pinnum Paadal Seyvaar,“ thus sings Sekkizhar Peruman. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, who went to Thillai, had a vision of Thillai Koothapperuman and composed a Thiru-Pathikam beginning with “Ariyaanai.” Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sings a Pathikam from his heart about Shiva Peruman, who is difficult to attain but easy for devotees, beginning with “Ariyaanai.” Sekkizhar Peruman describes that he worships the Peruman who performs the sacred dance in the golden Ambalam, which shines throughout all worlds, and sings many more Tamil Pathikams. The Thiru-Pathikam now sung, beginning with “Ariyaanai” The Thiru-Pathikam beginning with “Ariyaanai” is revered by devotees as the Periya Thiru-Thandaka Thiru-Pathikam.

This Thiru-Pathikam is a Thiru-Pathikam that devotees always cherish in their hearts.

Therefore, it is named Periya Thiru-Thandaka Thiru-Pathikam. Just as the names “Adaiyala Thiru-Thandakam,” “Thiruvadi Thiru-Thandakam,” and “Potri Thiru-Thandakam” came to those respective Thiru-Pathikams for specific reasons, similarly, this Thiru-Thandakam is named Periya Thiru-Thandakam because this Thiru-Thandaka Thiru-Pathikam, which begins with “Ariyaanai,” is a glorious Thiru-Pathikam that always resides in the minds of devotees. This Thiru-Thandaka Thiru-Pathikam, which begins with “Ariyaanai Anthanaartham Sinthaiyaanai,” is compiled as the first Thiru-Pathikam in the sixth Thiru-Murai. That is why Sekkizhar Peruman states that he sings the great Thiru-Thandaka Senthamizh, which begins with “Ariyaanai” and never leaves the hearts of devotees. The word “Ariyaan” here means that the Lord is difficult to perceive, see, and describe. “Ariya Kaatchiyaraay” is a Thiru-Paasuram composed by Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman.

The first line of Periya Puranam, “Ulagellam Unarnthu Otharku Ariyavan,” begins with the same idea.

Thus, even though Shiva Peruman is difficult to attain, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar made him accessible through his songs, which is the meaning here. That is why the next line says, “Adiyavarukku Ezhiyaanai.” Now, the Thiru-Pathikam: Thiruchitrambalam. “Ariyaanai Anthanaartham Sinthaiyaanai Arumaraiyin Akaththaanai” Anuvai Yaarkkum Theriyatha Thaththuvani Thenai Paalai Thikazh Oliyai Thevarkal Tham Konai Matrai Kariyaanai Naanmukanai Kanalai Kaatrai Kanai Kadalai Kulavaraiyai Kalanthu Nindra Periyaanai Perum Patru Puliyooranai Pesaatha Naalellam Piravaanaale. Kattranai Gangai Vaar Sadaiyaan Thannai Kaaviri Soozh Valam Soliyum Karuthinaanai Attrarkkum Alanthaarkkum Arul Seyvaanai Aroorum Puguvaanai Arinthom Anre. Matraarum Thannoppar Illathaanai Vaanavarkal Eppozhudhum Vanangiyeththa Petranai Perum Patru Puliyooranai Pesaatha Naalellam Piravaanaale.

Karumaanin Uri Thazhe Udaiyaa Veekki Kanai Kazhalkal Kalanthozhippu Anal Kaiye. The Lord, who, adorned with the crescent moon in His matted locks, dances with His mighty shoulders, while the hosts of celestials bow their heads to behold His divine form, beautiful as a deer’s gaze, and whose face is like the full moon; the Lord of Perumbarrappuliyur – days not spent speaking of Him are days not born. The Father worshipped by great ascetics, the Lord of the celestials, Hara, the youth who bestowed the elixir of immortality upon the celestials, the Great One who became the surging seas, the mountain ranges, the earth, the sky, the perfectly ordered stars, the eight directions, the two luminaries, and all else; the Lord of Perumbarrappuliyur – days not spent speaking of Him are days not born. The great support, the potent medicine that dispels the suffering of devotees, who, having appeared in the vast world, abandon all support, kin, and attachments. Having abandoned and restrained the external senses, and having transformed the fruit of great penance with women into spiritual bliss, and having removed all commonality, He is the great support for those who are able to meditate upon Him; the Lord of Perumbarrappuliyur – days not spent speaking of Him are days not born. He who is the consort of the sweet-tongued maiden, whose form is like a mountain to the elephant-headed god, who wears a garland of blossoming konrai flowers, who is the essence of the sacred Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, the radiant flame of Thiruvarur, surrounded by fragrant groves where bees hum, the unwavering lamp, the supreme reality; the Lord of Perumbarrappuliyur – days not spent speaking of Him are days not born.

The fruit of all endeavors, the sound of the seven strings, the Lord who made the mountain His bow when the celestials strove to destroy the demons who caused great harm. He who consumed the ocean’s poison; the great benefit for those ascetics whose minds are unshaken by the sidelong glances of women with humming tresses; the Lord of Perumbarrappuliyur – days not spent speaking of Him are days not born. He who wears the hide of a black elephant, the Lord of Thiru Ekambam, adorned with beautiful flowers, who is near to any devotee, who is immeasurable and unknowable to the celestials; the supreme light, the transcendent Lord, who dances so that earth and sky may worship Him; the Lord of Perumbarrappuliyur – days not spent speaking of Him are days not born. He who wears the crescent moon, not yet full, the primal Lord who is all three worlds, who destroyed the three cities of His enemies, the radiant light, the emerald, the honey, the milk; the beautiful one who resides in Thirukutralam.

The Lord who is skilled in the dance, the King, the embodiment of wisdom; the Lord of Perumbarrappuliyur – days not spent speaking of Him are days not born. The ancient, radiant light, a pillar of fire, whose glory could not be seen by the dark-hued Vishnu with red eyes, nor by the lotus-born Brahma, who dispels the confusion of the mind; the radiant light that transcends the two worlds, the sky, the seven worlds, and the cosmos; the Lord of Perumbarrappuliyur – days not spent speaking of Him are days not born.

This is the great Thiruththāndakam hymn beginning with “Ariyānai.” We shall continue our meditation.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 366. Thirunindrachcharukkam. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sang the Thiruppathikam beginning with “Ariyānai” before the Lord of Dance, Koothaperuman, who performs His divine dance in the Golden Hall of Thillai. That Golden Hall possesses a radiant light.

This light expands and illuminates all worlds. It is called the light of wisdom. That Akasha is not inert like ordinary space; it is the Akasha of wisdom, the Chidakasha. When this light of Shiva-gnana spreads, it expands immeasurably everywhere, and thus it is called Thiruchitrambalam.

There, Kootha- Peruman continuously performs the fivefold divine dance.

Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar composed that great Thiruththāndakam, embodying the sentiment that “days not spent speaking of the Koothaperuman who performs this dance of grace in Thillai are days not born.” The phrase “Perumbarrappuliyurānai” appears. Perumbarrappuliyur is one of the names for the sacred site of Thiruchitrambalam. The theme of this Thiruppathikam is “days not spent speaking of the Lord of Perumbarrappuliyur are days not born.” The Lord exists to be known and to be praised. Yet, He is easily accessible to devotees who remember Him with love. Both the Lord’s inaccessibility and His accessibility are explained in this Thiruppathikam.

Therefore, the days not spent speaking of Him are days not born – this is the essence of this Thiruppathikam. Since this Thiruppathikam indicates that this is the purpose of human life, Sekkizhar Peruman states that it is worthy for everyone to keep it in their hearts and practice it, never letting it depart from their thoughts.

The Lord is unknowable to all who possess animalistic understanding (pasu-bodham). Nevertheless, He resides in the minds of the Anthana. Anthana are righteous ones, great sages, and devotees. He resides in their minds. This is the general meaning of Anthana.

However, this Thiruppathikam was composed by Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar in Thillai.

Therefore, the term Anthana here should be understood as “Thillai Vazh Anthana” (the Anthana residing in Thillai), and thus it means “He who is in the minds of the Thillai Vazh Anthana,” implying that He is always present in their thoughts.

Thus, Shiva, who is unknowable to all who possess animalistic understanding and who resides in the minds of the Anthana, is the Witness (Kari). “Kari” means witness. He is the one who, from within, witnesses and understands all actions of living beings. He is the inner meaning of the Vedas, residing within the sacred scriptures. The epithet “Arumarai” (sacred Veda) is used here.

Therefore, He is the inner meaning of the Veda that speaks of liberation (moksha). He is subtle, subtler than an atom. If anyone attempts to realize the Lord through their own efforts, He is unattainable to those who strive with self-effort and ego to know Him. He is unattainable to them. He is the true reality, the leader of the celestials, the form of eternal light. He is the exalted one who works in conjunction with Vishnu, Brahma, fire, wind, the roaring ocean, and the lofty mountains.

He bestowed grace upon the sage Vyagrapada Muni, the tiger-footed sage, in Thillai. Days not spent speaking of the true glory of such a Lord, days not spent conversing about Him, are fruitless days. That is, days not spent speaking of the Lord are days devoid of the purpose for which this birth was taken. One might ask, “Are there not also the benefits of dharma, artha, and kama, the three pursuits of life, in this birth? Even if one does not speak of the Lord, are there not these benefits of dharma, artha, and kama?” If such a question arises, these benefits, when compared to the great benefit of divine bliss, are very insignificant.

Therefore, they are negligible benefits or minor benefits.

Thus, the days spent praising the Lord, speaking of His glory, which are actions that bring us the great benefit of divine bliss, are the days that fulfill the purpose of our birth. All other days are fruitless days. This is the theme and essence of this Thiruppathikam.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman states that he sang the great Thiruththāndakam beginning with “Ariyānai Anthanaardham Sindaiyānai.” Let us continue with the beautiful Tamil hymn, rich in truthful and exquisite words, beginning with “Senjadai Kattrāi Muttraththu Ilanilā” Erikkum. How does Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sing? With a mind enveloped in love, melting with devotion, with two sacred eyes shedding tears like rain, with a sacred mouth filled with words of praise for Shiva, and with an unwavering sacred heart engaged in constant service, he sings the Thiruppathikams. The Thiruppathikam sung at this time is the one beginning with “Senjadai Kattrāi Muttraththu Ilanilā Verikkum.” This Thiruppathikam is compiled as the twenty-second Thiruppathikam in the Fourth Thirumurai. Sekkizhar Peruman describes this Thiruppathikam with epithets such as “excellent truth,” “beautiful words,” and “richness.”

He thus enumerates the epithets of this hymn, which clearly illustrate its qualities. This Thiruppathikam is an excellent hymn; its excellence lies in showing the way and place to behold the Lord. It is a hymn of truth, proclaiming the Lord’s divinity. It is a hymn of beautiful words, composed in the sweet melody of Thirunerisai. It is a hymn of richness, abundant in meaning. It is a Tamil hymn, rich in words that convey that meaning.

It is a garland-like hymn; that is, each verse of this Thiruppathikam begins with the theme of the moon shining, and concludes with the theme of the Lord dancing with fire in His hand, thus strung together like a garland. Each verse of this Thiruppathikam begins with the moon: “Senjadai Kattrāi Muttraththu Ilanilā,” “Ēranār Ēru Thampāl Ilanilā,” “Sadaiyanār Sārndha Nīrttar Thaninilā,” “Paiyaravasaiththa Algul Paninilā,” “Ōthinār Vēdham Vāyāl Oli Nilā,” “Ōrudampu Iruvarāgi Oli Nilā,” “Mudhal Thanichchadaiyai Mūzhga Mugizh Nilā,” “Maraiyanār Mazhu Ondrēndhi Mani Nilā,” “Viruththanāyp Pālanāgi Viri Nilā,” “Pālanāy Viruththanāgi Paninilā,” “Madhiyillā Arakkanōdi.” Thus, each verse begins with the moon.

Similarly, each verse concludes by singing of the fire held in the Lord’s hand: “Thulangku Eri Ādumārē,” “Nīnda Eri Ādumārē,” “Anal Eri Ādumārē,” “Kanal Eri Ādumārē,” “Kanal Eri Ādumārē,” “Pirangku Eri Ādumārē,” “Nīnda Eri Ādumārē.” Thus, this Thiruppathikam is structured so that each verse ends with the Lord dancing with this fire.

Therefore, it is a garland-like Thiruppathikam. Sekkizhar Peruman has bestowed many such epithets upon this Thiruppathikam.

Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar sang this Thiruppathikam in an astonishing manner. Astonishment is a feeling of awe that arises in the mind when one experiences something profoundly.

Now, this Thiruppathikam is the twenty-second Thiruppathikam in the Fourth Thirumurai.

“Senjadai Kattrāi Muttraththu Ilanilā Erikkum Senni, Nanjadai Kandanaarai Kaanalā Naravanārum Manjadai Sōlai Thillai Malku Chitrambalaththē Thunjadai Irulkizhiya Thulangkeri Ādumārē.” “Ēranār Ēru Thampāl Ilanilā Erikkum Senni, Āranār Āru Sūdi Āyizhaiyāl Ōr Pāgam Nāru Pūnjōlai Thillai Navindra Chitrambalaththē Nīru Meyppūsi Nindru Nīndheriyādumārē.” “Sadaiyanār Sāndha Nīrttar Thaninilā Erikkum Senni, Udaiyanār Udai Thalaiyil Unpathum Pichchai Ētru Kadigol Pūnthillai” Thannul Karudhu Chitrambalaththē Adigalāl Ārkka Nindru Vanaleri Ādumārē. Paiyaravasaiththa Algul Paninilā Erikkum Senni Maiya Kanniyālum Mālum Ōr Pāgamāgi Seyyeri Thillai Thannul Thigazhndha Chitrambalaththē Kaiyeri Vīsi Nindru Kanaleri Ādumārē. Ōthinār Vēdham Vāyāl Oli Nilā Erikkum Senni Pūthanār Pūtham Sūzha Puliyuri Adhalanārthām Nāthanār Thillai Thannul Navīndra Chitrambalaththē Kādhil Venkulaigal Thāzha Kanaleri Ādumārē. Ōrudampu Iruvarāgi Oli Nilā Erikkum Senni Pāridam Pāni Seyya Payindra Em Paramamūrththi Kāridam Thillai Thannul Karudhu Chitrambalaththē Pēridam Peruga Nindru Pirangkeri Ādumārē. Mudhal Thanichcha- Kadaiyai Mūzhga Mugizh Nilā Erikkum Senni Madakkazhitru Arivai Pōrththa Maindharai Kaanalāgum Madaththu Vandraraiyum Sōlai Malku Chitrambalaththē Kadaththōr Aravamādak Kanalari Ādumārē. Maraiyanār Mazhu Ondrēndhi Mani Nilā Erikkum Senni Iraivanār Empirānār Ēththuvār Idargal Thīrppār Siraigal Nīr Thillai Thannul Thigazhndha Chitrambalaththē Arai Kalalārkka Nindru Vanalari Ādumārē.

Viruththanāyp Pālanāgi Viri Nilā Erikkum Senni Niruththanār Niruththam Seyya Nīnda Pun Sadaigal Thāzha Karuththanār Thillai Thannul Karudhu Chitrambalaththē Aruththamā Mēni Thannōdu Analari Ādumārē. Pālanāy Viruththanāgi Paninilā Erikkum Senni Kālanai Kālāl Kāyndha Kadavulār Vidai Ondrēri. Gnālamām Thillai Thannul Navīndra Chitrambalaththē Nīlam Sēr Kandanaarthām Nīndheri Ādumārē. Madhiyillā Arakkanōdi Mā Malai Edukka Nōkki Nidhiyendrōl Neriy Ūndri Nīdirum Pozhilgal Sūzhndha Madhiyam Thōy Thillai Thannul Malku Chitrambalaththē Adhisayam Pōla Nindru Analeri Ādumārē.

This is the Thirunerisai Thiruppathikam beginning with “Senjadai Kattrāi.” There is a place where we can behold the Primal Lord, Thiruneelakandan. He, wearing the moon on His head, dances in Thiruchitrambalam, within the form of the fire of the final deluge. As we have already seen, two important themes are discussed in this Thiruppathikam: one is the Lord’s head, where the moon shines, and the other is the divine form of the Lord dancing with fire in His hand. The phrase “Eriyāduthal” (dancing with fire) refers to the Lord dancing with fire in the palm of His hand. This fire in the hand of Lord Nataraja symbolizes dissolution (samhāram).

Therefore, it highlights the supremacy of the Lord as the cause of dissolution. The beginning of each verse symbolizes creation (srishti), the origin. It also symbolizes wisdom (gnana) through Thiruchitrambalam.

Therefore, it is understood that the Lord, being the cause of dissolution, can again bring forth creation. We can reflect here on the meaning of the first sutra of Sivagnanabodham, “Oduṅgi Malaththu Uḷathām.” Thus, the dance of the Lord of the Ambalam is a dance of grace that performs the fivefold functions. It bestows the bliss obtained through Sivagnanam. We can behold Shiva, the God who is difficult to see. Where can we behold Him? In Thiruchitrambalam, in Thillai Thiruchitrambalam, where He dances.

How can we behold Him? By seeing Him dancing with the moon shining on His head and holding fire in His hand. This is the theme of this Thiruppathikam. The God who is difficult to see, wearing the moon on His head and holding fire in His hand, His dance in Thillai Thiruchitrambalam appears as a wonder, does it not? While there are many aspects to describe in the divine form of Koothaperuman, from His sacred crown to His sacred feet, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, in each verse of this Thiruppathikam, has placed the moon-adorned head and the fire in the palm of His hand to signify both dissolution and creation. We must remember this here.

Thus, the Lord who performs this dance of grace has entered even my heart, which is as hard and unyielding as stone. However, the Lord is greater than the greatest and smaller than the smallest.

Therefore, His presence even in my heart is not a wonder.

Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar concluded this Thiruppathikam. Sekkizhar Peruman also points out that he sang it in an astonishing manner.

Thus, while Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar was worshipping and singing of Koothaperuman, who constantly performs His dance in Thillai, in Thillai Thiruchitrambalam, for the removal of the egoistic darkness of souls and for them to attain the light of wisdom and liberation, the devotees conveyed a message to him. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar listened to the message spoken by the devotees. Having heard the message from the devotees, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar prepared to depart from Thillai.

Let us meditate further. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 367. Thirunindrachcharukkam. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We have seen the Thiruppathikams composed by Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar in Thillai. While he was performing sacred service in Thillai, the devotees conveyed a message to him.

Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar listened to it. The Periya Puranam verse states: “The devotees heard the sacred words of the child-saint, who, by the grace of the red-eyed Lord who consumed poison, floated on the ocean at the end of an eon, and who, having been fed the milk from the sacred breast of the daughter of the mountain king, mixed with the overflowing Shiva-gnanam, partook of it and grew in wisdom.” When Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar was residing in Thiru-Thillai, the devotees there recounted to him the sacred history of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, which transpired in the nearby sthalam of Seerkazhi. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman lived in the same era.

Therefore, the events of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar’s life often intertwine with those of Aludaiya Pillaiyar, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman.

Thus, to understand Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar’s history, we must also keep in mind the events of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s life as they appear. Sekkizhar Peruman illustrates this truth throughout his work. We shall see.

So, at this moment, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar is residing in Thiru-Thillai, singing praises to the Lord.

At the same time, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman is bestowing grace in Seerkazhi. During this period, the devotees recount to Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar the sacred history of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, specifically how the Goddess Herself fed him the nectar. Upon hearing this, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar proceeds to Seerkazhi, and a meeting between him and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman takes place. This is the brief historical summary of this event. We shall elaborate on this as shown by Sekkizhar Peruman. The sacred sthalam of Seerkazhi possesses twelve sacred names, among which the twelfth sacred name for Seerkazhi is Thiru-Kazhumalam.

This sthalam is one that floats, never submerging in the deluge of the cosmic dissolution that occurs at the end of each yuga. Sekkizhar Peruman here refers to it as Thiru-Kazhumalam, which floated during the final yuga.

Thus, among the twelve names of Seerkazhi, the last is Thiru-Kazhumalam.

Furthermore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has sung Thiru-Viruttha Pathigams here under this very name, Thiru-Kazhumalam.
