In such a Seerkazhi, by the divine grace of Thoni-Appar, who is enshrined there and whose vehicle is the red-eyed bull, the daughter of Thiru-Malaiyarasan, Periya Nayaki, the Ambikai, mixed the growing wisdom, which caused Shiva to flourish, with Her sacred breast milk and fed it to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar hears this sacred history from the devotees in Thillai.

Here, it is mentioned, “by the grace of the one who rode the bull.” Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman sings that the Lord came and blessed him riding on a bull, as in “Thodudaiya Seviyan Vidaiyeri.” In this sacred verse, Sekkizhar Peruman sings “Vidai Ugaththar Thiruvarulaal” to signify this.

Thus, by the grace of the one who rode the bull, Ambikai fed him wisdom along with Her sacred breast milk. This history is extensively discussed in Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s Thiru-Puranam. The Lord, looking at the mountain maiden, the Mother, who resides in one half of His body, commanded, “Let the milk flowing from Your breasts be given as food.” As commanded by the Lord, the Mother fed him. What the Mother added and fed was the wisdom that caused Shiva to flourish. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s Puranam states that he is the Pillaiyar who causes Shiva to flourish in all stable and unstable beings. We can observe the flourishing of the path of Shiva in all worlds in many parts of Pillaiyar’s history.

The Shaiva world attaining prosperity through the sacred ash and even palm trees becoming imbued with Shiva are examples of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s deeds. All who witnessed Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred marriage attained Shiva. These are all examples.

Thus, Ambikai mixed the wisdom that caused Shiva to flourish, enabling beings to attain salvation, with Her sacred breast milk and fed it to him.

The devotees in Thillai recount to Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar all these sacred histories of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman: his incarnation, his attainment of wisdom, his receiving of the golden cymbals that make sound, and his receiving of the palanquin. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to this history as “Thiru-Vaarthai” (sacred word) in this verse. Generally, “Thiru” denotes Shiva, and here it refers to the words concerning Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. It pertains to the history.

The devotees speak of these things. The implication here is that devotees do not engage in idle talk but speak such sacred words. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has now reached Thillai and is performing darshan, is he not? Before Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar reached Thillai and performed darshan, Pillaiyar, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, had also visited Thillai, performed darshan, and departed.

Therefore, the devotees there recount this to Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing: “Upon hearing the sacred history of the great one, who, having consumed the divine milk from the Mother’s breast, immediately sang the garland of seven-fold melodious Tamil, showing ‘He is our Lord,’ and who is capable of speaking, the great one who came from Seerkazhi, upon hearing his glory, with wondrous love, with great love, a desire arose in his mind to worship his lotus feet. At that very moment, he worshipped the feet of the Lord dancing in the sacred hall, received His grace, and, casting off the disease of false birth, circumambulated the sacred streets, prostrating himself. He then worshipped and praised the boundaries of the sacred city, which pervades all worlds. He then worshipped and sang at Thiru-Narayur, a place of inexpressible glory, accompanied by a throng of devotees, with folded hands and a body covered in sacred ash. Those who saw him, their hearts melted and dissolved, showing forth compassion.

“Thiru-Navukkarasar, who floated on a stone in the ocean, then approached Thiru-Pukazhi, where the Lord, who spoke the Vedas in rich Tamil, resides.”

“Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman sings the sacred history of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar’s arrival in Seerkazhi in three sacred verses. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar hears the news that Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, having partaken of the divine milk from the Mother’s breast along with wisdom, immediately sang a garland of rich Tamil verses imbued with the seven melodies. Upon hearing the glories of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Pillaiyar, the great one who incarnated in Seerkazhi, capable of singing and pointing out Lord Shiva as “He is our Lord,” a wondrous emotion of great love arises in Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. The arising of love upon hearing is a characteristic of supreme devotion. As such great love arose, a desire to worship the lotus-like sacred feet of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman arose in Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar’s mind. Previously, when he sang the great Thiru-Thandagam in Thillai, a wondrous love for the Lord arose, which was due to the Lord’s gracious vision.

“That love arose when he saw the Lord.

“Here, a wondrous love arises in Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, and this wondrous love arises from hearing about the greatness of the devotee.

“Now, the wonder arose when he saw the Lord; that wonder arose when he heard about the greatness of the devotees. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman points out Lord Shiva as “He is our Lord,” does he not? He points out the one who is unattainable to others. He speaks of the one who is difficult for others to describe. Upon hearing such a sacred word, which embodies both the greatness and the simplicity of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, love arises in Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. Such is the great stature of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman.

“Perunthagai” (great stature) means that he incarnated not for any personal gain, but for the flourishing of Shaivism in this world. Is that not so? That greatness is referred to as “Perunthagai.” Thus, upon hearing the sacred history of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, not only does a desire to see him arise, but also a desire to worship Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman arises in Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. This indicates the maturity of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar’s spiritual state. It makes us realize his state. “It is rare to attain the grace of Shaivism, which is humble even in its lowliness,” says Sivagnana Siddhiyar.

“When Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar heard this sacred history of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, his desire to worship the feet of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman was greater than his desire to worship the Lord of Thoni-Puram, who blessed Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. This will be the next historical event. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s lotus feet are life-giving lotus feet, lotus feet that always reside in the hearts of devotees. Even to worship Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s lotus feet in one’s heart, one needs prior penance. Only with such prior penance can we worship Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s lotus feet in our hearts. Those who have performed such penance will directly attain those feet.

“We can see this through the twenty-fourth sacred verse in Nambiandar Nambi’s Aludaiya Pillaiyar Thiru-Andhadhi: “Arumbina anbillai archanaiyillai aran adikke virumbina maandarkku meippani seykilan poykamaindha virumbina ullathinerku engkane vandhu nerpattathaal karumbana neezh vayal soozh Kaalinaadan kalaladiye.” This is the twenty-fourth verse of Aludaiya Pillaiyar Thiru-Andhadhi. Nambiandar Nambi expresses wonder in this sacred verse, asking how he, who lacks even a single good quality, could have attained the lotus feet of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, which are not even available to those with good penance and loving hearts.

“Therefore, as the desire to worship such lotus feet intensified and merged with love, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar takes leave from Koothaperuman in Thillai and departs for Seerkazhi. Our reflection shall continue.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 368, Thiru-Nindrachcharukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar departs from Thillai. He worships the sacred feet of Koothaperuman and, having received Koothaperuman’s gracious permission, departs from there. Thillai is a sacred city that pervades all worlds. It is a city that is complete in all places due to the fullness of Gnana-Akasha.

“Everywhere is the sacred form, everywhere is Shiva-Shakti, everywhere is Thiruchitrambalam, everywhere is the sacred dance, everywhere is Shiva.

“Thus, the grace of Shiva, which resides everywhere, is His divine play.” Thiru-Mooladeva Nayanar has sung about the Thillai Koothu in the Ninth Thanthiram of Thiru-Mandiram, stating, “The seven worlds are the beautiful city, the five ancient akashas are the city, and in the south, the chakra He has sung about the Thillai Koothu, stating that the Supreme Light dances, having the sacred hall as its stage. He has sung all this in the Ninth Thanthiram of Thiru-Mandiram. The Bhuta Akasha, that is, the elemental ether, one of the five elements, is inert ether. It pervades the other four elements and provides space for them.

“However, what exists in Thillai is Gnana Akasha, Chid-Akasha. This pervades and excels in all worlds. In such a glorious Thillai, which is a sacred city pervading all worlds, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar worships the sacred feet of the Lord who performs the dance of grace in the sacred hall, receives Koothaperuman’s gracious permission, and then departs from there. Before departing, he circumambulates and worships the sacred streets of Thillai. He worships the sacred feet of Koothaperuman and departs after receiving His grace. The blessing of worshipping Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s feet is attained only through divine grace.

“Therefore, for these two reasons – to be united with that divine grace and to take leave when departing from Thillai – he worshipped the sacred feet of Thillai Koothaperuman.

“Similarly, we can recall here the history of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, who, when going to meet and defeat the Jains in debate at Thiru-Alavai, sought permission from our Lord before proceeding.

“Thus, worshipping the feet of Koothaperuman, he casts off false birth. Thiru-Navukkarasar circumambulates the sacred streets of Thillai, prostrating himself. After receiving the gracious permission of Ambalavanan, the Nayanar circumambulates the streets. It is mentioned here how he worshipped Thillai and its sacred streets. It is a known event in our Nayanar’s history that after receiving grace and departing from Thillai in this manner, the Nayanar never again returned to Thiru-Thillai.

“Thus, he departs from there, prostrating himself in the sacred streets of Thillai and taking leave.

“Here, Sekkizhar Peruman states, “Poibpiravirandu valam kondu ponthae” (having cast off false birth and circumambulated, he departed). “Ponthae” means departed. The suffix “ae” here indicates that he departed for Thillai. In the Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman Puranam, Sekkizhar Peruman similarly mentions, “Koothar arul pettru pontharuli” (having received the grace of Koothar, he departed), referring to the event of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar properly visiting Thiru-Thillai, performing darshan, and taking leave to proceed to Seerkazhi.

“Similarly, in the Eyarkon Kalikkama Nayanar Puranam, Sekkizhar Peruman sings, “Porpathiyai vanangi poy” (having worshipped the golden city, he departed), when Sundaramoorthy Swamigal visited Thillai for the second time.

“Thus, having taken leave in Thillai, circumambulated and worshipped the streets, and reached the sacred boundary of Thillai, worshipping that boundary as well, Sekkizhar Peruman sings, “Seppariya perumaiyinar Thiru-Narayur panindhu paadi sellvar” (the one of inexpressible glory worshipped and sang at Thiru-Narayur and proceeded). Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar worships Thiru-Narayur, a place of inexpressible glories. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, who set out from Thiruchitrambalam to go to Seerkazhi, worships the sthalam called Thiru-Narayur on the way and then proceeds to Seerkazhi. Thiru-Narayur is a sacred sthalam near Thiruchitrambalam. It is the sacred sthalam that was instrumental in making the Thiru-Murais available to us. Nambiandar Nambi incarnated there, developed devotion to Pollap Pillaiyar, and through Pollap Pillaiyar’s grace, discovered the location of the Thiru-Murais in Thiruchitrambalam, thus making them available to us.

“We have already reflected on that history at the beginning of Periya Puranam. In this Thiru-Narayur In this sacred sthalam, the Lord’s sacred name is Soundarya-Nathar, and the Goddess’s sacred name is Thripura Sundari. The sthala-tree here is the Punnai tree, and the sacred water is Karunya Theertham. It is the sacred sthalam where Pollap Pillaiyar, who revealed the Thiru-Murais to us, is enshrined. It is a sacred sthalam sung by Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman and Appar Swamigal. Nambiandar Nambi has also sung about this sacred sthalam, as has Kapila Deva Nayanar.

“Its name is Thiru-Narayur.

“Therefore, a stork worshipped the Lord here and attained liberation.

“The Lord granted liberation to a stork here.

“Thus, this sacred sthalam is called Thiru-Narayur. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar worships the Lord of such a glorious Thiru-Narayur and then departs for Seerkazhi. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar proceeds, surrounded by a throng of devotees. His hands are folded in anjali. The sacred form of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, adorned with sacred ash, radiates compassion, causing the hearts of those who behold it to melt and dissolve. It is mentioned that he is surrounded by a throng of devotees.

“Many devotees, aware of the Nayanar’s greatness, gather around him. These are the sacred devotees who accompany Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar from Thiru-Thillai.

“Furthermore, devotees from Seerkazhi come to meet, worship, and escort Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar.

“Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar arrives, surrounded by a throng of devotees, with the desire to worship the lotus feet of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman in Seerkazhi. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar arrives.

“Therefore, he comes with folded hands, worshipping the direction and the city where Seerkazhi is located. That form is a sacred form that causes the hearts of those who see it to melt and dissolve; it is a sacred form that radiates compassion. The Nayanar’s sacred form is arranged in such a way as to outwardly display the compassion within him.

“Therefore, the hearts of those who saw it first softened, then dissolved, and then melted. We can recall here how, previously, when Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar arrived at Thiru-Vathikai Veerattanam from Thiru-Padiripuliyur, all who saw the Nayanar in the sacred street of Thiru-Vathikai had their hearts melt and spoke of the Nayanar’s gracious history.

“Similarly, here, devotees surround him. It should be understood that the compassion held by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar is boundless, extending to all living beings. This mental state of compassion is outwardly manifested in the Nayanar’s appearance.

“Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, who crossed the ocean by floating on a stone, and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Nayanar, who spoke the written Vedas in rich Tamil, arrive near the sthalam of Seerkazhi. Sekkizhar Peruman uses these epithets to indicate that both are great individuals who received divine grace. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar is the Lord who reached the shore by floating on a stone in the ocean, while Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman is the one who conveyed the meanings of the unwritten Vedas, which are the sacred words of the Lord, in Tamil.

“Thus, the one who composed the sacred scriptures, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, arrives at Thiru-Sirkazhi. Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, who was directly taken into grace by the Lord through the gift of the colic disease, arrives. Hearing the news that Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal was arriving at Thiru-Sirkazhi, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, with a great desire to see Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, came forward, accompanied by many of his devotees.

“We will now extensively contemplate the meeting of these two great spiritual masters.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 369, Thiru-Nindra Sarukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman comes to the border of Thiru-Sirkazhi to welcome Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, who has reached the border of Thiru-Sirkazhi. He sets out from within Thiru-Sirkazhi and comes to its border.

There, a meeting of two great religious preceptors takes place. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman were Nayanmars who lived at the same time, Shaivite preceptors who lived at the same time.

Now, the period when Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman was staying in Thiru-Sirkazhi was after he had completed his fourth pilgrimage. In the sacred history of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, Thiru- Gnanasambandha Peruman undertook seven pilgrimages. The first pilgrimage was to Thiru-Kolakka, where he received the golden cymbal and returned. The second pilgrimage was when the Brahmins of Thiru-Nanippalli, the birthplace of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s mother, invited him, and he went there, transforming the desert land into fertile land by singing sacred hymns.

Then, after visiting Thiru-Valamburam, Thiru-Saikkadu, and Thiru-Venkaadu, he returned to Thiru-Sirkazhi. This was the second pilgrimage. The third pilgrimage was to Thiru-Then-Thirumullaivayil, Thiru-Mahendrappalli, and Thiru-Kurukavur, after which he returned to Thiru-Sirkazhi. The fourth pilgrimage undertaken by Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman was to worship Thillai, also known as Thiruchitrambalam, and then Thiru-Erukkaththampuliyur. After worshipping Thiru-Mudukunram and other sacred places, he received the pearl palanquin at Thiru-Nelvayil Araththurai and returned to Thiru-Sirkazhi, where he remained adorned with the sacred thread. It was during this time that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar came to Thiru-Sirkazhi.

He came with the desire to worship the lotus feet of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, having heard his sacred history.

Therefore, at this time, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman had completed his fourth pilgrimage and was staying in Thiru-Sirkazhi.

Now, the meeting of the two great preceptors takes place. The meetings between Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman occurred three times. This is the first of those meetings. The other three pilgrimages undertaken by Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman were: the fifth pilgrimage was the manifestation of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s avatar, which was to reject false religions and spread the light of sacred ash. That event itself was the fifth pilgrimage. The sixth pilgrimage was to visit Thondai Nadu and return.

The seventh pilgrimage was to Nallur Perumanam and attain the sacred feet of the Lord.

Therefore, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman is now staying in Thiru-Sirkazhi, having completed his fourth pilgrimage.

At that time, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar arrives at Thiru-Sirkazhi. This is the first of the three meetings between Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman and Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar comes to the border of Thiru-Sirkazhi with the desire to worship the lotus feet of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. Hearing of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar’s arrival, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, wishing to see him, comes to the border of Thiru-Sirkazhi. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman comes to the border of Thiru-Sirkazhi to welcome Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, who was blessed with the great fortune of being taken into grace by Lord Shiva through the sacred gift of the colic disease. The colic disease that afflicted Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar was the grace of the Lord; it was not a disease.

The elders’ conclusion is that as devotion to the Lord increases, any obstacles or sufferings are also to be seen as manifestations of the Lord’s grace.

Thus, Lord Shiva, who bestowed the grace of the colic disease and took him into grace, is the Lord. The Nayanar who was taken into grace is Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, with the desire to meet and worship him and experience that blessing, arrives there. Along with Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, devotees who, by divine grace, possessed a similar disposition to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, also accompany him. Sekkizhar Peruman sings about this wonderful meeting: “Thozhuthu anaivutru aanda arasu anbu uruga thondar kuzhaththidae sendru pazhuthil perum kathaludan adipaniya panindhavar tham karangal patri ezhuthariya malarkaiyal eduthu irainji vidaiyin mel varuvar thammai azhuthu azhaithu kondavar tham appareye ena avarun adiyen endrar.” This is the 182nd verse in Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam, and the 1447th verse in Periya Puranam. The verse begins with “Thozhuthu anaivutru.” As we have already seen, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, with great desire to see Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, comes bowing and approaching.

There, we have already seen that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar arrived with folded hands.

Therefore, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, who went with the desire to see him, also bows in return and approaches. Pillaiyar bowed and approached. Among the throng of devotees surrounding him, the ruling saint, with melting love, went and prostrated himself before Pillaiyar with great affection. He prostrated himself with melting love and great affection before Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, who had come to see him. When the object of his great love and worship appeared directly before him, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar prostrated himself at the feet of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. The love that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar held was a flawless, great love.

Flawless love means that the love that blossomed then never diminished but continued to grow. We can recall here the historical events where these two religious preceptors met twice more after this.

Thus, with flawless, great love, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar prostrates himself at the feet of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. He falls to the ground and worships at his sacred feet with eight limbs. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman takes the hands of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, who thus worshipped, with his indescribable lotus-like hands. He took the hands of Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, who prostrated himself before him, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman took the hands of Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal with his own hands. This is one of the expressions that signify the depth and preciousness of love.

Similarly, in the history of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, we will see instances where he took the hands of Kulachirai Nayanar and Mangaiyarkkarasi Ammaiyar, who prostrated before him. The hands of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman are indescribable lotus-like hands. They are sacred hands like lotuses, whose form cannot be written or described. Does not Thevaram say, “He is the Lord, who cannot be written or shown”? Just as the Lord cannot be written or copied, so too Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman possesses indescribable lotus-like hands. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman takes the hands of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, who prostrated before him, with such lotus-like hands.

Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, in turn, prostrates himself and takes the sacred hands of Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal.

Thus, bowing upon seeing each other is born of the abundance of love.

Here, the idea is that both bowed at the same time, making it impossible to distinguish who bowed first and who later. That is also the characteristic of devotees. One should not see disparities in the love of devotees. Only those who do not understand the true nature of the Nayanmars’ love will perceive such disparities.

Thus, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, taking the hands of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar with his indescribable lotus-like hands, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, having taken the hands of Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal and worshipped him, addresses Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal as “Appare.” Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar replies, “Adiyen.” It is at this moment that Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman addresses Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal as “Appare.” This name, Appar Swamigal, is still used today for Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. This reveals the depth of love Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman held at that time. He calls Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar “Appar.” “Appar” means one who is like a father. He calls him “Appare,” meaning “You are like a father.” Therefore, implying that it is not proper for him to prostrate, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman addresses Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal as “Appare.” At that time, Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal also says, “Adiyen.” Even though Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman addresses him with the status of “Appar,” Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal says “Adiyen,” meaning “I am always your servant.” He says “Adiyen” with the implied meaning that “I am always your servant, therefore, prostrating is fitting for me.” Here we can see that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar is the best example of the humility described in Shaiva philosophy.

Now, the next verse: “Ambigai sempor kinnaththu amutha gnanam koduppa azhukai theerndha sembavala vayppillai Thiru-Navukkarasar ena sirandha seerthi em” Our great people, in the assembly where the devotees attained bliss and the celestials praised, filled the world with the sound of Shiva’s abundance. This is the next verse. The child-saint, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, whose crying ceased when Mother Ambika fed him the nectar of wisdom from a golden bowl, and whose sacred mouth was like red coral.

Here, it is said that his crying ceased when Ambika gave him the milk of wisdom. There are two terms here: “azhukai” (crying) and “theerndha” (ceased). “Azhukai” refers to birth, and “theerndha” refers to liberation, its cessation. Because Pillaiyar partook of the nectar of wisdom, not only did his crying cease, but the path of the Vedas flourished, and the great Shaiva path manifested. The succession of elements flourished, and so on, as we will see in his history.

Therefore, the crying of Pillaiyar was the cause for all beings in this world to cease their crying and attain stability.

Here, the reference is that he was only three years old at that time, a tender age.

Therefore, the color of his beautiful sacred mouth shone like coral. Hence, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to him here as “Sembavala Vayppillai” (Child with a red coral mouth). When he cried, his mouth was coral-like in shape. When his crying ceased, that sacred mouth became the source for the birth of divine Tamil, bestowing Shiva, the ultimate reality, and gracefully embracing this world.

Therefore, “Sembavala Vay” (red coral mouth) refers not only to the color, but the ‘semmai’ (redness/perfection) in ‘sembavalam’ also implies that it bestows Shiva, the ultimate reality. Such is Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, who possesses a sacred mouth like red coral.

Here, Thiru-Navukkarasar is the king of tongues that bestow the ultimate reality, possessing the quality of a king.

Thus, both are special individuals of the same nature, which is implied here. Sekkizhar Peruman, who gave the epithet ‘Sembavala Vayppillai’ to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman in this verse, refers to Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar simply as ‘Thiru-Navukkarasar.’ At this point, which describes a significant part of the Nayanar’s history, Sekkizhar Peruman mentions Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar’s sacred name without an epithet. By mentioning it without an epithet, he conveys his unique greatness.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to him as Thiru-Navukkarasar at this point.

Thus, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman and Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal are great individuals who are always worshipped equally by Shaiva devotees. When these two great religious leaders met, the devotees who accompanied both of them raised a sound of Shiva’s abundance, overflowing with Shiva-ananda. All the devotees who witnessed the great sight of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman and Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal meeting, immersed in Shiva-ananda, chanted the sound of Shiva’s abundance, “Hara Hara Hara Hara.” It is a Shaiva tradition to chant “Hara Hara Hara Hara” when devotees are overflowing with Shiva-ananda. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that the sound raised by the devotees filled the entire world. The first word, “Ulagalam,” which the Lord of Dance, who performs the sacred dance in Thillai, gave to begin this Periya Puranam, Sekkizhar Peruman has used here to signify the greatness and importance of this event. It says, “Sivam perugum oli niraiththar ulagamellam” (They filled the whole world with the sound of Shiva’s abundance).

We shall continue our contemplation of this. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 370, Thiru-Nindrachcharukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. By the great penance performed by the Shaiva world, the sacred event of the meeting of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, who are the two eyes of the Shaiva religion, takes place. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, the ruling saint, rejoices that he has been blessed to worship the feet of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, the child-saint. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, the great benefactor of wisdom, rejoices at having been worshipped by Thiru-Navukkarasar, the master of words. When Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar was staying in Thillai, he heard devotees narrate the sacred history of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, and he desired to see him and worship his feet.

Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar rejoices that he has been blessed to see Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman and worship his feet, as he desired. This is the state of mind of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. As for Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, he rejoices that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar came directly to him without him having to seek him out, and that he was blessed to see and worship Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. Sekkizhar Peruman states in this verse, to indicate that the joy of Pillaiyar, who found him without seeking, was greater than the joy of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, who sought and found him, that “Arasu uvappa” (the king rejoiced) and even more, “Vallalar magizhchi ponga” (the benefactor’s joy overflowed). The love that filled the hearts of both for each other was complete, that love filled both hearts completely, leaving no room for anything else. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar towards Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman towards Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, held an unvarying love.

That unity mingled with love occurred here.

After this, with the desire to worship Thonippurathu Eesar, who resides in Thiru-Sirkazhi, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman come to the Thiru-Sirkazhi temple. Thonippurathu Eesar is the deity enshrined in the Thiru-Sirkazhi temple. When Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal came to Thiru-Sirkazhi, he first worshipped Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. Only then did he conceive the desire to worship Thonippurathu Eesar, the Lord residing in Thiru-Sirkazhi. The desire was very strong. Because the desire that arose in his mind to worship the lotus feet of Pillaiyar was fulfilled, he received that grace and reached Thonippuram.

Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar came to Thiru-Sirkazhi precisely because of his desire to see Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman and worship his feet.

Therefore, after first seeing and worshipping Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, he now intensely desires to worship Thonippurathu Eesar. Not only that, but the gathering of devotees emphasizes the Lord’s presence.

Therefore, it is a truth found in the scriptures of wisdom that joining the company of devotees is most beneficial. In the twelfth sutra of Sivagnanabodham, Meykandar Devar has stated, “Anbarodu mariyi malaraneyam malindhavar vedamum alayamthanum aran ena thozhume” (Worship the form and temple of those who are filled with love for the Lord, as Shiva himself). In this sutra, Meykandar Devar has placed the assembly of devotees first. He first mentions the assembly of devotees as “Neyam malindhavar vedamum” (the form of those filled with love), and then places the temple second as “alayamthanum” (and the temple).

Therefore, according to Sri Meykandar Swamigal, the truth established in this sutra is that one should worship the sacred form of devotees before worshipping the temple. Accordingly, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar first worships the sacred feet of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, and then has darshan of Thoniyappar, who is enshrined in the Thiru-Sirkazhi temple. Not only that, but Thoniyappar and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman in Thiru-Sirkazhi have an inseparable connection.

Therefore, whenever he worshipped Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, then It is also implied that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar worshipped Thoni-Appar. When one devotee meets another, all they do is remember, speak of, and worship Lord Shiva.

Thus, after these two great personages met, they desired to worship the Lord of Thoni-Puram, who is worshipped by the sea, and are now proceeding to the Thiru-Koyil of Seerkazhi. Sekkizhar then composes the following Thiru-Padal (sacred verse) about the two great spiritual leaders of the Saivite faith: “A unique ocean of grace overflowing, and an ocean of love for all the worlds, and the exalted Saivite path, the foremost of religions, received its two auspicious eyes, and to save the world, the one who consumed the dark poison, and the grace of the one who bore all the worlds.”

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman composes this verse, stating that the child-saint of clear artistic wisdom and the king (Thiru-Navukkarasu) went and reached the temple of the red-matted celestial being. In the Periya Puranam, at this very important juncture where two great Saivite spiritual leaders meet, Sekkizhar Peruman places such a wonderful verse. Sekkizhar Peruman uses three similes in this verse to describe how this meeting of these two great Saivite preceptors was. He sings that it was like the meeting of a unique ocean overflowing with grace and an ocean filled with love for all the worlds. He sings that they are like the two auspicious eyes of the Saivite faith. He sings that to save this world, Lord Shiva, who consumed the poison, Lord Shiva’s grace and the divine grace of Shakti, who bore all these worlds, are manifested in these two.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman sings in this verse that these two, the child-saint of clear artistic wisdom (Pillaiyar) and Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, united and reached the Thiru-Koyil of Thoni-Appar in Seerkazhi, which is the Thiru-Koyil of Lord Shiva. This sacred verse is praised and admired by all Saivite devotees for its excellence. This verse is one of the great illuminating lamps shining on the mountain of the Puranam. Sekkizhar describes the coming together of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman and Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal and their journey to the Lord’s Thiru-Koyil as follows: Peruman describes it in this verse with three similes.

First, he states the first simile: “A unique ocean overflowing with grace and an ocean filled with love for all the worlds.” He asks, “Are there not two great spiritual leaders?” He says that their meeting is like an unparalleled ocean overflowing with grace and an ocean filled with love, these two oceans that help all the worlds. He sings that it is like one overflowing with grace and one overflowing with love. “Love gives birth to grace as a child” is a saying from the Thiru-Kural. According to that, grace is love that overflows without limit; it is compassion. Pillaiyar called Nayanar “Appar,” so he refers to him as the ocean of love. In this verse, he refers to Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman as the grace obtained through that love.

Therefore, he calls Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal the ocean of love and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman the ocean of grace. He sings that these two great personages are coming together like these two oceans uniting to bring good to the world.

Now, the next simile is that these two are the two great auspicious eyes of Saivism. The Saivite faith is a religion that possesses the means to flourish. The primary Saivite path has received two such auspicious eyes: Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, as stated in this verse. The Saivite path was illuminated by these two great personages. The meaning here is that all people should perceive the Saivite path through their sacred utterances, namely Thiru-Kadaikkappu and Thevaram, which are like two eyes. Even though there are two eyes, the consciousness of the soul that enters and perceives through them is one.

Even if there are two eyes, the perception that the soul receives through these two eyes is a single perception. Only when the vision of these two eyes converges and blends does complete vision occur. The right eye and the left eye, these two eyes, one eye completes the vision of the other. The right eye of Saivism belongs to the Lord, and the left eye belongs to the Mother. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that these are the two auspicious eyes of Saivism. By stating “two auspicious eyes,” he implies that there are two types of merits: unexperienced merit, experienced merit, general merit, special merit, instrumental merit, and true merit.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman praises Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar and Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman in this verse as the auspicious eyes of Saivism.

Therefore, both of these eyes become the auspicious eyes of Shiva for the Saivite faith.

Next, Sekkizhar Peruman praises them as embodying both the grace of Lord Shiva and the divine grace of Shakti, who bore all these worlds. The grace of the Lord is revealed to us because He consumed the poison. The divine grace of the Goddess is revealed because she bore all these worlds.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman praises Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, the child-saint of artistic wisdom, as the grace of the Lord, and Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar as the grace of the Goddess in this verse. The reference to “Gnana-Kandru” (child of wisdom) indicates that Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman bestowed unparalleled artistic wisdom.

Thus, these three elements served as similes for the coming together of these two great personages. The meaning of this verse is that their meeting occurred inseparably, like grace and love uniting, like two eyes uniting in vision, and like Shiva and Shakti uniting in grace.

Therefore, in this verse, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman is referred to as “Kandru” (child) And Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal as “Arasu” (king). Sekkizhar Peruman praises Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman as the ocean of grace and Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar as the ocean of love. He praises Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman as the right eye among the two auspicious eyes of the Saivite faith and Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar as the left eye. He praises Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman as the grace of the Lord and Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal as the grace of the Goddess in this verse. Through these three similes, we must observe that love, spreading as grace, leads to the path of Shiva, and receiving the Lord’s grace, attains the state of liberation, and these three culminate in the single concept of liberation.

We can also see here the implication that love and grace are the grammar and प्रमाण (proof) of the Saivite path, and the grace of the Mother and Father (Ammai-Appar) is its fruit. We can also see here the truth that nothing else can compare to the divine path of grace and grace itself, in parallel to the coming together of these two great personages, who are immense in love.

Lord Shiva is incomparable. These great personages, who saw and delighted in Him within themselves and saw nothing but Lord Shiva, when they came together, the resulting supreme bliss of Shiva cannot be compared to anything else. Nevertheless, such similes are only perceptible to the divine eye of Sekkizhar Peruman. The Saiva Siddhanta meaning, which states that through two types of merit, love and grace occur respectively, and as a result of these two, love and grace, the Shiva-Gnana (divine knowledge) which is the grace of the Goddess arises, and thereby the attainment of the sacred feet, which is the grace of the Lord, is revealed in this verse. Pandit Thiru-Periyasamy Pillai notes this. Why did Sekkizhar Peruman use these three similes for this meeting of these two great personages?

Because in the Periya Puranam, the meeting of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman and Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal occurs three times.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman places three similes in this verse. This meeting, which took place in Thoni-Puram, Seerkazhi, is the first meeting. There is also a meeting in Thiru-Pukalur. The meeting lasted for a long time. During this meeting, when a famine occurred in Thiru-Vizhimillai, both of them received the sacred coins (Padikkasu) through the grace of Lord Shiva and fed the devotees, thereby nurturing the Saivite path in the world. They also performed the great deed of opening and closing the sacred doors in Thiru-Marai-Kadu, allowing the Vedic path to flourish and the great Saivite tradition to shine.

The third meeting takes place in Thiru-Poonthuruthi. This was their meeting when Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman went to see Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal. This is the third meeting.

Now, in the first meeting, Appar came to see the child. In the third meeting, Thiru-Poonthuruthi, the child came to see Appar.

There, in accordance with the divine utterance of the child, the king (Appar) carried his palanquin. To show that the inseparable grace of the Lord and the grace of the Mother were the similes for these actions, in the third simile, he said that the grace of the Lord and the grace of the Goddess were combined. Sekkizhar Peruman states in this sacred verse that the grace of the Lord and the grace of the Goddess are together. Sekkizhar Peruman mentions the word “Arul” (grace) in two places in this sacred verse. The first place where “Arul” appears is “Arutperugu Thanikkadal” (a unique ocean overflowing with grace). This arises from living beings and, by the grace of God, proceeds for the pure welfare of other living beings.

The second place where “Arul” appears is “Iraivanathu Thiruvarulum Iraiviyarathu Thiruvarulum” (the divine grace of the Lord and the divine grace of the Goddess). This refers to the grace of the Lord and the grace of the Goddess, which are the life within all beings and animate them everywhere.

Thus, in the third simile, two types of grace are mentioned. The grace of the Lord removes death. The grace of the Lord, who has a throat that consumed poison, removes death. The grace of the one who bore all the worlds, as the second type of grace, It comes to give birth and help remove both birth and death. The three similes mentioned here were used to compare the coming together of these two great personages. We should understand that they came together like grace and love uniting, like the right eye and the left eye uniting, and like the grace of Shiva and the grace of Shakti uniting.

The ocean here signifies immeasurable greatness. The eye here signifies the ability to see when shown, and grace here signifies the ability to see by showing.

Thus, these two great personages unite and worship the sacred feet of Thoni-Appar. They both proceed to the Thiru-Koyil of the Lord, who is enshrined in Seerkazhi, surrounded by groves where bees always sing melodies. They bow before the Thiru-Gopuram, which is the sacred form of the Lord, and enter the Thiru-Koyil. The Thiru-Gopuram stands before the Thiru-Koyil. This Gopuram is called a Sthulingam.

Therefore, it should be worshipped as Lord Shiva Himself, which is a rule of temple darshan. After worshipping in this manner and entering, both great personages circumambulate and worship the great Vimanam there.

Here, Vimanam refers to the structures above the inner shrines of the temples. Specifically mentioned here is the peak of Thiru-Thoni-Puram.

Thus, both worship Thoni-Appar.

Then Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman says to Appar Peruman, “Appar, please sing about your Lord, Shiva.” Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman states that Thoni-Appar belongs more to Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar than to himself, and asks him to sing about his Lord. Hearing this, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, with tears continuously flowing from his eyes, takes up the sacred word, which is a truthful language full of art that helps one realize Shiva, and sings the Thevaram, a sacred hymn. He stands before Thoni-Appar, who lovingly resides in Thiru-Thoni with Periya Nayaki Ammaiyar, and devoutly sings the Thevaram, a garland of beautiful Tamil. That Thevaram hymn begins with “Paarkondu Moodi.” We will continue to reflect on it. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 371, Thiru-Nindra-Charukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. In the Thiru-Koyil of Brahma-Pureeswarar in Seerkazhi, Thiru-Gnanasambandhar asks Thiru-Navukkarasar, who is having darshan of Thiru-Thoni-Appar, “Appar, please sing about your Lord.” At that time, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar composed two hymns. The first hymn begins with “Paarkondu Moodi,” and the second hymn begins with “Padaiyar Mazhuvondru.” Now, let us look at the verses of these two sacred hymns. The first sacred hymn is compiled as the eighty-second sacred hymn in the fourth Thiru-Murai. This sacred hymn, Thiruchitrambalam: “Paarkondu Moodi Kadal Kondagnan Nin Paadhamellam Naalaindhu Pullinam”

Eanthina enbar nalir madhiyam Kaalkonda van kai sadaiviritthu aadum Kazhumalavarkku aalanri mattrumundo Andha naali akalidhame Kadaiyaar kodi nedu maadangalengum kalandhilanga Udaiyaan udai thalai maalaiyum soodi ugandharuli Vidai thaan udaiya avvedhiyan vaazhum Kazhumalatthul Adaivaar vinaigal avai ezhuga naaldhorum aaduvanae Thiraivaaip perungadal muttham kuvippa mugandhu kondu Nuraivaai nuzhaichiyarodhi Kazhumalatthul azhundhum Viraiyaai narumalar soodiya vinnnavan than adikkae Varaiyaa parisu ivai naaldhorum nandhamai aazhvanavae Virikkum arumbadham vedhangal podhum vizhumiyanool uraikkil Arumporul ulluvar ke Kil ulagamuttrum erikkum paraiyodu boodhangal paada Kazhumala van niruttham pazhambadi aadum kazhal nammai aazhvanavae Sindhitthu ezhu maname ninaiyaamun Kazhumalatthai Bandhittha valvinai theerkavallaanai Pasupathiyai Sandhittha kaalam arutthum enrenni irundhavarkku Mundhi thozhu kazhal naaldhorum nandhamai aazhvanavae Nilaiyum perumaiyum needhiyum saala azhagudaiththaai Alaiyum peruvellatthu andru midhandha itthonipuram Silaiyil thiripuram moondru eriththaar tham kazhumalavar Alarum kazhaladi naaldhorum nandhamai aazhvanavae Muttrikkidandhu munneerin midhandhu udan moiththa amarar Suttrich kidandhu thozhappadugindradhu soozh aravan Thettrich kidandhu vengondral thundri ven Thingal soodum kattraich sadaimudiyarkku idamaya Kazhumalame Udalum uyirum oruvazhi sellum ulagatthullae Adaiyum unai vandhu adaindhaar amarar adiyinai keezh Nadaiyum vizhavudu naaldhorum malkum Kazhumalatthul Vidaiyandhanipadham naaldhorum nandhamai aazhvanavae Paravaik kadal nanjam undadhum illai ippaar muzhudhum Niravikkidandhu thozhappadugindradhu neendu iruvar Siramappadavandhu saarndhaar kazhaladi kaanbadharkae Aravak kazhaladi naaldhorum nandhamai aazhvanavae Karaiyaar kadal soozh ilangaiyarkon than mudi sidhara Tholayaa malaradi oondralum ullam vidhir vidhirndhu Thalaiyaaykidandhu uyarndhaan than kazhumalam kaanbadharkae Alaiyaa parisivai naaldhorum nandhamai aazhvanavae Thiruchitrambalam.

Now, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar’s The second sacred hymn sung. This sacred hymn is the eighty-third sacred hymn in the fourth Thiru-Murai, but only one sacred verse from this hymn has been found.

Now, that sacred hymn: “Padaiyar mazhuvondru pattriya kaiyin padhi vinavil Kadaiyar kodi nedu maadangal ongum Kazhumalamaam Madai vaai kuruginam paalai virithorum vandinangal Pedai vaai madhuvundu peraadhirukkum perumbadhiye.” Thiruchitrambalam. These two sacred hymns are the hymns composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar in Seerkazhi. These sacred hymns are dedicated to Thoni-Appar, who is enshrined in the Thiru-Koyil in the sacred town of Seerkazhi. Thoni-Appar is the Lord who revealed Himself and took possession of the child-saint (Aludaiya Pillaiyar).

Therefore, he Thiru-Navukkarasar also went there and sang hymns. In the Thiru-Koyil in Seerkazhi, there are three shrines: Brahma-Pureeswarar, Thoni-Appar, and Sattaiyappar.

Here, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar composed these hymns in praise of the sacred feet of Thoni-Appar. After composing these sacred hymns, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar proceeded to the sacred abode of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman and was served sacred food there. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred abode, his home, is currently located in the outer street outside the western gopuram entrance of the Seerkazhi Thiru-Koyil. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman did not allow Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar to stay anywhere else but welcomed him into his own sacred abode. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar then partook of the sacred food there. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, who teaches the world that feeding devotees is the first of the two great benefits for those born on earth, demonstrates it here.

“O Poombavai, do you leave without seeing the food served to the Rudra-Balgans of united character?” is a Thevaram by Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, composed in Thiru-Mayilai.

Therefore, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman welcomed Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar and the devotees who accompanied him into his sacred abode, prepared and served them sacred food with great honor. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar lovingly partook of that divine ambrosia. Partaking of the food was the action of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar; serving the food was the action of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. Sekkizhar Peruman thus presents the act of Nayanar partaking of the food in this Puranam, and the act of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman serving the food in the Puranam of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, with due emphasis. That is, in this sacred verse, he sings that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar partook of the sacred food. In the sacred history of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, Sekkizhar Peruman, singing about the same event, sings that Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman served the sacred food.

Thus, after partaking of the food, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar stayed for many days in the sacred abode of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman in Seerkazhi. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that he stayed there, and their renewed friendship and kinship grew like that day. “Kezhmai” means kinship; here, it refers to the great kinship of the Shiva-Ganas. If one speaks of kinship, there is also kinship without friendship; therefore, here, the poet specially sings of ‘friendship in the form of kinship.’ The meeting of these great personages, which began here, occurs again twice. This kinship, a great family of Shiva’s ganas, grows during the second meeting at Thiru-Pukalur, Thiru-Vizhimilalai, and Thiru-Maraikkadu.

Then, when the third meeting takes place at Thiru-Poonthuruthi, it flourishes, which Sekkizhar Peruman indicates by singing ‘grew and flourished.’ Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasar Nayanar stayed there for many days with Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman.

Here, Sekkizhar Peruman uses the word ‘udan’ (with). ‘Udan’ is a word that shows the uniqueness of Saiva Siddhanta, unlike any other religious doctrine. Its specialty is the mixture of two things, neither becoming one nor separate. We can recall and understand this by remembering the section explained under the Sivagnanabodham sutra, ‘Avaie Thaneyai’ (He Himself is they). During those days, the boundless joy that Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman and Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman experienced through their mutual conversation grew immensely. Many days passed with such mental joy. Conversing and associating with a mingling of feelings brings immense, boundless joy.

Due to the maturity of this experience, time passed unnoticed by them; time simply elapsed. In Saiva Siddhanta, there are two qualities referred to as ‘Anaintha’ qualities: one is being with the assembly of devotees, and the other is worshipping in temples.

Now, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar is among the assembly of devotees. While he is in this state, a desire arises in Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar to worship in temples, which is the other ‘Anainthor’ quality. This feeling arose in Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar to teach the world that both being with the assembly of devotees and worshipping in temples bring good to people. As a great desire to worship in temples arose, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar’s wish to visit the temples where Lord Shiva is enshrined on both banks of the Kaveri River became paramount. Although Lord Shiva is omnipresent, there are numerous sthalams where He is visibly enshrined in the Kaveri region. A yearning arose in Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar to behold such sacred sthalams of the Chola country, through which the Ponni River flows.

Therefore, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar departs from Sirkazhi. As he departs, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman also sets out with Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, and together they proceed to Thiru-Kolakka, a sacred place near Sirkazhi. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman bids farewell to Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar there, after worshipping at Thiru-Kolakka. From there, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar begins his pilgrimage to the sacred sthalams of the Chola country. When elders visit our home and then return, it is our tradition to accompany them for a short distance and see them off. In accordance with this tradition, Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman went as far as Thiru-Kolakka, which is near Sirkazhi, to bid farewell to Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar.

Although Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar departed from there, he carried the love of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman with him. Pillaiyar received the Nayanar’s love, and the Nayanar received Pillaiyar’s loving farewell.

Thus, having received his farewell, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar sets out beyond Thiru-Kolakka. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman returns to Sirkazhi. Having thus departed, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar visits the sthalams on the northern and southern banks of the Kaveri. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing about which sthalams he visited. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing in the Periya Puranam, song number 1454, which is the 189th sacred verse in the Puranam of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar: “Andar Arasu departed, and he went with him to Kolakka, worshipped, and returned with love. He also took leave and went beyond, to the places desired by the Lord of the Vedas: Thiru-Karuppariyalur, Thiru-Punkur, Thiru-Nidur, Thiru-Kurukkai, Thiru-Nintriyur, and Thiru-Nanippalli, among others, where the Lord with the eye on His forehead resides.

“He worshipped His feet and proceeded.” Sekkizhar Swamigal sings thus. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar visits and worships at all the places where the Lord of the Vedas desired to reside. Although Lord Shiva, the Lord of the Vedas, has no likes or dislikes, the text here states that He desired to reside in all the sacred places. What does this mean? It means that these are the places where the Lord desired to reside for the sake of souls, so that they might easily find and reach Him.

“Thus, the sthalams that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar visited on the northern and southern banks of the Kaveri, after Thiru-Kolakka, include Thiru-Karuppariyalur, Thiru-Punkur, Thiru-Nidur, Thiru-Kurukkai Veerattam, Thiru-Nintriyur, and Thiru-Nanippalli. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that he worshipped the sacred feet of Lord Shiva and proceeded further. Sekkizhar Peruman mentions many more sthalams.

“Therefore, we will continue to contemplate the references to those sthalams and the sacred verses that Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar composed for them.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 372, Thiru-Nindrachcharukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar departs from Thiru-Kolakka and begins his pilgrimage to the sacred sthalams of the Chola country, through which the Ponni River flows. Sekkizhar Peruman sings about all the sthalams he visited, in accordance with the twelfth sutra of Sivagnanabodham, “Alayam Thaanum Aran Ena Thozhume” (The temple itself is worshipped as a fortress). “To the places desired by the Lord of the Vedas: Thiru-Karuppariyalur, Thiru-Punkur, Thiru-Nidur, Thiru-Kurukkai, Thiru-Nintriyur, and Thiru-Nanippalli, among others, where the Lord with the eye on His forehead resides. He worshipped His feet and proceeded.

“He reached both banks of the Ponni River, where water flows, and sang of Thiru-Chemponpalli, where the bull is raised, and where tall peacocks dance. He sang of Thurai, the long bank of the Ponni, Thuruthi, Velvikudi, Ethirkolpadi, and many other sacred places of the Supreme Lord, praising them with beautiful Tamil verses, and then proceeded. He reached Avoor and Anjaaduvaar Kodikkavil, worshipped there, and then arrived at Aavaduthurai,” thus Sekkizhar Peruman concludes his song. He thus sings the history of Thiru-Navukkarasar’s journey from Thiru-Karuppariyalur to Aavaduthurai. He continues to sing about the other sthalams visited by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar in subsequent verses.

“Here, we will briefly contemplate the sthalams mentioned so far and the sacred verses sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar there, and then we will look at the other sthalams. From Thiru-Kolakka, the first sthalam Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar reached after departing was Karuppariyalur. This is located near Vaitheeswaran Koil, also known as Thiru-Pullirukku Velur, to its northwest. The present name of this sthalam is Thalainayiru. This sthalam is similar to the sacred sthalam of Sirkazhi, and therefore it is referred to as Melai Kaali.

“Here, the Lord’s sacred name is Aparadhakshameswarar (Lord who forgives sins), and the Goddess’s sacred name is Vichithra Valaiyambikai (Goddess with a wondrous bangle) or Kolavalai Nayaki. The sthala vriksham here is Kodimullai (a type of jasmine), the Theertham is Indra Theertham, and there is a red water lily pond. The deities on the hill are Thoniyappar and Sattai Nathar. For this sacred sthalam, one sacred verse composed by Thiru-Gnanasambandha Swamigal and one by Sundaramurthi Swamigal are available, making a total of two sacred verses. We saw that Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal visited this sthalam, but the sacred verse sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar for this sthalam is not available to us. There is a sthala puranam for this sthalam, consisting of 298 songs, composed by Maruthur Ambalavanar.

“This sthalam is located north of the Kaveri, south of the Vinayaka River, east of Thiru-Valikozhiputhur, and west of Sirkazhi. The sthala vriksham here is Mullai, which is called Kogudi Mullai, a type of Mullai. Since Mullai is the sthala vriksham here, this sthalam is named Yudhikavanam. Because the karma that causes birth is destroyed here, it is named Kanma Nasapuram. Since the Sun worshipped here, it is also named Adityapuri and Thalainayiru. It is named Thiru-Karuppariyalur because it bestows supreme knowledge and severs the root of birth.

“Like Sirkazhi, this sthalam is a Katumalai sthalam, where the Lord is enshrined in three tiers. Sattai Nathar is seated in the upper tier, which is Ratnagiri, and Thoniyappar is also present. Since this sthalam is located west of Sirkazhi and is similar to Sirkazhi, it also bears the name Melai Kaali. The Theerthams associated with this sthalam, as we saw, are Indra Theertham and the red water lily pond.

“In addition, there are eight Theerthams: Vinayaka Theertham, Surya Theertham, Vasishta Theertham, Hanuma Theertham, Nimba Pushkarani, Sanga Pushkarani, Potramarai, and the red water lily pond. When Indra desired a Theertham to worship the Lord in Sirkazhi, Vinayaka Peruman caused the water in Agastya’s kamandalam to flow as a river. That river flows here, hence it is named Vinayaka Nadi. Those who bathe in this river will gain ancient knowledge and will not experience sorrow. Surya, who lost his teeth for attending Daksha’s yagna, lost his radiance, and the world became dark.

“Therefore, everyone appealed to Surya, who then came to Thiru-Karuppariyalur, worshipped Kutram Porutha Nathar, created a Theertham before Him, and worshipped according to the prescribed rites. His ailment was cured, and he regained his lost radiance. Bathing in this Theertham on Sundays is highly auspicious. The competition between Vayu Bhagavan and Adiseshan is a well-known story to all of us.

“At that time, one of the peaks of Mount Meru, which was scattered, came here and transformed into Ratnagiri, a mountain.

“The Lord is enshrined here. Indrajit, the son of Ravana, worshipped at this sthalam. We know the story that after slaying Ravana in the Ramayana, Sri Rama performed Linga puja at Rameswaram.

“At that time, Rama instructed Hanuman to bring a Shiva Lingam within two ‘naligai’ (a short period). Hanuman went north. Realizing the great delay, Rama and Sita fashioned a Lingam out of sand and performed puja.

“At that time, Hanuman rushed back with a Lingam. He lamented, asking why they had performed puja and fashioned a Lingam before he arrived. Thinking highly of his bodily strength, he tied his sword to the Lingam and tried to pull it, but he could not move the Lingam. Hanuman was distressed. After much effort, Hanuman fell down, breathless. Seeing this, Sri Rama was saddened and lifted Hanuman, comforted him, and commanded him to perform penance to atone for his offense against Shiva.

“As he performed penance, Lord Shiva appeared before Hanuman and blessed him, saying that his offense would be removed if he went to Thiru-Karuppariyalur, also known as Kanmanasapuram, and worshipped there. Hearing this, Hanuman came here, performed puja, and worshipped the Lord.

“The Lord also bestowed His grace upon him. Amazed by the Lord’s compassion, Hanuman installed a Lingam in his own name in the northeast corner of this sthalam, created a Theertham for it, and performed worship. That sthalam is now known as Thiru-Kurugukka. The story of King Chitrangathan is also found in this sthala puranam. The Thiru-Uruvam (sacred form) of Nataraja Peruman in this sacred temple is very ancient, seated with widely spread red matted locks. One can see the antiquity and divine beauty shining in His sacred form.

“The sacred face of the Somaskanda Thiru-Uruvam expresses boundless joy through a gentle smile. There is a legend that a stork also worshipped at this sthalam. This is one of the temples belonging to the Dharmapuram Adheenam. These are the historical details of the sacred sthalam of Thiru-Karuppariyalur. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar worshipped here and sang a sacred verse, but due to our lack of merit, that verse is not available to us. Having thus worshipped Thiru-Karuppariyalur, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar next reached the sacred sthalam of Thiru-Nidur and worshipped the Lord there.

“After worshipping Thiru-Nidur, Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal proceeds to Thiru-Punkur.

“Therefore, he has sung about these two sacred sthalams, Thiru-Punkur and Thiru-Nidur, in a single sacred verse. That sacred verse is a Thiru-Thandaka Thiru-Pathikam titled ‘Thiru-Punkurum Thiru-Nidurum’.

“First, let us briefly contemplate the special features of this sthalam, Thiru-Nidur. Among the sacred sthalams sung in the Chola country, Thiru-Nidur is a sthalam sung by Thiru-Navukkarasar and Sundaramurthi Swamigal. The sacred name of the Lord here is Arut-Somanatheswarar, Nirthagana Priyar, Gana Nirthana Sankarar, Bhadrakaleeswarar. The sacred name of the Goddess is Adithya Abhayapradambikai, Vedanayaki, Aalalasundaranayaki, Veyuruththozhi Ammai. The sthala vriksham here is the Magizha tree. This sthalam is renowned for being worshipped by Soma and others.

“Vadimalaippillai of Thiru-Nidur has composed a sthala puranam of 400 songs. This sthalam is located on the northern bank of the Kaveri. This sthalam is mentioned in Sangam Tamil literature such as Akananuru and Purananuru. It is a town of enduring great fame, hence it is named Nidur, a name based on its characteristic. The sthala puranam explains the reason for its name Nidur, stating that it is a sthalam that remains indestructible even during the time of dissolution. “Even if the deluge comes, it remains undestroyed, hence it is always called the incomparable Nidur,” is a part of the sthala puranam’s song.

“The sthala vriksham is the Magizha tree, hence it is called Vakularanyam, Magizharanyam, and Magizhavanam.

“The Lord of this sthalam has the special name Padiyadiya Devar (Lord who danced and sang). The Goddess also has the name Adhikandhiyammai.

“The Lord here manifests as a Swayambhu Murthi. A crab worshipped Him and requested to merge with Him, and the Lord, in His grace, granted the crab’s wish. To make this act of grace known to the world, He appears with a net at the top of His sacred form. The Thiru-Nidur sthala puranam states that there are nine Theerthams for this sthalam: Ananda Theertham, Sengalinir Odai, Surya Theertham, Chandra Theertham, Indra Theertham, Bhadrakali Theertham, Munivarar Theertham, Paruthi Kundam, and Varuna Theertham. The information we get from the sthala puranam includes the histories of Indra’s worship, Chandra’s worship, Bhadrakali’s worship, the crab’s worship, Surya’s worship, and Sembiyan’s worship. Bhadrakali visited many sthalams such as Kedaram and Kasai, worshipped the Lord, and then came to Thiru-Nidur, also known as Vakularanyam.

“She bathed in the Kaveri, took a sacred dip in the Sengazhinir Vavi (red water lily pond), and also immersed herself in other Theerthams, worshipping Kanan Ruthra Sankarar at this sthalam. She herself was bestowed with the sacred duty of protecting Nidur under the name Aalalasundari by the Lord.

“Accordingly, even today, Bhadrakali, with the sacred name Aalalasundari, is enshrined in a north-facing shrine in front of the sacred temple and protects this sthalam. This sacred temple has an east-facing structure. To the south, there is a beautiful sacred pond. Beyond the Aalalasundari temple, to the south, is the Magizha tree, the sthala vriksham. The Goddess appears in a south-facing shrine. Upon entering further, there is a very large Ardhamandapam.

“Beyond that, in the circumambulatory path, one can worship the Nalvar who worshipped Somanathar, Bhairavar, Sapthamathas, Subrahmanya Kadavul, and also behold Sivalokanathar, Kailayanathar, and Viswanathar.

“Following that, one can visit the shrines of Thirumagal, Chandikeswarar, and Vedanayaki. A beautiful Koothapiran (dancing Lord) form, a sacred vision of the Lord who is pleased with the south, is enshrined here.

“The Lord is enshrined within as a Swayambhu Murthi, bearing the mark of the crab’s worship. Among the Utsava Murthams in the sanctum sanctorum are Somaskandar, Piriyavidai Amman, Vedanayaki, Bhogasakthi, Murugan, Valli, Deivanai, Munaiyaduvar Nayanar, Indra, Bhadrakali, and Mariamman. One can also enjoy seeing the forms of Lakshmi Narayanan, Rama, Lakshmana, Sita, and Hanuman, brought from a Perumal temple here. This is the birthplace of Munaiyaduvar Nayanar, one of the sixty-three Nayanmars. This is also the sthalam where the Nayanar attained liberation through his service. The sacred form of Munaiyaduvar Nayanar, with folded hands, is enshrined in this sacred temple.

“He served the devotees of the Lord and performed Maheswara Puja with the income from his profession, adhering to the unwavering path of love. There is a history that when Sundaramurthi Swamigal worshipped the Lord of Thiru-Nintriyur and was about to proceed to worship the Lord of Thiru-Punkur without worshipping the Lord of Thiru-Nidur, his true understanding blossomed, and he came here to sing and worship the Lord of Nidur before proceeding to Thiru-Punkur. We will see this in another section of the Periya Puranam. These are the special features and puranic stories of the sacred sthalam of Thiru-Nidur. Having worshipped here, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar proceeds to the sacred sthalam of Thiru-Punkur and there, the Lord sings praises. We have already extensively contemplated the history of the sacred sthalam of Thiru-Punkur when we discussed the Puranam of Thiru-Nalaipovar Nayanar.

“As we have already seen, Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal has sung a Thiru-Thandaka Thiru-Pathikam combining Thiru-Punkur and Thiru-Nidur. This Pathikam is compiled as the eleventh Thiru-Pathikam in the sixth Thiru-Murai.

“Now, that Thiru-Pathikam.

““Piravathe thondriya pemman thannai penathathar avarthammai penathathanai thuravathe kattaruththothiyai thu nerikkum thu neriyai nindran thannai thiramaya eththisaiyum thane aki thiruppunkur meviya sivalokanai niramamozhiyanaai niduranai nithanen enne nan ninaiyavarai.” (The Lord who appeared without birth, who does not care for those who do not care for Him, who taught the pure path by cutting off attachments, who became all directions with skill, the Sivaloka Lord residing in Thiru-Punkur, the Lord of Nidur with colorful words, what am I, a lowly one, that I do not think of Him?) “Pinanum mundranum anan thannai” pitharkku pithanai nindran thannai nandrangku arindhavarkkum thane aki nalvinaiyum theevinaiyum anan thannai sendrongi vinnazhavum theeyan anai thiruppunkur meviya sivalokanai nindraya nidur nilavinanai nithanen enne nan ninaiyavarai illanai evvidaththum ullan thannai iniya ninaiyadarkku innathanai vallanai valladaintharkku arulum vannam mattatharkku eththiraththum mattathanai sellatha sennarikke selvipanai thiruppunkur meviya sivalokanai nellal vilai kazhani niduranai nithanen enne nan ninaiyavarai kalai gnanam kallame karpiththanai kadu naragam saramame kappan thannai palavaya vedangal thane aki panivarkkku angange pattaranai silaiyal O Lord, who danced in the fire that consumed the cities, who resides in Thiru-Pungoor, the Lord of Shiva-loka, the Lord of Thiru-Needoor with its lofty jeweled mansions, O Righteous One! How can I, a humble one, not contemplate You? You who looked upon me, though I did not look upon You; You who became subtle, though I did not become subtle; You who created all, though I created nothing; You who do not approach those who do not approach You. You who consumed the poison of the southern sea without hesitation, the Lord of Thiru-Pungoor, the Lord of Shiva-loka, the Lord of Thiru-Needoor, whose boundless light never diminishes. How can I, a humble one, not contemplate You?

“You who wear what is not worn, You who are adorned with what is not adorned, You who are the flesh within the foul-smelling vessel, You the Supreme One whom none can see, You whose form shines with light, You the Lord of the lofty coral mountain, the Lord of Thiru-Pungoor, the Lord of Shiva-loka, the Lord of Thiru-Needoor with its water-filled fields. How can I, a humble one, not contemplate You? How can I, a humble one, not contemplate You? You who are tireless for the hidden treasure, You who became all things without diminishing, You who are ancient and yet ever new, You whose crown is adorned with flowing waters, the Lord of Thiru-Pungoor, the Lord of Shiva-loka, the Lord of Thiru-Needoor with its lofty jeweled mansions. How can I, a humble one, not contemplate You? Even the sharp-fanged serpent and Brahma, born from the cool lotus pond, cannot comprehend You.

“Who can know Your nature? Even those gods who claim to know cannot comprehend Your glorious, ankleted feet.

“The Lord of Thiru-Pungoor, the Lord of Shiva-loka, residing in the shady groves, the Lord of Thiru-Needoor with its water-filled fields. How can I, a humble one, not contemplate You? I, a humble one, believed all the lies told by those who stand tall, with hands smeared with ghee, and necks stretched out, eating with their hands, and thus I was caught by the fowlers. I escaped, not to be caught.

“The Lord of Thiru-Pungoor, the Lord of Shiva-loka, residing in the fertile lotus fields of Thiru-Pungoor, the Lord of Thiru-Needoor, with its water-filled gardens of water lilies. How can I, a humble one, not contemplate You? How can my foolish heart not scorn You? You who stand as one, without scorn. You who crushed the mighty mountain beneath Your feet, the Lord of Thiru-Pungoor, the Lord of Shiva-loka, who bestowed grace upon the demon king. You who wore the hide of the fierce elephant, the Lord of Thiru-Pungoor, the Lord of Shiva-loka, the mighty Lord of Thiru-Needoor.

“How can I, a humble one, not contemplate You?

“This is the Thiru-Padigam of Thiru-Pungoor and Thiru-Needoor, composed by Thiru-Navukkarasar Nayanar.

“Let us continue our journey with Thiru-Navukkarasar Nayanar on his pilgrimage and continue to reflect.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 373, Thiru-Nindra-Charukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, after worshipping Thiru-Pungoor, arrives at the sacred sthalam called Thiru-Kurukkai.

There, he prostrates before the Lord and sings Thiru-Padigams. Thiru-Kurukkai is one of the eight sthalams where the Lord performed heroic deeds, that is, one of the Ashta Veerattana Sthalams. It is the sthalam where Manmatha was burnt. The name of the Lord here in this Thiru-Kurukkai Veerattana Sthalam is Veeratteswarar. The name of the Goddess is Gnanaambikai. This sthalam is very close to Mayiladuthurai.

It is located on the road from Mayiladuthurai to Manalmedu, past Needoor. The Kadukkai tree is the sthala vriksha of this sthalam.

Therefore, this sthalam is called Kaduvana. This is the place where the Lord performed yoga, separated from the Goddess, and therefore it is also called Yogeesapuram. It is the place where Kama was incinerated, and therefore it is also called Kamadahanapuram. It is the sthalam that removed Lakshmi’s trembling, and therefore it is also called Kambakarapuram. When the sage Theerthavagu came to this sthalam and extended his hands, desiring the waters of the Ganga to perform ablutions for the Lord, his hands did not lengthen but remained short, and thus this sthalam was named Kurukkai. In addition to this, names like Harithakivanam and Gnanaambikai Puram are also found in the sthala puranam.

Harithaki means Kadukkai. It is called Harithakivanam. The Kadukkai tree is the sthala vriksha, and therefore it is called Harithakivanam. This temple is surrounded by four sacred walls and faces west. There are two prakarams. The Goddess is enshrined facing south, and a separate shrine has been built for Her.

In front, there is a large Vaval Thetri Mandapam. In the southwest corner, there are a granary and offices. In the inner prakaram, on the upper side, in the Thiru-Maligai Pathi, there are Utsava Moorthies, Subrahmanyar with Valli and Deivanai, and Lakshmi. In the eastern prakaram, the deities of Bhairavar, Sani Bhagavan, Vishnu, Surya, Chandra, and the Navagrahas are consecrated. There is a sthala vriksha in that prakaram. In the southern prakaram itself, Kurukkai Vinayagar, with Kurukkai Munivar, is enshrined in a separate temple.

Outside the sanctum sanctorum of the Lord, there are deities such as Kurukkai Brahmar, Lingodbhava Moorthy, Dakshinamurthy, and Nardana Ganapathy. Yogeeswarar is enshrined with the Goddess.

Here, the Lord’s name is Veeratteswarar, and the Goddess’s name is Gnanaambikai. The name of the Utsava Moorthy, Samharamurthy, is Yogeeswarar, and the Goddess is Poorniyammaiyar. This is Kamadahanapuram, and therefore there are Utsava Moorthies for Manmatha and his wife Rati. As we have already seen, this sthalam is one of the Ashta Veeratta Sthalams. The assembly hall of this sthalam is called Kamananga Nasani Sabai. It is also called Shambu Vinoda Sabai.

This sthalam is where the Lord burnt Kama, who had a sugarcane bow, and then, at the request of Rati and the worship of Nedumal, restored Kama to life. It removed the trembling of Lakshmi. The asuras This sthalam is where Muruga-kadavul came, worshipped, and received the trident to achieve victory. This sthalam is where Raghavan worshipped and performed ancestral rites. This sthalam is where Theerthavagu Munivar’s hands became short. This sthalam is where Mahavishnu, fearing Vanasura, was granted refuge.

This sthalam is where Brahma, who falsely claimed to have seen the crown, was deprived of his creative power by the Lord, and then, fearing and worshipping, regained his lost creative power. This sthalam is where Jayatvajan, who desired rice to grow throughout the Chola country, was blessed according to his wish. This sthalam is where the Lord’s idol was worshipped by Agastya Munivar. This sthalam is guarded by Kali and Durga. This sthalam has all these glories, including the worship of Rati and Kama. The incineration of Manmatha The heroic deed performed by the Lord, that history is known to all of us.

The place where the Devas gathered to witness Manmatha shooting his arrows is Devanur, near this sthalam. The place where Kama tied the thread to begin the battle is Kanganamputhur, a nearby place. The place where he bent his bow is Villiyanallur. The place where he bent his leg and aimed is Kalvalaimedu, Kavalaimedu. The place where Manmatha stood to shoot his five arrows at the Lord is Panjabana Nallur, Aivanallur. The place where Manmatha fell exhausted is Sothamangalam.

The place where Yama resided is Kootruvan Vazhkai, Koothur Vazhi. All the places surrounding this sthalam bear names related to this sthala history. The Chola country is praised as ‘Chola Nadu Sorudaitthu’ (Chola country is full of rice). This Thanjai Tharani, the Chola country, is filled with paddy fields and serves as a granary, and this sthalam is the reason for it. The history is as follows: Once upon a time, a king named Jayatvajan ruled the Chola country. He was a devotee of Kali.

In those days, the Chola country was a forest. Only varagu and other such grains grew there, but no paddy. This king desired rice to offer as amrita to the Devas. To obtain this boon, he went to Kasi and worshipped Viswanathar and Annapoorani Ammaiyar there.

One day, while he was bathing in the Ganga and worshipping thus, Annapoorani The Goddess appeared and asked what he desired. The king pleaded, “O Mother, no rice grows in the Chola country, so please remove this deficiency.” Accepting his plea, Mother Annapoorani said, “Visweswarar and I will reside in Kaduvana as Yogeeswarar and Gnanaambikai. Go there, bathe in the Soola Theertham, and worship.

“Then your wish will be granted.” The king thanked her and bowed. He then asked, “Mother, the Chola country is a forest. How will I know the place where you wish to reside?” To this, the Mother replied, “My dear, let your chosen deity, Kali, go before you, and you follow her. Wherever the sound of the bells on her body stops, wherever the flame on her body disappears, that is the place where we wish to reside,” she blessed. Immediately, the king thought of Kali, and she appeared with jingling bells and a blazing flame. The king bowed to her and followed her as she walked ahead.

“Upon reaching Thiru-Kurukkai, the sound of Kali’s bells stopped, and the flame also disappeared. The king understood the blessed words of Mother Annapoorani.

“Therefore, he considered this to be Kaduvana. He bathed in the Soola Theertham and praised Yogeeswarar and Gnanaambikai. While he was worshipping thus, one day, Mother Annapoorani came here as an old woman and appeared before the king, scattering white rice. It spread everywhere in that land. Seeing this, the king was astonished, thinking it was the Mother’s grace. He bowed and took leave.

“From that day onwards, the entire Chola country became a land where rice grew, providing food to the world as a granary. Even today, Thanjai Tharani remains a granary. The place where the flame from Kali’s body fell became a pit, and water filled it.

“From then on, that Theertham is known as Jwala Theertham. That Kali also guards this sthalam. Durga worshipped the Lord in this sacred sthalam before setting out to slay Sumbha-Nisumbha and Mahishasura. The Theerthams here are Soola Theertham, Gnana Theertham, Lakshmi Theertham, Rama Theertham, Brahma Theertham, Agni Theertham, Agastya Theertham, Homa Theertham, Kama Theertham, and many other Theerthams. Gnana Theertham flows north of the temple. It is now called Pazhavaru.
