“When the Lord performed yoga, the joyful stream that emerged from His sacred eye flowed northeast and became a large river. That is called Gnana Nadi and Gnana Theertham. Thiru-Kurukkai Temple is one of the Devasthanams under the administration of Thiru-Kailaya Paramparai Dharmapuram Aadheenam. These are all the puranic details and sthala history of Thiru-Kurukkai, and notes about the temple, composed by Thiru-Sirapuram Mahavidwan Meenakshi Sundaram Pillai. Thiru-Navukkarasar Swamigal has blessed this sthalam with two beautiful Thiru-Padigams.

“Let us continue to reflect on them.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 374, Thiru-Nindra-Charukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar is visiting the sthalams on the northern and southern banks of the Kaveri in the Chola country. He arrives at the sacred sthalam called Thiru-Kurukkai and worships the Lord there. We have briefly reflected on the sthala puranic details of Thiru-Kurukkai.

Here, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has blessed this sacred place with two Thiru-Padigams. The first Thiru-Padigam is compiled as the 49th Thiru-Padigam in the Fourth Thiru-Murai. In the ten sacred verses of this padigam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has sung, incorporating puranic details. He has included the puranic details from the eighteen Puranas and the Periya Puranam in each verse of this padigam. This is the unique and great specialty of this sacred sthalam and this Thiru-Padigam.

Now, this Thiru-Padigam is a Thiru-Nerisaipadugam.

“Aathiyil Piramanar thaam archithar adi inai keezh Othiya Vedhanavar unarumarunaralutraar Sothiyul sudarayth thonri sollinai iranthar palpoo Kothi vandarariyum solai Kurukkai Veerattanare.” (In the beginning, Brahma worshipped His feet, and those who recited the Vedas understood. He appeared as a light within light, transcending words, in the groves where many flowers are plucked by bees, the Lord of Kurukkai Veerattam.) “Neetrinai niraiya poosi nitthalam niyamam seythu Aatru neer poorithaattum anthananarai kolvan Saattru naal atrathenru tharumaraasarkay vantha Kootrinai kumaippar polum Kurukkai Veerattanare.” (He who smears sacred ash abundantly, performs daily rituals, and pours river water for ablutions. It seems He crushed Yama, who came at the command of Dharmaraja, saying the appointed day had come to kill the Brahmin, the Lord of Kurukkai Veerattam.) “Thazhaithathor aaththiyin keezh thaabara manalal kooppi Azhaithange aavin paa karanthu kondu aattakkandu Pizhaiththan than thaathai thaalai perungodu mazhuval” “Veasa kulaithathor amutham inthaar Kurukkai Veerattanare.” (Beneath a flourishing Aathi tree, he made a lingam of sand, and seeing him milking cow’s milk and performing ablutions, his father, who had erred, tried to kick him. He, the Lord of Kurukkai Veerattam, gave the nectar of Shiva-ananda to the one who cut off his father’s leg with a great axe.) “Silanthiyum aanaikkavil tharu nizhal panthar seythu Ulantha van iranthapothe Kochchengananumaka Kalantha neer Kaveri soozh Sonattu Chozhar thangal Kulanthanil pirappiththittar Kurukkai Veerattanare.” (The spider, having made a canopy of shade in Thiru-Anaikka, when it died, was reborn as Kochchenganan, in the lineage of the Chola kings of the Chola country surrounded by the mixed waters of the Kaveri, by the Lord of Kurukkai Veerattam.) “Eerudan ezhadarthan enni aayiram poo kondu Aarudaichchadaiyinaanai archithan adi inai keezh Verumor poo kuraiya meymalar kannai mindu Koorumor aazhi thanthar Kurukkai Veerattanare.” (He who subdued seven bulls, thinking of the Lord with matted locks, worshipped His feet with a thousand flowers.

When one flower was short, he plucked his own lotus-like eye and offered it.

The Lord of Kurukkai Veerattam gave him the discus.) “Kallinal erinthu kanji thaam unum Saakkiyanar Nellinar sorunamay neel visumbu aala vaithar Elliyangu erikai enthhi ezhil thigazh nattamaadi Kolliyam pan ugathar Kurukkai Veerattanare.” (The Saakkiyar, who threw stones and ate gruel, was made to rule the vast sky without eating rice. He, the Lord of Kurukkai Veerattam, who danced beautifully, holding fire in his hand at night, loved the Kollip-pan.) “Kaappathor vellum ambum kaiya” “Aiyathor iraichchi baaram thorp perum seruppu thottu Thooiya vaay kalasamaatti thee perum kannkal seyya Kuruthi neer ozhuga than kann koppathum pattrikkondar Kurukkai Veerattanare.” (He, the Lord of Kurukkai Veerattam, accepted the one who, with a protective victorious arrow in hand, and a burden of meat, touched his great leather sandal to his pure mouth as a kalasam, and with blood flowing from his great fiery eyes, plucked out his own eye.) “Niraimarai kaadu thannil neendheri deepam thannai Karai nirathu eli than mookku suttida kananru thoonda Nirai kadal mannum vinnum neenda vaanulagamellam Kuraivarak koduppar polum Kurukkai Veerattanare.” (In the dense Vedic forest, a rat, with its nose, stirred the long burning lamp, causing it to blaze. It seems the Lord of Kurukkai Veerattam granted the entire full sea, earth, and vast heavens without any deficiency.) “Anangu umai baagamaaga adakkiya aathimoorthi Vananguvaar idarkal theerkkum marunthu nal arunthavaththa Ganampullarku arulkal seythu kaathalaam adiyaarkku enrum Gunangalai kodupparp polum Kurukkai Veerattanare.” (The Primeval Being, who holds Uma as a part of Himself, is the medicine that removes the sufferings of those who worship Him. It seems the Lord of Kurukkai Veerattam, having bestowed grace upon the great ascetic Ganampullar, always grants virtues to His beloved devotees.) “Eduthanan ezhil Kailai ilangaiyar mannan thannai Aduthoru viralal oondra alaripoy avanum veezhnthu Viduthanan kai narambal Vedhageethangal paadu” “Koduthanar kotra vazhnaal Kurukkai Veerattanare.” (He, the Lord of Kurukkai Veerattam, who, when the king of Lanka tried to lift the beautiful Kailash, pressed him down with a single toe, causing him to cry out and fall, and then, when he sang Vedic hymns with the nerves of his hand, granted him a victorious life.)

In the ten verses of this padigam, Thiru-Navukkarasar Peruman has beautifully sung ten puranic stories. In the first verse, it says, “Aathiyil Piramanar thaam archithar” (In the beginning, Brahma worshipped). The primeval Brahma, that is, the first Brahma, worshipped Lord Shiva to understand the Vedas and thus perform the act of creation. The second verse, “Neetrinai niraiya poosi” (smearing sacred ash abundantly), narrates the story of Markandeya Maharishi. Thiru-Navukkarasar has sung that the Lord of Kurukkai Veera Thiru-Navukkarasar has sung that the Lord of Kurukkai Veera crushed Yama, who came at the command of Dharmaraja to take the life of Markandeya, who smeared sacred ash all over his body and performed daily Shiva puja according to the Vedas and Agamas, when his appointed lifespan was over. The third verse narrates the story of Chandeswarar Nayanar, beginning with “Thazhaithathor aaththiyin keezh” (beneath a flourishing Aathi tree).

It says that when Chandeswarar Nayanar’s father tried to kick the milk pots with his feet, seeing his son making a lingam of sand under an Aathi tree and performing ablutions for the Lord with cow’s milk according to the Agamas, the son cut off his father’s legs. The third verse says that the Lord of Kurukkai Veerattam gave the nectar of Shiva-ananda to such a Visara Sarmanar. In the fourth verse, the story of the spider and the elephant worshipping the Lord in Thiru-Anaikka The fourth verse narrates the story of the spider and the elephant worshipping the Lord in Thiru-Anaikka, and how the spider was reborn as Kochchenga Chola. In the fifth verse, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has sung the story of Thirumal, who incarnated as Krishna, subduing seven bulls at once, and then worshipping Lord Shiva’s feet with a thousand lotus flowers. When one flower was short, he plucked one of his own lotus-like eyes and offered it, and the Lord gave him the Chakrayudham (discus). The sixth verse narrates the story of Sakkiya Nayanar.

The seventh verse narrates the sacred story of Kannappa Nayanar. The eighth verse narrates the story of a rat in the sthalam of Vedharanyam, which stirred the lamp in front of the Lord’s shrine, and as a result, was reborn as King Mahabali. The ninth verse narrates the story of bestowing grace upon Ganampullar Nayanar. The tenth verse narrates the story of Ravana attempting to lift Mount Kailash. We know that in most of Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar’s Thiru-Padigams, the tenth verse contains details about Ravana.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has blessed this first padigam with ten puranic historical stories in its ten verses. The second Thiru-Padigam, Thiru-Kurukkai Thiru-Padigam, is compiled as the fiftieth Thiru-Padigam in the Fourth Thiru-Murai.

However, only two verses of this Thiru-Padigam have been found. That Thiru-Padigam is as follows: “Nediya Mal Piramanodu neer enum” “Pilayam kolla adiyodu mudiyum kaanaar aruchchunarkku ambum villum Thudiyudai vedaraagi thooiya manthirangal solli Kodi nedum ther koduthar Kurukkai Veerattanare.” (The Lord of Kurukkai Veerattam, whom the tall Vishnu and Brahma could not find the beginning or end of, became a hunter with a drum, spoke sacred mantras, and gave a flag-bearing chariot to Arjuna.) “Aaththama mayanum maalum anri matrozhintha thevar Soththam emperumaan enru thozhuthu thoththirangal solla Theerthamaam attami mun seerudai ezhu naalum Kooththaraay veethi ponthar Kurukkai Veerattanare.” (The Lord of Kurukkai Veerattam, whom even Brahma and Vishnu, and other remaining Devas, worshipped and praised as “Our Lord,” came out into the streets as a dancer for seven glorious days before the sacred Ashtami.) Thiruchitrambalam. This is the second Thiru-Padigam composed by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar for the sthalam of Thiru-Kurukkai.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, after worshipping the sacred sthalam of Thiru-Kurukkai, reaches the sacred sthalam of Thiru-Nindriyur. Thiru-Nindriyur is a village located between Vaidheeswaran Koil and Mayiladuthurai, a Thevaram-sung sthalam on the northern bank of the Kaveri. This is the nineteenth Thiru-sthalam among the holy places. The Lord’s holy name here is Mahalakshmeeswarar, also known as Lakshmipureeswarar. The Goddess’s holy name is Lokanayaki. The sthala-viruksham (sacred tree) here is the Vilamaram, and the Thirtham (sacred water body) is Lakshmi Thirtham.

This Thiru-Nindriyur sthalam has been sung about by the three great saints: Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, Appar Swamigal, and Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. The sthala-varalaru (temple history) states that a king, desiring to build a temple, came here and, upon digging the earth, saw blood gush forth. When he dug deeper, he found a Shiva Lingam and proceeded to build the temple. Due to the impact of the digging, a depression can still be seen on the top of the Shiva Lingam. In ancient times, this was also one of the Maada-koils built by Ko-Chengan Cholan. About a hundred years ago, when the Nagarathars undertook renovation, they rebuilt it in its current form.

It is said that a Lingam worshipped by Parasurama also exists at this site. The Moolavar (presiding deity) is a Swayambhu Murthy (self-manifested idol) with a tall Bana (pedestal). Selva Ganapathy bestows grace as the Sthala Vinayagar. The Muyalagan (dwarf demon) beneath the holy feet of Dakshinamurthy here is turned to the left, holding a snake in his hand.

The Lord is in a posture of bestowing grace upon him with His left hand. Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman has sung about the sacred Thirtham here as ‘Neelamalar Poigai’ (pond of blue flowers) in his Pathigam. Mahalakshmi worshipped Lord Shiva at this site and received His grace.

Therefore, the Lord of this sthalam is called Mahalakshmeeswarar and Lakshmipureeswarar. Because Mahalakshmi worshipped here, this town received the name Thiru-Nindriyur.

Now, let us look at the Thiru-Pathigam bestowed upon this site by Appar Swamigal. This Thiru-Pathigam is compiled as the twenty-third Thiru-Pathigam in the fifth Thiru-Murai, in the form of Thiru-Kurunthogai Thiru-Pathigam.

Now, that Thiru-Pathigam.

“Kodungan ven thalai kondu kuraivilai padungan onrilarai pali thernthu unpaar nedungan mangaiyar aattaiyar nindriyur kadungai kootruthaitthu itta karuthare veethi vel nedunganniyar vel valai neethiye kolar palathu nindriyur vedamothi vilangu ven thottarayi kaathil ven kuzhai vaiththa vengalvare putrinara aravam pulithol misai sutrinara sunnapporvai kondar sudar netrik kannudaiyar amar nindriyur patrinaraai patraavinai paavame paraiyin osaiyum paadalin osaiyum maraiyin osaiyum malki ayalalam niraiyum poom” “Pozhil soozh Thiru-Nindriyur uraiyum eesanai ulgum en ullamē sunaiyul neelam suzhiyum nedunganaal inaiyanenrenru esuvathu enkalo ninaiyum than vayal soozh Thiru-Nindriyur panaiyin eeruri porththa paramare uraippak kenmin num uchiyullaan thanai nirai pon maamathil soozh Thiru-Nindriyur uraipporkattraiyar aarivaro enil thiraiththuppaadi thiritharum selvare kanthiyur mukil polum karungaliri eralanaal ithu venkalo nindriyur pathiyaaga nilaayavan venriyerudai engal vikirthane nilaiyilaa vellai maalaiyan neendathoor kolaivilaal eyil koytha kodiyavan nilaiyinaar vayal soozhthiru” “Nindriyur uraiyinaal vinai oyume anjiyagilum anbu pattagilum nenjam vaazhi ninai nindriyurai nee inji maamathil eythu imaiyor thozha kunji vaanpirai soodiya koothane ezhiyana mozhiyaa ilangaikku irai kaliyinaal kayilayam eduththavan nezhiya oontravalaan amar nindriyur azhiyinaal thozhuvaar vinai alkume Thiruchitrambalam.” This is the Thiru-Pathigam bestowed upon Thiru-Nindriyur Thiru-sthalam by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar. Having worshipped the Peruman of Thiru-Nindriyur, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar proceeds to the Thiru-sthalam named Thiru-Nanippalli.

We shall continue our reflection on this. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 375. Thiru-Nindriya-Sargam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Having worshipped Thiru-Nindriyur, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar reaches the Thiru-sthalam named Thiru-Nanippalli. Thiru-Nanippalli is one of the Thiru-sthalams on the southern bank of the Kaveri River in the Chola country.

This sthalam is currently known as Punjai. Among the sthalams on the southern bank of the Kaveri, this is the forty-third Thiru-sthalam. The holy name of the Lord here is Natrunai Appar. The holy name of the Goddess is Parvatha Rajaputhri. The Sthala-viruksham is the Shenbaga tree and the Pinna tree. The Thirtham is Swarna Thirtham.

This sthalam was renovated by Parantaka Cholan, one of the ancestors of Rajaraja Cholan. Because an elephant directly came and worshipped in the Moolasthanam (sanctum sanctorum) of this sthalam, the sanctum sanctorum of this sthalam is very large.

Here, two Ambikas bestow grace with the holy names Parvatha Rajaputhri and Malaiyaan Madanthai. The Kaveri River flows here, coming from the east and turning back to the west. This is called Pasvamangini. This Thiru-sthalam is where Vinayagar performed Shiva Puja to atone for the sin of having tipped over the Thirtham from Agathiyar’s Kamandalam. The Durga of this sthalam bestows grace with a lion in her holy hand and in the posture of having destroyed Sumban and Nisumban. This Thiru-sthalam is the birthplace of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman’s mother, Bhagavathi Ammaiyar.

Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, seated on his father’s shoulder, came to this sthalam and sang about the Lord here, bestowing grace. In response to the devotees’ request, he sang about this place, which was a desert, as a coastal region (Neythal). This sthalam also transformed into a Neythal region. We will see all that history in the Puranam of Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman. It is a very ancient temple. Nal Thunai Eeswaram is the name of the sthalam.

In inscriptions, it is referred to as Thiru-Nanippalli Udaiyar Koil. The temple faces east. The side length of its square Garbhagriha (sanctum sanctorum) is twenty-four feet, making it a very large Garbhagriha. In its center, four pillars and four semi-pillars along the wall support it. The Mandapam called Nanippalli Kodivattam is very special. The space connecting the Ardha Mandapam and the Mukha Mandapam is sixteen feet.

In this space, four pillars with rounded Kumbhas (pot-like structures) stand, supporting it. The Mandapam called Nanippalli Kodivattam, located in this space, was named Mukha Mandapam Mumudichola Perambalam. This Mandapam, built by Rajaraja I, is supported by sixteen pillars. In the Deva Koshtams (niches), there are idols of Ganapathy, Agathiyar, and Dakshinamurthy. There are also forms of Lingodbhavar, Ardhanareeswarar, Brahma, and Durgas. In the middle of the Makara Thoranams (archways with crocodile motifs) above the Koshtams, there are sculptures.

There are sculptures depicting the Ramayana and explanations of the Kanda Puranam. All these are unique features of this site. As seen earlier, Nanippalli Kodivattam is very famous. The Kodungai of Avudaiyar Koil, Nanippalli Kodivattam, and the Vaval Nathi Mandapam of Thiru-Velimilai are renowned for their beautiful craftsmanship. A thousand years ago, the name of this site was Thiru-Nanippalli in Akkoor Nadu, located in Jayankonda Chola Valanadu. These are the sthala visheshams (special features) of the Thiru-Nanippalli sthalam.

Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, who visited this sthalam, has bestowed a Thiru-Pathigam. The Thiru-Nanippalli Thiru-Pathigam is compiled as the seventieth Thiru-Pathigam in the fourth Thiru-Murai. It is structured as a Thiru-Nerisai Thiru-Pathigam. Each verse of this Pathigam ends with “Nanippalli Adigalaare.” This refrain appears in seven verses. The last two lines of the eighth verse and the ninth verse are not available to us. The tenth verse has the refrain “Nanippalli Paramanaare.” The Lord of Nanippalli is a good support for devotees with compassion.

He removes the sins of those who think good thoughts. He bestows grace and removes our impurities daily. He does not let His devotees fall into hell. He bestowed grace upon the spider and Ravana. He made the poison given by the Samanars, which tormented me, into nectar.

Therefore, the idea of this Thiru-Pathigam is that if one worships and recites without forgetting the continuous practice of morning and evening, love for the holy feet of Lord Shiva will grow.

Now, that Thiru-Pathigam.

“Mutrunai aayinaanai moovarkku muthalvan thannai sotrunai aayinaanai sothiyai aathariththu utru unarnthu urugi oori ulkasivudaiyavarkku natrunaiyaavoolum nanippalli adigalaare pularnthakaal poovum neerum kondu adi potra maattaar” “Valam seythu vaayin noolaal vattanai panthar seytha silanthiyai arayanaakki seermigal arulavallaar nalanthigal solai soozhntha nanippalli adigalaare enpathum patthum aarum en ulle irunthu manni kan pazhakonrunindri kalakka naan alakkazhinthen shenbagam thigazhum punnai sezhunthiralkuravam vengai nanbu sey solai soozhntha nanippalli adigalaare panninaar paadalaagi pazhaththinil irathamaagi kanninaar paarvaiyaagi karuththodu karpamaagi enninara ennamaagi ezhulagu anaiththumaagi nanninaar vinaigal theerppar nanippalli adigalaare thunjirul kaalai maalai thodarchiyai maranthiraathe anjaluuthu othi” “Than naalum aran adikku anbaathaagum vanjanai paalchoraakki vazhakilaa amanar thantha nanju amuthaakkuviththaar nanippalli adigalaare semmalar kamalaththonum thirumudi kaanamaattaan ammalar paatham kaanbaan aazhiyaan agazhnthum kaanaan ninmalan enru angu etthum ninaippinai aruli naalum nammalam arupparpolum nanippalli adigalaare aravaththaal varaiyai sutri amararodu asurar koodi araviththuk kadaiya thonrum aala nanju amuthaa undaar viraviththam adiyaaraagi veedilaa thondar thammai naragaththil veezhavottaar nanippalli adigalaare.” Now, the eighth verse: “Mannule thiriyum pothu varuvana palavum kutram pannule purai puraiyan puzhuppothi pollal aakkai” is how it is structured. The second part of this eighth verse, those two lines, are not available to us. The ninth verse is also not available to us.

Now, the tenth verse: “Patthu mor iratti tholaan paariththu malaiyedukka patthu mor iratti tholgal padarudambadaravoonri patthuvaay geetham paada parinthavarkku arul koduththaar patthartham paraviyeththum nanippalli paramanaare.

“” Thus, having worshipped Thiru-Nanippalli, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar next reaches the sthalam named Thiru-Chemponpalli, as sung by Sekkizhar Peruman. That verse is as follows: “Mevu punal ponni iru karaiyum saarnthu vidai uyarththaar Thiru-Chemponpalli paadi kaavuyarum mayilaaduthurai neel ponni karai thurutthi velvikudi ethirkolpaadi paavuru sen” Tamil maalai paadi potri paramar thiruppathi palavum paninthu ponthē aavoorum anjaaduvaar kodikkaavil anainthu paninthu aavaduthan thuraiyai saarnthaar enru Sekkizhar Peruman paadugiraar. The meaning of this verse is that Thiru-Navukkarasar, having sung about Thiru-Chemponpalli of Lord Shiva, who raised the Rishabha flag, located on both banks of the Kaveri River, and having worshipped Thiru-Mayiladuthurai with its tall groves, Thiru-Thurutthi, Thiru-Velvidiyin, and Thiru-Ethirkolpadi on the long banks of the Kaveri, and having praised with garlands of beautiful Tamil songs, and having worshipped many other holy places of Paramasivan, then reached Thiru-Kodikkavu of the Lord who delights in the five sacred baths, worshipped there, and then reached Thiru-Aavaduthurai, the sacred Thiru-Aavaduthurai. The meaning of this verse is that Thiru-Navukkarasar reached Thiru-Aavaduthurai. The phrase “irukaraiyum saarnthu” (having reached both banks) should be understood as having visited all the Shiva sthalams on both the northern and southern banks of the Kaveri.

“Among these, some sthalams are directly opposite each other, and some are very close.

“Therefore, the method of Shiva temple darshan is to see and worship the sthalams as they are encountered.

“Thus, whether on the northern or southern bank of the Kaveri, he visited and worshipped the sthalams without following a single linear path. Those who undertake pilgrimage in this region of the Chola country will well understand its nature.

“Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, on his pilgrimage, worships Thiru-Chemponpalli, also known as Sempanar Koil, which is the forty-second sthalam among the sthalams on the southern bank of the Kaveri River in the Chola country. He worships Thiru-Chemponpalli, also known as Sempanar Koil, which is the forty-second sthalam among the sthalams on the southern bank of the Kaveri River in the Chola country. This sthalam is currently known as Sempanar Koil. There is one Thiru-Pathigam by Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman and two Thiru-Pathigams by Thiru-Navukkarasar for this sthalam. The name Sempiyan Palli, meaning a temple renovated by a Chola king, later became Chemponpalli. Sempiyan means Chola.

“Many Chola kings have renovated this temple. The temple’s name itself became the village’s name. It can also be said to be a temple roofed with pure gold. To the south and north of Sempanar Koil, there are two villages called Old Thiru-Chemponpalli and New Thiru-Chemponpalli. The temple is built facing east.

“The Lord faces east, and the Goddess faces west. To the right of the temple entrance is the Thirtham. Nandi and Balipeedams are at the temple entrance. After passing through the Kattai Gopura Vaayil (short tower entrance) with Panchamurthis, we enter the temple prakaram (circumambulatory path). There is only one prakaram. In the Kanni Moolai (southwest corner) is Vinayagar, and next to him, in the western prakaram, are the Nalvar (four saints), Murugan, Gajalakshmi, and Jeshtadevi.

“In the Garbhagriha Koshtams (niches of the sanctum sanctorum), to the south is Dakshinamurthy, to the west is Ardhanareeswarar, and to the north are Brahma and Durga. In the northern prakaram is the Chandesar temple. In the Lord’s sanctum, next to the Dvarapalakas, are Vinayagar, Suryalingam, Sundaralingam, and Subramaniyar. In the Snapana Mandapam are the Panchamurthis. At the entrance of the Ardha Mandapam, Chandi and Mundi serve as guardians. The Lord’s sanctum shines with great splendor.

“Thus, we reach the Moolasthanam, where the Lord is beautifully seated. The holy name of the Lord here is Arulmigu Thiru-Chemponpalliyar. He is also known as Swarnapureeswarar. The holy name of the Goddess is Maruvaar Kuzhali Ammai, and in Sanskrit, she is called Sugandhakunthalambikai. The idol of Bhikshadana in this temple is very much worth seeing; it is a beautiful idol. The Sthala-viruksham is the Vanni tree.

“The Thirtham is Surya Thirtham. The Ambika is depicted with two holy hands. The Puranic history states that Indra worshipped the Lord of Chemponpalli to kill Vrithrasura.

“Therefore, this sthalam is called Indrapori. Murugaperuman worshipped here before slaying Tharakasura, so it is called Skandapori. Agathiyar worshipped here and attained Purusharthas. Brahma worshipped here and gained the power of creation. Rathi worshipped here and attained Kama. Naga Kanniyargal worshipped here and attained good husbands.

“Vasishtar, the Dikpalakas, and Kaveri, among others, also worshipped here and received blessings. This is the sthalam where Veerabhadrar incarnated to cut off Dakshan’s head. In this sthalam, bones immersed in the Kaveri turn into flowering trees, used for offering to the Lord. There are six inscriptions in this sthalam. Thiru-Navukkarasar, who worshipped here, has bestowed two Thiru-Pathigams upon this site.

“We shall continue to reflect on them.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 376. Thiru-Nindriya-Sargam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar has bestowed two Thiru-Pathigams upon the Thiru-sthalam named Thiru-Chemponpalli. The first Thiru-Pathigam is a Thiru-Nerisai Thiru-Pathigam, compiled as the twenty-ninth Thiru-Pathigam in the fourth Thiru-Murai.

“Thiru-Chemponpalliyaare” is the refrain that appears in every holy verse of this Thiru-Pathigam.

The Lord is like honey and nectar within His devotees. He is a lamp in their hearts. He is the one who removes the deceit of the clear-minded. He resides as Shiva in their thoughts. He is a lover to His devotees. He is virtue and penance.

He is our Father who has seen the three periods of time and is righteous. He is the three hundred and sixty flowers. He is our Father. He is the one who bestowed the Vedas and their Angas. He is the one who resides in Thiru-Chemponpalli. This is the summary of this Thiru-Pathigam.

Now, this Thiru-Pathigam.

“Ooninul uyirai vaatti unarvinaarkku eliyaraagi vaaninul vaanvarkkum ariyalaagaatha vanjar naan enil thaane ennum gnanaththaar patthar nenjul thenum innamuthum aanaar Thiru-Chemponpalliyaare. Noyyavar vilimiyarum noolinun neriyai kaattum meyyavar poyyum illaar udal enum idinjil thannil neyyamar thiriyumaagi nenjaththul vilakkumaagi seyyavar kariya kandar Thiru-Chemponpalliyaare. Velliyar kariyar seyyar vinnvaravargal nenjul olliyar oozhi oozhi ulaga” “Agamathu ettha nindra palliyar nenjaththullaar panchamam paadiyaadum thelliyar kallam theerppar Thiru-Chemponpalliyaare. Thanthaiyum thaayumaagi thaanavan gnanamoorththi munthiya thevar koodi muraimurai irukkuch solli enthai nee saranam enru angu imaiyavar paraviyeththa sinthaiyul sivamathu aanaar Thiru-Chemponpalliyaare.

“Aarudai sadaiyarpolum anbarukku anbarpolum koorudai meyyarpolum kol aravavaraivarpolum neerudai azhagarpolum neythale kamazhu neermai serudai kamalaveli Thiru-Chemponpalliyaare. Gnanamum ariya vendin nanrena vaazhalutreer kaalamum kazhiyalaan kallaththai oliyagilleer kolamum vendaa aarvach settangal kurodha neekkil seelamum nonbumaavaar Thiru-Chemponpa” Paḷḷiyārē puṟikālē nēcam ceyya irunta puṇṭarīkattārum erikālē mūṉṟumāki imaiyavar toḻa niṉṟārum terikālē mūṉṟu canti tiyāṉittu vaṇaṅka niṉṟu tirikālam kaṭaṉ kaṇṭa entai tirucceppoṉ paḷḷiyārē kāruṭai koṉṟai mālai katirmati aravinoṭum nīruṭai caṭaiyuḷ vaitta nītiyār nītiyuḷḷār pāruṭu viṇṇum maṇṇum patiṉeṭṭu kaṇaṅkaḷētta cīruṭu pāṭalāṉār tirucceppoṉ paḷḷiyārē ōvāta maṟaivallāṉum ōta nīr vaṇṇaṉ kāṇā mūvāta piṟappilārum muṉikaḷ āṉārkaḷ ēttum pūvāṉa mūṉṟum muṉṉūṟṟu aṟupatum ākum entai tēvāti tēvar eṉṟum tirucceppoṉ paḷḷiyārē aṅkaṅkaḷ āṟu nāṉkum antaṉarkku aruḷicceytu caṅkaṅkaḷ pāṭa āṭum caṅkaraṉ malai eṭuttāṉ aṅkaṅkaḷ Uthirnthu sora alarida adarthu nindrum sengal vellerathu erum Thirucchempon Paḷḷiyārē.

“In the ninth verse of this Thiru-pathikam, it is stated, “Pūvāṉa mūṉṟum muṉṉūṟṟu aṟupatum ākum entai” (The three flowers and the three hundred and sixty become the Lord). For this, the commentator, Sivakavimani Aiyya, has written a note stating that the three flowers refer to the three mandalas, and the three hundred and sixty refer to the one hundred and eight fire flames, the one hundred and sixteen sun rays, and the one hundred and thirty-six moon phases, totaling three hundred and sixty. The three mandalas are the Sun, Moon, and Fire. He has specified the numbers for each mandala, and in total, He has written a note stating that it totals three hundred and sixty.

“Now, the second Thiru-pathikam for this Thiru-sthalam was composed by Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar. This is a Thiru-kurunthokai Thiru-pathikam. It is compiled as the thirty-sixth Thiru-pathikam in the fifth Thirumurai.

“Now, that Thiru-pathikam: Thiruchitrambalam. Kāṇarāta kaṭi poḻil vaṇṭiṉam tēṉarāta tirucceppoṉ paḷḷiyāṉ ūṇarātator veṇṭalaiyil pali tāṉarātōr koḷkaiyiṉ kāṇmiṉē eṉpum āmaiyum pūṇṭaṅkuḻitarvarkku aṉpum āyiṭum āyiḻaiyīr iṉi cempoṉ paḷḷiyuḷḷāṉ civalōkaṉai nam poṉ paḷḷi uḷka viṉai nācamē vēṟu kōlattar āṉalar peṇṇalar kīru kōvaṇa vaittukilāṭaiyar tēralāvatu oṉṟaṉṟu Thirucchempon Paḷḷiyār, the Lord who wears the Ganga, holding a white skull, wanders seeking alms. He is the one, yet many. Behold! He who wears the Ganga on His matted locks, who burned the three cities by His command, the Lord of Thirucchempon Paḷḷiyār whom the Devas worship, is the primordial Lord, the first of the three. Why does He, with a snake and the moon, become agitated?

“He is the Lord of Thirucchempon Paḷḷiyār with a glorious crown. He is the Dancer who shot the three cities with a bow. He holds a trident and a skull-staff. He has a dark throat and two bright eyes. He is the Lord of Thirucchempon Paḷḷiyār, with a body smeared with white ash. He holds a five-headed serpent in His hand, a fierce serpent.

“He who made the fierce serpent tremble, who wore the skin of the green-eyed elephant, the Lord of Thirucchempon Paḷḷiyār, the red-eyed bull-rider, removes the karma of those who approach Him. He who, when Narayanan and Brahma, unable to find His crown and feet, wandered in search, became a pillar of fire in Thirucchempon Paḷḷiyār. He who burned the three cities with a single arrow, and pressed down the king of Lanka, Thirucchempon Paḷḷiyār, bestows rare boons.

“As sung by Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal, “Kurikaḷum aṭaiyāḷamum kōyilum neṟikaḷum avar niṉṟatōr nērmaiyum” (Signs and symbols, temples and paths, and His upright nature), this Thiru-pathikam describes the place where the Lord manifests, His form, nature, principles, and the means to attain Him.

“Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, who composed two Thiru-pathikams in Thirucchempon Paḷḷi, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, who composed them, reaches Thirumayiladuthurai, also known as Mayuram. Let us go on contemplating.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 377, Thirunindrachcharukkam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, having worshipped the sacred sthalam of Thirucchempon Paḷḷi, also known as Sempanar Kovil, and sung a Thiru-pathikam there, reaches the sthalam called Thirumayiladuthurai. Thirumayiladuthurai, also known as Mayuram or Mayavaram, is the thirty-ninth sacred sthalam among the Thevaram-sung sthalams on the southern bank of the Kaveri. It is a very famous sthalam. Thirumayiladuthurai is a sthalam sung by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal, two of the four Saivite Samayacharyas.

This sthalam is known by the names Sri Gauri Mayuram and Thirumayiladuthurai. The temple in this sthalam is very The ancient temple has a beautiful nine-tiered gopuram, approximately one hundred and sixty-four feet high, at its eastern entrance. This temple has entrances in all four directions. The pillars called Anivettikkal in this temple are very intricately carved. The Deviyar temple is located to the north of the Lord’s temple, facing east. The name of the Lord of this sthalam is Mayuranathar.

The Lord manifests as a Swayambu Murthy with a captivating appearance. The names of the Goddess are Anjalai and Abayambikai. The Vinayagar of this sthalam is located to the south of the flagstaff, known as Periya Vinayagar. To the north of the flagstaff, Lord Arumugam is enshrined. In this temple, the Kumara Kovil, a temple for Lord Muruga, is located directly behind the Lord’s vimana. A Shiva lingam, representing the ancient tradition of this sthalam, is found in the outer prakaram, along the northern wall, facing east.

This small temple is called Adi Mayuranatha Swami Kovil. Inside this small temple, a copper idol of the Goddess in the form of a peacock is seen facing south. In the southwest corner of the Lord’s vimana, the idol of Vinayagar known as Agathiya Vinayagar is found. It is said that this idol was installed and worshipped by Agathiyar. In the Kalanjiyam outer verandah, Vinayagar is enshrined, known as Kalanjiyam Pillaiyar and Kanakku Pillaiyar. At the entrance of the temple’s granary, a Shiva lingam named Nathasarma is also found.

To the south of the Goddess’s vimana, a Shiva lingam named Anavidyambikai is also found. This sthalam has many sacred names such as Sutavanam, Sikkandipuram, Brahmapuram, Brahmavanam, and Thenmayilai.

The Lord here is called Brahmalingam because Brahma worshipped Him, Vallalar because He bestows everything, and Gauri Mayuranathar because He married Gauri. The Goddess here is known by the names Abaya Pradambikai, Abayambikai, Anjal Nayaki, and Anjalai because she gave refuge and protected the peacock that sought shelter in fear. Gauri, Indra, and Brahma have worshipped the Lord of this sthalam. Brihaspati, the preceptor of the Devas, also worshipped here and attained eloquence. Agathiyar installed and worshipped the primordial Lord Vinayagar and a lingam in this sthalam. Nathasarma and his wife Anavithai also worshipped here and attained the state of Sivasaayujyam.

Dileepa, the king of Ayodhya, also worshipped here. The Sapta Matrikas have also worshipped here. Among these histories, the history of Gauri’s worship and the attainment of liberation by both Nathasarma and Anavithai are celebrated with great significance here. The history of the Goddess taking the form of a peacock is narrated in the Sthala Puranam of this sthalam. When Daksha performed a yagna, Veerabhadra, sent by Lord Shiva to destroy the yagna, was destroying it.

At that time, a peacock in a nearby grove, in great distress, sought refuge with the Goddess. The Mother gave refuge to the peacock and protected it. After giving refuge to the peacock, the Mother, considering the disgrace caused by going to her father Daksha’s yagna without listening to her husband Lord Shiva, decided to end her life and immolated herself in the very state she was in. When the Devi disappeared, the memory of the peacock to whom she had given refuge was in her sacred heart.

Afterwards, when she wished to seek forgiveness and grace from her husband for having gone without listening to his words, the form of the peacock that was in her memory became her form. With that peacock form, she came to this sthalam and worshipped by plucking the tender leaves of the mango tree found here with her beak, The Devi regained her true form. Since the Devi, in the form of a peacock (Mayura), worshipped here, the Lord of this sthalam is called Mayuranathar. This town is known as Mayuram and Mayiladuthurai. The history of Nathasarma and his wife Anavithai receiving the Lord’s grace here is also narrated in the Sthala Puranam. Nathasarma, a Brahmin, and his wife Anavithai, by performing good deeds such as wearing sacred ash and rudraksha, and chanting with devotion, attained the Saloka state of being united with Lord Shiva and lived in Kailash.

While they were in this state, desiring to attain the higher state of Sayujya, they both worshipped Lord Shiva and prayed to the Lord, “O Lord, please bestow upon us, your humble servants, the state of Sayujya.” The Lord commanded them, “Go south and worship our sacred sthalams.” Accordingly, they went south and visited sthalams such as Thirumuthukundram, also known as Virudhachalam, and worshipped the Lord there. Finally, they reached Thiruvaiyaru and worshipped the Lord there daily according to the prescribed rituals.

One day, Aiyarappar appeared before them and asked, “O devotees, what is your wish?” They replied, “O Lord, we wish to bathe in a sacred tirtha superior to the Ganga, attain Sivagnanam, install a Shiva lingam, worship it, and merge with you in the state of Sayujya.

“Therefore, please show us your compassion. This is our wish.” The two of them said. Hearing this, the Lord of Thiruvaiyaru, Aiyarappar, said, “O devotees, the sthalam of Mayuram is the most suitable and glorious place to fulfill your wish. We will take you there. Come with us.” Then, Aiyarappar set out with the Goddess, and they also accompanied him.

“Aiyarappar, having arrived a little to the west of Mayuram, addressed the devotees, “Go and bathe in the Rishabha Tirtha, which is the Kaveri, worship Mayuranathar, who is enshrined in the seven sthalams including Thanthondiswaram, attain Sivagnanam in the Vallalar Kovil, which is called Uttaramayuram, and fulfill your wish by installing a Shiva lingam in Mayuram.” Thus, he commanded them. Accordingly, they fulfilled everything. When they approached to worship Mayuranathar, the Lord said to them, “O devotees, you shall install and worship my form on my left side. Your wife Anavithai shall install and worship a Shiva lingam on the right side of our Anjalai Nayaki.

“After that, we will fulfill your desire.” Then, both Nathasarma and Anavithai worshipped the Lord and prayed, “Please grant that devotees may also worship these forms installed by us.” The supremely compassionate Lord Sri Mayuranathar bestowed a great boon, saying, “Devotees who worship us and our Anjalai Nayaki will attain the benefits of worshipping us only if they also worship the Shiva lingams installed by both of you at the end.”

“Thus, after some days, Mayuranathar granted grace for both of them to merge and become one within the Shiva lingams they had worshipped. From that day onwards, it has been customary for devotees who worship the Lord and Goddess of this sthalam to finally worship the Shiva lingam on the right side of the Irani Vimana, known as Anavitha Eswarar, and the Shiva lingam named Nathasarma at the entrance of the temple’s granary.

“Furthermore, to illustrate that the form of Anavitha Eswarar is the symbol of Anavithammaiyar’s union, even today, only a sari and a parivattam are offered to that Shiva lingam. Aiyarappar, who guided them here, is enshrined in a temple on the upper street of this sthalam.

“Now, the tirthams in this sthalam: The Kaveri river flowing through this town is called Rishabha Tirtha. The Rishabha Tirtha is considered a very glorious tirtha. This tirtha is of great significance to South India. It is a well-known fact that bathing in this tirtha from the first day of the Aippasi month to the first day of the Karthigai month, known as Thula Kaveri Snanam, bestows great merit. Next is the Brahma Tirtha, which is the sacred tank located in this temple. It was in this tirtha that the Goddess, in the form of a peacock, bathed, worshipped the Lord, and regained her original form.

“Next is the Anavidya Saras. This tirtha is located on the lower street of this town. Currently, it is known as Aiyankulam and Theradi Kulam. Next is the Agathiya Tirtha. This is a square-shaped well to the east of the Dakshinamurthy shrine in the inner temple. Around this sacred sthalam, to the east of this town, In Thiruvizha Nagar, the Lord bestows grace as the ‘Lord who shows the way’.

“To the south, He bestows grace with the name ‘Lord who shows the word’. To the west, He bestows grace as the ‘Lord who shows the path’. To the south, He bestows grace as the ‘Lord who shows the hand’.

“Thus, the Lord bestows grace around this sthalam as four ‘Vallals’. To the east, in Thiruvizha Nagar, He bestows grace as the ‘Lord who shows the way’. Since Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who came to this sthalam, made the Kaveri flood subside and brought him here, the Lord is enshrined in Thiruvizha Nagar to the east of this town with the name ‘Lord who shows the way’. Since He bestowed eloquence upon Brihaspati, who desired it, Lord Shiva bestows grace in the village of Perumcheri to the south with the name ‘Lord who shows the word’. Since He guided the Devas who were confused and lost their way, the Lord bestows grace in Moovalur to the west with the name ‘Lord who shows the path’. Since He bestowed Sivagnanam upon Rishabhadeva and others who desired it, the Lord bestows grace in Vallalarkovil with the name ‘Lord who shows the hand’.

“Indra and the eight guardian deities, along with many sages, have worshipped Sri Mayuranatha Peruman and established many Shiva lingams and tirthams around this sthalam in their own names. Not only Devas, but also lower forms of life such as eagles, parrots, horses, foxes, cats, elephants, and monkeys have worshipped this Lord and attained blessings, and these histories are found in the Sthala Puranam. The Sthala Vriksham here is the mango tree, hence this town is called Su- This town is called Sutavanam in Sanskrit. In this sthalam, Mayuranathar, along with Goddess Uma in the form of a female peacock, performed a dance, taking the form of a male peacock. This dance is called Gauri Thandavam. Sri Mayuranathar gathered Thirumal, Brahma, and others in an assembly and married the Goddess who regained her original form in this sthalam.

“The assembly gathered for this purpose in this sthalam is called Adisabai.

“Now, the festivals celebrated in this temple: The Vasanthotsavam celebrated in this temple is the Brahmotsavam. The festival is celebrated throughout the month of Aippasi in this temple. On the first day of Aippasi, the five principal deities, with great pomp and splendor, proceed to the Kaveri and bestow tirtha. Among the three most important days celebrated in the month of Aippasi, This first day is one of them. Next is Aippasi Amavasai. As mentioned earlier, the tirtha will take place in the Rishabha Tirtha on Amavasai.

“Today’s tirtha has a special significance.

“Once upon a time, Nandi Devar, who became arrogant due to primordial reasons, was pressed down into the netherworld by Lord Shiva. The place where he was pressed down is the Thula Kattam of the Kaveri in this sthalam. Even today, his sacred form can be seen in the middle of it. This is why this tirtha is called Rishabha Tirtha. In this pressed state, he then prayed to the Lord, “O Lord, please bestow upon me the Sivagnanam that helps one truly understand your greatness.” On Aippasi Amavasai, the Lord appeared on the northern bank of the Kaveri and bestowed Sivagnanam upon Rishabhadeva. This sthalam is Vallalar Kovil, and the Lord residing here The Lord is called ‘Kai Kaattum Vallal’ (The Lord who shows the hand).

“The sacred rivers like Ganga and Yamuna come to this Rishabha Tirtha on the aforementioned Aippasi Amavasai to cleanse themselves of the sins of those who bathe in them, which is also a story told in the Sthala Puranam. It is a tradition in this sthalam that if one takes the Kaveri water from the Rishabha Thurai at noon on Amavasai and keeps it in a vessel, the water will not spoil for any number of years. The tirtha that takes place on the last day of every Aippasi month is called ‘Kadai Muzhukku’ (Final Bath). There is no one who does not know about this tirtha festival. Such a famous Kadai Muzhukku takes place here. Many people from Kashi to Kanyakumari come to this bathing festival and take a dip, just like the Kumbh Mela.

“And like the Mahamaham Tirtha in Kumbakonam, this festival is very special. Next is Mudavan Muzhukku, which takes place on the first day of the Karthigai month. People who have taken the Kadai Muzhukku do not leave without taking a dip on that day. People believe that if they do so, even the Kadai Muzhukku will be of no use. According to tradition, a lame man, intending to take the Kadai Muzhukku, rushed quickly, but the day had passed.

“So, he complained to Mayuranathar.

“At that time, the Lord gave him a boon, saying, “If you go and take a dip, you will attain blessings.” It is said that he also took a dip on the first day of Karthigai and attained liberation, which is a story passed down through generations. This Aippasi festival begins on the twenty-first day with a grand flag hoisting. On the fifth day of this festival, the tradition of the Goddess in the form of a peacock worshipping the Lord takes place. Around three in the evening, the Peacock Goddess proceeds to bathe in the Kaveri River and circumambulates the various pavilions erected in the Mayuranathar Temple. Around six-thirty in the evening, she customarily worships Mayuranathar in front of the Lord’s sanctum. On that day, the sight of the Peacock Goddess performing the Thandavam dance brings great thrill to the hearts and bodies of the people.

“On the seventh day of this festival, the sacred marriage (Thirukalyanam) takes place. Festivals such as Margazhi Darisanam, Thai Poosam, Shivaratri, Aani Thirumanjanam, Aadi Pooram, Avani Moolam, Navaratri, Karthigai Thirunal, etc., are celebrated at their respective times. The subsidiary temples of this sacred temple are the Pancha Viswanathar temples, where Lord Viswanathar is enshrined with the sacred name Viswanathar in various places in this sthalam. Finally, The Thiru Viswanathar Temple, the Balakkarai Viswanathar Temple, and another Viswanathar Temple are found on the northern bank of the Kaveri River, below the Vallalar Theertha Mandapam. Another temple is located at Thimmiyappa Nayakkan Padithurai. A Viswanathar Temple is situated between Mayuram North Street and the northern sacred wall of the temple.

“It is said that these five Viswanathar Temples were built and worshipped by the five sages: Kanvar, Gautamar, Agathiyar, Bharadwajar, and Indiran. The Saptha Mathars (Seven Mother Goddesses) have worshipped the Lord in this sthalam. The deities worshipped by the Saptha Mathars are as follows: Thanthondreesam, also known as the Suyambunathar Temple, is located between Mayuram and Pallavarayapattu. Next is Karunambettai, also known as Karunguyilnathanpettai, followed by Kanjatharu, which is called Anathandavapuram.

“Fourthly, Pasupatheeswaram, which is located between Vallalar Temple and Dharmapuram.

“Fifthly, Kazhukkani Mattam.

“Sixthly, Dharmapuram.

“Seventhly, Vallalar Temple. These seven temples surround this sacred site. These are the sthalams where the Saptha Mathars worshipped. The Abayambikai Sathagam, composed by Nallathukkudi Krishnaiyar, is a very famous work. The author of this sthala puranam is Thirusirapuram Mahavidwan Thiruvalar Meenakshi Sundarampillai, a great scholar and esteemed professor to eminent Tamil poets such as Thiruvaavaduthurai Adheenam Sri Vidwan and Maha U. Ve.

“Swaminatha Iyer. All these details are from the Mayiladuthurai Sthala Puranam and Sthala Visesha Kurippugal. Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal visited this sthalam and sang a Thiruppathigam. That Thiruppathigam is the Thirukkurunthogai Thiruppathigam, the thirty-ninth Thiruppathigam in the fifth Thirumurai.

“Now, that Thiruppathigam: Thiruchitrambalam. “Kollum Kaathanmai peyththuru kōlvalai uḷḷam uḷki uraikkum Thiruppeyar Vaḷḷal Maamayilādu Thurai urai veḷḷanthāṅgu saḍaiyanai vēṇḍiyē chiththam thēṟum seṟivaḷai chikkēnum pachchai thīrum en paiṅgoḍi pānmadhi vaiththa Maamayilādu Thurai araṇ koththinar poli konrai koḍukkilē aṇḍar vāḻvum amarar irukkaiyum kaṇḍu vīṟṟirukkum karuththu oṇrilōm vaṇḍusēr Mayilādu Thurai araṇ thoṇḍaṟpādhaṅgaḷ sūḍi thudhaiyilē veñjina kaḍungālan viraikilān añjiraappum piṟappum aṟukkalaam mañjan Maamayilādu.” (Gloss: The beautiful bangle-wearing woman, whose heart yearns for the Lord, utters His sacred name. The generous Lord of Maamayiladuthurai, whose matted locks bear the Ganga, is desired. The mind becomes clear, the dense bangles tighten, my tender creeper is cured.

“The Lord of Maamayiladuthurai, who wears the crescent moon, adorned with clusters of konrai flowers. We have no desire for the life of celestials or the abode of immortals. If we adorn ourselves with the sacred feet of the Lord of Maamayiladuthurai, where bees gather, the fierce Yama will not approach, and fear and rebirth can be cut off. The beautiful Lord of Maamayiladuthurai.) Thurai urai añjolāḷ umaipangan aruḷilē kuṟaivilōm koḍu mānuḍa vāḻkkaiyāl karainilāviya kaṇḍan eṇ thōḷinaṉ maṟaivalāṉ Mayilādu Thurai urai iṟaivaṉ nīḻkaḻal ēththiyirukkilē nilaimai sollu neñjē thavam eṇ seythāy kalaikaḷāy vallāṉ Kayilāya nanmalaiyan Maamayilādu Thuraiyan nam thalaiyinmēlum maṉaththuḷum thaṅgavē nīṟṟināṉ nimisaḍaiyāṉ viḍaiyēṟṟināṉ namai āḷuḍaiyāṉ pulaṉ māṟṟināṉ Mayilādu Thurai eṉṟu pōṟṟuvārkkum uṇḍō puvi vāḻkkaiyē kōlum pullum oru kaiyil kūchchamum thōlum pūṇḍu thuyaram uṟṟu eṉ payaṉ nīlamā Mayilādu Thuraiyaṉē nūlum vēṇḍumō nuṇṇuṇarnthōrkaṭ. (Gloss: In the grace of the Lord of Mayiladuthurai, the partner of the sweet-speaking Uma, we are not lacking due to this human life.

“The Lord with the dark throat, eight shoulders, and master of the Vedas, who resides in Mayiladuthurai. If we praise His long feet, tell me, O heart, what penance have you performed? The master of arts, the good mountain of Kailash, the Lord of Mayiladuthurai, who resides in our heads and minds, who is adorned with sacred ash, with matted locks, who rides the bull, who rules us, who transforms our senses. Is there any earthly life for those who praise Mayiladuthurai? What is the use of holding a staff and grass in one hand, feeling shame, and wearing skins, suffering? O Lord of the blue Mayiladuthurai, do the subtly discerning need scriptures?)

“Kē paṉaṅkoḷ āḍaṟava alkul pagīrathi maṇaṅkolach chaḍaivaiththa maṟaiyavaṉ vaṇaṅgu Maamayilādu Thurai araṉ aṇaṅguvōrpāl koṇḍa kōlam aḻagithē nīṇilā aṟavachchaḍai nēsaṉai pēṇilāthavar pēthuravōṭṭinōm vāṉilā Mayilādu Thurai thanai kāṇil ārkkum kaḍunthuyar illaiyē paruththa thōḷum muḍiyum poḍipaḍa iruththināṉ avaṉ inthisai kēṭṭalum varaththināṉ Mayilādu Thurai thoḻum karaththinār viṉai kaṭṭarum kāṇmiṉē Thiruchitrambalam. (Gloss: The Lord of Mayiladuthurai, the Vedic one, who holds the Ganga in his matted locks, whose waist is like a palm-tree, worshipped by those who adore Him, His form is beautiful. We have driven away those who do not cherish the Lord with the matted locks adorned with the long moon. If one sees Mayiladuthurai, which is in the sky, there is no severe suffering for anyone. He made the mighty shoulders and crowns crumble to dust. Upon hearing this, those who worship Mayiladuthurai with their hands, their karmic bonds will be cut off, behold!

“) This is the Thiruppathigam that Thirunavukkarasu Peruman bestowed upon Mayiladuthurai.

“Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, having worshipped Mayiladuthurai, continued his pilgrimage to Thiruthuruthi, Thiruvelvikudi, and Thiru Ethirkolpadi. Let us continue our reflection.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Three Hundred and Seventy-Eight, Thirunindrachcharukkam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal, having worshipped Thirumayiladuthurai, reached the sacred sthalam called Thiruthuruthi. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that he visited many sacred places such as Thuruthi, Velvikudi, and Ethirkolpadi. Thiruthuruthi and Velvikudi are sthalams located opposite each other on the two banks of the Kaveri. It is customary to consider these two as a single sthalam.

Thiruthuruthi is the thirty-seventh sthalam among the Kaveri South Bank sthalams. Velvikudi is the twenty-third sacred sthalam among the Kaveri North Bank sthalams. Thuruthi is now known as Kuthalam. Before marrying the Goddess in Velvikudi, Lord Shiva resided here as a celibate. He resided here as a celibate and recited the Vedas.

Therefore, he is known here as Utthara Vedeeswarar. Since he himself recited the Vedas he had composed, Swamigal is known as Sonnavaru Arivar.

Sundaramoorthy Swamigal praises him by this name, Sonnavaru Arivar Thuruthiyar, in his Thevaram. The sacred sthalam of Thiruthuruthi is now located on the Mayavaram-Kumbakonam road, known as Kuthalam. The Kaveri, which previously flowed on both sides of the sthalams that were like islands, now flows to the north of the temple. The Sthala Vriksham here is the Utthala tree, hence this sthalam is also named Utthala Vanam. This has evolved into Kuthalam. The sacred The temple is beautifully situated in the middle of the village.

There are two circumambulatory paths.

The Lord faces west, and the Goddess faces south. Both the Lord’s temple and the Goddess’s temple are separate, with circumambulatory paths for devotees to walk around. The western entrance is graced by a Rajagopuram. In the outer circumambulatory path, in the northwest corner, is the Sundara Theertham. On its western bank is the Sundaramoorthy Swamigal temple.

Here, the Lord’s sacred name is Uktha Vedeeswarar, also known as Sonnavaru Arivar. The Goddess’s sacred name is Amrita Mukilambikai, also known as Arumbannavanai Mulaiyar. The Sthala Vinayagar is Thunai Vantha Pillaiyar, and there are many other deities such as Manavalanathar and Narunjanthu Ilamulai Ammaiyar. In this sthalam, the Goddess worshipped the Lord, and the Lord appeared in visions. The Goddess, holding the Lord’s hand, bowed and requested, according to tradition, that the Lord marry her to the delight of her parents.

The Lord graciously replied, “It is good. We ourselves have ordained destiny in this world. If we do not act according to the destiny we have ordained, it may change.

“Therefore, we will marry according to it.” Here, there is a deity named Manavalanathar. This is the sacred form that appeared at the request of Uma Devi to marry her. It is located at the base of the Sthala Vriksham, in front of Uktha Vedeeswarar. Currently, only the sacred sandals (padukai) are visible. Narunjanthu Ilamulai Ammaiyar is the sacred image adorned with garlands and sandalwood paste for the marriage of the Goddess, hence she received this name. This sacred image of Manavalanathar is located opposite the sacred sandals.

“The Sthala Vinayagar is Thunai Vantha Pillaiyar. When the Lord set out from Kailash to marry the Goddess and came to this sthalam, Vinayagar also accompanied him, hence he is known as Thunai Vantha Vinayagar. This sthalam has many special features. This is the sthalam where Uma Devi performed Shiva Puja and married the Lord. Agni, having been blamed by everyone for destroying everything it touched, came to this sthalam to absolve himself of that sin. This sthalam cured Komalai, the wife of Vikrama Chola, of an incurable skin disease.

“This sthalam blessed Varuna by curing him of the disease called Salodaram. Kali worshipped here to receive the boon of guarding the town after witnessing the sacred dance. It was in this sthalam that the seven sages — Kashyapar, Angirasar, Gautamar, Markandeyar, Vasishtar, Pulastiyar, and Agathiyar — worshipped and received boons and the grace of the Lord. This sthalam bestowed compassion by curing the consumption of Shivabhaktan, the son of Pariccheda Muni, which was caused by past karma. This sthalam has many glories, such as Surya regaining his lost authority by performing penance here to attain the Lord.

“Thus, because Surya regained his former authority in this sthalam, the Lord bestowed his grace upon Surya.

“The Lord has blessed that those who come to this sthalam on Karthigai Sunday, bathe, and worship will attain supreme bliss and liberation. It was in this sthalam that the Lord stopped and blessed a Brahmin named Thiraschman, who was going towards Kasi without realizing the greatness of this sthalam. It was in this sthalam that Bharatha Muni worshipped and attained liberation with his wife. When Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, who was staying in Thiruotriyur, remembered the sacred form of the Lord of Thiruvarur and set out to go to Thiruvarur, his two eyes lost their light because he had broken his vow. After visiting many sthalams, he reached Kanchi and regained sight in one eye. As he continued towards Thiruvarur, he crossed the Kaveri and reached Avaduthurai.

“When he bowed there and moved away, At that time, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal’s body was afflicted with a skin disease, and his complexion turned dark.

“Then, he came to the Thiruthuruthi temple and worshipped the Lord, requesting, “O Lord, please cure this incurable disease that has afflicted your servant and bestow your grace.” The Lord graciously replied, “My dear one, let your sorrow cease. Bathe in the Padma Theertham.” Sundarar did so, bathed in that theertham, and rose. His skin disease was cured, and his sacred body appeared radiant.

“At that time, he sang a Thiruppathigam beginning with “Minnuma Megangal.” Thus, the theertham in which Sundaramoorthy Swamigal bathed is known as Thamarai Thadagam and Padma Theertham. It is located in the northwest corner of the temple. Sadananda Muni, the son of Gautama, bathed in this theertham for two Ayana periods as instructed by his father. This Theertham is also known as Sundara Theertham. On its bank, a temple is dedicated to Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. The other Theerthams of this sthalam include the Kaveri River, which flows north of the temple towards the east.

“This Theertham is very special.

“In addition, there are many other Theerthams around this sthalam, such as Agni Theertham, Kali Theertham, Pundareeka Theertham, Kama Theertham, Kathirava Theertham, and Markanda Theertham. The Sthala Vriksham is the Utthala tree. When the Lord came to marry the Goddess, this tree came with the Lord from Mount Kailash, by His command, to provide shade for Him. Upon arriving at this sthalam, the Lord placed it on His left side and, beneath it, in the sacred sandals of the Vedas, He also took His abode. Kakola Muni, Pulagan, Kuchchan, Vikraman, Vachchan, Somasekhar, Dharmasanman, Namarai, Sumathi, Soudarsana Muni, and others have worshipped here and received many blessings. This sthalam has mandapams such as the Alankara Mandapam and Theerthavari Mandapam.

“According to the Karana Kamika Agamas, five daily pujas are performed. On Karthigai Sunday and Thai Friday, the Lord goes in procession, gives darshan, and bestows Theertham. This sacred temple is one of the devasthanams under the administration of the Thirukailaya Paramparai Dharmapuram Adheenam. The other sacred names of the Lord of this sthalam are Vinguneer Thiruthuruthi Udaiya Mahadevar, Thirukkattrali Mahadevar, and Udaiyar Sonnavaru Arivar. The Sthala Puranam, called Thiruthuruthi Puranam, composed by Mahavidwan Meenakshi Sundarampillai, is available in poetic form. This Puranam contains one thousand six hundred and two Thiruviruththams.

“There are two Pathigams by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, one Pathigam by Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal, and one Pathigam by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal for this sthalam. Manikkavasagar Swamigal sings, “Thuruthi thannil aruthiyodu irunthum” (Even residing with desire in Thuruthi). In another place in Thiruvachagam, Manikkavasagar Peruman sings about this sthalam in the Kanda Pathu, song number three: “Urutheriya kaalaththai ul pugunthu en ullam manni karuththiruthi oon pukku karunaiyinaal aandu konda Thiruthuruthi meyaanai thiththikkum Sivapathaththai naayadiyen anikol Thillai kandenē” (I, a dog-like devotee, saw the sweet abode of Shiva in beautiful Thillai, the Lord of Thiruthuruthi, who entered my heart in an unknown time, settled there, entered my flesh, and ruled me with compassion).

“Now, let us look at the Thiruppathigam that Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal bestowed upon this sthalam. The Thiruthuruthi Thiruppathigam is compiled as the forty-second Thiruppathigam in the fourth Thirumurai. The Thiruppathigam begins with “Porunthiya Kurambai.” “Porunthiya kurambai thannai porulenak karutha vendaa iruththi eppozhuthum nenjull iraivanai eththuminkal oruthiyiaai paagam vaiththangu oruthiyiaich chadaiyil vaiththa thuruthiyan sudarinanaai thondanena kandavare. Savai thanai seythu vaazhvaan salaththule azhunthukindra ivai oru porulum alla iraivanai eththu minno avai puram moonru eythu adiyavarkku arulichcheytha suvaiyinai thirutthiyaanaai thondanena kandavare. Unni eppothu nenjull oruvanai eththu minno kanniyai oru paal vaiththu gangaiyaich chadaiyil vaiththu ponniyin naduvu thannull poompunal.” (Gloss: Do not consider this body, which is a temporary dwelling, as the ultimate reality.

“Always keep the Lord in your heart and praise Him. I, a devotee, have seen the Lord of Thuruthi, who placed one woman as a part of Himself and another in His matted locks, a radiant being. These things, living in deceit and sinking in water, are not real. Praise the Lord, who, by destroying the three cities, bestowed grace upon His devotees, the sweet Lord of Thuruthi, as I, a devotee, have seen. Always keep the one Lord in your heart and praise Him. He placed the virgin on one side and the Ganga in His matted locks, and in the middle of the Ponni, sacred water.)

“Poḻintha thōṇṭum thuṇṇiya Thuruthiyāṉai thoṇḍaṉēṉ kaṇḍavārē ūṇṭalai valiyaṉāgi ulagaththuḷ uyirkaṭkellām thāṇṭalai paṭṭu niṉṟu chārkaṉal agaththu vīḻa vāṉṭalai thēvar kūḍi vāṉavarkku iṟaivā eṉṉum thōṇṭalai Thuruthiyāṉai thoṇḍaṉēṉ kaṇḍavārē uḍalthaṉai kaḻikkaluṟṟa ulagaththuḷ uyirkaṭkellām iḍarthaṉai kaḻikka vēṇḍil iṟaivaṉai ēththu miṉṉō kaḍalthaṉil nañjam uṇḍu kāṇpari thāgi niṉṟa suḍarthaṉai Thuruthiyāṉai thoṇḍaṉēṉ kaṇḍavārē aḷḷalai kaḍakka vēṇḍil araṇaiyē niṉaimiṉīrkaḷ poḷḷalik kāyntha thaṉṉuḷ puṇḍarīkaththu iruntha vaḷḷalai vāṉavarkkum kāṇpari thāgi niṉṟa thuḷḷalai Thuruthiyāṉai thoṇḍaṉēṉ kaṇḍavārē. (Gloss: The Lord of Thuruthi, who appeared as if pouring forth, as I, a devotee, have seen. He, who became strong in body, stood as the head for all beings in the world, and fell into the fierce fire.

“The Lord of Thuruthi, whom the gods in heaven gathered and called out, “O Lord of the celestials,” as I, a devotee, have seen. If you wish to remove the suffering of all beings in the world who are about to shed their bodies, praise the Lord.

“The Lord of Thuruthi, who consumed the poison from the ocean and stood as an unseeable light, as I, a devotee, have seen. If you wish to cross the mire, meditate on the Lord. The generous Lord of Thuruthi, who resides in the lotus of the heart, which is like a dried gourd, and who is an unseeable dance even for the celestials, as I, a devotee, have seen.) Pāthiyil umaiyāḷ thannai pāgamā vaiththa paṇpaṉ vēthiyaṉ eṉṟu solli viṇṇavar virumbiyēththa sāthiyām chathurmuganum chakkaraththāṉum kāṇā sōthiyai Thuruthiyāṉai thoṇḍaṉēṉ kaṇḍavārē sāmaṉai vāḻkkaiyāṉa salaththuḷē azhuntha vēṇḍā thūmaṉal agilum kāṭṭi thoḻuthu aḍi vaṇaṅgu miṉṉō sōmaṉaich chaḍayuḷ vaiththu thoṉ neṟi palavum kāṭṭum thūmaṉath Thuruthiyāṉai thoṇḍaṉēṉ kaṇḍavārē kuṇḍarē samaṇar putthar kuṟiyaṟiyāthu niṉṟu kaṇḍathē karuthuvārkaḷ karuttheṇṇāthu oḷimiṉīrkaḷ viṇḍavar puṟaṅgaḷ eythu viṇṇavarkku aruḷkaḷ seytha thoṇḍarkaḷ thuṇaiyiṉāṉai Thuruthi nāṉ kaṇḍavārē piṇḍaththai kaḻikka vēṇḍil pirāṉaiyē piththaṟṟumiṉkaḷ. (Gloss: The virtuous one who placed Uma as a part of Himself, whom the celestials desired to praise, calling Him the Vedic one.

“The Lord of Thuruthi, a light unseen by Brahma and Vishnu, as I, a devotee, have seen. Do not sink into the deceitful life of the world. Show pure, good incense and worship His feet.

“The Lord of Thuruthi, who holds the moon in His matted locks and shows many ancient paths, the pure-minded one, as I, a devotee, have seen. O fools, Jains and Buddhists, who stand without knowing the truth and consider only what they see, do not heed their thoughts, but shine forth.

“The Lord of Thuruthi, the helper of devotees who shot down the cities of the enemies and bestowed grace upon the celestials, as I, a devotee, have seen. If you wish to shed the body, utter the name of the Lord.) Aṇḍaththai kaḻiya nīṇḍa aḍal arakkaṉ thaṉ āṇmai kaṇḍoththu kāl viralāl ūṉṟi mīṇḍaruḷi seytha thuṇḍaththu Thuruthiyāṉai thoṇḍaṉēṉ kaṇḍavārē Thiruchitrambalam. (Gloss: The Lord of Thuruthi, who, seeing the might of the powerful demon who stretched to the heavens, pressed him with His toe and then graciously restored him, as I, a devotee, have seen.

“) This is that Thiruppathigam. “What a wonder it is that I saw the Lord in Thiruthuruthi!” Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal states in this Thiruppathigam, “O people of the world, do not consider worldly life as real and sink into it. Praise that Lord!” This is the essence of the Pathigam.

“We shall continue with our reflection.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Three Hundred and Seventy-Nine, Thirunindrachcharukkam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal, having worshipped the Lord in Kuthalam, also known as Thiruthuruthi, visited many sacred places such as Thiruvelvikudi and Thiru Ethirkolpadi, and then reached Thirukodikka.

Therefore, he must have visited many other sacred places between Thiruvelvikudi, Thiru Ethirkolpadi, and Thirukodikka. Among those many sacred places are Thirumanjeri and others. It is known from this that Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal visited the sacred places of Thiruvelvikudi, Thiru Ethirkolpadi, and Thirumanjeri and sang Pathigams.

However, the Thiruppathigams composed by Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal for this sthalam are not available to us. Due to its scarcity, we do not have access to the Thiru-Velvikudi, Thiru-Ethirkolpadi, and Thirumanancheri sthalams, all of which are connected by a single history and a single purana. In Thiru-Velvikudi, the Lord’s name is Kalyana Sundareswarar or Manavaleswarar, and the Goddess’s name is Parimala Sugandhanayaki. The sacred waters are Mangala Theertham and Gauthaga Bandhana Theertham. A Thiru-Pathigam composed by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal for this sthalam is available. This is the twenty-third sthalam among the Cauvery North Bank sthalams that have received Thevaram hymns.

The Lord faces east and bestows grace as a Swayambhu Lingam. As previously seen, this is a Thiru-Sthalam that was sung about along with Thiru-Thuruthi, also known as Kuthalam. The parents of a girl, who was betrothed to a prince, passed away before the wedding.

After that, the bride’s family did not consent to the marriage. The prince came to this sthalam, worshipped the Lord, and requested that the postponed wedding be conducted.

Lord Shiva sent a Bhootham (spirit) to bring the girl and arranged their marriage. Near Thiru-Velvikudi, in Kuthalam, the Goddess incarnated as the daughter of Bharatha Maharishi. To marry Parameswaran, she observed a fast for sixteen Mondays, meditating on him and worshipping a Lingam made of earth. On the seventeenth Monday, Lord Shiva appeared as Manavaleswarar and granted her the boon of marriage.

Accordingly, Brahma tied the Kankanam (sacred thread) for the Goddess and performed the rituals, and the Lord consented to the marriage.

Therefore, this Thiru-Sthalam is called Thiru-Velvikudi. The next sthalam is called Thiru-Ethirkolpadi, which is Melai Thirumanancheri. This is the twenty-fourth sthalam among the Cauvery North Bank sthalams and is a sthalam that has received Thevaram hymns from Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. Melai Thirumanancheri is also known as Ethirkolpadi. This is the sthalam where Airavatham worshipped. The Lord’s name is Airavatheeswarar, and the Goddess’s name is Sugandha Kunthalambikai or Malarkuzhal Maadhu.

The sacred water is Airavatha Theertham. Since the Lord came to receive his devotee, the prince, who had married in the nearby Thiru-Velvikudi and was arriving in his wedding attire, like his maternal uncle, this sthalam was named Ethirkolpadi. There is no Brahmotsavam in this temple. The Thiru-Kalyanam (sacred marriage) of Kalyana Sundarar takes place in the nearby wedding sthalam, Thirumanancheri, in the month of Chithirai. In his groom’s attire, he proceeds to Ethirkolpadi. He will arrive at the temple.

The priest of this temple, considering himself the father of the Goddess, will welcome Kalyana Sundareswarar with full honors and offer him the customary gifts due to a son-in-law. After accepting this hospitality, the Lord will return to Thirumanancheri and marry the Goddess there. Another account states that after Bharatha Muni conducted the marriage of Lord Shiva and the Goddess in Thiru-Velvikudi, he invited the Lord to come to Melai Thirumanancheri, where he resided, once the marriage was complete.

The Lord agreed to come. Bharatha Muni went to receive the divine couple, the Lord and the Goddess, who were arriving in their wedding attire.

Therefore, this sthalam is called Ethirkolpadi.

Thus, Thirumanancheri is another sthalam connected with Kuthalam, Thiru-Velvikudi, and Thiru-Ethirkolpadi. Currently, the sthalam of Thirumanancheri is very famous as a prayer sthalam for those seeking marriage. This sthalam is called Thirumanancheri because Kalyana Sundaramoorthy Swamigal married Kokilambal Ambigai here. The Lord’s name is Uthvaganathar, and the Goddess’s name is Kokilambikai. It is believed that for the Lord’s sacred marriage ceremony, the seven oceans transformed into a garland.

Therefore, the seven ocean theerthams appear as a moat surrounding this temple. Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal came here and sang praises of the Peruman, but that Thiru-Pathigam is not available to us. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sang about the Lord of this sthalam, and that Thiru-Pathigam is available to us. Two women from the merchant community wished to arrange marriages between their descendants through giving and taking, and they made a vow.

However, one of the women gave birth to a tortoise. When they presented their grievances to the Lord of this sthalam, the Peruman, in his grace, transformed the tortoise-child into human form and then ensured that the vow they had made to each other was fulfilled, conducting the marriage. This is one of the histories here. It is widely known among the glories of the Lord of this sthalam that those whose marriages are delayed or obstructed will quickly be married if they offer a garland and perform archana to Kalyana Sundara Peruman, the Lord of this sthalam. Those who desire progeny will attain it by bathing in the Sapthasagara Theertham here and worshipping the Lord. The Moolavar (presiding deity) of this temple, built according to the Karana Agama tradition, is Sri Uthvaganathar, also known as Arul Vallanathar.

The Goddess is Kokilambal, also known as Yazhinum Menmozhiyal. Kalyana Sundarar appears in his wedding attire. We have information from inscriptions that this temple was renovated by Sembiyan Mahadevi. Annually, during the Chithirai month, on the Poosam star, the sacred marriage festival of the Lord and Goddess is celebrated with great pomp for three days. This entire town appears in wedding attire during these days. The five daily pujas, namely Thiruvananthal, Kalasandhi, Uchikalam, Sayarakshai, and Arthajamam, are performed.

Upon entering this east-facing temple, after passing the Rajagopuram, Ganapathi is seen. Next are the Dhwajastambam, Balipitam, and Mahanandi Mandapam. Varachithi Vinayagar is enshrined. Inside the temple, in the Dhwara Mandapam, Sri Uthvaganathar, also known as Arul Vallanathar, is beautifully seen with Dhwarapalaka Nandi in the Garbhagriham. In the Nirtham Mandapam, Natarajar bestows grace upon devotees while dancing. Opposite him, facing east, Kalyana Sundarar appears in his wedding attire.

Sri Kokilambal Ambigai, Yazhinum Menmozhiyal, is seated in a comfortable posture on the wedding platform, as a bride should be, which is a very beautiful sight. In the Devakoshtam are Bhikshatanar, Balaganapathi, Natarajar, Dakshinamurthy in Yoga form, Lingodbhavar, Brahma, Rahu, Durga, and Pazhaiyanthagar. In the temple’s southwest corner is the shrine of Azhagu Vinayagar, and in the Thiru-Maalai Pathathi, the shrine of Subramaniyar. Above the Lord’s sanctum, there is a shrine for Mahavishnu with Ubhaya Nachiyar, a shrine for Lakshmi, and images of Bharatha Maharishi and Sembiyan Mahadevi. Bhairavar, Suriyan, Saneeswarar, Pachaiyappanathar, Rudravaneeswarar, Pachaiyammai Nayaki, and Rudravaneeswari are in the lower Thiru-Maalai Pathathi.

As we have already seen, Thiru-Thuruthi (Kuthalam), Thiru-Velvikudi, Thiru-Ethirkolpadi (Melai Thirumanancheri), Thirumanancheri, and Thiru-Aavaduthurai are all sthalams where the Peruman bestows grace based on a single puranic history.

One day, Uma Devi worshipped Easwaran on Kailash and requested the boon to marry him once more and experience joy. Lord Shiva, with compassion, said, “In the coming Brahma Kalpa, I will marry you and bestow grace.” Umaiyal, saddened that the Lord had postponed the fulfillment of her wish for a very long time, that is, for a Kalpa, tried to act somewhat carelessly towards the Peruman. Because of this, Lord Shiva blessed Uma Devi to live as a cow on earth. Uma Ambigai, who had transformed into a cow, regretted her actions and appealed to the Peruman, who granted her the boon that he would soon marry her.

Therefore, as blessed by Lord Shiva, Uma Ambigai comes to earth as a cow. Mahalakshmi, Saraswati, Indrani, and other celestial women also took the form of cows and roamed with Uma Devi in places like Achukadu and Arasankadu on earth. Thirumal took the form of a cowherd and cared for all these cows. Uma Devi, in the form of a cow, daily poured milk to cool Lord Shiva’s Lingam. Lord Shiva, who was delighted to receive the impression of the hoof of Uma Devi in her cow form, decided to marry the Goddess as she wished. Uma Devi then incarnated in the sacrificial fire pit conducted by Bharatha Maharishi.

It is the history that Lord Shiva married Uma Devi, who thus incarnated, in Thirumanancheri. The Thiru- Sthalams associated with this history are as follows: In the village of Therazhundur, the Goddess was cursed to be a cow. In Asukadu, the Goddess took the form of a cow. In the Thiru-Sthalam of Komal, Thirumal took the form of a cowherd and cared for the cows. In the Thiru-Sthalam of Thirukuzhambam, the Lord received the impression of the cow’s hoof. In Thiru-Aavaduthurai, the Goddess, in her cow form, was granted liberation.

After that, the Goddess incarnated in the sacrificial fire pit conducted by Bharatha Maharishi in Thiru-Thuruthi, also known as Kuthalam. To marry Uma Devi, who thus incarnated, the Kankana Dharanam (tying of the sacred thread) and Mangala Snanam (auspicious bath) for the marriage were performed in Thiru-Velvikudi. In Kurumulaipalai, the Baligai Sthapanam (installation of the sacred pot) was performed. In Thiru-Ethirkolpadi, they welcome the Lord. In Thirumanancheri, the Peruman took the hand of Umaimangai Devi and married her. These are the details related to the sthalams of Thiru-Aavaduthurai, Thiru-Thuruthi, Thiru-Ethirkolpadi, Thiru-Velvikudi, and Thirumanancheri.

Thus, after visiting the sthalams of Thiru-Velvikudi, Melai Thirumanancheri (Thiru-Ethirkolpadi), and Thirumanancheri, Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal reaches the sthalam called Thirukodikka. Let us resume our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 380, Thirunindracharukkam, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal, having worshipped the sthalams of Thiru-Velvikudi, Thiru-Ethirkolpadi, and Thirumanancheri, reaches the sthalam called Thirukodikka. This sthalam is currently known as Thirukodikaval. The Lord’s name is Kotteeswarar or Kottinathar. The Goddess’s name is Thiripura Sundari or Vadivambigai.

The Sthala Vriksham is the cane tree. The Theertham is Sringa Theertham. This sthalam is named Thirukodikka because three crore Rishis worshipped here. The Srungodbhava Theertham is a sacred water body created by the horns of Nandi. This is the sthalam that absolved the Mathrugathi Dosham incurred by Parasurama, the son of Jamadagni Muni; the Brahmmahatthi Dosham incurred by Sri Rama; the Dosham incurred by Balarama for killing Prambalasuran; the Brahmmahatthi Dosham incurred by Veerabhadrar for killing many in Daksha’s Yagna; and the Mahagathiya Dosham incurred by Kali. Sriman Narayanan, in this sthalam, bathed in the Singodbhava Theertham, performed penance, and prayed for the liberation of three crore Devas, and this is the sthalam where he granted liberation to all of them.

This is the sthalam where Sudarsanan, a Vaishnava boy who was a great devotee of Shiva, received the divine grace to become Haradatta Sivachariyar. This is the thirty-seventh sthalam among the Cauvery North Bank sthalams. Across the Cauvery from here is the South Bank sthalam of Thiru-Aavaduthurai. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed one Thevaram, and Appar Swamigal composed one Thiru-Nerisaith Thirukkurunthogai and one Thiru-Thandagam, making a total of three Thiru-Pathigams. This sthalam has three Thiru-Pathigams. The Sani (Saturn) here is called Bala Sani (Child Saturn).

A Shiva Lingam is on his head. Instead of a crow, he has a Garuda as his vehicle. The Cauvery River flowing near this town flows northwards from south, as an Uttaravahini. The Sthala Vinayagar bestows grace with the name Karaiyetru Vinayagar. Approximately fifty inscriptions are found in this temple. The name of this Thiru-Sthalam is Thiru-Kodikka.

Five Shiva sthalams ending with ‘Ka’ are called Pancha Kaakkal or Pancha Ka Sthalams. This is one of the five sthalams: Thiru-Anaikka, Thiru-Kolakka, Thiru-Nellikka, Thiru-Kurugukka, and Thirukodikka. It is believed that the Goddess of this sthalam, Thiripura Sundari, blessed the great sage Sri Bhaskararaya to write a commentary on the Lalita Sahasranamam in her very presence. It is believed that the Goddess of this sthalam, Thiripura Sundari, blessed the great sage Sri Bhaskararaya to write a commentary on the Lalita Sahasranamam in her very presence. We saw that Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal, who visited this sthalam, composed three Thiru-Pathigams. Those Pathigams are as follows: The first Pathigam is the fifty-first Thiru-Pathigam of the fourth Thirumurai, a Thiru-Nerisaith Thiru-Pathigam.

“Nettri mel kanninane neeru meippusinane Kattai pun sadaiyinane kadal vidam paruginane Settravar purangal moonrum sevazhal seluthinane Kutramil gunathinane Kodikkavudaiya Kove Kadigamal konraiyane kapalam kai yendinane Vadivudai mangai thannai marbilor bhagathane Adiyinai parava nalum adiyavarkku arul seivane Kodiyani vilavadova Kodikkavudaiya Kove Neeru mei poosinane nizhal thigazh mazhuvinane” Gloss: “O Lord with an eye on your forehead, who smears sacred ash on your body, with matted hair, who drank the ocean’s poison, who burned the three cities of his enemies with red fire, O flawless one, Lord of Kodikka! O wearer of fragrant Konrai, who holds a skull in his hand, who has the beautiful maiden as a part of his chest, who always bestows grace upon devotees who praise his feet, O Lord of Kodikka, where banners flutter without ceasing!
