The Goddess took leave, praising Peruman, and, as per His command, arrived at Thiru-Anaikka with the Bhootha Ganas (celestial attendants) and her companions. The sages performing penance there saw the Goddess and worshipped her.

The Goddess desired to bathe in the various Thirthams here and worship Peruman. The Goddess’s attendants gathered all the necessary items for the worship. The Goddess, wishing to understand the nature of Mukti, which bestows bliss, decided to consecrate a Shiva Lingam made of sweet-tasting water.

Therefore, meditating on the sacred feet of the Lord, she gathered the Thirtham itself and consecrated it as a luminous Lingam. Due to this, this Lingam came to be known as Appu Lingam (Water Lingam). As the devotion of the Goddess grew, the Thirtham overflowed from that spot. It was named Srimath Thirtham. The Goddess performed Abhishekam to Peruman according to tradition, performed Shiva Puja, and offered praises.

One day, during this daily Shiva Puja, Peruman appeared to the Goddess on His Rishabam (bull mount). The Goddess, with her spiritual eye, beheld the Lord whom she could not perceive with her physical eyes. The Goddess, not for herself but for the sake of other beings, sought and received many boons from Shiva.

Afterwards, the Goddess requested Peruman to clarify the doubt she had initially asked on Kailash. Peruman addressed Uma Devi, saying, “You asked about the truth of Yoga. I will tell you now, listen. All worlds operate by Our grace.

“Therefore, just as a dance instructor first demonstrates the dance himself, We must first train the world.

“Thus, to enable the souls in the world to experience enjoyment, We embraced you and became a Bhogi (one who enjoys), and to enable them to attain true knowledge through Yoga and achieve salvation, We became a Yogi.” Peruman thus instructed the Goddess. The Goddess was greatly delighted. We can recall here Karuvur Devar’s eleventh verse in the Thiru-Pathigam of Gangaikonda Cholapuram in the Ninth Thiru-Murai, where he sings, “He who performs Yoga while with the maiden.” We can also recall here Appar Peruman’s third verse in the fiftieth Thiru-Pathigam of the Sixth Thiru-Murai, where he sings, “He who conquered the five senses while united with the beautiful maiden.” After hearing this instruction, the Goddess again asked Peruman, “I wish to understand Mala (impurity), Jiva (soul), Maya (illusion), Karma (action), true knowledge, and Mukti (liberation). Please instruct me on these.” Peruman clearly instructed her on their natures. To signify that the Goddess received instruction, the Swami Sannidhi (Lord’s shrine) faces west and the Amman Sannidhi (Goddess’s shrine) faces east in this temple.

“Therefore, such an arrangement is called an Upadesa Sthalam (place of instruction). Kachiappa Munivar, in his Thiru-Anaikka Puranam, has dedicated a chapter called ‘Gnana Upadesa Padalam’ (Chapter on the Instruction of Wisdom). In this chapter, Kachiappa Munivar has extensively described the nuances of Saiva Siddhanta that Peruman instructed to the Goddess. In the book titled Thiru-Anaikka Puranam.

“Now, fifthly, the history of Rama’s worship. When Rama returned after completing the destruction of Ravana and others, and rescuing Sita, the shadows of Ravana and Kumbhakarna followed Rama, threatening him. Rama, intending to dispel them, consecrated a Shiva Lingam at Rameswaram and worshipped it. Only Ravana’s shadow disappeared. Rama saw that Kumbhakarna’s shadow continued to follow him. As Rama was contemplating how to remove it, upon reaching the boundary of Jambukeswaram, Kumbhakarna’s shadow vanished like darkness before the sun.

“Rama was greatly pleased, bathed in several Thirthams, went to the Sannidhi, and worshipped Shiva, the Lord, and Akhilanda Nayaki. Afterwards, Rama met the sages there and recounted how the shadow had come, and how it had disappeared at the boundary of this sacred place. They told Rama, “In this sacred place, which is excellent in its Moorthy (deity), Sthalam (place), and Thirtham (sacred water), evils like ghosts, shadows, and diseases will not approach. If you cross the boundary of this place, that shadow will follow you again.

“Therefore, to ensure it never follows you, consecrate a Shiva Lingam here, worship it, and dispel it.” The sages advised Rama. Rama commanded Angathan to bring a Shiva Lingam. Angathan brought an emerald Lingam. Rama created a Thirtham to the west of the Lord’s Sannidhi, built a temple nearby, and, according to tradition, consecrated the new Lingam there. He worshipped and praised Peruman and the Goddess with a melting heart. Peruman appeared to Rama with the Goddess.

“Rama worshipped Shiva and the Goddess, then returned to Ayodhya and ruled the kingdom. The deity consecrated by Rama is known as Neelavinteeswarar. The Thirtham created by Rama is known as Rama Thirtham here.

“Now, sixthly, the history of Peruman wearing a pearl necklace. In Uraiyur, the capital of the Chola country watered by the Kaveri, a Chola king ruled. He was very devoted to Shiva and His devotees. He regularly performed the daily and occasional pujas in the temples where Shiva resided, without fail.

“At that time, winter ended and summer began, and the heat intensified. The Chola king who ruled Uraiyur then sent many items to Peruman residing in Thiru-Anaikka, the sacred place of wisdom, to alleviate the heat, and set out with his wife to have Darshan. Seeing the pearl necklace on his wife’s chest, the king, due to his devotion to Shiva, wished to adorn Peruman with that beautiful pearl necklace.

“At that time, as the king and his wife were bathing in the Kaveri, the pearl necklace worn by his wife slipped into the river. The king was greatly distressed that the pearl necklace, which he had intended to offer to the Lord, had slipped into the river. He praised Peruman in his thoughts.

“Then, crossing the Kaveri, he came to Thiru-Anaikka and had Darshan of Peruman.

“At that time, the temple priests performed Thirumanjanam (sacred bath) for Peruman with the Thirtham brought from the Kaveri.

“Then, by the grace of Shiva, the pearl necklace that had fallen into the Kaveri entered the Thirumanjana pot and, during the Abhishekam, fell onto Peruman’s sacred head along with the Thirtham. Everyone was astonished. The king also saw it and was amazed. He praised Peruman, saying, “O Lord, the leader who resides in Jambumoolam! How great is Your grace upon me! You, who removed the troublesome river, and adorned Your sacred head with the celestial river, causing wonder!” The fame of that king endures in the world even today.

“Sundaramurthy Swamigal has sung about this history in his Thevaram, in the song beginning “Tharamakiya Ponni.” Now, next, seventhly, the history of the sacred ash wall. Many days ago, when Kochchengan Cholan and other kings were performing renovation work on temples, by the grace of Peruman, a voice would always be heard from the sky, saying, “Perform all other works except the great wall.” Whenever they performed renovation work, this voice would be heard.

“One day, while renovation work was in progress, Peruman came as an ascetic, wearing saffron robes, with matted hair, rudraksha beads, and sacred ash. He began to build the sacred ash wall with carpenters and other laborers. He gave sacred ash as wages to the laborers. That sacred ash transformed into gold according to their work. The Siddhar who came as an ascetic performed many wonders and miracles. Such is the glory of that sacred ash wall.

“This sacred place possesses many such historical and Puranic narratives. There are seven Thiru-Pathigams sung by the Thevara Moovar (three great Shaivite saints) for this sacred place. There are three Pathigams by Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, three Pathigams by Appar Swamigal, and one Thiru-Pathigam by Sundaramurthy Swamigal, making a total of seven Thiru-Pathigams for this Sthalam. This Sthalam has been sung by the Moovar. The Thiru-Anaikka Puranam, composed by Sri Kachiappa Munivar, consists of twenty-one chapters. There is another Puranam called Thanthivana Puranam.

“Its author is said to be Kamalai Sri Gnanaprakasar. All these are details, special features, and historical accounts about Thiru-Anaikka Sthalam. May Arul Valar Sambu Moolathu Amuthalingesar live long! May Akilanda Valli live long! May the essence of the Vedas and Agamas flourish! May the glorious sacred city of Thiru-Anaikka live long!

“May all lands live long, O Mother! May the righteous Kaveri live long! May Akilanda Ammai live long! May all the abundant clusters of the earth live long! May the Lord of the world, who renounces attachment, live long in His true glory! May the sacred feet of the excellent Sambunathan live long!

“Thus, praising and extolling Jambukeswara and Akilandeswari Ammai, and praising the sacred feet of the Lord of Anaikkaval, we shall now contemplate the three Thiru-Pathigams bestowed upon this Sthalam by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 433, Thirunindrachcharukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar came to Thiru-Anaikka Sthalam, worshipped the Lord there, and sang Thiru-Pathigams. Appar Swamigal sang a total of three Pathigams for Thiru-Anaikka Sthalam. The first Thiru-Pathigam is the Thiru-Kurunthogai Thiru-Pathigam from the Fifth Thiru-Murai, the thirty-first Thiru-Pathigam from the Fifth Thiru-Murai.

“The Lord of the forest, cool and fragrant, some southerners do not drink the honey. They do not approach our Lord in Anaikka, but carry their bodies and wander like fools.” “O Lord of Anaikka, who stands near, without any flaw, for those who remove their crooked thoughts, make them righteous, and melt with devotion, knowing the path, holding onto the essence of the town.” “Without sorrow, without suffering, if you desire bliss, praise Him day and night. To those who contemplate, ‘My golden Lord is the Ruler,’ the Lord of Anaikka will be a friend.” “O Lord of Anaikka, who says ‘Ah!’ to all who praise His sacred feet with their tongues, without ceasing, and whose sins are removed by those who worship with their hands, saying ‘Protect me!’” “Worship without deceit, always. Avoid harsh words to attain liberation. To all whose hearts cool down, melting and melting, the Lord of Anaikka says, ‘Fear not!’” “Do not speak atheism, thinking the body is real.

“The five elements come like armies. To all who take refuge in Him without any hindrance, the Lord of Anaikka is a refuge.” “Before the nine gates of the flowing body are consumed by vultures, worship His sacred feet, offer pure flowers with your hands, and to those who weep, the Lord of Anaikka is a friend.” “O people of the world, who cannot comprehend when it rolls! Do not let evil deeds approach you firmly. To all who remove darkness and say, ‘He is the Lord,’ the Lord of Anaikka bestows grace.” “O my foolish heart, remember with love! The family and relatives that are destined for destruction, leave attachment and desire the supreme bliss of the Lord of Anaikka.” “The Lord of Anaikka, who is the beginning, who, when the king of Lanka, surrounded by the vast ocean, sang songs and played the Kinnaram, accepted his feet and bestowed grace.” The second Thiru-Pathigam is the sixty-second Thiru-Pathigam, Thiru-Thandaka Thiru-Pathigam, from the Sixth Thiru-Murai.

““What mother, what father, what relatives, what wealth is mine? Who are the good ones? No one will come to help when one dies. They will light the fire with small firewood and depart. O Lord of Thiru-Anaikka, the wealthy one, with the form of an ascetic, residing in the long Ponni river!

“If I attain Your golden feet, what else can I, Your servant, do with this body?” “You are the body, the life, the consciousness within it, and all else. You came into me without my knowing anything, and showed me both good and evil. O Lord with the honeyed Konrai flower, residing in Nindriyur, Shiva residing in Thiru-Anaikka! You are knowledge. If I attain Your golden feet, what else can I, Your servant, do with this body?” “You are incomparable. You live in harmony with this world.

“You stand with those who are not one with others. You are the one who protects me, who wanders, eating meager food, forgetting my true nature, and makes me subtle consciousness everywhere, and rules me, O beautiful Lord of Anaikka! You are the body, the life, the consciousness within it, and all else. You came into me without my knowing anything, and showed me both good and evil. O Lord with the honeyed Konrai flower, residing in Nindriyur, Shiva residing in Thiru-Anaikka! You are knowledge.

“If I attain Your golden feet, what else can I, Your servant, do with this body?” “You are incomparable. You live in harmony with this world. You stand with those who are not one with others. You are the one who protects me, who wanders, eating meager food, forgetting my true nature, and makes me subtle consciousness everywhere, and rules me, O beautiful Lord of Anaikka! O Father of the celestials, O Lord of Anaikka! If I attain Your golden feet, what else can I, Your servant, do with this body?” “You are in the hearts of those who remember You, O deceitful thief!

“You have the full moon in Your matted hair. You destroyed the three cities of those who opposed You. O Primeval One, who wore the skin of the elephant! O Lord with the blue throat, who rides the roaring bull! O Lord of Kailash mountain! I have reached Your ocean.

“O Lord who rules all worlds, O Lord of Anaikka! If I attain Your golden feet, what else can I, Your servant, do with this body?” “O Lord, who saved me, a servant, from being caught in the whirlpool of suffering in the ocean of this illusory birth, by helping my mind, which is like a wild elephant, with compassion, and placing love in me, O Invisible One! O Brahmin, who wore the skin of the fierce, intoxicated elephant! O Lord residing in Thiru-Anaikka! If I attain Your golden feet, what else can I, Your servant, do with this body?” “O Lord of Uraiyur, whose fame is enduring, O Lord of Kachi Ekambam, O Lord of Karona! You are supreme among those who worship You by scattering fragrant flowers.

“You wear snakes as ornaments. O Honey residing in Thiru-Anaikka, where the Ponni river with its waves and sacred waters overflows! O Lord of the celestials! If I attain Your golden feet, what else can I, Your servant, do with this body?” “O Lord with the dark, jewel-like throat, who is half of the Mother! O Lord with hands holding a deer, a great battle-axe, and fire! O Kankala, who destroyed Yama’s body!

“You are the past and the future. O Red One, whose sacred body is unknown! O pinnacle of the race of gods! O Lord residing in Thiru-Anaikka! If I attain Your golden feet, what else can I, Your servant, do with this body?” “O Lord with the young, surrounding army, O Lord with eight shoulders! You are the nature of those who bow down, saying, ‘There is none but You everywhere.’ O Lord with the bow, who holds the great mountain of fire in His hand!

“O Fire-dancer residing in Thiru-Anaikka! May my heart not wander, afflicted by small ailments. If I attain Your sacred feet, what else can I, Your servant, do with this body?” “O Lord with the red matted hair adorned with celestial waters! O path of the Vedas! O Lord who consumed the poison from the fiery ocean! O Lord of countless glories!

“If I, Your servant, can always remember You with my tongue, saying ‘My Lord,’ and behold You with my eyes, and always bathe in the abundant waters of Thiru-Anaikka, surrounded by beautiful groves, O Lord! If I attain Your golden feet, what else can I, Your servant, do with this body?” “O Lord with the bull adorned with a banner! You dance while the goblins sing and dance. O Youth who holds the beautiful maiden! O Lord of Thiru-Anaikka, O Lord of Mahakalathi! If I, Your servant, can come and serve Your feet, which crushed the mighty shoulders and heads of the king of Lanka, surrounded by the ocean, what else can I, Your servant, do with this body?”

“The third Thiru-Pathigam sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman for Thiru-Anaikka Sthalam is the sixty-third Thiru-Pathigam, Thiru-Thandaka Thiru-Pathigam, from the Sixth Thiru-Murai.

““I bathed in the abundant waters of Thiru-Anaikka, the Lord who wore the skin of the elephant, the one with an unaging mind, who made the mind and speech His own, who rode the bull, who is difficult to approach, who is the Father, my Lord, my Master, the one residing in Thiru-Anaikka, surrounded by the Kaveri with its fiery waves, the honey, the milk, the abundant waters.” “I bathed in the abundant waters of Thiru-Anaikka, the medicine, the one in the hearts of those who chant His name, the one with the crescent moon in His matted hair, the one who joyfully resides in my heart, the immortal, the unborn, the Lord of the Himalayas, the one who wore the skin of the fierce, intoxicated elephant, making Uma afraid, the one with the mighty battle-axe, the one who wandered from village to village seeking alms, the one residing in Thiru-Anaikka, the abundant waters. I bathed in the abundant waters of Thiru-Anaikka, the one with the unblemished white moon, the one who consumed the poison of the ocean and bestowed nectar upon the celestials, the one who is a relative and a support to all living beings, the inner meaning of Omkara, the one who created all worlds, the one who performs the act of creation, the one who destroyed the three cities of those who did not praise Him as the Lord, the one residing in Thiru-Anaikka, the abundant waters.” “I bathed in the abundant waters of Thiru-Anaikka, my Lord with the dark, jewel-like throat, the one with the white earring in His ear, the one with the garland of fragrant Konrai flowers, the one with the tiger skin as clothing, the one who is the great knowledge, beyond all else, the one with the jewel-adorned chest, the one with the matted hair, the one who is the chariot of the four divine Vedas, the one residing in Thiru-Anaikka, the abundant waters.” “I bathed in the abundant waters of Thiru-Anaikka, the truthful one without any falsehood, the virtuous one, the one who shot arrows at those who were not good, the one who is supreme in penance, the Lord who rides the bull, the one with the left hand, the one with the Kankala form, the one with the banner of the skull, the one with a body like fire, the red one, the one residing in Thiru-Anaikka, the abundant waters.” “I bathed in the abundant waters of Thiru-Anaikka, the one with the deer, the one with the battle-axe in His hand, the one who is a cluster of diamonds, the mountain of rubies, the one at the crown of my head, the one with the matted hair, the one who is stable with the ashes of the cremation ground, the one who strung the bow with the serpent as the string, the one who bent the Meru mountain as a bow to destroy the cities of those who did not remember Him, the one residing in Thiru-Anaikka, the abundant waters.” “I bathed in the abundant waters of Thiru-Anaikka, the primordial one, the sound of the fiery jewel, the one beyond the comprehension of the celestials, the supreme light, the meaning of the pure Vedas, the Brahmin who wore the ancient texts of flowers where bees gather, the one who taught righteousness, the one who cut off one of the five heads of Brahma, the one residing in Thiru-Anaikka, the abundant waters, with joy. I bathed in the abundant waters of Thiru-Anaikka, the one who rules the golden world for those who remember, praise, and extol the Lord of Kachi Ekambam without forgetting, the one with the army of Bhootha Ganas, the one who delights in dancing in the cremation ground, the one who desires alms, the one who shines like a coral cluster within my heart, the one residing in Thiru-Anaikka, the abundant waters.” “I bathed in the abundant waters of Thiru-Anaikka, the desired one, beyond the four Vedas, the one who protects from poverty and severe diseases, the one who is music, the one with countless virtues, the one who resides in Idai Maruthu and Eengoy, the one who rides the bull, the one who is the eight directions of the vast ocean, earth, sky, abundant fire, water, and wind, the one residing in Thiru-Anaikka, the abundant waters.” “He who looked at Kama and reduced his body to ashes, the one who was beyond the comprehension of Brahma and Vishnu in ancient times, the one who was like a blazing fire, the Lord of the celestials, the one who roared without fear.” Having destroyed the might of the Lankan king who lifted the mountain, and having relieved his distress then and there, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, praising and worshipping the Lord at Thiru-Anaikka, composes three Thiru-Pathikams. Sekkizhar Peruman then states: “Having worshipped the anklets that blessed the spider, and having sung many garlands of eloquent words, he bowed to the Lord of Thiru-Erumbiyur, whose matted locks shine.

“After singing, he worshipped the radiant Thiru-Chirappalli mountain, Thiru-Karkudi, and the prosperous Thiru-Paraythurai.” Thus, having worshipped the Lord of Thiru-Anaikka, who blessed the spider, and having sung Thiru-Pathikams, he then reached the sacred site of Thiru-Erumbiyur. After singing to the Lord there, he proceeded to Thiru-Chira- palli mountain and sang to Thayu-Mana Swamy there.

“Then, he proceeded to Thiru-Karkudi, also known as Uyyakkondan Malai, and sang a Thiru-Pathikam there. Afterwards, he reached the sacred site of Thiru-Paraythurai. All the places mentioned now are located near and within Thiru-Chirappalli. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman visits all these places, praises the Lord, and sings Thiru-Pathikams.

“Let us continue our reflection.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 434. Thiru-Nindra Sarukkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, having worshipped at Thiru-Anaikka, proceeds to the site known as Thiru-Erumbiyur, also called Thiru-Erumbur. This site, Thiru-Erumbur, is very close to Thiru-Chirappalli.

This sacred site, mentioned as Thiru-Erumbiyur in the Thevaram hymns, is located on the road from Thiru-Chirappalli to Thanjavur. It is near Thiru-Chirappalli and is a hill temple. According to legend, it is called Manikkoodam and Rathnakkoodam.

Furthermore, this site is also known by the names Thiru-Erumbipuram, Erumbeesam, Brahmapuram, Lakshmipuram, Madhuvanapuram, Rathnakkoodapuram, Manikkoodapuram, and Kumarapuram. These names are attributed to the worship of Brahma, Lakshmi, and Murugan. It is called Thiru-Erumbiyur in Tamil and Pipileeswaram in Sanskrit. Thiru-Erumbiyur is the place where the Devas worshipped the Lord in the form of ants. We saw that Thiru-Anaikka is the place where the elephant worshipped, and a spider also worshipped there.

Here, ants worshipped the Peruman. The temple faces east, situated on a hill. There are 115 steps from the bottom to the top. At the base, there is a circumambulatory path where chariot processions and festivals take place. On the hill, there are two circumambulatory paths: one inside the temple and another outside. Inside the inner circumambulatory path are shrines for Vinayagar and others, and in the outer circumambulatory path is the Amman temple.

The Vinayagar of this site is named Balachandra Vinayagar. The Moolamoorthy is known by the names Erumbeesar, Erumbeeswarar, Madhuvaneswarar, Manikkoodachala-pathi, Pipilikes- eeswarar, Manikkanaathar, and others. In inscriptions, names such as Thiru-Malai Azhwar, Thiru-Erumbur Azhwar, Thiru-Erumbiyurudaiya Nayanar, Thenkailayathu Mahadevar, and Adiththa Pattaragar are found. The names Pillaiyar Kshethra Baladevan and Pillaiyar Bhagavathi were given to some deities. Thiru-Navukkarasar refers to the Lord as a ruby on the mountain and a radiant flame in his Thiru-Thandagam. The Amman is known by names such as Narunguzhal Nayagi, Soundarya Nayagi, Madhuvanaveeswari, and Rathnambaal.

Now, regarding the sacred waters in the temple: Brahma Theertham, which is the temple tank in front of the temple, was established in the name of Brahma Devan. Since the sins of those who bathe in it are destroyed, it is called Pavanaasa Theertham. The float festival takes place in the month of Vaikasi, on the third day after the full moon. Next is Padma Theertham, which is located in the north-east direction of the temple, named after Lakshmi. The third is Madhu Theertham, named after the Devas. The fourth is Kumara Theertham, located north of the temple, named after Kumara Kadavul.

Additionally, there are Surya Pushkarani, Chandra Pushkarani, Kalyana Theertham, and other sacred waters. This site is praised as Then Kailayam and is said to be a fragment of Mount Meru. This temple, situated on a hill, is located amidst the fertile fields of the Marutham land. The Moolavar is a Swayambu Moorthy. Brahma, Thirumagal, Rathi, Indra, and other Devas, Agni, Murugan, Agasthiyar, Naimicha Munivar, and others have worshipped Lord Shiva at this site and received blessings. When Indra worshipped the Lord in the form of an ant, the Lord inclined His head and accepted it.

This is a unique glory of this site. The line “Kulichakkaiyan Erumbana Ahhrinaiyin Urukkodu” (He who took the form of an ant, a tiny creature) emphasizes this. It is also said that Karan worshipped here in the form of an ant. There are many inscriptions in this temple. Thiru-Kurunthogai and Thiru-Thandagam, hymns sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar, are dedicated to this site. There is also a Purana called Thiru-Erumbiyur Puranam.

This temple is glorious in terms of Moorthy (deity), Thalam (place), and Theertham (sacred water). Inside the inner circumambulatory path of this temple, next to the kitchen, there is a tunnel, but no details about it are known. In the North Street, there is a monastery of a great saint named Sri Kattai Kali Swamigal. The surrounding temples for this temple are Kailasanathar Temple to the north, Vinayagar Temple at the base, and Arasu Kaaththamman Temple as the village deity temple.

After the festival for this Amman, the festival in the hill temple takes place. Abhishekam and Aradhanai are performed daily for the Lord and other deities in this temple during the four periods of morning, noon, evening, and night. Abhishekam is performed for the Moolalingam without water touching it. Annually, a grand ten-day festival takes place in the month of Vaikasi. The festival begins on the Punarpoosam star during the waxing moon and concludes with Theerthavari on the Visakam star, followed by palanquin festivals and float festivals on subsequent days.

Once upon a time, there was a demon named Tharukasuran. He waged war against Indra and captured Devaloka. Indra went to Brahma to complain, and Brahma told him to go to Thiru-Erumbiyur, the Southern Kailash on earth, and worship the Lord.

Accordingly, Indra and other Devas, fearing Tharukasuran, took the form of ants and reached this site. They worshipped the Lord and expressed their grievances.

The Lord appeared with Uma Devi, granted them darshan, and promised to alleviate their sorrows, commanding the Devas to stay at this place for some time. Accordingly, Indra, along with the host of Devas, came and worshipped Erumbiyur Eesan here with black water lilies. This was the Lord’s command.

Therefore, Indra, in the form of an ant, worshipped the Lord daily with a thousand black water lilies. The Lord, inclining His sacred head, accepted that worship. The Purana of this site states, “Even the great Indra, in the form of an ant, surrounded and praised Erumbeesam.” To make this known to the people of the world, the Lord even today grants darshan with His sacred head inclined. Agasthiyar, the sage of the Kumbha, married Lopamudra and embarked on a pilgrimage, visiting many sacred sites. He came to this Rathna Koodam, Thiru-Erumbiyur, on the southern bank of the Kaveri, bathed in the Kumara Theertham there, and worshipped Rathnachalanathar and Rathnambaal according to Agamic rites.

One day, the Lord appeared with His consort and blessed him.

At that time, Agasthiyar requested the Lord to impart spiritual knowledge to him.

The Lord blessed the sage, saying that Murugapperuman would impart the knowledge. Agasthiyar then worshipped Murugapperuman. Murugapperuman, with His consorts, appeared on His peacock vehicle, granted darshan, and imparted spiritual knowledge to Agasthiyar.

Thus, Murugapperuman taught Agasthiyar the three realities of Pathi, Pasu, and Pasam.

Here, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman comes to this glorious sacred site of Thiru-Erumbiyur, also known as Thiru-Erumbur, and composes two Thiru-Pathikams. The first Thiru-Pathikam is the 74th Thiru-Pathikam of the Fifth Thiru-Murai, a Thiru-Kurunthogai Thiru-Pathikam.

“Virumbiyooruvidel madanenjame karumbinooral kandaay kalanthaarkkavan irumbinooral araathathor vendalai erumbiyoor malaiyaan engal eesane.” (O foolish heart, do not desire to wander; see the sweetness of sugarcane for those who mingle with Him. He is our Lord, the Lord of Erumbiyur mountain, with a skull that is not a mere iron skull.) “Pirangu senjadai pinagan penuseer karangu bootha ganamudai kannuthal” “Narunguzhal madavaalodu naadorum Erumbiyoor malaiyaan engal eesane.” (Our Lord, the Lord of Erumbiyur mountain, with fragrant locks, is with the young woman daily.) “Marunthuvaanavar thaanavarkku insuvai purintha punjadai punniyan kannuthal porunthu poonmulai mangai nallaalodum Erumbiyoor malaiyaan engal eesane.” (Our Lord, the Lord of Erumbiyur mountain, is the virtuous one with matted locks, who gave sweet taste to the Devas and Asuras, and is with the good maiden with adorned breasts.) “Nirangol kandathu ninmalan em mirai marangol ver kanni vaanuthal paagamay arampurintharul seytha em angnan Erumbiyoor malaiyaan engal eesane.” (Our Lord, the Lord of Erumbiyur mountain, is our pure Lord with a dark throat, who, with the beautiful-browed maiden as a part, performed dharma and bestowed grace.) “Narumpo nanmalar kondraiyum naagamum thurumbu senjadai thoomathi vaiththuvaan urumpon maalvarai pedaiyodu oorthorum Erumbiyoor malaiyaan engal eesane.” (Our Lord, the Lord of Erumbiyur mountain, with fragrant golden flowers, konrai, and snakes, with pure moon in His matted locks, wanders through towns with the golden mountain-like maiden.) “Karumbiyooruvana ainthula kaayaththil thirumbiyooruvana matrum palavula kurumbiyooruvathor kootagaththu inai Erumbiyoor aran seytha iyarkkaiye maranthu,” “Matrathu peridar naadorum thirumbi nee ninaiyel madanenjame puranjai kolak kurambaiyil ittu ena Erumbiyoor aran seytha iyarkkaiye inbamum pirappum irappum pinnodu thunbamum udane vaiththa sothiyaan anbane arane endru aratruvaarkku inbanagum Erumbiyoor eesane kanniraintha ganapavala thiral vinniraintha virisudar sothiyaan un nirainthu uruvaay uyiraay avan enniraintha Erumbiyoor eesane nirangol maal varai oon eduththalum narunguzhal madavaal nadukkai thida marangol vaalarakkan vali vaattinaan Erumbiyoor malai em mirai kaanmine.” (O foolish heart, do not daily remember other great sorrows; the nature that Erumbiyur’s Lord created, placing joy, birth, death, and sorrow together in this beautiful body, is the radiant one. He is the beloved Lord of Erumbiyur, who is sweet to those who cry out, ‘Beloved, Lord!’ He is the radiant light, full of coral clusters, filling the sky with spreading light.

He is the Lord of Erumbiyur, who fills your being, becoming your form and life. See our Lord, the Lord of Erumbiyur mountain, who, when the great mountain was lifted, and the fragrant-haired maiden trembled, crushed the strength of the mighty demon.)

Now, the next Thiru-Pathikam by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, the 91st Thiru-Pathikam of the Sixth Thiru-Murai, a Thiru-Thandaga Thiru-Pathikam.

“Panniya senthamizh ariyēn kaviyēn maattēn ennōdu panniraintha kalaigalāy thannai unthan thiraththu ariyā poriyilēnai than thiramum ariviththu neriyum kaatti annaiyaiyum aththanaiyum pōla anpāy adainthēnai thodarnthu ennai ālāk konda then Erumbiyūr malaimēl mānikkaththai sezhunjudarai senradaiya petrēn nānē.” (I do not know refined Tamil, nor am I a poet. I am an ignorant one who does not know your nature, though you are the arts that fill me. You made me know your nature, showed me the path, and like a mother and father, you lovingly embraced me, followed me, and made me your own. I have attained the ruby on the Southern Erumbiyur mountain, the radiant flame.) “Pazhungin nizhalul pathiththa sōthiyānai pasupathiyai pāsupatha vēdaththānai vizhinthazhuntha salantharanai vīttinānai vēthiyanai viņṇavanai mēvi vaiyam aḷanthavanai nānmukanai allal thīrkkum arumarunthai āmārariṇthu en uḷḷan theḷinthu Erumbiyūr malaimēl mānikkaththai sezhunjudarai senradaiya petrēn nānē.” (I have attained the ruby on the Erumbiyur mountain, the radiant flame, having understood and clarified in my heart that He is the light enshrined in the shadow of the fruit, the Pasupathi, the one in Pasupatha guise, who destroyed Salandharan who rose up, the Vethiyan, the celestial one, who measured the earth, the four-faced one, the rare medicine that removes suffering.) “Karuvai en than manaththiruntha karuththai gnāna kadunjudarai padinthu kidanthu amarar ēththum” “Uruvai aṇḍaththu oru muthalai ōtha vēli ulaki niṟai thoḻil iruthi naḍuvāy ninṟa maṟuvai venṟa kuḻal maḍavāḻ pākam vaiththa mayāṉaththu māsilā maṇiyai vāsaththiruverumbiyūr malaimēl māṇikkaththai seḻuñcuḍarai cenraḍaiya peṟṟēn nāṉē.” (I have attained the ruby on the fragrant Thiru-Erumbiyur mountain, the radiant flame, having worshipped the form that is the primal source of the universe, the one who stands in the middle of the ocean-girt world, the blemishless jewel in the cremation ground, who has the maiden with fragrant locks, who conquered blemish, as a part.) “Pakaḻi poḻinthu aḍalarakkar puṟaṅkaḷ mūṉṟum pāḻpaḍuththa parañcuḍarai paṟinthu taṉṉai pukaḻum anparkku iṉpamarum amuthai tēṉai puṇṇiyaṉai puvaṉiyathu muḻuthum pōka umiḻum ampoṟkuṉṟaththai muttiṉ tūṇai umaiyavaḷ tam perumāṉai imaiyōr ēttum tikaḻ erumbiyūr malaimēl māṇikkaththai seḻuñcuḍarai cenraḍaiya peṟṟēn nāṉē.” (I have attained the ruby on the shining Erumbiyur mountain, the radiant flame, having worshipped the supreme light who destroyed the three cities of the mighty Rakshasas with arrows, the nectar and honey that brings joy to devotees who praise Him, the virtuous one, the golden mountain that emits the entire world, the pillar of pearls, the Lord of Uma, praised by the celestials.) “Pāriḍaththudan pāḍappaṉiṟu naṭṭam payilvāṉai ayilvāy sūlam ēnti nēriḍum pōr mikavalla nimalaṉ taṉṉai nirmalaṉai ammalar koṇḍu ayaṉum mālum”

“Pāriḍanthum mēl uyarnthum kāṇāvaṇṇam paranthāṉai nimirnthu muṉi kaṇamēttum sīr Erumbiyūr malaimēl māṇikkaththai seḻuñcuḍarai cenraḍaiya peṟṟēn nāṉē.” (I have attained the ruby on the glorious Erumbiyur mountain, the radiant flame, having worshipped Him who dances with the Bhoothaganas, who holds the sharp trident, the pure one, the stainless one, who is very skilled in battle, whom Brahma and Vishnu could not see by digging down and rising up, who spread out, and whom the hosts of sages praise.) “Kārmukilāy poḻivāṉai poḻintha muṉnīr karappāṉai kaḍiya naḍai viḍaiyoṉṟu ēṟi ūrpalaṉum tirivāṉai ūradāka oṟṟiyūr uḍaiyaṉāy muṟṟum āṇḍu pēr eḻuththu oṉṟu uḍaiyāṉai nīḻnilavum an thīyum nīrum maṟṟai neṟiyilaṅku miku kālum ākāsamum vāṉilavu tārakaiyum maṇṇum viṇṇum maṇṇuyirum eṉṉuyirum tāṉāṉ sempoṉ āṇi eṉṟum añcaṉa mā malaiyē eṉṟum ampaḷa thiraḷ eṉṟum aṟinthōr ēttum seḻñerumbiyūr malaimēl māṇikkaththai seḻuñcoḍarai cenraḍaiya peṟṟēn nāṉē.” (I have attained the ruby on the glorious Erumbiyur mountain, the radiant flame, having worshipped Him who pours down like a dark cloud, who hides the ancient waters, who rides a swift bull and wanders through many towns, who owns Ottiyur as His town, who rules completely, who has a great name, who is the moon, fire, water, the mighty wind, sky, stars in the sky, earth, heaven, all earthly beings, and my own life, whom the knowing ones praise as a pure golden pillar, a great collyrium mountain, and a coral cluster.) “Aṟantariyā ūththaivāy aṟivil sinthai ārampa kuṇḍarōḍu ayarththu nāḷum maṟanthum” “Aṟanthiruvaḍikaḷ ninaiyamāṭṭā mathiyiliyēn vāḻvellām vāḻā maṇmēl piṟantha nāḷ nāḷalla vāḻā vīsaṉ pēr pithaṟṟi sīraḍimai thiṟaththul anpu seṟinthu Erumbiyūr malaimēl māṇikkaththai seḻiñcuḍarai cenraḍaiya peṟṟēn nāṉē.” (I, a foolish one with a foul mouth and ignorant mind, who daily forgets and cannot remember the sacred feet of dharma, my life is not a life; the day I was born on earth is not a day. I have attained the ruby on the Erumbiyur mountain, the radiant flame, having uttered the name of the Lord and filled with love for the path of sacred servitude.) “Aṟivilaṅku maṇaththāṉai aṟivārkaṉṟi aṟiyāthārtham thiṟattoṉṟu aṟiyāthāṉai poṟiyilaṅku vāḻaṟavum puṉainthupūṇḍa poṉṉiyaṉai poṟuthiraivāy nañcamuṇḍa kuṟiyilaṅkumiḍaṟṟai maḍaṟṟēn koṉṟaic caḍaiyāṉai maḍaitōṟum kamalamenpūccedi Erumbiyūr malaimēl māṇikkaththai seḻuñcuḍarai cenraḍaiya peṟṟēn nāṉē.” (I have attained the ruby on the Erumbiyur mountain, the radiant flame, having worshipped Him who has a shining mind, who is known only by the knowing and unknown by the ignorant, the golden one adorned with shining snakes, who swallowed poison from the ocean, whose throat has a shining mark, who has matted locks with konrai flowers, and whose lotus-like flower plants are in every channel.) “Arunthavaththiṉ peruvaliyāl aṟivathaṉṟi aḍal arakkaṉ thaḍavaraiyai eḍuththāṉ thiṇṭōḷ muṟinthu neṟinthu aḻinthu pāthāḷam muṟṟu muṉkai narampiṉai eḍuththukki” “Kītham pāḍa irunthavaṉai ēḻulakum ākkinaṉai emmāṉai kaimāviṉ urivaip pōrththa thirunthu eḻumpiyūr malaimēl māṇikkaththai seḻuñcoḍarai cenraḍaiya peṟṟē nāṉē.” (I have attained the ruby on the sacred Erumbiyur mountain, the radiant flame, having worshipped Him who was there to sing the song, who created the seven worlds, our Lord, who is covered with the hide of an elephant, after the mighty demon who lifted the great mountain had his strong shoulders broken, crushed, and destroyed, reaching the netherworld, and took out the nerve of his forearm.)

We shall continue with our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 435. Thiru-Nindra Sarukkam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, having worshipped at the sacred site of Thiru-Erumbiyur, proceeds to the temple of Thayu-Mana Swamigal, also known as Thiru-Chirappalli Mathrubhuteswarar.

There, he worships the Lord and sings Thiru-Pathikams. The Lord, Thayu-Mana Swamy, who is centrally enshrined on the hill in Thiru-Chirappalli, is famously known as Thiru-Chi Malai-Kottai. It is said that there is no one who does not know the Uchi Vinayagar (Ganesha at the summit) of this temple, as he is very famous. The Thiru-Pathikam sung by Thiru-Gnana Sambandha Peruman, beginning with “Nandrudaiyanai Theeyathilanai,” is dedicated to this site. A Thiru-Pathikam by Appar Swamigal is also dedicated here.

Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, in the twelfth Thiru-Pathikam, the general Thiru-Pathikam, mentions this site as a Vaippu-Thalam (a place mentioned in hymns) with the lines “Thengoorum Thiruchitrambalamum Chirappalli Paangur.” Manikkavasaga Peruman sang “Chirappalli Meviya Sivane Potri” in the Thiru-Vasagam Potri Thiru-Agaval. This site has many names such as Thiru-Chiramalai, Thiru-Chirapuram, Thiru-Chiragiri, Muththalaimalai, and Brahmagiri. The word ‘Palli’ means temple. This name Thiru-Chirappalli came about because a demon named Thirisiran ruled here, worshipped the Lord, and received blessings. Scholars also say that the name Thirisirapuram came about because this mountain has three peaks, namely the Swami, Amman, and Uchi-Pillaiyar. Since it is named after Brahma, it is called Brahmagiri, and because it appears like a bull when viewed from a distance, it is called Rishabachalam.

Due to its connection with Mount Kailash, it is specially referred to as Thenkailayam (Southern Kailash). Researchers state that names like Silaippalli, Silappalli, and Chirappalli arose from the meaning of ‘Palli’ (temple) carved into stone. This site stands prominently in the center of Thiru-Chirappalli, visible from anywhere in the city.

The Lord enshrined on the hill is known by names such as Sevvanthinathar, Thirumalai Kozhundhar, and Thayu-Manavar. In Sanskrit, the Swami is called Mathrubhuteswarar. The Amman’s sacred name is Sugandha Kunthalambikai, and in Tamil, Mattuvar Kuzhal Ammai. This mountain also has the name Thirumalai.

Therefore, the Lord is also known by the sacred name Thirumalai Perumanadigal, and this city is known as Chittambar. It is understood that since Sarama Munivar worshipped with Sevvanthi flowers, the Lord is called Sevvanthinathar. Because He is the sprout of the mountain, He is called Thirumalai Kozhundeesar. And because He came as a mother to help a woman out of love, He is called Thayu-Manavar. The local Vinayagar is called Sevvanthi Vinayagar. The Manikka Vinayagar shrine at the base of the temple is very famous.

Now, regarding the sacred waters associated with this temple: Kaveri, Sivagangai, Somarohini (also known as Brahma Theertham), Nandrudaiyan Theertham, Theeyathillan Theertham, and others. The Kaveri, which flows north of the town, is the Kudakavari. The Thiru-Pugal hymns, such as “Neelalai Soodiya Thiru-Chiramalai Mel Urai Veera,” inform us that the Kaveri flowed near the mountain in ancient times. Next is Sivagangai, which is located near the Naganatha Swamy Temple to the northwest of the temple. It is said that Ambikai performed penance here to marry the Lord. Next is Somarohini, also called Brahma Theertham.

It is a beautiful temple tank with a central mandapam, located on the western side of the temple. It was built by Viswanatha Nayakkar, who formerly ruled Thiru-Chi. Next is Nandrudaiyan Theertham, which is a short distance east of the temple, near the present Thiru-Chi railway station. Next is Theeyathillan Theertham, located south of the temple. The sixth day of the festival takes place. One can see that Thiru-Gnana Sambandha Peruman, in the first verse of his Thevaram for this site, placed these sacred waters, praised as Nandrudaiyan and Theeyathillan, within the hymn.

This site is called Dakshina Kailasa. It is called Dakshina Kailasa. From the bottom to the Swami shrine, the paths are covered. The Swami temple above the Amman temple is built as a multi-storied structure. Every year, on the 23rd, 24th, and 25th days of the Panguni month, the rays of the evening sun shine directly on the Moolalingam. This is called Surya Pooja.

There are two cave temples carved into the rock, both on and below the hill. In the upper cave, there are many inscriptions in Grantha and Tamil. There are many literary works about this site. The mountain is situated in the middle of the city, arranged so that anyone looking can have a darshan. In Sangam literature, this mountain is praised as Nedum Perungundram. In Agananooru, it is mentioned as “Karangisai Vizhavin Urandai Gunathu Nedum Perungundram.” According to the Purana, Of the three, Murthi (Deity), Sthalam (Holy Place), and Theertham (Sacred Water), Thiruvarur is especially renowned.

The liberation attained by being born in Thiruvarur, and the blessings easily obtained by merely uttering the name of this holy place, are affirmed by the sacred words of Appar Swamigal, who stated that even uttering its name with devotion dispels evil deeds. Those who circumambulate the hill on the auspicious days of Chithirai month’s beginning and end, and on the Poora Nakshatram and Navami Thithi, will receive their desired boons. On the auspicious day of Somavaram (Monday) combined with Rohini Nakshatram, and for those who bathe in Brahma Theertham and worship in Panguni month, all benefits will be bestowed. Those who bathe in Sivagangai on Purattasi Pournami, offer Thumbai flowers to the Lord, and worship Him, will attain a good life.

Once upon a time, the Devas came to worship Lord Shiva, who resides on Thiru-Kailashagiri.

At that time, Adiseshan arrived, and everyone praised and celebrated him. Witnessing this, Vayu Devan became extremely jealous and began to speak ill of Adiseshan. Subsequently, a competition arose between the two, asking: “Who is greater? Who is more powerful?” Adiseshan tightly bound Mount Kailash with his body. Vayu Devan began to blow wind with all his might, causing the entire world to tremble.

At that moment, three fragments broke off from Mount Kailash; one fell in Thiru-Kalaathi, another in Thiru-Siramalai, and the third in Thiru-Konamalai in Lanka. As these were fragments of Thiru-Kailashamalai, these three became known as Then-Kailash (Southern Kailash). Among these, Thiru-Siramalai holds greater significance as it is centrally located between Thiru-Kalaathi and Thiru-Konamalai.

Now, the sacred history of the Lord here, known as Mathrubhootheswarar and Thayumanavar Swamy: In the Chola kingdom, in Kaveripoompattinam, a merchant named Rathinagupthan, born into a merchant family, lived a domestic life with his chaste wife. By the grace of the Lord, he was blessed with a daughter named Rathinavathi. Rathinagupthan arranged the marriage of his daughter, Rathinavathi, to Thanagupthan, a merchant residing in Thiru-Siramalai.

Thus, Rathinavathi lived in Thiru-Siramalai with her husband, Thanagupthan. From the very first day she arrived in Thiru-Siramalai from Thiru-Kaveri-Poompattinam, Rathinavathi unfailingly and lovingly worshipped Sevvandhinathan. In due course, by the grace of the Lord of Siramalai, Rathinavathi became pregnant and reached the time of delivery. Hearing this news, Rathinavathi’s mother, who was in Kaveripoompattinam, set out with the necessary medicines, oils, and other provisions for her daughter.

At that time, the Kaveri River was heavily flooded.

Therefore, the Kaveri flood prevented Rathinavathi’s mother from reaching her daughter for the delivery. The daughter kept thinking, “My mother will come today, she will come tomorrow, she will bring the things I need.” The time of delivery drew near, but her mother did not arrive. At this moment, Rathinavathi prayed to Thiru-Siramalai Sevvandhinathar, whom she had been worshipping.

The Lord Shiva, known as Sankaran, Sivan, Sadashivan, Eesan, Eesanan, Pungavan, Thirupuranthakan, Puraathanan, Puraanan, Gangai Nayagan, Karaimidatru Irai, Nuthal Kannaan, our Lord, Iraamaiyan, the Lord of Siramalai, Pooranan, Paran, Paraparan, Velliyamporuppan, Kaaranan, Madananthakan, Kaalanai Kadindhon, Vaaranan thanai urithavan, Maraiporul Vaguthon, Naaranan thanakku ariyavan, the Lord of Siramalai, Lord Shiva, assumed the guise of Rathinavathi’s mother and arrived at Rathinavathi’s house, where she was suffering from labor pains. The daughter, too, rejoiced, believing the newcomer to be her mother. The mother and student, Lord Shiva, performed the necessary treatments. Rathinavathi had a smooth delivery, and a beautiful baby boy was born. The one who came as the mother stayed for a few days, protecting both the child and the mother. While this was happening, the flood in the Kaveri receded, and Rathinavathi’s real mother crossed the river and arrived at Rathinavathi’s house.

Rathinavathi was astonished when she saw her. She wondered how there could be two mothers. Immediately, Thayumanavar Swamy, Lord Shiva, who had come as the mother, disappeared and appeared in the sky on His Rishabha Vahanam (bull mount).

From that day onwards, the sacred name Thayumanavar became permanently associated with Siramalai Sevvandhinathar. Rathinavathi, too, having worshipped the Lord, shines even today as one of His devotees. This history is celebrated grandly on the fifth day of the temple’s Brahmotsavam.

Now, the history of the Lord facing west here: A sage named Saramamunivar established a Nandavanam (flower garden) for the Lord of Siramalai, cultivating Sevvandhi flowers brought from Naga Lokam, and daily worshipped the Lord with these flowers. During the reign of Paranthaka Chozhan in Uraiyur, also known as Kozhiyur, a flower merchant entered the sage’s Nandavanam, stole Sevvandhi flowers, and presented them to the king’s queen.

One day, the sage observed this secretly and reported it to the king. The king did not reprimand the merchant.

Therefore, the sage complained to the Lord.

The Lord of Siramalai turned His face from east to west. He caused a rain of mud to fall in Uraiyur with many clouds. The king and his pregnant wife had gone out. Uraiyur was destroyed by the mud rain. The mud rain continued to follow the king. Finally, the king died, falling into the Kaveri.

The queen, Bhuvanamadevi, who had fallen and escaped, was rescued by a Brahmin and gave birth to a baby boy. This child later became known as Karikal Chozhan.

Now, the history of Thanthonreesar: Jananatha Chozhan, born in the lineage of Manu, had a son named Suravathitha Chozhan. He ruled from Uraiyur, which was named Kozhiyur because a hen had defeated an elephant there.

One day, the Chozhan went hunting near Saramamunivar’s Nandavanam.

At that time, seven Naga maidens, daughters of Adiseshan, were going to worship Siramalainathar with Sevvandhi flowers. The king saw them and wished to marry them. They did not consent. The king went to Naga Lokam, obtained Adiseshan’s consent, married Kanthimathi among the maidens, received a Shiva Lingam and a sword from Adiseshan, and returned to his city. He consecrated the Lingam he had brought and performed worship. Kanthimathi, the Chozhan’s wife, out of intense devotion, obtained her husband’s permission and daily walked to Thiru-Siramalainathar to worship Him.

In due course, Kanthimathi became pregnant, and even during her pregnancy, she unfailingly visited the Lord.

One day, due to the sun’s heat, she became too weak to walk and fell on the way. She grieved, thinking that she would not be able to have darshan today. Immediately, Siramalainathar appeared as a Swayambhu Lingam at that spot and gave darshan to Kanthimathi. Since the Lord appeared as a Swayambhu, He was named Thanthonreeswarar. Kanthimathi praised the Lord in many ways and returned to her city. Her husband, Suravathithan, hearing of this miracle, built a separate temple for Thanthonreeswarar and arranged for worship to be performed.

This temple is on the road leading to Uraiyur.

Now, the history of the marriage of Mattuvar Kuzhali Ammai: Goddess Uma, desiring to worship Lord Shiva and marry Him, appeared in this holy place in the form of a small girl from a lotus flower and was raised by Sage Kathiyayana. As the Goddess’s hair naturally exuded a good fragrance, she was called Sugandha Kunthalambikai and Mattuvar Kuzhali. The Goddess bathed in the Theertham called Sivagangai and worshipped the Swayambhu Lingam that appeared nearby, performing penance. This place is known as Naganatha Swamy Temple. The Lord, intending to fulfill her original desire, appeared and gave darshan to the Goddess and married her. This marriage festival takes place on the sixth day of the Chithirai festival.

Now, the history of Thayumanavar Adigal: In the Chola kingdom, in Thirumarai Kadu, also known as Vedharanyam, about three hundred years ago, a Saiva Vellalar named Kediliyappillai lived. He served the government in Thiruchirappalli. Vijayaraghunatha Chokkalinga Nayakkar, having heard of Kediliyappillai’s good qualities, summoned him to Trichy and appointed him to the position of political accountant. While Kediliyappillai was working in Thiruchirappuram, he prayed to the Lord of this place for offspring. He already had a son named Sivachidambaram, but he had given that son in adoption to his elder brother.

Therefore, he prayed to the Lord for a son. He prayed to Thayumanavar Peruman. By the grace of the Lord, a beautiful baby boy was born. He named the child Thayumanavar, after the Lord. Thayumanavar grew up well. His mind was intensely focused on finding a Gnana Guru, receiving good instruction, and freeing himself from the cycle of birth.

He daily worshipped Sri Thayumanavar Peruman with love and devotion.

Then, one day, Mounaguru Swamigal, who belonged to the lineage of Thirumoola Nayanar, was on a pilgrimage and was in a state of samadhi in the Dakshinamurthy shrine in this temple. When Thayumanavar came for darshan as usual, like iron drawn by a magnet, he fell at the feet of Mounaguru, who was in samadhi, and pleaded. Mounaguru, seeing Thayumanavar’s ripened state, imparted spiritual instruction to him. Thayumanavar Swamigal shone as a recipient of Shiva’s experience, singing the song “Anging enaathapadi engum prakasamai aanandhapoorrthiyaagi arulodu nirainthathu ethu” (That which is everywhere, shining, full of bliss, filled with grace, without being here or there). He also gave to the world many sacred verses containing Siddhanta concepts, clarifying that Vedanta’s clarity is Siddhanta.

Therefore, he was known by the names Thayumanavar Adigal and Thayumanavar Swamigal.

Thus, Thayumanavar Swamigal lived a detached life, visited many holy places for darshan, and finally in Lakshmipuram, belonging to Ramanathapuram, he attained the sacred feet of the Lord in Nirvikalpa Samadhi. There is also a temple for Adigal there. His sacred verses are known as Thayumanavar Padalgal. In this temple, there are two cave temples carved out of the hill. One is on the hill and the other at the base. From the markings in the cave temple on the hill, it appears to have been built by the Pallava king Gunaparan, also known as Mahendravarman, who lived in the sixth century.

We have seen in the beginning of the history of Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal that Mahendravarman converted from Jainism to Saivism. This temple has many mandapams from the base to the top. There are the Aayirakkal Mandapam (thousand-pillared hall), Vahana Mandapam, Sahasralinga Mandapam, Noorrukkal Mandapam (hundred-pillared hall), Chithira Mandapam, Pathinaaru Kal Mandapam (sixteen-pillared hall), and Mani Mandapam. The great ones who worshipped the Lord of this holy place and received blessings include Brahma, Agasthiyar, Indra, Uma Devi, Jadayu, the Saptharishis, Thiruchiran, Rama, Arjuna, Hanuman, Vibhishana, the radiant Ayyanaar, Naga Kannigais, Saramamunivar, Vandu Chozhan, Rathinavathi, Mounaguru, and Thayumanavar Swamigal. The Hanuman Mudra worshipped by Hanuman is carved on the hill. It is also said that Agasthiyar, after worshipping here, pressed another equally tall mountain into the netherworld.

The Uchipillaiyar Temple on the mountain peak is very famous. The Mutt of Mouna Swamigal is located in this holy place. The affairs of the Mouna Mutt are still managed by the Dharmapuram Adheenam of the Thiru-Kailaya Paramparai. Daily rituals are performed excellently in this temple. Annually, in the months of Chithirai and Panguni respectively, the Chariot Festival and the Float Festival take place. In Chithirai and Vaikasi, Vasanthotsavams are held on the hill.

In the month of Aadi, a separate Aadi Pooram festival is held for the Goddess. The Sevvandhi Puranam, also known as Thiruchiramalai Puranam, was composed by Saiva Ellappa Navalar. It consists of eleven sections and five hundred and fifty verses. Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, who visited this holy place, composed one Thiru-Pathigam (decad of verses). It is the eighty-fifth Thiru-Pathigam, Thiru-Kurunthagai Thiru-Pathigam, in the fifth Thirumurai.

“Mattuvār kuzhalāḷoḍu mālviḍaiyiṭṭa māvukandhu ēṟum iṟaivaṉār kaṭṭu nīttavarkku iṉṉarulē ceyyum ciṭṭar pōlum cirāppaḷḷi celvarē.” (The Lord, who rides the great bull with the fragrant-haired Goddess, seems to be a noble one who bestows sweet grace upon those who have shed their bonds, the wealthy one of Sirappalli.) “Ariyaṉ talai veṭṭivaṭṭāṭiṉār ariyayaṉ tozhuthēttum arumporuḷ periyavaṉ cirāppaḷḷiyai pēṇuvār ariyaṉ tozha aṅkiruppārkaḷē.” (He who cut off the head of Ariyan and played with it, the great essence worshipped by Ariyan and Ayan, those who cherish Sirappalli will be there to worship Ariyan.) “Ariccirāppakal aivarāl āṭṭuṇṭu curiccirāthu neñcē oṉṟu collakkīzh tiruccirāppaḷḷi eṉṟalum tīviṉai nariccirāthu.” (O heart, do not be troubled by the five senses day and night; when one utters ‘Thiruchirappalli’ even once, evil deeds will not approach.) “Naṭakkum naṭakkumē tāyumāy eṉakku ētalai kaṇṇumāy pēyaṉēṉaiyum āṇṭa peruntakai tēyanātaṉ cirāppaḷḷi mēviya nāyaṉār eṉa nam viṉai nācamē.” (He who became my mother, my eye, and ruled over even me, a madman, the great Lord, the Lord of Sirappalli, our Lord, our karma is destroyed.) Only four of these sacred verses have been found; the other six verses are not available to us.

We shall proceed with our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 436, Thiru-Nindracharukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, having worshipped Thiru-Chirappalli, reached the holy place called Thiru-Karkudi, also known as Uyyakkondan Malai, on the western border of Thiru-Chirappalli. Uyyakkondan Malai is a temple situated on a small hill. Since the Lord resides on the hill, this place is called Karkudi. To uplift all beings, the Lord here is enshrined by the names Ujjivanathar and Uyyakkondan.

This holy place has been sung by the three great saints: Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, and Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. It is the place where Markandeya was blessed. The temple is located on the hill. There are steps from the bottom to the top. At the foot of the hill, there is a Theertham. After worshipping Ganesha at the base and ascending the steps, one reaches the outer circumambulatory path around the temple.

After circumambulating it and ascending further, one can reach the Natarajar Mandapam. The temple has three entrances: two facing south and one facing east. The shrines of the Lord and Goddess face west. There are two shrines for the Goddess; one faces east, and the main Goddess shrine faces west. One can circumambulate here and reach the Lord’s shrine for worship.

The Lord is a Swayambhu Murthi. This temple contains the Pathigam sung by Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, praising the various glories of Karkudi Mamalaiyar; the Pathigam sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, immersed in the joy of beholding the Lord of Karkudi; and the Pathigam sung by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, seeking refuge. The Lord’s sacred names are Ujjivanathar, Uyyakkondar, Ujjinathar, Muttheesar, and Karpaganathar. The Goddess’s names are Anjanakshi. The old Goddess shrine faces west. The Theerthams are Ponnoli Odai, Kudamurutti, Gnanavavi, Enkonakkinaru (octagonal well), and Narkonakkinaru (quadrangular well) – five Theerthams in total.

The Sthala Vriksham is the Bilva tree. Upamanyu Muni, Markandeya, Karan, the king of Eelam, and Arunagirinathar have worshipped here. When Markandeya worshipped the Lord in various holy places, upon reaching and worshipping this holy place of Thiru-Karkudi, he completed his sixteenth year. Karan, one of Ravana’s brothers, worshipped the Lord of this place and received His grace. Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, who visited this holy place, composed a Thiru-Pathigam in praise of the Lord of this place. It is the sixth Thiru-Pathigam, Thiru-Thandagam Thiru-Pathigam.

“Mooththavaṉai vāṉavarkku mūvā mēṉi mutalvaṉai tiruvaraiyiṉ mūkka pāmpu oṉṟu ārththavaṉai akkaravam āramāka aṇindhavaṉai paṇindhu aṭiyār aṭaindha” (The ancient one, the ageless primal one for the celestials, who bound a snake around his sacred waist, who wore a snake as a garland, whom devotees reached by worshipping him with love). “Aṉpōṭu ēththavaṉai iru varaiyil tēṉai ēṉōrkku iṉṉamudham azhiththavaṉai iṭaraiyellām kāththavaṉai karkuṭiyil viḷimiyāṉai karpakaththai kaṇṇāra kaṇṭēṉ nāṉē.” (With love, I saw with my own eyes the Karpakam, the Lord of Karkudi, who is praised, who gave sweet nectar to those who were not, who protected from all troubles.) “Ceyyāṉai veḷiyāṉai kariyāṉ taṉṉai ticaimukaṉai ticaiyaṭṭum ceṟindāṉ taṉṉai aiyāṉai noyiyāṉai cīriyāṉai aṇiyāṉai cēyāṉai āṉañcāṭum meyyāṉai poyyāthumillāṉ taṉṉai viṭaiyāṉaic caṭaiyāṉai veṟiththa māṉ koḷ kaiyāṉai karkuṭiyil viḷimiyāṉai karpakaththai kaṇṇāra kaṇṭēṉ nāṉē.” (I saw with my own eyes the Karpakam, the Lord of Karkudi, who is red, who is white, who is black, who is the four-faced one, who pervades all eight directions, who is the master, who is subtle, who is great, who is near, who is far, who is the true one who dances with the five elements, who is without falsehood, who rides the bull, who has matted locks, who holds the frightened deer in his hand.) “Maṇ athaṉil aindhai mā nīril nāṉkai vayaṅkeṟiyil mūṉṟai māruthatthiṉ iraṇṭai viṇ athaṉil oṉṟai virikathirai taṇmathiyai tārakaihaḷ tammiṉmikka eṇ athaṉil ezhuththai ēḻicaiyai kāmaṉ ezhil azhiya eriyumizhndha imaiyā neṟṟik kaṇ avaṉai karkuṭiyil viḷimiyāṉai karpakaththai kaṇṇāra kaṇṭēṉ nāṉē.” (I saw with my own eyes the Karpakam, the Lord of Karkudi, who is the five in earth, the four in great water, the three in shining fire, the two in wind, the one in sky, the spreading rays, the cool moon, the stars, the letter in numbers, the seven notes of music, who emitted fire from his unblinking third eye to destroy Kama’s beauty.) “Naṟṟavaṉai puṟṟaṟavaṉāṉai nāṉāthu nakuthalai ūṉ nayandāṉ taṉṉai muṟṟavaṉai mūvātha mēṉiyāṉai muṉṉīriṉ nañcam ugandhu uṇṭāṉ taṉṉai paṟṟavaṉai paṟṟārtham pathikaḷ ceṟṟa paṭaiyāṉai aṭaivārtham pāvam pōkka kaṟṟavaṉai karkuṭiyil viḷimiyāṉai karpakaththai kaṇṇāra kaṇṭēṉ nāṉē.” (I saw with my own eyes the Karpakam, the Lord of Karkudi, who is the good ascetic, who is the ascetic of the anthill, who desired the flesh of the smiling skull without shame, who is complete, who has an ageless body, who gladly consumed the poison from the primordial ocean, who is the one who holds, who has the army that destroyed the cities of his enemies, who is learned in removing the sins of those who approach him.) “Caṅkaithanai tavirththāṇṭa talaivaṉ taṉṉai caṅkaraṉai taḷaluṟu tāḻ mazhu vāḻ tāṅgum aṅkaiyaṉai aṅkamaṇi ākatthāṉai ākatthōr pākatthai amaravaiththa maṅkaiyaṉai mathiyoṭu mācuṉamum tammiṉ maruva viricaṭai muṭimēl vaiththa vāṇīr kaṅkaiyaṉai karkuṭiyil viḷimiyāṉai karpakaththai kaṇṇāra kaṇṭēṉ nāṉē.” (I saw with my own eyes the Karpakam, the Lord of Karkudi, who is the leader who ruled by dispelling doubts, who is Shankara, who holds the sharp axe in his beautiful hand, who has a gem on his body, who placed a part of the maiden in his body, who placed the bright water of the Ganga on his matted locks, along with the moon and the snake, to mingle with each other.) “Peṇṇavaṉai āṇavaṉai pēṭāṉāṉai piṟappiliyai iṟappiliyai pērāvāṇi viṇṇavaṉai viṇṇavarkkum mēlāṉāṉai.” (He who is woman, who is man, who is neither, who is without birth, who is without death, who is the great sky, who is superior even to the celestials.) “Vēthiyaṉai vēthatthiṉ kīthampāṭum paṇṇavaṉai paṇṇil vaṟu payaṉ āṉāṉai pāravaṉai pāril vāḻ uyirkaḷkkellām kaṇṇavaṉai karkuṭiyil viḷumiyāṉai karpakaththai kaṇṇāra kaṇṭēṉ nāṉē.” (I saw with my own eyes the Karpakam, the Lord of Karkudi, who is the Vedic scholar, who sings the hymns of the Vedas, who is the fruit of the melody, who is the earth, who is the eye for all living beings on earth.) “Paṇṭāṉai paranthāṉai kuvinthāṉ taṉṉai pārāṉai viṇṇā ivvulakamellām uṇṭāṉai umizhndāṉai uṭaiyāṉ taṉṉai oruvarunthan perumaithanai aṟiyavoṉṉā viṇṭāṉai viṇṭārtham puṟaṅkaḷ mūṉṟum vevvaḻalil venthu poṭiyāki vīḻa kaṇṭāṉai karkuṭiyil viḷumiyāṉai karpakaththaik kaṇṇāra kaṇṭēṉ nāṉē.” (I saw with my own eyes the Karpakam, the Lord of Karkudi, who is ancient, who is expansive, who is gathered, who is the earth, who swallowed and spat out all these worlds, who is the owner, whose greatness no one can know, who saw the three cities of his enemies burn to ashes in fierce fire.) “Vāṉavaṉai vāṉavarkku mēlāṉāṉai vaṇaṅgum aṭiyār maṉaththuḷ maruvippukka tēṉavaṉaith tēvar toḻu kaḷalāṉ taṉṉai ceykuṇaṅkaḷ palavāki niṉṟa eṉṟi kōṉavaṉai kollai viṭaiyēṟṟiṉāṉai kuzhal muzhavum iyampa kūtthāṭavalla kāṇavaṉai karkuṭiyil viḷumiyāṉai karpakaththaik kaṇṇāra kaṇṭēṉ nāṉē.” (I saw with my own eyes the Karpakam, the Lord of Karkudi, who is the celestial, who is superior to the celestials, who is the honey that entered the hearts of worshipping devotees, whose feet are worshipped by the Devas, who is the king who stood as many good qualities, who rode the wild bull, who can dance to the sound of the flute and drum.) “Kolaiyāṉai.” “Uripōrththa koḷkaiyāṉai kōḷariyai kūrampā varaimēl kōththa cilaiyāṉai cemmaitharu poruḷāṉ taṉṉai tiripuraththōr mūvarkku cemmai ceytha talaiyāṉai thatthuvaṅkaḷ āṉāṉ taṉṉai taiyalōr paṅkiṉaṉai taṉ kai ēnthu kalaiyāṉai karkuṭiyil viḷumiyāṉai karpakaththai kaṇṇāra kaṇṭēṉ nāṉē.” (I saw with my own eyes the Karpakam, the Lord of Karkudi, who has the nature of wearing the skin of a murderous elephant, who is the bow strung with a sharp arrow on the mountain, who is the substance that gives righteousness, who is the head who brought righteousness to the three in Thirupuram, who became the Tattvas, who has a maiden as a part of himself, who holds the crescent moon in his hand.) “Pozhilāṉai pozhilārum puṉkūṟāṉai puṟampayaṉai aṟampurindha pukalūrāṉai ezhilāṉai iṭaimeruthiṉ iṭam koṇṭāṉai īṅkōy nīṅkāthu uṟaiyum iṟaivaṉ taṉṉai azhalāṭu mēṉiyaṉai aṉṟu ceṉṟa kuṉṟaṭuththa aṟakkaṉ tōl neṟiya ūṉṟum kaḷalāṉai karkuṭiyil viḷumiyāṉai karpakaththai kaṇṇāra kaṇṭēṉ nāṉē.” (I saw with my own eyes the Karpakam, the Lord of Karkudi, who is the grove, who is the one with the grove of Pungoor, who is Purambayan, who is the Lord of Pukalur who performed righteousness, who is beautiful, who took his place in the middle of the Marudha tree, who is the Lord who resides in Eengoy without leaving, who has a body that dances with fire, whose foot pressed down the skin of the demon who approached the mountain that day.)

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, having worshipped Thiru-Karkudi, reached the holy place called Thiru-Parayathurai. This is one of the holy places on the southern bank of the Kaveri. On the banks of rivers, we can see many holy places that shine with the name ‘Thurai’ (ford/bank). Since the Lord is enshrined amidst the Parai tree groves on the bank of the Kaveri, it is called Parayathurai. The Parai tree is the Sthala Vriksham of this place. This tree is located in the western prakaram of the temple.

In Sanskrit, it is called Tharuga Vriksham. It is said that the shade of this tree is excellent for performing penance. It was formerly known as Tharugavanam, and it is associated with the history of the Lord going as Bhikshatana to Tharugavanam, removing the ego of the sages, and giving them darshan. It is located on the Thiruchirappalli-Karur road. The shrine faces east. Adjacent to the seven-tiered gopuram, which houses the Panchamurthis, there is a Vasantha Mandapam.

There is a small sacred pond. Adjacent to the mandapam, a seven-tiered gopuram adorns the temple. Passing through the gopuram entrance, one enters the Nandi Mandapam. In the first prakaram, there are the sixty-three Nayanmars, and subsidiary deities such as Vinayagar, Murugan, Mahalakshmi, and Durga, as well as the Navagrahas. In the Garbhagriha Koshtams, Dakshinamurthy and Ardhanareeswarar are present. The Lord’s shrine faces east, and the Goddess’s shrine faces south.

The Goddess’s shrine is in the Mahamandapam. The Panchamurthis are enshrined in the Snapana Mandapam. The Lord’s name here is Tharugavaneswarar, and in Tamil, Parayathurainathar. The Goddess’s name is Hemavarnambikai, and in Tamil, Pasum Pon Mayilammai. The Theertham is the Kaveri River. On the first day of Aippasi, the Lord, mounted on His Rishabha Vahanam, along with the Goddess, bestows Theertham in the Kaveri.

In inscriptions, this place is referred to as Utthamaseevi Chathurvedi Mangalathu Thiruparayathurai, and the Lord’s name as Parayathurai Mahadevar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sang one Thiru-Pathigam and Appar Swamigal rendered one Thiru-Pathigam for this Thalam, which is also referred to as Paraythurai Parameswaran. Manikkavasaga Peruman praised the Peruman of this Thalam in Thiruvasagam, Thiru-Agaval, saying, “Paraythurai Meviya Parane Potri.” In the fourth Thiru-Padal of Thiruvasagam Sethilapathu, he praised the Peruman of this Thalam as “Then Paraythuraiyai Sivaloka.” Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal, who visited this Thalam, rendered a Thiru-Pathigam, which is the thirtieth Thiru-Pathigam in the fifth Thirumurai, structured as a Thiru-Kurunthogai Thiru-Pathigam.

Karappar Kalam Adainthavar Tham Vinai Surukkumaru Vallar Gangai Senjadai Parappu Neervaru Kaveri Thenkarai Thirupparaythurai Meviya Selvare Mudinar Kali Yanaiyin Iruri Padinar Marai Nankinodu Aram. Sedanar Thenparaythurai Selvarai Thedik Kondu Adiyen Sendru Kanbene. Pattanetriyir Palmathikkitrinar Nattamaduvar Nallirul Emamum Sittanar Then Paraythurai Selvanar Ittamayirupparai Arivare. Munbelan Sila Molaimai Pesuvar Enbellam Pala Poondangulitharvar Thenparaythurai Meviya Selvanar Anbaray Irupparai Arivare. Podu Thathodu Kondu Punaithuvudan Thathavizh Sadai Sankaran Pathathul Vathai Theerkka Venrethip Paraythurai Sothiyanai Thozhuthu Ezhunthu Uyamine.

Nalla Nanmarai Othiya Nambanai Pallil Venthalaiyil Palikolvanai Thillaiyan Thenparaythurai Selvanai Vallaiyay Vanangi Thozhuvaymaiye. Neruppinar Kuvithalokku Nezh Sadai Paruppatham Matha Yanai Urithavan Thirupparaythuraiyar Thirumarbin Nool Porupparavi Izhu. Thulippunal Pondrathe. Ettavitta Idumanekkar Mel Patta Nunthuli Payum Paraythurai Sittan Sevadi Sendradaiyitrel Vittu Nam Vinai Ullana Vidume. Nerupparay Nimirthalokku Nezhsadai Marupparay Valaithalokkum Vanmathi Thirupparaythurai Meviya Selvanar Virupparayirupparai Arivare. Thondu Padiyum Thoomalar Thooviyum Indai Katti Inaiyadi Ethiyum Pandarangar Paraythurai Pangaraik Kandukondadiyen Uynthu Povane.

Arakkan Atral Azhitha Azhaganai Parakku Neer Ponni Mannu Paraythurai Irukkai Meviya Isanai Ethu Meen Porukka Num Vinai Poyarunganinai.

Thodarnthu Sinthippom. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 437. Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal, having had Darshan at Thirupparaythurai, continued his Thalam pilgrimage. Sekkizhar Peruman sings as follows: “Having worshipped other Thiru-Pathis and performed sacred services, he praised with Thiru-Pathigams. With abundant grace, he crossed the Kaveri, and reaching the northern bank, he arrived at Thiruppaingili, where the archers reside.” Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman describes the pilgrimage undertaken by Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Having worshipped Thirupparaythurai and other Thiru-Pathis nearby, he then crossed the Kaveri to the northern bank and reached the Thalam called Thiruppaingili, as sung by Sekkizhar Peruman.

Thirupparaythurai to Ari. He visited other Thiru-Pathis located nearby. These other Thiru-Pathis include Thiru-Alanthurai, Thiruchendurai, and similar places on the southern bank of the Kaveri.

However, Sivakavimani Ayyavargal notes that the Thiru-Pathigams sung by Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar for these places are not available. In the Dharumaiyatheena Periya Purana Vilakkam, it is noted that the nearby Thiru-Pathis mentioned in this verse are Thiru-Kadambanthurai and Thiru-Vatpokki. This is because one Thiru-Pathigam each, sung by Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, has been found for Thiru-Kadambanthurai and Thiru-Vatpokki.

Therefore, it is believed that he must have visited the Thalam of Kadambanthurai and Thiru-Vatpokki, which are south of the Kaveri from Thirupparaythurai, and then crossed the Kaveri to the northern bank to reach Thiruppaingili. This note is found in the Dharumaiyatheena Periya Purana Vilakkam.

Accordingly, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman arrives at the sacred Thalam called Thiru-Kadambanthurai.

Here, we have received a Thiru-Pathigam sung by Thirunavukkarasu Peruman in praise of the Lord. This Thalam, known as Thiru-Kadambanthurai, is currently called Kadambar Kovil and Kulithalai.

Here, the sacred name of the Lord is Kadambavaneswarar, Kadambavanathar. The sacred name of the Goddess is Balakujambal. The Theertham is the Kaveri. Those who worshipped the Lord here include Brahma, Vishnu, the Saptha Kanniyars, and others. The unique feature of this Thalam is that the temple is oriented towards the north, and the Lord also faces north. This is the only Thalam among the Thevara-sung Sthalams that faces north, which is a unique feature of this Thalam.

This is a unique feature of this Thalam. There are 274 Thevara-sung Sthalams, of which 127 are on the southern bank of the Kaveri. Among these, Thiru-Kadambanthurai is the second Thalam. Currently, everyone knows Kulithalai. This temple is located in the city of Kulithalai. Thiru-Kadambanthurai is one of the Thalam names ending with ‘thurai’.

It is currently known as Kadambar Kovil. Near Thiru-Kadambanthurai, on the southern bank of the Kaveri, are temples such as Rajendram, Pettaivaythalai, Vatpokki, Karuppathur, and on the northern bank are Thiru-Ingoy Malai, Musiri, Vellur, and other sacred places. On Thai Poosam day, the deities of these temples come to the Kaveri River and grant Darshan. It is customary to visit Kadambar Kovil in the morning, Vatpokki Malai in the afternoon, and Thiru-Ingoy Malai in the evening to receive great merit. It is customary to visit Thiru-Ingoy Malai in the evening and have Darshan of the deities there, which is considered highly meritorious. This is explained by the proverb: “Morning Kadambar, Afternoon Sokkar, Evening Thiru-Vengainathar.” To the east of Kadambar Kovil, outside the town of Kulithalai, is the Sri Meenakshi Sundareswarar Temple, which is a sub-temple of Kadambar Kovil.

This is the Thalam where Lord Shiva appeared in his wedding attire to the Brahmin named Vedasarma. Other temples include the Perallamman Temple, Mariamman Temple, Neelamega Perumal Temple, and others. This sacred Thalam has other sacred names besides Thiru-Kadambanthurai, such as Kadambai, Kadambavanam, Dakshina Kasi, Kulithanthalai, Brahmapuram, Chathurvedapuri, Kanthapuram, Sapthapuri, Vadmadurai, Gnanodayapuri, and others. These names exist. It is called Kadambanthurai, Kadambai, Kadambavanam because it had Kadambu trees. It is called Dakshina Kasi because it is located on the southern bank of the Kaveri, facing north, like Varanasi in the north.

It is called Kulithanthalai because it has cool groves. It is called Brahmapuram because Brahma worshipped here, built temples, and conducted chariot festivals. It is called Chathurvedapuri because Vishnu recovered the Vedas from Somakasura here. It is called Kanthapuram because Muruga worshipped here to remove his curse and received blessings. It is called Gnanodayapuri because Muruga attained enlightenment here. It is called Sapthapuri because the Saptha Kanniyars worshipped the Lord here and were freed from the Brahmahathi Dosha that afflicted them.

It is called Vadmadurai because the Brahmin Vedasarma performed penance here and witnessed the wedding scene that took place in Madurai. And so, this Thalam is known by these sacred names. The Sri Meenakshi Sundareswarar Temple in this town is the place where Lord Shiva appeared in his wedding attire to the Brahmin named Vedasarma. The name Kulithanthalai has evolved into Kulithalai and is now commonly used.

Here, as a symbol of the Saptha Kanniyars’ worship of the Lord, their idols are placed behind the Moolavar in the temple. The temple is situated amidst lush green groves, facing north. Among the north-facing temples, Varanasi in the north and Kadambar Kovil in the south are particularly significant. This is why this Thalam is called Dakshina Kasi. The Lord, Muruga, and the Goddess are all seated together, making the temple appear like a Somaskanda Murthy. The Kaveri River flows to the north.

Inside the temple, there are two circumambulatory paths, and outside, there is a street for the chariot procession. In front of the temple, there is a mandapam and an entrance. Inside, in the second circumambulatory path, to the east, there are a vehicle mandapam, a kitchen, a well, and a shrine for Kalabhairavar. In the southeast corner, there is the Brahma Theertham. In the northwest corner, there is the Navaratri Mandapam. Next to it, the Amman temple faces east.

Opposite, there are flagstaffs for the Lord and Amman, and a shrine for Paramnathar.

Following this, the inner gopuram entrance has three eyes. Passing through this, inside the first circumambulatory path, there are shrines for Natarajar, Navagrahas, and Chandikeswarar. To the south, there are shrines for Jeshtadevi, Nallvar, Arupathu Moovar, and Sekkizhar Peruman. To the west, there are shrines for Viswanathar, Vinayagar, Subramaniyar, Somaskandar, and Gajalakshmi. Agastya prayed, “Please initiate me into the Sri Panchakshara Maha Mantra.” The Peruman, adorned with all ornaments, appeared as Sundarar with Aralakesi Ambigai, placed His sacred hands on Agastya’s head, and initiated him into the Panchakshara Mantra. Agastya attained Jeevan Mukti. Agastya prayed to the Lord, “Since you have appeared to me at noon, you should be known by the sacred name Madhyana Sundarar. From today onwards, those who have darshan during the day should attain liberation.” The Lord granted his wish. This Sthalam is where the Peruman blessed a king named Veerasenan.

The Theertham created by Bharadwaja Muni through penance and the Theertham created by Vishnu in the form of a boar in the Agni direction are present here. To the north of this mountain is the Kanya Theertham created by Durga Devi.

There, she was freed from the sin of slaying Mahisha. Bathing in the Mahanadi there grants all siddhis. Since Durga Devi took Mahisha’s life with the sword granted by Shiva, it is said that the name Vaat- Naatpokki came into being. A herdsman from Kanchi, seeking progeny for his sister, came to this Sthalam and, upon his prayer being fulfilled, offered his head as a sacrifice. Due to his detachment, he is known as Vairaperumal. His shrine and a neem tree are located on the way to the mountain.

After the Deeparadhanai for Rathnagireeswarar, Deeparadhanai is performed for him, the guardian deity of the mountain. A herdsman from Kulithalai used to bring a pot of fresh milk daily for Abhishekam.

One day, a crow overturned the pot of milk, and the herdsman, grieved, decided to end his life. At that moment, the Lord appeared and said, “My devotee, do not grieve. This mountain is my form. The milk spilled on it is like an Abhishekam to me.” He then incinerated the crow.

Since then, crows do not fly here. The Sthala Purana states that the Lord appeared to Sundaramurthy Swamigal here as a Jyotirlingam and the entire mountain as rubies, and bestowed gold on a rock. That rock is called Pon Idum Paarai (the rock that gives gold). This event is part of the Chithirai Brahmotsavam on the fifth day. Since Durga’s curse was removed, two rock fissures, a sword-like rock nearby, and the Sapta Kannikas can be seen on the mountain. The legend says that when the seven maidens were struggling without shelter during heavy rain, the Lord created a cave-like structure between the rocks here and gave them refuge.

The people of Poompuhar, having left their city, settled here and, amazed, offered their twelfth share to the Lord.

Therefore, the Lord here is called Panirendam Chettiyar (the twelfth merchant). On Shivaratri or the days before or after, sunlight passes through a window directly facing the Lord and falls upon the Lord. In front of the Shiva Lingam, there is a water tank called Poyvasik Kopparai.

Here, ten pots of water are brought daily from the nearby Kaveri for the Lord’s noon Abhishekam. Even today, the descendants of the Panirendam Chettiyar family undertake this responsibility and conduct it through the temple priests.
