On the way to Srisailam from Vijayawada, there is the Tripurantakeswarar temple in Kumaragiri. Previously, devotees who walked to Srisailam would first have darshan here before proceeding.

“This is the place where Lord Muruga vanquished Tharakasura, hence it is called Kumaragiri. The greatness of this sthalam is discussed in the Srisaila Kandam. Siddavatam, described as the southern gateway of the sthalam, is very vast. It is a place where Agastya, Athri, Bhrigu, Vasishta, and other sages and Siddhas lived. The Skanda Purana, in the Sri Parvata Kandam, extensively describes the many forests, peaks, rivers, thirthams, and Shiva Linga forms present here. It is believed that by residing here, bathing in the Pinakini River, and having darshan of Siddheswarar, one can attain Jeevan Mukti.

“Here, one can find many Linga forms capable of granting Siddhi, such as Siddheswarar, Balasiddheswarar, Gandasiddheswarar, Kanyasiddheswarar, Ishtasiddheswarar, Vyama Siddheswarar, Bhasmasiddheswarar, Bhiksha Siddheswarar, Bila Siddheswarar, Pura Siddheswarar, and Jala Siddheswarar. The Skanda Purana states that by leaving one’s life here, one can attain the form of a Lingam. The Dakshinamurthy shrine in Siddavatam, on the banks of the Vadapennai River, is very famous. On the way from Kurnool to Hyderabad, At Alampur, there is the Yogambika Sametha Bala Brahmeswarar temple. In this temple, which has shrines for the Navabrahmas, Yogambika Devi appears.

“Here, Brahmeswarar himself is Kasi Viswanathar, and the Tungabhadra River is the Ganga. Just like in Kasi, there are shrines for Ganapathi and Kalabhairavar, and sixty-four ghats. Uma Maheswarapuram, which serves as the northern gateway to Srisailam, is located near Mannanur or Rangapuram on the way to Hyderabad. There are two Shiva temples, one on the mountain and one at its base. Rudradharakai is a thirtham. Kubera guards this sthalam.

“The Ratnakaram text states that if one plays the Mridangam in the Padmavathi cave, which is a short distance from here, the Goddess will appear, offer Amritam, and grant divine status. As the southeastern gateway to Srisailam, Somasilam is located on the banks of the Vadapennai River, on the Nellore-Kadapa route.

“The Lord is called Skanda Someswarar. Pushpagiri, also known as Prasunachalam, is the southwestern gateway to Srisailam. It is located on the banks of the Pennai River in Kadapa district, near Nandikotkur in Kurnool district. Sangameswaram is mentioned in the Srisaila Kandam as a sub-gateway, the northwestern gateway, to Srisailam. Seven rivers—Krishna, Veni, Thungabhadra, Bhimarathi, Mala, and Pavanachini—converge here. During eclipses, all seven oceans and all sacred thirthams converge here.

“Bathing in this Nivarthi Sangamam during such auspicious times is believed to yield the benefits of a Yaga. Eleswaram, the northern gateway to Srisailam, has been subjected to many invasions and is now submerged in the Nagarjunasagar dam. This sacred temple They have now renovated it. Many Shaiva monasteries were located in Srisailam. Over time, they disappeared, and five monasteries are currently found to the southwest of the Srisailam temple. These include the very ancient Kanda Madam, which has a shrine for Gandasiddheswarar and the perennial Kandakkarna Thirtham.

“Nearby are the Bhimasankara Madam and the Veerapathrar temple.

“Additionally, there are the Vibhuthi Madam, Rudraksha Madam, and the Sarangadhara Madam, where Sarangeswara Munivar lived. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Sundaramoorthy Swamigal worshipped this sthalam from Thirukalathi and composed sacred hymns from there. Among the twelve Jyotirlinga sthalams in India, Srisailam is one of the three Jyotirlinga sthalams that have received Thevaram Thirumurai hymns. One of them is Srisailam, and the other two are Rameswaram and Thirukedaram.

“Here, the Arjuna tree is the Sthala Viruksham, as we saw. Another Sthala Viruksham is called the Thripala tree. This Thripala tree is a combination of three trees: Methi, Ravi, and Juvi. Since Dattatreya performed penance under this tree, it is called Dattatreya Viruksham. This tree is located in the Vriddhamallikarjunar temple. There is also an ancient tree called Karaveeram here.

“The Krishna River flows at the base of the mountain where this sacred temple is located. This river is called Pathala Ganga. This mountainous region is praised. Srisailam mountain has eight peaks and nine Nandis. The eight peaks are Vaidoorya Sikaram, Paravali Sikaram, Roupiya Sikaram, Manikka Sikaram, Maragatha Sikaram, Brahma Sikaram, and Kema Sikaram. There are nine Nandis, namely Prathama Nandi, Naga Nandi, Vinayaka Nandi, Garuda Nandi, Shiva Nandi, Maha Nandi, Surya Nandi, Vishnu Nandi, and Soma Nandi.

“Similarly, there are nine temples here: Brahmeswaram, Janardhaneswaram, Varuneswaram, Hameswaram, Saptakoteeswaram, Moksheswaram, Indreswaram, Agneswaram, and Kukkuteswaram. Kings of the Chola and Vijayanagara dynasties, among many others, have performed renovations here at the Sahasralingeswarar Temple and Annapoorani Panchanadeeswarar Temple, which are built of marble. Seventy-two minor kings in Andhra, Islamic fought and re-established Hindu kingdoms. Among them, Attanki Vemareddy is notable. His family deity is the Murti in Tripurantakam. Praloyareddy declared himself a devotee at the feet of Srisaila Mallikarjunar.

“We learn from inscriptions that the Reddy kings built steps for devotees ascending Srisaila Hill. During the time of Krishnadevaraya, the eastern gopuram and mandapams in Rathaveedhi were constructed. The vimanam was gilded with gold. Chhatrapati Veera Shivaji Maharaj visited this temple and had darshan of the Lord.

“Later, when a Muslim invasion occurred at the Srisaila temple, history records that Maratha warriors fought fiercely and protected the temple. The descendants of those Maratha warriors still come here once a year to commemorate their ancestors. and worship. We saw that the eastern gopuram was built by Krishnadevaraya. The northern gopuram was built by the great emperor Chhatrapati Shivaji. The western gopuram was built very recently. The vimanam of Mallikarjuna Swamy was built about seven hundred and fifty years ago by Mylamma Devi, the sister of Kakatiya Ganapati Rajan.

“At one time, those who could not climb all the way to Srisailam meditated on Mallikarjuna Swamy by having darshan of Sikareswaram, the highest peak in the Srisaila mountains. From here, devotees offer bali to Veerasankara Swamy on this peak, which is a little higher, and perform abhishekam to the Lord, then have darshan of the Mallikarjuna temple spire from between the horns of Nandi. Near the Bhiman Kula spring, which merges with Pathala Ganga, is the Bhimeswara Swamy temple. is located. From Pathala Ganga, one can travel by raft on the Krishna River to reach the cave where Akkama Devi performed penance. One can also visit the Ishtakameswari temple located in the dense forest. After crossing the river by raft, one can reach Kadalivanam, where Dattatreya performed penance.

“To this glorious and magnificent Thiru-sthalam of Srisailam, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman came and composed a Thiru-pathikam. Let us press on with our contemplation.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Four Hundred and Fifty-One. Thirunindracharukkam. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. During his sacred pilgrimage to the Thiru-Kailash mountain facing north, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman arrived at Srisailam Thiru-malai and there praised the Lord and sang a pathikam. This Thiru-pathikam is the fifty-eighth Thiru-pathikam of the Fourth Thirumurai, composed in Thiru-nerisai.

Kanrinaar purangal moondrum kanaleriyaaga seeri nindrador uruvum thannaal neermaiyum niraiyum kondu ondriyaang umaiyum thaamum oor bali theerndhu pinnum pandri pin vedaraagi parupathai nokkinaare. (He who, enraged, burnt the three cities with fire, and stood in that form, possessing water and fullness, united with Uma, sought alms in many towns, and then, becoming a hunter after a boar, looked towards the mountain.) Katrama maraihal paadi kadaithorum baliyundthervaar vatralor thalai kai yendhi vaanavar vanangi vaazhtha mutravor sadaiyil neerai yetra mukkanthammai patrinaarkku arulhal seidhu parupatha nokkinaare. (Singing learned Vedas, seeking alms at every door, holding a dried skull in hand, worshipped and praised by celestials, He who received water in His matted locks, the Three-Eyed One, bestows grace upon those who cling to Him, and looked towards the mountain.) Karavilaamanatharaagi kaithozhuva. vaarkku endrum iravu nindreriyathaadi innarul seyyum endhai maruvalaaru purangal moondrum aattiya nagaiyaraagi paravuvaarkku arulhal seidhu parupatha nokkinaare. (My Lord, who dances in the night with fire, bestows sweet grace upon those who worship Him with pure hearts, who, with a smile, burnt the three cities of the enemies, bestows grace upon those who praise Him, and looked towards the mountain.) Kattitta thalai kai yendhi kanaleriyadi seeri suttitta neerupusi sudapinakaadaraagi vittitta vetkaiyaarkku verirundarulhal seidhu pattitta udaiyaraagi parupatha nokkinaare. (Holding a tied skull in hand, dancing fiercely with fire, smearing sacred ash, becoming a cremation ground dweller, bestowing grace upon those who have renounced desires, wearing a patched garment, and looked towards the mountain.) Kaiyaraai kapaalamendhi kaamanai kannaarkaaindhu meyyaraai menithan mel vilanguven neeru poosi uyvaraai ulkuvaarku uvakaihal palavum seidhu paiyara araiyil aarthu parupatha nokkinaare. (Holding a skull in hand, burning Kama with His eye, being truthful, smearing shining white ash on His body, bestowing many joys upon those who meditate on Him for salvation, wearing a snake around His waist, and looked towards the mountain.) Vedaraai veyyaraagi velathin urivaip poorthu odaraai ulagamellam ulitharvar umaiyum thaamum kaadaraai kanalkai yendhi kadiyathor vidaimeel kondu paadaraai boothanjuzha parupatha nokkinaare. (Becoming a fierce hunter, wearing the skin of an elephant, wandering all over the world, He and Uma, as forest dwellers, holding fire in hand, riding a swift bull, surrounded by singing bhoothas, and looked towards the mountain.) Megampol midatraraagi velathin urivai poorthu ekampam. mevinaraam imaiyavar paraviyeatha kaakambar kalararaagi kadiyathor vidai ondraeri paagam pennuruvamaanar parupatha nokkinaare. (He whose throat is like a cloud, wearing the skin of an elephant, residing in Ekambam, praised by the celestials, wearing a garland of skulls, riding a swift bull, half of His body being that of a woman, and looked towards the mountain.) Peridar pinigal theerkkum pingakan endhai pembaan kaarudai kandaraagi kapaalamor kaiyilendhi seerudai sengan vellereriya selvar nalla paaridam paani seyyap parupatha nokkinaare. (My Lord, the golden-hued One, who removes great suffering and diseases, whose throat is dark, holding a skull in one hand, the wealthy One riding a glorious red-eyed white bull, with good bhoothas singing, and looked towards the mountain.) Anganmaalludaiyaraay aivaraal aatrunaadhe ungal maal theeravendil ullathaal ulkiyeathum senganmaal paraviyethi sivan ena nindra selvar paingan velleru athu yeri parupatha nokkinaare. (If you wish to dispel your delusion, which is not overcome by the five senses, praise with your heart the wealthy One who stands as Shiva, praised by the red-eyed Vishnu, riding a green-eyed white bull, and looked towards the mountain.) Adalvidai oorthiyaagi arakkan thol adaravoonri kadalida nanjamunda karaiyani kandanaaraam sudar vidu meni thanmel sunnaven neeru poosi padarsadai mathiyam serthi parupatha nokkinaare. (He who rides a powerful bull, who crushed the demon Ravana, who consumed the poison from the ocean, whose throat is adorned, smearing shining white ash on His radiant body, adorning His matted locks with the moon, and looked towards the mountain.)

Thus, he worshipped the Lord of Srisailam and sang a Thiru-pathikam. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman thus praised Srisailam, a Thiru-sthalam where Vidyadharas, celestial beings, aerial beings, Siddhas, Kinnaras skilled in music, inhabitants of the Naga world, and other divine beings who wander at will, along with silent Shiva-gnanis, come and worship daily. Just as Kailash mountain is referred to simply as Thiru-malai without any adjectives, this Thiru-sthalam is also called Thiru-silambu, Thiru-paruppatham, Sri Parvatham, and Srisailam, to indicate that this place is equal to Kailash. He worshipped this glorious mountain and sang a pathikam. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, driven by his love to go to Thiru-Kailash, worshipped this mountain and proceeded further. This is the note here.

Thus, departing from Srisailam, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, with his mind fixed on the White Kailash, Thiru-Kailash mountain, and without any other desires, continues his pilgrimage towards Thiru-Kailash mountain.

Therefore, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman continues with only the desire to see Thiru-Kailash mountain, without any desire to visit other Thiru-sthalams, sacred rivers, or mountains. Many Shiva devotees join Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. They follow Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman goes ahead.

Thus, he crosses the Telugu-speaking country and then the Kannada-speaking country. He traverses many forest areas. Many types of forests are interspersed in this region. There are sacred river banks here. He crosses all the banks of the sacred rivers like Krishna, Godavari, and Mahanadi. As he travels through countries rich in resources, with large mountain passes and vast water bodies, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman also sings about Thiru-Gokarnam.

Similarly, he crosses Malava Desam. This Malava Desam is one of the fifty-six countries of Bharat Desam.

Thus, crossing Malava Desam and many dense, long forests, he goes to the region called Lada Bhumi. Lada is one of the fifty-six countries. This Ilada Desam, is a part of Bengal. Peruman mentions that there are many charitable institutions here. He refers to it as ‘Aramgal Neetum Ilada Bhumi’ (Land where virtues abound).

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman states that there are many charitable institutions in this country that provide food, lodging, medicine, and other facilities to travelers.

Thus, crossing Ilada Desam, he reaches Paithira Nadu. This is the land now known as Madhya Pradesh. It is a country located in the center of the Indian subcontinent. Arumuga Thambiranar mentions it as the country located west of Prayaga and east of Vinasam.

Thus, crossing this Madhya Pradesh, he reaches the great Thiru-sthalam of Varanasi, where the Ganges River flows. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman reaches the great Thiru-sthalam of Varanasi. Sekkizhar Peruman describes Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s arrival in Varanasi in this verse: “Anna naadu kadandhu Gangai anaindhu sendru valam kollum minnu veliyar Varanasi virippinodu panindhu udan pinnai anainthavar thammai angan oliyndhu Gangai peyarndhu poy mannu kaathal seyvin mannavar vandhu karsura munthinaar.” As we have already seen, he crosses many countries, which are subdivisions of the central part of Bharat Desam, called Madhyama Paithiram, and goes to that part of North Bharat Desam, a land where sacred rivers like the divine Ganges flow. In this land, rich in swans, the Ganges River flows. The Ganges River, which descended from the sky, flows here. It flows through the Himalayas, spreads across the land, and enriches this region.

The Ganges River, which flows from west to east until Varanasi, turns northward when it reaches Varanasi, flowing as Uttaravahini, encircles Varanasi, and then flows eastward again.

Therefore, Peruman sings, “Gangai anaindhu sendru valam kollum Varanasi” (Varanasi, where the Ganges flows and brings prosperity). It is a common prayer that one should visit Kashi at least once. There is no one who does not know about the glory of such a Kashi. Its greatness has been extensively and elaborately described in many books. It is a great Thiru-sthalam, one of the Thevara Vaippu Thalangal, where Viswanatha Peruman and Visalakshi Ammaiyar are clearly enshrined. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman sang in the Kaappu Thiruthandakam, “Mathilum Maakaanam Varanasi.” The Kasi Kandam states that this place is called Varanasi because the two rivers, Varuna and Asi, encircle this Thiru-sthalam from south to north as a boundary.

The saying “Kasiyil irakka mukthi” (Salvation upon death in Kasi) is a well-known fact throughout Bharat Desam. When Thirunavukkarasu Peruman was in Thiru-Kalahasti Thiru-malai, he set out northward with the desire to see the form of Thiru-Kailash mountain. He worshipped and bowed to Srisaila mountain and continued his journey swiftly without staying in any other Thiru-sthalam or place. When he arrived in Varanasi, due to its immeasurable glory, he worshipped Viswanatha Peruman here and performed sacred service. This is because the Lord of Kailash, whom he loved and sought, resides here as Viswanatha, surrounded by the Ganges.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman states that the Nayanar, who had traveled without any desire for other places, worshipped here with devotion. This is the Thiru-sthalam where the Nayanar, who went to worship the Northern Kailash, worshipped the Lord in the North.

The devotees who had followed Thirunavukkarasu Peruman until now stopped at this Thiru-sthalam. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, who departs from here towards Thiru-Kailash mountain, now traverses through difficult areas of uninhabited forests and mountains. Crossing the banks of the Ganges, he continues. He crosses vast forests that reach the sky. These are dense forest areas inaccessible to humans.

But Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, driven by his love to see the sacred vision of Thiru-Kailash, traverses these difficult terrains. He crosses these forest areas, which even groups of people fear to enter, alone. He continues without even consuming the leaves (fallen dry leaves), roots, tubers, and fruits that even Shivayogis and Shivagnanis consume as food. Shivayogis, with the intention of not harming plants, which are single-sensed beings, would consume parts of plants that are no longer useful to them, such as fallen leaves, dry leaves, roots, and tubers. This was the custom of our ancestors. Gnanis in a state of yogic silence would sometimes suffer from hunger.

Even then, they would seek and consume plant-based foods. Generally, they would awaken the inner fire through their feet and consume the nectar of meditation. They would consume such foods only when hunger arose.

But here, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, as if unaware of the feeling of hunger, swiftly traverses through the dense forests towards Thiru-Kailash mountain. He travels thus due to the strength of his surging love to see Thiru-Kailash mountain. He continues day and night, through cold and rain, without noticing anything.

Thus, continuing his journey, He continues day and night, through cold and rain, without noticing anything.

Thus, continuing his journey, he reaches the northern polar region, the foothills of the Himalayas. Even fierce predatory animals like tigers that roam at night, and snakes, did not harm Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. The ferocious animals, fearing to harm the Nayanar, kept their distance. The snakes not only refrained from harming him but also used their gems as lamps, showing the way and light to Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, and served him. It is noteworthy that even these animals, which always have a fierce nature, changed their disposition here. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman also crosses the fierce desert lands encountered in some places.

Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, firm in his penance, continues without even noticing the severe heat of the summer.

Thus, at night, and during the day, he crosses vast, impassable forests. The sacred feet of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman are capable of saving those who reach them. Even though those sacred feet were worn out, would Thirunavukkarasu Peruman forget Shiva Peruman, who resides in Thiru-Kailash with Uma Devi? No, he continues without forgetting. Even though the flesh of his feet wore away, he proceeds by crawling with his hands. He places his hands down, lifts them, and places them down again and again.

Even though his hands and wrists became worn and damaged, he did not mind it. As his love to see the sacred vision of Thiru-Kailash increased further and further, even though his hands were damaged, he propelled himself forward with his chest. His mind was in one direction, and his body’s effort was not in another direction; rather, the effort of his body, combined with his surging love, was a true, embodied, surging love. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s love matured further and further. Nevertheless, even amidst the cruel heat of the stony, fiery terrain, he continued his journey by propelling himself forward with his chest.

Propelling himself forward with his chest, his chest muscles wore away, and his ribs broke. Yet, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman continued without deviating from his goal. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s entire being was filled with the desire to see the sacred vision of Thiru-Kailash, and that being made a great effort to propel his body. His being was filled with eagerness.

Therefore, even though his chest Even though his chest wore away and his ribs broke, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s soul propelled his body, rolling and rolling, continuing his journey. “Maarpamum thasai naindhu sindhi varindha enbu murindhida nervarum kuri nindra sindhaiyin nesam eesanai nedu neet aarvam anguyirkondu kaikkumudampadangu oonkedda servarum pazhuvam purandu purandu sendranar semmaiyor appuram puralkindra neelidai angamengum arainthida sepparum kayilai silambadi sindhai sendrurum aathalaan meippurathil uruppu azhindhapin mella vandhu muyarchiyum thappurach cheyalinri annneri thanginaar Tamil aazhiyaar” - thus Sekkizhar Peruman presents the verses. Rolling and rolling with his body, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, whose entire body was worn out, stopped when he could no longer exert physical effort. His inner being, his mind, remained there with the thought of worshipping at the foot of Kailash.

Therefore, unable to proceed further, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, the ocean of Tamil, stopped there. The reason was that the Lord’s sacred body was greatly weakened. Even though his body was exhausted and lay without effort, the Tamil brilliance in his mind remained undiminished. That desire to see the sacred vision of Thiru-Kailash matured into love and he remained steadfast in the path of Shiva.

Let us continue to contemplate what happens next. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Four Hundred and Fifty-Two. Thirunindracharukkam. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, who had traveled a very long distance with great love to see the sacred vision of Thiru-Kailash, the Kailash, while crossing a desert land, found that after the outer limbs of his sacred body were worn away, even the effort to slowly propel himself forward ceased. Unable to perform any other action, he stopped there, unable to proceed further.

The reason for this was that the Peruman’s sacred body was greatly weakened.

Therefore, he remained there.

At this time, as Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman had requested, Shiva Peruman decided that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman should not proceed to Thiru-Kailash, but should remain on this earth for some more time and bestow many more Thiru-Pathigams upon the people of the world.

Therefore, Shiva Peruman did not grant Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman permission to ascend Thiru-Kailash at this moment. Shiva Peruman did not grant permission now because of His compassion for the souls of this world, desiring that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman should remain here for some more time and sing many more Thiru-Pathigams. “Mannu Theen Tamil Puviyin” Sekkilhar Peruman states here, “May he be praised again upon the earth of sweet Tamil.” He says, “Annatthanmaiyaar Kayilaiyai Anaivatharku Arulaar Mannu Theen Tamil Puviyin Mel Pinnaiyum Vazhutha Nan Nedum Punal Thadammum Ondru Udan Kadanthaar Pannagam Punai Paramaror Munivaraampadiyaal.” Sekkilhar Peruman composed this Thiru-Paadal. For the reason, “Mannu Theen Tamil Puviyin Mel Pinnaiyum Vazhutha,” Shiva Peruman did not grant Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman permission to ascend Thiru-Kailash.

At this time, every word in the phrase “Mannu Theen Tamil Puviyin Mel Pinnaiyum Vazhutha” is rich in meaning. The compassion that all the Thiru-Pathigams that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman is yet to bestow should reach the souls of this world, We saw that Shiva Peruman acts in this manner out of compassion.

Therefore, those Thiru-Pathigams of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman are referred to by Sekkilhar Peruman as “Mannu Theen Tamil Thiru-Pathigams.” “Mannuthal” means the quality of remaining eternally in the hearts of devotees. “Theen Tamil” means Thiru-Pathigams that possess both sweetness of meaning and ease of words. These Thiru-Pathigams include the Kailai Potri Thiru-Thandagams seen in the formless manifestation, the Kailai Kaatchi Kanda Thiru-Vaiyaatru Thiru-Pathigams seen in the manifest form, the many unique Thiru-Pathigams, Adaivu Thiru-Pathigams, and Nindra Thiru-Pathigams composed while residing and performing penance after building a Thiru-Madam in Thiru-Poonthuruthi, The general Thiru-Thandaga Thiru-Pathigams, specifically mentioned in Periya Puranam songs 1679 and 1680, the Thiru-Angamaalai Thiru-Pathigam, the Thiru-Pathigams sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman upon seeing and worshipping Thiru-Aalavaai Udaiyar, the spiritual Lord of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s Shiva Puja, that is, the Thiru-Aalavaai Thiru-Pathigams, the Thiru-Poovanam Thiru-Thandaga Thiru-Pathigams praising the qualities seen when the Lord appeared directly, the Thiru-Aaroor Thiru-Thandagam stating “I am not for the two karmas that lament within Maya,” the Thiru-Virutham seeking refuge in the Lord, the Thiru-Thandagam of being established at His holy feet. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman is yet to bestow all these Thiru-Pathigams in the upcoming sections of his sacred history.

Therefore, if Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman were to be granted the vision of Thiru-Kailash now, or if he were allowed to ascend Thiru-Kailash, all these Thiru-Pathigams would not reach the souls living in this world. Hence, out of compassion, Shiva Peruman is not granting Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman permission to ascend Thiru-Kailash now, so that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman may bestow all these Thiru-Pathigams in his future sacred history. Even if Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman were to go to Thiru-Kailash, he could still sing praises to the Lord in sweet Tamil from there. Nevertheless, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman must bestow all those Thiru-Pathigams upon this earth, because only if they are bestowed upon this earthly world will they be accessible to other souls.

Therefore, this is the great compassion shown by the Lord for the sake of other souls.

Thus, Shiva Peruman, who holds great compassion, desires that Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman should bestow all the previously mentioned Thiru-Pathigams, just as he has sung Thiru-Pathigams until now. Shiva Peruman, having such great compassion, decides to come in another form to the place where Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar is. At that spot where Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman stands, He creates a large pond filled with water. Near the pond thus created, Shiva Peruman walks in the form of a sage. He approaches very close to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sees the sage who has come in the form of a sage.

Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sees Shiva Peruman, who stood before him in the form of a sage. Shiva Peruman, in the form of a sage, addresses Thiru-Navukkarasar, saying, “Your body parts are all wasted, you are suffering greatly, your body parts are damaged, and you are now in great distress. Why have you come to this cruel desert?” Thus, Shiva Peruman, who came in the form of a sage, asks Thiru-Navukkarasar. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman replies. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman replies to the sage. Sekkilhar Peruman beautifully composes a Thiru-Paadal describing how the sage appeared in the eyes of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, Through it, Sekkilhar Peruman presents before our eyes the sacred form of Shiva Peruman who came as a sage.

The song is as follows: “Maasil Varkkalai Aadaim Maarpin Mun Noolum Thesudai Sadai Mavuliyum Neerum Meytthigalha Aasin Meytthavaraagi Nindravar Thamain Nokki Pesavutradhoru Unarvura Vilambuvaar Periyor.” Thus, this song is composed.

Therefore, Sekkilhar Peruman composes this song like a painting, bringing before our eyes the sacred form of the Lord who came as a sage. How does that sage appear? He appears in “Maasil Varkkalai Aadai.” “Varkkalai Aadai” means clothing made of tree bark. On his sacred chest, The sacred thread with three strands shines. He wears his matted hair as a crown, shaping it like a royal diadem. Sacred ash adorns his divine body.

He appears as a flawless true ascetic. “Aasil Meytthavam” means “Aasu Il Meytthavam.” “Aasu” means blemish or fault.

Therefore, “Aasu Il Meytthavar” literally means one who possesses true penance without blemish. However, the true meaning here is that the one who came in the guise of a sage was Shiva Peruman.

Therefore, “Aasu Il Meytthavar” correctly means that He came as a true ascetic to remove the blemishes, the malas, the faults of souls, to make them non-existent. This would be the correct interpretation. In the Mangala Vazhthu Paadal of Sivagnanabodham, the great Siddhanta scholars interpret “Malaivillaar” as one who removes the “malaivinai” (confusion or delusion) of other souls.

Similarly, here, “Aasuyil Meytthavar” does not mean that he is faultless, but rather that he is one who makes the faults of souls non-existent. This is the correct meaning.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman begins to answer the question posed by Shiva Peruman, who came in the guise of that ascetic. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, whose body parts were all wasted and who was unable to perform any action, now, upon seeing the sage who came before him and asked a question, looked at the sage, and a little Emotion arose, and Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman became capable of speech. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman replies to the sage who asked, “Despite your body being so wasted, and in this harsh desert, where are you going? What is the reason for your presence in this desert?” Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar replies, “O Sage, I have come with the desire to see and worship the Lord, Shiva Peruman, who resides on Thiru-Kailash with Uma Devi, whose hair is adorned with wandering bees, as I am His devotee. This is my intention. This is my goal.” “Vandulaang Kuzhal Malaimagaludan Vadakkaiyilai Andar Nayagar Irukkum Apparisu Avar Adiyen Kandu Kumpida Viruppodum Kaathalin Adainthaen.”

The Peruman composes this Thiru-Paadal, saying, “Konda En Kurippu Ithu Muniyee Enak Koora.” In this song, he refers to Uma Devi as “Malaimagal” (daughter of the mountain) whose hair is adorned with wandering bees. He has come here with the intention of going to Northern Kailash, inspired by the memory of worshipping Ammaiyappar (Shiva and Parvati) in Thiru-Kalaathi, referred to as “Thenaarthukka Gnana Poonkothaiyaal Paagaththaan.” Thus, the nature of Uma Devi remains firmly in Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s memory, causing him to speak in this manner. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman states that he wishes to go towards Northern Kailash.

Therefore, the implication here is that the desire to worship Northern Kailash arose from the memory of seeing Southern Kailash in Kalaathi. He states that his desire is to see the state in which Shiva Peruman resides with Uma Devi in Thiru-Kailash. The phrase “Irukkum Apparisu” appears in the song. “Apparisu” means “that state” or “that nature.” Sivakavimani Aiyya explains that the ‘a’ in “Apparisu” refers to “Pandu Arisu,” meaning something known previously. That is, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman had previously seen the sacred form of the Lord residing with Uma Devi in Thiru-Kailash when he was the sage Vakeesa.

Therefore, the meaning here is that he is now going with the intention of seeing it again.

Furthermore, he states that he desires that state, meaning the sacred form in which the Lord resides there. “Kandu Kumpiduthal” means the desire to see and worship with the outer eye. Although Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman continuously worships with his inner eye, his desire is to see and worship with his outer eye as well. This recalls the prayer made when moving from the state of inner worship (Antharyagam) in Shiva Puja to outer worship (Purapooja).

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman replies to the sage. The sage then replies to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. This is the 365th song: “Kailai Maalvaraiyaavathu Kaasini Marungu Payilum Maanudap Paanmaiyor Adaivatharku Elitho Ayil Kol Verpadai Amararum Anugutharku Arithaal Veyil Kol Venchurath En Seytheer Vanthu Ena Vilampi.” This is the next song. The sage addresses Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, saying, “Is that great Kailash mountain an easy place for the people of this world to reach? The great Kailash mountain is so glorious that the people of this world cannot reach it.

“It is so rare that even the Devas and others cannot reach it.

“Therefore, what will you accomplish by coming to this cruel desert filled with scorching heat?” Thus, the sage speaks to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. The song states, “Kaasini Marungu Payilum Maanidap Paanmaiyor Adaivatharku Elitho.” “Kaasini” means this earth. This is a confusing earth, a karma-bhumi where the fruits of good and bad deeds are experienced together. This earthly world, and those who reside in it, are human beings.

“Therefore, the sage states that Thiru-Kailash is a place inaccessible to these human beings. There is an inner meaning here: it is indeed a very difficult place for human beings to reach, an inaccessible place.

“However, although Thiru-Gnanasambandha Peruman, Thiru-Navukkarasu Swamigal, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, and others were born as humans in this life, they are great Acharyas who have transcended human nature and possess Shiva-nature.

“Therefore, the inner meaning here is that Thiru-Kailash is an easy place for those who have attained such Shiva-nature to reach.

“Thus, Kailash is a place inaccessible to souls with human nature, but not to great souls with Shiva-nature. The inner meaning here is that Kailash is a place inaccessible to souls with human nature, but not to great souls with Shiva-nature.

“Thus, the sage speaks to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman. Hearing this, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman replies to the sage. “Ena Vilangum Tholum Aagamum Thuvalum Munnool Muni Solla Aalum Nayagan Kayilaiyil Irukkai Kandallal Maalum Ivvudal Kondu Meelen Ena Maruthaar.” This is the next song. The sage says that the great Kailash mountain is a place inaccessible to human beings with human nature.

“Therefore, it would be right for you to return to where you came from. So, go back to your place and abandon the attempt to go to Kailash. When the Lord, who was in the form of the sage, spoke thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman replied, I will not return with this perishable body unless I have seen and worshipped the sacred form of Shiva Peruman, my Lord, residing in Thiru-Kailash. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman refuses. The sage says, “What have you done?” When he says it is right for you to return, it indicates the compassion and eagerness with which the sage, seeing Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s state, speaks out of pity.

“Thus, as he spoke these words with compassion and love, a movement appeared in the sage’s divine body, causing the sacred thread he wore to sway on his divine body. This was the physical manifestation that occurred in the sage’s divine body when he replied. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman states here, “Aalum Nayagan Kayilaiyil Irukkai Kandallal.” Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman refers to Shiva Peruman as “Nayagan” (Lord).

“Therefore, the inner meaning of using the word “Nayagan” here is that Shiva Peruman is the Lord, and it is His duty and responsibility to fulfill the desires of the souls who reach Him.

“Furthermore, when the sage says, “Even though your body is wasted, you are still going to Kailash; don’t, go back,” Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman refuses, saying, “Kondu Meelen.” That is, this body is bound to perish one day. So you say my body is going to perish, and therefore, I should go back.

“But even if not now, this body is certain to perish one day.

“Therefore, rather than dying on that day, if my body perishes in this noble endeavor of seeking Kailash, it is a good thing, he says, and refutes the sage’s statement. As soon as Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman said this, Shiva Peruman wished that this world should witness and be saved by the determination of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman.

“Therefore, the Lord, who had come in the form of a sage, vanished into the sky, revealing that it was He who had been speaking as the sage until then. At that moment, Shiva Peruman’s divine voice was heard from the sky. Shiva Peruman, as an ethereal voice, commanded, “O exalted King of Tongue, arise!” At that moment, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman All the sufferings in his body vanished. We had previously seen the sufferings in Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s body; all those vanished by the grace of Shiva Peruman, and Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman’s body shone with Shiva’s divine light. He arose and shone with such a body. The voice said, “O King of the exalted tongue, arise!” This was the ethereal voice of the Lord.

“Iru” (arise) truly means to rise from a state of physical inactivity and prostration, and “iruthal” (to be) means to remain on this earthly world for a long time, practicing Shiva-dharma, and finally, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman will remain at the sacred feet of the Lord, becoming the very form of Shiva-ananda gnana. The word “Iru” signifies both. The song goes thus: “Aangumatravar Thunivu Arinthavar Thamain Ariya Neengumaathavar Visumpidai Karainthu Neen Mozhiyaal Oongu Naavinukku Arasaney Ezunthir Endru Uraippa Theengu Neengiya Yaakkai Kondu Ezunthu Oli Thigalvaar.” Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, having risen and heard the divine voice of Shiva Peruman, arose and praised Shiva Peruman, presenting his request. “Annaley Ena Aandu Kondu Aruliya Amuthai Vinnile Marainthu Arul Puri Veda Nayaganai Kanninaal Thiru-Kailaiyil Iruntha Nin Kolam Nanni Naan Thozha Nayanthu Arul Puri Ena Paninthaar.” This is the next sacred verse. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman prostrated before the Lord, worshipped Him, and presented his request. He humbly requested, “O great Lord, the nectar who has graciously taken me as Your servant, the Lord of the Vedas who bestows grace by disappearing into the sky, please grant me the grace to see and worship with my own eyes Your sacred form residing in Thiru-Kailash.” Shiva Peruman then graciously responded with His divine voice as an ethereal utterance.

“We shall contemplate this further.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 453, Thiru-Nindracharukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. While Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman was undertaking the Thiru-Kailash pilgrimage, his body parts were wasting away, and at a certain point, he could no longer move.

At that time, Shiva Peruman assumed the guise of a sage, created a pond there, and appeared before Navukkarasu Peruman, asking, “Where are you going?” When Navukkarasu Peruman replied, “I am going to Thiru-Kailash,” the sage said, “Thiru-Kailash is a place inaccessible to human beings with human nature.

“Therefore, return the way you came.” Hearing this, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman firmly declared, “I will not return with this perishable body. I will only return after seeing the vision of Thiru-Kailash.” Shiva Peruman, wishing to reveal his steadfastness and courage to the world, The Lord Shiva, who had come as a sage, hid himself and, from the sky, spoke an ethereal voice, saying, “O King of Tongues, arise!” Hearing this, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman praised and worshipped the Lord, requesting, “You must show me the vision of Thiru-Kailai.” To this, Lord Shiva again responded with an ethereal voice. The verse is as follows: “Looking at the good devotee who rose in worship, the Lord, with a great sacred utterance from the sky, commanded, ‘Plunge into this pond, and you shall see Us in Thiru-Ayyatru in the manner We reside in Kailai, without blemish.’” Thus, the Lord responded in an ethereal form to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, who had requested to see the vision of Thiru-Kailai. He bestows grace. Did we not already see that when Lord Shiva came as a sage, he created a pond and appeared before him?

“Now, in an ethereal form, he addresses Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, saying, “Plunge into this pond, and you shall arise in Thiru-Ayyatru.

“Then, in Thiru-Ayyatru, you will receive the vision of our Thiru-Kailai. You shall go to Thiru-Ayyatru and behold the manner in which we are seated in Thiru-Kailai.” This is what Lord Shiva says in this verse. The special quality of Thiru-Ayyatru is that it removes all the imperfections of living beings.

“Here, Thiru-Nandi Devar performed penance and attained blessings, becoming the lord of the Shiva Ganas. And becoming the foremost of the Shiva Guru lineage, this special quality belongs to Thiru-Ayyatru, a flawless distinction.

“Here, the term ‘flawless’ (pazhuthu il) refers to ‘pazhuthu’ as fault or impurity, which we saw earlier. It denotes the innate impurity of souls, known as ‘aanava malam.’ In the first chapter of the Periya Puranam, in the section on the glory of Thiru-Malai, we have contemplated how Sekkizhar Peruman explained the glory of Thiru-Ayyatru in the forty-fifth verse.

“Accordingly, Lord Shiva bestows grace upon Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, who desired to see the vision of Thiru-Kailai, saying, “Go and behold that vision of Thiru-Kailai in Thiru-Ayyatru.” Thus, as Lord Shiva bestowed His grace, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, taking the sacred utterance of Lord Shiva upon his head, rose, worshipped, and sang a Thiru-Pathikam. He begins with “Vettragi Vinnagi Nindrai Potri” and bestows the Potri Thiruthandakam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, taking the Lord’s grace upon his head, rose and worshipped. Sekkizhar Peruman composed this verse: “He who desired the word ‘Vettragi Vinnagi Nindrai,’ who attained power, the Lord, chanted the five letters, and plunged into the sacred pond of flowing water, by divine command.” As soon as the Lord said He would show the vision of Thiru-Kailai in Thiru-Ayyatru, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sang the Thiruthandakam, “Vettragi Vinnagi Nindrai Potri,” praising the Lord. In each verse of this Thiruthandakam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman has graced it with the refrain “Kailai Malaiyane Potri Potri.” It is composed as the Thiru-Nodithanmalai Thiruthandakam, the Potri Thiruthandakam.

“In each of the verses within this Thiruthandakam, the word ‘Potri’ appears in nine places.

“Now, the Thiruthandakam that begins with ‘Vettragi Vinnagi’ is the Thiruthandakam dedicated to Thiru-Kailai Malai.

“Vettragi Vinnagi Nindrai Potri, Meelame Aal Ennai Kondaai Potri, Oottragi Ullae Olithaai Potri, Ovaatha Saththaththu Oliye Potri, Aatrragi Ange Amarnthaai Potri, Aarankam Naal Vedam Aanaai Potri, Kaatrragi Engum Kalanthaai Potri. Kailai Malaiyanai Potri Potri. Pichchaadal Peyodu Kandaai Potri, Piraviyarukkum Pirane Potri, Vayirchaadal Nandru Makizhnthaai Potri, Maruviyan Sinthai Pugunthaai Potri, Poychchaar Puram Moondrum Eythaai Potri, Pogaathan Sinthai Pugunthaai Potri, Kachchaaka Naakam Asaithaai Potri, Kailai Malaiyanai Potri Potri. Maruvaar Puram Moondrum Eythaai Potri, Maruviyan Sinthai Pugunthaai Potri, Uruvaakiyanai Padaithaai Potri, Ullaavi Vaangi Olithaai. Potri Thiruvaaki Nindra Thirame Potri, Desam Parava Paduvaai Potri, Karuvaakiyodum Mukile Potri, Kailai Malai Yanai Potri Potri.

“Vaanaththaar Potrum Marunthe Potri, Vandendran Sinthai Pugunthaai Potri, Oonaththai Neekkum Udalae Potri, Ongiyazhalaai Nimirnthaai Potri, Thenaththai Vaartha Thelive Potri, Devarkkum Devanai Nindraai Potri, Kaanaththiyaadal Ukanthaai Potri, Kailai Malai Yanai Potri Potri. Ooraaki Nindra Ulakae. Potri, Ongiyazhalaai Nimirnthaai Potri, Peraaki Engum Paranthaai Potri, Peyaraathan Sinthai Pugunthaai Potri, Neeraaviyaana Nizhalae Potri, Nervaaru Oruvaraiyum Illaai Potri, Kaaraaki Nindra Mukile Potri, Kailai Malai Yanai Potri Potri. Silluruvaai Sendru Thirandaai Potri, Devar Ariyaatha Deve Potri, Pulluyirkkum Potri Punarthaai Potri, Pogaathan Sinthai Pugunthaai Potri, Palluyiraai Paarththoorum Nindraai Potri, Pattrri Ulakai Vidaathaai. Potri, Kalluyiraai Nindra Kanale Potri, Kailai Malai Yanai Potri Potri. Pannin Isaiyaaki Nindraai Potri, Paavi Paavam Maruppaai Potri, Ennum Ezhuththum Sollaanaai Potri, En Sinthai Neenga Iraivaa Potri, Vinnum Neelanum Theeyaanaai Potri, Melavarkkum Melaaki Nindraai Potri, Kannin Maniyaaki Nindraai Potri, Kailai Malaiyanai Potri Potri.

“Imaiathu Uyiraathu Irunthaai Potri, En Sinthai Neenga Iraivaa Potri, Umaipaakamaakaththu Anaithaai Potri. Oozhiyelana Oruvaa Potri, Arumaiyaa Arunanjam Aarnthaai Potri, Aathi Puraananai Nindraai Potri, Kamaiyaaki Nindra Kanalai Potri, Kailai Malaiyanai Potri Potri. Moovaai Piravaayiravaai Potri, Munname Thondri Mulaithaai Potri, Devaathi Devar Thozhum Deve Potri, Sendreriyangum Paranthaai Potri, Aavaa Adiyenukkellam Potri, Allal Naliya Alanthaen Potri, Kaavaaik Kanaka Thirale Potri, Kailai Malaiyanai Potri Potri. Nediya Visum. Podu Kanne Potri, Neela Akalam Udaiyaai Potri, Adiyum Mudiyum Ikali Potri, Angondrariyaamai Nindraai Potri, Kodiyavan Kootrram Uthaithaai Potri, Koyilaayan Sinthai Kondaai Potri, Kadiya Uru Mudum Minne Potri, Kailai Malaiyanai Potri Potri. Unnaathu Urangaathu Irunthaai Potri, Vedam Unarnthaai Potri, Ennaayilankai Kon Thannai Potri, Iraiviralal Vaiththukanda Eesaa Potri, Pannaareesayin Sol Kettaai Potri, Pandeyan Sinthai Pugunthaa Po.

“Potri, Kannaiyulagu Nindraai Potri, Kailai Malaiyanai Potri Potri, Kailai Malaiyanai Potri Potri.

“Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman sings the Thiruthandakam, praising the Lord.

“Then, in accordance with the Lord’s sacred utterance, he plunges into the pond created by the Lord. He plunges, chanting the five letters, into that watery expanse in the northern foothills of Thiru-Kailai, to behold the vision of Shiva in Thiru-Ayyatru.

“Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman plunges, chanting the five letters. He plunges into this pond as commanded by the Lord, “Plunge and behold.” Who can comprehend the greatness of the grace of Lord Shiva, the foremost deity? To the astonishment of the entire world, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, the sage of divine knowledge, plunged into the pond situated in the snowy mountains and emerged from a pond in Thiru-Ayyatru. He emerged from a pond in Thiru-Ayyatru, where Lord Shiva, who holds Uma Devi in one part of His body, joyfully resides. Before narrating the event of Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, who plunged into a pond in the northern foothills of Kailai and emerged from a pond in Thiru-Ayyatru in the south, Sekkizhar Peruman begins with an introduction, asking, “Who knows the greatness of divine grace?” “Aathi Devartham Thiruvarul Perumai Yaar Arivaar?

“Potha Maathavar Panivarai Poykaiyil Moozhki Maathorpaakanar Makizhum Aiyaatril Or Vaavi Meethu Thondri Vandhu Ezunthu.” Sekkizhar Peruman composes the verse, “Ulakaelam Viyappa” (to the astonishment of the whole world). Aathi Devar is Lord Shiva. The actions of other deities are subject to the command of Aathi Devar and occur within a limit.

“But Aathi Devar is all-powerful; therefore, His acts of grace can transcend all boundaries and occur without limit. This is its implication.

“Thus, the greatness of the grace of Aathi Devar, Lord Shiva, can make the north and south, the path and the pond, align. For others, this is extremely rare; this is its inner meaning.

“Therefore, Aathi Devar is Lord Shiva; only He can perform such great acts of grace. “Is there anything impossible when the Foremost One stands before you?” We can recall this verse, the one hundred and thirty-second song, from another place in the Periya Puranam by Sekkizhar Peruman.

“Therefore, we can recall here the verse he sang.

“Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, who plunged into the pond created by Lord Shiva in the northern foothills of Kailai, emerged in the south at the Samudra Theertham, a tank located northwest of the Thiru-Ayyatru temple, and worshipped the Lord of Thiru-Ayyatru. This sacred tank is currently known as Samudra Theertham and Uppankottai Pillaiyar Kovil Kulam, located northwest of the Thiru-Ayyatru temple, presenting a sacred sight.

“Therefore, every year on Aadi Amavasai, the historical festival of this sacred vision of Appar Peruman is celebrated in Thiru-Ayyatru. The festival where the Lord granted Thiru-Kailai vision to Appar Swamigal in Thiru-Ayyatru is celebrated every year on Aadi Amavasai. All Shiva devotees throughout the month of Aadi Amavasai gather in Thiru-Ayyatru on the day of Aadi Amavasai and experience blissful joy upon witnessing the Thiru-Kailai vision shown by the Lord to Appar Peruman. The Nayanar, who plunged downwards into the pond in the Kailai foothills, rose upwards from the sacred tank of Ayyatru.

“Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman states, “Vaavi Meethu Thondri Vandhu Ezunthanar” (He appeared and rose from the pond). He states, “Ulakaelam Viyappa Ezunthanar” (He rose to the astonishment of the whole world). “Ulakaelam” is the first auspicious word given by Lord Nataraja of Thillai to Sekkizhar Swamigal for composing the Thiru-Thondar Puranam, the Periya Puranam. Sekkizhar Peruman has emphasized this auspicious word “Ulakaelam” in this sacred verse. He has sung it because this is a rare and great act of divine manifestation.

“Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman has sung this auspicious word “Ulakaelam” in this sacred verse.

“Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, who came ashore from the pond filled with fragrant flowers, realizing the greatness of Lord Shiva through his own experience, praises the Lord with tears streaming from his eyes, asking, “Is this the grace and compassion bestowed by our Lord?” Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, who plunged into the pond with his love for the Lord, now stands having risen from the pond of the Lord’s grace. The love Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman offered to the Lord; the grace the Lord bestowed upon him.

“Thus, the Nayanar, thinking, “This is the divine grace the Lord bestows upon me, even considering me.” Unable to bear it, his heart melted, and tears flowed profusely.

“Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, who rose from that sacred tank in Thiru-Ayyatru, proceeds into the sacred site of Thiru-Ayyatru. Our contemplation shall continue.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 454, Thiru-Nindrachcharukkam, Thiru-Navukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman plunges into the pond created by the Lord in the northern foothills of Kailai and emerges from a tank in Thiru-Ayyatru in the south. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, having emerged, passes through the streets of Thiru-Ayyatru. White flags adorn the streets leading to the Thiru-Ayyatru temple. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, having come ashore from the pond, approaches the temple to worship and praise the Lord of Thiru-Ayyatru.

At that moment, he beholds all living beings, both stationary and moving, known as ‘acharam charam,’ appearing with their respective companions. That is, all living beings in this world appear with their companions, presenting a vision to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman in Thiru-Ayyatru.

Here, ‘companion’ refers to the idea that male and female are companions to each other. Until now, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman had seen the world for a long time.

However, now, for the purpose of the Lord showing him a vision—that is, the vision of Thiru-Kailai in Thiru-Ayyatru, where Lord Shiva is seated with Uma Devi in Thiru-Kailai—He is about to show this sacred vision to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman.

Therefore, as a prelude to this, all living beings in this world, male and female, appear together, and the entire world appears as Shiva-Shakti. This is due to the divine grace of the Lord upon Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman.

Thus, to show His vision, the Lord first reveals it in this divided manner, and then He shows the state of Shiva and Shakti as a pair, a ‘charithai’ (conduct).

Then He shows His sacred feet to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman.

Now, in the Thiru-Pathikam sung by Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, in each verse of the Pathikam, he sings about living beings being male and female. Along with that, he sings, “Kanden Avar Thiruppaatham” (I saw His sacred feet) and “Kandariyaathana Kanden” (I saw what I had never seen before), describing the way the Lord shows His sacred feet.

Thus, we can see that this Thiru-Pathikam is structured to convey the experiential stages of coming from a philosophical form, a philosophical vision, to a Shiva vision.

Here, the verse states that both the stationary (acharam) and moving (charam) appear as male and female. We all know that among moving creatures, i.e., animals and humans, there is a male and female distinction.

But the verse also shows that even among stationary creatures, known as ‘acharam,’ i.e., plants, there is a male and female distinction. We also see in this verse that even among stationary living beings, that is, plants, there is a male and female distinction. Sekkizhar Peruman’s verse is: “Midaithu Neelkodi Veedhikal Vilangiya Aiyaarudaiya Naayakar Sevadi Paniyak Kandu Uruvaar Adaiya Appathi Nirpavum Charipavumana Pudai Amarntha Tham Thunaiyodum Polivan Kandaar” (He saw the Lord of Aiyaaru, whose streets were adorned with long banners, and as he approached to worship His sacred feet, he saw all the stationary and moving beings in that place, shining with their companions).

Now, the next verse is: “Pon Malai Kodiyudan Amar Velliyamporuppil Thanmaiyaam Padi Saththiyum Sivamaam Charithai Panmai Yonikal Yaavaiyum Payilvana Paninthe Mannu Maathavar Thampiraan Koyil Mun Vanthaar” (The great sage, having worshipped all the numerous species that practice the conduct of Shakti and Shiva in the manner of the golden mountain and the silver mountain, came before the temple of his Lord).

Thus, as Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman emerged from the pond, he saw this entire world as Shiva-Shakti.

The Lord showed eighty-four. All living beings, known as ‘yoni bhedas’ (types of birth), are divided by the Lord into two categories: Shakti and Shiva. All diverse forms of life, by their nature and qualities, are categorized as male and female within these two types.

The Lord has ordained that they naturally unite and live together. The Thiru-Virutham verse from Sivagnana Siddhiyar states: “Saktiyum Sivamaay Thanmai Ivvulakellam Otthav Aanum Pennum Unar Kunakuniyumaaki Vaiththanan” (He has placed this entire world, with its male and female, as the knower and the known, in the nature of Shakti and Shiva).

Accordingly, to visibly demonstrate that He Himself is the origin of the world, He has imprinted His identity throughout the world, making it known that living beings are divided into male and female by the Lord.

Therefore, the nature of Shakti and Shiva is practiced here, as stationary and moving beings stand with their companions. And this signifies the state where the Lord manifests with the Mother in Thiru-Kailai. Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman beholds this as the Lord reveals His grace, and he worships it. This vision serves as a prelude to the Thiru-Kailai vision that the Lord is about to show Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman in a short while.

Thus, Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman, having seen what the Lord revealed, approaches the Thiru-Ayyatru temple. He sees the Thiru-Ayyatru temple. That great temple appears to Thiru-Navukkarasu Peruman as the great Kailai mountain. Thiru-Mal, Brahma, Indra, and other deities, who are awaiting the Lord’s service, are also present. All behold and lovingly worship the sacred Thiru-Kailash mountain, and the sounds arising therefrom resonate distinctly everywhere. All the established Vedas chant distinctly.

The great temple seen there, like the great Kailash mountain, is praised by Brahma, Vishnu, Indra, and other great celestials with overflowing love and devotion, and all the great Vedas chant distinctly.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman composes this verse. This verse, comprising five feet, is structured as a Kalinilai Thurai.

Furthermore, in this verse and the subsequent five verses, Sekkizhar Peruman describes the vision of Thiru-Kailash.

Thus, the profound peace of concluding the direct vision of the Thiru-Kailash mountain with five verses, each a five-footed Kalinilai Thurai, is Maha Satha. We can perceive that it specifically points to the vision of Shiva-Murti. Devas, Danavas, Siddhas, Vidyadharas, Yakshas, and great ascetics and sages throng everywhere. The song of the beautiful-eyed Apsaras and the sound of the drums, exceeding the roar of the seven unfailing oceans, swell forth.

Thus, the next verse is formed. Devas, Asuras, Siddhas, Vidyadharas, Yakshas, and fitting great sages and ascetics are gathered everywhere. The song of the celestial Apsaras and the sound of the drums create a mighty roar, greater than the sound of the seven unfailing oceans. The Ganga and other sacred, divine great rivers, with auspicious, abundant waters, come and worship as great ponds. Everywhere, the vast great Gana-Nathas bow down. With overflowing joy, the Bhoota-Ganas and Vetala-Ganas praise.

The Vetala-Ganas praise. This is the next verse. The Ganga and other pure, divine great rivers come and worship as great ponds filled with auspicious water. Everywhere, the vast great Shiva-Gana leaders bow down. The Bhoota-Ganas and Pey-Ganas play various instruments and praise. There are seven great divine river goddesses in Kailash.

These seven great divine river goddesses fan Shiva when he processes. Such sacred waters have now gathered here, because the Thiru-Aiyaru temple appears as Thiru-Kailash, and those sacred waters have come here in the form of auspicious, water-filled ponds. All the Shiva-Ganas who exercise their guardianship and authority in Thiru-Kailash, have gathered here. The Shiva-Bhootas and Vetala-Ganas have also gathered here. Vetala is one type among the Bhoota-Ganas. Vetala is a type of Shiva-Gana, a ghost-host.

These are all playing instruments and praising. Various instruments producing different sounds are played. As if there were two great silver mountains, those who arrived there thought, as the great Nandi, with red eyes, stood before the bull. With the joy of the foremost benefit of ancient great penance, Nandi Peruman stood before the Lord, who appeared as a mountain at Thiru-Aiyaru.

Thus, the great Nandi, with red eyes, appears before it.

Therefore, as if there were two great silver mountains, those who arrived there thought, and this vision is displayed there. Nandi Peruman, acting on the Lord’s command, holds a golden staff in his sacred hand and is responsible for organizing and facilitating the worship of those who come to Kailash mountain to worship.

Therefore, here, the Thiru-Aiyaru temple appears as Thiru-Kailash mountain, and before it, Thiru-Nandi Devar appears. Those who have attained Shiva-nature and are worthy of directly seeing Shiva behold this vision. There is also a reference here that Thiru-Nandi Devar performed great penance and received grace at this sacred place of Thiru-Aiyaru. This specialty connects Thiru-Kailash and Thiru-Aiyaru. Our Lord Nandi, the first Guru-Natha for all our Guru lineage, is the Lord of the Adi-Deva’s temple, according to the sacred words. In accordance with these words, Nandi Devar, who is the chief of all Shiva-Ganas, appears.

He appears between the Lord and the assembly that came to worship the Lord. This is because Thiru-Nandi Devar stands between the Lord and the devotees who came to behold Him, serving both parties. We must remember here that the Lord commands Nandi Peruman, and according to that command, Devas, sages, and others are sent into Thiru-Kailash mountain by Thiru-Nandi Devar. The next, fifth sacred verse is the pinnacle of the Kailash vision. “On the silver mountain, with an emerald creeper, shining like a clear, great, luminous coral mountain, the Lord, who is the generous one, seated with the great mountain daughter on His left side, was first seen by the King of Words.” This is that sacred verse.

Thus, Thiru-Kailash mountain appears in the Thiru-Aiyaru temple. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman beholds it.

At that time, Shiva, the generous one, who is seated on the silver mountain with an emerald creeper, shining like a clear, great, luminous coral mountain, with Uma Devi on His left side, appears before Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar beholds the vision of Thiru-Kailash before his very eyes. Thiru-Kailash mountain appears as a silver mountain, radiating great light. On that silver mountain, the Lord is seated like a coral mountain. To the left of that coral mountain, the Ambika is seated like an emerald creeper, green and vibrant. The great temple of Thiru-Aiyaru itself appears as the great Kailash mountain.

On it, Rishabadevar appears as another great silver mountain. The Lord, who has graced him, appears like a coral mountain. Beside that coral mountain, Ambika is seated like an emerald creeper. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman saw that vision of Thiru-Kailash with his own eyes, as shown by the Lord. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman melts with emotion, thinking, “My Lord has shown all this to me out of His sacred grace!” He praises and worships Shiva, the generous one, who unreservedly bestows the great flood of His grace. He melts with emotion.

“Having scooped the ocean of joy with his eyes, with folded hands, he fell prostrate, rose, his body trembling, and before the celestials, he danced, sang, and wept. Who can describe what happened to that devotee there?” Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, having seen the vision of Thiru-Kailash there, scooped the ocean of joy with his two eyes, folded his hands above his head, fell before the sacred presence of Shiva, then rose, his entire body trembling. Standing before Shiva, the Lord of all living beings, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar danced, sang, and wept. Who can describe the wondrous spiritual experiences that occurred to that devotee at that time? No one can describe them. “Melting and melting within, standing, sitting, lying, rising, laughing, weeping, worshipping, praising, performing various dances, looking at the sacred form shining like the evening sky, shivering, when will I enter and stand, united with my precious jewel?” This is the eighth verse of Thiruvasagam, “Punarchi Pathu,” which comes to our mind here.

Therefore, who can comprehend the events of the state of spiritual experience attained by Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar here? Whenever the Lord comes to bestow grace upon souls, He comes on the bull, with the Mother, and in accordance with this, the state of spiritual experience attained by Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, who beheld that vision, is something indescribable. Sekkizhar Peruman, with the intensity of emotion arising in his sacred heart, feels that he is attempting to describe the indescribable, and thus, he composes these verses as if it were Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s own words, asking, “Who can describe this greatness?” What Sekkizhar Peruman intends to convey here is that he cannot describe this state of spiritual experience attained by Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, and not only that, no one else can describe it either.

Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, filled with inner joy through the vision he beheld, and being a great devotee of immeasurable love, worthy of partaking of that rare, unending nectar of divine grace, and possessing boundless penance, with boundless desire overflowing before him, began to sing sacred Thandagams praising the Lord with golden-hued matted locks. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, in this state, composed such sacred hymns.

We will continue to contemplate them. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 455. Thiru-Nindra-Charukkam. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. At Thiru-Aiyaru, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman beholds the vision of Thiru-Kailash and praises it, singing Thiru-Thandagams. These Thiru-Thandagams of praise are the Thiru-Thandagams of praise dedicated to Thiru-Kailash mountain.

There are a total of three Thiru-Thandagams of praise for Thiru-Kailash sung by Appar Swamigal. The first Thiru-Thandagam of praise begins with “Vettragi Vennagi Nindrai Potri.” This is the sacred hymn sung when Shiva appeared as a sage in the foothills of Kailash and then disappeared, revealing Himself through an ethereal voice.

At that time, he praised the Lord, seeing Him in His formless state.

Here, at Thiru-Aiyaru, he now beholds the vision of Thiru-Kailash. He sang two sacred hymns, two Thiru-Thandagam hymns of praise. These two hymns praise the Lord’s form, having seen Him directly in His manifest form and also in His formless-manifest form, which is the cause of the manifest form. As we have already seen, the joyful emotions and actions within Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, through his praise, further increase joy. Through these hymns, even the worlds and the living beings residing in them, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman has composed these sacred hymns for the Lord. There are two such sacred hymns, and the first sacred hymn, that is, the first sacred hymn sung now, is the second sacred hymn in the Thiru-Kailash sacred hymn, which begins with “Poraiyudaiya Bhoomini.”

This hymn is the 56th sacred hymn of the Sixth Thiru-Murai.

“Praise to You, who are the patient earth and water! Praise to You, the pure one with a host of Bhootas! Praise to You, who are in the heart full of fullness! Praise to You, who dwell in my heart unceasingly! Praise to You, who expounded the Vedas!

“Praise to You, who are worshipped by the celestials! Praise to You, who have a neck with a boundary! Praise, praise to You, Lord of Kailash mountain! Praise to You, the primal one who stood before! Praise to You, the ageless one with three eyes! Praise to You, who are near to those who stand in love!

“Praise to You, whose matted locks bear the bull! Praise to You, who are adorned everywhere with bones! Praise to You, Lord, who never leaves my thoughts! Praise to You, the fire that stands as an eye! Praise, praise to You, Lord of Kailash mountain! Praise to You, the moon that rose in the evening!

“Praise to You, who dwell steadfastly in my thoughts! Praise to You, who cut off past karmas! Praise to You, whose crown bears the crescent moon! Praise to You, the essence of sugarcane, Praise to You, who became the rare nectar for devotees! Praise to You, the sun that rose in the morning! Praise, praise to You, Lord of Kailash mountain!

“Praise to You, who cut off the karmas of the body! Praise to You, the Lord who radiates bright light! Praise to You, the moon on the spreading matted locks! Praise to You, the Lord of the many Ganas who dances! Praise to You, the light that shines brightly! Praise to You, who dwell in my heart that has appeared!

“Praise to You, the pearl that shines in the ocean! Praise, praise to You, Lord of Kailash mountain! Praise to You, who have a neck stained with poison! Praise to You, who gave a discus to Vishnu! Praise to You, who do not enter a mind filled with falsehood! Praise to You, who dwell in the heart that does not depart!

“Praise to You, who bathe in sacred white ash! Praise to You, the lamp praised by the great ones! Praise to You, who dance holding fire in Your hand! Praise, praise to You, Lord of Kailash mountain! Praise to You, whose crown bears the Ganga! Praise to You, who stand as the rare nectar for devotees!

“Praise to You, whose body is filled with water! Praise to You, who never depart from my heart! Praise to You, the sharp axe of the Maiden! Praise to You, who encompass the seven principles! Praise to You, whose neck is dark like a cloud! Praise, praise to You, Lord of Kailash mountain!

“Praise to You, who transcended the seven worlds! Praise to You, who stand as the ancient primal one! Praise to You, who cut off ancient karmas! Praise to You, who are praised by those on earth and in heaven! Praise to You, who are in the place where devotees praise! Praise to You, the light that watches over deeds!

“Praise to You, who are capable of blackening the neck! Praise, praise to You, Lord of Kailash mountain! Praise to You, the river that flows abundantly! Praise to You, who remove great diseases! Praise to You, who are in the hearts of those who melt and remember! Praise to You, the Lord who removes defects!

“Praise to You, the gold that shines nearby! Praise to You, who are not to be despised! Praise to You, the water that flows, dark and abundant! Praise, praise to You, Lord of Kailash mountain! Praise to You, Brahma on the beautiful lotus and Vishnu! Praise to You, who stood unknowable even when sought!

“Praise to You, the patient one who endured the five falsehoods! Praise to You, who took me as Your possession! Praise to You, who delighted in the true five elements! Praise to You, whose qualities are praised by the great ones! Praise to You, who flayed the skin of the elephant! Praise, praise to You, Lord of Kailash mountain!

“Praise to You, the Lord of the celestials placed above! Praise to You, who pierced the three flying cities! Praise to You, the virtuous King of Southern Lanka! Praise to You, who made him cry out when he lifted the mountain! Praise to You, the beautiful one who fiercely punished the flawed one! Praise to You, who punished even Yama, the god of time!

“Praise, praise to You, Lord of Kailash mountain!

“Now, the third hymn of the Thiru-Kailash Thiru-Potri Thiru-Thandagam. This is the second hymn of grace, now sung at Thiru-Aiyaru, after beholding the vision of Thiru-Kailash. It is the 57th sacred hymn of the Sixth Thiru-Murai, a Thiru-Thandagam hymn.

““Praise to You, the garland of beautiful songs! Praise to You, who stand unknowable in Your nature! Praise to You, whose crown bears the crescent moon! Praise to You, who are adorned with a pure garland of Datura! Praise to You, who delight in the five dances!

“Praise to You, who laughed when the enemies’ cities were destroyed! Praise to You, who flayed the skin of the wild elephant! Praise, praise to You, Lord of Kailash mountain! Praise to You, who cut off karmas that do not tremble! Praise to You, who are seated beneath the Banyan tree! Praise to You, the clever one, with clever earrings!

“Praise to You, the chief who smears ash on His body! Praise to You, who create worlds that do not oppose! Praise to You, who bestow grace that never returns! Praise to You, the eye of the radiant sun! Praise, praise to You, Lord of Kailash mountain! Praise to You, who are red, black, and white!

“Praise to You, who possess inexhaustible wealth! Praise to You, the Lord, the great one, the small one! Praise to You, whose color is the sky! Praise to You, the fierce one, the solitary one, the near one! Praise to You, who possess unperformed sacrifices! Praise to You, the Lord, the beautiful one, who holds the deer in His hand!

“Praise, praise to You, Lord of Kailash mountain! Praise to You, who rule the world! Praise to You, who bestow nectar to devotees! Praise to You, who have no trace of cunning! Praise to You, who consumed the poison of the surrounding ocean! Praise to You, who possess great majesty!

“Praise to You, who delight in my steadfast thoughts! Praise to You, whose vision is greatly unknowable! Praise, praise to You, Lord of Kailash mountain! Praise to You, the primal one who is always remembered! Praise to You, who possess an ageless form! Praise to You, my Father, the Lord, who is contemplated!

“Praise to You, who delight in the seven notes! Praise to You, the steadfast husband of the Maiden! Praise to You, who are both mantra and tantra! Praise to You, the Lord of the virgin Ganga on Your head! Praise, praise to You, Lord of Kailash mountain! Praise to You, who are worthy of all the worlds!

“Praise to You, who possess the knowledge of consciousness! Praise to You, the divine flame that is fire! Praise to You, who possess the eight-armed form! Praise to You, who are unknowable to all the celestials! Praise to You, who possess knowledge and humility! Praise to You, who gave the discus to Vishnu!

“Praise, praise to You, Lord of Kailash mountain! Praise, praise to You, who possess thoughts beyond thoughts! Praise to You, whose qualities are beyond comprehension! Praise to You, who are enshrined in melody! Praise to You, who practiced with song and lute! Praise to You, who rose higher and higher into the sky!

“Praise to You, who are above the great ones, above the great ones! Praise to You, who have an eye on Your forehead! Praise, praise to You, Lord of Kailash mountain! Praise to You, the moon in the matted locks that do not end! Praise to You, the form that is entirely sacred ash! Praise to You, the partner of Uma, with a slender waist!

“Praise to You, who stood unseen by those who sought You! Praise to You, who know the servitude of devotees! Praise to You, who established the city of love! Praise to You, who pierced the three strong cities! Praise, praise to You, Lord of Kailash mountain! Praise to You, who stand to be praised and worshipped!

“Praise to You, the virtuous one, who is unknowable! Praise to You, who dwell above the praising sky! Praise to You, who have eight thousand hundred names! Praise to You, the Lord, who are a lamp to the four directions! Praise to You, who are unknowable to Brahma and Vishnu! Praise to You, the seed for all directions where the wind blows!

“Praise, praise to You, Lord of Kailash mountain!

“The tenth verse of this sacred hymn is not available to us.

“Thus, to the delight of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar’s heart, the Lord, who is seated in Thiru-Kailash with His consort, graciously revealed the form of Kailash before the pure devotee, who stood in worship, making His presence manifest in Thiru-Aiyaru.

“Then, Shiva graciously concealed that Kailash vision. While Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar was still worshipping the vision of Thiru-Kailash, Shiva graciously concealed that sacred vision. This is because whether beings see or do not see is not due to their actions, but rather due to the Lord’s action of revealing and concealing for the sake of beings. The implication here is that if He shows us, who would not see? Who would see if the Lord with an eye on His forehead does not show? This is also the inner meaning of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s sacred words.

“In this verse, it is said that He graciously created this sacred vision. Before this, from 1640 to 1644, Sekkizhar Peruman described the vision of Thiru-Kailash in five verses. That is a reference to the vision of Sadashiva-Murti. Since this verse mentions that He made that sacred vision disappear, this sacred verse refers to the Adhomukha Darshanam.

“Thus, Shiva, having granted the vision of His form in Thiru-Kailash to be seen in Thiru-Aiyaru, later graciously concealed it. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, who had undertaken the sacred service of the Lord’s feet, was bewildered, yet his heart was filled with even greater joy than before. Realizing the nature of the Lord’s grace that had shown him this vision of Thiru-Kailash, he joyfully began to reveal the message of grace he had seen, for the salvation of the world. Sekkizhar Peruman describes how he sang that hymn in the following verse: “He sang, ‘I saw the Lord with the crescent moon on His head, with the daughter of the mountain, in the faultless, cool Tamil words, in the sacred hymns, the primal Lord in Thiru-Aiyaru, with all moving and non-moving beings, with their beloved consorts.’” These are the sacred words of Sekkizhar Swamigal. Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar, his heart gladdened by the vision of Thiru-Kailash he had seen, began to sing the sacred hymn that starts with “Madhar Piraikanniyanai.” He began to sing the sacred hymn composed of faultless, cool Tamil words.

“The implicit meaning of this sacred hymn is that he sang with the idea, “I saw the primal Lord in Thiru-Aiyaru, with all moving and non-moving beings, with their beloved consorts.” “Madhar Piraikanniyanai Malaiyan Magalodum” is the beginning of this sacred hymn. This also serves as the hymn’s summary. This sacred hymn is a “Kotharu Thiru-Padigam.” “Kothu” means fault. A sacred hymn that removes faults. “Kothu” refers to the impurities of souls. As a “Kothatra Tamil-sol” (faultless Tamil word), this sacred hymn is structured to remove the impurities of souls.

“Here, Thiru-Navukkarasar Peruman refers to this one Thiru-Pathigam, which begins with “Matharpirai Kanniyanai.” However, in the Thiru-Padal, how does he compose it? He says, “Matharpirai Kanniyanai Malaiyan Magalodum” in beautiful Tamil, not referring to this Thiru-Pathigam in the singular, but in the plural as “Thiru-Pathigangal.” This is because each verse in this Thiru-Pathigam is considered a Thiru-Pathigam in itself. The name of the Thiru-Pathigam has come to its verses. Such is the specialty of this Thiru-Pathigam. This Thiru-Pathigam is the third Thiru-Pathigam in the fourth Thiru-Murai, set in the Gandhara Pann.

“Bododu neer sumandhe thee puguvavar pin puguven Yaadhum suvadupadaamal Aiyaaru adaigindra podhu Kaadhan mada pidiyodum kaliravana kanden Kande navar thiruppaadham kandariyaadhana kanden Kande navar thiruppaadham kandariyaadhana kanden Pozhilanganniyinai poonthukilaalodum Vaazhiyambotriyandre thee vattamittaada varuven Aali valavanindre thum Aiyaaradaigindra podhu Kozhi pedaiyudan koodi kulirndhu varuvana kanden Kanden avar thiruppaadham kandariyaadhana kanden Kanden avar thiruppaadham kandariyaadhana kanden Eripirai kanniyinai ezhaiyaalodum paadi Muritha ilaiyangaleettu mugam alarndaada varuven Ari thozhugum vellaruvi Aiyaaradaigindra podhu Vari kuyil pedaiyodee vaigi varuvana kanden Kandenavar thiruppaadham kandariyaadhana kanden Kandenavar thiruppaadham kandariyaadhana kanden Pira ilanganniyinai peyvalaiyaalodum paadi Thuraiyilam pan Malarthoovi tholai kulira thozhuven Ara ilam poonguyilum Aiyaaradaigindra podhu Siraiyil pedaiyodaadi seval varuvana kanden Kande nabar thiruppaadham kandariyaadhana kanden Kande nabar thiruppaadham kandariyaadhana kanden Edumathi kanniyanai e thilaiyaalodum paadi Kaadodu naadu malaiyum Thozhudaadaaven Aadal amarndhuraigindra Aiyaaradaigindra podhu Pedai mayilodum koodi pinaindhu varuvana kanden Kanden avar thiruppaadham kandariyaadhana kanden Kanden avar thiruppaadham kandariyaadhana kanden Thanmathi kanniyinai thaiyal nallaalodum paadi Unmeli sindhaiyanaagi unaraavurugaa varuven Annal Marundhuraigindra Aiyaaru adaigindra podhu Vanna pagandhilodaadi vaigi varuvana kanden Kande nabar thiruppaadham kandariyaadhana kanden Kande nabar thiruppaadham kandariyaadhana kanden Kadimathi kanniyinai kaarigaiyaalodum paadi Vadivodu vanna mirandum vaai venduva solli vaazhven Adiyinai aarkkum kazhalaan Aiyaaradaigindra podhu Idi kural annadhor enam isaindhu varuvana kanden Kande navar thiruppaadham kandariyaadhana kanden Kande nabar thiruppaadham kandariyaadhana kanden Virumbu mathi kanniyanai melliyalaalodum paadi Perum pulkaalaiyezhundhu perumalar koyyaa varuven Arungalam ponmaniyondhum Aiyaaru adaigindra podhu Kalandhu varuvana kanden Kande nabar thiruppaadham kandariyaadhana kanden Kande nabar thiruppaadham kandariyaadhana kanden Murpirai kanniyanai moy kuzhalaalodum paadi Patri kayirukkillain paadiyum naadaa varuven Atrarul petru nindraarodum Aiyaaradaigindra podhu Natrunai pedaiyodaadi Naarai varuvana kanden Kanden avar thiruppaadham kandariyaadhana kanden Kanden avar thiruppaadham kandariyaadhana kanden Thingal mathi kanniyanai the mozhiyaalodum paadi Engarul nalgum kondhai ena kini enna varuven
